name: Rhode Island Current
title: Remote meeting access improves in some RI communities, slips backwards in others, ACLU report finds
description: Since the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Rhode Island began tracking remote access to public meetings in 2023, some of the state’s most closed-off public bodies still have not expanded options for people who cannot attend in person, according to an updated ACLU report released Tuesday. The July 2026 edition of “Remote Access to […]
text:
The ACLU of Rhode Island says remote access to public meetings has improved in some communities since 2023, while other local councils and school committees continue to offer limited options. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)Since the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Rhode Island began tracking remote access to public meetings in 2023, some of the state’s most closed-off public bodies still have not expanded options for people who cannot attend in person, according to an updated ACLU report released Tuesday.
The July 2026 edition of “Remote Access to Public Meetings: A Review of Rhode Island City and Town Councils and School Committees” found modest improvements in some municipalities and stagnation in others. It focused on four forms of access: livestreamed meetings, recorded meetings, online agenda documents and the option for members of the public to participate remotely.
Of Rhode Island’s 39 city and town councils, only 11 appeared to offer all four forms of access, according to the ACLU report. Of the state’s 34 school committees, only two offered all four forms of access from afar. 
“The importance of allowing residents to follow what’s happening in their communities, and have a voice even if they cannot physically be at meetings, cannot be overstated,” Zoe Chakoian, the ACLU of RI’s spokesperson and communications associate, said in a statement announcing the report, which she drafted with her colleague Megan Khatchadourian. 
“If we have learned anything since 2020, it’s that virtual access is possible for every council and committee to offer should they choose to,” Chakoian added.
The report bases its findings on reviews of municipal websites, agendas posted online and other related documents. Draft copies of the ACLU’s findings were also sent to the councils and school committees before publication to give the public bodies an opportunity for feedback and corrections.
Remote access is important, the report notes, because residents’ ability to participate in public meetings should not be dependent on whether a resident can drive at night, arrange childcare, take time off work, or be physically able to travel and enter government buildings. 
“The decisions that are regularly made by city and town councils and school committees markedly affect residents’ lives every day,” Steven Brown, the ACLU of RI’s executive director, said in a statement. “At the very least, there is simply no excuse in this day and age for any of these public bodies to fail to livestream or record their meetings or post their agenda packets online.”
Brown added that constituents in places lacking some or all remote access options should “demand them from their elected representatives.”
  29 of 34 school committees and 34 of 39 councils livestream 

There has been some progress, the ACLU report noted, with four municipal councils and eight school committees having improved at least one of the four practices since the ACLU’s initial review in May 2023.
On the other hand, three school committees — North Providence, Tiverton and Woonsocket — have reduced remote options since the ACLU began tracking them in 2023. The report says those three committees stopped posting complete agenda packets online or otherwise increased difficulty in accessing the documents. 
Representatives for those school committees had not responded to a request for comment as of late Wednesday afternoon. 
Livestreaming options remain relatively common among both councils and committees after the needed infrastructure and tech was put in place during the pandemic era. The updated report notes that 34 municipal councils and 29 school committees livestream their meetings, while 36 councils and 29 school committees host archives of their recorded meetings on town websites or platforms like YouTube.
Some open meetings more open than others, new ACLU report finds

Rarer is the actual opportunity to participate remotely, with but a dozen councils and four school committees offering such an option to residents. That equates to about one-third of councils and 12% of school committees offering virtual participation, in the ACLU’s calculation.
The ACLU has repeatedly supported legislation to enhance access to public documents, including those discussed during open meetings. That includes testimonies from the organization to support comprehensive legislation that would reform Rhode Island’s Access to Public Records Act (APRA). 
The legislation has been introduced and defeated multiple years in a row — including the 2026 legislative session, which ended in June. Among a smorgasbord of public records reforms, the failed legislation includes a stipulation which would require public bodies to proactively post or link relevant documents alongside agendas before meetings take place. Current open meetings law requires agendas, but not packets of discussed documents, to be posted before meetings.
Brown wrote in his May 2026 testimony when the Senate version of the APRA-reforming bill was up for a hearing that it had “been almost fifteen years since the General Assembly passed legislation updating and strengthening” Rhode Island’s public records law.
“Time has demonstrated the acute need for continued reform of the law, as the public’s critical ‘right to know’ is thwarted all too often by provisions in APRA that are ambiguous, weak or fail to address key issues that promote meaningful access to public records,” Brown wrote.
Where there are no online options
The report lists five public bodies which provide none of the four forms of access studied in the report: The Exeter and West Greenwich town councils, plus the Exeter-West Greenwich, Johnston and New Shoreham school committees. 
But at least one of those public bodies — the New Shoreham School Committee — has started livestreaming and archiving meetings on its YouTube channel, labeled the Block Island School Committee. The channel’s oldest livestreamed video is from March 2026.
A representative for the school committee could not be reached immediately Wednesday, but former Superintendent Mike Convery told Rhode Island Current in February 2025 that the district was in the process of collecting bids for a vendor to install a broadcasting system at the Block Island School, which serves approximately 126 students in grades K-12. 
Asked about the discrepancy, Chakoian said the organization sent the report to all councils and school committees before publication for feedback. 
“We sent all the councils and committees the report in advance of publishing for feedback, and certainly accept updates going forward,” Chakoian wrote in an email Wednesday.
The ACLU website notes that at least one other public body, the Cranston School Committee, allows more remote access than the published report suggests. The school committee “does allow remote participation, however this is not indicated on the agenda or website,” the ACLU’s website notes.
The full report is available on the ACLU’s website.



 What’s changed since 2023?

Four city and town councils expanded access:

Barrington and Foster now livestream their council meetings; the latter also archives the videos on YouTube.
Tiverton’s agenda packets are now posted online — albeit on two different sections of the town website, the ACLU report notes. Burrillville has also started posting packets online, but limits available selections to the most recent three meetings.

Nine school committees expanded access:

Coventry now allows remote participation through Zoom, but does not list the option on its agendas.
​​Cumberland, North Smithfield, Pawtucket and West Warwick now post agenda packets online. Cumberland, however, does not post them until noon on the day of the meeting.
Foster-Glocester, Middletown and New Shoreham/Block Island (although not noted in the report) began livestreaming and archiving meetings. Scituate has also started to livestream its meetings.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Pillen announces picks for tax incentive-eligible ‘opportunity zones,’ a slate stretching statewide
description: LINCOLN — A handful of Nebraska mayors — including one who has watched his town’s biggest employer flee — stood with Gov. Jim Pillen on Wednesday to announce the governor’s 28 picks for tax incentive-eligible opportunity zones. The recommendations span the state, from Scottsbluff in western Nebraska to Omaha, where 10 areas were selected. One […]
text:
Norfolk Mayor Shane Clausen at the podium, flanked by Gov. Jim Pillen. From left to right are Mayors Linda Taylor of McCook, John Fagot of Lexington, John Ewing Jr. of Omaha and Maureen Larsen, director of the Nebraska Department of Economic Development. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — A handful of Nebraska mayors — including one who has watched his town’s biggest employer flee — stood with Gov. Jim Pillen on Wednesday to announce the governor’s 28 picks for tax incentive-eligible opportunity zones.
The recommendations span the state, from Scottsbluff in western Nebraska to Omaha, where 10 areas were selected.
The Tyson beef plant in Lexington, shown in December. (Photo by Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
One of Pillen’s census tract selections is in Lexington, home to the former Tyson Foods plant, which in the next few days will fully close, said Mayor John Fagot. About 3,000 jobs were lost earlier this year as production ceased. Fagot expects an opportunity zone designation to help strengthen his town.
“We’re going forward,” Fagot said during a press conference at the State Capitol. “We’re going to build our community, we’re going to go forward in every aspect.”
Pillen expects opportunity zone incentives to help create jobs and boost construction of affordable workforce housing — a need laid out in various reports and widely discussed in the Nebraska Legislature and city governments. 
Fagot said he foresees more housing construction in his town as well. Some might think the Tyson shutdown opened up housing stock, but he said the city hasn’t “had a whole lot of exodus.” Many former Tyson workers took jobs in nearby communities.
In naming his recommended slate, Pillen said he foresees incentives encouraging public and private partnerships and sparking economic development.
“My expectation is there’s going to be a lot of wood being thrown in the air quickly, a lot of concrete going down, because there are a lot of people really excited,” said Pillen.
Congress originally established the federal opportunity zones program through the Tax Cuts and Job Act of 2017. Its purpose was to promote investment and drive growth in low-income and economically disadvantaged communities. Parties that invest in designated zones can benefit from tax incentives.
HUD Secretary Scott Turner, flanked by Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, visits the Micro Market in the Highlander redevelopment site in May. He was in Omaha in part to promote opportunity zones. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
The program was extended permanently under the 2025 law President Donald Trump calls big and beautiful. The so-called Opportunity Zones 2.0 program takes effect in 2027. Pillen called it a “significant upgrade.”
He and Larsen said there were enhanced provisions benefiting rural areas, stricter eligibility criteria, more reporting and accountability requirements, and an updated capital gains deferral provision. Investors can roll capital gains into a qualified opportunity zone fund and defer or reduce their existing capital gains taxes. If the investment is held for at least a decade, capital appreciation generated by the investment becomes tax-free.
U.S. Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner visited Omaha in May, appearing with Pillen and Ewing, in part to promote opportunity zones.
Nebraska was allowed to nominate a quarter of areas deemed eligible under federal criteria. Larsen said 112 were eligible, and the 28 picked by Pillen were submitted to the U.S. Treasury Tuesday for certification.
She described the interest in the zones as extraordinary, saying cities submitted applications for 107 of the 112 eligible areas.
Among the 28 are 10 in Omaha and five in Lincoln, the state’s two most populated and urban cities. Others are in Alliance, Ogallala, North Platte, McCook, Lexington, Hastings, Columbus, Norfolk, Fremont, Bellevue, Crete and Beatrice.
Larsen said state officials, in narrowing candidates, looked for investment readiness, economic needs and potential community benefit before submitting their preference to the governor. 
Pillen said the state tried to get ahead of the rest of the nation in naming recommendations, but said at least one other state was ahead of Nebraska.
McCook Mayor Linda Taylor speaks during a press conference with Gov. Jim Pillen in August 2025 when he announced that an ICE detention center was to be located in McCook. (Photo by Brigham Larington/McCook Gazette)
“We want to lead the way but we want to make sure we play winning ball,” he said.
Larsen said an early start allows communities to start recruiting investors to tap the incentive to develop housing and other eligible projects.
“By doing it this early we’re giving communities, we’re giving developers and we’re giving those officials time, more time to go out and get those investments so that we get the bigger bang for a buck and those investments land right here in Nebraska.”
Also at the press conference were Omaha Mayor John Ewing, Norfolk Mayor Shane Clausen and McCook Mayor Linda Taylor.
Clausen said an opportunity zone designation offers Norfolk another way to compete, another tool for economic development and a way to lure developers.
Ewing foresees opportunities for more affordable housing construction in the nominated tracts. “I greet this news with hope.”
Taylor said a designation is an “important piece” to further economic development in southwest Nebraska. “We have a lot of small communities around us and we all depend on each other.”

name: National
title: Cyclosporiasis outbreak surges to over 4,173 confirmed cases
description: The number of cases of cyclosporiasis — a parasitic infection linked to contaminated water or food that causes severe intestinal issues — has more than doubled to over 4,173 cases across 41 states this week, up from the 1,645 confirmed cases in 34 states reported last week by the federal Centers for Disease Control and […]
text:
Salad greens for sale at a bodega in Astoria, New York. The number of cases of cyclosporiasis has more than doubled to over 4,173 cases across 41 states this week. (Photo by Shalina Chatlani/ Stateline)The number of cases of cyclosporiasis — a parasitic infection linked to contaminated water or food that causes severe intestinal issues — has more than doubled to over 4,173 cases across 41 states this week, up from the 1,645 confirmed cases in 34 states reported last week by the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Cyclosporiasis causes symptoms that include watery or “explosive” diarrhea, nausea and stomach cramps. The surge in cases had made 2026 the worst year for the infection on record.
The CDC estimates that there are likely more than 7,400 additional cases that have not yet been confirmed. No deaths have been reported, but 308 people have been hospitalized, more than double the 141 hospitalizations reported last week.
State and federal officials suspect there are multiple sources of the outbreak, but they have connected at least 1,644 cases in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio and West Virginia to shredded iceberg lettuce grown in central Mexico and sold by Taylor Farms.
Michigan, the first state to report an outbreak, reported 7,171 cases and 102 hospitalizations as of July 16. Indiana, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, and Indiana also have seen high case counts, alongside New York City.
Salad greens scrutinized as cyclosporiasis outbreak spreads

The Association of State and Territorial Health Officials, which represents public health agencies across the country, said labs have a hard time tracking case connections because cyclospora is a parasitic genome that is more complex than the bacterial pathogens that cause other foodborne illnesses. As a result, state and local heath investigators must resort to reviewing restaurant and grocery receipts, menus and supply chain records, according to the organization.
“Case interviews and traceback investigations are often time intensive, creating a burden on state and local public health infrastructure,” senior analyst Heather Tomlinson and environmental health director Courtney Anderson wrote.
North Carolina had confirmed more than 560 cyclosporiasis cases as of July 20. Dr. Carl Williams, state public health veterinarian for the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services, told reporters on Tuesday that the state has relied heavily on its 86 local health departments to track cases.
Williams said twice weekly calls with the CDC also have been helpful.
“The CDC has been very responsive to us and the other states,” Williams said during the briefing. “But as you can imagine, I mean, it’s a lot to go through.”
Stateline reporter Shalina Chatlani can be reached at schatlani@stateline.org.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Conservative public interest firm joins AI free speech election lawsuit
description: A public interest law firm, the Hamilton Lincoln Law Institute, has joined a First Amendment lawsuit against a 2025 state law that limits artificial intelligence use in campaign materials. Hamilton Lincoln Law said that it’s joining because of concerns about free speech restrictions.  The lawsuit is being brought by former Republican legislator Dan Bartel af[...]
text:
A sign noting where to vote by precinct is on display at the Helena Civic Center during a primary vote on Tuesday, June 2, 2026 in Helena, Montana. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)A public interest law firm, the Hamilton Lincoln Law Institute, has joined a First Amendment lawsuit against a 2025 state law that limits artificial intelligence use in campaign materials.
Hamilton Lincoln Law said that it’s joining because of concerns about free speech restrictions. 
The lawsuit is being brought by former Republican legislator Dan Bartel after Rep. Eric Albus, a Hi-Line Republican and former legislator Jennifer Carlson, running for a state House seat in the  Bozeman area, filed a Commission of Political Practices complaint against an organization, Accountability in State Government, over mailers. Bartel is the treasurer of the political committee.
Albus and Carlson accused Bartel and Accountability in State Government of breaking a new state law that says generative AI content cannot be used with messages regarding political candidates or parties within 60 days of the start of voting in any given election. 
The political committee ran mailers depicting each candidate with pride flags and buttons while accusing Albus and Carlson of using taxpayer money for a “woke agenda.”
The mailers used digitally altered photos of the candidates, adding the pride flags and buttons. Albus and Carlson said it violated a law that Democratic lawmakers had pushed for during the 2025 session.
That COPP complaint is pending while the law is challenged in Helena District federal court.
Hamilton Lincoln Law Institute, which describes itself as existing to “defend civil liberties” and “challenge government overreach,” filed a brief along with Bartel’s lawyer, Matthew Monforton, late last week. The firm is based in Washington, D.C.
The suit was initially filed on May 5. Both Monforton and Hamilton Lincoln attorney Adam Schulman said the law was a free speech issue. 
“There is absolutely no reason why the government should be telling private citizens what they can and cannot say about their political opponents,” Monforton said Wednesday.
Schulman, whose organization has been involved in other generative AI lawsuits, said there’s angst around the technology, but that doesn’t mean it needs to be outright banned. 
“When something’s unknown, you have to err on the side of speech until you can show that the market can’t respond to this by counter speech and other measures,” Schulman said in an interview, pointing to Elon Musk’s social media site as an example. “X is developing tools, community notes, and things like that. Things that are AI get flagged by private speakers rather than the government stepping in and prohibiting this.”
Meta — which owns both Facebook and Instagram — have also added labels to AI-generated content, but even so critics have still maligned parts of the company’s misinformation policy.
“Obviously AI is not very well understood, so there’s a lot of fear around the technology,” Schulman said. “Throughout history, that really hasn’t been different. The same thing was said about video games, comic books before that.”
Even so, there was legislative and national worry about the impacts of generated content that seems real — but isn’t — on voters ahead of the 2024 election cycle.
Those laws also came as discussion was swirling about digitally-altered videos and content used toward the end of the general election, as generative artificial intelligence tools took substantial leaps around that time in access, affordability, and realism.
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is under the Department of Homeland Security, issued a report on AI in elections in January 2024 while President Joe Biden was still in office, ahead of the federal elections that year. CISA, created in 2018, is the nation’s main cybersecurity and cyberdefense agency.
“Malicious actors can use generative AI tools to reduce the costs and increase the scale of cyber incidents and foreign influence operations,” the 2024 CISA report says, going on to say generative AI can be used to create malware that evades cyber defenses. 
It could also be used for “denial of service attacks,” which entails flooding websites with massive amounts of data, which overwhelm or stop them, which the report warns could include election sites. There’s also worries that the technology could be used to “deep fake” people, particularly their voices.
The CISA report added the techniques aren’t new, but they are now easier and cheaper to deploy.
“Malicious actors may also use generative AI to assist in deploying phishing and social engineering techniques, generating lifelike audio in any individual’s voice, creating highly realistic fake images, powering counterfeit social media profiles, and producing deepfakes to support influence operation narratives,” the report said.
Montana Democratic minority legislative leaders Rep. Katie Sullivan and Sen. Pat Flowers favored the new law because “we’ve opened the floodgates” as far as how generated artificial intelligence content is circulated. They said deepfake artificial intelligence use in elections should be outlawed.
But the law also has carveouts for media usage of broadcasting AI images for the purpose of “satire or parody,” which the briefs argue isn’t fair.
And it argues that even if there is misinformation, it’s still protected.
“False political speech is still protected speech,” the brief says, adding, “Elections have always been a noisy ruckus of misinformation. Because the Act regulates political speech for a reason other than avoiding corruption, it is unconstitutional.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Planned Parenthood endorses Pingree, says rivals can’t be trusted on abortion rights
description: Planned Parenthood’s local political arm endorsed Democratic candidate Hannah Pingree on Wednesday, saying she is the only candidate in the gubernatorial race who would expand abortion rights while arguing her Republican and independent opponents cannot be trusted to protect them. At a press conference announcing the support of the Planned Parenthood Maine A[...]
text:
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree speaks at a July 22, 2026 press conference in Portland, Maine about her support for abortion rights that earned her the endorsement of the Planned Parenthood Maine Action Fund. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/ Maine Morning Star)Planned Parenthood’s local political arm endorsed Democratic candidate Hannah Pingree on Wednesday, saying she is the only candidate in the gubernatorial race who would expand abortion rights while arguing her Republican and independent opponents cannot be trusted to protect them.
At a press conference announcing the support of the Planned Parenthood Maine Action Fund PAC, President and CEO Nicole Clegg said, “there is too much at stake for the people of Maine this November.”
“There is only one person we can trust to lead our state, to protect our rights, and safeguard access to basic, essential, life-saving healthcare, and that is Hannah Pingree,” she added.
The endorsement also underscored one of the clearest policy divides in the race. While Pingree has pledged to expand abortion protections, Republican Bobby Charles has described abortion as “abhorrent.“ Rick Bennett, a Maine senator and former head of the Maine Republican Party who withdrew from the GOP last year to run as an independent, said he supports preserving Maine’s existing abortion laws, but Planned Parenthood said his voting record in state government proves otherwise. 
Maine is among the roughly 26 states that have protected or expanded access to abortion since the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade four years ago. The next governor will determine whether that support continues. 
Since 2022, outgoing Democratic Gov. Janet Mills has passed shield laws that protect abortion providers, required health insurance companies to cover abortion care and added at least $8 million in state funding for reproductive health care providers including Planned Parenthood. 
“As governor, Hannah will continue to build on that work,” Clegg said. “She’ll be a foil to whatever Trump and Republicans in Congress throw at us.”
If elected, Pingree said she would enshrine the right to abortion in the Maine Constitution, protect access to abortion medication, including mifepristone, and ensure ongoing funding for reproductive health care providers. 
She also spoke about the attacks on reproductive health care by President Donald Trump’s administration, including banning Planned Parenthood and other abortion providers from receiving Medicaid reimbursements and cutting access to contraceptives.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“When Washington D.C. and the federal government come for our rights, the states are the line of defense, and governors are truly the firewall,” Pingree said at the Planned Parenthood office in Portland on Wednesday. “A governor has to stand up and say, ’not in my state, and not while I am in charge.’”
Pingree also criticized her opponents, calling Charles an “anti-abortion extremist” and highlighting Bennett’s past votes against funding family planning services and enshrining abortion protections in Maine’s constitution. Clegg agreed, adding that she believes Charles would do “everything in his power to take access away.”
“And given the fact that we don’t have Roe v. Wade anymore, that’s gotten a lot easier for governors to do,” she said.
Both Charles and Bennett pushed back on Pingree and Clegg’s attacks.
“Hannah Pingree has failed Maine women and families,” Charles said in a statement provided to Maine Morning Star. When asked if he would protect or overturn Maine’s existing reproductive rights laws, he said he would “uphold any existing state and federal laws as Governor.” In the March interview with News Center Maine when Charles condemned abortion, he did not specify any changes he would make to current Maine laws, although he said he supported the Supreme Court decision ending the federal right to abortion.
Bennett, who has served in both chambers of the Maine Legislature on and off since 1990, said in an emailed statement that he has “always supported a woman’s right to choose.” 
He cited a bill he cosponsored three decades ago that would have codified Roe v. Wade in Maine law, as well as his 92% rating from Planned Parenthood Maine Action Fund last year, which he said reflected his support for reproductive health access. However, the organization gave Bennett a 38% rating during the 2023-24 legislative session because of his votes against bills that would have enshrined the right to reproductive autonomy in the Maine Constitution, protected reproductive care providers in Maine from prosecution under other states’ laws, mandated insurance coverage of contraceptives and established state funding for family planning services, among others.
Asked about that score, Bennett said in an emailed statement that while it “reflected a particular set of votes at a particular time, my core belief has remained the same: I trust women, I support reproductive freedom, and as Governor, I will defend Maine’s protections.” 
Addressing his varying support for the issue over the years, Clegg said, “You can certainly cherry pick votes if you want to present a particular position or give people an impression that you’ve been a lifelong supporter of reproductive rights or Planned Parenthood.” She added, “We know Rick Bennett’s voting record over his career doesn’t support that.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas lawsuit accuses drugmakers of undermining access to discount program
description: Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin sued multiple major drugmakers Tuesday, alleging they undermined healthcare providers’ access to a federal drug discount program. The 22 defendants include 13 drug manufacturers, their related corporate entities and data management firm Second Sight Solutions. The complaint filed in Polk County Circuit Court claims the d[...]
text:
From left: Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin (fifth from left) announces a lawsuit against several prescription drug manufacturers on July 22, 2026. Behind Griffin are (from left) Arkansas Pharmacists Association CEO John Vinson, University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences Director of External and Local Governmental Relations Marq Golden, Arkansas Pharmacists Association Government Affairs Director Deborah Wolfe, pharmacist and Republican state Rep. Brandon Achor of Maumelle, UAMS Director of Agency and Health System Affairs Jenna Goldman, Community Health Centers of Arkansas CEO Lanita White, Baptist Health 340B Program Manager Tanya Moore, Arkansas Hospital Association Director of Analytics and Financial Policy Donald McCormick, and Mena Regional Health System CEO Paul Ervin. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin sued multiple major drugmakers Tuesday, alleging they undermined healthcare providers’ access to a federal drug discount program.
The 22 defendants include 13 drug manufacturers, their related corporate entities and data management firm Second Sight Solutions.
The complaint filed in Polk County Circuit Court claims the defendants, among them Pfizer and Bristol Myers Squibb, engaged in deceptive business practices and violated Arkansas’ 2021 law requiring drugmakers that participate in Medicaid to sell discounted drugs to contract pharmacies.
Arkansas was the first state to pass such a law, and several other states have followed suit. The Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America, known as PhRMA, challenged Arkansas’ law in federal court. 
Drug manufacturers lose appeal of Arkansas law on discounts to hospitals using outside pharmacies

That litigation ended in 2024 when the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear PhRMA’s appeal of a lower court ruling that federal law does not preempt Arkansas law.
Griffin said Wednesday the defendant drug companies have since put rules in place that are “so burdensome and so prohibitive” that the 340B drug discount program can’t function as intended.
Under the 340B program, established in 1992, pharmaceutical companies that participate in Medicaid must sell outpatient drugs at discounted prices to clinics, community health centers and hospitals that primarily serve low-income patients. The federal government expanded the program in 2010 to allow independent pharmacies to dispense drugs on behalf of hospitals and clinics.
Drug companies illegally limited how many independent pharmacies they work with and required data reporting for healthcare organizations to receive the program’s benefits, Griffin said.
“They’re looking for a way to be in the program, to have access, but to limit their downside financially,” Griffin said at a news conference. “They sort of want to have their cake and eat it too.”
AstraZeneca, one of the defendants, declined to comment on ongoing legal proceedings. Pfizer, Bristol Myers Squibb and Eli Lilly all did not respond to emails requesting comment.

340B-complaint 
Three of the defendants — Eli Lilly, Sanofi and Novo Nordisk — faced a 2022 lawsuit from then-Attorney General Leslie Rutledge, accusing them of conspiring with the three largest pharmacy benefit managers to inflate the cost of insulin. Last year, the Pulaski County Circuit Court case was grouped into multi-state litigation from 444 lawsuits over insulin prices.
Pharmacy benefit managers serve as middlemen to negotiate prescription benefits among manufacturers, distributors, pharmacies and health insurance providers. Arkansas passed a first-of-its-kind law last year to ban PBMs from holding a permit to operate a drugstore. A federal judge temporarily blocked the law before it could go into effect.
The suit asks for the court to find the defendants liable for violating the Arkansas Deceptive Trade Practices Act and fine them $10,000 per offense. If the court grants the state’s request, the defendants should pay the state more than $1 billion, Griffin said.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho ranks third in wage growth nationally, report shows
description: Idaho’s average hourly wage in 2025 rose by 4.7% from 2024, ranking the state third nationally for percentage increases during that time, according to a press release by the Idaho Department of Labor. That amounts to a $1.31 increase per hour statewide, with the average wage for all occupations listed at $29.41 in 2025. The […]
text:
The Idaho Department of Labor's administrative office is located on Main Street in Boise. (Christina Lords/Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho’s average hourly wage in 2025 rose by 4.7% from 2024, ranking the state third nationally for percentage increases during that time, according to a press release by the Idaho Department of Labor.
That amounts to a $1.31 increase per hour statewide, with the average wage for all occupations listed at $29.41 in 2025. The median wage, or the midpoint between lowest and highest earners, also increased, jumping from an hourly $22.34 in 2024 to $23.06 one year later.
The report, although showing an increase in average wages since 2024, also comes as the lowest percentage increase since 2022.  
Average wages grew by 8.3% from 2022 to 2023, and again by 5.1% from 2023 to 2024, as reported by the Idaho Capital Sun. The latest percentage increase would be the lowest in that three-year cycle.


“One of the strongest indicators of a healthy economy is when Idahoans see bigger paychecks and greater take-home pay,” Gov. Brad Little said in a press release boasting the figures. “Rising wages mean more opportunities for families, more confidence for workers, and more prosperity in communities across our state.”
Increases also spread across all seven Metropolitan Statistical Areas (MSAs) in Idaho, meaning that growth could be felt statewide, with the greatest percentage increase being in the southwestern parts of the state.
The southwestern region reached an average hourly wage of $30.76, and it became the only region to pass $30 per hour in 2025, according to the press release. 
Even so, wage increases confront a simultaneous rise in the cost of living, as gas, housing and other necessities see frequent price jumps in response to national and local conditions. 
The required living income for single adults without dependents stood at $49,091 in 2026, according to MIT’s Living Wage Calculator. 
That’s $2,000 above the median statewide annual income of $47,970 reported by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Employment did not lag behind wages, as reported employment numbers grew 1.5% from 2024 – an increase of more than 12,000 people employed.
Fast Food and Counter workers made up the largest occupation, totaling over 25,000 workers, with 24,880 General and Operations managers following at a close second.
For more information, including a county-by-county breakdown of average wages, top occupations in the state and other data points, visit: https://lmi.idaho.gov/data-tools/oews/.

name: VTDigger
title: Is it safe to eat lettuce? Upper Valley experts answer key questions on cyclosporiasis outbreak
description:
So far Vermont has had no cases linked to the national outbreak, a Health Department spokesperson said Monday.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Is it safe to eat lettuce? Upper Valley experts answer key questions on cyclosporiasis outbreak.
text:
Danielle Pappo chooses bags of spinach from Killdeer Farm and lettuce from Crossroad Farm while shopping at the Co-Op Food Store in White River Junction, Vt., on Friday, July 17, 2026. “It’s more fun to shop up here honestly because they have so much local stuff,” said Pappo, of Palmer, Mass., who is staying in the Upper Valley while working as a baker at King Arthur Flour. Dawn Archambeault, director of marketing and consumer relations for the Co-op Food Stores said the grocer has seen an increase in sales of local produce as news has spread of a cyclospora parasite outbreak linked to lettuce from Taco Bell locations in five states. “It’s not hurting us, it’s helping our local providers,” said Archambeault. Photo by: James M. Patterson/Valley News

This story by Clare Shanahan was first published in the Valley News on July 20, 2026.
The Twin States have remained mostly insulated as cyclosporiasis outbreaks continue around the country, but consumers may still have questions about the illness.
As of Sunday, New Hampshire has recorded six cyclospora infections so far in 2026 with none linked to a national outbreak, according to the state Department of Health and Human Services.
There have also been no cases linked to the national outbreak in Vermont, Department of Health spokesperson Kyle Casteel confirmed Monday. Casteel declined to say how many cyclosporiasis cases the state has seen in 2026, but said the number is “within the typical range.”
The situation progressed on Friday when Salinas, California-based Taylor Fresh Foods, a national produce distributor, issued a voluntary recall for all iceberg lettuce sourced from farms in central Mexico between June 29 and July 16. The lettuce was distributed in New Hampshire but not Vermont, according to the recall.
Taylor Fresh Foods’ lettuce includes Marketside-branded products sold at Walmart, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Though the recall is ongoing, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration walked back a claim Sunday that a sample of Taylor Farms’ lettuce had tested positive for the parasite.
“FDA has notified Taylor Farms and continues working with the firm to ensure product implicated in this outbreak has been removed from the market,” the agency wrote.
The CDC and FDA are investigating cases around the country of the illness that comes from food and drink contaminated with feces. Last week, the agency linked an outbreak across five Midwestern states with Taylor Farms lettuce sold at Taco Bell.
As of July 13, the CDC has confirmed 1,645 cases of cyclospora infection and 141 hospitalizations across 34 states. More than 5,100 suspected cases “require further analysis,” according to the agency.
Cases of cyclosporiasis are recorded annually in summer months in the U.S., but it is typically less pervasive.
The CDC recorded 717 cases of the infection in 2024 with more than 300 linked to international travel. Annual cases have been consistently on the rise since 2020.
How will I know if I have cyclosporiasis and when should I contact a healthcare professional?
Cyclosporiasis is a gastrointestinal illness caused by a parasite. Common symptoms include watery diarrhea, loss of appetite, weight loss, cramping, bloating, increased gas, nausea and fatigue.
It usually takes about a week to develop symptoms after consuming the parasite, Dr. Gabriela Andujar Vazquez, Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center’s hospital epidemiologist, said Friday.
The illness can last about a month, Andujar said. Symptoms can also start to lessen and then return, so patients experiencing symptoms should seek medical attention. There is an antibiotic available to treat the infection, she explained.
“It can resolve on its own,” Andujar said. “(…) But, it will be painful. It will take weeks for it to run its course.”
Patients also run a high risk for dehydration, which is often what brings people with cyclospora infections to the hospital, Andujar said.
How does it spread and how can I avoid getting sick?
Cyclospora is typically introduced to the U.S. in imported produce, Andujar said. The parasite can live in produce for weeks to months and cause an infection when consumed.
“Anything that’s fresh that we eat raw typically that is contaminated and we don’t clean well with running water could potentially cause a case of cyclosporiasis,” Andujar said.
The illness is not contagious if a person is sick at home. It can spread if you “don’t practice good hygiene” like not properly cleaning bathrooms or hands, Andujar explained. The parasite needs proper conditions like the right temperature to become infectious.
“It needs a perfect-storm type of situation,” she said.
Nonetheless, patients who are sick with any kind of gastrointestinal illness should avoid handling food for themselves or others “unless you’re very good about proper safety with food handling and hand-washing.”
The CDC recommends washing hands with soap and water after handling raw fruits and vegetables, washing and scrubbing produce thoroughly and cutting away damaged or bruised areas. For produce that is not consumed raw, cooking to at least 158 degrees Fahrenheit will kill the parasite.
Where is it safe to acquire produce?
While possible, the risk of contracting a cyclospora infection from local farms, farmers markets or your own garden is very low, Andujar said.
Cyclosporiasis has historically only been introduced into the U.S. food system from produce grown internationally, Andujar said. The one risk is if a sick individual is handling food at a farm, farmers market or restaurant and not following safety protocols like proper hand-washing.
Norwich Farmers’ Market Manager Nica Meiloch-Blinn said similar national health concerns typically drive up business for produce vendors.
“People like to buy from smaller local producers/owners where they know their farming practices and can speak directly to how they farm and grow,” Meiloch-Blinn said in a Friday email. “Our producers also have excellent safety and health track records and I think when the public is avoiding pre-packaged lettuce mixes what better place to look for alternatives then your local farmers market.”
The Co-Op Food Stores in Hanover and Lebanon, New Hampshire, and White River Junction have seen a “pretty hefty” increase in customers purchasing “ultra-local” produce available at the grocery stores, like from Edgewater Farm in Plainfield, New Hampshire, said Dawn Archambeault, director of marketing and consumer relations for the co-op.
While Archambeault declined to give specific numbers for the shift, she said it is clear customers “are feeling a little safer” with local produce than big brands.
As for food prepared in store, Archambeault said co-op staff will typically put together sandwiches and meals using produce from local suppliers like Black River Produce in Springfield or grown in hydroponic systems, so “we don’t see any concern there.”
The co-op does carry Taylor Farms lettuce, but none of the products come from Mexico where the outbreak may be linked to, Archambeault said. Salad mixes sold at the stores come from California, Canada and Florida.
As of Monday morning, neither a supplier nor the Food and Drug Administration had notified the co-op of a recall for the specific products they sell, so products have not been pulled off shelves, Archambeault said.
“We try to stay the course of relying on the info that we get from the FDA and other entities like that,” Archambeault said. “But, most importantly from the distributor and the supplier and sort of letting people make their own decisions.”
Decisions like the FDA walking back positive results Sunday have made the situation even more complicated, Archambeault said.
How can I know that produce is safe?
The CDC, FDA and state agencies are continuing to monitor outbreaks and cases around the country, including testing and reporting positive cases of the illness and testing potentially contaminated products like Taylor Farms lettuce.
Consumers should throw away any recalled produce, wash surfaces that may have touched recalled produce with hot soapy water or a dishwasher, and ask restaurants where the lettuce they use has come from if they don’t know the source, according to the CDC.
The co-op is keeping a close eye on the situation. If the federal government or suppliers recall co-op products, the store will contact all members and customers who bought them, Archambeault said.
“There’s daily conversations that are happening here and it’s on the forefront of our minds.”
Other local entities using large amounts of produce are also keeping an eye on the situation, like the nonprofit Hartford Community Coalition, which distributes 3,800 free summer meals per week to students in Hartford and Lebanon.
Friday’s meals included caesar salad, said Executive Director Emily Zanleoni.
While she was not aware of the outbreak, Zanleoni said HCC’s kitchen director was keeping an eye on it and questioned whether caesar salad was still the right choice for the day.
“When there’s an issue with supply we get hit pretty hard,” Zanleoni said. “I have to really think about that.”
Zanleoni said employees confirmed that the lettuce was not from Taylor Farms. Kitchen staff rinsed the produce an additional time and decided to go forward with the planned meal for the day.
“That’s why we rely on people who are experts on making sure that our food is sourced well and taken care of before it gets distributed,” Zanleoni said. “I’m grateful we can rely on our kitchen experts.”

name: VTDigger
title: Enough with the excuses. Help Vermont’s loggers.
description:
Finch Paper's closure is the latest in a string of mill shutdowns, and Vermont's conservation policy is threatening the industry's survival.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Enough with the excuses. Help Vermont’s loggers..
text:
This commentary is by William Sargent, a lifelong Vermont woodsman and the author of the memoir “50 Years a Dirt Forester: Always Outside and Never Behind a Desk.”
Since the announcement of the closure of the Finch Paper mill in Glens Falls, New York, on July 17, I’ve received multiple emails, texts and phone calls asking for my take on the situation.
Without a doubt, it is one of the most impactful events in my 50-plus-year career as a forester in Vermont. The economic impact on loggers, truckers, landowners and anyone involved in the forest products industry in the Northeast is immense. A facility that has been buying pulpwood from the region’s loggers since 1865 will stop making its own pulp from local logs and will transition to buying it from suppliers outside the area.
At a speaking engagement this past winter, I was asked if the tariffs were the biggest single event that I’d been involved in throughout my career. I said then that if Finch Paper ever closed, that would be much bigger and impact more people. 
Those words have come back to haunt me. 
Someone said to me recently, “It’s just one mill. What is the big deal? Just sell it somewhere else.” This person, like many others, has no idea of the sheer volume of the low-grade material purchased by Finch Paper. The wood yard handled about 60 tractor-trailer loads of roundwood seven days a week, or 420 loads weekly. An average of 20,000 trucks annually. By comparison, the biggest mills in Vermont take in around 75 to 80 loads weekly. In addition to it being a loss of volume, there are no other markets available for some of their intake. No one else in the Northeast purchases low-grade hemlock pulp. There’s no doubt that the loss of this market will have a huge long-term impact.
Loggers and truckers across the Northeast are a pretty resilient crew. They will adjust. They did it when the mills across Bennington County closed. Burke Lumber closed. They adjusted. They did it after the fire at Rutland Plywood in 2014 and the more recent closing at A. Johnson Company in Bristol. They will figure out a way to bounce back from this. 

READ MORE

Legislators have asked what they can do to help. It is a nice thought, and I’m not going to go off on a tangent about the lack of help the forest products industry has gotten in the past. Tempting but not productive. I’ll offer one major suggestion and save the others for another day. 
Please stop allowing our working lands to be conserved and protected out of existence by out-of-state organizations. Stop the sale of carbon credits on land in the current use program. It is a shell game. Insist that we do something with our state and federal lands. Make them multiuse again. Forestry uses have been forgotten. 
I’m pretty sick of the excuse that we are doing all we can with our limited resources. These are the things that will help your local loggers and truckers survive in the long term. It is the Vermont way. Make it happen.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Trump highlights Republican candidates, urges Senate to pass SAVE Act during Cobb County visit
description: MARIETTA, Ga. — Facing what is likely to be a difficult midterm election in Georgia and across the country, President Donald Trump touted his economic platform during a visit to Wheeler High School in Cobb County Wednesday.  Several Republican candidates for statewide office had speaking slots, giving the official White House event a distinctly partisan […]
text:
President Donald Trump visited Wheeler High School in Cobb County Wednesday, July 22, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderMARIETTA, Ga. — Facing what is likely to be a difficult midterm election in Georgia and across the country, President Donald Trump touted his economic platform during a visit to Wheeler High School in Cobb County Wednesday. 
Several Republican candidates for statewide office had speaking slots, giving the official White House event a distinctly partisan tint.
Trump tries to shift attention away from woes with glitzy Trump Accounts rollout

To an audience of roughly 3,000 people, the president promoted his newly launched child investment accounts and cast his opponents as “communists” who were threatening to bankrupt the country. But in a wide-ranging 75-minute speech, he also criticized members of the U.S. Senate for failing to pass his signature election bill, known as the SAVE America Act.
The bill would require voters to show proof of citizenship, such as a birth certificate or passport, before being able to cast a vote. 
But Trump has repeatedly demanded that lawmakers enact the bill, which stalled in the Senate last month largely over concerns that it would create chaos ahead of the November midterms. He refused to sign a landmark, bipartisan housing bill last month over lawmakers’ failure to pass the act and centered last Thursday’s primetime address on the bill.
Trump’s appearance at the public high school had the tone of a campaign rally, with a wide array of downballot Republican candidates appearing onstage to pitch themselves to Georgia voters. He also castigated U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff, a Georgia Democrat running for reelection, for voting against many of Trump’s policy priorities.
Jackson shares stage with Trump; Collins stays in Washington
Cobb County, which was once a reliably red area, flipped blue for the first time in decades during the 2016 election, and has stayed blue since. And despite multiple polls showing Democratic candidates in the lead over Republicans statewide, numerous speakers argued that Georgia is still a GOP stronghold, dubbing the state “Trump Country.”
Rick Jackson, the Republican nominee for governor, recounted his childhood growing up in foster care, and praised First Lady Melania Trump for launching her “fostering the future” initiative. 
“Affordability is not a political problem. Affordability is a business problem. It requires business solutions, just like this man’s been doing all his life,” Jackson said in comments praising Trump. 
Lieutenant governor candidate Greg Dolezal, attorney general candidate Sen. Brian Strickland and secretary of state candidate Rep. Tim Fleming were also among the speakers.
“This is a red state,” Dolezal told the crowd during his speech, appearing to echo false claims of Trump winning Georgia during the 2020 election. “We proved it in 2020, we proved it in 2024, and we’re going to prove it yet again this year in 2026.”
Three counts — including one conducted by hand — affirmed former President Joe Biden’s narrow 2020 victory in Georgia.
Congressman Mike Collins, who is running to unseat Ossoff in the U.S. Senate, was initially scheduled to attend the event, but later said he was needed in Washington D.C. to vote on legislation. 
Democratic officials sharply criticized the event, with state Rep. Lisa Campbell, a Kennesaw Democrat who represents a Cobb County-based House district, accusing Trump of hosting a political rally “at our public school using our tax dollars.”
Protesters line the street in Marietta on the day of President Donald Trump’s appearance at a public high school about a mile away. Jill Nolin/Georgia Recorder
“The sheer audacity and height of hypocrisy to dismantle the Department of Education and then host a campaign rally at a public school,” Campbell said. 
Ahead of Trump’s speech, protesters lined the sidewalk outside of a shopping center in Marietta about a mile from the school, with cars enthusiastically honking their approval as they passed. Many of them waved school-themed signs, such as “keep MAGA out of our schools” or giving Trump failing grades. A smaller group of protesters also gathered closer to the venue. 
Anna Ferraro, a teacher who lives in Paulding County, said she was tired of Trump “butting into everything” and was particularly unsettled by his appearance at a Georgia public school. Ferraro said she became interested in protesting when she saw others doing it and now she hopes her efforts will have the same effect on others. 
“I’m not just sitting on my phone saying I hate Trump. I’m actually out here trying to make a difference and showing people that they can make a difference,” Ferraro said. 
Democratic candidates were quick to blast their opponents for their participation in the event. 
“A picture is worth a thousand words. Today, Rick Jackson stood next to Donald Trump to again pledge he will be Trump’s ‘favorite governor,’” the Democratic nominee for governor, Keisha Lance Bottoms, said in a statement. “There’s a clear choice in this election: Rick Jackson would work for Donald Trump, I will work for Georgians.” 
Scanning the crowd
The president’s visit attracted a mix of loyal Republicans and curious voters from around the metro Atlanta area. 
Kazi Safi, a 19-year-old Marietta resident who is originally from California, said he attended the event as an observer, not necessarily a supporter of Trump. He said he has several concerns about the way the country is being run, including with immigration policy, politicians accepting money from interest groups and the Iran war.
“I’ll admit I was more of a fan of Trump’s first term,” Safi said. “I agree that we should take out illegal immigrants, but I feel like there’s a process to do that.”
While he approves of some of Trump’s policies, Safi said he does not support Collins and is undecided about Jackson, arguing that voters shouldn’t “blindly” support candidates just because of their party affiliation.
“I feel like Georgia needs a Republican governor,” he said. “Americans should take the time to do their research and then vote based off where they align.”
Another attendee, a 60-year-old Cobb County resident Leasa Brandenburg, said she was excited for the president’s visit, though she was hoping to learn more about Georgia’s top-ticket Republican candidates like Jackson. 
“It’s kind of like meeting somebody and then going out on a date with them,” she said. “You have to date them several times to find out what they’re all about, what they like, what they don’t like, and to determine whether or not they’re someone that would fit in your life.”
She said she was still waiting to see where Jackson lands on a variety of different issues, adding that she’d like to see Republican candidates move past the 2020 election.
“That doesn’t matter anymore. It doesn’t matter to anybody,” she said.
Andra Gillespie, a professor of political science at Emory University, said events like Trump’s rallies are aimed at energizing reliable Republican voters rather than appealing to moderates.
“The idea is to get them so charged up that you basically establish a lead that would be difficult for Democrats to [overcome],” she said.
For candidates like Jackson, who narrowly defeated Trump-endorsed candidate Burt Jones in the race for governor, Gillespie added, the event is a chance to consolidate support from both wings of the Republican Party.
“What I suspect he’s going to do is to use this as an opportunity to reach out to those Jones supporters and say ‘still come out and support me with the same fervor that you would have supported Burt Jones if he had been the nominee,’” she said. “And then he’s going to do a pivot towards voters in the middle and then play up his outsider credentials in order to try to have the best of both worlds.”
Georgia Recorder staff Jill Nolin, Ross Williams and Ellie Fivas contributed to this report.

title: Henderson City Council rejects data center moratorium
description: The Henderson City Council rejected a proposal Tuesday to implement a six month moratorium on new data center applications, instead choosing to change the city’s development agreement process. The vote followed nearly two hours of public comment from community members who largely urged the council to move forward with a proposal introduced by Henderson Mayor[...]
text:
The City of Henderson has not received any new data center applications, but city oficials say staff has been working on revising the city’s development agreement process since April with data centers in mind. (Photo: City of Henderson)The Henderson City Council rejected a proposal Tuesday to implement a six month moratorium on new data center applications, instead choosing to change the city’s development agreement process.
The vote followed nearly two hours of public comment from community members who largely urged the council to move forward with a proposal introduced by Henderson Mayor Michelle Romero to implement a 180-day pause on applications for new data centers. 
Council members directed staff to develop a framework that could be used to update development agreement standards for data center applicants. Those standards would address water consumption, electrical demand, noise impact, and a distance limitation from residents. 
Romero agreed an update to the city’s development agreement process would allow the city council to evaluate data center applications “on a case-by-case basis” using a framework based on the best available information. 
“A development agreement proactively gives us the ability to change the codes now and adaptively update them as technology changes,” Romero said. “We may or may not ever get an application, but at least we would be ready with a framework that we can rely on.”
Henderson Community Development and Services Department Director Eddie Dichter said the City of Henderson has not received any new data center applications, but added that city staff has been working on revising the city’s development agreement process since April with data centers in mind. Currently a Google data center is the only one in the city.
“A moratorium is temporary to some degree, they are only defensible for up to a certain point, usually that’s up to 12 to 18 months before you have to make some permanent changes to your code,” said city attorney Nicholas Vaskov.
City officials said the new framework would include public input across two public meetings.
Across Nevada the rapid rollout of data centers has pushed local municipal governments to address the growth of data centers in the state. 
In June, the Reno City Council voted to implement a temporary data center moratorium before adopting new regulations sometime next year. A month before, the Nye County Water District Governing Board unanimously approved an emergency order requesting that the Nye County Commission place a moratorium on data centers in the Pahrump Valley.
In May, the Boulder City planning commission voted unanimously not to recommend the construction of Townsite Solar 2 LLC’s data center on city-owned land. The developer responded by moving to get the construction of the data center approved on federal land.
The Boulder City Council followed by unanimously voting to appeal the approval of the first data center on U.S. Bureau of Land Management land.

title: Leading Dem on US House education panel, advocates blast student loan changes
text: WASHINGTON — Education experts and advocates warned Wednesday that the recent federal student loan system overhaul stemming from the GOP’s mega tax and spending cut law will drive borrowers to private lenders and could derail their higher education plans. U.S. Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia, the top Democrat on the House Committee on Education and Workforce, convened a panel to blast the sweeping loan changes, as well as separate, ongoing efforts from President Donald Trump’s administration to dismantle the Education Department and its impact on the federal student aid system. “Student loan debt now exceeds $1.7 trillion. Borrowers need clear guidance and certainty,” Scott said. “Instead, they’re forced to deal with uncertainty and chaos created by an administration that has systematically weakened the federal student aid system.”   Scott criticized Education’s plans to transfer core student aid functions to the Treasury Department. Under an interagency agreement, or IAA, announced in March, Treasury will take over Education’s responsibility for collecting on defaulted federal student loan debt in what marks the first step in a multi-phase process toward Treasury taking on the entire federal student loan portfolio. The Virginia Democrat said Treasury “has no expertise serving students or institutions of higher education or monitoring servicers for accuracy.” Meanwhile, the Education Department finalized regulations — most of which took effect July 1 — that implement sweeping student loan system changes outlined in the GOP’s “big, beautiful” law.Scott said that the sweeping changes to the federal student loan system originating from that law are “compounding the issues that have risen from the dismantling of the Education Department.” Borrowing limitsAmong the major changes are new loan limits for graduate and professional students, a restructured repayment system that gives new borrowers only two plans to choose from and the elimination of a key loan program for graduate and professional students that allowed for unlimited borrowing.Wil Del Pilar, senior vice president at the nonprofit policy and advocacy group EdTrust, said the mega tax and spending cut law “restricts access to federal graduate lending, pushing many borrowers, especially those from low-income and middle-income backgrounds, many of whom are students of color, into the hands of private banks.” Del Pilar, who was deputy secretary of postsecondary and higher education for the Pennsylvania Department of Education, said that would present a series of challenges for borrowers. “That means higher interest rates, fewer consumer protections, stricter credit requirements, and flat-out denials for some, forcing those students to halt their educational journey,” he said.Access to graduate education Clare McCann, managing director of policy and operations at the Postsecondary Education and Economics Research Center, said her organization was “very concerned that for many borrowers who want to continue to pursue a graduate education, that they will find themselves locked out of the private market or unable to access affordable loans without a qualified cosigner.” McCann, whose organization is housed at American University, added that the center’s research suggested almost 40% of student borrowers subject to the new caps have either poor or no credit scores, making them unlikely to be able to borrow money in the private market without a cosigner.McCann noted that allowing largely unlimited graduate lending is “unwise” and “puts both students and taxpayers at risk,” while calling on Congress to “allow students to borrow enough to make high-return investments in themselves, so long as their loans remain affordable and repayable based on the salaries students should expect.” Ellen Keast, a spokesperson for the department, defended the student loan system overhaul, in a statement shared with States Newsroom on Wednesday. “Blank checks to universities resulted in tuition skyrocketing for American students and families. Mass student loan forgiveness failed in nearly every courtroom it entered. The student loan portfolio is at a fiscal cliff because the last Administration perpetrated the lie that students do not need to repay their loans,” Keast said. “The Trump Administration is righting these wrongs – all while implementing historic reforms to federal student aid that will drive down the cost of college and simplify student loan repayment.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: After fire and flooding, Cox declares a state of emergency in 3 Utah counties
description: Gov. Spencer Cox declared a state of emergency Wednesday in three rural Utah counties after weeks of devastating wildfire and floods, a first step to unlock possible federal disaster aid.
text:
A section of highway 137 near Beaver, Utah, after being damaged by fire and flooding in a photo shared on July 15, 2026. (Photo courtesy of U.S. Forest Service) Gov. Spencer Cox declared a state of emergency Wednesday in three rural Utah counties after weeks of devastating wildfire and floods, a first step to unlock possible federal disaster aid. 
The governor’s declaration for Beaver, Piute and Sevier counties comes after the Cottonwood Fire — for a time the largest in the nation — burned more than 97,000 acres in the area’s Tushar Mountains. Monsoon rains over its burn scar caused flash flooding and flows of debris over the weekend, forcing evacuations and causing damage to homes, roads, and drinking water systems. 
“Utahns have endured an incredibly difficult wildfire season, and now many of these same communities are facing life-threatening flooding caused by those fires,” Cox said in a prepared statement, thanking the crews keeping communities safe. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The governor’s office noted this wildfire season is one of the state’s most destructive in recent memory, torching 380,000 acres statewide. The Babylon Fire, burning in southeast Utah, is among the biggest in the country, at more than 107,000 acres and 95% containment. 
Cox noted his order would help provide “every available resource” to help local communities respond and prepare for flood risks throughout the summer. The move activates an emergency operations plan, allowing the state to pursue hazard mitigation funding and request help from other states and the federal government if needed. 
President Donald Trump has said repeatedly that he’d like to reduce the size and scope of the federal government’s role in managing disasters, saying last summer that “We want to wean off of FEMA and we want to bring it down to the state level.” 
In Utah, Cox said recent flooding in Wayne County claimed the lives of Provo Fire Captain Spencer Long, his wife Katrina and their sons Reid, Thayne and Gage, calling the deaths a “heartbreaking loss.” 
“It’s a painful reminder that flooding can become deadly in moments, particularly in and below burn scar areas,” the governor said. “We urge every Utahn to heed warnings, avoid flooded areas and never underestimate the power of moving water.”
State Forester Jamie Barnes agreed. She said the danger will remain for some time. 
“Burn scars can remain highly unstable for years, creating dangerous flooding and debris flows with even relatively small storms,” Barnes said in a prepared statement. 
Eighteen Utah counties have declared local emergencies related to wildfire, flooding or drought since April, according to the governor’s office. The executive order expires after 30 days unless extended by the Legislature.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming GOP endorses candidates ahead of primary election, but says it won’t spend party funds backing endorsees
description:
The endorsements are the latest development in a dispute over the party’s say in who is a Republican in Wyoming. 
The post Wyoming GOP endorses candidates ahead of primary election, but says it won’t spend party funds backing endorsees appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
While the Wyoming Republican Party endorsed candidates in the state’s top races this week, GOP Chairman Bryan Miller says the organization will not spend money to support those candidates ahead of the primary election in August. 
“We obviously can’t put ads in the papers and do all those different things. We’re not going to do that,” Miller told WyoFile on Wednesday, referring to a state statute that prohibits a political party from backing one of its candidates over another before the primary. 
More specifically, it is a misdemeanor for a political party to expend any party funds “directly or indirectly in the aid of the nomination of any one person as against another person of the same political party running in the primary election,” according to state law. 
However, Miller said, state law does not forbid the party from vetting and endorsing candidates — a process the party began in April when it voted to adopt bylaws designed to fortify the party’s ability to determine who is Republican in Wyoming and who is not. In June, the GOP sued the state, challenging the constitutionality of the law that restricts party spending. 
“We do vetting, and we can do endorsing,” Miller said Wednesday. “It is the ability to get that out to the public after the fact that we are hindered on, and that is one heck of a violation of our constitutional rights.”
Historically, the party has backed whichever Republican won in the primaries. But more recently the party has been more selective in supporting candidates after they’ve won in August. The party, for example, only donated to certain Republican nominees ahead of the 2024 general election, according to campaign finance data. 
Park County’s Tim Lasseter hydrates during the Wyoming Republican State Convention on Saturday, April 25, 2026, in Douglas. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)
The party, as the federal lawsuit describes, “would like to contribute amounts determined by its leadership to one Republican candidate in various competitive, opposed primaries whom the party determines is most aligned with the WYGOP’s platform.” 
The party also says in its legal complaint that it would like to spend money publishing and distributing voter guides ranking and expressly endorsing candidates based on their alignment with the GOP platform. It also seeks to publish that guide online. 
Those actions are currently illegal, the lawsuit states, but such statutes are unconstitutional.
“The State of Wyoming has no compelling interest in preventing a political party from expressing a preference among its own primary candidates or in dictating how a political party allocates its private funds among such candidates,” the complaint states.
For several years, the Wyoming Republican Party has argued in various court challenges that because it is a private group, state laws ought not to govern its organizational structure and internal business. Opponents, meanwhile, say the organization can’t ignore the law, particularly since the party has public duties such as filing vacancies in elected offices like secretary of state or schools superintendent.
The party announced its endorsements in a Tuesday press release, citing a Monday meeting in which its state central committee “evaluated candidate records, platform fidelity, and core conservative principles.”
“This process is not about party leadership picking winners and losers, nor is it about telling anyone how to vote. It is about transparency,” Miller wrote in the press release. “The Wyoming Republican Party Platform was written and passed by grassroots delegates from all 23 counties. Our endorsement simply highlights candidates whose platform pledges and track records most closely align with those grassroot conservative principles.”
The endorsements largely align with the right flank of the party as well as the Wyoming Freedom Caucus, and include: U.S. Rep. Harriet Hageman for U.S. Senate; Secretary of State Chuck Gray for U.S. House; Col. Brent Bien for governor; Rep. Rachel Williams for secretary of state; Rep. Scott Smith for treasurer and Rep. Tom Kelly for superintendent of public instruction.

title: The new Route 7 project is a waste of money
description:
The Pittsford-Brandon Route 7 project isn't needed, and the funds would be better spent elsewhere.

text:
Dear Editor,
Vermont’s federal legislators have secured $19.7 million in federal funding for reconstruction of Route 7 between Brandon and Pittsford. The goal is to add truck climbing lanes and wider shoulders for cyclists. The work will take two years and will inevitably lead to huge traffic backups during that period. In my opinion, this short stretch of road is already quite safe, and most people drive sensibly on it.

READ MORE

Furthermore, even after the wider shoulders are built, it will not be particularly safe for bicyclists, and there are alternative routes for them that are both scenic and safer.
I am sure that other more useful road projects in Vermont could use that $19.7 million.
Louis Meyers
Shelburne, Vt.
