name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Polls show Hong leading with almost half of voters undecided
description: State Rep. Francesca Hong (D-Milwaukee) is leading the four other Democrats in the primary campaign for governor in a new Marquette Law School poll, a sign of her continued momentum, while more than 40% of primary voters remain undecided. The poll was conducted July 8 through 16 — around the same time that the Democratic […]
text:
State Rep. Francesca Hong (D-Madison) is leading in the Marquette Law School and internal polls conducted by her rivals. Hong speaks at a candidate forum hosted by the Wisconsin Technology Council in November 2025. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)State Rep. Francesca Hong (D-Milwaukee) is leading the four other Democrats in the primary campaign for governor in a new Marquette Law School poll, a sign of her continued momentum, while more than 40% of primary voters remain undecided.
The poll was conducted July 8 through 16 — around the same time that the Democratic primary field changed dramatically — failing to capture Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez’s exit from the race and the reentry of Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley with the endorsement of Gov. Tony Evers.
Charles Franklin, the poll’s director, said upon it’s release that there is  “plenty of room for change” in the race.
Hong led her primary opponents, excluding Crowley, with 26% support among Democratic primary voters, with 45% undecided. The poll included Rodiguez, who dropped out after it was completed, but not Crowley, who had not reentered the race.
Hong has led the Democratic field in each Marquette Law School poll released this campaign cycle so far. 
“Consistency counts for something,” Franklin said. “And we see that consistency over this entire time.” 
Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes had 15%, Rodriguez had 11%, Joel Brennan garnered 2% and 1% supported state Sen. Kelda Roys.
Some Democrats are skeptical of how Hong, a democratic socialist, will perform in November against presumptive GOP nominee U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany.
The new Marquette poll also showed that Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes was the only candidate who polled ahead of Republican candidate Tom Tiffany. Barnes had 44%, while Tiffany had 40%. 
Hong in a matchup against Tiffany polled at 40% to Tiffany’s 43%.
The Hong campaign pointed out  that among likely voters the poll showed Hong and Tiffany tied at 44%.
“This poll puts to rest the claim that our campaign cannot compete statewide,” Hong said. “We are building the multiracial, multigenerational and working-class coalition it will take to defeat Tom Tiffany and deliver universal childcare, fairer and cheaper health care, fully funded public schools and permanent affordability for Wisconsin families.”
Franklin said the takeaway from the poll is that the race is close. Another poll will be released next Wednesday, the day after the candidates are scheduled to debate.
Barnes and Crowley both released internal polls seeking to highlight their advantages, though each poll also showed Hong leading. 
The internal poll from the Crowley campaign showed Hong with 35% of the vote, Barnes with 15% of the vote and Crowley at 14%. His campaign highlighted that after people were provided with information about the candidates he jumped to 22% of support — 11 percentage points behind Hong. 
The internal poll from the Barnes campaign showed Hong at 39%, Barnes at 26% and Crowley at 11%. 
A poll conducted by the Roys campaign found that Hong polled at 29% followed by Barnes at 21%, Crowley at 11% and Roys at 7%. According to the poll when voters were provided with information about Roys, their support shifted to 25% Hong, 21% Roys and 16% Barnes.
“We are proud of our momentum, but as they say: Polls do not decide elections – people do,” Hong said. “Over the next 20 days, we will keep traveling, organizing and working to earn every vote in every corner of Wisconsin.”
Hong’s opponents target her in new TV ads
Hong’s Democratic primary opponents have begun to target her in campaign ads. 
Crowley does not mention Hong by name in his first ad released since getting back into the race, but highlights a Milwaukee Journal Sentinel article about Republican groups investing more than $2 million in ads that seeming aimed at boosting Hong’s campaign.

“The Republicans have made their choice,” Crowley says in the ad, “spending millions of dollars on candidates they know they can beat. It’s time for Democrats to make our choice.” He also highlighted Evers’ endorsement.
The Barnes campaign also focused on the Hong ads purchased by the Republican Governors’ Association.
“There’s nothing more important than beating Trump’s handpicked candidate Tom Tiffany, and polls show I’m the only candidate in this race who can,” Barnes said in a statement. “That’s exactly why we are seeing the Republicans meddle in our primary with over $3 million to boost my opponent who Tom Tiffany beats in every poll.” 
Joel Brennan, the former head of the Department of Administration, who has consistently polled behind his opponents in the primary, released an ad Tuesday that flashed photos of  the three frontrunners, all of whom are people of color. 
“She’s a proud socialist,” Brennan says as Hong’s photo is displayed on screen. “He lost statewide before,” he says over an image of Barnes. “A couple weeks ago, he dropped out,” he says over an image of Crowley.
The ad does not mention Roys, who, like Brennan, is white. 
“They’ll all lose to Republicans in November,” Brennan says in the ad, before talking about himself. 

His campaign has received pushback for targeting the candidates of color in the race. 
According to the Milwaukee Courier, the Democratic Party of Wisconsin Black Caucus Executive Board responded to the ad by saying it is “extremely disappointing that Joel Brennan released an ad saying none of the candidates of color running for governor could win in November following previous comments in May on this issue.”
Brennan’s campaign said in a statement that the ad was meant to highlight that there are other candidates running apart from the three promoted by “Madison insiders”.
“Each candidate has to make their own case, and the ad points to the facts about others running, why Joel is the strongest candidate to beat Tom Tiffany and what he’ll do for Wisconsin as governor,” the Brennan campaign said in a statement. 
Hong released her own ad this week that goes after Tiffany, not her Democratic opponents. She called him an “anti-abortion,” an “election denier” and an “Epstein pedophile protector” and said he “sides with the powerful, not the people.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Ryan Peterman seeks secretary of state records on voter data shared with DOJ
description: Democratic Secretary of State candidate Ryan Peterman said Iowans “deserve answers” from Secretary of State Paul Pate on how voter data shared with the federal government is being used. Peterman held a news conference Wednesday on the steps of the Iowa State Capitol, where he announced he was filing four public records requests through the […]
text:
Democratic Secretary of State candidate Ryan Peterman held a news conference at the Iowa State Capitol July 22, 2026 announcing that he was filing public records requests on the Secretary of State's office decision to share voter registration data with the U.S. Department of Justice. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Democratic Secretary of State candidate Ryan Peterman said Iowans “deserve answers” from Secretary of State Paul Pate on how voter data shared with the federal government is being used.
Peterman held a news conference Wednesday on the steps of the Iowa State Capitol, where he announced he was filing four public records requests through the Freedom of Information Act to obtain information on voter registration data provided by Iowa to the U.S. Department of Justice.
Pate, a Republican, announced in May that the state had complied with a DOJ request to turn over voter registration data, including personally identifiable information like driver’s license and Society Security numbers. Pate said the decision to provide this information to the federal government came after consulting with his office’s legal team, as well as the Iowa Attorney General’s Office, which confirmed the U.S. attorney general had the power to demand this information under the federal Civil Rights Act.
Peterman, who is running against Pate in the 2026 general election, said he has heard extensively from voters who are critical of Pate’s decision to share voter information with the federal government.
“As I travel all across Iowa on the campaign trail, the most common issue Iowans have raised for the past three months is their concern about their sensitive information being handed over to a partisan Department of Justice in the federal government,” he said. “I’ve heard from Iowans who are furious at our Secretary of State for doing this, who are worried about how their information will be used, and they’re right. Enough is enough. It’s time we all get some answers.”
In other states, some secretaries of state and attorneys general have reached a different conclusion and have refused the DOJ’s demands for this data. The federal department has then challenged these decisions in 30 states, as well as Washington, D.C., in court. According to the Brennan Center for Justice, 16 of these cases have been dismissed.
Peterman said these court cases prove Pate’s office had reached the wrong conclusion.
“To date, there has not been a single judge that has ruled states are required to hand this information over to the federal government. Not a single one,” Peterman said. “It is very clear that Secretary Pate did not have to give away Iowans’ sensitive information. He chose to. Now, this personal data is already in the hands of the Department of Justice. There’s no going back from that. But as Iowans, we still deserve answers.”
Pate said in a statement that the SOS office “spent considerable time reviewing the Department of Justice’s request,” and determined using available information and the state’s legal guidance that it was the correct decision to comply with the request.
“This was not a decision we made lightly,” Pate said in a statement. “We were assured the data would be protected as required under federal law. The information we provided to the federal government included publicly available information and information generated and provided by government institutions. The Department of Justice is responsible for some of the nation’s most sensitive information, and we are confident they can protect this data accordingly.”
Pate also added, “we continue to remind the federal government that the U.S. Constitution places responsibility for election law and voter lists with the states, and we expect that to be respected as federal duties are carried out.”
The four public records requests, filed after the news conference, seek records from the SOS office in four categories: information regarding material provided to the DOJ in response to their request for voter registration data, communications between SOS staff and the DOJ, as well as between the SOS staff and the Iowa attorney general’s office, about the request, and internal memoranda, guidance and meeting materials “explaining how and why the office responded to the federal request.”
“These are straightforward, and I hope the Secretary of State’s office will comply so that Iowans can get some answers,” Peterman said. “But when and if we do get some transparency, this isn’t the end of this story. Paul Pate had the chance to fight for Iowans. Instead, he betrayed their trust. They failed to protect their personal information. That deserves accountability. It’s clear that it’s time for new leadership in this office, leadership that actually works for Iowans.”
The Democratic candidate also announced his “Public Service Agenda” at the news conference, listing pledges including protecting Iowans’ personal information, increasing transparency efforts and collaborating with local officials.
“This is the culture I want to bring to the Secretary of State’s office,” he said. “Iowans deserve transparency, they deserve accountability, they deserve a Secretary of State stands up and fights for that.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont pledges eviction reform as tenants, lawmakers condemn corporate landlord
description: Gov. Ned Lamont joined a group of tenants and lawmakers in Hartford to call on Alpha Capital to improve conditions at its properties.
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont joined a group of tenants and lawmakers in Hartford Wednesday to call on a corporate landlord to improve conditions at its properties and address long-standing concerns. 
Alpha Capital, which owns 365 properties across Connecticut, was asked to attend to Wednesday’s gathering at the Legislative Office Building, to hear tenants’ complaints. But the company declined.
“While we appreciate your invitation, we are not in a position to attend the proposed meeting in its current format,” CEO Tyler Smith wrote in a letter addressed to the meeting’s organizers.
Hannah Srajer, president of the Connecticut Tenants Union, addressed the company’s response Wednesday. “We are offering you a way out of this mess, and the way out is to respect the people that pay your bills, to listen to them and come to solutions. … Give us a call. We’ll set a meeting. Let’s resolve these issues before we have to take it further.” 
Among the concerns tenants raised Wednesday was eviction — residents being displaced from their homes, in some cases without cause. For several years now, state lawmakers have raised legislation that would require landlords to provide a reason when they evict renters, but it has failed to reach the governor’s desk. 
This year, Senate Bill 257 died without a vote in either chamber. The controversial bill would have ended no-fault or lapse-of-time evictions, which typically occur at the end of a lease, at larger apartment complexes. These protections already exist for seniors and people with disabilities.
According to Luke Melonakos, vice president of the Connecticut Tenants Union, no-fault evictions make up about 11% of all evictions in Connecticut. However, he added that the figure does not “reflect many more unwanted displacements of people who were forced to move but didn’t want to go to court.” 
At one of the company’s properties in Middletown, nearly all of the tenants were evicted last fall. And in October, Alpha Capital planned to send 40 eviction notices to the city of New London — but the company eventually backed down after facing public pressure, Melonakos said. 
At Wednesday’s event in Hartford, Lamont and state lawmakers, including Housing Committee co-Chair Martha Marx, D-New London, pledged to push for eviction reform legislation again during next year’s General Assembly session.
“Just-cause eviction. We didn’t quite get that over the finish line. We’re going to get that done this next coming cycle,” Lamont told the tenants Wednesday.
In a legislature where nearly one out of five lawmakers is a landlord, the proposal faces obstacles.
“I am looking at all of those legislators that don’t support it, or are rolling their eyes, or nervous about what the landlords are going to think. We are talking about an entire state of renters who have no protection,” Marx said Wednesday.
State Senator Martha Marx, D-New London, speaks during a press conference organized by members of the Connecticut Tenants Union regarding Alpha Capital at the Legislative Office Building in Hartford on Wednesday, July 22, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Public
Harry Bryant, a 63-year-old veteran who has lived at the Middletown property for almost 10 years, said he repeatedly received eviction notices.
“They gave everybody eviction notices. Jeez, out of a full house, there were maybe five left over the age of 60,” Bryant said. 
For many tenants, eviction concerns were only one of many grievances they described at Alpha Capital-owned properties. Several complained about maintenance issues, rent hikes, as well as difficulties communicating with their landlord. 
Mark C. Ball, a 57-year-old tenant who lived at another Alpha Capital-owned property in Middletown, said the building’s long-broken elevator has made it difficult for him and others with disabilities to access the building. Ball uses a wheelchair.
“I was stuck in the elevator for an hour and a half. I fell off the elevator,” Ball said. “After Alpha Management took over the building, everything went downhill.” 
Karen Quinn, an 83-year-old tenant from Bay Point Apartments in East Lyme, said she had to deal with heating problems.
“Both winters, I had trouble with the electricity and the heating… this last winter, on Dec. 26, the heat went off completely,” Quinn said.
In a statement to the Connecticut Mirror, Alpha Capital’s Smith said the company “is committed to providing safe, quality housing and investing in communities throughout Connecticut.”
He said many properties the company has purchased were already in a state of disrepair and that the company has spent millions of dollars renovating the buildings it’s acquired.
Smith declined to comment on individual concerns, but said in the statement, “We understand that changes in ownership can be difficult, particularly for long-term residents, and we do not dismiss those concerns.”
Marx said housing remains the top concern for many of her constituents and for residents statewide, and she offered support for the tenants gathered Wednesday. 
“We are talking about a person’s home. A person’s home is not a safety net. It is what we all deserve,” Marx said.
Lamont echoed that message. “There are a lot of people trying to take advantage of you in this day and age…That’s not going to happen here in Connecticut. You deserve a place to be. You deserve a place you can call home. You deserve a place where the landlord treats you with respect,” he said.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska budget hole grows to over $1 billion, with 5 months before next legislative session
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska lawmakers will likely have to contend with two separate budget deficits when they reconvene for the 2027 legislative session, with the combined shortfall currently set over $1 billion. Legislative Fiscal Analyst Keisha Patent confirmed the situation at a Tax Rate Review Committee meeting on Wednesday. There, she provided lawmakers with a n[...]
text:
The Nebraska State Capitol. (Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska lawmakers will likely have to contend with two separate budget deficits when they reconvene for the 2027 legislative session, with the combined shortfall currently set over $1 billion.
Legislative Fiscal Analyst Keisha Patent confirmed the situation at a Tax Rate Review Committee meeting on Wednesday. There, she provided lawmakers with a new financial status report, showing a $208 million deficit projected for the ongoing two-year budget that runs through June 30, 2027, and a $864 million projected deficit for the next biennium spanning from July 1, 2027 to June 30, 2029.
Lawmakers spent the 2026 session working to fill a fluctuating shortfall that hit its peak at roughly $646 million — the second consecutive session the Nebraska Legislature has dealt with a budget deficit. They ended the session with a $6 million surplus that was erased before the session officially ended due to monthly tax receipts that fell below economic forecasts.
Since then, three additional months of tax receipts came in below forecasts, leading to an estimated deficit of $223 million. Patent said the estimation changed to $208 million primarily because of standard accounting adjustments that cover transfers that are authorized in state law.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
The true size of the deficits lawmakers will have to work with won’t be set until late October, when Nebraska’s Economic Forecasting Advisory Board has its next meeting. There, Patent said the board will make projections for the current budget cycle, the next biennium, and the following biennium that covers 2030 and 2031.
The latest estimates were no surprise to term-limited state Sen. Ben Hansen of Blair, who chairs the Tax Rate Review Committee. He said he was familiar with where the state’s finances stood as he was monitoring the latest tax receipts.
“The rubber meets the road now,” Hansen said. “What are we going to do about it? I think there’s going to be some tough decisions.”
Hansen noted it’s a bit uncommon for there not to be a special session called when the state’s tax receipts consistently fall below forecasts. There have been no signs from lawmakers that they are interested in a special session, though Hansen said he would be open to it only if senators were committed to having “serious discussions” rather than letting it devolve into a “circus.”
Gov. Jim Pillen has indicated that he does not plan on calling a special session on the budget, instead issuing a memo earlier this month announcing a 5% spending reduction across all state agencies. If fully implemented, this would create roughly $276 million in savings per fiscal year, according to Pillen spokeswoman Laura Strimple.
“The governor’s actions will ensure state agencies have enough momentum on reducing spending when the Legislature convenes in January,” Strimple wrote in response to a question about a possible special session.
The memo prompted questions about whether the governor has the authority to reduce the state’s budget without legislative approval. Hansen said he believes it is within the governor’s authority to adjust the budgets of code agencies, which report directly to him, but there may be more gray areas in areas of the budget that are governed in statute.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: ‘It’s not over’: Landry, Murrill tout consequences for New Orleans after AG indictment
description: Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry and Attorney General Liz Murrill said there will be fallout for New Orleans officials following now-rescinded criminal charges against Murrill.
text:
Gov. Jeff Landry expresses his frustration with New Orleans  officials Wednesday, July 22, 2026, after a criminal indictment against Attorney General Liz Murrill, right, was withdrawn earlier in the day. (Photo by Piper Hutchinson/Louisiana Illuminator) Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry and Attorney General Liz Murrill said there will be fallout for New Orleans officials following now-rescinded criminal charges against Murrill. 
Murrill and Landry said during a Wednesday news conference that although the special prosecutor has dropped the charges, it is not enough to prevent accountability for the city leaders Murrill accused of weaponizing the criminal justice system against her. 
“It’s not over,” Murrill said. “You can’t be friends with somebody who wants to put you in jail for 80 years. Mutual professional courtesy and professional working relationships, absolutely. We have always extended that to the city of New Orleans and its leadership, no matter how bad their decision making is.” 
Before her indictment was withdrawn earlier Wednesday, Murrill faced 16 criminal charges related to a letter she sent in May to Mayor Helena Moreno, District Attorney Jason Williams and five members of the New Orleans City Council. The attorney general warned the officials they were acting illegally by attempting to circumvent a new state law that consolidated the city’s dual court clerk offices.
On July 2, an Orleans Parish grand jury handed up an indictment against Murrill for public intimidation and malfeasance in office. Moreno and Williams have said they did not instigate the court investigation into the attorney general.
‘There was NO crime’: Charges against AG Liz Murrill dropped

Murrill and Landry, both Republicans, were visibly upset during Wednesday afternoon’s news conference, both raising their voices as they expressed their anger with Democrats Moreno and Williams. Murrill repeatedly maintained her innocence and alleged the charges were only brought due to city leaders’ political affiliations.
Murrill said she is pursuing consequences not because she’s angry but because she believes that if the grand jury system can be used to indict a sitting attorney general, she believes it can be weaponized against anyone. 
The mayor and district attorney did not respond immediately to a request for comment about the remarks from Landry and Murrill.
Moreno, Williams and the council members sent letters Tuesday to special prosecutor Laurie White asking her to drop the charges against Murrill. White did so Wednesday morning.
Murrill said her attorneys had filed subpoenas in the criminal case seeking public records from New Orleans’ officials related to their efforts to name an interim clerk of court. A court hearing was set for Friday regarding the subpoenas, according to the attorney general. City officials sought to withdraw the indictment against Murrill, but she said it was not an effort to smooth relations between state and city leaders.
“I think it’s because they want to hide records,” Murrill said.
New Orleans’ leaders might have broken some of the same laws Murrill was accused of violating, she said.
The governor has already directed Louisiana State Police to investigate the grand jury that charged Murrill. Landry declined to comment on what he called an “ongoing investigation.”
A day after the indictment, U.S. Rep. Clay Higgins, R-Lafayette, wrote to FBI Director Kash Patel asking him to suss out whether the grand jury was properly convened or used for political retaliation. The federal agency typically does not confirm whether it’s launched an investigation. 
Landry also suggested Williams and City Councilman JP Morrell, both lawyers, should be disbarred. 
Murrill said she will pursue civil litigation and intends to seek reimbursement from the state for her ongoing legal costs, which she pegged at $250,000. 
In addition to the investigations, Landry said state lawmakers have expressed interest in convening a special session to explore taking more control of the Orleans Parish court system. Unlike the state’s other 41 judicial districts, Orleans has separate civil and criminal courts. 
Landry can call a special session for any topic as long as he gives lawmakers seven days notice before convening the session. 
During the legislative session that ended June 1, Republican lawmakers voted to eliminate three Orleans Criminal Court judgeships. Funding was also revoked for 10 district attorneys in the city, with the money directed to other parishes, in addition to the criminal clerk of court’s office being abolished. 
This is a developing story.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: 5 plead guilty in SC prison bribery case
description: COLUMBIA — A South Carolina prison guard, inmate and three relatives of the inmate pleaded guilty Wednesday to wire fraud in a bribery case, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office. Lowanda Atkinson, a 52-year-old guard at Lee Correctional Institution, accepted more than $550,000 from inmate Jason Brown and his relatives over the course of nearly […]
text:
Department of Corrections Director Joel Anderson looks at a collection of confiscated drones, often used to smuggle contraband such as cellphones into prisons, outside Broad River Correctional Institution on Friday, Sept. 12, 2025. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — A South Carolina prison guard, inmate and three relatives of the inmate pleaded guilty Wednesday to wire fraud in a bribery case, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office.
Lowanda Atkinson, a 52-year-old guard at Lee Correctional Institution, accepted more than $550,000 from inmate Jason Brown and his relatives over the course of nearly five years, according to prosecutors. In exchange, Atkinson smuggled cell phones, tobacco and drugs into the prison, which inmates sold.
Former SC corrections worker sentenced for smuggling contraband: ‘A message needs to be sent’

Atkinson spent the money on luxuries such as plastic surgery and an SUV, according to prosecutors.
“Atkinson’s scheme is an example of law enforcement corruption, and we will not tolerate that in South Carolina,” U.S. Attorney Bryan Stirling, former prisons director for the state, said in a news release.
Mary Ann Hickman Brown, the inmate’s mother; Christopher Hickman, his brother; and Adrianna Conyers, his nephew’s mother, all pleaded guilty to bribing Atkinson as well.
Brown was serving a 25-year sentence for a murder conviction, along with 10 years for arson and five for grand larceny, according to inmate records.
Each of the five people faces up to 20 years in prison, plus three years of supervised release and up to $250,000 in fines. Sentencing will come at a later date.
“This person took advantage of the trust given to her and conspired with inmates and their families to flood our prison with deadly contraband,” prisons director Joel Anderson said in a news release. “I’m glad they are all being held accountable for their crimes.”
Another inmate and friend were charged with wire fraud related to the case. Their cases are still pending.



5 plead guilty in bribery case

Lowanda Atkinson, a 52-year-old prison guard from Kershaw County, pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit honest services wire fraud.
Jason Brown, a 43-year-old inmate, pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit honest services wire fraud.
Adriana Conyers, a 37-year-old relative of Brown’s from Sumter County, pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit honest services wire fraud.
Christopher Hickman, the 46-year-old brother of Brown from Richland County, pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit honest services wire fraud.
Mary Ann Hickman-Brown, the 64-year-old mother of Brown from Clarendon County, pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit honest services wire fraud.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Trump reportedly to visit Michigan as Gordie Howe Bridge opening proceeds without joint ceremony
description: As the Canadian government plans to celebrate the opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge on Friday — a ceremony that was planned to be a joint effort with the Americans but was later canceled — President Donald Trump reportedly plans to visit Michigan Monday to potentially support his endorsed candidates for the U.S. Senate […]
text:
President Donald Trump addresses the Detroit Economic Club at the MotorCity Casino on Jan. 13, 2026. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)As the Canadian government plans to celebrate the opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge on Friday — a ceremony that was planned to be a joint effort with the Americans but was later canceled — President Donald Trump reportedly plans to visit Michigan Monday to potentially support his endorsed candidates for the U.S. Senate and the gubernatorial election.
Trump’s potential visit to Oakland County was first reported by The Associated Press Tuesday, but an event has not been confirmed or notice sent to the media about a rally on Monday. 
A message seeking comment from the White House Executive Office of the President was not returned at the time of publication. This story will be updated once a response is received.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Trump has endorsed both Republican U.S. Rep. John James of Shelby Township, who is seeking the nomination in the Aug. 4 gubernatorial primary, and former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers of White Lake, who is the lone candidate on the GOP side of the U.S. Senate race.
Rogers will go on to face either Abdul El-Sayed or U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens of Birmingham following the results of next month’s primary contest. Recent public polling has shown Stevens with a narrow lead, though the race remains competitive.
James faces businessman Perry Johnson in August, who is running a self-funded bid to knock off James in the primary. He has not been endorsed by Trump. If the president does visit Monday and stumps for James, it will be the only Trump-sanctioned event in Michigan that week. Johnson is planning a tailgate event with some of his key surrogates on Monday, which he has labeled a Trump Tailgate, but the Trump team pushed back this week on social media, reiterating that the president has not endorsed Johnson’s campaign.
Meanwhile, Monday is the slated opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge on both sides of the span. Trump and the Canadians have been locked in a trade war over Trump-imposed tariffs that began after Trump returned to office for a second term. The bridge’s opening had been stalled multiple times as Trump and the Canadians worked out their differences. 
The Gordie Howe Bridge between Detroit and Ontario, Canada, remains closed. July 7, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Part of that conflict had to do with the financing agreement for the bridge, which would allow Canada to collect bridge tolls to recoup costs for building the new border crossing. The U.S. government declined to finance construction of the bridge, leading Canada to cover the upfront costs under a financing agreement.
A breakthrough finally occurred and a new deal on the bridge tolls appeared in recent months, and a joint-nation, pre-opening ceremony was planned for Friday at the Bridge.
But after Trump leveled new tariffs on Canada, the plan for a joint ceremony was scuttled.
A Canada-only opening ceremony is still planned for Friday.
A spokesperson for the Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority told Michigan Advance the bridge will be open to traffic on Monday.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Every New Hampshire policy debate should start in the same place, with the same question
description: Nobody can end the suffering of others, but everybody has the power to reduce it. Out in the world, it is easy to spot the affirmative embrace of that option. A door is held for the person behind, a retiree becomes a community volunteer, a “Let me help you with that” floats across a big-box […]
text:
Protesters gather outside of the State House in Concord during a "No Kings" rally on Oct. 18, 2025. (Photo by Dana Wormald/New Hampshire Bulletin)Nobody can end the suffering of others, but everybody has the power to reduce it.
Out in the world, it is easy to spot the affirmative embrace of that option. A door is held for the person behind, a retiree becomes a community volunteer, a “Let me help you with that” floats across a big-box parking lot. The rejection of the option is evident, too: A middle finger is flashed in traffic, a server is scolded by a diner for not meeting some arbitrary benchmark, a lie is delivered without compunction.
The same option holds true for public policy. We can start with the question, “Is this thing we are proposing intended to reduce suffering or is it meant to increase it, if only for some?” The answering can get tricky, but there are instances where complexity never truly arises, such as with human rights. When rights are denied based on something core about a person’s very existence, the intent is to deliver real suffering solely to alleviate the sense among others that they are suffering that existence.
New Hampshire’s debate over LGBTQ+ rights is a prime modern example. Some lawmakers want to repeal discrimination protections for transgender people, which would inflict real suffering on real people, and for reasons that never rise above intolerance. They do not want to acknowledge or understand another’s existence and resent being asked to try.
Even so, most people inherently apply the question of suffering to the positions they take, and that’s why you hear arguments from those who favor anti-LGBTQ bills about protecting girls and girls’ sports, and the security of locker rooms and restrooms. It makes some people suffer to think they are inflicting suffering, even when it’s at the expense of people they reject, and so they play mental games with themselves to designate their cruelties as a service to an imagined greater good.
Wisdom is little more than the ability to detect such games in ourselves. 
In many ways, the immigration debate is the same. There is a perception among some that the existence of people in America who lack the proper paperwork creates suffering for proper citizens. The explanations for why this is so run the gamut from the absurd (migrants eating pets) to the dubious (strains on housing and social services) to the fanatical (extreme isolationism and xenophobia). 
A good-faith debate over a new national immigration policy would be almost infinitely complex at the level of suffering, but the only point of the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign is to inflict suffering as punishment and deterrence. There’s nothing complex about it. Meanwhile, the human toll of that campaign is observably real — on victims, yes, but on witnesses and communities, too. And, again, any reduction in a “greater” suffering is imagined — and it requires the elevation of conspiracy theories and bigotry above human decency and due process.
It takes a special kind of person to physically separate families, to be the one to tackle a parent in front of a child who, in that moment, understands only that they’ve lost everything. If the question of suffering even arises for an agent of ICE, the mental games they play to explain away their cruelties would have to be extraordinary. 
The present harm of the president’s deportation effort is incalculable, and it is just the beginning. The lasting harm will haunt this nation for generations.
But cruelty is the primary currency of the Trump administration, and so any optimism that things will improve on that end in the next two years is misplaced. My hope for New Hampshire, however, is that the fundamental question of suffering is where every policy debate begins from now on. 
With our conversations about public education, that means clearly establishing from the outset that our schools are not something inflicted on taxpayers but a core tenet of society itself: that every child, regardless of family wealth or status, is owed an opportunity for a meaningful academic and social foundation provided by their community. Our charge is to find ways to pay for public schools, not dream up new ways of destroying them. 
When we talk about housing, I hope that we can start at the importance of welcoming new neighbors with lower incomes rather than the wish to “preserve town character” for existing residents. 
When we discuss investments in early care and education, I hope that we begin by considering how challenging it is to be a young working parent of modest means in a state with such a high cost of living — and the many ways those young working parents of modest means are critical to New Hampshire’s present and its future. 
When we debate elder care, I hope it is with the primary understanding that everyone grows old if they’re lucky — and not one of us can predict what our physical, mental, or financial capabilities will be when we get there.
Most of all, I hope we can begin to acknowledge something fundamental about our current divides, all of them: There is a big difference between the suffering we send out into the world to be absorbed by others and the suffering we create for ourselves and so must endure.

title: WA agency director out as Ferguson installs an interim leader
description: The director of Washington’s Department of Enterprise Services is out and the leader of another agency is in charge temporarily, Gov. Bob Ferguson announced Wednesday. Director Matt Jones, a Ferguson cabinet member who went on personal leave July 9, stepped down from the leadership post but is still employed by the agency, according to Ferguson’s […]
text:
Employment Security Department Commissioner Cami Feek joins Gov. Bob Ferguson at a press conference in May. On Wednesday, Ferguson named Feek as the interim leader of the Department of Enterprise Services. (Photo courtesy of Employment Security Department)The director of Washington’s Department of Enterprise Services is out and the leader of another agency is in charge temporarily, Gov. Bob Ferguson announced Wednesday.
Director Matt Jones, a Ferguson cabinet member who went on personal leave July 9, stepped down from the leadership post but is still employed by the agency, according to Ferguson’s office. 
Matt Jones has stepped down as director of the Department of Enterprise Services. (Photo from Department of Enterprise Services)
Spokespeople for the agency and governor’s office remain mum on why Jones took leave and how long it will last. There are no allegations of criminal wrongdoing, a Department of Enterprise Services official said last week
Ferguson tapped Employment Security Department Commissioner Cami Feek to serve as director through a transition of an unspecified length of time. The department manages state facilities, among other duties. It has more than 900 employees, a $280 million operating budget, and a $1.2 billion capital program, according to the agency’s website.
Feek is a veteran public servant having worked stints with the attorney general’s office, Washington State Patrol and General Administration, forerunner to the Department of Enterprise Services. She joined the Employment Security Department in 2017 and played a leading role in launching the state’s Paid Family and Medical Leave program. 
Former Gov. Jay Inslee appointed Feek as commissioner in 2021 and Ferguson has kept her in that post. Before that, she served as the department’s acting commissioner, deputy commissioner and chief operating officer.
With Feek taking over for Jones, Martin McMurry, chief operations officer for the Employment Security Department, will serve as interim commissioner.
There will be a recruitment for a new Department of Enterprise Services director, agency employees were told in a Wednesday memo from Chief Operations Officer Jo Aiken.
Wednesday’s announcement did not explain what role Ferguson may have played in Jones’ decision to leave the leadership post. Nor did it provide a timeline for finding a permanent replacement.
Jones began his state career at the Department of General Administration in 2006 and has been with the Department of Enterprise Services since it was formed in 2011. He guided the Capitol Campus and Visitor Services Division for seven years before being named interim chief operations officer in October 2024, according to the agency.
Ferguson named Jones acting director of the department on Jan. 12, 2025, appointing him to the top post last July.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

title: US House approves joint measure to curb Congress’ stock trading, require voter ID
text: WASHINGTON — U.S. House Republicans passed a measure to curb stock trading by members of Congress that was packaged with an unrelated voter ID bill, part of President Donald Trump’s push for major federal involvement in elections.The legislation passed by a vote of 232-198. All Republicans and 13 Democrats voted in favor.The bill faces possible headwinds in the narrowly split Senate where 60 votes are required for passage. Republicans control the upper chamber with 53 members, to Democrats’ 47 members. The House-passed bill, sponsored by Rep. Bryan Steil, R-Wis., would require voters to present a current state-issued driver’s license or identification card, passport, valid military or veteran ID, or tribal government-issued ID card to be able to vote. The base bill, the Stop Insider Trading Act, would prohibit members of Congress and their spouses and close family members from purchasing certain stocks, and require a public notice and waiting period prior to selling stocks.Violators could face a penalty of $2,000 or 10% of the transaction value, whichever is greater, plus any net gain realized from the transaction over a specified time period. The bill would govern investments issued by a publicly traded company. Some investments would be exempt, including widely held investment funds and investments held in a trust. Also, a spouse’s or dependent’s transactions made on behalf of another person, or held as part of a job benefits package would also be exempt.Voter IDBut it was the voter ID bill that attracted most attention as lawmakers debated the measure this week.Under the bill, if a voter doesn’t have one of the listed physical forms of identification, state election officials can issue a provisional ballot. The voter would then have three days to provide the accepted ID or an affidavit that the voter doesn’t have one because of religious objections to being photographed.Additionally, state officials would be prohibited from accepting absentee ballots unless the voter attaches a copy of a valid ID, the last four digits of their Social Security number with an affidavit that they cannot obtain a photo ID, or a notarized statement that the voter personally completed their ballot.During Monday’s House Rules Committee debate of the bill, Democrats criticized Republicans for removing a state grant provision from the voter ID section of the bill that would have covered voters’ individual costs of acquiring IDs. Democrats also panned the bill for going further than state laws in Florida and Wisconsin that are considered among the nation’s strictest. As of April 2025, 36 states had some form of voter ID law on the books, though they vary in restrictions, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.Rep. Joe Neguse, D-Colo., asked Steil why Wisconsin state law allows some university IDs at the voting polls, while his federal bill does not.“Plenty of constituents of yours at a variety of different colleges and universities that you represent … right now comply with what has been described by others as the most strict voter ID law in the country by using their college ID. But their congressman is championing a bill that would tell them that they can no longer do that,” Neguse said.“Great question,” Steil replied. “Universities across the country, including in my home state, issue IDs to noncitizens, issue IDs to illegal immigrants.”Not as restrictive as SAVE America ActAttaching the voter ID legislation to a bill curbing lawmakers’ stock trading appears to be Republicans’ compromise with the president’s eagerness for a more restrictive bill that faces a slim to nothing chance of clearing Congress.Trump is pushing Republicans to pass an even broader federal election regulations bill dubbed the SAVE America Act. That bill would require additional documents, such as passports and birth certificates, to register to vote. Critics say it would upend state management of elections.Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., has warned there are not enough votes in the Senate to pass Trump’s preferred bill.The president promoted the legislation in a primetime address July 16 when he declassified evidence that he said showed attempted election interference by China in 2020.Experts say the documents released did not prove Trump’s claims, and critics panned the speech as the president’s attempt to undermine trust in the upcoming November midterm elections that will decide control of Congress.House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., praised the joint stock trading and voter ID bill Tuesday, saying “probably in excess of 9 out of 10 Americans support both measures.” Johnson also said House Republicans “will continue to hammer” Trump’s messaging about elections.Dems objectHouse Democratic leadership urged members to vote “no” on the bill because it would allow lawmakers and close family members to continue buying and selling stocks. Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon, D-Pa., said Americans “have had it” with stock trading by federal lawmakers.“They are fed up with it. Congress needs to enact a comprehensive ban on members of Congress as well as the president, the vice president and members of their families from owning or trading individual stocks or having other financial dealings,” Scanlon said Monday.Scanlon’s amendment to replace the GOP-sponsored stock trading bill with the text of Rhode Island Democrat Seth Magaziner’s more restrictive bill, dubbed the Restore Trust in Government Act, failed. Magaziner’s bill also includes restrictions on the president, vice president and their families.Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., characterized the bill on the House floor Tuesday as a “fake stock trading ban.” “I want to be very clear: their bill does not block insider trading, no matter what it's called,” Jayapal said.They also objected to the voter ID portion.The measure “would functionally eviscerate mail voting by forcing Americans to include photocopies of their IDs alongside their mailed ballots,” according to House Minority Whip Katherine Clark’s email to members ahead of the vote Wednesday.Additionally, Clark, a Massachusetts Democrat, castigated the bill’s “narrow set of acceptable photo identification in order to cast a ballot in a federal election.”The Congressional Black Caucus issued a statement Tuesday slamming the bill.“House Republicans are not serious about enacting a meaningful congressional stock trading ban,” the Democrat-aligned group said. “The combined Stop Insider Trading Act and Voter ID Act — which incorporates provisions from the voter-suppressive, so-called SAVE America Act — would allow Members of Congress to continue owning, selling, and, in some cases, purchasing individual stocks while simultaneously imposing stricter voter ID requirements that would make it harder for millions of eligible Americans to vote, including by mail.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Husker legend Tom Osborne officially inducted into Nebraska Hall of Fame
description: LINCOLN — Husker legend and former Congressman Tom Osborne is officially the next member of the Nebraska Hall of Fame after a commission gave unanimous approval Wednesday at Gov. Jim Pillen’s urging. Pillen, a former Husker defensive back in the 1970s under Osborne as coach, made it no secret that the original Legislative Bill 1159 […]
text:
Former Husker football coach Tom Osborne, center, speaks at a February 2023 event with Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, just behind Osborne, at which Pillen designated the month as “Nebraska Mentoring Month.” (Courtesy of Nebraska Governor’s Office)LINCOLN — Husker legend and former Congressman Tom Osborne is officially the next member of the Nebraska Hall of Fame after a commission gave unanimous approval Wednesday at Gov. Jim Pillen’s urging.
Pillen, a former Husker defensive back in the 1970s under Osborne as coach, made it no secret that the original Legislative Bill 1159 introduced at his request, which passed as part of LB 596, was written for his mentor. The intent was always for the governor-appointed Nebraska Hall of Fame Commission, of which the governor is a nonvoting member, to add Osborne as the first living member, or at least someone matching specific qualifications tailored to Osborne, 89.
“His love of Nebraska and the people in Nebraska, what he’s done for Nebraska, is just absolutely second to none,” Pillen told reporters after the vote. “That we’re able to recognize him is a really, really special day.”
Former Nebraska head football coach and former U.S. Rep. Tom Osborne testifies against legislative efforts to legalize online sports wagering on Wednesday, July 31, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Jim Rose, a radio commentator and former Huskers broadcaster from Valley, made the nomination, praising the legal change that took effect Saturday allowing Osborne to be nominated and ending a 35-year waiting period after someone’s death for them to qualify.
“Though that policy assured induction of only the most enduring among us, it also robbed today’s Nebraskans of recognizing and amplifying the pathway of life for those still with us,” Rose said.
The commission did not make any other nominations and approved Osborne in a 7-0 vote.
‘Goosebumps’
Pillen said he got “goosebumps” at the meeting and told commissioners his mentor is “best of the best of the best of Nebraskans.” He told reporters Osborne has a global impact and a “ripple” effect through his Teammates mentoring nonprofit and deserves to be honored forever.
“The trophies, those are all going to tarnish with time,” Pillen said. “His commitment to people and his commitment to youth has inspired us all to try to do better than what we ever thought we could do.”
State Sens. Dan Lonowski of Hastings, center right, and Danielle Conrad of Lincoln, right, meet at the front of the legislative chamber on the relevance of a Lonowski amendment to a legislative package led by the Government, Military and Veterans Affairs Committee. That committee’s legal counsel, Dick Clark, center left, also meets with the group including Clerk of the Legislature Brandon Metzler, left. March 5, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The original LB 1159 referenced parts of Osborne’s resume that were so narrow, only Osborne would qualify — a member of the U.S. House of Representatives, head football coach and athletic director at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln and a graduate of Hastings High School. 
In that case, some lawmakers raised the possible constitutional concern of “special legislation.”
Former State Sen. Dan Lonowski of Hastings, Osborne’s hometown, led LB 1159 for Pillen. Lonowski changed the requirements to be any living Nebraskan who has a “record of achievement” in public service, leadership in collegiate athletics and volunteer youth mentorship activities.
Lonowski’s amendment passed with little fanfare and also outright eliminated the former requirement that any future Nebraska Hall of Fame inductees be dead for at least 35 years to be considered for inclusion. Before 1998, the waiting period was 10 years.
The new law took effect Saturday.
The Hall of Fame Commission can name just one new member every five years. Osborne won’t count toward that limit, however.
Future nominations expanded
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen. June 15, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., in a Wednesday reporter call before the meeting, said Osborne “certainly belongs in the Nebraska Hall of Fame” but said he wanted to leave it up to commissioners whether they wanted to give the honor to Osborne and break precedent.
“Tom Osborne is a man of character and integrity,” said Ricketts, a former two-term governor. “He has done a lot for our state serving, obviously, not only the University of Nebraska but here in Washington, D.C., as well. I think he’s very deserving of being in our Hall of Fame.”
Osborne served three terms in the U.S. House of Representatives (2001-07) for Nebraska’s sprawling 3rd Congressional District. He was succeeded in 2006 by U.S. Rep. Adrian Smith, R-Neb., after Osborne narrowly lost the Republican nomination for governor in 2006.
There were 27 members of the Hall of Fame before Osborne, whose busts are displayed in the Capitol. The last inductee was slain civil rights leader Malcolm X, an Omaha native whose bust was installed in 2024 after a years-long fight to include him.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen speaks in favor of naming his former Huskers coach Tom Osborne to the Nebraska Hall of Fame to the governor-appointed commission on Wednesday, July 22, 2026, in Lincoln. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Osborne will also receive a bust, which legislative analysts estimated to cost $45,000. However, Pillen led fundraising efforts and said about 10 to 12 players donated to cover the cost for taxpayers. Pillen said the bust should be done within a month or so, and he’s working on scheduling an induction ceremony.
“Traditionally it’d be here in the Rotunda, but we’re thinking there might be a better place, and a place where Nebraskans could really, really enjoy and celebrate and all together say ‘thank you’ in kind of a big venue someday,” Pillen said with a smile.
Nominations are also open for who would be now the 29th inductee. With the removal of the 35-year waiting period, any Nebraskan, living or deceased, can be nominated, director Daryl Bohac of the Nebraska State Historical Society confirmed.
Nominations for the next 29th inductee, for the 2025-29 inductee cycle, are due by Dec. 31.

title: US House GOP pushes through budget blueprint for Iran war funding, farm aid
text: WASHINGTON — Republicans in the U.S. House on Wednesday approved their outline for the third party-line budget measure of the second Trump administration, though they won’t be able to begin work on that package until they reach agreement with their Senate colleagues on a plan forward. The 216-214 vote on a budget resolution sets up a confrontation between GOP lawmakers in Congress over exactly how much funding to provide for the war in Iran and farm assistance as well as whether lawmakers should pay for it by cutting spending elsewhere. House Republicans proposed a total of $95 billion in spending in their budget resolution. The instructions in that blueprint would allow four committees to eventually write bills that would spend up to $60 billion on the military, $13 billion on intelligence agencies, $12 billion on agricultural assistance and $10 billion on some sort of grant program for states that implement voter ID laws. But work on that package can only begin after Republicans in both chambers vote to approve the same budget resolution with identical sets of reconciliation instructions. Third time aroundHouse Budget Committee Chairman Jodey Arrington, R-Texas, said during floor debate that the GOP has used the reconciliation process twice to achieve policy goals that wouldn’t garner Democratic support. The first time was last year, when Congress approved the “big, beautiful” law. The second occurred earlier this year, when lawmakers approved three years of funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Border Patrol without new constraints on federal agents. Both were signed into law by President Donald Trump.“Here we are, reconciliation 3.0, supporting our troops in their time of need,” Arrington said. “Just baseline battlefield readiness. Bullets and bombs to finish the job.”The yet-to-be-written reconciliation package, he added, would also likely "strengthen our food supply” and "safeguard the integrity of our elections.”Pennsylvania Democratic Rep. Brendan Boyle, ranking member on the panel, said that Republicans’ support for the two earlier packages and this budget outline shows they aren’t focused on bringing down costs for Americans. Boyle also questioned whether campaign promises from GOP candidates to lower the annual federal deficit were genuine, given that this and the previous party-line laws will have a substantial impact on the national debt. “Yes, that’s right, the same crowd that loves to cry crocodile tears about deficit and debt whenever there’s a president in the White House who's a Democrat — cumulatively now they have added $5 trillion to our national debt, more than any other 18-month period in the history of Congress,” he said. “And they’re about to add $100 billion more.” Senate GOP not on boardSenate Republicans don’t fully agree on their House counterparts’ proposed spending level, with some wanting considerably more in defense funding, and others looking for ways to offset the costs. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said during a Tuesday afternoon press conference that he’s unlikely to bring any budget resolution to the floor until after lawmakers figure out a way to fund the government ahead of the Oct. 1 shutdown deadline. Congress’ budget resolution is just a blueprint, similar to a blueprint for building a house. It isn’t a bill and never goes to the president for his signature. Lawmakers use a completely separate process to fund the government through a dozen annual appropriations bills. But since lawmakers are nowhere near close to finishing that appropriations task before the start of the new fiscal year they must agree to some sort of short-term spending bill to avoid another shutdown this fall. The House this week passed a stopgap bill that would extend that deadline until Dec. 4, but it doesn’t have the support needed to advance in the Senate, where leaders from both political parties are working toward a bipartisan compromise. Thune said he expects the Senate will vote on its stopgap spending bill before leaving for the August recess, which could delay work on a budget resolution until that chamber returns in mid-September.  “It’s possible that that would be something that would get punted into September,” he said.That could lead to a significant time crunch for Republicans if they want to use the complex budget reconciliation process to enact their party-line defense and farm aid spending package before the November midterm elections. There are just three weeks in September when both chambers are scheduled to be in session before lawmakers depart for their five-week October break.And while the House can approve the budget resolution and an eventual party-line package without taking up a single amendment on the floor, the Senate process is considerably more arduous. The Senate has unlimited amendment debate on both measures, giving Democrats in that chamber dozens of opportunities to challenge Republicans on spending and policy choices.That’s not necessarily an ideal scenario for Republican Senate leaders, who hope voters will allow the party to hold onto its narrow majority for another two years. Shauneen Miranda contributed to this report.

title: Vermont Conversation: ‘I’m sorry that this isn’t what we promised.’ Immigration attorney Jill Martin Diaz on fear and hope in Vermont’s immigrant community
description:
Martin Diaz, who is the executive director of the Vermont Asylum Assistance Project, warns that “rights and protections are being stripped away every day in mundane-seeming memos and orders from courts.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Conversation: ‘I’m sorry that this isn’t what we promised.’ Immigration attorney Jill Martin Diaz on fear and hop[...]
text:
The Vermont Conversation with David Goodman is a VTDigger podcast that features in-depth interviews on local and national issues. Listen and subscribe for free on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get podcasts.
Jill Martin Diaz, executive director of the Vermont Asylum Assistance Project in Burlington in Aug. 2025. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown is intensifying. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents detained over 10,000 people just in the last week of June. This month, ICE agents killed two men in less than a week, including a young Columbian father in Maine who reportedly had legal status. Despite the Trump administration’s insistence that it is only arresting “the worst of the worst,” most of the people arrested by ICE have no criminal convictions.
Fear is now a constant in immigrant communities.
“It’s like watching a slow car crash every day,” said Jill Martin Diaz, an immigration attorney and executive director of the Vermont Asylum Assistance Project.
VAAP is a rapidly growing legal services and technical assistance organization for immigrants. Since becoming VAAP’s first paid staff member in January 2024, Martin Diaz now oversees a paid staff of 10, a network of 28 volunteer attorneys and over two dozen volunteer interpreters, among others.
VAAP is also the hub of a newly formed network that now offers coordinated immigration legal services throughout the state. The network includes the Association of Africans Living in Vermont, the Center for Justice Reform Clinic at Vermont Law and Graduate School, Vermont Afghan Alliance, and Vermont Legal Aid. 
“We’ve seen a really steady stream of people being arrested in Vermont,” said Martin Diaz. VAAP attorneys make weekly visits to Northwest State Correctional Facility and report encountering an average of 12 to 18 immigrants in detention.
Martin Diaz warned that “rights and protections are being stripped away every day in mundane-seeming memos and orders from courts. And we’re just watching the system slip between our fingers as we’re trying to support Vermonters to access their needs.”
Anxiety has been compounded by a Supreme Court decision that allows the Trump administration to end temporary protected status. The decision may result in the loss of legal protection for over a million immigrants who have fled war or environmental disasters in their home countries.
Martin Diaz said this Supreme Court decision will impact several dozen Haitians, some of whom have lived in Vermont for decades and “find themselves now without temporary protected status, vulnerable to being arrested by ICE and prosecuted for removal proceedings, and most acutely unauthorized to work.”
Martin Diaz formerly taught immigration law at Vermont Law and Graduate School, directed its Center for Justice Reform Clinic and practiced at Vermont Legal Aid, and was a lecturer in the department of social work at the University of Vermont. In 2023, Martin Diaz was named by the LGBTQ+ Bar Association as one of the 40 best LGBTQ+ lawyers under 40 and has received awards from the Vermont Bar Association and American Civil Liberties Union of Vermont.
Martin Diaz said “that for every terrifying story about ICE hurting people, killing people in the streets, the stories about unfair things happening in courts of law, there are also stories of hope, of the system working as it should, of things going well, that doesn’t make the news.”
The attorney and activist concluded with a message for immigrants who are fearful: “I’m just so sorry that this is happening. I’m sorry that this isn’t what we promised.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Conversation: ‘I’m sorry that this isn’t what we promised.’ Immigration attorney Jill Martin Diaz on fear and hope in Vermont’s immigrant community.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Indigenous and federal officials urge outcry on proposed rollback of Chaco protections
description: Joey Sanchez, the chair of the All Pueblo Council of Governors, stood outside the U.S. Capitol Wednesday with dozens of tribal leaders and New Mexico’s entire federal delegation to protest a Bureau of Land Management proposal to unwind mining protections around Chaco Culture National Historical Park as just a week remains for the public to weigh in on the pl[...]
text:
A view of the Pueblo Bonito at Chaco Canyon National Historical Park, which tribal leaders and advocates say is threatened by the Trump administration’s efforts to undo federal protections against oil and gas drilling. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)Joey Sanchez, the chair of the All Pueblo Council of Governors, stood outside the U.S. Capitol Wednesday with dozens of tribal leaders and New Mexico’s entire federal delegation to protest a Bureau of Land Management proposal to unwind mining protections around Chaco Culture National Historical Park as just a week remains for the public to weigh in on the plan.
The Bureau of Land Management recently opened a two-week period for the public to comment on a proposal to eliminate or shrink the 10-mile mining protections around Chaco, a spiritually and culturally significant site for many of New Mexico’s pueblos and tribes. Members of New Mexico’s federal delegation quickly denounced the plan when the comment period opened last week, and many noted that BLM and U.S. Department of the Interior officials had not visited with the Indigenous communities that the decision would impact.
As a chorus of Indigenous leaders and politicians spoke at Wednesday’s event, they urged New Mexicans to submit a public comment on the BLM plan through its online portal.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Chaco is not a museum…it is a living cultural landscape,” Sanchez said Wednesday. “The pueblos have protected Chaco for thousands of years, and we’re not going to stop today.”
U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) joined Sanchez in Washington, D.C., Wednesday and said that Chaco Canyon “is not for sale.” 
New Mexico has already positioned itself as a national leader in oil and gas production, and it’s done so without sacrificing sacred sites, Heinrich, who serves as ranking member of the U.S. Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, said.
“We produce far more electrons than we consume and we have never had to sacrifice our most sacred places to do that,” he said. “And we should not do that going forward.”
Each of New Mexico’s U.S. senators and representatives, all Democrats, spoke out against the proposal at Wednesday’s event and said it was an “insult” that the federal government would allow just two weeks for public comment on a plan that could undo years of work to install Chaco’s current protections. In 2025, they proposed legislation that would make those protections permanent.
U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) questioned whether it’s necessary to drill any closer to Chaco than what is currently allowed. The BLM’s current proposal lists three options: eliminate the 10-mile buffer zone; cut it in half; or keep it intact.
U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) spoke alongside New Mexico pueblo and tribal leaders in Washington, D.C., on July 22, 2026, to oppose a Bureau of Land Management plan to eliminate or reduce mining protections around Chaco Culture National Historical Park. (Screenshot)
Chaco sits in northwest New Mexico, near the Navajo Nation and the Four Corners region. About 1,000 years ago, it was the San Juan Basin’s cultural and economic hub, according to the U.S. National Park Service.
“A molecule of gas from Chaco is the same as a molecule of gas outside that 10-mile buffer zone,” Leger Fernández said. “That molecule of gas could be easily, easily developed outside and without disturbing the 4,700…archaeological sites within that 10 miles. If we let the bulldozers of the oil and gas companies destroy any of those 4,700 sites, they can never be reconstructed.”
State leaders push back on BLM plan
State lawmakers have also taken up the fight against the BLM’s plan. Rep. Derrick J. Lente (D-Sandia Pueblo) on Tuesday called on Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham and several state agencies to present a unified front against the federal plan.
“Chaco is not a bargaining chip, and it is not an ordinary parcel of federal land. It is the ancestral home of our people and a place of continuing ceremony and prayer,” Lente said in a statement. “As a Pueblo person and as a legislator, I refuse to stay quiet while our tribal sovereignty is ignored and our sacred lands are opened to extraction.”
In a statement to Source NM, a spokesperson for Lujan Grisham wrote that she is “fiercely opposed” to the Trump administration’s proposal and noted that state Cultural Affairs Secretary Debra Garcia y Griego wrote a letter to BLM officials, urging them to keep the current protections in place.
The governor “is working through appropriate channels to push back on this terribly shortsighted and reckless plan, including submitting official administration correspondence in opposition back in April and communicating with New Mexico’s congressional delegation,” Lujan Grisham’s Communications Director Michael Coleman wrote in an email to Source NM. “She encourages Rep. Lente, other members of the New Mexico Legislature and the general public to also submit letters in opposition to help protect Chaco Canyon.”

title: The real problem in Alaska schools: school boards
description: The Mat-Su school board recently passed a policy to arm classroom teachers. I’ve been struggling to find the right word to describe it. The district claims the policy is about “maintaining a safe and secure learning environment.” In a profession obsessed with research-based decision making, nothing supports the claim that armed teachers make schools safer, [[...]
text:
Deputy Matanuska-Susitna Borough School District Deputy Superintendent Katie Gardner and Superintendent Randy Trani discuss a concealed-carry weapons proposal during a regular school board meeting at the Matanuska-Susitna Borough School District in Palmer on May 5, 2026. (Photo by Amy Bushatz/Mat-Su Sentinel)The Mat-Su school board recently passed a policy to arm classroom teachers. I’ve been struggling to find the right word to describe it.
The district claims the policy is about “maintaining a safe and secure learning environment.” In a profession obsessed with research-based decision making, nothing supports the claim that armed teachers make schools safer, especially when there hasn’t been a gun-related death in an Alaskan school in over twenty-five years. The board claims the policy will not “change the educational environment.” When you hide guns in classrooms, the environment changes immediately. 
The board’s concealed carry program will cost an estimated four hundred and fifty thousand dollars — roughly forty-five thousand dollars per gun. With forty-nine schools and over one thousand teachers, guns will be in a fraction of schools. The chance a gun related incident will happen near an armed teacher is miniscule. The cost of “protecting” such a tiny number of classrooms is fiscally irresponsible. 
This isn’t even the worst part of the policy. The school board is arming themselves. According to the policy, the superintendent can approve to arm board members. If the superintendent denies a board member’s request, they can appeal the decision… to the board!
I don’t support arming teachers, but arming board members is absurd. First, board members are rarely in school buildings. Their usefulness as security is next to nothing. Second, most board members have no training in classroom management, school procedures or deescalation. Third, because board members are not regular participants in classrooms they have no understanding of individual students, classroom dynamics or school culture necessary to understand volatile situations.
Finally, and I can’t stress this enough, board members are not school employees. In fact, they are barred from being employees by Alaska Statute AS14.14.140. It begs the question, why do board members need guns at all? To threaten people in board meetings? Outside a board meeting, individual board members have no authority. 
There is simply no logic that justifies arming board members. Then again, logic is hardly a motivating factor these days. Guns don’t belong in classrooms, books do. An expensive lesson the Mat-Su board had to learn from a federal judge. And while they claim this policy will “maintain a safe” environment, they literally struck the phrase “safe spaces” from their library policy and have actively made their schools less safe for LGBTQ students.
All of this brings us to the real problem: school boards. Nothing prevents school boards from enacting irrational policies like this. Many board members have no experience in education. No training is required of board members. Every year we put the fate of our schools into the hands of people whose only requirement for eligibility is a pulse and valid voting registration. 
It was a struggle, but I finally found a word to describe this situation: asinine.

text:
Iowa State University will lead four research projects selected by the U.S. Department of Energy for its Genesis Mission initiative. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowa State University researchers are contributing to a new, national consortium with their efforts to integrate artificial intelligence with different areas of study and development.
The Ames university announced in a news release that ISU will lead four projects and collaborate on four more for the Genesis Mission, an initiative created by the U.S. Department of Energy to use AI and accelerate research and innovation in areas like advanced manufacturing, biotechnology, nuclear energy and semiconductors.
The Department of Energy announced the awards Wednesday, according to the release. Department of Energy national laboratories, including the Ames National Laboratory, are also partners in the initiative, including corporations like Amazon Web Services, Dell Technologies, Google Public Sector, IBM, Microsoft, NVIDIA, OpenAI, Palantir and more.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“As an institution, we’re honored and excited to support the Department of Energy in its historic Genesis Mission,” said ISU Vice President for Research Peter Dorhout in the release. “The innovations our faculty are spearheading show how intelligent, data-rich tools can open new frontiers and accelerate discovery that delivers profound economic impact to our constituents and stakeholders throughout Iowa and around the nation.”
The four ISU-led projects span translational AI, statistics, agronomy and mechanical engineering within the university, and each project includes partners from other national labs. ISU’s Translational AI Center is leading a project to develop “decentralized, cooperating AI agents that share compact insights to generate stronger hypotheses.” The department of mechanical engineering will head the creation of an AI platform to model production system conditions to help successes found in labs to achieve large-scale production.
Statistics and computer science experts at ISU will work to build AI tools for predicting cloud behaviors with the goal of developing “an easy-to-use and real-time AI retrieval framework to enable atmospheric and energy science discovery,” the release stated.
ISU faculty are also working on projects led by the University of Kentucky, Battelle Memorial Institute-Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Auburn University. Computer engineering will also combine with mechanical engineering, translational AI and agronomy for a project aimed at developing an AI framework for linking plant genetics to performance and predicting biological traits.
According to a news release from the Department of Energy, the Genesis Mission announced a total of 278 awards that include 342 partner organizations and institutions, selected from “the largest response to a funding opportunity in DOE history.” The Genesis Mission initiative is “designed to double America’s scientific productivity,” the release stated.
“The extraordinary response to this Genesis Mission application process demonstrates that America’s scientific community is ready to reimagine how discovery happens,” said Under Secretary for Science Dr. Darío Gil in the Department of Energy news release. “Through the Genesis Mission, we are bringing together the nation’s leading researchers, institutions, and technology partners to build the next generation of scientific capability. We look forward to seeing these teams demonstrate new research workflows that accelerate discovery and reveal what is possible when AI and science advance together.”
