name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: ACLU sues Penn State Health over canceled gender-affirming care procedure
description: Plaintiffs say the procedure was scheduled at Penn State Health St. Joseph Medical Center but canceled for violating Catholic doctrine.
text:
Attorneys say hospital administrators "abruptly" canceled a gender-affirming procedure, saying it would violate Catholic doctrine. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)A new lawsuit accuses Penn State Health of violating a Pennsylvanian’s civil rights when a hospital “abruptly” canceled a gender-affirming procedure less than 24 hours before it was scheduled. 
Doctors for EJ Stiles, who is nonbinary and has a gender dysphoria diagnosis, recommended a mastectomy “to align their outward presentation with their gender identity,” according to the filing. 
The lawsuit states that administrators at Penn State Health St. Joseph Medical Center in Reading, Berks County, claimed such a procedure would violate Catholic doctrine. 
“I did everything right. I followed my doctors’ advice and trusted Penn State Health after they made me feel there was a place for patients like me. But being denied care so suddenly, simply because of who I am, was a devastating eye-opener,” Stiles said in a press release. 
“If an institution’s biases can so easily lock transgender and nonbinary patients out of care, then our health care system is operating with holes that need to be addressed. We all deserve equal access to health care, and to be served by institutions that honor their responsibility to treat us with dignity,” they continued.
2026.07.21-Stiles-Complaint-filed-no-exhibits
 
The American Civil Liberties Union of Pennsylvania and Patterson Belknap Webb & Tyler LLP filed the lawsuit on Stiles’ behalf in the Court of Common Pleas of Dauphin County Tuesday afternoon. Defendants include Penn State Health, Penn State Health St. Joseph and Pennsylvania State University. 
Though St. Joseph Medical Center identifies as a Catholic hospital, it is part of Penn State Health, a network of public hospitals. Plaintiffs argue that it violated the Pennsylvania Human Relations Act and Equal Amendment Act as well as “religious freedom provisions in the Pennsylvania Constitution by exercising state authority to enforce religious doctrine.”
States reject plan to block gender-affirming — what HHS calls 'sex rejecting' — care

“EJ Stiles has the right to access the same health care options as any other patient, and those decisions are between a patient and their doctor,” said Rich Ting, a senior staff attorney at the ACLU of Pennsylvania. “EJ’s surgery at a Penn State Health hospital being canceled based on religious beliefs is an outrageous and illegal action that put EJ’s health and well-being in jeopardy for months. If hospitals controlled by a public university can reap the benefits of state funds, then they must be bound by the same constitutional and equal protection mandates as all other state-funded institutions.” 
Penn State Health didn’t immediately return a request for comment.
Healthcare providers across the country have scaled back gender-affirming care, even in Democratic-led states, following the Trump administration’s threats to transgender healthcare. 
Just over half of states ban gender-affirming care for minors, and 29 states restrict sport participation — though such a prohibition hasn’t advanced in Pennsylvania.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Gov. Kay Ivey signs executive order creating commission to study screen-based learning
description: Gov. Kay Ivey Wednesday afternoon signed an executive order creating a commission dedicated to studying screen-based instruction. The Commission on Screen-Based Instruction will study the risks, usage and benefits of screen-based instruction in K-12 classrooms across the state. “Responsible use of classroom screen time is a top priority of my administration,[...]
text:
Gov. Kay Ivey delivers the State of the State Address at the Alabama State Capitol on Tuesday, Jan. 13, 2026, in Montgomery, Ala. On Wednesday, Ivey signed an executive order that created a commission to study screen-based instruction in K-12 classrooms across the state.(Estela Muñoz for Alabama Reflector)Gov. Kay Ivey Wednesday afternoon signed an executive order creating a commission dedicated to studying screen-based instruction.
The Commission on Screen-Based Instruction will study the risks, usage and benefits of screen-based instruction in K-12 classrooms across the state.
“Responsible use of classroom screen time is a top priority of my administration, and while we are already making a difference by passing two signature laws to address it, we can still do more,” Ivey said in a statement Wednesday afternoon. “Children’s overexposure to screens is a barrier to classroom learning and the acquisition of critical emotional and social skills. We must continue exploring the proper role of screen time in classrooms of all ages.”
During the 2026 regular session, Ivey signed HB 78, sponsored by Rep. Jeana Ross, R-Guntersville. The bill set screen time limits for children up to five years old in licensed child-care facilities. Ross also filed HB 584 which would have expanded the limits for all public school students, but the bill failed to pass before the Legislature adjourned in April.
Last year, Ivey signed the FOCUS Act into law which prohibits cell phones in classrooms and requires local boards of education to have internet safety policies.
The newly-created commission will submit a final report on its findings to Ivey, the Legislature and the Alabama State Department of Education by Dec. 1.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Governor announces change to survivor benefits investment for foster care youth
description: Gov. Kim Reynolds announced Wednesday that Iowa will change how the state manages Social Security survivor benefits for foster children with deceased relatives, allowing the child to retain this money for the future. The governor and Larry Johnson, principal deputy director of the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services, announced the change during a […[...]
text:
Gov. Kim Reynolds spoke on changes Iowa is making to Social Security survivor benefits for children in the state's foster care system in a news conference at Foster SQUAD in Ankeny July 22, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Gov. Kim Reynolds announced Wednesday that Iowa will change how the state manages Social Security survivor benefits for foster children with deceased relatives, allowing the child to retain this money for the future.
The governor and Larry Johnson, principal deputy director of the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services, announced the change during a news conference at Foster SQUAD, a foster care support organization in Ankeny. Reynolds said the change to survivor benefits comes as Iowa seeks to work on the national initiative led by First Lady Melania Trump to provide more support to foster families and help children in the system live independently and successfully as adults.
“I have directed Iowa Health and Human Services to preserve survivor benefits using the most appropriate account type for each eligible child, so that he or she may use the money in the future to support their life’s goals, whether that means pursuing an education, purchasing a home, or achieving financial stability. So this change aligns well with other financial support that already exists for young Iowans who transition out of the foster care system,” Reynolds said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Previously, federal survivor benefits for eligible children in foster care were put toward the cost of foster care. Under the new system, Reynolds said, funding will be placed in accounts that can then be returned to a family if the child is reunited with their family or if they are adopted or gain a permanent guardianship within 12 months of entering the foster system. If the child remains in foster care for more than a year, the federal dollars will be invested through a combination of the 529 education savings plan and an escrow account, or through an IAble account if eligible.
After the child leaves the foster care system, the accounts will be transferred to them, with the money available for spending on certain expenses like education, housing and transportation.
The change came at the request of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, the governor said, and builds on other work being done in Iowa to improve the state’s foster care system. Reynolds highlighted other efforts to improve foster care in Iowa, like the collaboration between Iowa HHS, the Administration for Children and Families and the Google Public Sector “to develop a new comprehensive child welfare information system,” as well as a law signed this year making changes to Iowa’s foster care training requirements.
Johnson said the investment for survivor benefits is “another step Iowa is taking to ensure eligible foster youth have every opportunity to succeed.”
“These efforts reflect the dedication of our child welfare workforce and the collaboration of partners who share a common goal: building a stronger system that helps children and families thrive,” Johnson said. “Protecting and investing survivor benefits reinforces this strategy by giving eligible youth additional resources to build sustainability, pursue education and employment, secure housing, and meet other essential needs as they move into adulthood.”
Social Security survivor benefits are only available to children in the foster care system if they are unmarried and their parent died when they were age 17 or younger, if they are ages 18 or 19 and still in school full time, and if they developed a disability at age 21 or younger. Survivor benefits are also paid in certain circumstances to married children, stepchildren, adopted children, grandchildren, and step-grandchildren, according to the Social Security Administration. Officials at the news conference said in Iowa, the change will impact a small percentage of children in the state’s foster care system.
Johnson said “the state will cover the cost of the care for foster care” that survivor benefits currently go toward.
“It is a small amount of children, but it will make a difference for them,” Johnson said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Sign here. And here and here too? Nomination form protocol challenge sparks debate.
description: The Rhode Island Board of Elections rejected an attempt by a Rhode Island independent gubernatorial candidate to oust one of his competitors from the November ballot. Yet the question of whether voters have to write their own names and addresses on candidate nomination papers remains unresolved. The elections panel denied Ken Block’s challenge to fellow […]
text:
Independent gubernatorial candidate Ken Block, left, tried unsuccessfully to get the Rhode Island Board of Elections to eliminate Jasjit 'Jay' Gotra from the Nov. 3 ballot because the nomination papers turned in by Gotra's campaign. (Photos by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)The Rhode Island Board of Elections rejected an attempt by a Rhode Island independent gubernatorial candidate to oust one of his competitors from the November ballot. Yet the question of whether voters have to write their own names and addresses on candidate nomination papers remains unresolved.
The elections panel denied Ken Block’s challenge to fellow independent gubernatorial candidate Jay Gotra’s nomination papers because Block did not complete the entire objection form. The board’s unanimous vote Monday affirms that both candidates handed in enough valid voter signatures to qualify for the November ballot. A third independent running for governor, C.D. Reynolds, is also on the ballot.
The decision sidesteps Block’s argument: that Gotra should be tossed because the handwriting on his nomination papers suggests that Gotra printed the name and address for each voter himself while voters signed their names. 
“When you look at the entire sheet, and it’s done in the same hand, it doesn’t give anybody confidence is all I’m saying,” John Pagliarini, an attorney for Block’s campaign, told the elections board Monday. “I am not saying any of these signatures are fraudulent. What I am saying is, it looks problematic.”



Quotation







When you look at the entire sheet, and it’s done in the same hand, it doesn’t give anybody confidence is all I’m saying. I am not saying any of these signatures are fraudulent. What I am saying is, it looks problematic. 


– John Pagliarini, an attorney for Ken Block’s gubernatorial campaign


Signature fraud headlined recent state election cycles, including in the 2023 special election for Rhode Island’s 1st Congressional District, where forged signatures, including names of dead people, were found on Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos’ nomination papers. Two campaign workers were later sentenced to probation for criminal charges for the fraud. Matos, who still qualified for the ballot, was never linked to the crime, but finished a distant fourth in the primary after being an early front-runner. 
In 2024, forged signatures were flagged on the nomination papers for Republican presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and the No Labels party, which petitioned for state party recognition with the intent of propping up a third-party presidential candidate. The bipartisan group never ended up backing a candidate and has since been removed as a state party. Four people who worked for the out-of-state vendor hired to collect signatures for No Labels were indicted by a state grand jury in October 2024 on various voter and signature fraud charges, Tim Rondeau, a spokesperson for the Rhode Island Attorney General’s office, confirmed Wednesday. Two of the four defendants in the case have been sentenced, while the other two are still wanted, Rondeau said. The sealed indictments were first reported by GoLocalProv on July 18. 
The scandals prompted changes to state laws, coupled with more training for election administrators and candidates on the signature-gathering and verification requirements. But no one had ever quibbled over who fills in the name and address on the papers before the signatures.
John Pagliarini, left, an attorney for Ken Block’s gubernatorial campaign, and independent candidate Jasjit ‘Jay’ Gotra, right, speak to the Rhode Island Board of Elections at its meeting on Monday, July 20, 2026. (Screenshot)
Open to interpretation 
State law does not offer much help.
“Every voter signing a nomination paper shall sign in person with his or her name, place of residence, and street number, as it appears on the voting list,” the 1947 statute reads.
To Block, the “shall” applies not just to the signature, but the penning of the name and address.
“It’s pretty black and white,” Block, 60, of Barrington, said in an interview Monday, before the board meeting.
But Ray Marcaccio, legal counsel for the election board, had a different take. Marcaccio pointed to a 1952 state Supreme Court order stemming from an election dispute over a Woonsocket candidate’s signatures. The court order allows for a “more generous interpretation” of state law in signature disputes, Marcaccio said. 
“So long as the signature is penned by the endorser, then the remaining, so long as it’s permitted, can be done by a third party,” Marcaccio said.
Pagliarini maintained that the appearance of “hundreds” of signatures on Gotra’s nomination papers bearing the same handwriting for voters’ names and addresses was problematic. He also named two, more recent Supreme Court decisions as evidence to support a stricter conformance to the state law on signature gathering. 
“If you want a lesser approach, then the board should recommend to the General Assembly the need for clarity,” Pagliarini said. “This is such a blind spot in election law. Your guidance is needed.”
No guidance was given Monday. 
Instead, the board rejected the challenge because Pagliarini did not list every single name and signature being disputed on the objection letter, instead writing “form is not applicable” on the space given on his objection letter. The objection included 21 sheets from Gotra’s nomination papers as examples of what Pagliarini claimed were “hundreds” of names and addresses filled out by someone other than the voter. 
To write out every single name and line in question would be “impractical,” Pagliarini said, noting the 24-hour turnaround between when nomination papers were made available and when challenges were due to the Rhode Island Department of State. 
Gotra seized upon the technical error as reason to dismiss the complaint, pointing out the perceived hypocrisy in Block’s challenge about rules, while not following the rules himself.
The board ultimately agreed that it could not take on the responsibility of identifying which of the 1,538 names Gotra submitted — 1,069 of which were already approved after a vetting by local election administrators — included names and addresses written by someone other than the signatory.
Seeking clarity 
Several board members said they wanted to pursue more clarity on the issue in a future meeting.
“I think we need to revisit this and include this as part of our guidance,” Randy Jackvony, board member, said during the meeting. “People don’t run for office every day. We need to help them understand, to do their best to follow the rules.”
Gotra, owner of a now-defunct solar sales company who remains under investigation by the AG’s office for predatory and deceptive sales tactics, said that he did not write voters’ names and addresses on his papers, except for a handful of “very elderly” voters to help them. 
“My interpretation of the rules is very simple: when a person came up to sign the document, and there was a husband and wife, the husband would come up and sign the document, write his name, write his wife’s name and address and say ‘honey can you sign it,’” Gotra said. “I just presumed I needed to make sure they had to sign, and the signature had to match.”
Gotra said he collected most of the signatures himself, with a regular booth outside the food court in the Warwick Mall and another day stationed outside the Rhode Island DMV in Cranston. A first-time candidate, Gotra, 44, of East Greenwich, praised the process and state agencies that oversee elections for clear instructions for candidates. 
“I’ve dealt with a lot of state agencies in many ways,” Gotra said. “I am so impressed and so amazed by our elections process. How welcoming they are. The instructions were clear. It was beautiful and perfect.”
Block, who has run for governor twice before under different parties, said the opposite: that there were too many cumbersome and convoluted technical requirements for candidates to run for office.
“It’s a do-or-die process, and if you don’t do one thing right, you’re dead,” Block said.
If elected governor, Block said he would push for legislation clarifying the signature gathering process, and for separate policies extending the amount of time for candidates to submit challenges to nomination papers. 
“Our compressed calendar is a recipe for problems,” agreed John Marion, executive director for Common Cause Rhode Island. “There are many problems that could be alleviated if our election calendar was extended.”
Rhode Island Secretary of State Gregg Amore has pushed lawmakers to change the state elections calendar to allow more time and relieve pressure during various stages of the state election cycle. But the effort has fallen flat; the 2026 companion bills failed to advance out of either chamber, without even a preliminary hearing on the Senate side.
Another Amore initiative, to create an online signature portal for nomination papers to be signed and vetted, also stalled in the Senate committee this year despite passing in the House. 
The elections board meets again at 1:30 p.m. Thursday to review challenges to the nomination papers for Arlette Hidalgo, a Democratic candidate for state representative in District 12; Ana Borges, an independent Pawtucket mayoral candidate; and two Democrats running forPawtucket School Committee. 
The primary is Wednesday, Sept. 9, with a Nov. 3 general election. Early voting for the primary begins on Aug. 20.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Judge denies motion to block a federal judge from starting as UK dean
description: A federal judge denied a motion to temporarily prevent a federal judge from starting as the next dean of the University of Kentucky College of Law.  Last week, professor Ramsi Woodcock filed a lawsuit against the incoming dean, Judge Gregory Van Tatenhove, as well as UK President Eli Capilouto, Provost Robert DiPaola and the university. […]
text:
UK Provost Robert DiPaola, left, and incoming Law dean Judge Gregory Van Tatenhove, right, speak to reporters. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)A federal judge denied a motion to temporarily prevent a federal judge from starting as the next dean of the University of Kentucky College of Law. 
Last week, professor Ramsi Woodcock filed a lawsuit against the incoming dean, Judge Gregory Van Tatenhove, as well as UK President Eli Capilouto, Provost Robert DiPaola and the university. Among Woodcock’s requests were asking the court to block Van Tatenhove from becoming dean of the law school and preventing UK administrators from appointing or reappointing a dean over the objection of a majority of faculty. 
The case had been originally filed in the U.S. Eastern Kentucky District Court, but has since moved to the Western District, as Van Tatenhove served in the Eastern District. District Judge Benjamin J. Beaton, of the U.S. Western District of Kentucky, is now presiding over the case. 
Beaton denied a motion for a temporary restraining order from Woodcock. Joe Childers, who is representing Woodcock, said he will now seek a preliminary injunction. 
UK announced Van Tatenhove, who was appointed to the bench by Republican President George W. Bush, as the next dean of the college earlier this year, but the choice has been met with criticism. 
Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear blasted UK administration this spring for the choice, saying he was “losing confidence and growing increasingly concerned” with the management of the state’s flagship institution. Associate deans at the law school wrote a February email to DiPaola that faculty felt Van Tatenhove was an “unacceptable” candidate as he lacked “qualifications to be granted tenure,” which could risk the school’s accreditation with the American Bar Association. 
Beshear renewed his questions about Van Tatenhove’s appointment during a Thursday press conference, as well as his disapproval over a  $3.2 million payout to retiring UK Director Mitch Barnhart. 
UK spokesperson Jay Blanton previously said Van Tatenhove was to start as the law dean on Monday. 
“We are pleased that Dean Van Tatenhove is here at UK and excited about the outstanding leadership he will provide for the Rosenberg College of Law,” Blanton said Wednesday.

name: WyoFile
title: Forest Service OKs cattle in Wyoming allotments with history of grizzly conflict
description:
The tracts in northwest Wyoming were retired from sheep grazing a decade ago via a buyout deal with conservationists. Environmental advocates have asked the Bridger-Teton National Forest to reconsider.
The post Forest Service OKs cattle in Wyoming allotments with history of grizzly conflict appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Cattle growers can use a roughly 48-square-mile swath of the Gros Ventre Range this summer that was retired from sheep grazing a decade ago, and rangeland watchdogs are raising questions about the process federal land managers used to authorize the restocking.
Controversy over the Bridger-Teton National Forest’s decision to temporarily allow cattle stocking in four allotments known collectively as the Elk Ridge complex is heightened by a 2016 voluntary buyout deal struck to protect bighorn sheep in the area. Woolgrower Mary Thoman agreed to waive her permit to graze sheep in the complex in exchange for an undisclosed sum in a deal that was funded by the Wyoming Wild Sheep Foundation, Sagebrush Habitat Conservation Fund and other groups. Many of those involved assumed that deal effectively withdrew the allotments from all grazing, not just sheep. Then about five years ago, cattlemen led an effort to stock domestic cows and calves there instead. The Bridger-Teton never completed its analysis of that proposal and the allotments have remained vacant of sheep and cattle ever since.

Wyoming Game and Fish Department large carnivore biologist Zach Turnbull probes a dead cow in July 2020, looking for evidence of carnivore bites. (Angus M. Thuermer, Jr./WyoFile)

Now, up to 650 cattle have been temporarily approved to run on the allotments in 2026 and 2027. Explaining the shift, Bridger-Teton Jackson District Ranger Chad Hudson pointed to a 2025 wildfire that raged through adjacent allotments used by the Upper Green River Cattlemen’s Association.
“The Dollar Lake fire did severely impact about 15,000 acres of the Upper Green River Rangeland management area,” Hudson told WyoFile. “The temporary use of the Elk Ridge allotments provides a critical short-term solution to a fire-related forest deficit and …  supports the recovery of the fire-damaged area.” 
The four grazing areas in question — the Elk Ridge, Rock Creek, Lime Creek, and Tosi allotments — total about 31,000 acres. They’re located about 30 miles southeast of Jackson, and the westernmost acres, in the Tosi Creek drainage, include portions of the Gros Ventre Wilderness. Others farther east are in the Green River drainage.
The authorization for the Upper Green River Cattlemen’s Association to run its cattle in the area is briefly described in the Bridger-Teton’s “Annual Operating Instructions” for its Pinedale Ranger District, which states that an unspecified number of livestock would be allowed to graze there “if necessary.” 
“A small group of people came up with this concept,” Hudson said, “to use adjacent acres to provide adequate forage, but also rest those burnt acres.” 
Parties that generated the idea include the Sublette County Conservation District, Wyoming Game and Fish Department, The Nature Conservancy and the Upper Green River Cattlemen’s Association, Hudson said. 
Some livestock industry watchdogs aren’t pleased with the arrangement. 
‘Beyond flimsy’ rationale
Bondurant resident John Carter, who runs the Yellowstone to Uintas Connection, formally asked Bridger-Teton leadership in a July 5 letter to reconsider its approval of cattle grazing at the Elk Ridge complex, and to release a plethora of related documents. 
“This request is not based merely upon disagreement with the decision to authorize grazing,” Carter wrote. “Rather, it arises because the administrative history of these allotments, the Forest Service’s own environmental analyses, and the agency’s current monitoring information raise significant questions regarding the basis for authorizing livestock grazing after nearly a decade of vacancy.” 
Upper Green resident Jonathan Ratner doesn’t buy that the Dollar Lake Fire was the true reason for the restocking. The blaze, which nearly burned down his house, didn’t burn the non-forested meadows and shrublands used by cattle, he said. 
The Bridger-Teton National Forest released this photograph of the early stages of the Dollar Lake Fire showing an air tanker dropping retardant in an effort to control the blaze. (Bridger-Teton National Forest)
“Their rationale is beyond flimsy,” said Ratner, a former Bridger-Teton rangeland scientist who’s a longtime critic of public lands grazing. “The federal government is not allowed to act arbitrarily and capriciously, and they’ve manufactured rationale that can’t withstand even the slightest examination.” 
Ratner and Carter argue that the public was improperly cut out of decisionmaking and that federal land managers haven’t met their legal obligations. And they also take issue with Bridger-Teton’s reliance on a 1978 environmental assessment to temporarily allow cattle on the allotments 48 years later. Additionally, the duo say the Forest Service misrepresented its plan in a review conducted to comply with the Endangered Species Act. 
That review, known as a biological assessment, found the restocking would “not be expected to have any additional impacts to grizzly bears” — a conclusion that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service agreed with in a May letter. 
“They concurred,” Hudson said. “Given the proximity, it’s essentially the same bears and the same cows” as the previous grazing arrangement.
The Elk Ridge complex is sandwiched between allotments where the Upper Green River Cattlemen’s Association runs cows each summer after driving its herds up the Green River Drift. For over a dozen years, the area has seen a remarkable concentration of grizzly bear-cattle conflict. Despite efforts to diminish depredations, the conflicts have continued to grow more common, often with lethal outcomes for both species. Between 2010 and 2024, there were 964 “confirmed conflicts” on the Upper Green allotments and 50 grizzly bears killed by wildlife managers as a result, according to Fish and Wildlife Service data. 




Click to enlarge: The Bridger-Teton National Forest compiled this map showing the Elk Ridge complex allotments in relation to adjacent Upper Green allotments during an Endangered Species Act compliance process because the area is a hotbed for conflicts with “threatened” grizzly bears. (U.S. Forest Service)
Conservation groups’ bought out the Elk Ridge sheep allotments mostly to protect bighorn sheep, not grizzlies: The Whiskey Mountain and Jackson herds had a “high risk of interaction,” and that interspecies mingling can cause catastrophic diseases in the wild sheep. But the Forest Service noted in a 2016 letter to the bought-out permittee that there’d been “significant predation from both grizzly bears and wolves” and that “recurrent scatter events associated with predation continue.” 
For that reason, the Forest Service officials stated they “would not restock these allotments with domestic sheep” and that additional National Environmental Policy Act analysis “would be necessary” before restocking cattle. 
EIS coming soon
Although the Forest Service didn’t complete the NEPA review it started in 2021, Hudson anticipates a new analysis soon. 
“We are, most likely, going to look at more of a permanent option and kick off an [environmental impact statement] this fall,” Hudson said. “But as far as this temporary authorization, if needed, we relied on [the 1978] environmental documents.” 
Sagebrush Habitat Conservation Fund Vice President Jon Marvel, who contributed to the 2016 buyout, said that he’s still waiting to see the authorization. 
“They haven’t supplied a copy of any document that actually authorizes this temporary two-year use,” Marvel said. “It’s illegal, let’s get that straight.” 
Marvel and others who were involved in the 2016 buyout were not part of discussions as the Bridger-Teton assessed the temporary restocking. Wyoming Wild Sheep Foundation executive director Katie Cheesbrough learned that cattle could move back onto the allotments come Aug. 15 when she took WyoFile’s call.
“We’re not necessarily upset with the thought of cattle being restocked,” Cheesbrough said. 
Domestic sheep bail out of a truck and onto Jim Magagna’s leased pastureland in July 2023. In the background, Kristy Wardell, who runs the Thoman Ranch’s sheep operation, wields a prod to encourage the stubborn sheep to leave the vehicles. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
But she wondered what the restocking meant for the future effectiveness of  grazing allotment buyouts, which are a conservation tactic the Wyoming Wild Sheep Foundation has heavily relied on historically. Between the 1990s and 2017, her organization put over $300,000 into “quite a few” buyouts. 
“It really begs the question: Is this tool viable anymore?” Cheesbrough asked.
Cheesbrough also shared concerns about the Forest Service process, and broader changes to restocking procedures under the Trump administration that diminish the public’s ability to weigh in. 
“There’s not that opportunity to go through the NEPA process and have public comment and analyze what the proposal is,” Cheesbrough said. “We would be interested to look at the analysis, and comment. I do anticipate engaging with it, if we are allowed to.” 
The U.S. Department of Agriculture has directed national forests to expand access to and prioritize permitting vacant and closed grazing allotments. Trump administration undersecretary Michael Boren told Forest Service line officers in a June 12 memo that they should “utilize emergency authorities” to “expedite authorization of livestock use.” 
Hudson, the Jackson District Ranger, said that the restocking is “consistent with the current administration’s agenda and desire to increase access for our [livestock] producers.” But the federal directives weren’t the driving force, he added. 
“It’s really a reaction to the Dollar Lake Fire,” Hudson said. “The analysis that we’ll do starting this fall is being a little bit more proactive, too.” 
Authorizing long-term cattle grazing in the Elk Ridge complex would give cattle ranchers “options when and if their allotments are impacted” by future wildfires, he said. 
Upper Green River Cattlemen’s Association President Coke Landers told WyoFile he was unavailable for an interview this week. Although Wyoming Stock Growers Association lobbyist Jim Magagna drove earlier efforts to restock vacant Bridger-Teton allotments, he said he wasn’t particularly engaged in recent changes to the Elk Ridge complex. 
Still, Magagna was pleased with and defended Bridger-Teton’s decision.
“Nobody’s asking for more head of livestock out there,” Magagna said. “They’re just asking for more land to be available, and it gives the permittee more flexibility.”
“It seems like it’s a win-win for everyone,” he added.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A state Senate primary could bring major changes to CT education
description: Sen. Douglas McCrory is facing a three-way primary next month that could have a major impact on K-12 education in Connecticut.
text:
Hartford-based Democratic Sen. Douglas McCrory is facing a three-way primary next month that could have a major impact on K-12 education in Connecticut.
McCrory is the Senate co-chair of the Education Committee, making him a leading voice on which education bills are taken up and passed along to the full General Assembly. 
His two Democratic challengers are also deeply involved in education: Rep. Maryam Khan of Windsor led the passage of significant special education reforms last year and also sits on the Education Committee, while Ayana Taylor serves as the president of the Windsor Board of Education.
McCrory, a veteran legislator who is the subject of an ongoing federal criminal investigation, lost the Democratic nomination to Khan in the spring, but voters will have the final say on who advances to the general election. Early voting begins Aug. 3, and primary Election Day is Aug. 11.
CT Mirror spoke with all three candidates about how they would approach some of the most pressing issues in K-12 education in Connecticut. All three candidates agreed that the state needs to do more to support under-resourced schools and ensure every child has access to a quality education, but they differed, sometimes sharply, in how they propose to get there. 
Here’s what they had to say.

Maryam Khan (left) and Ayana Taylor (center) talk after the first round of voting during the Democratic convention for the state’s 2nd Senate District. Both Khan and Taylor are challenging Sen. Doug McCrory for the senate seat covering Hartford, Bloomfield and Windsor.  Credit: Andrew Brown / CT Mirror

Doug McCrory
McCrory said his top education priority is “making sure all our children have access to a quality education, regardless of where they live … and providing them choices. Public school choices.” 
That includes addressing how Connecticut funds its schools, which just about everyone agrees needs to change. Public schools in Connecticut rely heavily on local property wealth to cover rising costs, meaning those in under-resourced areas often struggle to provide critical services and staff up classrooms.
McCrory said he wants to “level the playing field” by putting state resources into the places that need more support. That includes fixing the Education Cost Sharing grant, Connecticut’s main state funding system and the focus of a state commission studying school financing. Critics argue the formula drastically underestimates how much money schools need from the state, forcing some districts to repeatedly make deep cuts to stay solvent.
But McCrory said he doesn’t think pumping more dollars into ECS will fix the problem on its own. He said the state also needs to “have a harder look” at outcomes.
If low-income students remain concentrated in specific districts, McCrory said, “there’s no data that says, ‘Just pour and pour money in it, and you’re gonna get better outcomes.’”
The real solution, McCrory said, is to give kids from under-resourced communities the opportunity to study with kids from more affluent communities.
“The research shows that, you place them in environments where they’re around other children who are not in poor communities, they’ll do better,” McCrory said.
This is where the longstanding issue of segregation comes into play. A recent study found Connecticut is one of the most economically and racially segregated states in the U.S. The authors of the study argued this high segregation is highly detrimental to students. McCrory concurred.
“We have segregated outcomes when it comes to our children in this state of Connecticut,” he said.

Sen. Doug McCrory, D-Hartford, poses for a photo. Credit: Courtesy / McCrory for Senate 2026

McCrory’s own Senate district has been the staging ground for one of Connecticut’s biggest segregation fights: Sheff v. O’Neill. The Sheff plaintiffs argued Hartford students lacked educational opportunities because they were effectively segregated from their wealthier suburban peers. The state Supreme Court agreed, leading to the creation of a school choice program to voluntarily integrate students from Hartford (predominantly Black and Latino) and the surrounding towns (predominantly white).
However, while Sheff arguably created new opportunities for many students, critics have argued it hasn’t resolved the underlying inequities at play and has siphoned dollars from Hartford Public Schools. Today, the district faces a multimillion-dollar deficit.
“I think the concept behind Sheff was a good concept. The unfortunate thing is, it was voluntary,” McCrory said. He added that demographic changes in the state have made the underlying concept “a little more problematic.”
“I think we have to move on from Sheff and come up with alternative solutions to … integrate our schools,” McCrory said. “We have to go Sheff level 2 and have a conversation about what’s really working and what our parents really need.”
The root of Connecticut’s segregation, McCrory said, is housing. Building affordable housing in more affluent communities would in theory reduce segregation and give more lower-income families access to quality schools; however, McCrory said he’s skeptical the state can actually build enough, at least in the near future.
Ultimately, McCrory came back to where he started: putting more resources into struggling schools — but doing it in a creative or innovative way. 
His ideas included boosting salaries for teachers who work in under-resourced districts; creating more opportunities for field trips and other activities outside the typical school day; encouraging districts to offer Saturday school programs run by community members; and expanding access to charter and magnet schools. 
McCrory was the only candidate to offer full-throated support for Connecticut’s school choice programming. Municipal or neighborhood schools lose a portion of their state funding whenever a student enrolls in a choice program (like a charter or magnet school), which critics say puts undue strain on local districts. But McCrory pushed back on that.
“That’s not true, because we have different funding mechanisms for charter schools, magnet schools and our traditional public schools,” McCrory said.
Here’s a rough example: Say Hartford gets $11,000 per student from the state. A student enrolls in a magnet school, and $4,500 follows them. That means Hartford still receives $6,500 — “for a child they’re not even educating,” McCrory said.
“No one loses,” he added.
Special education is another issue expected to see heightened attention during next year’s legislative session. On that topic, McCrory said his first concern is the rapid rise in the number of students being tagged with disabilities in Connecticut. The number of special education students has grown despite an overall decline in student enrollment in the last 20 years, and he wants to know why.
“And my concern is, why are there such a disproportionate number of young men of color labeled special ed?” McCrory said.
As the number of children receiving special education services has increased, the ability of schools to provide those services has come under increasing strain. Some schools struggle to afford the necessary paraeducators and teachers, even though federal law requires them to meet each student’s needs.
Asked what he thinks the solution to that might be, McCrory suggested collaboration between school districts could help. 
“If these communities can come together and work in collaboration, they can build capacity,” he said. For example, multiple smaller districts could pool resources to share a speech pathologist.
In January, a report to the State Department of Education found problems in how schools are held accountable for the special education services they provide. In theory, parents can file complaints against schools they feel are not handling their children appropriately, but those options are often ineffective or hard to access. Some schools end up shifting the burden back onto parents: For example, it’s not unheard of for schools to call a parent multiple times a week to have a disruptive child picked up early.
When asked about this practice, McCrory described it as “unacceptable” and basically a form of harassment.
“That child may need a one-to-one para, you know, and this district might not want to pay for it, right? So it comes down to a finance, a funding thing,” McCrory said.
He said schools need to follow students’ IEPs and the state needs to provide resources so districts can hire the appropriate staff. To that end, he voiced support for the SEED grant, which funds in-district special education services and which Khan helped pass into law last year. However, McCrory said, he wished the SEED grant included funding for inter-district programming. Right now, the money only goes toward individual districts.
Literacy is another top-of-mind issue for many in Connecticut. The state passed major literacy reform in 2023, and some schools have reported improved reading scores in the years following. But McCrory said he’s nowhere near satisfied as a large proportion of the state’s students remain far behind.
Reducing the number of students per classroom, especially in earlier grades, would help, McCrory said. He also wants the state to look into how colleges and universities are preparing teachers themselves.
“A lot of people that’s coming out of our schools of education are not properly prepared to teach literacy, and we have to change the way we do that,” McCrory said.
McCrory leaned into his record to argue why he deserves another round representing the 2nd Senate district. He has the most legislative experience of the three candidates, having been elected state representative in 2004 and state senator in 2017. 
“I know what can get passed, and I know what won’t get passed,” McCrory said.
And he touted his decades of experience in education — he has worked as both a teacher and administrator and is now employed by the Capitol Region Education Council, or CREC, which provides public school choice options to students in the greater Hartford area.
Among the legislative achievements he’s most proud of are increasing the diversity of Connecticut’s teachers, which also improves outcomes for students; instituting a requirement that schools teach financial literacy; adding Black and Latino studies as a required subject; and the creation of a $10,000-a-year scholarship for aspiring educators.
But there is a shadow hanging over McCrory this election: an FBI investigation into how the senator directed the Blue Hills Civic Association to send state taxpayer money to various other organizations, some run by close associates. A CT Mirror investigation found McCrory held sway over the nonprofit until its abrupt and shocking collapse in April 2025.
Despite the ongoing federal investigation, however, neither of McCrory’s opponents opted to mention the scandal when discussing why they were running against him. McCrory himself said it hasn’t come up when he’s out knocking on doors, either. And he pointed to the passage this year of a bill to regulate earmarks, which he said he supported “100%.” The bill was widely seen as a response to the investigation.
“I just want to be clear: Douglas McCrory doesn’t write checks,” McCrory said.
Maryam Khan
Khan said she thinks the top priority for education in Connecticut right now has to be special education.
“It’s the No. 1 issue that has come up as being the biggest cost driver, the largest shortage area,” Khan said.
And, she added, “I know we’ve identified reading as a big concern, so I would say both of those.”

State Rep. Maryam Khan, D-Windsor, speaks with reporters after winning the Democratic endorsement in the August 2026 primary for the 2nd Senate District. Credit: Andrew Brown / CT Mirror

Special education costs are an issue Khan already knows well. In 2025 — her third year as a legislator — she helped lead the passage of HB 5001, a bill focused on easing special education costs for districts. The bill created the SEED grant, which funds schools’ in-house special education services, and capped the rates providers can charge schools for outplaced students. That latter change is something Khan expects will come under pressure during next year’s legislative session.
“There is going to be a push by the private special ed providers to try to remove it,” Khan said. “It’s something that we really have to grip onto.”
At least one prominent Connecticut special education advocate has criticized the rate setting portion of the bill, but Khan maintained it was an important provision.
“The state has to have a system in which they set rates so that districts are protected, because public education relies on tax dollars, and if you don’t have the money, they will have to cut something,” Khan said.
Outplacement costs tend to be very high, but until the passage of 2025’s HB 5001, those were the only special education costs for which the state would reimburse public schools. Khan said that led districts to favor outplacement over in-house services, a trend she’d like to change.
Funding more special education resources for districts themselves, she said, would not just save money on outplacements but also “use the money more appropriately” given that kids learn better closer to home.
Asked about school compliance — and the parents getting frequent calls from schools to pick up their children early — Khan suggested the issue is part of something broader.
“This is behavioral issues that are going up with students,” Khan said. “Students are having more behavioral needs, and districts are not able to provide what students need, and so then they’re calling parents for this.”
Part of the solution, Khan said, is to reconsider “what education needs to look like in 2026.”

Rep. Maryam Khan, D-Windsor, speaks at a press conference outside the Parker Memorial Community Center on May 15, 2026. Credit: Theo Peck-Suzuki / CT Mirror

“Children are not required in their daily life to have as much physical activity as they would have maybe like 30, 40 years ago, when they were still helping out at home more,” Khan said. “So you have children that have a lot of physical energy and no way to release it.”
Revamping classrooms to include less sitting and listening to lectures would help with that, Khan said. The state can help incentivize that process, she said, through initiatives like a competitive grant for a pilot program.
For the students with more acute behavioral needs, Khan said, the state needs to ensure schools can hire enough social workers.
“You’ll see a lot of schools with like 600 students and one social worker,” Khan said. 
“If you have more resources in terms of social workers that are able to work with students on behavioral issues, on emotional issues, on just emotional regulation, then those students can actually stay in school,” Khan said.
To that end, she’d like to see the SEED grant — the other part of HB 5001 — increase. Fully funded, the grant would provide around $180 million, but legislators have only funded a fraction of that.
Speaking of school funding more generally, Khan said she thinks Connecticut has to start “incentivizing regionalizing to some degree.”
“That doesn’t necessarily mean regionalizing schools but regionalizing services,” she explained. Like McCrory, she said she supported encouraging districts to partner for shared services. Some districts do so already, Khan said, but she’d like to see the state incentivize it more.
Khan said she had hoped to bring forward legislation allowing districts to pool their SEED money in the most recent legislative session — thereby resolving the very issue McCrory brought up with the SEED grant — but it wasn’t taken up by the Education Committee.
In a sharp divergence from McCrory, Khan said she feels the Education Committee’s focus on expanding school choice is one of the main reasons the state has yet to address the problems in its funding system.
“I don’t believe [expanding school choice] is going to solve the problem. I think it creates more inequities within our current system, but I feel like a lot of the conversations at the state level in the legislature revolve around school choice,” Khan said.
She pushed back on McCrory’s assertion that municipal schools don’t really lose money when students enroll in choice programs.
If “10 children leave Hartford Public Schools, they’re leaving from 10 different schools. You’re not going to be able to cut a teacher. You’re not going to be able to cut any resources. You’re not saving any money,” Khan said. But the district still has to pay tuition for all 10 of those students.
Ultimately, Khan said, “the state creates these choice programs, and I think the state needs to then fund them.”
That’s not her only concern with choice programs, either. Khan also criticized what she sees as a lack of oversight. Municipal schools have boards of education that serve under the town’s elected government, which is ultimately accountable to local voters. Those same local governments, however, have little to no authority over choice schools. The state makes the decision on which new schools are approved.
“The town’s can’t do anything … They [choice schools] self-govern,” Khan said.
She said the leadership on the Education Committee — which includes McCrory — takes a view of school choice that is out of step with most parents.
“I have never once heard a parent say to me, ‘I would like more choice opportunities for my child,’” Khan said. “Every single time, it’s, ‘Why is it that my child has to go out of the city? Why does my child have to get on a bus at five a.m. … so that they can get good reading education?”
That, she said, is what motivated her to challenge McCrory for his Senate seat.
“Unfortunately, it feels like, as an educator, that we are in the minority party on that committee because of the constant push to just privatize education or create more school choice opportunities,” Khan said.
“Privatizing education” tends to evoke conversations around private school vouchers, which Connecticut does not have. However, Khan said, privatization here happens in other ways. For example: a reading program or assessment developed by a private company that the Education Committee ends up mandating schools to adopt.
“No district has said, ‘Hey, … we need help teaching reading because we don’t know what to teach,” Khan said. And yet, she said, that new program becomes a required reading intervention.
As an example, she pointed to 2023’s Right to Read legislation, which mandated schools adopt specific science of reading-aligned curricula. Khan said she agrees with the push to align reading instruction with the science of reading, but she expressed skepticism that mandating schools drop their existing curricula to buy specific state-sanctioned programs had worked out.
“We’ve now implemented [Right to Read] for about four years, so by that logic, we should have different reading scores now, and we have not seen a shift,” Khan said. “But [those new programs] cost Connecticut schools millions of dollars to purchase on their own. The state did not help them.”
As a result, Khan said, some districts ended up cutting teaching positions to finance the new curricula.
She added, “If you’re making districts buy private programs based on private lobbyists that have come to lobby your legislature, that is still privatization.”
(Some districts, such as New Haven, have reported improved reading scores in lower grades after Right to Read, but the number of students reading below grade level remains high.)
Khan said Right to Read’s “blanket” approach didn’t work well in a state where literacy rates vary drastically from one district to another.
“So, if certain districts have lower rates of reading scores, and we know that they also have, let’s just say, an absence of early childhood [education] in that district, then the answer is not ‘make them buy new curriculum.’ The answer is how can we increase early literacy in this district,” Khan said.
When asked about segregation, Khan turned toward her own experience growing up as an immigrant in New York. Most of her classmates were also immigrants from low-income families, but because the school was well-resourced and boasted strong supports for multilingual learners, Khan said, she and her siblings all learned to read on time — even though their parents couldn’t help. Her father was a laborer; today, all four of his children own their own homes.
Khan’s takeaway: “Even with the economic and racial segregation, you can still have good outcomes.”
The problem in Connecticut, she said, is that the outcomes aren’t good. And that, she suggested, is about resources.
She pointed to Sheff as an example.
“What the state did to address [Sheff] is to try to solve the segregation issue, but [it] never solved the resources issue,” Khan said. “So now Hartford Public Schools has less ability to actually make an impact than it did when that case was even brought.”
Ayana Taylor
Taylor said her top education priority is funding, an issue she said is top of mind for her as both a member of the Windsor Board of Education and a mother of a child with autism whose services she had to fight for. She highlighted the cost of special education, the rising costs for schools in general and the problems with the ECS formula as all being “top of mind.”

Ayana Taylor, the chairwoman of Windsor’s Board of Education, talks with her supporters before the Democratic convention for the state’s 2nd Senate District. Taylor is challenging state Sen. Doug McCrory, D-Hartford, for the second election cycle in a row.  Credit: Andrew Brown / CT Mirror

But, she said, “you have to crawl before we walk.”
“It’s not a quick snap of the finger to say, ‘OK, how do we fund all this?’ Because everything’s going to come back to taxpayers,” she said.
She aligned with McCrory and Khan on schools sharing resources, especially for special education needs like speech pathologists.
“It saves taxpayers money, expands opportunities for students,” she said.
She also said she likes the idea of schools sharing programming. As an example, she pointed to her cousin, a Windsor student who attended an agricultural program at Glastonbury and ultimately became a veterinarian. That agricultural program wasn’t something Windsor itself could offer, but because the districts collaborated, students from both benefited. 
A state senator, Taylor said, could “be advocating for dollars for a data dive, or to have consultation to see what something like that could look like.”
At the same time, Taylor expressed some criticism of Connecticut’s choice programs, though she said repeatedly that she supports families having options.
“Being smart about investing in our community schools. … You know, another elephant that’s in the room, the choice programs and students going all over the place,” Taylor said.
She later said, “I am seeing oftentimes more schools than we have kids to go to them. That’s what I’m seeing.”

Windsor Board of Education President Ayana Taylor poses for a campaign photo. Credit: Courtesy / Ayana for State Senate

Taylor also asserted that neighborhood schools do, in fact, lose money to choice programs. She pointed to Hartford as an example.
“What Hartford found is that as students were leaving … and going to CREC or magnet or charter, money follows the child. And so what [that] leaves behind is half-empty schools and classrooms, and we still have to pay the overhead as taxpayers,” Taylor said.
And she noted that it costs money to bus kids to choice schools, which may be farther away than their neighborhood school. 
“When you’re thinking about going back to investing properly in our neighborhood schools … there’s a cost savings there,” Taylor said.
Taylor also criticized how the state calculates the cost to districts to educate students. Right now, the ECS formula gives every student the same starting “cost,” then runs that number through a complex array of weights to arrive at a final funding amount. Taylor suggested the process is missing the mark.
“The cost to educate my daughter … and my son are two different numbers,” she said.
“I think we really need to be specific about the data, and really have a partnership and be in collaboration with our towns and cities to ask what they need … so that the state isn’t just” making things up, Taylor said.
Bringing a new degree of collaboration to the state legislature was a major part of how Taylor described her candidacy.
“It’s a lot of silo work in education, if you can imagine. And what happens when you continue to work in silos for so long, you don’t realize that, ‘Oh, we’re actually all fighting for the same things,’” Taylor said.
She said she’s beginning to see that kind of collaborative energy emerge between school boards, including the one she leads, and she’d like to bring it to the statehouse.
“Being part of conversations and being in coalition prior to session time,” Taylor said. “As soon as the school year starts, those are the times for your town halls. … Not waiting until session when you’re overwhelmed by everything coming at you.”
This is the second time Taylor has primaried McCrory. She said her decision to run for the state Senate grew out of her experiences as a helper and leader in the community — the kind of person people reach out to when they need an answer to just about any kind of question.
“People are asking for change. I am reliable. People call me … I respond, I’m accessible, and so I just became a person, an advocate, for the people,” Taylor said.
When it comes to segregation, Taylor said, her top priority is ensuring the quality of a child’s education doesn’t depend on where they live. Like McCrory, she expressed concerns that marginalized students avoid the teaching profession.
“The disparities of the amount of teachers that are coming into the profession are … the diversity is still lacking,” Taylor said.
When asked about Sheff, Taylor turned back to neighborhood schools.
“If our community schools, if all schools were equitably funded … there would be no Sheff vs. O’Neill,” she said.
Taylor did say she thinks “the choice should be there for parents” to send their kids to a Sheff school instead of a neighborhood district. But she reiterated that she wants more emphasis put onto bringing the latter “up to snuff.”
“We, first things first, need to find out, why aren’t we equitably funding all of our schools?” she reiterated.
Taylor said it’s no surprise that many students opted to leave Hartford Public Schools when new choice programs came about.
“If your child’s neighborhood school is leaking … it would make sense that parents would want to go to the shiny new school,” Taylor said. “I think that we lose something by kiddos not going to school with the neighborhood friends, the lack of community built.”
When it comes to special education, Taylor said, one of her big concerns is that many parents won’t even discuss their children’s needs out of shame. 
“There’s a systemic barrier there with certain communities culturally,” Taylor said. “So kiddos are going so long without being diagnosed … for fear of diagnoses.”
This, Taylor said, leads people ultimately into “going along to get along.” Sometimes, she said, that looks like parents being told everything is fine when it might not be. She herself struggled to get services for her son because he knew two words too many to be accepted into a birth-to-three program.
“If you’re not a person like Ayana Taylor … [with] a speech and language pathologist in my family, to push back, things go unchecked,” Taylor said.
She said the process of getting services is also just confusing for many parents.
“I’m hearing that a lot from parents saying, ‘I did not know what I didn’t know.’ They were speaking to me in acronyms,” Taylor said.
She said she wants the state to do more to promote unconscious bias training and “making sure we are meeting families and parents where they’re at.” That’s also something she feels would help address the problem of schools repeatedly calling parents to pick their kids up early.
“When a child is melting down … the first thing should be making sure that we get to the root of the problem, and then practicing restorative practices to make sure that the child feels comfortable coming back into the setting,” Taylor said.
She also said the state should do more to track where such cases are occurring and thereby hold districts more accountable.
As for literacy, Taylor said universal pre-K is a top priority. Kids who start school at kindergarten often lack important soft skills and may already be behind in developing reading skills.
“I’m always thinking ahead, that if we get out in front of it we won’t be so far behind moving forward,” Taylor said.
She also expressed support for improving Tier 2 and Tier 3 supports — that is, additional support services available to students beyond general instruction — and reducing class sizes.
“Our educators are doing their very best, but that’s classroom sizes. It’s more supports. It’s more preventative and early interventions for any disabilities and things of that nature,” Taylor said.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas to pay more than $1.1 million for wrongful conviction in baby’s death
description: TOPEKA — A Kansas man wrongfully convicted of murdering his infant nephew will receive $614,205 from the state of Kansas after spending more than nine years in prison. Christopher Dale Lyman was convicted of first-degree murder and child abuse in the 2013 death of the baby, deputy attorney general Robert Hutchison told the State Finance […]
text:
Robert Hutchison, deputy attorney general, spoke to the State Finance Council at its virtual meeting July 21, 2026, about an overturned conviction of a Kansan. (Kansas Reflector screen grab of State Finance Council virtual meeting)TOPEKA — A Kansas man wrongfully convicted of murdering his infant nephew will receive $614,205 from the state of Kansas after spending more than nine years in prison.
Christopher Dale Lyman was convicted of first-degree murder and child abuse in the 2013 death of the baby, deputy attorney general Robert Hutchison told the State Finance Council on Tuesday. Lyman was accused of shaking the baby, causing his death, and in February, a Kansas court overturned the conviction.
The state also will pay $498,077 in attorney’s fees for Lyman’s counsel, Hutchison said. The total dollars being paid will come from the tort claims fund, he said.
As part of the agreement, Lyman will be entitled to enroll in the state’s healthcare plan and receive tuition assistance, Hutchison said.
“It was a difficult case for the state, for the plaintiff and for the victim’s family, who we were in contact with while the case was proceeding the second time,” Hutchison said.
Lyman’s conviction was overturned on appeal for ineffective assistance of counsel and the prosecution withholding evidence about an expert’s qualifications from the defense, Hutchison said.
“The prosecution ultimately decided not to retry the case, not because they felt Mr. Lyman was innocent, but because of complications with evidence and the family of the victim’s desire to move on from the case and also their belief that the defendant did not actually commit the crime,” Hutchison said. 
The baby’s cause of death was in “great dispute” between two experts, one of whom believed the infant died of shaken baby syndrome and another who offered different testimony, Hutchison said. 
Members of the State Finance Council questioned the amount being paid to Lyman’s attorneys and whether there was any limitation on those fees. Hutchison said any amounts exceeding $25,000 require the attorneys to offer proof of their billing amount.
“There’s no cap under the statute,” he said. “We had proposed one a couple of years ago of, I believe, $100,000, but that proposal ultimately was not successful.”
Hutchison said the Attorney General’s Office, upon reviewing the attorney’s bill in Lyman’s case, made motions to reduce the amount and he estimated they saved the state about $200,000. He said the case took years in litigation and required multiple trial experts.
In other business Tuesday, the State Finance Council approved a payout of $35,000 “as a settlement and compromise” in a case filed by the U.S. Department of Justice against the Kansas Department of Health and Environment. The council discussed the case in executive session.
In that case, Stacy Gonzales was employed by the Finney County Health Department in a position funded as part of a KDHE grant, according to court records. Gonzales, who was a member of the U.S. Army National Guard, alleged she was fired after KDHE deputy director Jennifer VandeVelde, made comments implying she would have to choose between her career and the military based on Gonzales’ deployments and training.
Gonzales made an official complaint in 2018 through the Veterans’ Employment and Training Service, which investigated and determined that KDHE had been in violation of federal rules that protect military members’ jobs when they deploy, court records said.
The court ruled the health department, not KDHE, was Gonzales’ employer, but the case is currently being appealed.
The resolution approved by the council said Attorney General Kris Kobach recommends the $35,000 payout and “the delay of the requested action may invalidate all settlement options available to the attorney general.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Livingston County enters ICE cooperation agreement; sheriff says it ‘doesn’t change anything’
description: On Monday, the Livingston County Sheriff’s Office signed a 287(g) agreement — a formal cooperation agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement that gives local law enforcement agencies “the authority to perform specified immigration officer functions under ICE’s direction and oversight.” The agreement signed in Livingston County is for the Warrant Ser[...]
text:
Livingston County Sheriff Mike Murphy speaks at "Crime and Safety" press conference held by the Trump campaign in Howell. Aug. 20, 2024. Photo by Jon King.On Monday, the Livingston County Sheriff’s Office signed a 287(g) agreement — a formal cooperation agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement that gives local law enforcement agencies “the authority to perform specified immigration officer functions under ICE’s direction and oversight.”
The agreement signed in Livingston County is for the Warrant Service Officer model, which “allows designated immigration officers to serve and execute administrative warrants on aliens in their custody,” according to the ICE website. 
Livingston County Sheriff Mike Murphy, who is also a Republican candidate for state Senate, told Michigan Advance in an interview that this agreement will not change the actual actions that his officers are taking on the ground, as they were already cooperating with ICE and other Department of Homeland Security agencies. 
“We have always cooperated with other agencies, whether state, federal, local, doesn’t make any difference,” he said, specifically referring to detainer requests from other agencies for individuals held in the Livingston County jail. “We have always done that for ICE.”
“If another bona fide law enforcement agency says, ‘Hey, please hold this person, because we’ll come get them,’ then by all means, we’re going to hold them. That’s what we do,” he added.
Livingston County Sheriff and Michigan state Senate candidate Mike Murphy at U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett’s (R-Charlotte) 2026 campaign kickoff. April 17, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance
As for why his office would sign the agreement now, Murphy noted that he was initially resistant to signing any memorandum of understanding, because it was already their policy. However, the office wanted to apply for a new Department of Justice grant opportunity that can be used for equipment for immigration investigations. However, a stipulation of that grant is that only agencies with 287(g) agreements or plans to enter such an agreement were eligible to apply. 
“All that does is basically allows us to detain illegals and legitimately serve them with notice that they’re being detained for immigration,” he said of the 287(g) agreement, noting that he intentionally did not sign an agreement in the Task Force Model, which allows for more direct immigration enforcement by local officers. “There’s a reason that there’s local law enforcement, and there’s a reason that there’s federal law enforcement. We both enforce different laws.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Immigrant rights advocates were swift to criticize the decision to enter the agreement — Livingston County is the state’s 10th-most populous, and includes major highway connections to cities including Detroit and Ann Arbor, where ICE has had a notable presence. 
A Facebook post from the Michigan Immigrant Rights Center urged residents and those concerned about the agreement to contact Livingston County officials and tell them to rescind the agreement. 
The group said in a fact sheet about the agreements that the 287(g) program, “has been shown to result in racial profiling, be costly for localities, target individuals with little or no criminal history, and harm the relationship between police and local communities.”
Livingston County is the eighth jurisdiction in Michigan with an active 287(g) agreement, joining five other counties and two municipalities. It is the second agreement signed this year in Michigan — but the first, signed by the Saginaw County village of Oakley, was rescinded just months later by the Oakley Village City Council.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Beshear reverses 4% Kentucky Medicaid provider cuts
description: “Today is not a magic wand. It’s not a magic bullet."
text:
Hundreds of Kentuckians with disabilities and their loved ones and advocates came to Frankfort and pleaded with elected officials to find a way to protect the services they receive through Medicaid waivers. July 17, 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)FRANKFORT — Thanks to an “unanticipated” corporate income tax payment and revenue surplus, Gov. Andy Beshear announced Wednesday that Medicaid providers will not suffer a 4% reimbursement cut after all. 
Beshear said $255 million from the taxes, as well as additional revenue, will delay any cuts to Medicaid reimbursement through this fiscal year, which ends at the end of next June. 
It will also fund the state’s senior meal program and Michelle P. Waiver slots, which are Medicaid waivers for Kentuckians with intellectual or developmental disabilities who need nursing facility or immediate care facility level of care. 
Beshear said he does not know which company submitted the tax payments — “and the Department of Revenue isn’t allowed to tell us” — and therefore said not to count on that money every month. He also said that “this isn’t any type of data center payment.” 
“Thanks to strong fiscal management by my administration and a strong economic surge late in the fiscal year, we turned a $156 million deficit into a $476 million surplus,” Beshear said during a press conference in Frankfort. “Additional good news… we believe that the surge is going to continue.”  
This comes after hundreds of Kentuckians rallied in Frankfort for a reversal of the cuts, especially those affecting Medicaid waivers, last Friday.  
Kentuckians with disabilities, advocates say looming 4% Medicaid cut is a ‘threat’

The Beshear administration had, in June, informed various providers they would see a 4% reduction in Medicaid reimbursement starting Aug. 1. He said Wednesday that new notices will go out to providers “shortly.” 
Beshear blamed the budget passed by the General Assembly this year for forcing his hand toward the cuts, while lawmakers said he could better manage the money they provided. 
Beshear is redirecting $4 million into the Senior Meal program, fully funding all authorized Michelle P. Waiver slots and putting $18 million into the road fund. The latter was a point of contention between his administration and the General Assembly. When Beshear, in May, signed an executive order to reduce the gas tax by 10 cents (and later, he extended the reduction to localities that asked him to), lawmakers said the move would cost the state’s road project fund $26.8 million for one month. 
At that time, Sen. Jimmy Higdon, the Lebanon Republican who chairs the Senate Transportation Committee, said lawmakers could consider reducing road funding from local governments that participate in the gas tax reduction. 
Beshear said all the financial changes announced Wednesday only apply to this fiscal year and said the legislature “absolutely” needs to reopen the budget in January and ensure enough funding for the next fiscal year.  
“Today is not a magic wand. It’s not a magic bullet,” Beshear said. “There are still people out there suffering, but I know that there will be fewer that suffer in order to get their services because of this movement.” 
This story may be updated.
