name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Consumer advocates seek breakup of BlackRock as it attempts to buy AES Indiana parent company
description: Consumer advocacy groups say BlackRock’s attempt to get a controlling stake in utility AES means the private equity firm needs to be broken up.
text:
New filings contest the purchase of AES Indiana by BlackRock. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)Consumer advocacy groups say BlackRock’s move for a controlling stake in utility company AES means the private equity firm needs to be broken up. 
In a complaint to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission filed Monday, the Citizens Action Coalition of Indiana and two other groups argued that if a planned purchase of AES by investors were to proceed, BlackRock affiliates would control over half of the utility. That includes BlackRock’s management of the California Public Employees’ Retirement System stake in AES.
Public Citizen and the Private Equity Stakeholder Project joined the Hoosier Citizens Action Coalition in the complaint.
The Federal Power Act gives FERC authority to approve public utility acquisitions only if “consistent with the public interest.” The groups argue that level of control is not.
“It is more important than ever for regulators to carefully examine whether the financial incentives driving Wall Street investments are compatible with the long-term public interest of utilities that power Americans’ homes and businesses,” said Nichole Heil, a senior climate and energy researcher at the Private Equity Stakeholder Project, in a news release. “FERC should give this BlackRock transaction that level of scrutiny.”
FERC previously granted holding companies like BlackRock blanket authorization for purchases in utilities, an approval designed to “encourage greater investment in utilities by mutual funds.” But blanket authorizations still have some limitations, including not owning more than 20% of the voting shares of any one utility company.
BlackRock affiliates, the advocate groups argue, would exceed 50% control if the purchase were to proceed.
AES announced earlier this year that it had agreed to be purchased by BlackRock and other investors — and become a private company — in a $33-billion deal expected to close in late 2026 or early 2027. It’s just one of numerous attempts by private equity firms to purchase public utilities amid a surge in data center demand for electricity.
Other members of the investor group are Swedish private equity firm EQT and the sovereign wealth fund of Qatar
AES Indiana services more than 500,000 retail customers in Indianapolis and surrounding areas.
Firms like BlackRock “are the last people we should want to be running our public utilities,” said Kerwin Olson, executive director of Citizens Action Coalition.
“The aim of private equity firms is to extract as much profit from the assets that they own,” Olson told the Indiana Capital Chronicle. “And in this case, that asset would be our public utility.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: New education commissioner is an ‘outstanding choice,’ Erika Donalds says
description: Henry Mack won approval as Florida’s next education commissioner Wednesday, having been recommended by Gov. Ron DeSantis and deemed an “outstanding choice” by someone particularly close to DeSantis’ potential successor. Erika Donalds, a school-choice advocate and wife of GOP gubernatorial frontrunner U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds, praised Mack, “our next commissio[...]
text:
The Florida Historic Capitol dome. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Henry Mack won approval as Florida’s next education commissioner Wednesday, having been recommended by Gov. Ron DeSantis and deemed an “outstanding choice” by someone particularly close to DeSantis’ potential successor.
Erika Donalds, a school-choice advocate and wife of GOP gubernatorial frontrunner U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds, praised Mack, “our next commissioner of education,” following his confirmation.
The Board of Education has the responsibility of appointing the state education commissioner. But, as was the case this time, the governor can recommend candidates to the panel, comprising gubernatorial appointees.
In a social media post, Erika Donalds posted a picture with Mack from the Board of Education meeting Wednesday in Orlando. She wrote, “Florida students won today!”
“Congratulations to Dr. [Henry Mack], our next Commissioner of Education,” Erika Donalds wrote in part, “Thank you, [Gov. Ron DeSantis] and State Board of Education members for this outstanding choice.”

Florida students won today!
Congratulations to Dr. @HenmackIII, our next Commissioner of Education — an innovator and proven leader with experience across the education spectrum, most recently as U.S. Assistant Secretary of Labor.
Dr. Mack believes in academic excellence and… pic.twitter.com/342v9cndTu
— Erika Donalds (@ErikaDonalds) July 22, 2026

“Welcome home, Henry!” Erika Donalds concluded.
Of note, the Donaldses are particular interested in education policy.
Erika Donalds, a self-described “education entrepreneur,” is founder and chair of OptimaEd, a virtual reality education company, with other roles with classical schools and education choice foundations.
Byron Donalds, as a member of the Florida House, was chair of the PreK-12 Quality Subcommittee and vice chair of the PreK-12 Appropriations Subcommittee. He sponsored the House version of the Hope Scholarship Program in 2018, now law. He sponsored various other education bill during his time in the state Legislature.
“It is an honor beyond words to be entrusted with stewarding Florida schools at this pivotal moment and I approach this responsibility with the utmost respect for the work that you’ve already accomplished and the work that Gov. DeSantis has led under his visionary and bold leadership,” Mack said during the confirmation hearing.
In thanking interim commissioner Paul Burns, Mack said “It is just a profound honor, Paul, to think about the next however many years I’m lucky to serve, to do it side by side with you,” adding: “It is going to be an amazing next few years together for the great state of Florida for the students that we serve.”
The Donalds campaign did not immediately respond to a Phoenix question Wednesday about his preference for education commissioner should he win the election.
The education commissioner who served most of former Gov. Rick Scott’s terms, Pam Stewart, left on Jan. 8, 2019, the day DeSantis first took his oath of office. Richard Corcoran began as commissioner that same day.
Mack’s return
Last week, DeSantis announced he was recommending Mack, a former Florida Department of Education official now serving as President Donald Trump’s assistant secretary of labor.
The board followed suit and unanimously approved Mack Wednesday.
DeSantis recommends Trump administrator, former Florida official, to be next ed commissioner

Mack worked in the department from 2019 until 2023 as a chancellor, focusing on colleges and career education. He then spent a year at Northwest Florida State College as provost.
During his time at the department, he served alongside Eric Hall, now president of Pasco-Hernando State College.
“I have great admiration for who he is and who he has been and the things that he has accomplished and the things that he will continue to do for this great state,” Hall said during public comments. “Being a part of President Trump’s administration, helping to bring those relationships to our state, only further strengthens the role that Florida plays in being a national leader.” 
Board members did not ask any questions of Mack.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In December, Mack was confirmed by the U.S. Senate to serve as assistant secretary of labor under Trump, overseeing the federal department’s Employment and Training Administration. 
Former Education Commissioner Anastasios Kamoutsas pointed, on social media, to “Dr. Mack’s distinguished record,” adding that he’s “positive that [Mack] will ensure Florida remains positioned as the national leader in education and workforce development.”
Carole Gauronskas, vice president of the Florida Education Association, which has often sparred with the DeSantis administration over education policy and teacher salaries, gave a positive statement for Mack. 
“We look forward to working collaboratively with Dr. Mack and enjoy the fruit of all of your hardwork,” Gauronskas said during public comment. 
The commissioner position opened earlier this month when Kamoutsas left to become president of Polk State College. In the meantime, Senior Chancellor Paul Burns was interim commissioner.
Mack is the fourth commissioner to serve under DeSantis. Two interims have served, too.

name: Source New Mexico
title: More than 10,000 New Mexico kids have lost federal food assistance in last year, new analysis shows
description: The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities’ analysis released Tuesday says new burdens on states and households have coincided with more than 1.5 million children nationwide losing their SNAP benefits, including more than 10,000 in New Mexico.
text:
More than 18,000 New Mexicans, most of them children, lost federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program funding over the last year, according to a new analysis from the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. (Courtesy The Food Depot)More than 10,000 New Mexico children have lost federal food assistance benefits in the year since Congress enacted a sweeping spending bill, according to a new analysis from a Washington, D.C.-based think tank.
The spending bill President Donald Trump signed last July imposed new work requirements and other burdens on households seeking food assistance from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. It also included stiff penalties for states that have high rates of errors in implementing the program, causing states, including New Mexico, to quickly impose new paperwork requirements. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities’ analysis released Tuesday says those new burdens on states and households have coincided with more than 1.5 million children nationwide losing their SNAP benefits, roughly one-third of the estimated 4.5 million people who lost SNAP since Congress passed the law.
The center’s analysis looked at the period between July 2025 and April 2026 and determined that roughly 18,000 New Mexicans lost SNAP in that period, including more than 10,000 children. 
In a news conference Wednesday morning detailing their analysis, center leaders said the swift dropoff of SNAP recipients should compel Congress to delay penalties for states that don’t reduce errors by deadlines set in the law or to give states more funding to reduce errors. 
“States are working hard to reduce their error rates, but they’re up against the wall,” Vice President for Food Assistance Ty Jones Cox said. “The law didn’t give them any time or resources to do so, so that creates an enormous incentive for states to slash their error rates by any means necessary, and that’s what we’re seeing: more paperwork, shorter certification periods, more red tape, even if it means eligible families lose benefits they’re entitled to.”
New Mexico could face a penalty of at least $150 million if it does not reduce its error rate from 16.8% — which is the third-highest in the nation — to less than 6% by October 2027. 
The New Mexico Health Care Authority recently imposed new verification requirements for SNAP applicants’ incomes and household sizes, and the authority is working to improve its data collection and caseworker training to minimize the number of SNAP over- and underpayments made to SNAP recipients.
Citing a hunger ‘crisis,’ US mayors call for end to federal SNAP cuts

The center examined data from 19 states with readily available data regarding children enrolled in SNAP. New Mexico’s proportion of children who lost SNAP — 56% — over the last year was among the highest. 
Health Care Authority officials did not immediately respond to Source NM’s emailed request for comment Wednesday. 
More-recent HCA data reviewed by Source NM shows that the trend in SNAP disenrollment has continued through June, with approximately 7,000 additional people losing SNAP between April and June. That HCA data does not specify how many of them are children. 
The center’s analysts say they cannot identify whether lack of funding or new barriers on households is the primary driver in reducing SNAP enrollment. But they ruled out the possibility that SNAP households’ economic well-being have improved enough in the last year that they no longer need the food assistance. 
“Grocery prices are still rising,” Jones Cox said. “Unemployment has been largely flat since before the law passed. Real wages have actually declined. People need food assistance today just as much as they did a year ago, and they’re simply being cut off from assistance as states scramble to limit their exposure.”

title: US Senate Dems press Mullin to ensure all immigration agents have body cameras
text: WASHINGTON — A supermajority of the U.S. Senate Democratic Caucus has asked Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to deploy body cameras to all federal immigration officers, following deadly shootings of immigrants in Texas and Maine.In a July 19 letter addressed to Mullin, 38 Senate Democrats and Maine’s Angus King, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, requested information about the shootings this month in Houston of 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and in Biddeford, Maine, of 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero. Neither man was the initial enforcement target when Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers stopped their vehicles, the Department of Homeland Security has said.“The unnecessary loss of life in these incidents demands immediate, thorough, independent, and transparent investigations (including the full involvement of local and state law enforcement personnel), along with a comprehensive examination of enforcement protocols, training, and operational approaches necessary to prevent such tragedies,” the senators wrote.The lawmakers pressed Mullin about providing body cameras to immigration officers, pointing out the Congress has allocated $175 billion to the department since last year. From that funding, DHS planned to hire up to 10,000 ICE officers.“While DHS has previously acknowledged that body-worn cameras promote public trust and increase officer and public safety, accountability, and transparency, the Department has clearly not prioritized acquiring cameras,” the senators wrote.None of the ICE officers involved in the shootings were wearing body cameras. “Contrary to recent statements made by the Department and the White House, DHS has had more than sufficient time and funding to procure and deploy a body-worn camera for every officer before the end of 2025,” they wrote.Enough fundingCongressional Republicans last year used a special legislative maneuver to allocate roughly $175 billion to DHS for immigration enforcement, detainment and deportations, without needing Democratic support. They used the same move following the shutdown this year to fund $75 billion for ICE and Border Patrol through September of 2029. Republicans used the maneuver that allows party-line votes after Democrats refused to provide more funding for DHS unless restraints were placed on ICE and Border Patrol officers following the killings of two U.S. citizens — Alex Pretti and Renee Good — by federal immigration agents in Minnesota in January. Among Democrats’ demands at the time was that immigration officers wear body cameras. Top Trump officials, including then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, said body cameras would be provided to immigration agents.“The recent tragedies confirm that neither of these commitments were honored,” senators wrote in the letter.Traffic stops unpausedWhite House border czar Tom Homan said over the weekend that ICE officers will wear “at least one body camera” during traffic stops.Following the two killings this month, DHS instructed immigration officers to pause vehicle stops, but President Donald Trump quickly instructed the department to continue the policy.  During the second Trump administration, federal immigration officers have shot 22 people and killed six, including three U.S. citizens. Most of the shootings stemmed from traffic stops.In the letter, senators also sought information about DHS’s plan to have an independent investigation into the killings, the vetting process for new immigration officers, the department’s procedures for vehicle stops and any additional oversight and reporting requirements DHS is implementing.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Ryan Walters, top adviser settle lawsuits with fired state employees
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Taxpayers will cover $132,000 in lawsuit settlements owed to two fired Oklahoma State Department of Education employees who sued former state Superintendent Ryan Walters and his senior adviser. Cheryl McGee and Matt Colwell each sued Walters and Matt Langston in Oklahoma City federal court in 2023. Both had been fired that year […]
text:
Former state Superintendent Ryan Walters speaks during a meeting of the Oklahoma State Board of Education on Sept. 25 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Taxpayers will cover $132,000 in lawsuit settlements owed to two fired Oklahoma State Department of Education employees who sued former state Superintendent Ryan Walters and his senior adviser.
Cheryl McGee and Matt Colwell each sued Walters and Matt Langston in Oklahoma City federal court in 2023. Both had been fired that year for sharing agency information with individuals outside of the Education Department.
They contended Walters and Langston violated their First Amendment rights by putting an overly broad restraint on their speech. Because Walters and Langston were acting within the scope of their authority as agency officials, the state of Oklahoma is responsible for paying both plaintiffs’ settlements, under state indemnification laws.
Education Department spokesperson Tara Thompson confirmed the money owed will come out of the agency’s funds.
“We are hopeful this settlement brings OSDE one step closer to a resolution of outstanding legal issues so that our attention and resources can be focused on serving the students of Oklahoma,” Thompson said.
Walters and Langston deny any legal violations, according to the settlement agreements, which Oklahoma Voice obtained from the Education Department.
The defendants signed the agreements on June 26 “solely for the purpose of avoiding further expenses of litigation,” and the settlements in no way represent an admission of liability, the documents state.
Matt Langston, senior advisor and campaign manager for former state Superintendent Ryan Walters, attends a Legislative Office of Fiscal Transparency committee meeting Oct. 29, 2024, at the Oklahoma State Capitol. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Their attorney, W. Caleb Jones, declined to comment on the case. 
Walters and Langston didn’t return requests for further comment. Both left the Education Department in September when Walters accepted a position leading an anti-teacher-union organization.
McGee, the agency’s former executive director of school based mental health, was awarded $100,000. She will keep half of the funds — a $30,000 payment and another $20,000 for wage loss, according to her agreement. The second half will go to the law firm representing her, Hammons, Hurst & Associates. 
Colwell settled for $32,000. Half will go to his attorneys and the other half for himself and for wage loss.
Attorney Mark Hammons, who represents both McGee and Colwell, said the settlements are a “source of vindication” for his clients.
“I think our government has to perform better than it did in this case,” Hammons said. “These are individuals who were willing to stand up and do the right thing. Of course, like a lot of people who stand up and do the right thing, they get punished for it.”
McGee was fired May 25, 2023, for sharing an email from Langston with the news media, according to her lawsuit. In the agency-wide email, Langston threatened employees with termination if they were found to have leaked information to the press. He later said he had formatted the emails with subtle differences so he could identify which employees had leaked.
Colwell was fired the next day after sharing concerns about a teacher signing bonus program with the Attorney General’s Office and with a state representative, according to his lawsuit. He sent a memorandum explaining the teacher pay plan could contravene federal and state requirements and could result in millions in extra costs.
Walters established signing bonuses of up to $50,000 to lure qualified classroom teachers from out of state or back into the profession from other career fields. 
The program attracted more than 500 teachers to Oklahoma school districts, but it caused controversy when the Education Department realized it had paid a few teachers in error and threatened to claw back the money.
Two of the affected teachers, Kharis “Kay” Bojorquez and Kristina Stadelman, sued the agency and Walters in Oklahoma County District Court. All parties agreed in October to voluntarily dismiss the case, court records show.
Hammons, who also represents the two teachers, said the state gave up on its attempt to claw back their signing bonuses.
The cases are a few of many filed against Walters and the Education Department during his tenure in office. Plaintiffs sued the former state superintendent over open meeting and open records concerns, religious freedoms, alleged defamation, revocation of a teacher’s certification and other disputes.
“The state was littered with complaints about his conduct. Things were undone as soon as he left,” Hammons said. “I would be embarrassed if I had been in that position and my legacy was having gotten sued all the time successfully and having gotten sued because I was being vindictive to people over political purposes.”

name: WyoFile
title: Northern Arapaho Business Council crafts policy governing ‘outside organizations’ after sermon sparks outrage
description:
Protests, Sunday services continue after Foundations for Nations pastor goes viral with call for tribal members on the Wind River Reservation to reject their traditional spiritual ways.
The post Northern Arapaho Business Council crafts policy governing ‘outside organizations’ after sermon sparks outrage appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
RIVERTON—The fallout after a controversial July 5 sermon by Foundations For Nations Pastor Sarah Lucas has endured, and this week, the Northern Arapaho Business Council announced a new policy: Outside organizations like the church must consult with and receive authorization from the business council to conduct activities on land under the tribe’s jurisdiction.
The sermon sparked outrage and national headlines for its call on tribal members to reject their traditional spiritual ways. On the last day of the Northern Arapaho Sundance Celebration, Lucas condemned traditional practices as idol worship.
“The pipe cannot hear your prayers,” she told parishioners in a video that has since gone viral. “It’s just a piece of material, right? And this is a cycle that they’re caught up in, and this is all they’ve ever known.”
As protesters gathered last Sunday outside the church on the Wind River Reservation just outside Riverton, Northern Arapaho’s records department was busy conducting an extensive audit, scouring documents to determine whether Foundations For Nations had ever received authorization from the business council to set up shop on the reservation.
Turns out, according to a Northern Arapaho Business Council statement outlining the new policy, Foundations For Nations Church had not.
The business council has sent a formal notice to the church’s leadership requesting a meeting within 10 days to discuss Foundations For Nations’ “mission, leadership, funding, activities and any documentation it believes demonstrates authorization to operate on lands under tribal jurisdiction,” the business council wrote in its Monday statement.
The new request for a meeting with church officials comes on the heels of an initial meeting shortly after the sermon, on July 10, when the Northern Arapaho Business Council told Foundations For Nations it was no longer welcome on the reservation and needed to leave.
But church officials have doubled down, instead continuing to hold Sunday services as protesters gathered along the highway. Foundations For Nations instead asked its membership for donations for an anticipated legal battle over the tribe’s directive to leave.
The sermon
Established on the reservation in 2017, the church also operates a food shelf in Riverton. Its website advertises a “multi-cultural, multi-generational church made up of people from all different backgrounds,” and focuses much of its ministry on children’s programming.
The church shared a video of the July 5 sermon online, as it typically does each Sunday. But this time, the video quickly spread on social media as tribal members decried Lucas’ portrayal of traditional practices and recalled a painful history of forced assimilation.
In her sermon, Lucas urged her congregation to be watchful in the “spirit realm” and reflected on a busy week for the church. 
“But are we fighting the spiritual temperature in the atmosphere?” she asked. “Where it says ‘tear down the altars, tear down the idols?’ And this nation gathered this week and they prayed, and they prayed to pipes, and they prayed to their ancestors, believing that this is their way for their freedom to get free from addiction, for people to be healed from their sickness, and this is what this culture did this week. 
“And we went on as church as normal, but here’s the thing. I feel like we’ve got to pray this morning before moving on. I feel like we’re going to pray for this nation this morning, and we’re going to pray for our Indigenous nation, for our tribe this week as they’re coming out of this, because we know that Jesus is enough. He’s enough. It’s not Jesus plus. It’s Jesus everything, he’s everything … Jesus is the chain breaker. He is the only god that we should be praying to.”
The backlash was swift, and with it came threats. A large protest was held July 7 outside the church, which quickly moved to its food shelf in Riverton and then outside city hall. The food shelf was temporarily closed in response.
While the church itself has not released a statement, it has engaged in comments on Facebook. 
“No wonder we have to carry guns,” the church wrote. “But keep agitating the protestors, you are part of the problem!” 
In another comment, Foundations For Nations described harassment the church and its parishioners have faced: “Your protestors aren’t peaceful! Yelling profanity as church goers going into church. Driving onto the property at the end of service trying to block our exits. Flipping us off as we leave! The threats of danger and violence that your protestors are writing on their signs or social media post[s] does not show you are a peaceful people!”
By July 10, church officials had met with the Northern Arapaho Business Council, which reportedly ordered the church to leave the reservation. The meeting, church leaders wrote in a statement to members, was “marked by intense opposition.”
Church leaders’ message to members was clear about their intent to remain on the reservation and continue preaching there.
“We are standing firmly on the truth of the Word of God concerning idol worship,” they wrote, describing “ongoing death threats and threats to burn our church.” 
Legally, they said, the church “cannot be removed in this manner.” The message added: “We are in contact with legal counsel and are preparing to pursue this in federal court as soon as possible in order to uphold our Constitutional rights to preach the gospel … We are not stopping.”
A new tribal policy
“This policy is not about preventing anyone from practicing their religion,” Northern Arapaho Business Council Chairman Keenan Groesbeck said in the Monday statement from the business council. “It is about respecting the sovereign government of the Northern Arapaho Tribe. Any outside organization seeking to conduct organized activities within our jurisdiction should first communicate with the elected leadership of our Nation and work in partnership with the tribe.
“The business council further recognizes the historical relationship between many Christian institutions and Native Nations, including the devastating legacy of forced assimilation, boarding schools, and efforts to suppress Indigenous languages, cultures, and spiritual traditions.” The business council statement continued: “These historical experiences make it especially important that any outside organization engaging with the Northern Arapaho people do so through respectful government-to-government consultation and with a full understanding of tribal history, culture, and sovereignty.”
Sunday service
On Sunday, July 19, a handful of protesters gathered outside the church as parishioners trickled in. Though the numbers had dwindled from initial protests in response to the sermon, those gathered said they were committed to sending a message to church leaders.
“We’re going to continue to protest,” said Alice Thomas as Sunday service was held inside. “I don’t think not giving an apology is a good thing.”
Thomas, who said she is a member of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and practices traditional spiritual ways too, said the two did not need to be at odds. 
“My religious and traditional side — they coincide with one another. I’ve never had a church authority come and tell me ‘This is wrong,'” she said. “Our traditions come from the Bible.”
Protesters said just before the Sunday service got started that they’d had a conflict with a security guard patrolling the grounds. Riverton resident Fred Poutray had set up a shade canopy, and witnesses said the security guard took issue with its placement and threw it in a ditch, ripping it. 
The security guard then allegedly asked Poutray: “You going to fight me, old man?” and “chest bumped” Poutray during the argument.
Bureau of Indian Affairs officers responded after protesters called police about the incident. Because Poutray is white, they tapped the Fremont County Sheriff’s Office to handle the call.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Department of Public Health holds hearing on marijuana rescheduling
description: A group of conservative activists Wednesday registered objections to the federal rescheduling of marijuana with the Alabama Department of Public Health (ADPH). The ADPH held a public hearing following the April decision by the Trump administration to move marijuana from a Schedule I drug, meaning it has the greatest potential for abuse and least legitimate [[...]
text:
Mock medical cannabis tinctures in a display case at Callie's Apothecary in Montgomery, Alabama, on May 14, 2026. The Alabama Department of Public Health Wednesday heard from members of the public for rescheduling marijuana from Schedule I to Schedule III. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)A group of conservative activists Wednesday registered objections to the federal rescheduling of marijuana with the Alabama Department of Public Health (ADPH).
The ADPH held a public hearing following the April decision by the Trump administration to move marijuana from a Schedule I drug, meaning it has the greatest potential for abuse and least legitimate use, to a Schedule III drug with substances considered to have a low to moderate potential for physical and psychological dependence.
Former President Joe Biden planned to have rescheduling occur in 2024, but hearings on the matter were canceled in early 2025.
In May, the governing body of ADPH voted to object to the federal rescheduling of marijuana to give the agency more time to determine how to implement it. Alabama State Health Officer Dr. Scott Harris, the head of ADPH, said during the meeting that the department “fully intends” to implement the change.
Activists speaking at Wednesday’s meeting cited several concerns.  
Eagle Forum Executive Director Becky Gerritson said the change would “not only harm children, but we believe it will worsen Alabama’s mental health crisis.”
“Rescheduling marijuana from a Schedule I to a Schedule III puts it on the same level as Tylenol with codeine. This sends a powerful message to the public that this drug has an accepted medical use, and presents a relatively low risk,” Gerritson said. “ADPH’s policy should follow the evidence, not public opinion or commercial pressure.”
Greg Davis, the chief executive officer of the Alabama Citizens Action Program (ALCAP), a conservative organization that represents churches across the state, also spoke in opposition to the rescheduling.
“Whether we call it medical or whatever we want to call it, or however someone gets it, however it comes to them, whether it’s on the corner street or whether it’s in a doctor’s office or at a dispensary, it doesn’t really matter. The effects can be the same, and so I would just urge everyone, on behalf of our churches across the state, who oftentimes deal with the devastation, to oppose this rescheduling in Alabama,” he said.
Susan Short, a member of the public, said she opposed the rescheduling because of the effects it has on teens.
“Teens do not know that marijuana could possibly make you psychotic at 19 years of age for the rest of your life,” she said. “We are losing an entire generation of young people because we have normalized and commercialized and glorified this addictive and harmful substance.”
Under the Compassion Act passed by the Alabama Legislature in 2021, a minor under the age of 19 cannot obtain medical marijuana without approval from a parent or guardian and without a qualifying medical condition. If approved, the minor can only receive medical marijuana that contains no more than 3% tetrahydrocannabinol (THC).
Callie’s Apothecary, a dispensary in Montgomery, sold the first legal medical cannabis in the state last month.
Joey Robertson, CEO and president of Wagon Trail Med-Serv, the sole proponent of the rescheduling at the meeting, said not following what is happening on federal level could instill distrust between patients and doctors and the state.
“This is a controlled program in the state of Alabama that has nothing to do with children outside of those that qualify for those medications,” he said. “This has nothing to do with the illicit market, which will grow no matter what, and really does not care if the federal government or Alabama reschedules from Schedule I to Schedule III.”
General counsel for the ADPH said after the hearing a decision must be made after Aug. 5.

description: Wisconsin Republican U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson was named chairman of the Senate budget committee Tuesday, taking up a position left vacant after the death of Sen. Lindsey Graham earlier this month.  Johnson was the fourth highest ranking Republican on the committee, but received the chairmanship because Sens. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Mike Crapo (R-Idaho) alre[...]
text:
Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., talks to a reporter in the basement of the U.S. Capitol on Thursday, Oct. 23, 2025. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)Wisconsin Republican U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson was named chairman of the Senate budget committee Tuesday, taking up a position left vacant after the death of Sen. Lindsey Graham earlier this month. 
Johnson was the fourth highest ranking Republican on the committee, but received the chairmanship because Sens. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Mike Crapo (R-Idaho) already chair the Judiciary and Finance committees and Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) is on his way out of the Senate after losing his May primary.
In a statement, Johnson called Graham an “American patriot” and said he’ll “be sorely missed.” He added that he wants to focus on exposing fraud in government. 
“As chairman for the remainder of the year, I intend to maximize this opportunity to define the fiscal challenge we face, help expose the fraud in government programs, and work with the House, the White House, and my Senate colleagues to enact as much of President Trump’s agenda as possible,” Johnson said. 
Republicans in Congress are currently attempting to pass a third budget reconciliation bill of the term before November’s midterm elections — with a focus on providing the Department of Defense with more funds for the war in Iran, further cutting government benefit programs and passing the SAVE America act to put more restrictions on voting. 
A Johnson spokesperson previously told the Wisconsin Examiner that he would “work diligently” to pass a reconciliation bill.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium to get $400 million in federal settlement
description: The federal government has agreed to pay the Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium $400 million to settle claims of inadequate cost coverage over several years. The settlement, announced on Tuesday by the U.S. Justice Department, stems from a lawsuit filed by the nonprofit tribal health group in 2021 against the Department of Health and Human […]
text:
The Alaska Native Medical Center is reflected in the campus pond on Sept. 9, 2022. The hospital is among several facilities on the Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium campus in Anchorage. ANTHC is the nation's largest Native tribal organization. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)The federal government has agreed to pay the Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium $400 million to settle claims of inadequate cost coverage over several years.
The settlement, announced on Tuesday by the U.S. Justice Department, stems from a lawsuit filed by the nonprofit tribal health group in 2021 against the Department of Health and Human Services, which operates the Indian Health Service.
At issue in the case are “contract support costs,” the term for the expenses necessary for administration, facilities maintenance and other functions that support the healthcare services that tribal organizations provide through contracts with the federal government.
In a statement, the Justice Department acknowledged that the federal government owed ANTHC money to cover contract support costs.
“This settlement reflects our commitment to resolving litigation fairly and ensuring that federal resources are appropriately directed toward serving Native communities,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said in the statement. “We are pleased to have reached an authorized agreement that benefits American Indian and Alaska Native communities and remains consistent with the legal framework established by Congress.”
Natasha Singh, ANTHC’s president and chief executive officer, characterized the settlement as a fair resolution of a longstanding dispute over costs borne by the organization.
“ANTHC welcomes the authorization of this settlement, addressing contract support costs that have long been owed to Tribes that assumed responsibility for delivering healthcare on the federal government’s behalf. This settlement marks an important step toward ensuring that resources accurately reflect the true cost of operating a complex Tribal health system and advancing self-determination in healthcare,” Singh said in a statement.
For more than a decade, different tribal health organizations have claimed that the Indian Health Service was underpaying contract support costs. There is a history of litigation and Congressional action over the issue.
In 2024, the U.S. Supreme Court weighed in. Ruling in a case concerning tribes in Arizona and Wyoming, the court said the Indian Health Service is obligated to pay the full costs of contract support services.
Those costs are necessary for tribal health organizations to provide medical services, the 5-4 ruling said. If the costs are not fully covered by the IHS, “the tribe would have to divert some program income to pay such costs, or it would have to pay them out of its own pocket,” amounting to a penalty for pursuing self-determination under federal law.
The settlement is in line with that 2024 ruling, as well as with the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act, the federal law through which tribal organizations administer their own healthcare programs, the Justice Department said.
ANTHC is the nation’s largest tribal health organization. At its approximately 140-acre campus in east Anchorage, it operates the Alaska Native Medical Center, which is one of the state’s biggest hospitals, along with various in-patient services, research and epidemiology services and an environmental health program, among other functions. It provides services throughout the state.
The consortium, formed in 1997, has embarked on a facilities expansion program, enlarging the hospital’s emergency department and constructing a skilled nursing facility for patients needing extended care, along with other periodic upgrades.
Singh, in her statement, said the ANTHC board had “committed resources toward long-standing needs across our system of care” in anticipation of the settlement announced Tuesday. Those commitments include the investments in the ongoing construction projects, she said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: UMMC to take over Greenwood Leflore Hospital Aug. 1
description: Notices taped to the front door inform patients of the closing of outpatient and cardiac rehabilitation services at the Greenwood Leflore Hospital, Wednesday, April 29, 2026, in Greenwood. The hospital is scheduled to closed on June 15th.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Nearly four years after negotiations collapsed over a potential takeover of the long-struggling Greenwood Leflore Hospital by the University of Mississippi Medical Center, the state’s only academic medical center is set to assume operations of the Delta hospital on Aug. 1. 
A federal bankruptcy judge on July 16 approved a plan for the donation of the 25-bed public hospital, which is owned by the city of Greenwood and Leflore County, to UMMC.  At a Tuesday Greenwood City Council meeting, Gary Marchand, the hospital’s former interim CEO who became a consultant for the hospital’s board, called this the “last hurdle” to completing the transfer.
Gary Marchand talks about the state of the hospital on Wednesday, Sept. 20, 2023. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“As I speak here today, the university is on our campus,” Marchand said. “They’re making sure the IT — their clinical information systems — are up and running, the connectivity works, etc. We’re ready to switch over.” 
The Greenwood hospital has struggled financially for years, with its problems worsening during the COVID-19 pandemic. Officials have repeatedly warned it was near to closure. Its plight intensified in 2025 due to a dispute with the Mississippi Division of Medicaid over the repayment of debts the hospital owed. 
The hospital will be renamed UMMC Greenwood and will add to the university medical center’s existing services in the area, which include obstetrics and gynecology, internal medicine and pediatrics clinics and an AirCare helicopter base. 
UMMC operates seven hospitals and 35 clinics. In addition to its main campus facilities in Jackson, UMMC has hospitals in Grenada, Holmes and Madison counties. 
“We look forward to serving the Greenwood community and surrounding areas as part of our commitment to providing the highest quality health care to the citizens of Mississippi,” Dr. Alan Jones, associate vice chancellor for health affairs, said in a statement to Mississippi Today. 
UMMC declined to answer Mississippi Today’s questions about whether the takeover would result in service changes or layoffs. On Tuesday, Marchand said medical center staff are meeting with existing employees about available positions in Greenwood and its other hospital locations. 
The hospital has roughly 400 employees, according to documents filed in bankruptcy court. About 40 of these employees will be retained to complete the hospital’s business matters after Aug. 1.
Greenwood Leflore Hospital’s services, including the emergency room, operating room, skilled nursing care and cancer care, will continue uninterrupted when UMMC takes over, Marchand said. He said the Greenwood hospital expects to take approximately 18 months — and likely less — to wind down its corporate affairs before the entity is dissolved. 
UMMC will take on the hospital’s Medicaid liabilities and deferred maintenance responsibilities in the transaction, Marchand said Tuesday. A key sticking point in the 2022 talks between UMMC and the Greenwood hospital was the outstanding debts the hospital owed to Medicare and the funds necessary for deferred maintenance on hospital facilities, because UMMC did not want to be responsible for the costs after a transition.
“Greenwood Leflore Hospital will not have a dispute with Medicaid come August 1,” Marchand said.  
Several of the hospital’s properties are not included in the transfer, including its Itta Bena Clinic, which is scheduled to close at the end of July. Greenwood Leflore Hospital has operated the primary care clinic since 1997, serving the nearby town of Itta Bena’s more than 1,500 residents. 
Delta Health Center, a Mound Bayou-based federally qualified health center with 17 locations, is interested in reopening the clinic and rehiring its employees, Deputy CEO Neuaviska Braugher told city council members Tuesday. 
Greenwood City Council President Ronnie Stevenson said the city could not consider the possibility until after the transfer to UMMC is complete, noting that such an arrangement would need approval from the bankruptcy court judge. 
“I want to see the Itta Bena Clinic remain open,” he said. “Unfortunately, it will close July 31.” 
‘A long road’
Greenwood Leflore Hospital faced a litany of financial challenges over the past several years. Before the pandemic began, the hospital was losing $7 million to $9 million a year.
The pandemic only worsened the hospital’s precarious financial condition. To keep its doors open, the hospital shut down departments and clinics, went up for lease multiple times, drew down millions of dollars in credit, and pursued a more lucrative hospital designation. In 2023, the hospital suspended the use of 173 beds to control costs, according to an audit. 
The hospital’s financial challenges worsened in 2025. In June, the Division of Medicaid notified the hospital it would recoup $5.5 million in state-directed payments, or supplemental funds intended to offset low Medicaid reimbursement rates. The overpayments stemmed from the division’s calculations based on old data that did not reflect lower patient volumes after the hospital closed its labor and delivery and intensive care units in 2022.
The hospital and state agency reached an agreement to give both sides more time to negotiate a plan for the debt repayment in December as Marchand warned that the hospital was one day away from making its last payroll. 
But even with additional time, it was clear the hospital was in a dire financial situation, Marchand said. Hospital leaders approached three larger hospital systems about taking over operations of Greenwood Leflore. UMMC was the only interested party. 
In February, Greenwood Leflore Hospital signed a letter of intent to discuss the possibility of UMMC taking over its services, Mississippi Today reported. 
But the hospital’s conflict with Medicaid was not over. Recoupments were scheduled to resume in March, but hospital officials said they would likely force the facility to close. In response, a Hinds County chancery judge ordered Medicaid to temporarily stop collecting the money.
In April, the hospital laid off 86 staff members and closed clinics. Days later, it filed for bankruptcy, a move officials said would give it time to negotiate the transaction with UMMC. 
In June, the Hinds County chancery judge ordered the Mississippi Division of Medicaid to make a scheduled payment of roughly $2.4 million to Greenwood Leflore Hospital after the agency said it planned to withhold the funds. The Delta hospital argued that missing a payment would force it to close imminently and jeopardize its proposed agreement with UMMC. 
Inside the wood-paneled Greenwood City Council chambers Tuesday, Marchand was greeted with handshakes and kudos from attendees. One man in a brimmed hat reached out to shake his hand and offer congratulations. 
“It’s been a long road,” Marchand replied.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: ‘There was NO crime’: Charges against AG Liz Murrill dropped
description: The special prosecutor in the criminal case against Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill has dropped the charges at the request of New Orleans officials who were purported victims in the case.  Laurie White confirmed in text messages Wednesday she has declined to prosecute all 16 counts, including eight counts of public intimidation and eight counts […]
text:
A Louisiana Senate committee blocked legislation backed by Attorney General Liz Murrill that could have moved thousands of cases from juvenile to adult court. (Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)The special prosecutor in the criminal case against Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill has dropped the charges at the request of New Orleans officials who were purported victims in the case. 
Laurie White confirmed in text messages Wednesday she has declined to prosecute all 16 counts, including eight counts of public intimidation and eight counts of malfeasance in office, against Murrill. Her action followed letters sent to her Tuesday by New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno, Orleans Parish District Attorney Jason Williams and five city council members asking her to drop the charges against Murrill.
“This case should have NEVER been started because there was NO crime,” Murrill said in a statement. “This outcome will not deter my efforts to get to the bottom of this. The irresponsible and illegal actions that led to this abuse of the criminal justice system need to never happen again.” 
White’s decision to withdraw the charges marks a turning point in a tumultuous and politically charged dispute that began in May when Murrill wrote to city officials warning she could charge them under the state’s usurper laws if they tried to hold a special election for a consolidated court clerk’s position. Republican state lawmakers had passed legislation in the spring that effectively prevented Calvin Duncan, a formerly incarcerated man who was exonerated and became a lawyer, from taking office after winning election to the clerk’s position.
Murrill’s letter prompted complaints from Moreno and her supporters that the attorney general’s message could be interpreted as a criminal threat.
An Orleans Parish grand jury handed up an indictment July 2 against Murrill, though Moreno and Williams have said they did nothing to initiate the investigation that led to the charges.
In text messages Wednesday, White distanced herself from the political dispute. 
“I performed my responsibilities as an appointed prosecutor in accordance with the law,” White said. “It is important to understand that the grand jury brought this indictment, and that what followed was in accordance with their judgment. I respect the grand jury’s service and actions, as we all should, and thank them for their service. 
“Extraordinary interference in this situation has been truly unfortunate, and we should all hope that it doesn’t set a precedent,” White added. 
The lingering question: Who’s behind the indictment of AG Liz Murrill?

On the day the court unsealed the indictment, White told reporters the grand jury initiated the investigation on its own, a statement that led Murrill’s defense team to suggest in a news conference that day that someone was “tampering” with the grand jury. 
Affidavits filed Monday into the court record from several of White’s colleagues and attorneys not connected to the case back up White’s public statements about how the grand jury decided to indict Murrill. 
In one of the affidavits, noted New Orleans defense lawyer Pat Fanning wrote that he got a call from White on July 1, and she told him she tried to talk the grand jurors out of indicting Murrill but didn’t think they were listening. 
Another affidavit came from one of Murrill’s own employees, Assistant Attorney General Daniel Smart, who said he ran into White in the courthouse garage on the day of the indictment and struck up a conversation asking her why she was there. 
“She explained to me that she was there with the grand jury … She mentioned that she was attempting to not have the grand jury vote on the indictment today, but it seemed as though they wanted to,” Smart stated in his affidavit.  
Murrill’s letters to New Orleans leaders and the ensuing indictment wasn’t the first time she has faced accusations of threats. 
Last year, the attorney general sent a pointed letter to Duncan during his campaign for the Orleans Parish Criminal Court clerk’s election, warning him of legal consequences for what she claimed were conflicts of interest surrounding his exoneration. The claims were later debunked, and Duncan supporters labeled the letter as an unlawful suppression of his First Amendment rights.   
In April, state Rep. Brian Glorioso, R-Slidell, gave a lengthy speech on the floor of the Louisiana House of Representatives accusing Murrill of using “coercion and possibly even threats” to pressure his colleagues into voting for legislation she wanted passed. Glorioso, an attorney, likened Murrill’s actions to the politics of tyrannical governments. 
Murrill denied making threats and demanded a public apology, prompting Glorioso to ask for forgiveness in the House the next day. 
With the charges against her being dropped, Murrill said she will continue her own criminal investigation into what she claims was illegal misconduct surrounding the case. 
This is a developing story.

title: Trump attends dignified transfer of four fallen soldiers at Dover Air Force Base

text:
President’s July 22 visit highlights Dover’s central role in receiving service members killed overseas
DOVER, Del. — President Donald Trump traveled to Dover Air Force Base on Wednesday to attend the dignified transfer of four U.S. Army service members killed in attacks connected to the conflict with Iran.
The visit was not a campaign stop or public event. Trump arrived at the base Wednesday morning and joined military leaders and family members for the transfer ceremony before departing Delaware shortly before 1 p.m.
Trump stood on the flight line with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and saluted as military carry teams moved four flag-draped transfer cases from an aircraft. The remains were then taken to the Air Force Mortuary Affairs Operations facility at Dover.
Before arriving, Trump described the ceremony as one of the most difficult responsibilities of the presidency.
“We’re going to honor our heroes,” Trump told reporters before traveling to Delaware. “It’s one of the hardest things to do as a president.”
The four soldiers died in separate incidents in Jordan and Iraq.
First Lt. Tyler James Feehan, 25, of Ewa Beach, Hawaii; Sgt. Angel S. Rampersad, 28, of Ozone Park, New York; and Pvt. Isabella Gonzales, 19, of Carrollton, Texas, were killed when an Iranian missile struck sleeping quarters at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan.
Sgt. Michael Emmanuel Swinton, 30, of Spring Lake, North Carolina, was killed at Erbil Air Base in Iraq during the controlled detonation of a downed Iranian attack drone.
Trump met privately with the families of the fallen service members. Senior military officials and members of Congress also attended the ceremony.
The president’s attendance underscored the national significance of the losses and once again placed Dover Air Force Base at the center of the country’s military mourning process.
Dover is home to the nation’s largest military mortuary and serves as the primary arrival point for U.S. service members killed overseas. Mortuary personnel identify and prepare remains before they are released to families for burial.
The July 22 ceremony marked Trump’s third dignified transfer at Dover since the Iran conflict began in February.
The deaths brought the number of U.S. service members killed in the conflict to 18. Hundreds of others have been injured.
The visit also came as lawmakers in both parties continued to question the cost, duration and objectives of the conflict. Trump has defended the military campaign and warned that Iran would face further consequences for attacks on American troops.
For Delaware, the visit highlighted Dover Air Force Base’s unique and solemn national mission. The base has long served as the place where fallen service members return home and where presidents, military leaders and families gather to honor them.

title: Johnson’s ‘Trump Tailgate’ spurs backlash from Trump team; he calls James endorsement ‘bad advice’
description: Republican gubernatorial candidate Perry Johnson is hosting a “Trump Tailgate” on July 27 — but he’s not endorsed by President Donald Trump, and his branding of the event has him in hot water with the president’s campaign team. Team Trump, the official X account for the Trump campaign, posted in response to the event that “Perry […]
text:
2026 GOP gubernatorial candidates Perry Johnson (left) and John James (right) | Photos by Andrew Roth/Michigan AdvanceRepublican gubernatorial candidate Perry Johnson is hosting a “Trump Tailgate” on July 27 — but he’s not endorsed by President Donald Trump, and his branding of the event has him in hot water with the president’s campaign team.
Team Trump, the official X account for the Trump campaign, posted in response to the event that “Perry Johnson is a NEVER TRUMPER who ran against @realDonaldTrump in the 2024 election,” calling him out for hosting the event with Trump’s name on it when his primary opponent, U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township) received the president’s endorsement.

Perry Johnson is a NEVER TRUMPER who ran against @realDonaldTrump in the 2024 election.
Now in the Michigan governor’s race, he’s hosting a “Trump Tailgate” despite not having the Trump endorsement.@JohnJamesMI is the ONLY Trump-endorsed candidate, a state POTUS won BIG in… https://t.co/9TWpZzSYci
— Team Trump (Text TRUMP to 88022) (@TeamTrump) July 21, 2026

Johnson responded directly to the post, saying, “I love President Trump and proudly support him. I have said time and time again I think he is our greatest President,” before posting an hour later a clip of himself speaking in support of Trump at the 2024 Republican National Convention. A spokesperson for his campaign deferred to that statement in response to a request for additional comment.
“Team Trump’s post pretty much sums it up,” Alyvia Bailey, James’ campaign press secretary, said. “Perry Johnson is a never-Trumper who spent $30 million running against President Trump. President Trump gave his complete and total endorsement to John James. Perry Johnson should stop gaslighting voters.”
James also reposted the Team Trump post with a bullseye emoji in response. 
Johnson’s tailgate is being held the same day — and in the same county — as Trump is expected to hold a rally in Michigan. 
Asked at a news conference about Trump’s event, Johnson doubled down on a sentiment he expressed shortly after the president’s endorsement of James was announced — that he made that decision on bad advice from his team. 
“I think President Trump’s been a very good president. I never would deny that, but he has a group of advisers that often don’t give him the best possible advice,” he told reporters, citing recent primary losses by Trump-endorsed candidates in Georgia and Iowa. 
Perry Johnson speaks to reporters about the impact of utility company donations in elections. July 22, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Johnson has repeatedly referenced the Trump endorsement directly in his criticisms of James on social media — following two debates between Johnson, James and former Attorney General Mike Cox, who has since dropped out of the race, he posted about “Trump endorsed liberal John James.” On the day of Trump’s endorsement, Johnson said that “Trump-backed statewide candidates like John James, Tudor Dixon, Matt DePerno, and Kristina Karamo all came up short when it mattered most.”
Despite those criticisms, he has remained steadfast in his support for the president, including in a debate in early July, when he said that he could not imagine a situation where a Trump administration policy was harming Michigan, but called Trump “very rational” in terms of how he might respond to that scenario. 
Trump’s Monday rally is expected to be in Oakland County — where the county Republican Party’s chair and vice chair, Vance Patrick and Terri Nallamothu, endorsed Johnson in a move that drew the ire of state party leadership. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Patrick and Nallamothu specifically said that their statement was “issued in a personal capacity, not in any official capacity relating to the Oakland County Republican Party,” but Michigan GOP Chairman Sen. Jim Runestad criticized them for invoking their offices in the statement. 
“The spirit of the Oakland County Republican Party bylaws is straightforward: party leadership should remain neutral in contested primaries unless the Executive Committee formally authorizes an endorsement. That protects the grassroots’ right to choose their nominee without interference from those entrusted to lead the organization,” Runestad said in a statement on X. “Every Republican is free to support the candidate of their choice. But when party officers repeatedly invoke their leadership roles and responsibilities to persuade Republican voters, many will reasonably view that as an endorsement from the Chairman and Vice Chair—not simply two private individuals.”
Patrick and Nallamothu to themselves in their endorsement as “leaders of the largest Republican county organization in Michigan,” which Runestad quoted in his own response to emphasize his dissatisfaction with the statement. 
Patrick is also listed as a featured guest at Johnson’s “Trump Tailgate” — which has not been rebranded publicly in spite of the pushback from the president’s team. 
“Perry Johnson doesn’t just have the opportunity to win the governor’s race. He has the opportunity to lift every Republican running alongside him. By continuing to aggressively fund his own campaign while allowing more resources to flow to down-ballot races, Perry can help build the kind of coordinated statewide effort our party needs,” Patrick and Nallamothu said. “As county party leaders, that matters enormously. Our responsibility is not simply to elect a governor. It is to elect Republicans at every level of government, and we believe Perry Johnson gives us the best opportunity to do exactly that.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado health officials still unable to investigate tuberculosis case at ICE detention facility
description: Colorado public health officials are still unable to investigate at least one tuberculosis case at an immigration detention center in Aurora, as the private company that runs the facility missed a deadline to give more information and allow health workers inside the building. “The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment still has not received […[...]
text:
The Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention center in Aurora, operated by private prison firm GEO Group, is pictured on Jan. 30, 2025. (Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Colorado public health officials are still unable to investigate at least one tuberculosis case at an immigration detention center in Aurora, as the private company that runs the facility missed a deadline to give more information and allow health workers inside the building.
“The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment still has not received access to the facility or all of the information needed to determine who may have been exposed and ensure they receive appropriate testing and treatment,” CDPHE spokesperson Hope Shuler wrote in an email. “The Governor and CDPHE leadership have demanded contact with facility leadership multiple times, including sending written questions, and we remain ready to work together to complete the investigation.”
Shuler wrote that lawyers for The GEO Group, the company that operates the detention center for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, have stated that there are no confirmed or suspected cases of tuberculosis at the site, but it is impossible for CDPHE and the Adams County Health Department to verify that claim without a public health contact investigation.
“A complete investigation remains necessary because people who were recently infected may initially test negative,” she wrote.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Colorado law requires public health agencies to investigate confirmed tuberculosis cases. Adams County health officials became aware of one laboratory-confirmed case and issued a public health order on June 25 to require compliance from GEO. CDPHE then gave GEO a July 17 deadline for information and access, which went unanswered.
Immigration advocates press for action on tuberculosis case at Aurora ICE facility

Immigration advocates believe there has been more than one case, and an unnamed person detained in the facility told The Guardian last week that at least 12 people have tested positive for the disease.
Staff from the offices of Rep. Jason Crow of Aurora and Sens. Michael Bennet and John Hickenlooper of Colorado, visited the facility on July 15 and wrote in a report that ICE said it can “deny facility access to local officials as they are a federal facility.” Hickenlooper’s office submitted a formal inquiry with the Department of Homeland Security over the issue, spokesperson Madeleine Hughes said.
During that visit, GEO and ICE staff told the lawmakers there were no active tuberculosis cases at the facility and one person was being monitored. Correspondence to Crow’s office from July 17 also noted that GEO conducted its own contact investigation and identified 61 people exposed to the initial case, according to the report. GEO placed those people in a “precautionary cohort.” The staff members also noted very high temperatures inside the facility, which align with reports from advocates that the air conditioning is not working. Temperatures in the Denver metro area have approached or hit 100 degrees Fahrenheit in recent days.
“ICE is out of control and needs to be reined in,” Crow said in a statement. “When our immigration detention system is driven by corporate greed, it allows corporations like GEO Group to cut corners on medical care and safety to benefit their bottom line.”
An unnamed ICE spokesperson said last week that the facility is complying with Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidelines on communicable diseases.

title: Amore says no signs noncitizens were registered to vote in Rhode Island
description: The same French multinational biometrics technology company behind the motor voter system in New Jersey where a software glitch mistakenly registered 6,600 noncitizens to vote — of whom a few hundred did so — also provides software and equipment for the state of Rhode Island. But Rhode Island Secretary of State Gregg Amore said Wednesday […]
text:
The Rhode Island Division of Motor Vehicles office on Valley Road in Middletown. (Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current)The same French multinational biometrics technology company behind the motor voter system in New Jersey where a software glitch mistakenly registered 6,600 noncitizens to vote — of whom a few hundred did so — also provides software and equipment for the state of Rhode Island.
But Rhode Island Secretary of State Gregg Amore said Wednesday there is no evidence that the state’s system improperly registered noncitizens to vote. Amore said staff from his office had requested a meeting with the Division of Motor Vehicles (DMV) and its vendor to conduct a comprehensive review to ensure no one was improperly registered. The Elections Division has also requested a complete system review with the Division of Motor Vehicles.
“At this time, there is no indication that a similar issue has occurred here,” Amore said in a statement. “The RI Department of State remains confident in the integrity of Rhode Island’s voter rolls.”
Idemia Identity & Security USA LLC, with North American headquarters in Reston, Virginia, was paid nearly $5.2 million between August 2021 and June 2025, according to the state’s Transparency Portal.
The company offers DMV services and equipment, including producing physical driver licenses and ID facial recognition, in over 30 states.
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill revealed Tuesday that about 6,600 noncitizens were registered to vote because of a software glitch in the state’s automatic voter registration system managed by Idemia. The malfunction at the state’s Motor Vehicle Commission mistakenly registered them when they applied for driver’s licenses and identification cards between June 2023 and June 2024.
Fewer than 400 of the people have voted since they were registered to vote, Sherrill said.
Since 2019, the Rhode Island DMV has conducted a regular audit of a randomized selection of driver records to ensure that database entries match paper records, according to the Secretary of State’s office. That process would identify any irregularities in registrations so that they could be immediately rectified, Amore said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Barr sponsors effort to regulate intoxicating hemp-derived products ahead of federal ban
description: U.S. Representative Andy Barr, R-KY, is sponsoring a bipartisan effort, backed by Kentucky’s hemp industry, to regulate intoxicating hemp-derived products ahead of an effective ban of such products spearheaded by Kentucky’s senior U.S. Senator, Mitch McConnell.  The Lawful Hemp Protection Act would create a regulatory framework for consumable hemp products t[...]
text:
A line of THC-infused beverages on a desk before state lawmakers during a committee meeting at the General Assembly. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)U.S. Representative Andy Barr, R-KY, is sponsoring a bipartisan effort, backed by Kentucky’s hemp industry, to regulate intoxicating hemp-derived products ahead of an effective ban of such products spearheaded by Kentucky’s senior U.S. Senator, Mitch McConnell. 
The Lawful Hemp Protection Act would create a regulatory framework for consumable hemp products that have tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, the intoxicating compound that gives users a “high” feeling when consumed. 
Last year, McConnell successfully passed a provision into federal law that bans hemp-deprived products containing more than 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container, what hemp industry advocates and U.S. Sen. Rand Paul decried as a ban on a growing market for intoxicating hemp-derived edibles, beverages and other consumables. 
McConnell had said he wanted to close a loophole created with his legalization of industrial hemp through the 2018 Farm Bill that allowed companies to market intoxicating hemp-derived products to children. His provision for intoxicating hemp-derived products would go into effect in November. 
Barr’s bill, supported by Democratic Minnesota U.S. Rep. Angie Craig, would allow the sale of such products with three distinctions: Sales would be limited to those 21 years of age and older, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration would be tasked with setting limits on THC amounts per hemp-derived product, and the advertising of such products to children would be prohibited. 
In a statement, Barr said his Lawful Hemp Protection Act protects “Kentucky agriculture, safeguards consumers, and establishes a commonsense regulatory framework that allows this important industry to continue to grow while ensuring products are safe and kept out of the hands of children.
“Kentucky has demonstrated that hemp can be successfully regulated while supporting farmers and protecting consumers,” Barr said. “This legislation builds on that success by creating a national framework that rewards responsible producers, eliminates bad actors, and ensures consumers have confidence in the products they purchase.”
The bill has the backing of hemp industry groups including the Kentucky Hemp Association and the Wine and Spirits Wholesalers Association, according to a release from Barr’s office. 
Dee Dee Taylor, the president of the Kentucky Hemp Association, in a statement also called for an extension of the November deadline of the effective ban on such products. 
“An extension will give lawmakers the time needed to build a durable federal framework that protects public health, respects successful state regulatory programs like Kentucky’s, and preserves economic opportunities for American agriculture,” Taylor said.

text:
U.S. Senate candidate David Costello ended his bid for the Democratic nomination on July 22, throwing his support behind Troy Jackson. (Official campaign photo)Troy Jackson’s presumptive Democratic U.S. Senate nomination became even more likely Wednesday, as one of the two other remaining candidates withdrew from the race. 
David Costello, who reentered the race after losing to previous nominee Graham Platner in the June primary, announced he was dropping out Wednesday morning. 
“Based on the delegate makeup, there is no realistic path forward,” he said in a statement to Maine Morning Star. “We’ll be supporting Troy Jackson going forward.”
Costello confirmed he has officially withdrawn with the Maine Democratic Party. Political newcomer Saundra Pelletier, who works in the pharmaceutical industry, remains on the ballot alongside Jackson. 
Costello’s exit follows nearly all other candidates dropping out over the weekend, when it became clear the delegates each county selected to send to the nominating convention were overwhelmingly supporters of Jackson, the former Maine Senate president and logger from Allagash, who came in third in the Democratic gubernatorial primary last month.  
The Maine Democratic Party will be replacing Platner, who dropped out after an accusation of sexual assault earlier this month, thorugh a convention on Saturday in Bangor, where 601 delegates will vote. Of that total, 101 are members of the party’s state committee and 500 were chosen from the counties this past weekend.  
Of the 500, 478 are aligned with Jackson, based on a comparison of the results and a list of supportive delegates Jackson’s campaign released. However, delegates are not pledged to any one candidate and can vote for whoever they’d like to at the convention.

text:
DoorJame #6 will feature four local bands, vendors and food on July 25 in downtown Wilmington
By George D. Rotsch, Editor of Delaware LIVE
WILMINGTON, Del. — The Queen will take live music beyond its theater doors July 25, closing part of Market Street for a free outdoor concert featuring four local bands.
DoorJame #6 will take place on the 500 block of North Market Street outside The Queen. The event will feature performances by The Headies, Death by Indie, The Recusants and New Habit, along with local vendors and a food truck.
Attendees are encouraged to bring chairs and spend the day enjoying music in the heart of downtown Wilmington. Admission is free.
The lineup highlights Wilmington’s independent music scene. Death by Indie is a Wilmington-based art-rock band, while The Recusants are an emerging local band featured as part of the Wilmington Music Festival. New Habit also performed at the Wilmington Music Festival, giving the DoorJame lineup another connection to the city’s broader music scene.
The outdoor format allows The Queen to accommodate music fans, families and visitors who may not regularly attend a ticketed indoor concert. It also gives emerging musicians and small vendors an opportunity to reach a larger downtown audience.
The Queen, located at 500 N. Market St., is one of Wilmington’s principal live entertainment venues. Its schedule includes local performers, national touring acts, tribute concerts, comedy and community programming.
Events such as DoorJame also help bring foot traffic to Market Street, where restaurants, shops and other businesses can benefit from people gathering downtown.
By eliminating the cost of admission and moving the performances outdoors, The Queen is making live music accessible to people who might not otherwise purchase concert tickets. The block-party atmosphere also gives visitors room to bring chairs, visit vendors, buy food and stay for multiple performances.
The event continues The Queen’s role as both a concert venue and a platform for Wilmington-area artists. For emerging bands such as The Recusants and New Habit, appearing at a Queen-sponsored event offers exposure to new listeners and an opportunity to perform as part of a professionally organized downtown program.
