name: Mississippi Today
title: Beaches closed as Tropical Storm Bertha crawls along the Gulf Coast
description: This NOAA satellite image taken at 11:40 a.m. EDT on Wednesday, July 22, 2026, shows Tropical Storm Bertha in the Gulf of Mexico. (NOAA via AP)
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Tropical Storm Bertha was creeping along the Gulf Coast toward the edge of Louisiana on Wednesday, spinning off strong winds far from its center and closing beaches from Florida to Mississippi.
The wind and storm surge were the main threats for the Deep South states. Parks and piers were closed up and down the coast, as were some low-lying roads. A tropical storm warning stretched from parts of the Florida Panhandle over to Louisiana, including metropolitan New Orleans and Lake Pontchartrain, National Hurricane Center said.
Landfall, expected later Wednesday, was a lesser threat.
“Landfall really doesn’t have a whole lot of meaning in this particular case,” said Robbie Berg, a warning coordination meteorologist at the hurricane center.
READ MORE: Getting ready for the 2026 hurricane season
Tropical storm force winds extended about 100 miles from the center of the storm, the hurricane center said. Bertha was centered about 55 miles northeast of the mouth of the Mississippi River by mid-morning. It was moving west at 6 mph with maximum sustained winds of 50 mph.
Storm surges up to 4 feet were possible in Louisiana from the Mississippi River mouth to the Alabama-Mississippi state line, forecasters said. Rain totals were forecast between 2 to 4 inches, with higher amounts possible in isolated areas.
Elsewhere in the U.S. this week, a line of storms generated reports of tornadoes stretching from Cincinnati to New Jersey. Torrential rains caused flash floods Tuesday night that swamped homes, washed out bridges and led to water rescues in West Virginia, authorities said.
Sandbag distribution sites are set up
Authorities in Mississippi, Louisiana and Florida opened sites to provide sandbags to residents who may be impacted by Tropical Storm Bertha. Double-red flag warnings were posted along some beaches, closing them to swimmers.
“For locals, this is just another storm,” said Candice Henderson, manager of the Crab Trap, a beachside restaurant that was packed Tuesday on Pensacola, Florida’s Perdido Key. “When you’re on vacation and it’s raining, you either shop or you go out to eat.”
Bertha is the second tropical storm of Atlantic season
Bertha is the second tropical storm of the Atlantic hurricane season. Tropical Storm Arthur in June brought heavy rainfall to the southeastern U.S.
Bertha could dump heavy rain on coastal areas of Mississippi that are still recovering from flooding brought by Arthur that destroyed and damaged homes.
Hurricane Fausto in the Pacific is far from land
In the eastern Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Fausto churned far from land Wednesday. The hurricane was hundreds of miles west-southwest of the southern tip of Baja California with maximum sustained winds of 80 mph.
It was forecast to gradually strengthen and the hurricane center warned that ocean swells generated by Fausto could cause life-threatening surf and rip tide conditions on the Baja California coast.
___
Associated Press journalists Julie Walker in New York and Kim Chandler in Montgomery, Alabama, contributed to this report.

name: VTDigger
title: Brattleboro weighs a municipal tax hike to aid the local hospital’s endangered birthing center
description:
The selectboard may hold a special Town Meeting to ask residents to help subsidize a facility that’s losing money due to cost and staffing challenges and declining births.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Brattleboro weighs a municipal tax hike to aid the local hospital’s endangered birthing center.
text:
A crowd of about 100 people rally July 14 in support of the birthing center at Brattleboro Memorial Hospital. Photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger
BRATTLEBORO — As medical groups call for higher state reimbursements to help Brattleboro Memorial Hospital’s birthing center stay open, local leaders are debating whether to ask residents to assist by raising municipal taxes for an unspecified donation.
“The choice belongs to the taxpayer, and it’s one that deserves an open, transparent and thoughtful public discussion,” Selectboard member Peter Case told his colleagues Tuesday of hopes to hold a special Town Meeting as early as September. “Property values, economic development, emergency care, physician recruitment and the community’s ability to attract young families all depend on a strong hospital.”
The not-for-profit regional healthcare hub, facing a projected $14.5 million overall budget deficit after recent management upheaval, announced July 1 it would close obstetric services within the next six to nine months if it can’t find a way to cover estimated unit losses of $4.8 million this fiscal year.
“The BMH Birthing Center’s financial challenges stem from structural issues that affect rural hospitals across Vermont, including inadequate reimbursement for obstetrical services, declining birth volumes and rising costs,” the hospital said in a statement Wednesday. “These are challenges that require both immediate assistance and long-term policy solutions.”
In a letter released this week, seven medical groups representing 3,000 Vermont clinicians urged Gov. Phil Scott and the state Agency of Human Services to help the hospital by raising Medicaid obstetric reimbursement rates to match those paid for other primary care services.
Medicaid pays for nearly half of Windham County births, the groups noted — a ratio higher than the state average of 36.9%.
“The Department of Vermont Health Access has the authority to increase reimbursement for these services immediately,” wrote the heads of the Vermont Medical Society, Vermont Academy of Family Physicians, Vermont Nurse Practitioners Association, Planned Parenthood of Northern New England and state branches of the American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Nurse-Midwives and American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.
The state has received the letter but has yet to respond, an Agency of Human Services spokesperson told VTDigger Tuesday afternoon.
For its part, the five-member Brattleboro Selectboard voted unanimously Tuesday night to explore holding a special Town Meeting to consider a tax hike to aid the birthing center.
Local leaders haven’t discussed a specific proposed sum above their current $27 million annual budget, although Town Manager John Potter offered a memo Tuesday with a potential range of $100,000 to $1 million.
“The model we’re talking about here would be a one-time special assessment that would not be baked into the budget going forward,” Selectboard Chair Oscar Heller said.
The hospital is the only Vermont facility providing obstetrical services in Windham and Windsor counties, with the nearest alternatives located in New Hampshire at Cheshire Medical Center in Keene and Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center in Lebanon.
Rural hospitals in Vermont and nationwide have cut birthing services in recent years, including Copley Hospital in Morrisville and Springfield Hospital. 
Brattleboro hospital officials weren’t present at Tuesday’s selectboard meeting.
“The willingness of the selectboard to explore every available option, including potential municipal support, reflects the deep value our community places on ensuring families can continue to access labor and delivery services close to home,” the hospital said in a statement Wednesday. “We continue to pursue a comprehensive solution that includes state support, philanthropy and other sustainable funding opportunities.”
Several residents at Tuesday’s meeting questioned the usefulness of a tax hike, noting a hospital-distributed list of talking points said “while one-time grants are helpful and appreciated, they do not address the ongoing structural funding gap.”
Residents also said the town has yet to address its own costly problems, be it repairing infrastructure or replacing its aging public works garage and public swimming pool — each carrying multimillion-dollar price tags.

READ MORE

“We cannot afford to fund what the municipality needs,” said Dick DeGray, a former selectboard chair who voiced the belief that many people rallying for the birthing center were citing more fears than facts. “This has become a heart issue, not a head issue. We need to do our homework.” 
Real estate agent Susan Bellville asked local leaders to seek financial help from the 21 other towns in Vermont, New Hampshire and Massachusetts that rely on the facility.
“It makes absolutely no sense for Brattleboro to be standing there attempting to raise money to help the hospital when we have absolutely no buy-in from anybody else who uses it,” Bellville said.
The selectboard has yet to publicize another session on the matter, although members suggested Tuesday they could schedule a follow-up discussion for as early as next week.
Residents have expressed growing frustration with local spending. A year ago, Brattleboro defeated a proposed municipal budget for the first time in its Town Meeting history, rejecting a $25 million initial plan that would have raised taxes 12.1%. This spring, residents approved the current municipal budget’s 6.3% tax increase only after considering a call for level funding.
“If we keep raising taxes,” resident Randy Blodgett said in proposing the lower number earlier this year, “when do we break people’s backs?”

title: Trump administration claims court victory in mandatory detention
description: The Trump administration claimed a rare court victory for its embattled immigration detention policy when an appeals court, covering three states with large detention centers, agreed to stay court rulings that freed three Texas immigrants during an appeal.  The 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, in a terse Jan. 21 ruling, agreed to stay three Texas […]
text:
Louisiana State Police and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement make an arrest last year. A federal appeals court covering Louisiana, Mississippi and Texas delivered a rare court victory for the Trump administration’s mandatory detention policy. (Photo courtesy of ICE)The Trump administration claimed a rare court victory for its embattled immigration detention policy when an appeals court, covering three states with large detention centers, agreed to stay court rulings that freed three Texas immigrants during an appeal. 
The 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, in a terse Jan. 21 ruling, agreed to stay three Texas court rulings that freed men who have no criminal record, and U.S. citizen children, who had arrived in the U.S. illegally years ago. The decision applies to Louisiana, Mississippi and Texas, where many immigrants from around the country are transferred in the latest escalation of immigration arrests. The next step in their cases is a court hearing Sept. 24. 
Brett Shumate, a U.S. assistant attorney general, called the ruling “an extraordinary precedential order making clear that illegal aliens do not have a constitutional right to roam free in the United States during their removal proceedings” in a social media post early Wednesday.  
Flouting Trump policy, federal judges are freeing immigrants from mandatory detention

That assessment met skepticism in a post from Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a senior fellow at the American Immigration Council, which defended the immigrants in court. 
“It’s an unreasoned stay order. In what world is that precedential?” Reichlin-Melnick wrote in a post. The Trump administration had asked for  a “precedential” ruling to help stop what it called a “flood” of federal court cases freeing immigrants held under the policy.  
The new detention policy, implemented in a July 2025 memo, threatens millions of immigrants with imprisonment without bond if they crossed a border illegally to get into the United States, no matter how long ago or whether they’ve applied for asylum. Without bond means they must be detained while awaiting court action.
The policy is a key part of the Trump administration’s stated goal to get to 1 million removals a year, including deportations and voluntary returns.
Statistics released July 20 by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement show about 2,000 detainees a month have been freed by court-ordered bond hearings. Many federal judges, even Trump appointees, have ruled against the Trump administration’s policy of mandatory detention for many immigrants. The U.S. Supreme Court is likely to rule on the legality of the policy in its October term. 
Other courts have treated the detention policy differently, resulting in wildly different results across the country. A California class action case ruled the policy unconstitutional, requiring bond hearings for the immigrants. During an appeal, it only applies to the Los Angeles area, though judges in other states have cited the ruling to free immigrants or grant them bond hearings.  A Nevada court made a similar ruling in March. 
Appeals courts covering 10 states have ruled the detention policy is unconstitutional without a class-action designation that could make it applicable nationwide.  Meanwhile the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, covering Arkansas and several Midwestern states, also upheld the Trump policy, helping to set up a Supreme Court case to settle the issue in the fall term.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: State Police gets funding boost for cadet classes in new spending plan
description: Pennsylvania’s new budget includes $16.2 million to train new state troopers and grow the ranks of the state police.
text:
A State Police vehicle equipped with new lights and sirens in their Harrisburg transportation building on Jan. 29, 2026. (Photo by Ian Karbal/Capital-Star) Emily Scolnick is a 2026 Dow Jones News Fund intern at the Pennsylvania Capital-Star. 
Pennsylvania’s new budget includes $16.2 million to train new state troopers and grow the ranks of the state police. Funding for the law enforcement agency has been included in each of Gov. Josh Shapiro’s four budgets, allocating a combined $63 million in funding for four new training classes each year. 
More than 600 cadets have joined the department since Shapiro took office, according to a release from the state police. The governor made a campaign promise to add 2,000 troopers during his first term. 
This year’s allocation covers training for four cadet classes, totaling 380 troopers. The agency will also receive a $4.5 million increase for its information technology and statewide radio systems, which help the police communicate and respond to emergencies of all kinds across the commonwealth. 
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Funding remained flat for the agency training programs for municipal police departments, vehicle inspection, fingerprint identification, and firearm background check programs. 
“Protecting the communities within our Commonwealth is at the foundation of everything we do,” Lieutenant Colonel George L. Bivens, acting state police commissioner, said in a statement. “Funding from this budget continues to deliver real results, ensuring our members have the resources available to meet the challenges of policing in today’s society.”
About 67% of the state’s 2,554 municipalities rely on full- or part-time state police coverage, a number that has remained fairly static in recent years. 
However, the number of communities that troopers provide full-time coverage for has slightly increased over the past five years, according to a state police spokesperson.
The state’s complex hiring process for boroughs and first class townships, as well as financial pressures that make municipal police forces harder to support have been driving that trend, according to Logan Stover, the policy and legislative director for the Pennsylvania State Association of Boroughs. 
“Oftentimes, newly graduated officers are more likely to work in a 2nd Class Township because they do not have to go through the long hiring process that is required in boroughs,” he wrote in an email. “This leads to a distinct disadvantage for boroughs attempting to hire full-time officers.” 
Advocates have pushed for reforms to the state’s Civil Service process, which requires multiple rounds of testing during a hiring process that can take up to nine months, Stover said.  
And as the costs of infrastructure projects and fire and emergency services increase, “the financial pressure of providing a full-time police department on a municipality’s budget could be another factor leading to increased reliance on PSP coverage,” he added. 
In 2023, the Shapiro administration eliminated the college credit requirement for applicants seeking to join the state police. Since then, applications have increased by 69%. 
Violent crime and homicides have decreased by 16% and 39%, respectively, during the same timeframe, according to a state police release.

title: Troy Jackson has already raised more than $1 million for Senate bid, campaign says
description: Presumptive Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson announced he’s raised more than  $1 million since he entered the race earlier this month.  That’s essentially equivalent to the total he’d raised throughout his previous months-long bid to be the Democratic gubernatorial nominee. However, it is still a far cry from the $11 million cash on hand […]
text:
Troy Jackson looks at results on a projector on election night (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)Presumptive Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson announced he’s raised more than  $1 million since he entered the race earlier this month. 
That’s essentially equivalent to the total he’d raised throughout his previous months-long bid to be the Democratic gubernatorial nominee. However, it is still a far cry from the $11 million cash on hand incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins reported as of the last filing deadline.
Since launching his bid for U.S. Senate, Jackson has received 27,283 contributions from 24,669 individual donors, according to his campaign, which did not respond to questions about these donations, such as the state of origin or average size.  
Those details are not yet publicly available as the latest Federal Elections Commission filings are from before former nominee Graham Platner exited the race following an accusation of sexual assault that led Democrats, including Jackson who had previously rallied alongside Platner, to call for him to drop out. Jackson swiftly entered the race to replace him. 
Over $613,000 of the more than $1 million his Senate campaign has raised came in since Sunday, which is when it became apparent Jackson had secured the majority of delegates that will be officially selecting the new nominee on Saturday in Bangor. 
The Maine Democratic Party decided to replace Platner through a convention of 601 delegates — 500 chosen from the counties and 101 being members of the party’s state committee. Of the 500 chosen from each county over the weekend, 478 are aligned with Jackson, based on a comparison of the results and a list of supportive delegates Jackson’s campaign released. 
However, delegates are not pledged to any one candidate and can vote for whoever they’d like to at the convention. Only two other contenders remain in the running: David Costello and Saundra Pelletier.
The latest state campaign finance filings due Tuesday show Jackson still has about $156,000 cash on hand for his gubernatorial campaign, however by law he is barred from using any of that money in his new bid for a federal office.

title: Walz skips specifics in new ‘Lynne’s Commitment to Nebraskans’ platform in governor’s race
description: LINCOLN — Former State Sen. Lynne Walz, Nebraska’s Democratic nominee for governor, unveiled her platform and day-one commitments Wednesday should she unseat Republican Gov. Jim Pillen, while sidestepping specifics at times about what they would look like. The proposed “Lynne’s Commitment to Nebraskans” offers aspirations for the early days, long-term priori[...]
text:
Former State Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont hosts her ninth listening session in Lincoln as part of her 2026 exploratory bid for governor. She plans to finalize a decision whether to run in early 2026. Dec. 13, 2025. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Former State Sen. Lynne Walz, Nebraska’s Democratic nominee for governor, unveiled her platform and day-one commitments Wednesday should she unseat Republican Gov. Jim Pillen, while sidestepping specifics at times about what they would look like.
The proposed “Lynne’s Commitment to Nebraskans” offers aspirations for the early days, long-term priorities and values for her administration should she win her uphill bid for governor. These range from addressing Nebraska’s growing deficit, a change from a $1.2 billion surplus four years ago to more than $750 million in the hole, to carrying out the legalization and regulation of medical cannabis as voters demanded in 2024.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen of Columbus, a Republican at center, is running for reelection against former Democratic State Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, left, and Rick Beard of Omaha, the nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW party. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
In a Monday interview with the Nebraska Examiner ahead of the rollout, she at times struggled to name specifics on what some of her commitments would look like.
“I don’t have the specifics, just to be honest with you, on how we’re going to do each of these actions,” Walz said. “I just know that these are actions that we want to put in motion on day one.”
Day One promises
Her listed day one actions are to:

Restore fiscal discipline, transparency and accountability in the governor’s office.
Declare Nebraska “open for business again.”
Assemble working groups of industry and community leaders to craft a 10-year, comprehensive plan to grow the economy.
Declare Nebraska as “agriculture and livestock friendly” and develop an agricultural advisory council.
Call on the Legislature to restore $3 million to the Veterans’ Aid Fund cut this spring. The fund provides temporary aid to veterans, spouses and dependants when an emergency disrupts their “normal method of living” and other resources aren’t immediately available, according to the Nebraska Department of Veterans’ Affairs.
Sign an executive order immediately legalizing medical cannabis with a doctor’s prescription and fire members of the voter-created Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission if they “can’t pass meaningful regulations in a timely manner that accurately reflect what Nebraskans voted for.”
Reject “any and all forms” of school vouchers, whether state or federal dollars, that subsidize attendance costs for students in private schools.
Hire an independent auditor to investigate waste, fraud and abuse of power.

The former two-term state lawmaker from Fremont also pledged to hold unscripted town halls statewide and appoint Republicans, Democrats and nonpartisans to cabinet posts. She also has said she would “absolutely” debate her opponents this year. Pillen has said he won’t.
A ‘resources’ divide
Walz, at multiple times in the interview, said she didn’t have all the answers and noted there would be a transition period if she defeated Pillen. She noted Pillen has more resources, alluding to his incumbency and his raising of more than $12 million in the last four years. He had more than $9.6 million in his campaign account by mid-June, compared to about $674,000 for Walz.
Walz talks priorities, pivot from Nebraska primary election to Nov. 3 faceoff

Walz has been outpacing all former Democratic candidates for the office in fundraising since at least 2002, though, based on available records. The last Democrat to win the governor’s race was Ben Nelson, who was reelected to a second term in 1994. He is also the last Democrat to win any statewide office, in 2006, in his reelection to a second and final term in the U.S. Senate.
If Walz had the same resources as Pillen, she said, it would “make this conversation a lot easier, but I just don’t.”
Results of a listening tour
Walz said the ideas are the result of a listening tour from what started initially as an “exploratory” bid for governor. She toured the state with a big poster board and would write down voters’ ideas at each stop on what was important to them.
“I wanted to make sure that people knew I was listening and that I am making a commitment to people that we will continue to listen, that we’ll work together and that we will really focus on the priorities that people talked about, what really matters to them and their families,” Walz said.
Pillen talks priorities, pivot from Nebraska primary election to Nov. 3 faceoff

She has explained her lines in the sand around the state budget, such as no across-the-board cuts, which she calls “irresponsible and lazy leadership,” and to always ponder downstream effects. Asked to define what fiscal discipline, transparency and accountability would look like, she said it is about values of honesty, transparency and working hard and being a role model for respect and kindness.
Walz pledged to release her public schedule, a practice previous governors followed but that Pillen didn’t adopt when he took office in 2023, and she criticized his office for saying he doesn’t have a state-issued phone and refusing to hand over records around his cellphone use, as first reported by the Flatwater Free Press. His office has sought to downplay that reporting.
Opponents respond
Taylor Sliva, Pillen’s campaign manager, said Wednesday that the governor is a “proven common-sense leader with a record of results,” which he said includes historic tax cuts, protecting farmers and natural resources, investing more money “than ever before” in K-12 education and ending corporate welfare for “Big Tech” data centers.
Sliva said Walz’s record, by contrast, “is wrong for Nebraskans.”
When Pillen’s team made similar arguments when she launched her campaign in January, a spokesperson said the governor’s team was distracting from the “real issues that matter.”
On Walz calling Pillen’s budget handling “irresponsible and lazy,” Sliva also fired back.
“Jim’s never been called lazy in his life,” Sliva said. “From raising his kids and grandkids to running a family farm to traveling this state to address everything from property taxes, wildfire recovery and honoring our veterans. Jim Pillen’s working overtime to serve the state he loves.”
Rick Beard of Omaha, a Legal Marijuana NOW candidate for Nebraska governor, meets with voters at a developmental disabilities community listening event on April 30, 2026, in Lincoln. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Rick Beard of Omaha, the nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW party, described Walz’s platform as a “real soft, word-salad approach to this campaign in the situation that we’re all in.”
He criticized her for ignoring topics he feels candidates should address, such as a moratorium on data centers, community surveillance, getting money out of politics, the Israel-Iran war, Islamophobia and Pillen’s comments about Palestinians or Nebraska wildfires. He said she also avoids the tax potential of medicinal cannabis and that the medicine is already legal.
“It’s just a very safe, typical Democrat approach to this whole thing,” Beard said Wednesday. “It’s a nice letter, but it really doesn’t say anything and doesn’t really have a plan.”
Former State Sen. Brett Lindstrom, a registered nonpartisan from Omaha, launched a petition drive seeking to be the fourth candidate on the ballot. His signature deadline is Aug. 3.
Taxes and medical cannabis
Pillen has made property tax relief a key tenet of his platform, which the former Husker defensive back dubbed “The Pillen Playbook.” Pillen sees expanded property tax relief achieved through expanded sales taxes. Walz, too, said voters in her former Dodge County-based Legislative District 15 called for reform to property taxes above all, not sales or income taxes.
Walz said she wouldn’t follow Pillen’s approach to add sales taxes to pay for relief. As for how she’d address property taxes, she still hasn’t specified her own approach but has said the state needs to grow its economy as a way to expand relief.
Commissioners on the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission during an April 13, 2026, meeting. From left, Commissioners Bud Synhorst of Lincoln, Jim Elworth of Nebraska City, Lorelle Mueting of Gretna (interim chair) and J. Michael Coffey of Omaha. All but Mueting also serve on the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
She said she would meet with all 49 state senators to understand their priorities and build a plan together focused on “finding common sense solutions for those pressing issues.” She also wants to bring together “industry leaders” to craft one-year, five-year and 10-year growth plans.
“We’re excited to showcase Nebraska as being the heart of the country,” Walz said, saying the state should be number one in a variety of industries.
Currently, state law already legalizes possession of up to 5 ounces of medical cannabis with a physician’s recommendation. Walz pledged an executive order to “immediately” do the same. 
Asked specifically what her order would do or add, she said she didn’t have “all the answers.”
In a follow-up statement, Walz said she doesn’t have a “personal wishlist” but that regulations “should be rooted in science and compassion to help those who would benefit from this medicine.”
Said Walz: “I want to make sure we have commissioners in place that believe in this medicine and medical experts in the room to ensure our patients who are suffering from cancer, PTSD, epilepsy and other serious conditions get the medicine they need and in the form that works best for them. Right now the proposals are so restrictive that families are telling me this is not what they voted for.”
Advocates for medical cannabis join together before a public hearing at the Nebraska State Office Building in Lincoln, Nebraska, on state-drafted regulations for the new medicine approved by Nebraska voters in November 2024. Oct. 15, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The state commission, as voters approved in 2024, consists of the three members of the Liquor Control Commission and up to two at-large members. All five are gubernatorial appointees.
Beard said while Walz talks about new businesses, “she doesn’t mention the one thing that’s the biggest thing that we can do” with medical cannabis.
Pillen has made clear that he’ll only support a tightly regulated system that has zero chance of allowing recreational marijuana, which longtime advocates have sharply criticized.
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers, a former senator who served with Walz for six years, has been more critical of medical cannabis in general and voters’ 2024 approval. The Nebraska Supreme Court hasn’t yet ruled in a Hilgers-led case challenging the validity of the laws.
Asked how she would work with Hilgers should he win reelection, or his Democratic opponent, former Assistant Attorney General Jocelyn Brasher, Walz spoke broadly.
“I guess I have a hard time understanding, to be honest with you, that when the people have spoken, the people have spoken,” Walz said. “I just think it’s our job as government in general to uphold the will of the people first and foremost.”
Schools and audits
In a similar vein, Walz again confirmed she would reject any federal or state program seeking to offset costs of attendance at private schools. Voters rejected a $10 million program in 2024, the second version to be put into law. 
Walz, as a lawmaker, did not take a position on supporting either of two “school choice” laws in 2023 or 2024, but she’s been in firm opposition since the statewide vote.
Pillen was the first governor to sign up for a new federal tax credit program beginning in January, which would allow people to donate up to $1,700 to scholarship-granting organizations nationwide to support private, public and home school students. U.S. Rep. Adrian Smith, R-Neb., ushered that federal program into law.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, center, smiles with local private school students after ceremoniously signing a proclamation for “National School Choice Week” in the state. Jan. 28, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Walz said Nebraskans were clear and that she would reject the program outright. Pillen has said he’ll continue seeking to ensure all K-12 students are in a school that is the “right fit” for them.
To Walz’s pledge for an independent auditor, she said Auditor of Public Accounts Mike Foley is doing a “great job, impeccable” and has a major duty to look at fraud and abuse not just within the state but for all political subdivisions.
Foley, the lieutenant governor under former Gov. Pete Ricketts, is running unopposed for what would be his fourth nonconsecutive term this fall.
“He is doing a great job, but he’s one person,” Walz said.
Walz said her hire would look for waste, fraud and abuse but also note what is and isn’t working. She says that’s especially important to fix the “Pillen budget crisis.”
“It’s really going to be important for us to evaluate where cuts should happen and what long-term negative effects they may have that will make the problem worse,” Walz said. “We’re bringing in someone to help us fix the budget crisis.”
Addressing a ‘budget crisis’
Pillen, in an interview last week, had a simple message for those criticizing his handling of the budget and slashing income taxes during his first year in office: “Thank you.”
He touted Nebraska earning an AAA rating from Moody’s, a global financial risk assessment firm, in 2025 and 2026. It is the highest Nebraska has ever received.
“Nebraskans were sick of continuing to have more and more taxes,” Pillen said. “… Our budget’s in great shape. … So, yeah, I’ll take credit for that. Thank you.”
State lawmakers gather on the final day of Nebraska’s 2026 legislative session. Not pictured: State Sens. Jana Hughes of Seward and Dan Quick of Grand Island. April 17, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The Veterans’ Affairs agency head, appointed by Pillen, supported cuts to the Veterans’ Aid Fund and said it wouldn’t hurt services. Pillen has said that’s how he’s tasked his team to approach cuts. Multiple veterans’ advocacy groups urged lawmakers to reconsider.
“We want to restore the funds to their previous level so that veterans and their families are taken care of when they face emergencies,” Walz said in a statement. “These veterans have given so much for our country, the least we can do is help them in their time of need.”
Walz’s team plans to release more details on her platform in the coming month in two installments. 
Each batch will include three components from among the following: addressing the “Pillen budget crisis,” fixing Nebraska’s “broken tax system,” growing Nebraska communities and business, growing agriculture, supporting Nebraskans and restoring good governance.
“Today, I’m making a commitment to Nebraskans that I will stay focused on the issues that matter most in your everyday life,” Walz said in a letter accompanying her platform. “I will work tirelessly to better the lives of all Nebraskans.”

title: Republican challenger narrowly outraises NM US Rep. Vasquez, but trails with cash on hand
description: New campaign finance reports show that the campaign for an Albuquerque Republican challenging incumbent U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) in the Nov. 3 general election has narrowly raised more money than his opponent, although Vasquez’s campaign has a strong cash-on-hand advantage.
text:
Greg Cunningham, an Albuquerque Republican challenging incumbent U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.), raised just shy of $1,000 more than Vasquez in the second quarter of this year, but significantly trails him in terms of cash on hand. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)New campaign finance reports show that the campaign for an Albuquerque Republican challenging incumbent U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) in the Nov. 3 general election has narrowly raised more money than his opponent, although Vasquez’s campaign has a strong cash-on-hand advantage.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The latest campaign finance filings, which cover April through June, offer a glimpse into a competitive race for a district that represents much of southern New Mexico and a portion of Albuquerque. Vasquez first won election to the 2nd Congressional District seat, which was previously held by Republican Yvette Herrell, in 2022 by less than one percentage point. 
Greg Cunningham, the Republican nominee who handily won his party’s primary for the race after his opponent bowed out, announced that he raised nearly $902,000 in the second quarter of this year — just shy of $1,000 more than Vasquez. Vasquez’s campaign has about three times the amount of cash on hand, though.
“There are some individuals and organizations who feel that CD 2 will be a competitive race. Usually, people don’t like to contribute money unless they feel like the candidate has a shot,” Brian Sanderoff, president of the Albuquerque-based firm Research and Polling Inc., told Source NM.
Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham signed off on redrawn congressional districts in late 2021, following the 2020 U.S. Census. That redistricting introduced portions of Albuquerque, which Sanderoff said are considered Democratic strongholds, into the otherwise rural district.
“Greg Cunningham does have one challenge to address in whether the mood of the nation could impact his competitiveness…most analysts feel the Democrats will flip the U.S. House,” Sanderoff said. “His strategy is going to have to be to cut his losses in Bernalillo County.”
Cunningham in a statement announcing his fundraising efforts said he believes the latest fundraising reports show that district residents want “a Congressman who actually shows up for them, not a far-left radical like Gabe Vasquez who voted to raise taxes on families and against securing our border.”
“New Mexico deserves better, and this quarter proves our district is ready to flip,” he wrote.
Vasquez’s campaign manager, Patricia Socarras Santiago, in a statement to Source NM, wrote that Cunningham has shown an allegiance to President Donald Trump and raised hundreds of thousands of dollars in “MAGA money.”
“New Mexicans cannot be bought off and they deserve someone who is actually fighting for them,” she wrote. “That fighter has always been Gabe Vasquez, and that’s why New Mexicans will re-elect him in November.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Nolan Xavier Wells’ independent autopsy can’t rule out foul play
description: Friends and family of Nolan Xavier Wells gather for his funeral at Center Pointe Church in Ocean Springs on Monday, July 20, 2026.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
An independent pathologist said he could not rule out foul play in the death of Nolan Xavier Wells and urged further investigation is needed to answer multiple lingering questions, according to his autopsy released Wednesday.
Dr. Roger Mitchell Jr. wrote in his July 19 report released at a news conference in Chicago that he encountered multiple challenges when he examined the body of the 18-year-old, whose death has received national attention. 
Wells, who was Black, traveled by boat to Horn Island in the Gulf Coast with a mostly white group of friends on the Fourth of July. Video from that day showed a mostly white crowd on the barrier island. 
“For these reasons, this pathologist cannot rule out if any intervening, nonaccidental factors contributed to or caused the death of Nolan Wells,” said attorney Ben Crump, reading Mitchell’s report results during the news conference at the NAACP national convention in Chicago. 
“He said, based on examination of the body, he cannot rule out foul play. This is significant.”
Mitchell noted decomposition of the body made it difficult to tell whether there were bruises or abrasions on his skin. 
He also said he was unable to examine Wells’ airway and lungs for the presence of water and his stomach for its contents. Mitchell said he did not receive parts of Wells’ throat, leading him to say that he can’t rule out a neck injury as a contributor to Wells’ cause of death.
Mitchell performed the independent autopsy in Washington, paid for by former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick, whose organization has an initiative to provide free autopsies for people who died in custody of law enforcement, corrections officers or immigration officials. 
Monday, after Wells’ funeral, Crump said weather delayed the transport of Wells’ body for the independent autopsy. Mitchell also received the body nearly a week after the state had completed its autopsy. 
It is not known whether the independent autopsy findings match or contradict those determined by the state. 
The State Medical Examiner’s Office completed its autopsy July 7, but has not released the findings report because some test results including toxicology are still pending, Jackson County Coroner Bruce Lynd Jr. said Tuesday. The state will provide the report to the local coroner’s office, but Lynd said release of results would have to come from the prosecutor’s office.
Neither Jackson County District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath, who met with the family last week, nor a representative in her office responded to a request for comment.
The Jackson County Sheriff’s Department has provided limited information about its investigation and has not responded to Missisisppi Today’s requests for comment. Sheriff John Ledbetter has told ABC News he suspects Wells drowned, even though the investigation remains open. 
In suspected drowning deaths, it is important to confirm how a person entered the water. Mitchell said he wasn’t able to see the condition of Wells’ body closer to July 4, so he was unable to determine whether Wells was conscious or unconscious when he entered the water and whether he was forced in. 
Because of the amount of decomposition on the body, Mitchell conducted a number of additional examinations to rule out blunt force injuries.
He examined the tissue on the back of Wells’ neck and skull and found a 12 by 8 inch focal area and red discoloration. Mitchell said he couldn’t determine its cause and it could not have been observed during the state’s autopsy because the medical examiner didn’t dissect that area. 
Crump said he hopes the Mississippi medical examiner will give Mitchell the opportunity to see its photographs and observations about the condition of Wells’ body closer to when it was first pulled from the water. He said Mitchell’s findings should be included in the evidence presented to a grand jury. 
The release of the autopsy results comes days after Wells’ burial and funeral in Ocean Springs, which hundreds attended. 
Christine Wonsley, mother of Nolan Xavier Wells, center, is comforted by attorney Ben Crump, left, and her husband, Elmore Wonsley, during Wells’ funeral at Center Pointe Church in Ocean Springs on Monday, July 20, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
During his eulogy for Wells, the Rev. Al Sharpton announced a $50,000 reward from his organization, the National Action Network, to anyone who could provide information leading to an arrest and conviction. Within a day, the reward amount grew to $125,000 through a match from filmmaker Tyler Perry, who also paid for Wells’ funeral service, and a pledge from NFL Hall of Famer Terrell Owens, who attended the funeral. 
Wells celebrated the Fourth of July with others by taking a boat to Horn Island, one of the Gulf Coast’s largest barrier islands where people are known to dock boats, wade in the water and walk on the white sand shore. Hundreds of people were on the island that day, according to photos and videos.
Wells was reported missing after he did not return to Ocean Springs. Investigators have said Wells told his friends he wanted to stay behind to talk with a woman and that he planned to get a ride off the island. Two days later, a U.S. park ranger found his body off the northwestern tip of Horn Island. 
Wednesday morning, Wells’ family, their attorney Crump released the preliminary autopsy results on the last day of the NAACP’s 117th national convention. 
Last weekend, the NAACP’s national board of directors adopted a resolution that offered condolences to Wells’ family and one that called on local, state and federal authorities including the U.S. Department of Justice to complete an in-depth and transparent review of how Wells “came to be left” on the island and what happened before his body was found. 
NAACP national president Derrick Johnson speaks during a town hall meeting hosted by the NAACP in Jackson, Miss., on Monday, Oct. 24, 2022.  Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis
NAACP president and CEO Derrick Johnson, who lives in Mississippi, said at the press conference that narrative matters in Wells’ case because it seems that law enforcement has repeated what other people are saying instead of investigating for themselves. 
Wells’ mother Christine Wonsley said at the press conference Wednesday that since her son’s death, members of the public have degraded her family, called her racist and questioned fundraising efforts and her and her husband’s parenting. But she said the family is leaning into their faith, support of each other and support from the community. 
The family has asked for help from Crump, Sharpton, the NAACP and others because they haven’t received it from local authorities, she said. 
“It is our hope that our local authorities will do what they need to do,” Wonsley said, now that the preliminary autopsy results have been released.

title: Six Indiana cities close on low-interest state loans for housing projects
description: The Indiana Finance Authority closed on more than $25 million in low-interest loans for housing developments in six Hoosier cities and towns throughout the state, the agency announced in a news release Wednesday. The loans come from the Indiana Residential Infrastructure Fund — a revolving-loan fund created by statute three years ago to support housing […]
text:
The Indiana Finance Authority closed on six low-interest loans designed make it easier for cities and towns to build new housing. (Getty Images)The Indiana Finance Authority closed on more than $25 million in low-interest loans for housing developments in six Hoosier cities and towns throughout the state, the agency announced in a news release Wednesday.
The loans come from the Indiana Residential Infrastructure Fund — a revolving-loan fund created by statute three years ago to support housing development through low-interest municipal loans.
Once a city pays off its loan, the money becomes available for other communities.
The agency recently closed on $25 million in loans for:

Arcadia: $3 million
Attica: $1.7 million
Austin: $1.19 million
Elkhart: $10 million
Fort Wayne: $8.15 million
Terre Haute: $1.575 million

“Indiana’s economy is growing, and our housing supply needs to grow with it,” Gov. Mike Braun said in the release. “These investments will save local communities money while helping them ensure Hoosier families have access to a variety of housing options.”
The low-interest loans will save cities $6.2 million in aggregate principal and interest costs, said Sherry Seiwert, director of the loan program for the Indiana Finance Authority.
To date, the Indiana Finance Authority has closed more than $87 million in loans for housing developments in 20 cities and towns throughout the state since 2024, according to the release.
Seventy percent of the loans are reserved for cities or towns with a population below 50,000 people by law.
About the projects
Arcadia, population 1,500, will use its $3 million loan to develop 264 singe-family detached homes.
Attica will build 29 single-family lots, the first phase of an 87-lot project for the rural city of 3,500.
A new housing development in Austin will see the creation of 119 single-family homes, 60 triplex units and 72 apartments. The first phase of the project—made possible through the city’s $1.19 loan—is expected to yield 54 single-family homes.
A $10 million loan to Elkhart will help finance the city’s redevelopment of an abandoned mall into a mixed-use housing development, anticipated to include 140 housing units, a health center, job training center and retail space.
Other projects include development of 182 single-family lots and 240 multi-family rentals in Fort Wayne, and a 50-unit development along Terre Haute’s trail system.
The list of cities that closed on loans excludes St. Joseph and New Carlisle, which had been selected by the Indiana Finance Authority in December for $4.5 million in low-interest loans.

text:
Fruit is displayed at an Anchorage grocery store. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma’s cyclosporiasis cases, the parasitic infection that causes stomach cramping and “explosive diarrhea,” have more than doubled since last week.
The state’s Department of Health has recorded 170 confirmed cases of the intestinal illness, most of which have been reported this month. There have been 12 hospitalizations but no deaths, according to the department. Just over half of the state’s infections have been reported in women, and it has affected people from 9 to 94 years old.
The Centers for Disease Control reports 4,173 confirmed cases across 41 states since May 1. The CDC expects this number to rise as it analyzes over 7,400 additional cases local and state health departments have reported. There have been 308 hospitalizations nationwide from cyclosporiasis, but no deaths as of Monday.
On Friday, the Food and Drug Administration announced a recall of iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico, which was served in restaurants like Taco Bell in five states. On Monday, acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas announced this was a false positive, but the agency still recommends against eating the company’s lettuce as it investigates possible causes of the outbreak.
The CDC recommends washing produce thoroughly, and if possible, cooking it to at least 158 degrees to kill the parasite. It advises against drinking untreated water.
Common symptoms of cyclosporiasis include diarrhea, loss of appetite and stomach pain. Treatment includes antibiotics and rehydration.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: UConn study highlights CT families’ childcare struggles
description: More than half of families found childcare expensive. And towns in CT's northeast corner and lower Fairfield County struggled most for spots.
text:
Communities across Connecticut, regardless of socioeconomic profiles, are struggling to access childcare options, often due to a lack of affordable options or available spots, according to a new study. 
The 2025 Parents/Caregiver Survey, led by a University of Connecticut researcher in collaboration with 140 partner organizations and the state’s Office of Early Childhood, found that 53% of families across the state found childcare to be too expensive.
The study also found families of toddlers — from 18 months to 35 months — were having the most difficult time accessing care, with nearly half of those respondents searching for care or on a waitlist. Accessing care was especially challenging for low-income families.
Caregivers struggled most to find drop-in care, weekend care, full-time care and care for school vacation days, while the least sought-out type of care was overnight and school age care, according to the study.

University of Connecticut researcher Samantha Lawrence, an assistant professor in the UConn School of Social Work, surveyed 3,719 parents and caregivers across Connecticut in the third iteration of the survey, which was also conducted in 2020 and 2022. Lawrence called the survey “a really important first step to hold us accountable, to make change.”
Around a quarter of respondents said that they care for their children themselves, while nearly half used childcare centers. Two-thirds of respondents reported at least one barrier to accessing childcare. The most common obstacle was cost, followed by waitlists, lack of available openings, distance and the inability to access financial assistance programs like Care 4 Kids.
Notably, caregivers in two regions in the state with vastly different demographic and geographic profiles — a swath of the northeast and a couple of towns in lower Fairfield County — are finding it especially challenging to find spots, according to the study. 
A grouping of towns — Brooklyn, Canterbury, Killingly, Putnam, Sterling, Thompson and Plainfield— had the greatest percentage of parents searching for childcare and/or on a waitlist, at 71% in 2025, when the survey was conducted. The Early Start Network in Greenwich and New Canaan came in a close second at 66%. 
Around a third of parents across the state say that their current childcare does not meet their needs.
But change is already underway. A historic investment in early childhood education by Gov. Ned Lamont’s administration promises to reform the sector, with the eventual goal of offering such care at no cost to all families making less than $100,000 and capping care at 7% of income for families making more.
At a press conference on Wednesday, Office of Early Childhood Commissioner Elena Trueworthy said that the survey provides direction on where the system may be falling short and where it’s working, information that will inform decisions going forward.
“Your experiences are really helping to shape the now and the future of early childhood care across our state, and we are listening,” she said, adding that Connecticut has the resources to do better for families.
Treasurer Erick Russell said on Wednesday that marginalized communities, including people of color and those living in rural areas, are most impacted by the struggle to find childcare. When children don’t have those opportunities, it also limits their opportunities for learning and cognitive development in the crucial early years.
“I’m proud of the work being done in Connecticut to address many of these issues,” he said. 
Russell, who estimated the endowment at around $723 million currently, said the investment in early childhood is also part of a broader picture of investing in the state’s economic health. “This is all going to be something that is going to be lifting up our state, that’s going to help fill these 80,000 jobs we have to get people back to work,” and contribute to the longterm economic health of the state, he said.
Comptroller Sean Scanlon told those gathered Wednesday a story about how his dad, a house painter, bartered an early childhood education program with his services to enroll Scanlon. “That’s what parents do. We find a way to make it work, it’s not easy,” he said. It’s a struggle for a diverse group of families, “whether you live in the richest part of Connecticut or the most rural part, it doesn’t matter.”
The survey’s results reflect this.
Lawrence said that the northeast corner of the state struggles with a variety of access concerns, from the need for more full-time care options to the proportion of parents traveling long distances to access childcare.
In the lower Fairfield County towns, availability is fluid especially in the summer months, said Louis Josephson, the CEO of Family Centers of Greenwich. He said his group currently has spots available. It provides sliding-scale tuition assistance and scholarships, as well as full-day care.
“I’ve heard about this as a longstanding phenomenon, that families are finding it really challenging to find the right slot for the right age child in the Greenwich community at a price they can afford,” he said. As for the need reflected in the survey for more spots, “We’re not feeling it, but it doesn’t mean it’s not happening.” 
At Wednesday’s press conference, Vanessa Hawke recounted her experience when she, then a stay-at-home mom, was asked to become the deputy director of the Connecticut Early Childhood Alliance. She struggled to find her son a childcare spot and ended up bringing him to her first day of work.
She said she cobbled together childcare through 30 hours at two different centers. The amount her family paid was more than their mortgage, she said. 
“We all know the work isn’t done yet,” Hawke said. Putting more money into the endowment will mean kids get the care they need in years to come, she said.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Storms bring flash flooding, damaging winds to parts of West Virginia
description: Tuesday’s storms brought 5 to 6 inches of rainfall and damaging winds to parts of West Virginia, leading to flash flooding, landslides, road closures and other dangers throughout the state, officials said.
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey posted this photo of the Walmart parking lot in Weston, West Virginia, following Tuesday's flooding across the state. (Photo courtesy of Gov. Patrick Morrisey's X account)Tuesday’s storms brought 5 to 6 inches of rainfall and damaging winds to parts of West Virginia, leading to flash flooding, landslides, road closures and other dangers throughout the state, officials said.  
Gov. Patrick Morrisey declared a state of emergency Tuesday evening for all 55 counties in the state because of the storms.
Flood warnings were still in effect Wednesday morning for Taylor, Harrison, Barbour, Upshur and Tyler counties as well as northern Pleasants County, Joe Curtis, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service at Charleston, told West Virginia Watch.
“In all of those places, there was a lot of water that fell yesterday,” Curtis said. “Some of those places saw 6 inches or more of rainfall, specifically in Upshur County and also part of Harrison County. So we saw a whole lot of rain in those areas, and there still is some lingering high water today, which is why we still have that flood warning in effect for lingering high water.”
Morrisey said in a social media post late Tuesday that the state Division of Natural Resources had been involved in 33 water rescues, and first responders were working through the night to protect lives and assist communities impacted by the storm.
Several people were rescued from high water in Upshur County, according to reporting by West Virginia MetroNews. High water blocked U.S. Route 33 at the Interstate 79 exit at Weston, MetroNews reported. 
Uphur County officials on Wednesday urged residents to stay home to avoid flooding, if at all possible.
“Many roadways are flooded or may become hazardous with little warning,” the Upshur County Sheriff’s Office wrote in a Facebook post. “Staying off the road helps keep you safe and allows first responders, utility crews and emergency personnel to respond quickly to those in need.”
The sheriff also warned people not to drive through flooded areas and to follow weather reports. 
The American Red Cross is responding to the flooding, setting up shelters in the Buckhannon Church of the Nazarene, Lewis County High School and Philippi Middle School, according to a social media post from the organization. 
Curtis said there were also reports of straight-line wind in areas of the state, including northern West Virginia as well as the Interstate 64 corridor, including Huntington and Charleston.
“(There were) quite a bit of tree down reports from yesterday’s storms,” Curtis said. He said the weather service has not yet determined whether the winds were due to a derecho. 
The weather service has also not yet determined whether tornadoes were a part of Tuesday’s weather events. 
“We’re still gathering that information. We’re still doing some investigation and we don’t have anything at the moment,” Curtis said. 
Morrisey said the state National Guard would deploy liaison officers to assist county emergency operations centers and swift-water rescue teams to assist local responders. 
About 100 Guard members were expected overnight in the Elkins, Weston and Buckhannon areas, and another 200 expected to arrive by mid to late morning Wednesday, Morrisey said. 
“State and local agencies will remain on the ground for as long as it takes to help affected communities,” Morrisey said. 
This is a developing story and may be updated.
