title: Missouri lawmakers fight utility bid to bypass competition on new power lines
description: Electric companies in the Midwest say new large scale powerlines are needed to get more energy onto the grid to serve big power consumers such as artificial intelligence data centers. Now, the utilities argue reducing competition is the fastest way to do it. A group of nine electric transmission utilities, including Ameren and Evergy, is […]
text:
As power-hungry data centers proliferate, states are searching for ways to protect utility customers from the steep costs of upgrading the electrical grid, trying instead to shift the cost to AI-driven tech companies. (Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Electric companies in the Midwest say new large scale powerlines are needed to get more energy onto the grid to serve big power consumers such as artificial intelligence data centers. Now, the utilities argue reducing competition is the fastest way to do it.
A group of nine electric transmission utilities, including Ameren and Evergy, is asking federal energy regulators for the right of first refusal to build and operate new multi-state, large-scale powerlines.
The group, called “Grid Acceleration Coalition,” filed a request with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) in April to exempt certain projects from the competitive bidding process or to put it on hold for five years. If approved, utilities operating in both the Midcontinent Independent Systems Operator (MISO) territory and the Southwest Power Pool (SPP) would be the default developer for any large multi-state transmission projects.
Northeast and mid-Missouri is situated in MISO territory while the western part of the state and some of southern Missouri’s grid is facilitated by SPP.
In their plea to federal regulators, transmission utilities stress how delays on infrastructure projects hurt progress.
“To meet spiking load growth, we must build the transmission needed to connect new large loads and generation,” the request reads. “If we succeed, we will win the race to achieve dominance in artificial intelligence (‘AI’), rebuild our nation’s manufacturing base, and ensure we have the infrastructure needed to extract our nation’s oil and gas resources.”
Davis Strobridge is director of regulatory strategy for ITC, one of the largest transmission companies in the country. He said it can take 16 to 20 months to select a company to build a large-scale powerline.
“We need rules and regulations that do things quickly and don’t have red tape involved, and removing this solicitation requirement would absolutely do that,” Strobridge said.
But in recent months, a number of state lawmakers have spoken out in opposition. Legislators from Missouri, Iowa, Montana, Wisconsin and Kansas have sent letters to the FERC urging the agency to deny the transmission companies’ request.
State Sen. Tracy McCreery, a Democrat from Kirkwood, said she fears there would be “no regard for cost” if the utilities had the right of first refusal. She said halting the competitive bidding process would raise project costs that then get passed onto customers.
“Without competition, there would be no motivation for these investor-owned utilities to do things in an economical manner,” she said.
In a letter to federal energy commissioners, McCreery said infrastructure costs for transmission and distribution are the primary driver of her constituents’ rising utility bills. McCreery writes that nearly a quarter of Missourians have unaffordable energy burdens, meaning they spend 6% or more of their household income on utility bills.
“We are putting so much strain on Missouri families and we have to just say stop. Let’s use some common sense,” McCreery said.
State Rep. Ben Keathley, a Republican from Chesterfield, also sent a letter to FERC echoing McCreery’s concerns.
 Faster and cheaper is the goal

More than a year ago, President Donald Trump declared a national energy emergencyand made new electric generation and transmission infrastructure a priority.
Transmission utilities say the project solicitation process to bid on and win the ability to build powerlines delays grid upgrades and hurts the ability to get new power plants online. But consumer advocates and lawmakers say without competition costs will increase.
Prior to 2011, the transmission companies operating as a regulated monopoly in a certain area had the right of first refusal for building new transmission lines. A policy called “Order 1000” changed that, opening up large scale powerline projects to a competitive process. Developers from across the country, as well as incumbent utilities, could submit proposals to win the project.
“In 2011, the environment we were in was a really low load growth environment … and so we almost had the time to experiment with the policy and it wasn’t impacting our electric grid,” Strobridge said. “Fast forward, obviously, we’re in an unprecedented time. The demands that are coming that utilities are experiencing right now are almost incomprehensible.”
Paul Cicio is chairman of the Electricity Transmission Competition Coalition, a group advocating against the utilities’ recent request. He said lobbying in state legislatures to reduce competition has been intense in the MISO region.
“Because these same utilities couldn’t get legislation in their home state, now they’re petitioning the federal government to bail them out to help them and prevent competition,” he said.
The companies’ request before federal energy regulators states that electricity demand is “increasing at a rate unseen since World War II, particularly in MISO and SPP.”
The transmission utilities’ request makes clear utilities want to take advantage of the current AI data center development boom and build assets to facilitate the increased electricity demand — which they say the competitive project “solicitation” process hinders.
“Any purported benefits of solicitations — which are uncertain and, at best, small — are almost certainly overwhelmed by the costs of foregone benefits of AI development,” the request reads.
In an email to KBIA, Evergy spokesperson Courtney Lewis said the current way the country goes about building large powerlines hurts the ability to meet growing electricity demand and threatens the region’s ability for economic growth.
“As one of the home utilities in the region, Evergy is well positioned to build transmission,” Lewis said. “We own and operate the local power grid that the lines connect to, and we are staffed to monitor and quickly respond anytime there is an issue that could impact service to our customers.”
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission is expected to rule on the utilities’ request this fall.
This story was originally published by KBIA. It can be republished in print or online.

name: WyoFile
title: Amid Wyoming’s elder care crunch, adult day center offers respite and companionship
description:
In a rapidly aging state where family members often provide unpaid care, Among Friends in Casper is a place for seniors to engage and connect under supervision. 
The post Amid Wyoming’s elder care crunch, adult day center offers respite and companionship appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
CASPER—A live-in caretaker for her mother, Michele Hand nearly cried from relief when she talked about the value of Casper’s new Among Friends Adult Day Center. 
“It’s just such a blessing,” she said. 
Between tasks like laundry and lawn mowing, house cleaning and cooking, Hand said, it was nearly impossible to give her mother, Agnes, who lives with dementia, the attention she deserves. Now she has help. 
On days like this Thursday in July, Hand dropped her mom off at Among Friends. The center affords Hand a little alone time unburdened from worries about her mom’s well-being. Access to daytime care is not just good for the younger Hand, she noted. 
“It’s good for mom to be around someone who’s not me,” Hand said. “They do such creative things, and she has friends.”
Agnes Hand became pals with Dorothy Sneathen the day they met at Among Friends. They’ve been glued together since. The women found each other soon after they arrived that Thursday. Even though it was likely they had forgotten one another’s names, they could recognize a friend.
Later, when they couldn’t remember the instructions they were given at craft time, it was also OK. They cracked jokes and seemed plenty entertained as they occasionally glued paper flowers to pages.
Dorothy Sneathen and Agnes Hand work on crafts at Among Friends Adult Day Center in Casper on July 9, 2026. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
Along with the four other people attending Among Friends, they ate lunch, did chair aerobics and sang when a music therapist stopped by for a session. One man pieced together puzzles, another played with fidget toys and others participated in a memory exercise. They hugged staff and held each other’s hands. 
“Giving them a little joy is so rewarding,” said Program Director Becky Bouzis.
In Wyoming, where the fastest-growing population is 65 and older, about 106,000 adults are family caregivers, according to AARP data. Unpaid caregiving can sap budgets, pull people out of the workforce and cause significant emotional distress. Family caregivers handle everything from grocery shopping to complex medical tasks, often with little training. About 80% pay out of their own pockets to meet loved ones’ needs, according to AARP.
“It’s hard, hard, hard,” Bouzis said. That’s where Among Friends comes in; the facility offers trusted respite for caregivers 
“It’s just so good for people to get a break,” Bouzis said.
Family affair
Bouzis operates Among Friends with her mother, Lona Cantine. Both are registered nurses; they actually attended Casper College nursing school together in the ‘90s. 
The inspiration for Among Friends grew from personal experience. Helping care for a mother-in-law with dementia, a grandmother with Parkinson’s and an uncle with multiple chronic health conditions laid bare the strains of caregiving. Juggling work is tricky, paying for in-home help is prohibitive and ensuring patients get the human connection they need is difficult.
Bouzis also had a sister-in-law who developed early onset Alzheimer’s. Before the disease took hold she was extroverted and active, Bouzis said. Once she developed it, the family wished there was a place for her to socialize. Because the disease caused her to become suspicious, in-home care failed miserably. 

Becky Bouzis and her mother, Lona Cantine, operate the new Among Friends Adult Day Center in Casper. Both are long-time nurses. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)

“We asked ourselves, ‘Why isn’t there a place she could go and find some joy?’” Bouzis said. “A place where we would know she was safe, we would know she was fed. And we could still keep our jobs and do our things with our own families.”
With backgrounds in clinical administration and neurological medicine, Bouzis and Cantine decided to create that place. They considered an in-home operation, but once they learned about Department of Health requirements, Bouzis said, they realized they “had to go big or go home.” With a larger facility in mind, they wrote a business plan, and Bouzis dovetailed it into her capstone project while earning her master’s degree. 
Bouzis and Cantine found a space on Casper’s Poplar Street that has previously held a travel agency, pregnancy center and dance studio. 
They gave it a full renovation, creating not just a facility that meets requirements for ADA and health department licensing, but also a destination that feels inviting, Bouzis said. “We wanted it to feel homey,” she said.
Textile art, potted plants and neutral colors help achieve that. With cabinets of puzzles and games, rows of new recliners and a large communal table, the space feels more like a contemporary rec center than anything. 
Seniors exercise at Among Friends Adult Day Center. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
Still, they stock medical and sanitary supplies, and the mother-and-daughter nurses meet required medical credentials. Employees have dementia care training, and a dozen volunteers go through background checks and training.
Bouzis’ daughter-in-law manages the kitchen, her son built the website and her father waters the plants and delivers food. 
“It’s truly a family affair,” she said.  
Day in the life
Among Friends runs on a daily schedule that includes lunchtime, movement, crafting and memory exercises. In that way and others, it has parallels to a children’s daycare facility. 
Clients, for example, sometimes struggle with goodbye when their caregiver drops them off. Occasionally they don’t want to eat or need to rest. 
Navigating such moments can require a deft touch, a kind of natural talent that certain people also display with children. The work also requires constant attention. While Cantine led a group memory activity using prompt cards, another volunteer stuck close to a client who is prone to head for the exit and distracted him when he approached the door. Bouzis, meanwhile, met with a client’s caregiver in her office.
For clients, gathering for group activities can bring out silliness and long-buried memories. Gerry Thorvaldson broke into dance when a music therapist began performing a song, and Agnes Hand joined in with her arms in the air. And, of course, there were Hand and Sneathen’s nonstop antics. 
Among Friends Adult Day Center volunteer Joan Davies dances with client Gerry Thorvaldson on July 9, 2026 during a music therapy session. Thorvaldson, who lives with dementia, began dancing as soon as the music started. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
Midway through craft time, a new client arrived. The small woman with bright eyes and a deeply lined face was wheeled in by a relative. 
When the relative disappeared into Bouzis’ office, Hand and Sneathen were by her side instantly, chatting familiarly and holding her hand before introductions even took place.
“You look only 29 like me!” said Sneathen. She and Hand dissolved into laughter. 
Cantine explained to the client all the ways the center could make her more comfortable: snacks, drinks, activities and friends. 
“This is your place,” Cantine told her. 
Solution for some
A month after its June opening, Among Friends had 12 clients. The facility is available to people over the age of 50 who live at home or with caregivers and meet other criteria. 
That’s not to say it’s for everyone. Some people have medical needs that go beyond the scope of its services, Bouzis said, while others get too confused or uncomfortable without their caregivers. And then of course families have to be able to afford it. 
The center is currently private-pay and accepts long-term care insurance, though Bouzis said she is working to get approved for Medicaid and Veterans Affairs coverage. Fees range from $14.50-$26 an hour depending on client needs — which is less than average rates for private in-home care. 
Cantine also recently launched the Still Me Foundation, which aims to financially support older adults in Natrona County with expenses that help them remain at home and independent. Still Me funds could help pay for care at Among Friends, among other expenses. 
For families it works for, Among Friends has been a lifeline. Agnes Hand’s daughter, Michele, said it’s obvious to her that a lot of thought and care goes into creating a quality experience. 
“It’s a very special place,” Hand said. “We’re very thankful.”
Part of the goal, Bouzis said, is to stave off two perils related to elder care. First, Among Friends keeps seniors from languishing in social isolation that is all too common for elderly folks. And second, it relieves caregivers from the mental burden of around-the-clock supervision. 
Alzheimer’s, for example, can be as damaging, if not more so, on the health of the caregiver, she noted. 
“If we can do anything to alleviate that for a little while for people, we’ve done our job,” Bouzis said.

title: ‘Material Connections’ showcases Wyoming women’s artwork
description:
Wyoming Women’s History House celebrates women artists with new exhibit and workshops.
The post ‘Material Connections’ showcases Wyoming women’s artwork appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A found-object sculpture resembling sideways lampshades hangs on one wall. Voices from the sculpture’s audio track fill the air with a poem. Rocks, landscapes, a pair of shoes and old photographs fill the other walls. This eclectic exhibition is “Material Connections,” on display at the Wyoming Women’s History House.
What do the artworks have in common? They offer commentary from women artists on what it means to be a woman in both the past and present. Going back centuries, women have been and are still underappreciated in the visual arts. “Material Connections” seeks to change that. 
Wyoming Women’s History House is a free museum highlighting women instrumental to the suffrage movement in Wyoming. The museum celebrates female firsts and seeks to inspire the next generation of women to be leaders in their fields. 
“Material Connections” features seven artists working across a range of media, offering a glimpse into the breadth of work Wyoming women artists produce.
Wyoming artists
Rocio Gomez Sandoval, born in Michoacán, Mexico, is a mixed media artist who now lives in Laramie. She uses techniques and materials often associated with women and crafting that aren’t considered fine art. 
“I use embroidery because I like using traditional [women’s] techniques to make art,” Gomez Sandoval said. “I want to say just by choosing this media, we are here, we were here, and we were always making art.” 
Gomez Sandoval’s pieces in the show focus on the life and death of women. One piece uses a fancy photo of a long-dead woman that ended up in a thrift shop, discarded by her loved ones, to explore abandonment. Another piece focuses on death and a mother’s milk. Gomez Sandoval dislikes when people categorize her work as women’s art. Instead, she sees art as a universal thing that doesn’t need divisions or separations based on her gender or ethnicity.  
Artists Tawni Shuler and Rocio Gomez Sandoval explore what it means to be a woman through their artwork in “Material Connections.” (Calla Shosh/WyoFile)
Sadie Winter is a multidisciplinary artist. She has three landscape prints in the show. Winter made the ink for two of the prints from foraged earth materials from Pilot Hill. For Winter, process is important in her work to help ground it in a place, material or tradition. Many of Winter’s mentors in the arts have been women, from her ceramics mentor to people who didn’t consider themselves artists like her grandmother. 
“A lot of times what I see is, like, what have been understood as like traditionally marginalized crafts,” Winter said, like textile arts and collage, “are not elevated to the level of fine arts until a man does it,” Winter said. 
“I wonder how much of it is internalized, like with my grandmother,” Winter said. “She’s an incredible fiber artist, quilter, embroidery artist, but doesn’t really consider herself to be an artist. So some of that I think is internalized and then some of it is also like societal pressures.”
Katie Christensen, an artist and self-described feminist, currently works in mental-health care. She helped organize “Material Connections,” by reaching out to the artists and curating the show. One of her works is a caustic print of bleeding-heart flowers, which her grandmother grew. The flowers are also tied to her great-grandmother’s homestead. 
Artist Katie Christensen stands next to her work Mother’s Son. Christensen curated “Material Connections.” (Calla Shosh/WyoFile)
“It’s kind of an homage to all the really strong women in my life,” Christensen said. 
Her other piece features two rocks in boxes. The first rock was the last gift given to Christensen by her father before he died. The other is a rock from her husband. Together, the three pieces are titled Mother’s Sons.  
Christensen recognizes that women have lacked visibility in the arts. However, solving this problem can’t be done with just women alone. 
“Men are just as important in this story as women” Christensen said. “We’re at the Women’s History House, and I think it’s very women-forward, but we need men just as much as we do need women and women’s equality.
“And I think that’s kind of an important piece as to why I also named the collection of work I did Mother’s Sons.”
Connect with the artists
The Wyoming Women’s History House will host five workshops over the next few months, providing the public with an opportunity to make art alongside the artists, while learning their processes and techniques.  
Joanne Mai, director of the Wyoming Women’s History House, hopes the workshops and exhibit will build a sense of community. “One of the things that we really notice about the women that we feature here is that they were really instrumental in building community in Wyoming,” Mai said. 
“So that sense of community is really important to us. And so we really want to bring people in to connect with each other, to learn from one another and to start to build new communities.”
Wyoming Women’s History House hopes to host future exhibits highlighting Wyoming women in other fields, including music and writing. 
Laramie artist Cassidy Post unveiled a new mural for the Wyoming Women’s History House, depicting Louisa Swain and Nellie Tayloe Ross. This is Post’s first mural. (Calla Shosh/WyoFile)
Alongside the exhibit is a new mural by artist Cassidy Post. Painted on a building next to the Wyoming Women’s History House, it depicts Louisa Swain and Nellie Tayloe Ross, two historic Wyoming women. Swain was the first woman to vote and Ross was the first female governor. 
The mural is a permanent fixture and was coincidentally finished the day before the “Material Connections” opening exhibit. 
“Material Connections” is open through Labor Day weekend, at 317 S. 2nd Street in downtown Laramie.

title: With political attack ads, crazy cashes in on lazy
description:
Every election season, attack ads turn complicated votes into simple lies — and count on us not to check, writes guest columnist Christy Mathes.
The post With political attack ads, crazy cashes in on lazy appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The commercial rolls across my television again.
The music is dark. The voice is ominous. The message is terrifyingly simple: Eric Barlow supports transgender surgeries for children. 

Opinion

The claims are packaged with the certainty of established fact and repeated often enough that viewers may recognize them before they ever think to question them.
I have seen variations of these advertisements repeatedly on streaming TV. I have not yet captured the final disclaimer identifying who paid for them, so I am not going to accuse any candidate, campaign or organization of creating them.
I will not condemn dishonesty and then make an allegation I cannot prove. But we can dissect the ads. The claims alone reveal a familiar strategy: Isolate one vote, strip away the language and amendments, ignore the surrounding record and attach the most explosive conclusion possible.
This is where crazy cashes in on lazy.
Not because Wyoming voters are stupid or truly lazy. We are busy. Most people do not have time to read every bill, amendment and legislative digest whenever a frightening commercial interrupts their evening.
The people creating these messages know that. They feed on it. 
Consider the accusation that Barlow supports transgender surgeries for children.
In 2023, he voted against Senate File 111, “Child abuse-change of sex,” in committee. That vote is real. So is the explanation left out of the commercial.
Barlow argued that the bill did not adequately define the criminal intent required for prosecution and questioned whether its definitions would accomplish its stated purpose.
Legislators are not elected to vote on bill titles. They are responsible for the language that will actually become law.
In 2024, Barlow supported Senate File 99, “Children gender change prohibition,” a differently written prohibition on specified gender-transition procedures for minors. He voted for it in committee and on the Senate floor.
The complete record is not that Barlow supports surgeries on children. It is that he opposed one bill he believed was legally deficient and later supported a revised prohibition that became Wyoming law.
You may disagree with his original vote. But using it to claim he supports the very procedures he later voted to prohibit is not an honest description of his record.
It is a true vote dressed up to tell a lie.
The school-choice claim is even more brazen. Barlow was a named sponsor of Wyoming’s 2024 education savings account bill. However, that bill was amended more than 30 times. Its primary House sponsor said it had been changed so dramatically that even he could no longer support the Senate version.
Barlow voted against that heavily amended version. He later served on the conference committee that negotiated a compromise and voted for the final legislation that became law.
That is not the record of someone who simply opposes school choice. It is the record of a legislator who sponsored one version, opposed a substantially changed version and supported the final compromise.
The same distortion appeared in a June 3 Breitbart article criticizing Barlow over his vote against Wyoming’s 2025 immigration omnibus bill.
The introduced bill was 20 pages long and addressed employment, public benefits, driver’s licenses, law enforcement, immigration-status investigations, detention and a million-dollar appropriation.
Barlow joined 19 other senators in voting against it. Were all 20 secretly in favor of illegal immigration? Of course not.
A person can support immigration enforcement while opposing a specific enforcement mechanism. A legislator can support the goal of a bill while objecting to its scope, cost, constitutionality, wording or unintended consequences.
A no vote means, “I do not support this bill in this form.” It does not automatically mean, “I support the opposite of everything mentioned in its title.”
This is bigger than Eric Barlow. Similar campaign materials have been called out for targeting other Wyoming lawmakers by reducing complicated records to flashy and sometimes inaccurate talking points.
We need to stop screaming for transparency from candidates while allowing anonymous political money to operate in the dark.
The goal is not to help voters understand a decision, but to create an emotional association powerful enough to survive any later correction. The lie gets ominous music, professional editing and repeated airtime. The truth gets a hurried Facebook post fighting an algorithm for exposure.
One of the most egregious defenses of this kind of politics I have heard is: “I can say whatever I want. It’s your job to prove it’s a lie.” No. That’s not true. And it’s not a defense. It’s a confession.
The burden of proof belongs to the person making the accusation. In the year of America’s 250th anniversary, we should remember that the First Amendment protects the right to speak freely. It was never meant to become a shield for reckless lies, anonymous cruelty and deliberate character assassination.
There is also responsibility among those who witness it.
Barlow was among 35 Wyoming candidates who signed the Become Peacemakers pledge, promising civility, courage and love for their political enemies. He has publicly defended his own record. What I have yet to see is another signer step forward and say that deliberately distorting an opponent’s record is unacceptable, even when the attack benefits their own side.
That silence matters.
Bullying does not survive on the bully’s power alone. It survives because others look away. Silence becomes permission. Compliance becomes participation.
You do not have to support Eric Barlow. You do not have to agree with his votes. But disagreement does not justify deception.
The next time a commercial tells you what a candidate “really believes,” pause.
Who paid for it? What did the bill actually say? What does the full record show?
And if you are willing to spend thousands throwing mud at someone’s name, have the courage to put your own name and face on the bucket.
Say it. Prove it. Sign it.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: The biggest barrier to teen mental health isn’t treatment.
description: The tragedies at Myers Park High School have prompted necessary conversations across Charlotte about youth mental health and what more can be done to support young people before they reach a crisis point. Those conversations matter. But while the recent discussion has centered on one school and one community, the challenge is hardly unique to Mecklenburg Cou[...]
text:
Photo: Getty Images.The tragedies at Myers Park High School have prompted necessary conversations across Charlotte about youth mental health and what more can be done to support young people before they reach a crisis point.

Those conversations matter. But while the recent discussion has centered on one school and one community, the challenge is hardly unique to Mecklenburg County.


Across North Carolina, more than one-third of high school students report feeling persistently sad or hopeless. At the same time, 94 of the state’s 100 counties face shortages of mental health professionals, and 43 counties have no child psychiatrist at all. The need is clear. The question is how we respond.


For years, much of the public conversation around youth mental health has focused on access to treatment. Treatment is critically important, but experience has taught us that another challenge often comes first: ensuring young people are identified, supported and connected to care before a situation becomes a crisis.


In our work with schools, county governments, healthcare providers and community organizations across North Carolina, we’ve learned that the biggest barrier is rarely a lack of caring or commitment. Parents care. Teachers care. Counselors care. Providers care.


The challenge is that the people and systems responsible for supporting young people are not always connected in the moments that matter most — and that lack of connection has serious unintended consequences.


Schools may recognize warning signs but lack immediate access to behavioral health resources. Families may know their child needs help but struggle to navigate a complicated system or pay for care. Providers may have expertise but no direct connection to the students who need it most. When those gaps exist, young people fall through the cracks.


That’s why conversations about youth mental health should focus not only on treatment, but also on identification and intervention.


Identifying a student who may be struggling is often more difficult than people realize. Warning signs are not always obvious, and no single teacher, counselor, parent or provider sees the full picture. The students most in need of support are often the easiest to miss.


Schools play a vital role because they are often the first place those warning signs emerge. But schools cannot be expected to carry this responsibility alone. Neither can families, providers or local governments.


The most effective approaches bring those partners together before a crisis occurs.


Across North Carolina, communities are pursuing that goal in different ways, but the strongest efforts share a common characteristic: they create clearer pathways between schools, families and behavioral health providers.


In Wake County, Alliance Health’s innovative school-based partnership model served more than 600 students in a single school year. Among students experiencing a behavioral health crisis, 93% were successfully connected to needed treatment. And students returning from psychiatric residential treatment also saw positive results, with 100% successfully transitioning back to school with coordinated support designed to help them continue their recovery and remain engaged in the classroom. Alliance recently expanded a similar initiative to schools in Durham County as well.


The lesson is not that one program can solve every challenge facing young people. It is that better outcomes occur when the right partners are aligned around a student’s needs and support is available before a crisis deepens.


This is where North Carolina has an opportunity.


Rather than asking any one institution to shoulder more responsibility, we should continue strengthening the partnerships that help educators, families, healthcare providers and community organizations work together. We should continue investing in approaches that make behavioral health services easier to access, easier to navigate and easier to coordinate.


After a tragedy, communities often ask what could have been done differently. A better question is what we can do sooner.


We cannot prevent every crisis. But we can build stronger pathways to identify struggling young people, connect them to support and ensure help is available before a moment of crisis becomes a lifelong tragedy.


That is a goal every North Carolinian should be able to support.


Ann Oshel is Senior Vice President of Community Innovation and Impact at Alliance Health. She oversees programs and partnerships that connect schools, healthcare providers, local governments and community organizations to improve access to behavioral health services and support healthier communities across North Carolina. She is based in Apex, North Carolina.

title: Alabama Public Television board votes to pay for public survey using emergency fund
description: The Alabama Educational Television Foundation Authority (AETFA) Tuesday voted to fund a survey that would be conducted by a Republican-aligned company through Alabama Public Television’s rainy day fund. The survey, which would be conducted by McLaughlin & Associates, a national survey research and strategic services company, could cost the commission $47,400[...]
text:
Members of the Alabama Educational Television Commission listen to a speaker during a meeting on July 21, 2026 in Birmingham. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama Educational Television Foundation Authority (AETFA) Tuesday voted to fund a survey that would be conducted by a Republican-aligned company through Alabama Public Television’s rainy day fund.
The survey, which would be conducted by McLaughlin & Associates, a national survey research and strategic services company, could cost the commission $47,400 plus travel expenses if needed if the current version of the contract remains in place. The survey will inform the board of what viewers want from APT programming.
The method of funding drew criticism from members of the authority and APT staff.

“We’ve had other nominations shot down to actually fill this foundation’s board and actually do what we need to do to raise money, and we’re not doing that,” said Logan Glass, a member of the authority and the Alabama Educational Television Commission (AETC), which oversees APT.  “And to make matters worse, we’re being fiscally irresponsible. Just like we did with this poll. That’s not fiscally conservative policy what we did.”
Melissa Austin, chief financial officer for APT, also did not agree with the vote.
“It’s the rainy day fund. It’s for emergency purposes,” she said. “We didn’t use the rainy day fund nine months ago when we unfortunately had to lay off 11 people because of the defunding.”
It’s unclear if the survey can be paid for using the account. According to the AETFA Statement of Investment Policy Objectives and Guidelines, the rainy day account can be used when a proration happens so late in the fiscal year it cannot be budgeted for.
Prior to the AETFA’s meeting, the AETC discussed the contract received by McLaughlin. Austin said the contract’s current state left many questions.
“The other clarification that we need to get is they mentioned voters receiving a text invitation that they would get the phone information from a voter database,” Austin said. “We had a conference call with them (McLaughlin) last Monday, and after the call, they ended up clarifying that they would use all adults in Alabama and that they would not use the voter database. But then we received the contract which mentions voters, so we’ve got to get clarification and correction on this as well.”
Austin said APT also had questions about McLaughlin & Associates designating itself as APT’s media buyer in the current version of the contract. 
AETC member Pete Conroy said during the meeting that the commission should postpone discussions until the contract was ready, citing  questions that needed to be answered.
AETC Chair Ferris Stephens pushed back on Conroy’s argument.
“I don’t think we need to postpone this anymore, he said. “I think now’s the time to do this.”
The survey was approved by the commission in April to gauge how Alabamians felt about the Public Broadcasting Station (PBS). 
Last year, the commission discussed disaffiliating from PBS after funding for the Corporation for Public Broadcasting was cut by the Trump administration. The move sparked backlash from APT viewers. Gov. Kay Ivey sent the commission a letter saying the commission should conduct a survey if they chose to disaffiliate from PBS. 
Stephens after the meeting said it’s the commission’s “duty” to conduct the survey, citing a section from the Code of Alabama that gives the AETC the power to “survey, study and appraise the need for an overall plan for the use of television facilities available for noncommercial educational use in the state.”
William Green, the vice-chair of the AETC, said after the commission’s meeting there’s a misunderstanding of what the survey will be used for.
“There was a misconception that the reason for the survey is to get rid of PBS. And I admit that maybe (it) did come up at first,” he said. “But right now, the purpose of it is to find out what they want to see.”
Conroy said after the meeting what the poll is and what it should be are “two different things.”
“The message was pretty clear to me from the chairman and select commissioners, that the poll was to be conducted by a conservative pollster for a predetermined outcome which would not be kind to PBS’ relationship to APT in the future,” he said.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee gubernatorial candidates take on eclectic legislation, pass few bills with gravity
description: Tennessee’s Republican gubernatorial candidates are far from prolific lawmakers, passing little legislation during their tenures in the state legislature and Congress. State Rep. Monty Fritts’ biggest claim to fame is passage of the so-called “chemtrails” bill that was panned by critics as “nonsense.” The measure passed with ease in 2024 to stop the potentia[...]
text:
U.S. Rep. John Rose, left, in December proposed the repeal of a measure that would let eight U.S. senators, including Sen. Marsha Blackburn, sue the government.  (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee’s Republican gubernatorial candidates are far from prolific lawmakers, passing little legislation during their tenures in the state legislature and Congress.
State Rep. Monty Fritts’ biggest claim to fame is passage of the so-called “chemtrails” bill that was panned by critics as “nonsense.” The measure passed with ease in 2024 to stop the potential release of climate-controlling chemicals into the atmosphere.
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn of Franklin often touts her efforts in turning back a state income tax while serving in the state Senate in 2001, encouraging Capitol protests that, ultimately, turned into a rock-throwing affair. 

#TBT 2001-The Tennessee Tax Revolt kept an income tax out of the state and I am glad to have helped lead the charge! pic.twitter.com/WJc6j63Hnr
— Sen. Marsha Blackburn (@MarshaBlackburn) October 30, 2014
Yet she also co-sponsored a bill while serving in the U.S. House that was designed to help people obtain medication but wound up flooding small communities with highly-addictive opioids, according to multiple reports stemming from an investigation by the Washington Post and “60 Minutes.” At the time, her staff said Congress would try to improve the law if it caused “unintended consequences.” 
U.S. Rep. John Rose grabbed attention in December 2025 by proposing the repeal of a provision in national defense funding that allowed eight senators, including Blackburn, to sue the government for half a million dollars over the FBI’s subpoena of their phone data in connection with the investigation into President Donald Trump’s effort to overturn the 2020 election. Senators would have been able to collect for each time the feds looked at their data. The measure was passed as part of the effort to end a federal government shutdown.
Rose said, in part, on the House floor, “… when we sent our funding bill to the Senate last week, we gave Senate leadership a taste of their own medicine and forced them to choose between this policy or reopening the government.”
Breaking down bills
When Fritts sponsored the “chemtrail” bill, he told the Lookout that it dealt only with “geoengineering” purportedly to be done by the federal government and said he wasn’t concerned about a connection to “chemtrail” conspiracy theories that governments and other groups are running a secret program to add “visible plumes” containing toxic chemicals to the atmosphere similar to contrails or vapor trails released by aircraft engine exhaust, which is made up mainly of water in the form of ice crystals.
“Chemtrail” bill set for House circuit described as “nonsense”

Other than that bill from two years ago, Fritts, a two-term legislator, passed House Bill 873 in 2025, a measure that makes it more difficult to bring civil action for negligence against makers of knives, body armor, pepper spray, silencers, gun clips and devices that speed up the discharge of semiautomatic weapons. Fritts supports the state’s permit-less carry law but believes Tennessee should pass what is called true “constitutional carry,” which would remove the state’s “intent to go armed” law and prohibitions on guns in parks and on college campuses.
Fritts’ failed legislation stretched from a measure that would have removed the state sales tax on items bought through the supplemental food program for Women, Infants and Children (WIC) to another that would have prohibited the use of vaccines containing mRNA, a technology used in the COVID-19 vaccine that caused hysteria because of vaccination requirements in some circles.
Aside from his effort to prevent senators from collecting billions from the federal government, Rose sponsored the “Housing Supply Expansion Act of 2025,” which removed the requirement that manufactured houses have a chassis that allows them to be moved after installation. The idea is to cut the cost of young and low-income families to buy homes as rent escalates.
Blackburn sponsored the Kids Online Safety Act, a measure requiring tech companies to put safety features on their platforms to protect children. Another measure she is backing sets up federal guidelines for protections dealing with artificial intelligence.
Recently, Blackburn renewed a bill to prevent foreign nationals from gaining U.S. citizenship by giving birth to children in the United States. She sponsored the bill after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down Trump’s executive order banning birthright citizenship.

title: Pro-data center group trying to change opinions in NC with ad campaign
description: A pro-data center lobbying group has poured $367,272 into an advertising campaign in North Carolina touting the economic and business benefits of data centers. The industry is facing an uphill publicity battle in North Carolina. Community pushback against data centers has grown dramatically in recent months. More than two dozen counties and cities have passe[...]
text:
Close-up of a data center. (Photo: Comezora/Getty Images) A pro-data center lobbying group has poured $367,272 into an advertising campaign in North Carolina touting the economic and business benefits of data centers.
The industry is facing an uphill publicity battle in North Carolina. Community pushback against data centers has grown dramatically in recent months. More than two dozen counties and cities have passed moratoriums on new data centers, and two bills in the state legislature would impose new regulations on the industry.
North Carolina Connects, the group behind the ads, has sponsored pro-data center billboards, television, and audio commercials across the state over the past month. The group bought 747 ad spots across all channels, with 189 of them on Fox News and 90 on Spectrum News Raleigh. 
The ads try to counter common critiques of data centers, including increasing demand for energy and their impact on water supply and quality. They also trumpet what they say are the benefits of data centers, including generating jobs and tax revenue that can be used to fund schools, hospitals and local infrastructure. 
The highly-produced ads feature female narrators’ voices over landscapes, neighborhoods, workers at an electrical site, and happy families in their homes, presumably in N.C.
“North Carolina data centers — committed to paying their costs so North Carolina families don’t,” one of the commercials says.  
 North Carolina Connects is an offshoot of America Connects, which backs similar media campaigns in other states.
America Connects started as Virginia Connects in June of 2024, but underwent a name change in February after expanding to other states. The group’s corporate filing in Virginia only lists three people: Chairman Kevin Hughes, President Josh Levi and Treasurer Allison Gilmore.
All three also serve in leadership roles at the Data Center Coalition, a pro-industry lobbying group. Levi is the president and CEO of the organization, Gilmore is the chief operating officer, and Hughes is the treasurer of the board of directors. 
The Data Center Coalition describes itself as a nonprofit organization that advocates for data centers through public outreach and public policy advocacy. 
Among its members are Google, Microsoft and CyrusOne — which operate major data centers in North Carolina — and Amazon, which is building a $10 billion data center campus in Richmond County. CyrusOne, which operates a data center near Research Triangle Park, has proposed a $900 million data center in Lee County, despite the opposition of some residents. 
Lee County residents demand pause on NC data center, claiming deception

“Through North Carolina Connects, the industry seeks to better explain the role of data centers to the public — including how they operate, why they are important to our daily lives and the 21st-century economy, as well as information about the industry’s responsible usage of water and its commitment to paying for the energy it uses,” Levi, president of the Data Center Coalition, wrote in a statement to NC Newsline.
Mary Maclean Asbill, state director of the Southern Environmental Law Center, says she wishes data centers would put their money towards addressing community concerns instead of ads.  
“I would like to see evidence, not just some fanciful tale told on a television ad,” she told NC Newsline. “I would like to see — and communities would like to see — proof of what are these great jobs you’re talking about, and how did you come up with these numbers?”
State lawmakers could consider proposals to regulate the industry when they return from break July 27.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Secretary of state candidates say North Dakota elections are secure, fair and free
description: North Dakota’s Republican and Democratic candidates for secretary of state agree the state’s elections are secure, free and fair in response to President Donald Trump’s election integrity speech. In a primetime national address last week, Trump said election infrastructure across the country, including voting machines, ballot tabulators, voter rolls, electio[...]
text:
Republican Secretary of State Michael Howe, left, and Democratic-NPL secretary of state candidate Ryan Braunberger. (Photos courtesy of Secretary of State's Office and Braunberger)North Dakota’s Republican and Democratic candidates for secretary of state agree the state’s elections are secure, free and fair in response to President Donald Trump’s election integrity speech.
In a primetime national address last week, Trump said election infrastructure across the country, including voting machines, ballot tabulators, voter rolls, election pollbooks and official election results websites were exposed to hacking and other exploitation from foreign countries and other non-state groups.
The Trump administration released a batch of documents after the speech, but they provided no proof that broad interference occurred or affected an election outcome.
Republican Secretary of State Michael Howe and Democratic challenger Ryan Braunberger, a state senator from Fargo, in interviews said voter information and voting results are secure in North Dakota. 
Howe said while he couldn’t speak for other states, he believes North Dakota’s elections are secure and conducted in a free and fair manner.
“We’ve got proof of citizenship,” Howe said. “If you are getting a new North Dakota identification card, you have to prove your citizenship at that point. You need a North Dakota ID to vote in our elections.”
Voter rolls 
Howe said every North Dakotan who receives an ID is put into the state’s voter file, managed by the North Dakota Department of Transportation, which includes people under age 18 and those who are noncitizen permanent residents of North Dakota. Those residents would be flagged at their polling location check-in tables as not eligible to vote.
Trump cites potential hack of US elections in speech slammed for stoking voter fears

“The only way (ineligible people voting) could happen is if there is an administrative error at the DOT,” Howe said. “Possible, sure. Anything is possible. But highly, highly unlikely.”
The Vital Records Division of the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services provides daily updates to the voter file for people who have died, Howe said.
Braunberger said he’s not worried about ineligible voters casting ballots in the state, even if they do have North Dakota ID cards, because of the check-in system used at polling locations to verify a voter’s eligibility.
“Obviously, we ask at the polling stations, ‘Are you 18? Are you a North Dakota resident? And, are you a U.S. citizen?’ If you are caught lying in any of that stuff, you are open to prosecution,” he said. 
 Sharing voter info

North Dakota’s voter file has not been shared with the Department of Homeland Security, and the department has not asked the state to share it, Howe said.
Braunberger said North Dakota should continue to protect the privacy of North Dakota citizens. It would also be difficult for a secretary of state to share that data because it is owned by the Department of Transportation.
 Hack attacks

Howe said he participated in briefings conducted by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and FBI ahead of the 2024 election, when he was made aware that foreign adversaries may try to acquire voter data, but to his knowledge, no attempts have been made to access that information in North Dakota.
“I’ve got full faith and confidence in our North Dakota (Information Technology) systems that are protecting the integrity of the election process on that front,” Howe said.
Braunberger said NDIT is constantly monitoring hacking threats, and he is certain the state’s voter file is secure. He added motor vehicle departments in other states notify North Dakota when people move out of state and acquire new ID cards, which then updates the voter file.
Voting absentee? Mind your signatures, North Dakota election officials say

Paper ballots 
Howe stressed North Dakota uses paper ballots in every election that can always be audited.
Both candidates noted that touch-screen voting machines and ballot tabulators are not connected to the internet and still produce a paper ballot.
“Every single one of the ballots that are out there are paper, even when you use the express machine, you get a paper read out of it, and that’s what gets counted,” Braunberger said
Howe described the method for counties submitting election results as using a military-grade encryption portal. He agreed that the state’s method for compiling results is secure.
 Mail-in ballots

In North Dakota, mail-in ballots are only sent to residents who submit applications to vote by mail. Signatures are verified against the application and those that don’t match are set aside to be verified by the voter or evaluated by county canvassing boards.
“I’ve even talked to people in the Legislature who have had their ballots flagged because their signatures did not match, so our systems are working,” Braunberger said. “And they go down to the county auditor to validate that it is truly them.”
Howe and Braunberger said the only potential problem they see with mail-in voting in North Dakota stems from potential delays in delivery by the U.S. Postal Service.
Lawmakers approve earlier deadline for North Dakota absentee ballots to align with Trump order

“The North Dakota Legislature has put all the processes in place to make sure one person, one vote, and that your vote is counted accurately, securely and in a fair manner,” Howe said. 
Braunberger said a law passed in 2025 by the Legislature requiring ballots to be in the hands of election officials by the time polls close on Election Day needs more educational outreach to ensure voters are aware of the new deadline. 
Braunberger said Trump’s election integrity rhetoric without proof was “dangerous” and reduces the confidence in election systems across the country.
“I think we need to boost our confidence in election systems, especially since we’ve had such apathy in people willing to vote at all,” Braunberger said. “We need to be increasing that, because we need more civic engagement … and his speech creates more mistrust.”
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Fallout from student column sparks press freedom scrutiny in Grand Junction
description: The staff advisor to the Orange & Black, Grand Junction High School’s student newspaper, was reassigned less than two weeks after another teacher complained about a student-penned column about the Israel-Gaza conflict. The Grand Junction High School administration had attempted on numerous occasions to block the newspaper from publishing various content, and[...]
text:
Eli Shultz, left, and Alek Purser, right, former student journalists with Grand Junction High School’s Orange & Black student newspaper, pose outside the school Monday. (Photo by Sharon Sullivan/Colorado Newsline)The staff advisor to the Orange & Black, Grand Junction High School’s student newspaper, was reassigned less than two weeks after another teacher complained about a student-penned column about the Israel-Gaza conflict.
The Grand Junction High School administration had attempted on numerous occasions to block the newspaper from publishing various content, and the column about Gaza may have been the final straw, said Steve Fox, who served as the newspaper’s advisor for five years. 
“I was totally unprepared for (the reassignment),” he said.
Fox was notified May 14, he’d no longer be advising the student newspaper — after the May 4 publication of “Why is Gaza Important — American tax dollars fund genocide,” an op-ed written by then-senior Alek Purser for the newspaper’s fourth-quarter print edition. 
A Colorado Newsline public records request uncovered emails from high school social studies teacher Mark Carris sent to Fox and administration staff condemning the Gaza piece. He said the piece contained “outright racism,” “bigotry” and “Nazi propaganda​,” and suggested Purser deserved punishment and removal from the program. Carris is faculty advisor for the school’s Young Conservatives club.

Eli Schultz, the Orange & Black editor-in-chief at the time, said there was never any backlash from students, the administration or other faculty regarding the column. Marie Calkins,  a previous editor, described the piece as a “researched article with cited sources.”
Purser, Schultz, Fox and incoming Orange & Black editor-in-chief Mason Strippel met with Principal Jory Sorensen in May and were told the administration found nothing wrong with the Gaza piece and did not agree with Carris’ comments toward one of its students, Purser said.
A few days later, “on the day of graduation I find out that Fox has been reassigned,” Purser said. “I don’t think that was a coincidence. I think they didn’t want Eli or Mason — the incoming editor-in-chief — to write about it.”
Free speech group considers next steps
The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, a national free speech nonprofit based in Philadelphia, has become involved in the case. On July 14, Marie McMullan, FIRE’s student press counsel, sent an email to Sorensen, Assistant Principal Jared Burek, and Mesa County Valley School District 51 Superintendent Brian Hill informing the administration of “Colorado’s New Voices law, which prohibits public schools from reassigning an advisor for acting to protect student expression.” 
In an email to Newsline, McMullan wrote: “The district did not provide Fox with any documentation as to why he was reassigned, but student leaders at the Orange & Black sounded the alarm that it was in response to the paper’s content. That reporting led us to reach out to Fox to do public advocacy. We wrote to the district calling for it to reverse its decision and to fulfill our public records request on July 14. A representative from the district responded to our public records request that same day, and we received some records on July 15.”



Quotation







It is ironic that the administration would threaten the one thing that inspired me most as a high school student — the one thing I truly thought Grand Junction High School did better than any other school.


– Alek Purser, former student journalist at Grand Junction High School


McMullan said the organization will consider its next steps after it hears back from the school district.
Schultz, who was editor-in-chief during the 2025-26 school year, said Sorensen tried to squash a news story about a discrimination lawsuit against the principal, Assistant Principal Josh Warinner, and the district, brought by former girls basketball coach Sydni Brandon.
Sorensen called Schultz to his office to dissuade him from publishing the story, Schultz said. “He said he felt disrespected and that the article would put him in a bad light.”
The newspaper staff determined it was relevant news and published the story.
Sorensen declined to be interviewed for this story.
Complaints from ‘stakeholders’
Marie Calkins, the 2024-25 Orange & Black editor-in-chief, wrote in a June column titled “Student Press freedom under threat at GJHS” in Grand Junction’s Daily Sentinel newspaper, that over the past two years, the administration “has attempted to censor, review, and repress several articles and elements within the publication.”
During her tenure as editor-in-chief, Calkins said the administration tried to stop the publication of a cover photo of a large group of football fans because it contained an image of a student wearing a T-shirt with the words “I Hate Milfs.” Calkins and Schultz both described the photo as overall positive, and showing school pride.

Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



Sorensen had asked for prior review and engaged in restraint regarding the photo — which is when a school official tells a publication not to publish something and acts against them doing so, Calkins wrote. The administration backed down after students said that would be a violation of the First Amendment and that state law guarantees students’ freedom of the press.
Fox continues to advise the school’s yearbook staff and teach journalism classes. He also advises Colorado Mesa University’s student newspaper, The Criterion. Calkins is studying mass communications at CMU and writes for The Criterion. She expressed concern that Fox’s replacement lacks journalism experience and did not apply or interview for the newspaper advisor position at the school.
During Fox’s five-year tenure advising the Orange & Black, the newspaper has won multiple statewide awards from the Colorado Student Media Association. For the 2024-25 school year the staff won 19 awards for writing, design, photography and podcasting. The newspaper also garnered state awards in 2023 and 2022, and a special national award in 2021 for its coverage of the aging high school building.
“The Orange & Black has been a newspaper for more than 100 years,” Schultz said. “It has a big legacy. It’s sad to see what’s happening currently.”
Colorado Newsline contacted Assistant Principal Heather O’Brien and Carris, the teacher who made the complaint, but they both declined to be interviewed for this story.
Caught off guard
Other articles considered controversial by the administration have included stories critical of AP classes, and the Tiger Portfolio — a graduation requirement where students must create a web site, said Fox.
“It’s hard for me to tell you what triggered (the reassignment). I have not been told,” Fox said.
“Complaints from various stakeholders” – a term that FIRE calls “vague” — was the only reason given for his reassignment, Fox said. “It’s tough to swallow, for sure. I’m not sure what it means. I’m not sure of the complaints and where they’re from.”
While Fox said he is preparing to return to Grand Junction High School to teach the English classes, he would prefer to resume his role as newspaper advisor. 
Purser said he is pursuing a career in journalism because of his experience writing for the school newspaper under Fox’s leadership. He plans to study journalism and political science at DePaul University in Chicago this fall.
Purser said Carris’ response to his opinion piece caught him off guard. For his final piece before graduation he said he wanted to write about an important topic to raise awareness of the issue and urge students to exercise their right to vote. 
“It is ironic that the administration would threaten the one thing that inspired me most as a high school student — the one thing I truly thought Grand Junction High School did better than any other school,” he said in an email. “I hope they choose to protect the best thing they had rather than to destroy it”
Calkins also expressed concern about how Fox’s ouster will affect the newspaper.
“I think the reassignment of Mr. Fox without any kind of process seems suspicious,” she said. “It’s become just a club. It is no longer a place for education of journalism. I wouldn’t be going into journalism if not for (Fox) and the program he created.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: How we can build a future for farming in Arkansas
description: It’s not hard to find data that points to a farm crisis in our state.  Arkansas not only lost 166,000 acres of farmland in five years, but also led the country in farm bankruptcies in 2025. There’s no shortage of reasons why this is happening: land prices have soared, land is lost to development, older […]
text:
A farmhouse sits along a gravel road near Elgin, Iowa. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)It’s not hard to find data that points to a farm crisis in our state. 
Arkansas not only lost 166,000 acres of farmland in five years, but also led the country in farm bankruptcies in 2025. There’s no shortage of reasons why this is happening: land prices have soared, land is lost to development, older farmers are aging out of the profession and there’s a lack of resources for younger farmers to take their place. 
This crisis puts farmers like Jacob Rowell, owner of Kings River Produce, at a crossroads. Despite being an experienced vegetable farmer, Jacob once considered leaving vegetable production altogether. He lacked the infrastructure needed to grow his business but couldn’t justify investing in improvements on property he didn’t own. 
Growing his business was simply out of reach. What Jacob needed was affordable, protected farmland, and a partnership that could help him scale his business. It’s clear that we need more investment in people and programs that can meet the needs of a new generation of farmers. 
Through agricultural conservation and supportive partnerships, it’s possible to meet those needs in northwest Arkansas. The region has a rich agricultural history, and it’s critical that we protect both the land and the ability to make a living farming it. 



Let us know what you think...


 


Furthermore, local farms cultivate not only fresh food, but opportunities for community and connection. When farms disappear, so do those opportunities. 
The Conservation Fund’s Farms Fund program recently debuted in northwest Arkansas and demonstrates how conservation is a tool that can be used to protect the future of local farming. 
The Farms Fund follows a unique model that involves buying valuable farmland, connecting up-and-coming farmers with that land and putting permanent protections on that land so it can be used for farming forever. 
The fund then enters leases with farm businesses to provide a pathway to ownership. During the lease, the Farms Fund works with these businesses to help them grow. It’s a win-win-win situation: land is saved, farmers thrive and surrounding communities get greater access to fresh, healthy food. 
This program recently partnered with Jacob and Kings River Produce to lease a farm in Berryville, a little over an hour away from booming areas like Fayetteville and Bentonville. 
While growing the business on this new property, Kings River Produce will be able to help supply more fresh, local food to the region. Jacob is also collaborating with a mentor farmer who will help him optimize his production techniques. He’ll be able to pass that knowledge down to new farmers, who can grow their own produce. This could help strengthen vegetable production throughout Arkansas at a time when in-state vegetable production has become more rare. 
With conserved farmland, a strong partnership and the opportunity to own the farm in four years, what was once out of reach for Jacob can become reality. 
The Farms Fund’s debut in northwest Arkansas will help meet the needs of not only farmers, but of surrounding communities. Northwest Arkansas is one of the fastest growing regions in the United States, and its population is predicted to double to 1 million by 2050. With population growth comes a greater demand for food, which can quickly become overwhelming at a time when food is becoming less and less affordable. 
Nearly 30% of Arkansas residents face food insecurity – one of the highest rates in the country. The more local food we produce, the more accessible it is to everyone. Well-resourced programs that support local food growers like Kings River Produce help meet a critical community need. 
Innovative partnerships and programs like this one in northwest Arkansas can be replicated nationwide. The Farms Fund, for example, has had success in Chicago, Atlanta and Charlotte. 
In 2025, the farm businesses we partnered with produced more than 1 million pounds of food. Imagine what we could do if we continue to build out these partnerships throughout the state of Arkansas, as well as around the country. 
Through conserving at-risk farmland, and helping farm businesses grow on that land, a future for farming in Arkansas is possible. Investment in this work will not only support farmers like Jacob, but growing metro communities that need greater access to fresh food. 
It takes a village to sustain local farming, but with the right resources and partnerships in our tool belt, we have what it takes to make it happen — one farm at a time.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: ‘We speak from different pulpits:’ New WV bishop says he doesn’t see himself as Trump opponent
description: The new leader of the Catholic church in West Virginia came to the United States years ago as an undocumented immigrant, and he’s spoken against President Donald Trump’s crackdown on immigration, but Rev. Evelio Menjivar-Ayala doesn’t see himself as an opponent to the president. They just have different perspectives and roles, he said.
text:
Rev. Evelio Menjivar-Ayala, the 10th bishop of the Diocese of Wheeling-Charleston, is seen during his installation services July 2, 2026, in Wheeling, West Virginia. (Photo courtesy of the Diocese of Wheeling-Charleston)The new leader of the Catholic church in West Virginia came to the United States years ago as an undocumented immigrant, and he’s spoken against President Donald Trump’s crackdown on immigration, but Rev. Evelio Menjivar-Ayala doesn’t see himself as an opponent to the president. They just have different perspectives and roles, he said. 
“One is political, and another is religious,” he told West Virginia Watch. “He speaks as a president that has obligations that I don’t have — to protect the people, to protect the (U.S.) border, and I have the obligation just to bring the gospel and be a father, a pastor to everyone.
“So I would say that… we are in different situations,” he said. “So it’s not opposition. It’s just that he has some responsibilities that I don’t have, and I have some responsibilities that he doesn’t have. So we speak from different pulpits, I would say.”
Menjivar, who was the United States’ first Salvadoran bishop, was appointed May 1 by Pope Leo XIV to be the 10th bishop of the Diocese of Wheeling-Charleston. He was installed July 2 in Wheeling. 
The reverend, 56, was a child during the civil war between the U.S.-backed Salvadorian government and a coalition of guerilla groups.
Menjivar said he feared if he stayed in his home he would be drafted into the conflict. 
“The only way to kind of save my life or, you know, to have a future was just leaving El Salvador,” he said. “So that’s how the plan came to be. 
“And obviously I didn’t have the opportunity to come documented, so I did what many, many immigrants were doing: So (I) just took my backpack and set to the north, undocumented,” he said.
Menjivar made two unsuccessful attempts to enter the U.S. before being smuggled across the border in the trunk of a car in 1990. 
Weeks after arriving in Los Angeles, he got a work permit to stay in the United States. It wasn’t until 1996, when he was working as a youth minister, that he became a permanent resident through a religious visa, he said. 
He’s been a United States citizen since 2006. 
Menjivar was religious growing up, but said he didn’t see a future as a priest in the church in Salvador while it was being persecuted during the war. 
He was around 10 in 1980 when Salvadorian Archbishop Oscar Romero was assassinated while celebrating mass. The same year, four American catholic missionaries — three nuns and one lay worker — were raped and shot to death by members of the Salvador national guard in an attack that sparked international outrage. 
He said seeing the violence against the church helped to solidify his faith, requiring him to take it more seriously. 
“It becomes a faith that has to be proven,” he said. “It stops being a cultural faith, that is sometimes the problem, that you are just culturally religious. But in this case, it’s something that you take more seriously, knowing that there is a risk by believing and by practicing that faith.”
Menjivar discovered his vocation in the ministry after coming to the United States and getting more involved with his parish, working as a youth minister, he said. 
After completing seminary and a master’s degree in theology, he was ordained for the priesthood in 2004. In 2023, he became auxiliary bishop for the archdiocese of Washington.
The bishop has criticized the Trump administration’s policies, comparing immigrants’ plight to the suffering of Jesus in a Holy Week essay last year. 
While West Virginia voters have overwhelmingly supported Trump in the last three presidential elections, the bishop said he doesn’t see West Virginia as “red.” He sees it most as green because of the vegetation, he said. 
“I don’t see things as red or blue. I’m here as a pastor, and I’m going to see everything through that perspective,” he said. 
He said the church’s responsibility during the Trump administration is the same it’s always been — to defend the human dignity of everyone. 
“Jesus is our model. He’s our teacher, and he gave us beautiful parables: the parable of the Good Samaritan: who will have compassion for that person in the road?” he said. “And we help people without asking, without questioning their status. We just help because they are human beings. 
“So that is, I would say, our stand, when we defend life, immigrants, the poor, the marginalized workers,” he said. “It is through that perspective that we need to defend and uphold the dignity of every person, from conception to natural death.”
Menjivar is not a stranger to West Virginia. He bought a cabin in the Lost River area of Hardy County during the COVID-19 pandemic. He also helped in a Spanish-speaking community in Martinsburg soon after being ordained, he said. 
“What I love about West Virginia is that sense of community,” he said. “I have gone to parish festivals and I see that everybody knows each other, you know, and the joy of sharing. And one of the things that happen here is that people like to talk.”
He said West Virginia is much more similar to his home in rural El Salvador than the D.C. area where he served previously. 
“It seems like the pace here is a little slower than Washington,” he said. 
Menjivar said he comes to the role of bishop here without an agenda or goals. He first wants to learn more about West Virginia and what the issues are here, he said. 
The church is planning to have a series of 17 meetings throughout the state, during which the bishop will hear from parishioners. They hope to have the meetings done by the end of October.  
“My only plan these days, these coming months, is to go out listening to the pastors, to the priests and to the people, and perhaps then we can come up with some goals for the diocese,” he said. “But these are going to be whatever the pastors and the people present. I mean, what do they see as pressing needs?”
