name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: The history of Indianapolis lives in old newspaper archives. Can we get to it?
description: Back in the day, when newspapers were flush with resources, they had internal libraries or archives of all of their stories, casually referred to as morgues. It was common practice for reporters to “check the morgue” before writing any story about the community. Reporters could learn the history of almost anything in Indianapolis by checking […]
text:
The Indianapolis Public Library still has bound editions of some historical newspapers like this 1916 edition of The Indianapolis Freeman. According to Encyclopedia of Indianapolis, Edward E. Cooper launched The Freeman in 1888, claiming it to be the only illustrated African American journal, the "Harper's Weekly of the Colored Race." Its issues are available online through the Library of Congress. (Photo by Tracey Compton/Public Editor)Back in the day, when newspapers were flush with resources, they had internal libraries or archives of all of their stories, casually referred to as morgues. It was common practice for reporters to “check the morgue” before writing any story about the community.
Reporters could learn the history of almost anything in Indianapolis by checking the morgue. There were clip files — a collection of physical articles — for historic buildings, every neighborhood in the city, people, issues and events. The files were refreshed every morning when librarians would cut up dozens of copies of that day’s newspapers, then neatly fold the clippings and add them to the relevant files. 
Today, our records are digitized, which means anyone can access them from anywhere. And the economic tides have washed away newsroom resources, including staff librarians and the morgues they maintained. While some archivists and editors say it’s beneficial having more access to information at your fingertips, I asked them if something might have been lost to journalists and the community when physical clip files disappeared. 
Editors at both the IndyStar and the Indianapolis Recorder told me that their journalists are adept at historical research, and pointed to examples where their reporters delved into the past, either to explain a traumatic event, give context to an anniversary, or update a story. The IndyStar’s story about 1970s life in the Circle City and The Recorder’s stories highlighting Black History Month illustrate this. 
But do journalists bring history into their reporting often enough? 
Take, for example, Gov. Mike Braun’s recent announcement that the state will end its Minority and Women’s Business Enterprises Program and Indiana’s Diversity Business Enterprises Program, which sought to strengthen the opportunities for minority and women business owners to get state contracts. These laws were passed by our state legislature in 1983. Why? What was happening back then? What’s different today?
Every news outlet that covered this announcement explained Braun’s reasoning and relied heavily on reactions from legislators and community groups. But they all lacked historical context.
Any number of current issues would benefit from more robust research and reference to the historical context to help news consumers understand how we got here. 
 The art of discovery: what’s lost in the digital era

April Hines is the journalism and mass communications librarian for the University of Florida Libraries. She helps students and researchers zero in on exactly what they’re looking for, maneuvering through all sorts of information repositories. The move from physical archives to digital has created many efficiencies for the public and journalists, she said. But it’s not without consequences.
“When you had those clip files, or a newspaper index, and you had content organized by subject, you had the element of discovery,” Hines said. “So you might open a clip file labeled ‘lawsuits’ and then you might find a lawsuit that you never even knew happened. So with keyword searching, you have to have a keyword to search for; you have to know what you’re searching for.”

Tulsa World reporter Randy Krehbiel knows this process well. In reporting on the 100th anniversary of the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre for his newspaper’s coverage and two books he’s written on the subject, he delved into his newspaper’s clip files and archives.

“By doing that, and I didn’t really plan it this way, but by kind of immersing myself in these newspapers, it helped me understand better what it was like to live in 1921 and how that was similar and different to living at that time to 80 years later,” Krehbiel said. 

Reporting on this story was a massive undertaking. He started working on the story in 1999. He read every issue of the Tulsa World from June 1, 1920 to the end of 1922 and every issue of a competing newspaper, the Tulsa Tribune, for the calendar year 1921.

Krehbiel’s one of few reporters in his newsroom who still knows how to access the newspaper’s morgue and does so frequently. The Tulsa World no longer has anyone to maintain the clip files. New reporters are shown where they are but that’s about it, he said. Krehbiel counts this as a loss for daily news coverage.

“I think it’s really hard for a young reporter to go to a city council meeting and they walk in there and they don’t know any of the history of any of the people in that room and they’re trying to follow what’s going on,” he said. “The history helps you understand, again, why they think what they think and say what they say…it’s just amazing how there are these thought strands that continue for generations.”

Krehbiel said that his assignment to cover the anniversary of the Tulsa Race Massacre and to create an archive for the paper was part of a broader effort by Tulsa World to better understand the Black community in Tulsa. 

News outlets in Indianapolis also bring stories from the past into the present.

At the Indianapolis Recorder, which bills itself as the third oldest Black newspaper in the country, editor-in-chief Camike Jones said it is a “standing recommendation” that her reporters consult the paper’s archives when writing stories.

“I encourage it at all times because I do think the context matters and I do believe that having that historical understanding matters,” she said.

To celebrate Martin Luther King Jr. Day this year, she had the paper reprint The Recorder’s 1968 opinion piece by civil rights leader Whitney M. Young Jr., which explains his response to King’s assassination. Recently, she’s also used the paper’s historical archives to tell the story of a bootleg cab kingpin and to update the story of St. Philips Episcopal Church at their 125th anniversary. 

Jones wants the public to know that they can access all of The Recorder’s stories starting in the early 2000s on the paper’s website. Stories before then are available through the Hoosier State Chronicles, Indiana’s statewide digital archive of historic newspapers, operated by the Indiana State Library. Both can be accessed by anyone, for free with an internet connection.

The IndyStar readers with paid subscriptions have access to the paper’s digital archive, going back to December 1845, through Newspapers.com. Executive editor Ryan Martin told me that members of the IndyStar’s staff “extensively reference the archives for reporting projects and initiatives.”
 
I want to hear from you. Please write to me at indypubliceditor@poynter.org.



That shows up on a regular basis in their Sunday editions’ Retro Indy features. And recently, Arts and Creativity reporter Domenica Bongiovanni used the paper’s archives to tell the real story behind the film “Dead Man’s Wire,” and in her reporting on the Children’s Museum carousel. 

“Our journalists are some of the strongest researchers I’ve worked with,” Martin said. “Their attention to history is clearly referenced in their accountability reporting.”

Journalism has changed since the advent of digital archives and the loss of physical ones, and how the community experiences the news has changed as well. I asked Hines, the UF librarian, what the community has lost with the digitization of news archives.

“I think what’s lost is, you know, newspapers are the first record of history,” she said. “So many times when you look up a photograph or what actually happened or those first kind of primary source accounts, a key place you’re going to find those is in a historical newspaper. But, if it hasn’t been digitized, if it hasn’t been made publicly available—or it’s stuck behind a paywall—then it’s much less accessible to those who could benefit the most.”

The digitization process is an expensive investment that not all newsrooms can make, Hines said. She’s even heard of some newspapers throwing their archives, especially photo morgues, in the trash, unable to find a suitable place to house them. 

 News consumers have options to dig deeper

“It is a win for everyone to be able to see newspapers online,” Maria McCauley, America Library Association president, told me in an email. “It is also wonderful to be able to view any archival material online, as accessibility is key. But very little can replace the experience of looking and researching something in person.” 

The newspaper morgues of the past offered reporters ideas, reference points, and historical context. Since the digital age, two things have happened: reporters don’t need the physical copies anymore and newsrooms don’t have the money to maintain physical archives.

We’ve gained access to a trove of digitized newspapers, and we’ve also lost something as a community. News coverage today requires that the public come with some basic level of understanding of the past because the news doesn’t always hold the depth of historical context that it used to. As a news consumer, you have options beyond the news outlets themselves to see this history.

Maire Gurevitz, director of collections at the Indiana Historical Society, reminded me that their collection contains news records in print, film, and audio. Here are the resources available to the public online or at the historical society:

The Indianapolis Recorder’s photo morgue
The Indiana Jewish Post & Opinion and the Illiana News from the state’s Jewish community
El Amigo del Hogar and the Latin Times, newspapers from Northwest Indiana’s Latino community
Periodicals that document the state’s LGBTQ+ community, found in the Michael Bohr Collection of the Indy Pride Chris Gonzalez Library and Archives
WTLC’s Like It Is, Indianapolis’ first predominately Black-owned and operated radio station
Hoosier State Chronicles, Indiana’s historical newspapers’ collection, operated by the Indiana State Library

If you’re adept at using these resources, you’ll be a more informed and critical news consumer. 



				Please join me at my next News & Nibbles: Let’s Talk Media event at the Glendale branch of the Indianapolis Public Library this Thursday, July 23 from 10:30 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. (3660 E. 62nd St., Indianapolis, IN 46220)

title: Mothers tell governor they’d be unemployed, homeless without childcare vouchers
description: Mothers told Indiana Gov. text:
Indiana Gov. Mike Braun admires a welcome message, delivered to him by a child, at Shepherd Community Center's Minnie Hartmann Neighborhood Childcare facility on Tuesday, July 21, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Mothers told Indiana Gov. Mike Braun on Tuesday that they would be unable to work — risking homelessness — without childcare vouchers for their young kids.
“I wouldn’t be able to work without it,” said Jasmine Williams, whose children attend Shepherd Community Center’s Minnie Hartmann Neighborhood Childcare facility in Indianapolis.
“I feel like it has helped my kids have stability, and they have learned a lot, from crawling to graduating pre-K,” Williams told Braun. “… I wouldn’t be able to do it without Minnie Hartmann and CCDF. I don’t think I make enough at home to pay for this every week, plus all my bills.”
Braun spoke to the mothers after a tour of the facility.
Jasmine Williams, left, and Kendra Chavez talk to Gov. Mike Braun about the significance of low-income childcare aid during his visit to Shepherd Community Center’s Minnie Hartmann Neighborhood Childcare facility on Tuesday, July 21, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
He is pushing to increase the state’s contribution to the Child Care and Development Fund, a mostly federally funded program that provides vouchers to children from low-income families, in the next biennial budget. The legislative session begins in January.
“If you want to keep growing the economy, that’s going to be a central part,” Braun said of childcare.
Until recently, CCDF had been closed to new children since December 2024, when enrollment peaked at 69,000 and a waitlist was created. Braun’s administration previously said the program would not expand until 2027, citing funding constraints after a dismal revenue forecast.
But more recent forecasts are markedly rosier. Braun in April secured a $200 million injection from the state’s General Fund to reopen CCDF to an estimated 14,000 children. Enrollments began late May — when the waitlist numbered about 35,000 — and are expected to continue through September.
The Braun administration will propose adding another $200 million per year to the budget line item for early childhood learning, Family and Social Services Administration officials have said.
Kendra Chavez said her oldest child, Ella, began attending Shepherd during the pandemic, after being abused at an in-home daycare. It was a “struggle,” Chavez said, to cover childcare costs for a younger sibling who was on the CCDF waitlist until recently. She is a single parent.
The voucher “meant a lot to me, because that helped put more funding towards my children’s future, making sure that they’re fed, making sure … our bills are paid,” Chavez told Braun. “A little bit less stress on me as well. And it’s also in a nurturing environment where I know they’re taken care of.”
Sarina Donahue, who is also a single mother, said she has the “minimum” left for groceries after paying her bills.
“Without CCDF … my child and I would either be living with a family member or on the streets,” she said. “… Hopefully, it gets me back on my feet to where I can get a better-paying job and maybe not have to rely on it. But for now, that’s my rock.”
Amber Hood cradles her infant while speaking to Gov. Mike Braun during his tour of Shepherd Community Center’s Minnie Hartmann Neighborhood Childcare facility on Tuesday, July 21, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Providers have also struggled, with some closing infant-specific rooms or entire facilities when children that would’ve gotten CCDF vouchers did not during the freeze.
Jay Height, executive director of Shepherd Community Center, told Braun that the childcare facility has 60 to 70 kids but has the capacity for up to 140 — “if the funding is there.”
Assistant Executive Director Andrew Green said about half of enrolled children are receiving vouchers, which is less than the usual 75%. Some of those without can still receive discounts.
The facility serves largely low-income working parents and their children.
Braun has also called on businesses to do their part, highlighting a recent law expanding eligibility for Indiana’s employer child care tax credit to small businesses with up to 500 employees.
“Every business in this state ought to be interested in that, if they’re complaining about not having the workforce,” he told reporters. “… They should be interested, again, in paying for a good portion of it, and that’s why we’re going to try to offer them incentives to get involved broadly across the state.”
“Government can only do so much,” Braun added. But, he said, Indiana is “probably in the best position of any state, per capita” to help out.

title: Rogue puffins visit NH to source snacks, but breeding colonies unlikely for the Granite State
description: Every summer, New Hampshire’s seacoast draws visitors in droves, from sunbathing tourists to ravenous greenhead horseflies. Less expected are Atlantic puffins, which are rare in the state year-round and in summertime become so uncommon that a sighting triggers a statewide birdwatching alert. One of those alerts went out early this July, when eBird user Brade[...]
text:
An Atlantic puffin off the Isles of Shoals, in Rye, in January 2024. A puffin is an uncommon sight in New Hampshire year-round, but especially rare in summertime, when most of the birds are nesting in island colonies off the coast of Maine. A bird spotted offshore of Rye this July was likely looking for food, scientists said. (Photo courtesy of Jim Sparrell/NH Audubon)Every summer, New Hampshire’s seacoast draws visitors in droves, from sunbathing tourists to ravenous greenhead horseflies.
Less expected are Atlantic puffins, which are rare in the state year-round and in summertime become so uncommon that a sighting triggers a statewide birdwatching alert.
One of those alerts went out early this July, when eBird user Braden Tingle reported an Atlantic puffin (also known as a common puffin, or by the Latin name Fratercula arctica) near Rye’s Star Island.
The puffin, Tingle reported, flew past a boat and landed near some black guillemots, a species of seabird related to puffins and known to nest on the Isles of Shoals, before taking off once more and heading east over the open sea.
Tingle could not be reached to discuss the sighting. But New Hampshire Audubon, which tracks rare fowl throughout the state with the help of online reports like Tingle’s, confirmed the observation by analyzing the included photos, said community science project leader Grace McCulloch. The puffin was noted in an Audubon Rare Bird Alert issued on July 6.
“The Atlantic Puffin was a rare and exciting sighting!” McCulloch wrote in a Friday email. Puffins do not breed in New Hampshire; in North America, their southernmost known nesting ground is Eastern Egg Rock, in midcoast Maine. Star Island, where New Hampshire’s puffin was reported this July, is part of the Isles of Shoals, an archipelago about 6 miles offshore from Portsmouth and about 86 miles southwest, as the puffin flies, of Eastern Egg Rock.
New Hampshire Audubon receives only a few reports each year of puffins in New Hampshire waters, McCulloch said. Almost all of those occur far offshore.
“They are not something you would see from Hampton Beach,” she said.
Sightings are especially uncommon in summer, when the birds are nesting and raising chicks on the northern islands where they were born. 
So what might bring a puffin so far from home at the height of nesting season? 
Most likely, the seabird’s journey to the Granite State was gastronomically motivated, said Don Lyons, director of conservation science at the Audubon Seabird Institute in Bremen, Maine. Puffins forage and dive for various species of small fish, sometimes traveling long distances to find prey.
“Puffins are, you know, at all times of year, worried about where their next meal is going to come from — like us,” Lyons said. “So most likely, when a puffin is spotted away from a nesting colony, they’re out foraging.”
In summer, puffins generally stick to foraging in shallow waters around their colonies. The distance this particular puffin appears to have ventured from a colony during summer indicates that it is likely unattached, Lyons and McCulloch said. It may be, for example, a young bird that hasn’t begun to nest, an older bird without a mate, or a partnered bird whose egg or chick failed to survive.
The Northeast U.S. is the southernmost tip of breeding territory for Atlantic puffins, which nest on rocky islands across the North Atlantic. But at one time, the birds were substantially more common in the Northeast, scientists say. 
The exact extent of their former range is unknown, due to limited historical records and the difficulty of observing the birds on land, where they burrow under rocks to nest, Lyons said. But history is clear that colonists pursued puffins relentlessly for meat, eggs, and feathers until they were nearly extirpated from U.S. shores. 
A dwindling population of birds held on at Maine’s Matinicus Rock, where Audubon eventually posted wardens for their protection. But other islands where the seabirds once made their nests were wiped completely bare.
Eventually, a groundbreaking experiment that began in the 1970s, involving transplanted chicks and puffin dummies, restored breeding colonies to two islands in Maine. And two other islands have seen puffin colonies reestablish naturally, both in northern Maine near Acadia National Park. 
Atlantic puffins are listed as vulnerable on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Red List. Among the threats they face, Lyons said, is climate change, which unbalances ocean food chains. This is especially concerning for puffins in the Gulf of Maine, where water is warming faster than almost any other ocean surface water in the world. 
Marine heat waves cause fish to change their behavior, Lyons said. When the fish species puffins rely on for food flee to cooler waters, this can force the birds to eat suboptimal species. One example of this is the Atlantic butterfish, which thrives in warmer water and so is less apt to migrate away during a marine heat wave. But the butterfish is round — “It’s what we call deep-bodied,” Lyons said — and tough for young puffins to swallow. When butterfish are all a parent can bring home to the nest, a chick may starve. 
Puffins also depend on healthy habitats in the open ocean, where they spend the nine months of the year they are not nesting. During this period, puffins’ range expands, stretching southward and out to sea. The Northeast Canyons and Seamounts Marine National Monument, set aside by then-President Barack Obama in 2016, was protected in part because of its importance for puffins, Lyons said.
The status of the monument has fluctuated with shifts in presidential administrations since then, with President Donald Trump taking steps to remove restrictions on commercial fishing within the monument during both his administrations. Yet the area is still protected from other development or uses, and provides an important habitat for the birds, Lyons said. 
Nonetheless, puffins are generally increasing in number on the few Maine islands where they’re found, Lyons said. Eventually, their population growth will slow, he expects, as space diminishes on those rocky shores. It’s unlikely, but not impossible, that they would then expand out to inhabit other islands. 
More robust puffin populations will increase sightings of the birds, including on foraging trips down south. But it’s unlikely, Lyons said, that the puffins would ever take up permanent residence in New Hampshire.
In fact, scant records make it hard to say whether there ever were puffin colonies in what is now New Hampshire to begin with, Lyons said.
On one hand, the birds prefer islands miles out at sea, out of reach from predators like mink, apt swimmers that would happily cross a mile or two of water if they smelled the promise of a seabird colony. Islands like the Isles of Shoals fit at least that criteria. But being fairly sandy, they don’t have much habitat that would appeal to rock-nesting puffins, Lyons said.
“Probably, not very many puffins would ever consider it,” he said. “But, you know, never say never.”
Puffins generate excitement anywhere they go, Lyons said. 
“Puffins are really iconic,” he said. “People really find them charismatic, and fun to view. … When they show up somewhere new or unexpected, that is a fun and exciting event.”
Future sightings of brave puffins far afield in places like New Hampshire will depend on the conservation of nesting colonies where they exist already, in Maine and northward, he added.
“Hopefully, we’ll keep the puffin populations well protected here, and there can be plenty of sightings in the future,” he said.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Biddeford leaders call for justice after ICE shooting. Residents are demanding action.
description: Biddeford officials are calling for justice and accountability for the killing of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who was shot on July 13 by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent. Residents, meanwhile, are demanding that their local leaders take stronger action to protect the community, which they say has been threatened for months by federal […]
text:
Biddeford residents have a moment of silence for Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who was shot by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent, during a July 21 city council meeting. (Photo by Lauren McCauley/ Maine Morning Star)Biddeford officials are calling for justice and accountability for the killing of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who was shot on July 13 by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent. Residents, meanwhile, are demanding that their local leaders take stronger action to protect the community, which they say has been threatened for months by federal immigration authorities.
For the first city council meeting since Guerrero’s shooting, Biddeford Mayor Liam LaFountain read a proclamation into the public record calling for a thorough, transparent investigation into the shooting, and for the federal government to cease its “reckless and deadly” enforcement activities as well as reform the nation’s “broken and inhumane” immigration system. 
“We’d like to be clear about why we are here tonight,” said LaFountain, addressing the roughly 90 people who attended the Tuesday meeting, which was moved from its usual city hall location to Biddeford High School in order to accommodate the expected crowd. “We’re not here because of where Johan was born, we’re not here to make a political point. We’re here because Johan was a member of this community, our community.”
LaFountain also emphasized his ongoing support for Guerrero’s wife, Karolina Rojas Alvarez, who broke her silence last week to remember him as a loving and devoted husband and father.
“Tonight and across Maine there are immigrant families carrying a fear that the rest of us are not asked to carry,” he continued, “that fear is paralyzing…To our immigrant neighbors, you belong, you are part of who Biddeford is, and you should not have to carry this weight alone.”
During the public comment period, many residents pointed to the strong community response, including days of protests and a growing memorial at the corner of Hill and Pool streets where Guerrero was shot, as well as how people have been working together to support their immigrant neighbors since the federal government’s enhanced immigration enforcement operation in January.
But they said they wanted to hear more from their elected leaders about what is being done to protect the people of the city. Some suggested coordinating with other Maine cities that have large immigrant populations, passing ordinances banning face masks or unidentified law enforcement, making the city’s police cars more well-marked, requiring Biddeford police to intervene when residents are being threatened, and making a permanent memorial to honor Guerrero.
A memorial for Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero is shown on July 15, 2026, at the intersection where the 25-year-old was fatally shot by ICE agents in Biddeford, Maine. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)
It’s unclear what legal authority municipalities have to rein in federal immigration enforcement, but community members shaken by their presence the past several months called on their leaders to take more proactive steps.
“The mayor’s statements have been necessary and tonight’s proclamation may properly honor Johan, but statements and ceremony will not make us safe. They do not answer the question before us: What do this city council and this mayor intend to do?” said Sam Pecor, who ran unsuccessfully for city council in November. 
Pecor added, “political responsibility includes what government bodies do after recognizing a danger — a danger that we recognized in January. Limited power is not no power.”
Tophe Thorne, who works for the immigrant support and advocacy group Presente! Maine, said the group warned officials in the winter that “the longer that ICE remained embedded in our communities, the more likely it was that someone was going to die…and here we are, six months later, standing here, proven right in the worst possible way.” 
Guerrero was the 22nd person shot at by federal immigration officers during President Donald Trump’s second term. The Columbian national was not the target of the federal officers and had legal work authorization to work in the U.S.
Sam Bullock was a neighbor of Guerrero and told the council that for months ICE has been “very present” in their neighborhood. “Unfortunately for me as a resident, what happened on Monday was an incredibly tragic inevitability,” Bullock said.
She said other neighbors have shared with her how frightened they’ve been since the winter surge. 
“I’ve seen my immigrant neighbors pull their kids out of school. I’ve seen my immigrant neighbors be pulled out of cars by ICE in front of the children who are at the bus stops,” Bullock said, “the parents are terrified, the children are terrified.” 
“I’ve done what I can as a community member,” Bullock added, “but I feel so very let down by my elected officials that this was allowed to happen for so long.”
LaFountain, who was only sworn in last December, previously told Maine Morning Star that the state has been responsive and helpful in supporting the community through the aftermath of the shooting.
“They’ve been giving us the information that they can — and that’s appropriate — and we’re going to continue to ask for that,” he said. The Maine Attorney General’s office is conducting an independent investigation into the shooting.



Quotation







When something this big happens, and it happens on your watch as a leader, history is going to remember you. What did you do?


– Mufalo Chitam, Maine Immigrant Rights Coalition


Throughout the week, protesters called to “get ICE out of Maine.” State law cannot dictate the actions of federal authorities while they perform their lawful duties, per the U.S. Constitution’s Supremacy Clause. Maine has passed several laws that aim to rein in unlawful action and stop local cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. 
Biddeford police already do not cooperate with ICE. LaFountain said last week that the agency was “not notified of ICE’s interaction prior to them coming to the city…and I don’t see that changing.”
LaFountain’s proclamation also compared the law enforcement standards of the Biddeford Police Department with ICE agents’ lack of body cameras, use-of-force policies, and lack of de-escalation training.
“The enforcement agents of the United States Government fell far short of the professional standards routinely upheld by local police departments throughout Maine,” the resolve reads.
Several city council members said Tuesday they appreciated the comments and that there have already been discussions about what more could be done.
Abigail Woods, who represents Ward 2 where Guerrero lived, said she’s committed to taking action. “This does take all of us. You all have showed up, we have showed up,” Woods said. “We have a little bit more power that we should utilize, but you all have power as well. There’s power in the words you spoke tonight.”
Mufalo Chitam, executive director of the Maine Immigrant Rights Coalition, said history will remember what action the city leaders take.
“When something this big happens, and it happens on your watch as a leader, history is going to remember you. What did you do?” she said. “Let the immigrants remember that change came from a small town in Maine called Biddeford, let change come from this small town.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Former Eau Claire Council President Emily Berge’s insurgent campaign in the 3rd CD
description: Emily Berge, the former president of the Eau Claire city council and a candidate in the Democratic primary for Wisconsin’s 3rd Congressional District, was working the window of the Wisconsin Farm Bureau milkshake stand at the Trempealeau County fair on July 18 when a woman asked her if she knew the Farm Bureau was for […]
text:
Congressional candidate Emily Berge meets with La Crosse area local elected officials at Bodega Bar in downtown La Crosse on July 18. (Photo by Henry Redman | Wisconsin Examiner)Emily Berge, the former president of the Eau Claire city council and a candidate in the Democratic primary for Wisconsin’s 3rd Congressional District, was working the window of the Wisconsin Farm Bureau milkshake stand at the Trempealeau County fair on July 18 when a woman asked her if she knew the Farm Bureau was for Republicans. 
To Berge, who had been at an event with the left-leaning Wisconsin Farmers Union the day before, the critique didn’t make sense. 
She’s running an underdog campaign against Rebecca Cooke — a former political fundraiser, business owner and waitress who nearly won the seat in 2024 and entered the race with massive advantages in fundraising, name recognition and support from high-profile national Democrats. Left, right or center, she is looking to pick up every vote she can get.
Former Eau Claire Common Council President Emily Berge serves milkshakes out of the Farm Bureau stand at the Trempealeau County Fair. (Photo by Henry Redman | Wisconsin Examiner)
Wisconsin’s 3rd CD is currently represented by U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden and leans Republican at its baseline, according to the Cook Political Report. 
Whoever wins the Democratic primary is going to have to pick off some people who have voted for Van Orden, President Donald Trump or both while not losing the support of organic farmers in Viroqua or tattoo artists in La Crosse.
For Berge, that means slinging milkshakes in Galesville, riding the tilt-a-whirl with Democratic state legislators in West Salem, grinding coffee beans with baristas in La Crosse and attending every county fair, dairy breakfast, cranberry festival and parade between Platteville and Eau Claire. 
After announcing her candidacy in April last year over the objections of the national Democratic party, Berge and her husband Mike realized by November that their old Subaru Outback wasn’t up for the rigors of a congressional campaign and bought a used Hyundai. In the subsequent eight months, they’ve driven 18,000 miles criss-crossing the district. 
Cooke, who previously worked for the centrist group Third Way, has burnished her moderate bonafides by forcefully denouncing left-wing policy proposals such as defunding the police and abolishing ICE while touting endorsements from the centrist congressional Blue Dog Caucus, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Michigan U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, a member of the fiscally moderate New Democrat Coalition running as a centrist for the U.S. Senate. She’s also been endorsed by U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders. 
The National Republican Congressional Committee still calls her “Commie Cooke.” 
At the end of the most recent reporting period, Cooke had raised $8.3 million since the start of 2025 — outraising Van Orden — and still has $2.4 million in cash on hand. Back in 2022, Cooke fought her way to  a surprise second-place finish in the Democratic primary for the seat. The winner of the primary, state Sen. Brad Pfaff, lost to Van Orden by 3.7 points. In 2024, Cooke won the primary and then lost to Van Orden by 2.7 points, although she outperformed Vice President Kamala Harris and U.S. Sen. Tammy Baldwin in the district on the same Democratic ticket. 
This year her name recognition and support from national Democrats, including an early endorsement from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, vaulted her to the front of the 2026 race. 
This spring, her campaign touted internal polling that put her more than 40 points ahead of Berge. 
But with three weeks before the Aug. 11 primary, political observers, voters and the Berge campaign feel like the gap is closing. 
Grassroots candidate vs. ‘the Establishment’
An oversimplification of the race would be to describe it as a contest between Berge the progressive and Cooke the moderate. That characterization is somewhat true: On healthcare for example, Berge supports Medicare for All while Cooke has called for more incremental policy changes. 
One of the biggest spats of the primary campaign has centered around LGBTQ issues, with Cooke repeatedly fumbling and recanting when asked in several forums if she would vote for a federal ban on conversion therapy. 
Cooke’s back and forth drew criticism from Van Orden for “flip-flopping”
During a May forum in La Crosse, Cooke said the question of conversion therapy should be left to local decision makers. At a June forum in Platteville she said she wouldn’t vote for a conversion therapy ban only to release a statement soon after saying she misunderstood the question and she would vote for a ban. At the final forum of the campaign last week in Eau Claire, Cooke said she does “not support conversion therapy whatsoever” but did not say how she’d vote on a ban. 
Berge, a trained mental health counselor, has been unequivocal in her support of a federal ban on conversion therapy at each forum and noted that she led Eau Claire’s efforts to pass a local ban on the practice. 
More than any particular policy difference, in an election cycle in which the brand of the Democratic party establishment has become toxic, the race has become a swing-seat contest between a candidate who appears determined to shake every hand in western and central Wisconsin against a consultant-backed candidate with poll-tested talking points.
Emily Berge speaks with voters at the Democratic Party booth at the La Crosse County Fair. (Photo by Henry Redman | Wisconsin Examiner)
Recently filed campaign finance reports show that Cooke’s campaign has spent almost $500,000 on political consultant fees since January of this year. Across her entire campaign, Berge has spent $578,000. 
“It’s kind of that classic tension between the national party and local activists,” Anthony Chergosky, a political science professor at UW-La Crosse, said. “I think that we have seen some ideological differences between the two, but also I think maybe like a bit of a broader conversation here about the value of a competitive primary and the extent to which national political figures should be intervening in these nomination contests.”
Berge, drawing on her experience serving as the president of the Eau Claire common council, is convinced that voters in this cycle are less focused on the exact policy particulars and more interested in someone who comes across as authentic and promises to act with the best interests of the people at heart. 
“It’s not necessarily what, but it’s how. It’s how you show up,” Berge told the Wisconsin Examiner. “That’s what I learned on council. That’s why I ran for council. You know, it’s how you show up, how you lead. It’s about being a bridge between your constituents, city hall or D.C. I think that’s what people want.” 




Quotation







It's kind of that classic tension between the national party and local activists


– UW-La Crosse Professor Anthony Chergosky



Without the cash to pay for its own polling, the Berge campaign is instead looking for other clues that she has the late momentum. On rural roads and residential streets in the district, Berge’s red, white and blue signs far outnumber Cooke’s green ones. The campaign chose to go without an office to save the rent money, but it does have 600 volunteers making calls, writing postcards and helping manage the campaign Reddit account. 
“We just always get different new people joining us,” Berge said. “I mean, I kind of have my core group of volunteers who have been with me since day one, but we’re like a snowball going down the mountain, you know, and we’re just collecting more and more people, and so we can just keep going and growing and growing.” 
The Berge campaign also believes that over multiple campaign cycles, voters’ views on Cooke have solidified — and not necessarily in a positive way. Near constant Republican messaging accusing her of being far left-wing, support from the DCCC in a cycle when voters are incensed with national Democrats, questions swirling around her background of political work — made worse by her recent request to delay the filing of her personal financial disclosures until after the primary — and bad blood from previous campaigns have soured people on Cooke, Berge campaign staff say. 
Additionally, Berge’s supporters say, Cooke’s reputation with the 19 county parties within the district has been harmed by the perception of a coronation by people outside the district and the fact that she hasn’t shown up much. 
“Certainly, the Democratic Party of Wisconsin is aware of how unhappy most of the county parties in the third district were with that early DCCC endorsement,” Kim McMullen, chair of the Monroe County party said. 
McMullen added that Berge has been far more visible in her area.
Berge greets a voter at the La Crosse County fair. (Photo by Henry Redman | Wisconsin Examiner)
“I certainly think having more time on the ground in the county has made a difference for the Berge campaign in terms of name recognition and seeing her as an individual with a real response and plan for various policies,” she said. “Let’s put it this way: all of the candidates for a 3rd CD race have been invited to attend many events, and Emily has been the most engaged thus far. As far as I’m aware, more people within the party have actually been at events with Emily Berge than with the Cooke events, because there was only one Cooke event since the campaign started last summer.”
The same pattern holds in Portage County, the far eastern wing of the district and the home of former state Rep. Katrina Shankland, whom Cooke beat in the contentious 2024 primary.
Gary Hawley, co-chair of the Portage County party, said hurt feelings about Shankland and the Cooke campaign’s failure to show up until recently have left the county “heavy Berge.” 
Campaign finance reports show that Cooke recently placed a $3 million television ad buy and has spent nearly $500,000 on direct mail to voters. 
In a statement, Cooke touted the support she’s received from local elected officials and unions. 
“Our campaign is meeting with Wisconsinites in every corner of our district and building the coalition to flip this seat,” she said. “I’m proud to have earned support from over 50 local leaders who know I’ll fight for their communities, 15 Wisconsin labor unions because I’ll fight for working people, and trusted leaders like Senators Tammy Baldwin and Bernie Sanders who know I’ll be their ally in taking on the career politicians and elites squeezing the rest of us. I will keep working to earn every single vote to win, because Wisconsin deserves a representative who will take on Trump and fight to lower prices, go after the corruption, and actually put us first.” 
Chergosky said that Cooke’s initial financial advantage and name recognition might be too much for the Berge campaign to overcome — though a close-fought Cooke win could portend something about her support heading into November.
“I do think as we get towards the primary, the candidates will start setting expectations in terms of what would be a good night for them, in terms of what would be a good night, a night that feeds momentum into the general election,” he said. “I think it is widely expected that Cooke will win the primary. So perhaps the more interesting question is the margin of victory …  because that could tell us something about the enthusiasm for her within the Democratic Party base.” 
Still, the Berge campaign sees a path. 
Both candidates are from Eau Claire, but Berge’s recent local government service there could be enough to sway a big win in the district’s second largest county. Shankland won 84% of the vote in Portage County in 2024.
If Berge performs well there while squeaking out a lead in the hub of La Crosse County and chipping away at Cooke’s 2024 margins in the more rural counties, it could be enough to pull off the upset. 
“On our worst night we give her a heart attack,” Nicholas Padesky, Berge’s campaign manager, said of Cooke. 
At each stop Berge made during a packed Saturday of campaigning, Berge’s staff had to drag her away from conversations with voters. She said that she might have disagreements with lots of voters on the issues, but she’ll work to make sure they all know she cares about them. 
“I may not have agreed with Emily on that, but I know she cares deeply about our community,” Berge said, describing voters’ experience with her in local government, which she hopes to translate to her campaign. 
And she believes she can get that message across without selling out the progressive voters and marginalized communities at the core of the Democratic primary electorate — saying she can see opportunities for compromise on lots of issues, including guns, data centers and zoning issues, but not on civil rights. 
“If it’s about civil rights or human rights or constitutional rights, if it’s about humanity, I’m not gonna compromise,” she said.

title: What’s ‘The Secret’ to success? Donald Trump and Norman Vincent Peale might be able to tell you.
description: Back in 2006, talk show host Oprah Winfrey made the book and movie “The Secret” household names. “The Secret” promotes the idea that you can get anything you want. This is achieved by practicing the power of positive thinking and applying a number of certain mental practices to gain your objective. One not-so secret about […]
text:
President Donald Trump speaks during a rally at Mount Rushmore National Memorial on July 3, 2026 in Keystone, South Dakota. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)Back in 2006, talk show host Oprah Winfrey made the book and movie “The Secret” household names.
“The Secret” promotes the idea that you can get anything you want. This is achieved by practicing the power of positive thinking and applying a number of certain mental practices to gain your objective. One not-so secret about “The Secret” is this idea is not new. Author Rhonda Byrne said she learned the principles in a book published in 1910 called “The Science of Getting Rich.”
When this book and movie came out, I was first concerned, then appalled, by the number of friends I knew who were sucked into its whirlpool of self indulgence and greed.
I spoke with my friend Elmer Green (he and his wife were the founders of biofeedback therapy), and he told me this stuff was “old hat.” He and his wife, Alyce, had dealt with this idea in the mid-20th century after the publication of yet another version of this concept was published. They had shared the same worries. That book came out in 1937 and was called “Think and Grow Rich.”
What concerns me is not whether this approach works. It actually does work. If you follow the steps outlined in these books and are guided by their principles, you can — if you practice correctly and long enough — get almost any thing you want.
This is a terrible idea.
First, it is selfish. None of these books talk about our responsibility as members of a society and of a planet with limited resources. They promote unbridled greed with slick justifications. Worries about pollution (“The Secret” came out when Hummers and other giant, gas-guzzling vehicles were in fashion) and concerns about taking resources from others are just “stinkin’ thinkin’.” The faulty assumption is that we can all have everything we want without regard for anyone else’s needs, finite resources or the health of our sacred planet.
This philosophy blames people personally for everything that happens to them. Diagnosed with cancer? You must have been thinking negatively. Got food poisoning at your favorite restaurant? It wasn’t the broken refrigerator but you who failed in some way. Born with a disease of some kind? That was also bad thinking on your part, perhaps in the womb.
I was dismayed by the number of people I met in my bodywork therapy office who felt at fault for things they had no way of controlling. Being an employee at a company that closed. Being a passenger in an airplane crash. And so on. Of course, there are choices we make and things we do that influence what happens to us, but to believe that our own actions contribute 100% is destructive magical thinking.
Finally, this philosophy promotes the false idea that things can make you happy.
If I had seen that pay off, even once, I could understand why people may want to try. But getting everything you think you want doesn’t make you happy — at least not anyone I have met. I’m not talking about the basics of food, shelter and clothing. If you lack basic needs and get them, you will be happier. That is a given. But it is not clear from current research that once you have achieved a solid foundation having more will make you happier or give you greater purpose or well-being.
These books promise you not just material things but also fame, power and reputation. In my experience, attainment of these will likewise not make you happy. Have you ever met someone resting in genuine wellbeing based on material wealth or reputation?
It is fine to have those things or not. The problem begins if our basic wellbeing is tied to them.
Look to President Donald Trump. He is one of the most successful proponents of “The Secret” I have ever seen. Trump’s minister was Norman Vincent Peale — from childhood until Peale’s 1993 death. The clergyman taught an early version of the Prosperity Gospel, a kissing cousin to “The Secret” dressed up in ecclesiastical robes. Trump took those teachings to heart. He rocks them hard. And he wins. And wins and wins and wins.
People are infuriated by Trump’s denial of facts and insistence on his reality, or alternate facts as they have been called. He is not denying facts. In his mind, he is practicing the power of positive thinking. Willing what he wants to be true. And it works, at least sort of. Trump continues to get everything he wants over and over again — at least sort of.
A central premise of the Secret is every person for themselves. If others have problems because of your actions, that is their problem, not yours. Each person for themselves. But I ask you, despite Trump’s continued assertion that he gives himself an A+ in everything, does he look happy to you? Would you aspire to “win” like him?
The ideas contained in these types of books will not bring you happiness. They may well harm you, your family and the world around you.
My friends were quite upset when I voiced my concerns regarding “The Secret” back in 2006. I spoke at length to anyone who would listen about what a danger this mindset is. Green and I presented our concerns at a conference and caused quite a bit of consternation among attendees.
To friends who argued with me back then, I am here to say a very sorrowful “I told you so.” This was my very concern: someone practicing these teachings who craved power, coupled with greed and a lack of regard for others. What damage could they do? We are finding that out right now, and so far the damage is pretty catastrophic.
Is the remedy to practice the secret against Trump and his goals for our country? Nope. Read my paragraphs above.
The remedy is luckily not only the way to fix our problems. It also carries the seed of genuine well being. Practice radical caring and kindness. Care for ourselves by all means, but make our acts of self care acts of divine selfishness (this is a term I coined that means self care for the benefit of yourself and everyone else too). We fill our own cup so we can be present and fill everyone around us. Love with compassion for yourself and all others, including Trump and his followers.
Love and compassion are not excuses to act like a doormat. I do not suggest blindly accepting and allowing bad behavior or ignoring actions that do harm. Absolutely not! We do not love the bad behavior or actions of ourselves or other people. That would be silly and destructive. This type of love is not personal. Nor is it dependent on outer circumstance. This aspiration of loving kindness is genuinely wishing wellbeing for everyone we encounter.
There is logic in this approach. People who are genuinely happy (called eudaemonia), are resting in a state of ease and wellbeing not dependent on outer circumstances. Our aspiration of loving kindness for ourselves first and then for others is to find this state. People who are genuinely happy don’t harm others because they are content. When we are genuinely content, it naturally follows that our actions become more wise and less harmful.
Why would we not wish this for every single person we encounter?
As we take action to right this ship of a world that has tilted so terribly wrong, do so with love. Love the sad broken people acting with ignorance and greed. Love them, even as we cast ballots and call for accountability. Do all we can to educate, inform and encourage people to act in ways that help us all.
When we stumble, let others help us too. Through that intention and action, we will come to find that genuine well being comes from a foundation of interconnection, compassion and care for all beings.
To me, that is the real secret.
Laura Mead is a retired bodywork therapist, meditation teacher, artist and sometimes assistant documentary filmmaker. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Natural resources commission gets new chairman amid recent turmoil
description: The Indiana Natural Resources Commission on Tuesday elected a new chairman, who acknowledged the recent upheaval on the citizen-led panel. Former state Rep. Kevin Mahan takes over after four recent resignations. The members who left have criticized a new process used by the Indiana Department of Natural Resources they say cuts out meaningful input by […]
text:
The Indiana Natural Resources Commission meets on Tuesday, July 21, 2026. (Screenshot of livestream)The Indiana Natural Resources Commission on Tuesday elected a new chairman, who acknowledged the recent upheaval on the citizen-led panel.
Former state Rep. Kevin Mahan takes over after four recent resignations. The members who left have criticized a new process used by the Indiana Department of Natural Resources they say cuts out meaningful input by the commission.
“This commission has been through a lot of change over this short period of time. We should not pretend otherwise. I want to recognize the members who recently left the commission,” Mahan said. “They devoted many years, some of them decades, to Indiana’s natural resources and to this body, and they cared very deeply about both. And their service does deserve much respect.”
He also gave credit to Gov. Mike Braun for his “commitment to conservation and stewardship.”
One key change has roiled the commission. Historically, the group would preliminarily propose rules before voting to adopt them, giving the board a chance to have direct say.
Instead, Department of Natural Resources Director Alan Morrison began posting preliminary approvals himself, which is permitted under Indiana administrative rules. The commission learned about the change in March, when they were asked to OK a rule the members had not previously seen.
Under the new process, board members can’t make changes to the rules proposed by Morrison and would have to attend public hearings to provide input.
Mahan — a former Blackford County sheriff who was a Republican Indiana House member in 2010-19 — conceded the change, saying “some steps in the process may be handled differently than they were in the past, but our role is not ceremonial … public notice and comment are not boxes to check; they are part of making sound decisions and maintaining public trust.”
He has asked Morrison to give a standing report at each meeting on provisional, interim and permanent rules in the process and other orders issued since the last meeting.
“This will ensure people will know what is happening and what is coming next,” he said.
Mahan said he will work closely with Morrison, agency officials and fellow commissioners.
“We will not always agree, and not every question will be easy. But we will treat everyone with respect,” he said. “Our decisions do affect people, and I think we need to remember that it will also affect communities, wildlife, public lands, and water resources throughout Indiana. That work deserves care and openness, and it also deserves a commission that people can trust.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: The Pennsylvania Capital-Star earns seven 2026 Keystone Awards
description: The Pennsylvania Capital-Star has been recognized by the Pennsylvania NewsMedia Association with seven Professional Keystone Media Awards in Division III for its work in 2025, including five First Place honors.
text:
Law enforcement officers stand outside the governor's residence on April 13, 2025, after a fire led to the evacuation of Gov. Shapiro and his family. It is being investigated as arson. (Ian Karbal/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)The Pennsylvania Capital-Star has been recognized by the Pennsylvania NewsMedia Association with seven Professional Keystone Media Awards in Division III, which is for multi-day publications with a circulation of up to 9,999. 
The number of awards is an all-time high for the organization. Five were first place honors, which is another record for us.
I’m particularly proud that the majority of the awards honor our coverage of some of last year’s top stories in the commonwealth. They include the firebombing of the governor’s residence, the chaotic impact Trump administration cuts had on Pennsylvania’s federal workforce and how the elimination of federal tax credits on health insurance premiums were hurting some Pennsylvanians.
Judges awarded the team — Peter Hall, Ian Karbal, John Cole and myself — first place for Breaking News coverage for its work to provide details and context for the April 13 attack on the governor’s residence and the man responsible for it. Coverage of what led Cody Balmer to an act of terrorism earned the staff a second place award in the Ongoing News category. 
A worker at a fracking facility wears a NIOSH-approved respirator. (Image provided by the CDC, 2016)
Ian was honored with a first place award for News Beat Reporting for his persistent coverage of an underreported yet critically important issue — federal employee cuts in mine safety programs based in Pennsylvania. Among the stories included in the entry was the detailing of a move to halt almost all work at an Allegheny County lab that certifies the nation’s N95 masks and other respirators. 
He and I earned a first place award for Headline Writing, as well. 
Whitney Downard joined the Capital-Star in November 2025 and immediately started looking into the impact of the pending expiration of federal tax credits that reduced health insurance premium costs for Pennsylvanians using Medicaid. Her profile of Jamie and Carrie Wright of McKeesport and their struggles to come to terms with a 265% increase in their monthly premium was honored with a first place in the News Feature Story category. 
Now, you may know I’m a bit of a history buff. So not long after I took the helm at the Capital-Star, I followed up on a tip about how one man’s hunt for information about his great-uncle’s military service led him to the small French community of Gathemo, which in turn decided to honor the men of Pennsylvania’s 28th Division who liberated it in 1944. I soon learned how it also inspired an effort to find other families connected to the nine soldiers who gave their lives in the battle for Gathemo, but had no idea about their loved ones’ role in the fight.
The aftermath of the battle between the 28th Division and German troops in Gathemo, France, in August, 1944. (Screenshot from National Archives film)
I’m thrilled to say the story was honored with a first place award in the Feature Story category. It also earned a second place award in the Features Video category. Pvt. Irwin S. Fox’s family contributed photos and a recording for an audio slideshow featuring the soldier’s voice, nearly 81 years after his death around Gathemo.
You share in the recognition of the Pennsylvania Capital-Star’s work. Whether you know it or not, you play a role in our ability to — paraphrasing former Radio Television Digital News Association Executive Director Dan Shelley — commit “flagrant acts of responsible journalism” every day. 
You make it all possible simply by reading our stories, sharing our work, subscribing to the Morning Guide newsletter and donating your hard earned money to support our efforts to connect the dots on how policy decisions in Harrisburg and Washington, D.C., impact you and your community.
So from Emily, Peter, Whitney, Ian and me, THANK YOU for holding us to a high standard every day and for trusting us to bring you factual, contextualized, nuanced and honest reporting on the policies and people shaping our great commonwealth. 
We are eternally grateful.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: In Ohio case, federal judge says warrantless ICE arrests are illegal, but denies motion to stop them
description: A federal judge sitting in Cincinnati, Ohio on Friday ruled that federal authorities are making illegal immigration arrests. Then she dismissed a case seeking to stop the practice. U.S. District Judge Sarah D. Morrison, a 2018 Trump appointee, ruled that Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents had made many arrests in Ohio that “deeply trouble the […]
text:
A masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent knocks on a car window in Minnesota on Jan. 12, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)A federal judge sitting in Cincinnati, Ohio on Friday ruled that federal authorities are making illegal immigration arrests. Then she dismissed a case seeking to stop the practice. 
U.S. District Judge Sarah D. Morrison, a 2018 Trump appointee, ruled that Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents had made many arrests in Ohio that “deeply trouble the Court.” They were illegal, she said, because they were made without a warrant and without making a determination that a person would flee before a warrant could be obtained.
One federal official “testified that almost all of his agency’s arrests are warrantless,” the judge’s order said.
Then she dismissed the case because she said the plaintiffs didn’t do an adequate job of showing the Trump administration is likely to keep making such arrests. She made the ruling even as ICE insists it doesn’t need warrants.
Groups defending the immigrants who brought the case were not pleased.
“The opinion from the court confirms what we already knew: ICE violated the law and arrested our clients illegally,” said Angela Plummer, executive director of Community and Refugee Immigration Services, one of the groups representing the plaintiffs. 
“Unfortunately, we are living in a world where documented human rights violations alone are insufficient to compel court action to stop them.”
The case was brought in March by four people who argued warrantless immigration arrests were so common that the case should be a class action and include all similarly situated people.
As the Trump administration tries to arrest 3,000 immigrants a day, critics say it’s run roughshod over due process, sweeping up people who are here legally and even some citizens.
In her ruling, Judge Morrison agreed with the plaintiffs that before making arrests, ICE agents need to have both probable cause to believe a person is in violation of immigration law and is likely to flee before a warrant can be obtained.
“Upon a fulsome review of the record in this case, it is clear that (ICE agents) have, in some instances, unlawfully arrested and detained non-citizens in Ohio without a warrant and without a probable cause determination of their likelihood of escape,” Morrison’s ruling said. “Some of the accounts offered by Plaintiffs and (the class) they wish to represent about how individual agents effectuated arrests deeply trouble the Court.”
One of the plaintiffs in the case was Moises Javier Aguilar Peralta, 38, who came to Ohio from Honduras in 2023, sought asylum and got a work permit, Social Security number, and a driver’s license. 
On Dec. 18, as he walked out of a Columbus Home Depot with materials he needed for work, four masked men in civilian clothes stopped him. When he told them he had an active asylum case, the agents told him it wasn’t valid and arrested him, the suit said.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
They didn’t ask him any questions to determine the legality of his presence in the country or to determine if he was a flight risk, it said.
As with the other plaintiffs, Peralta was held — and unable to support his family — for weeks and lived in a state of terror after his release, his lawyers said.
As of late March, around 670 immigrants in Ohio were in ICE detention.
“Countless of these individuals were arrested and detained without a warrant and without any pre-arrest, individualized determination of probable cause,” the plaintiffs said.
They asked Morrison to certify the case as a class action and order the government to stop making improper warrantless arrests. 
Judge Morrison rejected the request, saying the four original plaintiffs didn’t adequately show they were likely to be re-arrested. But if the class were certified, re-arrests among that much-larger group would have been much more likely.
Morrison acknowledged the pressure Trump is putting on ICE to make thousands of arrests a day. She also heard from U.S. Border Patrol Acting Deputy Patrol Agent in Charge Steven Vorholt.
“Agent Vorholt, a supervisor who oversees and evaluates the field operations of USBP agents and their supervisors, testified that almost all of his agency’s arrests are warrantless,” Judge Morrison wrote.
In addition, she acknowledged that other courts have found that federal agents are making illegal, warrantless immigration arrests. 
And ICE’s own website flatly says its agents don’t need warrants to arrest people they believe are in violation of immigration law.
“ICE does not need judicial warrants to make arrests,” it says. “Like all other law enforcement officers, ICE officers and agents can initiate consensual encounters and speak with people, briefly detain aliens when they have reasonable suspicion that the aliens are illegally present in the United States, and arrest people they believe are illegal aliens.”
Even so, Judge Morrison said the plaintiffs fell short because they didn’t show federal immigration arrests are always warrantless or that the agencies have a written policy to act illegally. She cited internal documents saying agents needed to get warrants in cases where escape wasn’t imminent.
“In this case, Plaintiffs have not shown that all of Defendants’ agents always make warrantless arrests without determining the non-citizen arrestee’s likelihood of escape,” she wrote. 
“Nor have Plaintiffs shown that either ICE or CBP adopted a written policy of unlawful conduct. Although the Court finds that Plaintiffs have shown for jurisdictional purposes that Defendants authorized their agents, through an unofficial custom or practice, to make unlawful warrantless arrests in Ohio, Plaintiffs have not convinced the Court that Defendants are sufficiently likely to subject them to another arrest under that practice.”
Freda Levinson, the chief legal officer of ACLU of Ohio, found a partial victory in the ruling.
“This ruling is deeply disappointing and frustrating, but it also recognizes that federal agents are wantonly conducting haphazard arrests in clear violation of the dictates and the Immigration and Nationality Act,” she said in a written statement.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Stop approving Wisconsin’s energy future one docket at a time
description: In a recent guest column, I argued that Wisconsin’s clean energy future is about affordability, jobs, manufacturing and economic competitiveness. The next question is equally important: Not one regulatory docket at a time. Wisconsin stands at one of the most consequential energy crossroads in its history. Artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing and e[...]
text:
Wisconsin needs a comprehensive energy plan. State Capitol and renewable energy collage by Henry Redman. (Photos by Baylor Spears and Marga Buschbell-Steeger/Getty)In a recent guest column, I argued that Wisconsin’s clean energy future is about affordability, jobs, manufacturing and economic competitiveness.
The next question is equally important:
How should we build that future?
Not one regulatory docket at a time.
Wisconsin stands at one of the most consequential energy crossroads in its history. Artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing and electrification are driving electricity demand faster than anyone anticipated. The Public Service Commission’s draft Strategic Energy Assessment projects peak demand could increase by more than 40 percent by 2032, with more than 70 percent of that growth tied to just three proposed hyperscale data centers.
Those investments present tremendous economic opportunities. They also require smarter planning.
Today, the PSC is evaluating the Foundry Ridge and Red Oak Ridge methane gas plants alongside transmission projects, data center tariffs, utility investments, and other major infrastructure. Each proceeding examines a single project. None asks the broader question:
Taken together, are these investments the lowest-cost, lowest-risk path to Wisconsin’s energy future?
Without comprehensive resource planning, regulators have little opportunity to compare alternatives before committing customers to decades of infrastructure costs.
Affordable electricity is economic development.
The decisions made today will determine what Wisconsin families, businesses, manufacturers, and farmers pay for electricity for decades. They will also affect water resources, public health, and our state’s long-term competitiveness.
This is not an argument against growth. Wisconsin will continue to attract investment in advanced manufacturing, artificial intelligence, and data centers. The question is not whether growth occurs, but whether it is planned responsibly so that large energy users pay the costs they create rather than shifting risks onto everyone else.
Planning should begin by comparing complete portfolios of resources instead of evaluating projects in isolation.
Before approving new methane gas plants, regulators should determine whether expanded battery storage, demand response, distributed energy resources, energy efficiency, and additional wind and solar generation can provide the same reliability at lower long-term cost and lower financial risk.
The cleanest megawatt is often the one that never has to be generated.
Demand response is infrastructure. Every megawatt shifted away from peak demand reduces pressure on the grid and can delay or eliminate the need for costly new power plants. Large customers, including data centers, have enormous opportunities to shift demand through operational flexibility and advanced controls.
Battery storage also deserves greater attention. Increasingly, it competes directly with natural gas by providing reliability during periods of peak demand while avoiding decades of fuel costs and emissions.
Water belongs in this conversation as well.
Both data centers and methane gas plants can require substantial water for cooling. The proposed Red Oak Ridge facility alone could consume hundreds of thousands of gallons each day. In rural Wisconsin, where farms, private wells, trout streams, wetlands, and local economies depend on reliable water supplies, those impacts deserve careful scrutiny before permits are approved.
Natural gas will likely remain part of Wisconsin’s energy mix during the transition. But every new gas plant also commits customers to decades of fuel-price risk driven by commodity markets, pipeline constraints, extreme weather, LNG exports, and geopolitical uncertainty. Clean energy resources, by contrast, have no fuel costs and are often the lowest-cost, fastest-to-deploy options available.
Reliability and clean energy are not competing goals.
Modern planning can deliver both.
Wisconsin should also modernize its regulatory framework by evaluating the cumulative impacts of related infrastructure investments. Generation, transmission, data centers, water use, and utility planning are interconnected. They should be planned together, not approved one docket at a time.
Wisconsin has everything it needs to lead: world-class manufacturers, innovative businesses, skilled workers, abundant renewable resources, productive farmland, and a clean energy economy that already employs more than 75,000 people.
Wisconsin does not have an electricity shortage.
It has a planning challenge.
Planning reduces costs. It improves reliability. It protects water resources. It strengthens economic competitiveness.
Most importantly, it allows Wisconsin to build an energy system designed for 2050, rather than one modeled in 1990.
Instead of approving Wisconsin’s energy future one docket at a time, let’s build it through one comprehensive plan.
