name: Georgia Recorder
title: It’s decision time for the Okefenokee Swamp’s proposed World Heritage designation
description: Georgia’s Okefenokee Swamp could soon be elevated to the same level as Yellowstone National Park, the fjords of Norway or Australia’s Great Barrier Reef. The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization’s World Heritage Committee is meeting this week in Busan, South Korea, with an agenda that includes deciding whether to add the 400,000-a[...]
text:
A kayaker paddles through Chase Prairie in the Okefenokee Swamp on Nov. 13, 2025. Credit: Justin Taylor/The Current GA/Catchlight Local/Report for AmericaGeorgia’s Okefenokee Swamp could soon be elevated to the same level as Yellowstone National Park, the fjords of Norway or Australia’s Great Barrier Reef.
The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization’s World Heritage Committee is meeting this week in Busan, South Korea, with an agenda that includes deciding whether to add the 400,000-acre Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge to its list of World Heritage sites.
Established in 1972, the list is intended to aid “in the protection of the cultural and natural heritage of outstanding universal value,” according to UNESCO.
Being recognized as a World Heritage site would be a major boost for the Okefenokee and Georgia, said Environment Georgia Director Jennette Gayer.
Justin Taylor/The Current
“I think it is recognition that the Okefenokee is really one of a kind, that we are lucky in Georgia to have such a beautiful, biodiverse, special place, and it will mean that the entire world recognizes how special the Okefenokee is,” she said.
The swamp is considered a good candidate for selection because it is one of the world’s largest naturally driven freshwater ecosystems and it serves as habitat for an enormous number of species, including amphibians, reptiles, mammals, birds, fishes and invertebrates, according to UNESCO documents. Because it is the source of rivers rather than their recipient and because the land has been well-managed, it remains largely unchanged by human activities compared with other wetlands, UNESCO says.
If it’s approved, it will become the 27th World Heritage site in the United States, with other sites including the Grand Canyon, the Everglades and the Great Smoky Mountains.
A local debate
If you spend enough time out on the Okefenokee, you’re likely to run into Rodney Thompson of St. George, who, with his wife, Tina, runs the YouTube channel Blackwater Outdoor Journeys. The channel showcases the couple’s canoeing, camping and fishing expeditions in the Okefenokee and other locations in Georgia and Florida.
Thompson grew up on the swamp, hunting, fishing and enjoying the natural beauty.
Rodney Thompson of YouTube channel Blackwater Outdoor Journeys paddles through the Okefenokee. Photo courtesy Rodney Thompson/Blackwater Outdoor Journeys.
“Me and my dad and my brothers, we grew up, and every Saturday, especially early spring – they say when the yellowflies get to bitin’, the warmouths get to bitin’ also – so when you start seeing yellowflies, you’d start seeing us in the swamps, trying to catch them warmouth, and we loved doing that,” he said.
Thompson said he  first learned about the proposal to make the swamp a World Heritage site when he started seeing opposition.
“I started seeing signs, you know, ‘Keep UNESCO out’ and all that kind of stuff,” he said. “I didn’t really understand what it was until I started really doing the research on it and what kind of impact it was going to have.”
Some locals oppose the designation because they say it could draw large numbers of tourists, potentially damaging the swamp and changing the local way of life.
Thompson said he ultimately supports the designation, but he is sympathetic to those arguments. He cited a 2024 Conservation Fund report finding that the number of people visiting the Okefenokee per year could double from 800,000 to 1.6 million by 2035 if it becomes a World Heritage site.
“I don’t know how Charlton County could handle that, Clinch County,” he said. “I mean, Fargo has a Dollar General. That’s about all. They ain’t even got a restaurant.”
Thompson characterized towns like St. George and Fargo as “dying,” but said he hopes increased tourism could inject new life. The Conservation Fund projects the region could see 750 jobs, $79 million in economic output and $11.1 million in annual tax revenue.
“Heck, we only got a Dollar General about four years ago,” he added. “So that tells you how small we are. But I think that if it’s done right and you’ve got the right people behind it, I think that it can have a positive impact on these smaller communities.”
Political football
The land deal announced Friday presents a second time a mining proposal near the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge was thwarted due to public outcry. Joe Cook/Georgia Rivers
Others who oppose the designation say they fear association with the United Nations would undermine U.S. sovereignty.
An online petition opposing the measure gained over 1,000 signatures.
“A specialized agency of the United Nations, UNESCO, gains major influence of our region through its World Heritage Committee, comprised of 21 foreign nations, which emphasizes furthering the goals of its parent organization, the United Nations,” the petition reads.
If the classification is approved, the refuge would continue to be owned and managed by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. In a FAQ on its website, the service says the designation would not affect the ability to hunt or fish on the property in accordance with state laws or subject the area to any kind of UN policy. UNESCO monitors sites and potential threats but does not have ownership or management rights over the land.
President Donald Trump has pledged to withdraw the U.S. from UNESCO effective at the end of the year.The U.S. previously withdrew from the organization during Trump’s first term and re-joined under former President Joe Biden. The nation’s departure is not expected to have an effect on the Okefenokee’s prospects as membership in UNESCO isn’t required for addition to the World Heritage list.
Not an end to the threat
The designation would not stop all threats to the swamp.
Last year, environmentalists celebrated after an Alabama-based company scrapped plans to mine valuable minerals near the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge, but the designation would not stop others from developing near the swamp in a way that could harm the ecosystem.
Advocates have rallied behind a bipartisan attempt to protect Trail Ridge from mining.
“The reality is there are still many acres of land that are adjacent to the Okefenokee that we know contain minerals that people want to mine that are not protected, that could be mined without regard to this designation,” Gayer said. “We hope that this would influence regulators to think twice about another effort to mine adjacent to the Okefenoke, but the reality is we still have unprotected lands that people could mine on.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Elon Musk, 3 other billionaires put $12 million behind pro-Ramaswamy super PAC in Ohio governor race
description: The world’s richest man is officially invested in the 2026 Ohio governor’s race. Elon Musk, a former trillionaire and former co-leader of the unofficial Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) with now-Republican nominee for Ohio governor Vivek Ramaswamy, donated $5 million to a super PAC backing Ramaswamy in May, according to campaign finance reports rel[...]
text:
CEO of Tesla and SpaceX Elon Musk speaks last year at the Conservative Political Action Conference in Maryland.(Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)The world’s richest man is officially invested in the 2026 Ohio governor’s race.
Elon Musk, a former trillionaire and former co-leader of the unofficial Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) with now-Republican nominee for Ohio governor Vivek Ramaswamy, donated $5 million to a super PAC backing Ramaswamy in May, according to campaign finance reports released last week.
Musk joined billionaires Jeffrey Yass, Ratmir Timashev, Bill Ackman, and Ross Stevens as the primary backers of V-PAC: Victors, Not Victims, a super PAC dedicated to supporting Ramaswamy’s election bid.
The billionaires have given V-PAC a combined $37 million so far, more than 88% of its total funding. About 98% of V-PAC’s second-quarter contributions, or $12 million, came from Musk, Timashev, Ackman, and Stevens.
“I do not think it’s surprising that billionaires support other billionaires running for office,” said Catherine Turcer, executive director of watchdog group Common Cause Ohio.
A super PAC can raise and spend unlimited amounts of money, but it cannot directly coordinate with a candidate’s campaign committee. Individuals can only contribute up to $7,000 per election cycle to a candidate’s campaign committee, which has more restrictions on what it can do.
While super PACs often throw their full weight behind their preferred candidates, Case Western Reserve University law professor Atiba Ellis emphasized that they carry their own agendas.
“This outsized amount of money can drown out what could be a dialogue about the issues in the governor’s race,” he said.
In any case, he added that voters should expect even more political advertising in what is set to be one of the most expensive governor’s elections in state history.
Democratic nominee for governor Dr. Amy Acton is narrowly outraising Ramaswamy in 2026, at least according to their most recent campaign committee filings. But without a super PAC backing her —  or $25 million of her own money to put in the race as her opponent did — Ramaswamy holds a large cash advantage. 
Acton promises to reform Ohio’s campaign finance system to make it more transparent if elected, according to her campaign platform. 
Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Acton’s campaign committee said in a statement that the billionaires’ donations were only more evidence that Ramaswamy’s “scam policies would enrich himself and his fellow billionaires while raising costs for Ohio’s working families.” 
V-PAC and Ramaswamy’s campaign committee did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Ohio isn’t for sale,” Acton wrote on social media in response to Musk’s donation. “Not now. Not ever.”
V-PAC bought a round of ad placements shortly after the billionaires’ donations, spending over $8.1 million in June on a 30-second ad against Acton. The super PAC reported $25.8 million in cash balance at the end of the second quarter.
Musk, Yass, and Ackman are no strangers to political lobbying. Musk spent over $250 million to support President Donald Trump in 2024. He was also extremely active in the 2025 Wisconsin state Supreme Court election, even appearing to hand out $1 million checks to two Wisconsin voters.
A bipartisan panel in Wisconsin later found that those checks likely violated state election law.
His donation in the Ohio race has not been flagged as problematic in any way.
“Even though this gift may be above board, voters should inquire about what his motives are in terms of influencing this election,” Ellis said.
Yass, the richest man in Pennsylvania, gave V-PAC $20 million before the primary. A co-founder of investment company Susquehanna International Group with an estimated net worth of $65.7 billion, Yass has poured hundreds of millions of dollars into politics to advance support for private school vouchers. 
Ackman, a hedge fund investor, donated $1 million to V-PAC in June. He was one of the most vocal opponents against New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s electoral campaign and gave super PACs $1.75 million to oppose him.
Timashev is a newcomer to the political scene in comparison. He had never made a political contribution in Ohio or at the federal level until the second quarter of 2026, when he gave V-PAC $5 million in May. 
The tech entrepreneur left Russia after the fall of the Soviet Union to study at The Ohio State University, eventually amassing most of his wealth through informational technology company Veeam Solutions.
Timashev made Ohio State’s largest single donation ever in 2023, giving $110 million to create the university’s Center for Software Innovation. He has said he aims to bring 100 artificial intelligence startups to Columbus through his own venture capital firm, turning Ohio’s capital into “the next Silicon Valley.” 
But in April, three former executives sued Timashev and the venture capital firm on allegations of fraud and civil conspiracy. They later filed another lawsuit claiming that public statements by the firm about their firing — including a LinkedIn post announcing that Sen. Jon Husted’s son, Alex Husted, would take their place — were defamatory.
The executives claim he hired them away from their previous companies with promises of $50 million in funding that never came, and when they complained, he fired them. Timashev countersued in federal court, alleging that the three executives misappropriated $8 million and stole trade secrets.
Like Timashev, Stevens is best known for donating to his alma mater. After graduating from the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School of Business in 1991, he became the founder and CEO of Stone Ridge Holdings Group, a Wall Street asset management company.
In 2019, he became the founding donor of Wharton’s Stevens Center for Innovation in Finance. But four years later, he pulled $100 million in funding from the university over how Penn’s then-president handled antisemitism on campus. She resigned days later.
Stevens gave $5 million to V-PAC in early 2025, the most he has given to a single PAC registered at the federal level, and added another $1 million in May.
Because super PACs cannot coordinate with candidates, they can use their outsized platform to steer elections in unintended directions, Ellis said. Super PACs can raise issues that their preferred candidates may want to avoid, putting pressure on candidates to address them.
Ramaswamy left DOGE in January 2025 after his relationship with Musk and President Donald Trump reportedly grew tense.
“Even though it’s unlikely that a supportive PAC is going to try to steer the agenda of a candidate, it’s certainly possible,” Ellis said.
When wealthy donors make large political contributions to a single-candidate super PAC like V-PAC, Turcer said there is “always a worry” that they will influence policymaking.
“There’s a sense that you dance with the one who brung you,” she said.

title: Ohio US Sen. Bernie Moreno blows hot air over Canada wildfire smoke
description: When the super wealthy crave next-level prestige and power as elected royalty in Washington, they are already accustomed to being the center of attention. But being a VIP lawmaker on Capitol Hill lets them be stars on the national stage. It’s heady stuff, even for zillionaires. Some promptly grab the spotlight to steal the show […]
text:
Ohio Republican U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno speaks with reporters in the Capitol building in Washington, D.C., on Thursday, Jan. 8, 2026. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)When the super wealthy crave next-level prestige and power as elected royalty in Washington, they are already accustomed to being the center of attention. But being a VIP lawmaker on Capitol Hill lets them be stars on the national stage. 
It’s heady stuff, even for zillionaires. Some promptly grab the spotlight to steal the show — or at least make news and TV appearances on the regular. 
Generating sensational headlines for pure clickbait — in lieu of conducting serious policymaking for constituents — is the stand-alone goal. Ohio Republican U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno, a former luxury car dealer, is good at it. 
He sells sensation over thoughtful governance like a pro. The Westlake Republican has made dozens of appearances on Fox News and triggered a bunch of media coverage as a MAGA performer, bless his heart. 
Last week Moreno stewed as toxic smoke from climate-driven Canadian wildfires enveloped Cleveland and other Ohio communities. 
It was bad. Would the senator address the gravity of the event soberly or warn of worse to come if man-made global warming continued to accelerate and intensify air-choking fires at home and up north? 
Would Moreno point to the real time risks of highly hazardous wildfire smoke as proof of a planet heating up and suggest urgent course correction — that doesn’t include pumping massive amounts of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere? 
Not this guy. Moreno saw smoky exposure to terrible air quality in the Great Lakes, Northeast and Mid-Atlantic states as an opportunity to exploit for personal gain and went full-on tinfoil. 
He assigned villainy to the powerful winds pushing wildfire smoke from Canada into the U.S. and polluting the air for millions in a thick, acrid haze. 
He charged Canada’s “failed leadership” with perpetrating an “atrocity” on the U.S. and said Canadian officials should be punished for not properly maintaining their vast, highly combustible boreal forest (that covers about 1.3 billion acres and stretches from Yukon and the Alaskan border to Newfoundland and Labrador in the east). 
The sheer magnitude of the forest, its remoteness and hard-to-get-to wilderness areas (often only accessible by air), the acute limits on firefighting efforts, were all lost on Moreno. 
So, too, was the whole cause and effect part of the impossible-to-put-out wildfires actively burning across Canada. 
Moreno simply ignored what has driven the frequency and severity of Canadian wildfire seasons; higher temperatures brought on by the rate of global warming nearly doubling in the last decade. 
Hotter, drier conditions prime the landscape to burn. A lightening strike in a parched forest can ignite a massive burn. That’s what happened in about 71% of the burned area in Canada between 1990-2023. 
Bottom line? Climate change has increased heat and drought and made wildfires more numerous and severe in dry forests north and south of the border. 
At this writing there are over 900 active wildfires in Canada and just under 500 in the U.S. But the summer is yet young and smoke-filled cities are on track to become the new norm as long as fossil fuels — coal, oil and gas — remain the biggest contributors to global warming. 
But the spotlight-loving Moreno was clearly not interested in doing a deep dive on the problem last week to assess the best solution. 
He wanted to get political mileage out of a “wildfire pollution emergency” by bashing Canada (and scoring points with the felon-in-chief he flatters). 
Moreno immediately blamed our longest and closest ally for allowing plumes of smoke to blow into the U.S. — as if Canada controlled the wind. “We will not tolerate this incompetence,” huffed the MAGA cowboy.

Moreno milked his moment in the haze by introducing a performative, if not passable, Senate bill to impose sanctions on Canada over wildfire smoke affecting U.S. air quality. 
“Canada’s government failed to invest in wildfire prevention methods, including forest thinning, fuel reduction, prescribed burns and stronger enforcement against arson,” said the statement from his office — without evidence or understanding about boreal forests. 
Moreno’s measure would also sanction Canadian officials found “responsible” for the fires, revoke their visas, block their assets, and formally express Congress’ opinion that the Canadian ambassador is a “persona non grata” until the wildfire smoke is gone.
Trump piled on Moreno’s rhetoric with his brand of hysteria. 
“The United States is being unnecessarily invaded by filthy, polluted, and unhealthy air” and “we are holding Canada responsible,” he bleated and threatened to levy additional tariffs for the air invasion. 
Other Republicans took the same tack as Moreno. The House Republican Conference chair accused Canada of doing nothing to keep the wildfire smoke over there. “Stop exporting your smoke into out skies. Enough is enough!”
The fire-breathing partisans, who deny the reality of climate change and aggressively promote more fossil fuel pollution over renewable, clean energy alternatives, removed all doubt about their willful indifference to the facts or shameless intent to leverage a serious public health issue for political points. 
Forget the scary trajectory we’re on with wild weather extremes every other week from supercharged storms and record flooding to scorching heat and forest infernos. 
It’s so much easier to lob attention-getting salvos for click bait, right? 
Worked for Moreno. 
He made state and national news with his insane rip on Canada blowing smoke and appeared on The Ingraham Angle on Fox News. But he didn’t come close to clearing the air.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: What the wildfire smoke is telling us
description: Recent fires in California and smoke from Canadian wildfires drifting across the Northeast are different events, but they point to a shared reality: wildfire conditions and smoke do not respect borders. Together, they raise a broader question about what is making dangerous fire conditions more likely and how the consequences reach communities here. Science d[...]
text:
Recent fires in California and smoke from Canadian wildfires drifting across the Northeast are different events, but they point to a shared reality: wildfire conditions and smoke do not respect borders. 
Together, they raise a broader question about what is making dangerous fire conditions more likely and how the consequences reach communities here.
Science does not say that rising temperatures caused a particular spark. Wildfires may be ignited by lightning or people, and forest management matters. A warming atmosphere changes the conditions in which fires burn.
Researchers studying eastern Canada’s extraordinary 2023 fire season found that warming caused by human activity made peak fire weather at least twice as likely and about 20 percent more intense. Warmer temperatures and lower humidity dry vegetation, making severe fires more likely.
The United States should also recognize its role. More than four fifths of our energy consumption still comes from petroleum, natural gas, and coal. Burning fossil fuels is the primary driver of the warming atmosphere, contributing to hotter and drier conditions that can make fire weather more dangerous. Focusing only on where the fires are burning leaves out our own part of the story.
The health consequences are neither abstract nor distant. The Environmental Protection Agency reports that wildfire smoke can worsen respiratory and cardiovascular disease and contribute to premature death. During the widespread wildfire smoke events that reached the United States in 2023, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found that asthma related emergency department visits were 17 percent higher than expected on smoke days.
Those visits become medical bills, missed work, prescription costs, pressure on hospitals, and public expense. The burden is often greatest for children, older adults, people with existing health conditions, outdoor workers, and families who may not be able to afford air filtration or lose a day’s income by staying home. Smoke can also cancel outdoor work, youth activities, and community events.
We pay for fossil fuels once at the pump or through our utility bills. We then pay a second, less visible bill through health care costs, lost wages, taxes, disrupted lives, and the growing expense of responding to extreme weather events.
The atmosphere does not recognize national borders. Smoke over Connecticut is not simply something another country is doing to us. It reflects decades of fossil fuel use and energy choices across borders, including our own.
Moving away from harmful fuel sources will take time. But delay is not free. The smoke is sending us a signal, and we are already paying the bill.
Mike Urgo is the former First Selectman of North Stonington and Founder of People for Planet and Democracy.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Before CT families pay more, Eversource must prove its worth
description: The question before PURA is whether Connecticut families and businesses are being asked to pay more than necessary.
text:
For many Connecticut families, opening up the electric bill has become another source of stress. 
It’s the parent deciding whether to keep the air conditioner running during a heat wave. It’s the senior on a fixed income wondering what else they have to cut to make ends meet. It’s the small business owner watching utility costs eat into already thin margins.
Now those customers could soon see their electric bills rise again.
Eversource has filed its first electric rate case in eight years, seeking an annual increase of either $451 million or $727 million, depending on whether recent storm-related costs are included. If approved as proposed, the average customer’s bill would increase by about 11 percent (without storm costs) or 18 percent (with storm costs).
Connecticut families and businesses already pay some of the highest electric bills in the country. That’s why Eversource’s rate case must receive rigorous scrutiny from the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority. As a regulated monopoly, Eversource faces no competition. PURA exists to provide accountability that the market cannot.
No one questions that Connecticut needs a safe and reliable electric grid. We all want fewer outages after storms and an electric system that can support our clean energy future. The real question isn’t whether we should invest; it’s whether Connecticut families and businesses already stretched by the high cost of living are being asked to pay more than necessary.
That’s why this rate case cannot become a rubber stamp.
PURA has an important responsibility: to make sure customers pay only for investments that are truly necessary, reasonably priced, and in the public interest.
Every dollar that isn’t carefully scrutinized comes directly out of a family’s monthly budget or a business’s bottom line. This review must look beyond the traditional utility playbook. For too long, utilities have relied on expensive poles-and-wires projects while overlooking lower-cost solutions that can deliver the same or better results.
PURA should require Eversource to prove that every proposed investment was prudent, that lower-cost alternatives were fully considered, and that customers are not paying for unnecessary or gold-plated infrastructure. Connecticut has opportunities to reduce costs by investing in solutions such as energy efficiency, battery storage, demand response, and other non-wires alternatives that can improve reliability. Those solutions should be the first option – not the last.
Customers should also see something in return if rates increase. Investments should modernize the grid in ways that help people save money over time, including new electric rates that make technologies like heat pumps more affordable to use and reduce energy costs for families and businesses alike.
Conservation Law Foundation is participating directly in this case as an intervenor. We will advocate for rigorous oversight, challenge unnecessary spending, and fight for investments that lower costs, strengthen reliability, and deliver real benefits to the people paying the bills.
Connecticut families shouldn’t have to choose between keeping the lights on and paying for groceries. Small businesses shouldn’t have to absorb avoidable utility costs that make it harder to hire workers and grow. If customers are being asked to pay more, they deserve the confidence that every dollar has been carefully examined and every reasonable opportunity to reduce costs has been pursued.
Connecticut families and businesses deserve affordable energy, a reliable grid, and a utility that earns – not assumes – the public’s trust.
Jamie Flynn is the Conservation Law Foundation’s Vice President for Connecticut.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Rethinking prisons and the notion of rehabilitation
description: What is the purpose of prison? Punishment, certainly, but do you have an expectation that our prisons are rehabilitating the ones they're incarcerating?
text:
I have been incarcerated in Connecticut for a little over 20 continuous years, since I was 18 years old. Sadly, my story is by no means unique. There are hundreds of people incarcerated in Connecticut prisons for crimes they committed as teenagers.
There are thousands of individuals who have been incarcerated for a decade or more (many of whom have decades-long sentences).  But this piece is not about the propriety of those sentences. Rather, I’d like people to think about what is actually going on in the state’s prisons day-in and day-out.  What is the purpose of prison? Punishment, certainly, but do we (do you) have an expectation that our prisons are rehabilitating the ones they’re incarcerating?
If I told the average uninformed citizen that there is startlingly little focus on the notion of “rehabilitation” for prisoners serving lengthy sentences, would this come as a surprise? Indeed, Connecticut’s correctional model increasingly shifts the focus of resources on individuals as they get closer to release. For those with lengthy sentences, the majority of those sentences will be spent idle and unstructured.
For the first 16 years of my incarceration this was the case.  The focus of Connecticut’s Department of Correction  has been this ubiquitous notion of “safety and security” which means: keeping prisoners locked in their cells for as much time as possible, limiting prisoner interaction, restricting prisoners’ movement and privileges.
Around 2022, as the COVID pandemic was winding down, we started to see a change–or rather, we started to make a change for ourselves.  At the Cheshire Correctional Institution, a group of “lifers” (people doing 20+ year sentences) proposed an idea for a novel housing unit that would focus on rehabilitation, and personal development, all while creating a more positive and therapeutic space. The truly novel aspect of this unit was not the notion that we (prisoners) want better for ourselves but, rather, that we would be the change makers–no longer relying solely on the DOC, whose focus lay elsewhere.
Thus the H.O.N.O.R. Program was born.  H.O.N.O.R. is an acronym for Honesty, Ownership, Nobility, Obligation, and Respect — lofty ideals that we strive to live by. This program offers about 90 incarcerated individuals with the opportunity to engage in peer mentoring across a variety of topics. Collectively, we have the lowest incident rate in a prison housing nearly 1,300 individuals, with zero incidents of violence in over two consecutive years of operation.
The advent of this program coincided with Gov. Ned Lamont’s signing of the Protect Act  an executive order that limited the use of solitary confinement and guaranteed minimum out-of-cell time per day, ostensibly for structured activities. When this order went into effect, prisons in the state went from 22-hour-plus lockdown by default to granting a minimum of five and a half hours of out of cell time per day. The crucial second component of this increase was programming opportunities, but this has been conspicuously slow in coming to fruition — except for those of us who made it for ourselves.
The goal of this program is not only peer support for one another but, eventually, to give back to our peers at large (the other ~1,210 people at Cheshire).  The goal is to be peer mentors and facilitators to those same individuals who have decades-long sentences and little to hope for.
We do not claim to be perfect and we can’t do this alone. If your preference for incarceration includes opportunities for a positive change, then perhaps the H.O.N.O.R. Program is something that the state should be called on to support. 
Perhaps, we can create a shift in corrections that sees more positive opportunities and environments for prisoners and staff. And let’s not forget, the ultimate goal of all of this is to create better people to eventually return to society — to create a safer society for everyone.
Ian Cooke is incarcerated at the Cheshire Correctional Institution.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Ellsworth found guilty of official misconduct in criminal trial
description: HELENA — Former Montana Senate president Jason Ellsworth was found guilty of official misconduct – a misdemeanor – on Tuesday evening in Lewis and Clark District Court in Helena.   He could face a $500 fine or as many as six months in jail.  Sentencing is scheduled at 3 p.m., Sept. 10. As the verdict was read, […]
text:
Sen. Jason Ellsworth, R-Hamilton, sits during as his guilty verdict is read in his trial on Tuesday, July 21, 2026, in Lewis Clark District Court in Helena, MT. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)HELENA — Former Montana Senate president Jason Ellsworth was found guilty of official misconduct – a misdemeanor – on Tuesday evening in Lewis and Clark District Court in Helena.  
He could face a $500 fine or as many as six months in jail. 
Sentencing is scheduled at 3 p.m., Sept. 10.
As the verdict was read, Ellsworth bowed his head slightly, before staring ahead. Neither he nor his lawyers offered comments to the media after the trial, and neither did state prosecutors. 
Ellsworth was found guilty of circumventing the state’s normal contracting process, and trying to steer more than $100,000 of work to a close associate. That work included tracking bills from the Senate Select Committee on Judicial Oversight and Reform ahead of the 2025 Legislative Session. The two initial contracts for the work totaled more than $100,000, which should have triggered additional scrutiny and a bidding process. 
On Tuesday afternoon, both sides made their closing remarks to the jury, which began deliberation around 3:40.
“Public office is a public trust, not a personal favor,” state attorney Stephanie Robles said in the prosecution’s closing arguments. “Taxpayer money belongs to the public. Procurement laws exist to protect everyone equally. The defendant doesn’t get to decide when those laws apply. When someone uses their public office to benefit a friend, they betray that trust.”
Stephanie Robles, an attorney for the state, delivers closing arguments in Jason Ellsworth’s official misconduct trial. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)
Ellsworth’s attorneys, meanwhile, said he was not trained on state contracting procedures, had asked for help, went through proper procedures and that ultimately the contract was approved by the state after the two agreements merged into one.
They told the jury that Ellsworth was unaware he was doing anything wrong, and that if the contract was illegal, the state should have cancelled it. Defense attorneys pointed out that a number of state employees worked on the contracts and approved them. 
An attorney for the State of Montana characterized it differently, saying they were trying to “fix” the contract problem and were trying to protect taxpayers, said Daniel Guzynski, who gave the state’s rebuttal to the defense.
He added that they had to do that because “of the egregious position that the senator put everybody in.”
Eventually, the contract was cancelled when the body started investigating it.
No money was paid on the contract. 
Ellsworth’s attorneys have also said he was within his power as Senate President to spend the money and execute the contracts. Defense attorneys have also said rushing to spend the funds was warranted because if they weren’t spent, they would go back to the Governor’s Office in just several days’ time.
Ellsworth was also traveling during much of the time leading up to the contracts. He didn’t return back to Montana until Dec. 24, 2024, about a week before the money would revert to the governor’s office. Ellsworth’s attorney said it was critical to cinch up the project because the  Senate Select Committee on Judicial Oversight had been given $500,000 for work on judicial reform and Ellsworth wanted to spend the money, his attorneys said.
“The state’s trying to make this out like this is some fun kickback contract. Just for funsies, and we’re going to give somebody some money. That’s not what this is at all,” said Martin Judnich, a defense attorney for Ellsworth. “This was a very serious contract about an issue that was extremely important to the Montana Senate.”
That committee put forth 27 bills during the 2025 Legislative session, many of them controversial and, along with property tax, became the major discussion point of the Montana Legislature.

title: Republicans in US House approve stopgap spending bill ahead of Oct. 1 deadline
text: WASHINGTON — The U.S. House approved a stopgap spending bill Tuesday that would keep the government up and running through the fall, sending it to the Senate, where lawmakers expect to rework the measure.Congress must pass a government funding bill before the new fiscal year starts on Oct. 1 in order to avoid a shutdown just weeks before the November midterm elections.The 220-205 mostly party-line vote represents House Republicans’ opening salvo in negotiations, though without Democratic support it won’t be able to advance in the Senate. House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., said during floor debate that GOP leaders hope passing the stopgap spending bill months before the start of the next fiscal year will avoid another shutdown. “For anyone questioning this legislation, the facts are simple — it extends the government funding deadline to Dec. 4, denying any party the opportunity to manufacture leverage before elections,” Cole said. “It contains no poison pills or partisan riders. It prevents harmful disruptions to our national security and the vital programs our constituents rely on.”Connecticut Democratic Rep. Rosa DeLauro, ranking member on the committee, opposed the stopgap, saying it would “allow Homeland Secretary (Markwayne) Mullin to transfer billions of dollars to the Border Patrol.”Republicans, she said, “refused” to change that aspect of the bill after Democrats “shared language to fix it.”“We cannot in good conscience allow billions of dollars to flow to these agencies without major reforms to keep our constituents safe from further violence,” DeLauro said. Democrats don’t want a government shutdown but also don’t want “to rush” the process and omit the list of anomalies just sent up by the White House, she said. Those tweaks to funding levels are commonly added to stopgap spending bills but weren’t included in House Republicans’ measure because it was written before the White House sent a list of requested anomalies to lawmakers Monday. “There are over 50 programs listed by the agencies to take some action so that they can be protected during a continuing resolution,” DeLauro said, using the technical term for a short-term funding bill. The changes would support wildfire suppression activities, housing assistance for tens of thousands and programs that help people in rural communities afford their utilities.“Rushing this bill to the floor haphazardly without carefully considering the various needs that must be met is no way to govern,” DeLauro said. “And it is irresponsible.” Senate anticipates changesSenate Appropriations Committee Chairwoman Susan Collins, R-Maine, said earlier in the day that she was working with the committee’s top Democrat, Washington Sen. Patty Murray, to draft a continuing resolution of their own. “It appears that there is good faith on the Democratic side to try to pass the CR and avoid a government shutdown, which is always a disaster,” Collins said. Murray said the House’s stopgap spending bill has “problems” that will need to be fixed in order to move through the Senate.“We just got the anomalies last night and both of us are trying to figure out the best way to get it put together,” Murray said. Appropriations statusLawmakers must lean on a stopgap spending bill because they will, once again, fail to complete work on the dozen annual government funding bills before the deadline. The House has passed three of its spending bills. The Senate hasn’t passed any, in part, because the committee hasn’t released a single bill. The two chambers will need to begin negotiations at some point to settle on a total spending level for the 12 bills and how that roughly $1.9 trillion will be broken down among thousands of federal agencies and programs. That means the earliest the full-year government spending bills would become law is during the lame-duck session that is set to last for about five weeks between the election and the start of the new Congress in January. Lawmakers could also pass a series of stopgap funding bills instead of completing negotiations on the full-year appropriations bills.

text:
A summary sheet is seen during ballot review on Tuesday, Aug. 27, 2024, at the headquarters of the Alaska Division of Elections in Juneau. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)The first two votes in Alaska’s Aug. 18 primary election have already been cast.
According to records published by the absentee and petition office of the Alaska Division of Elections, two voters — one in South Carolina and another in Hawaii — returned their ballots on July 17.
Thousands more voters will cast their ballots in the coming weeks. Absentee ballots were mailed to overseas and military voters starting July 2, and absentee ballots will start going out to the general public on July 24. Early in-person voting starts Aug. 3.
In the primary, voters will pick one candidate for each office. The top four vote-getters for each race, regardless of party, will advance to the general election on Nov. 3.
If there are four or fewer candidates running for a particular office, all candidates advance to the general election.
For Alaska’s statewide races, that isn’t an issue. There are 17 people running for governor, each running on a combined ticket with a lieutenant governor candidate:
 

Tom Begich and Julia Hnilicka (Democratic)

The governor is soliciting applications for that district after temporarily suspending Brad Molnar from t[...]
text:
The Montana State Capitol in Helena on Wednesday, April 26, 2023.  (Photo by Mike Clark for the Daily Montanan)Gov. Greg Gianforte is soliciting applications for a temporary appointment to the Public Service Commission.
In a news release Tuesday, Gianforte said qualified candidates must live in District 2, south-central Montana, and will serve until July 9, 2027.
The governor is soliciting applications for that district after temporarily suspending Brad Molnar from the Public Service Commission for a year.
The PSC regulates monopoly utilities in Montana including NorthWestern Energy. It is made up of five commissioners elected by district.
The governor and Molnar both described the suspension as unprecedented. Both are Republican, as are the other current Public Service Commissioners.
Gianforte earlier said a report into allegations of professional misconduct against Molnar points to “unlawful conduct,” including sex discrimination and retaliation.
The PSC voted 3-2 to adopt the report including a recommendation that the commission request Molnar’s suspension by the governor.
Molnar is fighting the suspension in Lewis and Clark District Court.
A court filing Tuesday requests an order to stop the defendants — Gianforte and Commissioners Jeff Welborn, Jennifer Fielder, and Annie Bukacek — from seating another commissioner.
The suspension is taking place as the Public Service Commission is dealing with at least a couple of significant issues, including data centers and a proposed merger between NorthWestern and Black Hills Corp.
In an email, lawyer Matthew Monforton said Molnar is willing to fight for Montana families as a commissioner and should stay on the job.
“Every dollar an unregulated data center doesn’t pay is a dollar a Montana family does, which Molnar objects to and which is why Gianforte wants him replaced,” Monforton said.
In an earlier letter, Gianforte said he suspended Molnar because he violated the public trust, and his actions would normally have resulted in him being fired.
The news release from the Governor’s Office said the application form to serve as a temporary commissioner is available electronically at governor.mt.gov/PSCappointment.
The deadline to file is Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026, and applications will be made available to the public, the news release said. 
The news release said from Thursday, Aug. 6, through Thursday, Aug. 20, the public will be given the opportunity to provide letters of support or other comments regarding the applicants at governor.mt.gov/PSCappointment.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: New Orleans leaders ask special prosecutor to drop charges against AG Murrill
description: A possible truce in the months-long discord between state leaders and New Orleans officials emerged Tuesday when Mayor Helena Moreno, District Attorney Jason Williams and five city council members asked a special prosecutor to drop criminal charges against Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill.
text:
New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno and other city leaders have asked a special prosecutor to dismiss criminal charges against Attorney General Liz Murrill. (Photo by Robert Stewart/Verite News)A possible truce in the months-long discord between state leaders and New Orleans officials emerged Tuesday when Mayor Helena Moreno, District Attorney Jason Williams and five city council members asked a special prosecutor to drop criminal charges against Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill.
“New Orleans and Louisiana have too much at stake to remain consumed by conflict,” Moreno and the council members said in a letter sent to Laurie White, who was appointed to investigate alleged threats Murrill made toward the city officials.
An Orleans Parish grand jury handed up a 16-count indictment July 2 against Murrill on charges of intimidation and malfeasance in office. The investigation centered on a letter Murrill sent to the mayor, DA and council members after they took action to install an interim clerk of court. 
In a letter she sent to the city leaders in May, Murrill said Gov. Jeff Landry had the authority to remove the officials from their elected seats after they had circumvented a new state law that combined Orleans Parish’s two court clerks’ offices. Council members appointed an interim clerk, retired Judge Calvin Johnson, and scheduled an election for Nov. 3 for voters to pick a permanent office holder.
Murrill insisted the combined agencies were under the control of the remaining clerk, Chelsea Richard Napoleon, and the Louisiana Supreme Court ruled in her favor. She threatened to jail Johnson if he performed any of the clerk’s duties.
Johnson wrote his own letter to White asking her to dismiss the charges against Murrill.
In his letter to White, Williams said the “prosecution of Mrs. Murrill is a distraction from the  work to which I have dedicated myself.” 
The district attorney recused himself and his office from the matter soon after the indictment, and it isn’t publicly known who, if anyone, instructed the grand jury to investigate Murrill. 
White did not respond immediately to a voice mail seeking comment Tuesday evening. 
Efforts to reach Murrill were directed to her attorney, Laura Cannizzaro Rodrigue, who wasn’t immediately available for comment.
Tuesday’s letters are the latest development in an escalating dispute that has pitted Republicans Landry and Murrill against the leaders of the state’s largest Democratic bastion. 
A week ago, the governor called the city to heel, saying “New Orleans thinks they’re so special,” as he stressed the need to right-size its court system with separate criminal and civil sections. 
“That parish is going to operate exactly like the rest of this state, and the people of this state want that,” Landry said.
This is a developing story.

name: Daily Montanan
title: New study finds short-term rentals contribute $755M to Montana economy
description: Short-term rentals in Montana boosted the economy and generated more than $755 million in visitor spending in 2025, according to a new study from the University of Montana’s Bureau of Business and Economic Research. Most of the activity — 60% — is focused in Bozeman and Kalispell, near Yellowstone National Park and Glacier National Park, […]
text:
Visitors to Yellowstone National Park walk around Old Faithful in May 2020. Tourists who stay at short-term rentals generate economic impact for Montana, especially near Yellowstone and Glacier National Park, finds a 2026 report from the Bureau of Business and Economic Research at the University of Montana. (Photo by Jacob W. Frank, courtesy of National Park Service)Short-term rentals in Montana boosted the economy and generated more than $755 million in visitor spending in 2025, according to a new study from the University of Montana’s Bureau of Business and Economic Research.
Most of the activity — 60% — is focused in Bozeman and Kalispell, near Yellowstone National Park and Glacier National Park, said the report, “Short-term Rentals in Montana: Economic Contributions and Trends.”
But the report said other places such as Billings also experience benefits, although they may draw more stays from business travelers than tourists.
Jeff Michael, director of the BBER, said Tuesday a tourist staying in a short-term rental typically stays longer in one location and drives around less, spending fewer dollars on gas and more on lodging.
“A lot of that lodging goes right into the pocket of a Montana household very frequently — not exclusively,” said Michael, who conducted the study with BBER economist Brietta Russell.
He said Airbnb provided $30,000 for the study, and it evaluated the benefits of short-term rentals.
The study references an earlier report from the UM Institute for Tourism and Recreation Research on nonresident spending, which found visitors who stayed in a short-term rental spent most of their money on arts, entertainment and recreation, followed by food and beverage stores.
“This is a distinction from the average visitor to Montana, who typically spends the largest amount on gasoline,” said the study on nonresident visitors.
The BBER study acknowledged that short-term rentals are at times controversial because of possible impacts on the overall housing market. However, it said any effects on the housing market are “beyond the scope of this report.”
The study found that in 2025, short-term rental guests booked more than 430,000 stays, supporting the following:

$356 million in rental income for hosts;
5,559 jobs statewide;
$277 million in labor income; and
$797 million in total value added to Montana’s gross domestic product.

“In the broader discussion of short-term rentals, the ability to host and engage more creatively in the growing tourism market does provide benefits for Montanans,” Russell said.
Russell said one outcome that impressed her was the impacts generated from short-term rental hosts as opposed to the nonresident visitor spending.
The study found income for just one type of short-term rental (home shares, or private rooms) ranged from $586 to $1,648 a month, “a significant source of supplemental income to households.”
“We saw a lot of activity in several different industries coming from hosts and how they used their revenue that they generated,” Russell said.
For example, revenue from short-term rentals may be used to offset other housing costs or even on health care, according to the BBER.
The report also said short-term rentals generate tax revenue for Montana, $47.6 million in all. It said they generated $40.8 million from a lodging sales tax and a tourism tax, and $6.7 million in local resort taxes in some communities (the resort tax is applicable to roughly 20% of the short-term rentals).
In 2025, short-term rentals in Flathead County generated the largest amount of visitor spending, $207 million; it was followed by Gallatin County at $152.2 million; Madison County at $85.8 million; and Park County at $64.3 million, the report said.
“At the lowest activity level, the Central Eastern region hosted over 40,000 reservation nights in 2025, resulting in an estimated 112 jobs, $4.3 million in labor income, and $12 million in value-added to the region’s (gross domestic product),” the study said.
The “unique nature” of those rentals allows travelers to pay hosts directly for “one of the largest parts of their trip,” which is lodging, the report said.
“Of the $754.5 million spent by guests, $510.5 million went toward their lodging,” the study said. “The revenue was received by hosts, increasing local household consumption and contributions to the economy.”
A record number of out-of-state visitors spent roughly $5 billion in Montana in 2024, according to an earlier study from the UM Institute for Tourism and Recreation Research. 
Michael said the money from short-term rentals is part of that impact.
“Without a short-term rental option, some dedicated properties would be used exclusively as a second home for the owner, while others might shift to medium-term rentals, which cater to guests who stay between one to six months,” the report said.
In Montana, a wide gap exists between the median household income and cost of a median home, and many communities are struggling to figure out how to provide more affordable housing.
Daniel Sidder, director of the Housing Whitefish nonprofit, said short-term rentals play a role in affordability, “but they are by no means the reason we have unaffordable homes to purchase and rent in the community.”
Whitefish is a high-cost area in Montana, and Housing Whitefish is focused on stabilizing the rental market and increasing options for people in the town.
In that community, around 400 registered short-term rentals represent 7% to 8% of all housing units, but close to 20% of all homes are classified as “dark homes,” or ones used only seasonally, Sidder said in an email.
In Whitefish specifically, he said, he believes second homes are the bigger issue when it comes to housing affordability.
“When looking at the housing challenges that Whitefish is facing, (short-term rentals) play a role — without them there would be more options for renters and buyers — but banning them, for example, would not solve the broad housing affordability challenges in the community,”  Sidder said.
The report said vacation rentals have always been present in Montana, but by 2026, more than 21,000 properties were operating on Airbnb or VRBO, associated with more than 8,000 hosts.
“This includes properties that have operated as short-term rentals prior to joining platforms that facilitate hosting and marketing (short-term rentals),” the report said.
The report said most of the revenue generated from short-term rentals is received as rental income, and in 2025, Montana residents received an estimated $356 million from hosting a short-term rental.
“This income was spent in the broader economy and generated additional economic activity across the state,” the report said.
It outlined non-lodging expenditures by short-term rental guests, for a total $243.95 million, including:

Arts, entertainment and recreation for $79.71 million,
Food services for $61.9 million,
Food and beverage stores for $31.86 million,
Gasoline stations for $31.53 million,
Retail trade for $22.39 million, and more.

In a statement provided by the BBER, Montana Chamber of Commerce CEO Todd O’Hair said the study shows short-term rentals are an economic driver, as the business community has witnessed.
“This is not a niche market,” O’Hair said in a statement. “Short-term rentals have resulted in more visitors coming to Montana, spending more money and creating an economic impact we all benefit from.”

title: Here’s who is leading in campaign funding for Iowa’s midterm races
description: New campaign finance reports from the fundraising period of May 27 to July 14 show millions of dollars have poured into Iowa’s statewide elections, including the attorney general’s race. Incumbent Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird continues to lead her Democratic opponent, Nate Willems, in fundraising, but Willems is gaining momentum. Bird raised more than $[...]
text:
Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird spoke to supporters at her annual "Bird Barn Bash" fundraiser at the Dallas County Fairgrounds in Adel Aug. 2, 2025. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)New campaign finance reports from the fundraising period of May 27 to July 14 show millions of dollars have poured into Iowa’s statewide elections, including the attorney general’s race.
Willems gets a fundraising boost
Incumbent Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird continues to lead her Democratic opponent, Nate Willems, in fundraising, but Willems is gaining momentum.
Bird raised more than $1.96 million during the most recent fundraising period. After expenditures, she currently has more than $6.89 million on hand.
Bird’s campaign received a large contribution from the Republican Attorneys General Association Action Fund organization in Washington, D.C., receiving $1.5 million during the latest reporting period.
Willems raised $1.94 million during the time span, including $1.5 million from the Democratic Attorneys General Association’s PAC. After expenditures, Willems’ campaign has more than $2.67 million on hand, a large increase from the last fundraising period, where he had $875,000 on hand.
Sand outraises Lahn in latest reports; both received millions from party PACs

Incumbent Pate trails in funding
Ryan Peterman, Democratic candidate for secretary of state, leads incumbent Republican Paul Pate in fundraising efforts.
Peterman raised more than $51,200 over the latest reporting period, bringing his cash on hand to more than $166,000 after expenditures.
Pate raised just $2,110 during the fundraising period, bringing his total cash on hand to more than $90,000.
Pate, who has served as Iowa’s secretary of state in nonconsecutive terms since 1994, has trailed Peterman in funding throughout 2026.
Wettach leads lieutenant governor in auditor’s race fundraising
Lt. Gov. Chris Cournoyer, a Republican running for state auditor, is trailing behind her Democratic opponent, Taylor Wettach, in fundraising.
Cournoyer raised more than $144,000 during the latest fundraising period, bringing her total cash on hand to more than $133,000, a big increase from the previous fundraising period, where she had just $3,226 on hand.
Wettach raised more than $272,000 during the most recent reporting period. After expenditures, Wettach has more than $763,000 on hand.
The state auditor contest is for an open seat. It currently is the only statewide office held by a Democrat, Rob Sand, who is running for governor.
Naig leads in ag secretary fundraising
Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig leads his Democratic opponent, Chris Jones, by a wide margin in cash on hand.
Naig raised more than $179,000 during the latest reporting period, bringing his total cash on hand to more than $672,000.
Jones raised $110,000 over the course of the reporting period. After expenditures, Jones has more than $98,500 on hand.
Incumbent Smith leads treasurer race fundraising
Iowa Treasurer of State Roby Smith, the incumbent Republican, leads Democratic challenger John Norwood in fundraising efforts.
Smith raised more than $149,000 during the latest fundraising period. He currently has $358,300 on hand.
Norwood raised more than $56,000 during the reporting period. After expenditures, Norwood has more than $58,000 on hand.



Federal fundraising roundup
In Iowa’s U.S. Senate race, U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson is currently outpacing state Rep. Josh Turek in total cash on hand, with $6.7 million compared to Turek’s $2.3 million. For the first time this election cycle however, Turek raised more money than Hinson, with $2.8 million in the period compared to Hinson’s $2 million. Turek spent more than $1.1 million during the last period, while Hinson spent more than $1.3 million. According to Fox News’ latest election forecast, this U.S. Senate race is considered a “toss-up,” with a recent Fox News poll showing Turek up by 4 percentage points.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: State Supreme Court rules warrantless searches by Pa. game officials are unconstitutional
description: Property owners have a greater right to privacy on their land under the Pennsylvania Constitution than under the U.S. Constitution, the state Supreme Court ruled Tuesday.
text:
Conemaugh River running through the remnants of the South Fork Dam used to create a man-made lake for the South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club. (	karenfoleyphotography/Getty Images)Property owners have a greater right to privacy on their land under the Pennsylvania Constitution than under the U.S. Constitution, the state Supreme Court ruled Tuesday.
The decision is in favor of a pair of western Pennsylvania hunting clubs. They challenged the constitutionality of two provisions in the Game and Wildlife Code that permitted state game wardens to enter private land, but not homes or buildings, without warrants.
“This is a victory for all landowners in Pennsylvania,” said Frank Stockdale, president of the Punxsutawney Hunting Club in a release. “Generations of members have come to this club to relax, to bond, to laugh, and to find peace. It’s a private place … that’s what makes it so special. Today, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court honored that privacy.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
The Institute for Justice, a public interest law firm, represented the clubs.
“Today, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court affirmed that private land is not public property. It’s yours, and that means you get to decide who enters it. If government officials want to invade your posted land without your consent and spy on you, they need to get a warrant,” said Joshua Windham, a senior attorney at Institute for Justice.
The state attorney general’s office, which represented the Game Commission, declined to comment.
In the summer of 2013, a state wildlife officer accused a Pitch Pine Hunting Club member of illegally feeding bears outside a cabin on the 1,100 acre property. The officer admitted that he had been watching the member and his guests for several days to catch violations, but ultimately left without citing anyone.
After that and other interactions with wildlife officials, members of the Pitch Pine Hunting Club and the nearby Punxsutawney Hunting Club in Clearfield County sued the Pennsylvania Game Commission, asking the Commonwealth Court to find the laws unconstitutional. 
The Game and Wildlife Code provisions allowing warrantless searches are enabled by a 1924 U.S. Supreme Court decision establishing that Fourth Amendment protection against warrantless searches does not extend to “open fields,” such as farmland or woodland well away from dwellings.
The Commonwealth Court ruled against the hunting clubs in 2023 and they appealed to the state’s highest court. 
In the lead opinion for the unanimous Supreme Court, Justice Kevin Brobson said the court’s own 2007 decision in a case called Commonwealth v. Russo, upholding the warrantless search provisions, was decided incorrectly. 
“We conclude that slavish adherence to our decision in Russo must give way to the greater privacy and property protections afforded under Article I, Section 8 of our state charter,” Brobson said. “As our jurisprudence in this area has evolved, the Court’s reasoning and result in Russo have not aged well.”
Article I, Section 8 of the Pennsylvania Constitution is roughly equivalent to the U.S. Constitution’s Fourth Amendment, establishing the right to be free from unreasonable search and seizure. The Supreme Court’s ruling centers on a slight difference in the wording of the two.
Whereas the Fourth Amendment protects the people’s right to be “secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects” from unreasonable searches and seizures, the state constitution uses the word “possessions” in the place of “effects.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In the Russo decision, the state Supreme Court upheld the conviction of a hunter who had been charged with baiting bears after he reported bagging a black bear within minutes of the season opening. 
The court rejected the hunter’s claims the searches that revealed evidence of baiting were constitutionally invalid. In its analysis of the Article I, Section 8 protections the court reasoned that the word “possessions” was equivalent to the word “effects,” in meaning personal property, not real property. Therefore, the Open Fields Doctrine established by the 1924 U.S. Supreme Court ruling was not barred under the state constitution.
The Supreme Court ruled Tuesday, however, that the court erred in finding that the term “possessions” is limited to personal items, and that historically, Pennsylvania law has considered “possessions” to include land.
“Article I, Section 8 provides Pennsylvania citizens with greater protection than the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution as it relates to the open fields of any landowner that has demonstrated a reasonable expectation of privacy by taking sufficient steps to exclude intruders therefrom,” Brobson wrote. 
“Accordingly, the Commission’s officers, employees, and representatives, as well as any other government officials, must obtain a warrant based upon probable cause or satisfy one of the recognized exceptions to the warrant requirement before entering such property,” the court said.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: USDA reversal on crop insurance change welcomed by farm groups
description: The U.S. Department of Agriculture is reversing course on a change to a federal crop insurance policy to allow farmers to buy more protection if weather or field conditions prevent them from planting a crop.  USDA had eliminated the option to buy additional prevented planting insurance going into the 2026 growing season. This raised concerns […]
text:
Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins speaks in Fargo, N.D., on April 22, 2025. She was invited by North Dakota Sen. John Hoeven, left. (Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor) The U.S. Department of Agriculture is reversing course on a change to a federal crop insurance policy to allow farmers to buy more protection if weather or field conditions prevent them from planting a crop. 
USDA had eliminated the option to buy additional prevented planting insurance going into the 2026 growing season. This raised concerns from growers in North Dakota, where the buy-up option has been a popular risk-management tool.  
In a Tuesday hearing of the Senate Agriculture Appropriations Committee, U.S. Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., asked Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins where the department stood on the policy. 
“We are 100% supportive of that and are moving forward to execute that buy-up option,” Rollins said. 
Farmers face greater risk with planting insurance option removed

The change will restore the 5% buy-up option, which provided additional coverage for more than 67 million acres across the country in 2025. North Dakota accounted for 10 million of those acres, Hoeven said. 
Justin Sherlock, past president of the North Dakota Soybean Growers Association and a director with the American Soybean Association, said restoring the buy-up option is welcome news, but that farm groups felt that USDA was required by law to offer it.  
He said defending crop insurance in general was the bigger issue. 
“It was the concern that this could be a bigger infringement upon the crop insurance program as Congress intended it.” 
While he was encouraged by Rollins’ comments, Sherlock said he would like to see the change noted in the Federal Register or in a formal statement from USDA.
Prevented planting was not a major issue in North Dakota this year, but Sherlock did benefit from hail insurance on some land in Griggs County. 
“I wouldn’t be farming without it,” Sherlock said of federal crop insurance.  
Hoeven credited working with Chair Sen. John Boozman, R-Ark.,and Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., of the Senate Agriculture Committee on emphasizing the need to return to the previous policy.   
“Given the challenges facing farm country, we worked very hard to restore this prevented plant buy-up option to provide our producers with an additional layer of protection when disaster prevents them from planting their fields,” Hoeven said in a news release.
