name: Michigan Advance
title: Campaign records show Maasdam refunded Palantir executive’s contribution
description: After receiving a $3,500 campaign contribution from a Palantir Technologies executive, one Democrat seeking the nomination in Michigan’s competitive 7th Congressional District chose to return the money. In September, Matt Maasdam, a former Navy SEAL and military aide to President Barack Obama, received $3,500 from Mehdi Alhassani, the head of government oper[...]
text:
Retired Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam speaks at a candidate forum for Michigan's 7th Congressional District hosted by the Eaton County Democratic Party and Indivisible Michigan 7th District. April 8, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan AdvanceAfter receiving a $3,500 campaign contribution from a Palantir Technologies executive, one Democrat seeking the nomination in Michigan’s competitive 7th Congressional District chose to return the money.
In September, Matt Maasdam, a former Navy SEAL and military aide to President Barack Obama, received $3,500 from Mehdi Alhassani, the head of government operations for Palantir Technologies, a data analytics company criticized for its contracts with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Alhassani previously served as a special assistant to the deputy national security advisor under Obama.
Maasdam’s campaign refunded the contribution on Feb. 9, according to campaign finance records.
Headquartered in Denver, Colo., Palantir has faced scrutiny from groups including the ACLU, Amnesty International and the American Immigration Council for its role in expanding surveillance through large databases that use machine learning technology to identify patterns. 
Since 2014, the company has run the Department of Homeland Security’s Investigative Case Management platform, which provides case-tracking capabilities and allows individuals to perform investigative research to build cases. The company received a $30 million contract in 2025 to upgrade the platform. According to the contract, the work is intended to streamline the “selection and apprehension operations of illegal aliens,” track self-deportation and streamline the deportation process from apprehension to removal.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Our campaign does not have any money from Palantir employees,” Emma Grundhauser, a spokesperson for Maasdam’s campaign, said in a statement. “Matt received a contribution last year from a former colleague in the Obama White House. When it came to our attention that the donor worked for this group, we returned the contribution.”
Throughout his campaign, Maasdam has called for greater accountability and oversight for ICE and Department of Homeland Security officials, calling out “reckless ICE agents” as a threat to the Constitution in his campaign’s first ad.
“Matt has been clear over the course of this campaign that Donald Trump has weaponized ICE into a paramilitary force that is terrorizing American communities and treating people like enemy combatants, and he believes we need to clean house at ICE and fundamentally overhaul the agency,” Grundhauser said, noting Maasdam supports ending mass raids, requiring warrants for arrests and searches and independently prosecuting agents who break the law.
Maasdam’s Democratic opponents have also spoken out against ICE conduct, with former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink calling for an overhaul of the agency, while political organizer William Lawrence has pledged to hold ICE accountable for unconstitutional conduct.
Neither Brink nor Lawrence has received campaign contributions from Palantir employees, according to a search of the Federal Election Commission’s campaign finance database.
All three Democrats are vying to run in November against U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte), who has received $7,000 in contributions from Palantir Chief Technology Officer and Executive Vice President Shyam Sankar.
When asked about the contribution, Barrett campaign strategist Jason Roe told Michigan Advance it was the first he’d heard of it. 
“I don’t think we have any heartburn about their modest contribution,” Roe said. “It’s not necessarily a reflection of what Tom’s views are on what they care about, but probably recognition that they think Tom is a thoughtful member of Congress.”
Border security was a key issue for Barrett’s 2024 campaign, with Barrett casting his first vote in Congress in support of the Laken Riley Act. That legislation requires Department of Homeland Security officials to detain noncitizens arrested for burglary, theft, larceny, shoplifting, assault of a law enforcement officer, or any crime that results in death or serious bodily injury to another person. The law also permits states to sue the government over “alleged failures” related to immigration enforcement.

name: VTDigger
title: Judge denies bid by suspect’s lawyers in border patrol agent killing to change records screening process
description:
Attorneys for Teresa Youngblut had called on the federal judge overseeing the death penalty case in Vermont to set a new system after what they described as “failures” with the current method.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Judge denies bid by suspect’s lawyers in border patrol agent killing to change records screening process.
text:
The Federal Building in Burlington on Friday, September 5, 2025. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

The defense team for a suspect charged in the fatal shooting of a border patrol agent in Vermont more than a year ago has lost its bid to change how certain records are screened before determining whether they can be released to the government.
Lawyers for Teresa Youngblut in a new court filing Monday in federal court in Burlington called on Judge Christina Reiss to change the system set up last fall to protect against the disclosure of privileged or protected pretrial detention records to the prosecutors. 
They cited an instance where they alleged that the government had inadvertently “received and reviewed” certain information due to issues with the screening system established last fall. The protocol was put in place to protect “privileged’ records, such as attorney and client communications, as Youngblut remains detained awaiting trial. 
“Because of that lapse, the government has received and reviewed privileged information regarding the identity of a member of the defense team,” the defense filing stated.
The filing later added, “These failures demonstrate that the Protocol is insufficient to protect Youngblut’s constitutional and evidentiary privileges in this capital case.”
Reiss, in a ruling Tuesday afternoon, denied the defense request for a hearing to reconsider the system she put in place in September that created a protocol that included the court’s review of certain records. 
“Defendant must identify authority for her contention that the identity of a defense team member is privileged,” Reiss wrote in her order.
“The purpose of the protocol is to prevent inappropriate dissemination of attorney-client privileged communications and attorney-client work product to the government,” the judge added. “The court reviewed the communications in question and determined that none of them fell within these categories.”

READ MORE

The defense filing this week follows another one earlier this month in which Youngblut’s attorney argued that evidence disputes a version of events from federal authorities about what led up to the deadly shootout in January 2025 in Vermont.
Youngblut, 22, of Seattle, faces several federal charges, including murder, in the fatal shooting of U.S. Border Patrol Agent David Maland during a traffic stop on Interstate 91 in Coventry on Jan. 20, 2025.
A passenger in the vehicle Youngblut was driving, Felix Bauckholt, a German national known as Ophelia, was also killed in the shootout. 
Prosecutors have stated in court filings, if convicted, they will seek the death penalty for Youngblut. Vermont does not have the death penalty under state law. However, this case is brought under federal law where the death penalty is permitted.
Youngblut, who was arrested shortly after the shooting, has been held in custody without bail since in various facilities in Vermont and out of state.
Youngblut’s defense team has argued at earlier hearings in the case that strict protocols needed to be in place to prevent the government from obtaining records, such as certain medical and attorney and client privilege information, stemming from Youngblut’s detention.
Youngblut’s attorneys have said there was a need for a “heightened scrutiny” with the prosecution seeking their client’s execution. 
Steven Barth, an attorney for Youngblut, could not be reached Tuesday for comment. 
A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for Vermont, which is prosecuting the case, declined comment Tuesday, stating in an email, “The U.S. Attorney’s Office does not comment as a general policy on ongoing litigation, and will file our response on the docket when due.”
Youngblut and Bauckholt had been connected by law enforcement to a loosely linked group known as the Zizians, whose members have been tied to six homicides across the country in recent years.
The Zizians have ties to Bay Area communities of rationalists, a movement of philosophically-minded people who focus on logical reasoning and are interested in artificial intelligence and software engineering. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Judge denies bid by suspect’s lawyers in border patrol agent killing to change records screening process.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: State-ordered study says opioid settlement money should target treatment for incarcerated people
description: South Dakota should spend opioid settlement money in the coming years to address the needs of people entering or leaving prisons and jails, according to an assessment prepared for the state Department of Social Services. The department commissioned the $325,000 statewide needs assessment to help guide the state’s investment of settlement dollars. The inadequ[...]
text:
An opioid rescue kit, which includes a naloxone kit inside, is stationed on the third floor of the South Dakota State Capitol, near the Senate chamber on June 3, 2026. The kit is next to an emergency defibrillator, which is used for cardiac arrests. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota should spend opioid settlement money in the coming years to address the needs of people entering or leaving prisons and jails, according to an assessment prepared for the state Department of Social Services.
The department commissioned the $325,000 statewide needs assessment to help guide the state’s investment of settlement dollars. The inadequacy of the programs and services for addicted people in the justice system was a major takeaway, the department secretary told members of the Legislature’s budget committee on Monday at the Capitol in Pierre.



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



“This is a more intense addiction once you get to that level of opioid use disorder,” Secretary Matt Althoff said. “We still see, as is so often the case, the justice involvement. Laws get broken, they become incarcerated or they become prosecuted, and they are also struggling with addiction.”
The money comes from the makers and sellers of opioid painkillers linked to spikes in addiction and overdose deaths. South Dakota is expected to receive about $99 million in settlement funds through 2038. The state’s collected $32.8 million so far, with 70% of the money tagged for statewide dispersal and 30% going directly to localities.
Thus far, the state has awarded all but $2.7 million of its share through a three-tiered grant system, with awards ranging from $5,000 on the low end to more than $50,000 on the high end. The largest single award went to Avera Health, which is using its grant for an addiction-focused psychiatric residential treatment facility in Sioux Falls.
Medication-assisted addiction treatment
In the future, treatment for those released on supervision could involve the use of medications for opioid use disorder, a class of pharmaceuticals that, at therapeutic levels, deaden the craving for the drugs without producing the high or spurring a higher tolerance and a need for higher doses.
The Department of Corrections already offers the medications inside its institutions, but it has concerns about the availability of the drugs and follow-up care on the outside, said Brenna Koedam, who leads the Department of Social Services’ Behavioral Health Division.
The two departments have discussed where they might begin with a collaborative effort, Koedam said, which could be with eight outside prison locations for follow-up care to parolees using the medicines. 
South Dakota awards $7.8 million from opioid settlement to combat addiction

The Department of Social Services and Unified Judicial System have also begun talks on the drugs’ possible use for people on probation, Koedam said. On Tuesday, court system spokeswoman Alisa Bousa said the state courts are interested in “any additional educational and engagement tools that would benefit the probationers.”
At the legislative meeting, Koedam told lawmakers that a stigma and “misconceptions” still surround buprenorphine, methadone and naltrexone, the three medications approved for opioid use disorder by the Food and Drug Administration. 
The department needs to “continue to get the education out there in regards to how effective these medications can be” when administered as part of an addiction treatment program, said Koedam.
Rep. Terri Jorgenson, R-Piedmont, wanted to know how long people take the drugs, on average.
“This isn’t a lifelong thing, is it?” Jorgenson said. 
Koedam told her the answer is complicated and depends on the individual. Some, she said, may use them long-term.
Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, said she recognizes that reliance on a non-intoxicating medication is preferable to opioid use, but asked if “we’re trading one addiction for another addiction.”
For some people, Koedam said, such medicines can be “maintenance” medications, not dissimilar to drugs for blood pressure or depression that people commonly take for a lifetime. Some people, she said, will remain on the anti-addiction medicines “for the course of their lifetime.”
Sen. Red Dawn Foster, D-Pine Ridge, urged the department to prioritize “innovative” approaches to addiction for those inside institutions.
“I know a lot of inmates are self-medicating, so this is some type of need,” said Foster, referencing the use of illicit substances in prisons and jails.
Next steps for funding
Questions of ongoing funding bubbled up throughout the meeting. Jorgenson said the settlement money is finite and noted the department’s mention that the award amounts will grow smaller as 2038 draws near.
Howard, meanwhile, said “I’m seeing a lot of new programs,” and said she wasn’t convinced that taxpayers won’t be expected to keep paying for them.
State revamps use of opioid settlement money by offering ‘transformative’ grants up to $2 million

“When somebody comes and asks for this grant, have you considered saying, ‘I need your commitment that you aren’t going to ask for ongoing dollars from this,’” Howard said.
The department denied a sizable stack of funding applications because it prioritized programs that wouldn’t need ongoing money from the state, Althoff said.
“Why did we say ‘no?’ Because a lot of it was not sustainable,” he said.
The next round of funding awards will prioritize applications in the mid-range of the department’s three-tiered grant system, which it calls “organizational” grants of up to $50,000.
The small awards were designed for projects at the idea stage, Althoff said, while the large ones were more about developing infrastructure. Over the next year, the goal will be to get projects into the operational and sustainable stage. 
Near the end of the briefing, Sen. Paul Miskimins, R-Mitchell, praised the department’s willingness to take on opioid addiction. Miskimins, a retired dentist who said he tightened his approach to painkiller prescriptions as their addictive nature became clear, said he hopes lawmakers and the general public remember the human cost of the drugs behind the settlement money.
“One of the finest ladies in my practice was arrested for stealing medications out of a medicine chest at a rummage sale because she was addicted and hiding it from everybody in the world,” said Miskimins. “She was a Sunday school teacher.”
Opioid settlement dollars

name: DC
outlet: News From The States - Fair. Fearless. Free.
title: Number of women seeking a governor’s seat hits an all-time high
text: WASHINGTON — New data reveals the number of women running in the 2026 elections is slightly up from 2024, but experts say there is still progress to be made with women’s representation in public office overall. The number of women running for governor has reached an all-time high this election cycle, and the number seeking a seat in the U.S. House of Representatives could also set a record, according to July 20 data from The Center for American Women and Politics, or CAWP. The center, part of the Eagleton Institute of Politics at Rutgers University, collects data on women’s representation in federal, state and local government. The center also conducts research and runs educational programs on the role of women in politics. Its mission is to increase female involvement in public life. Women in the midtermsThere are 85 women major-party candidates running for governor across 36 states this year, a number that significantly exceeds the previous record of 69, set in 2022. Fifty-one of those women are Democrats, another record, and 34 are Republicans. On the congressional level, 580 women are currently major-party contenders for the U.S. House, a figure that is just three away from the 2018 and 2020 record of 583 women candidates. That record could be broken once Louisiana reaches its candidate filing deadline for the House on Aug. 7, according to CAWP.  The number of Democratic House candidates who are women has already reached an all-time high at 387. The remaining 183 women running are Republicans. In the Senate, 64 women from major parties are running for a seat, exactly half of them Democrats and half of them Republicans. The record for women Senate candidates was set in 2022 at 70. Fairly high numbers of women would need to emerge as Senate candidates in Maine and South Carolina to beat that record of 70, said CAWP Director of Data Chelsea Hill during a media briefing with other CAWP research experts on Tuesday.A day before the briefing, Republican Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina, who was sworn in July 14 to replace her late brother, Lindsey Graham, announced plans to run for a full six-year term following the encouragement of President Donald Trump. Although record numbers of congressional women candidates have not yet been reached in either the U.S. House or Senate, the overall number of women running for Congress is up compared to the last election cycle. In 2024, the number of women who sought seats in Congress dropped after having previously increased for three consecutive cycles, a phenomenon that CAWP later described as “evidence of stalled progress toward gender parity,” Hill said. Despite the increase in women seeking office over the years, female representation is still low when taken as a percentage of all candidates running for Congress and state governors. According to another set of CAWP data from July 20, women make up 27% of total candidacies for the U.S. House and 23.9% of the total for the Senate in 2026. About 25% of gubernationarial candidates are women. Milestones within reach But at the same time, CAWP experts said at the media briefing, there are many milestones women could achieve in the 2026 election cycle, including firsts for women in certain government positions and for “women of specific racial and ethnic backgrounds and within either party.” They pointed to current Sens. Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee, a Republican, and Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota, a Democrat, who are both running to become the first women to serve as governors of their respective states. And Deb Haaland, the former U.S. secretary of the Interior currently running in New Mexico, could become the first-ever Native American woman governor in any state if she wins in November. At the congressional level, names such as Milat Keros, Aisha Wahab, Denise Powell and more have the potential to break barriers for women in public office. Keros is in place to become the first Black woman to represent Colorado, Wahab the first Middle Eastern or North African woman to serve from California and Powell the first Democratic woman to represent Nebraska in Congress.At the end of the media briefing, CAWP Scholar and Director of Research Kelly Dittmar said the center’s 2026 candidacy data could be used as a tool to study and open up a broader discussion about women’s political pathways, nodding particularly to Blackburn and Klobuchar’s gubernatorial runs. “When we think about women moving to be chief executives of a state as a potential pathway to the presidency, (it’s) also something we need to always keep our eye on,” she said. CAWP’s data focuses on major party candidates and will continue to be updated regularly to account for upcoming state filing deadlines and congressional primary results.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Union objects to Trump administration move to privatize security at Tampa International Airport
description: Officials with the union representing transportation security officers at more than 400 U.S. airports are criticizing the decision by the Trump administration and officials with Tampa International Airport to privatize security operations there next year. The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) notified the American Federation of Government Employee[...]
text:
Tampa International Airport, via airport website.Officials with the union representing transportation security officers at more than 400 U.S. airports are criticizing the decision by the Trump administration and officials with Tampa International Airport to privatize security operations there next year.
The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) notified the American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) Monday that the agency intends to launch a privatization called TSA Gold+ at airports in Tampa, Charleston, South Carolina, and Des Moines, Iowa, in 2027.
The AFGE says the new program would put private contractors in control not only of security screening but the screening technology itself — machines that detect guns, explosives, and other prohibited items. While TSA staff would provide oversight, they would no longer directly screen passengers or carry-on items at those airports.
“Make no mistake — this is a major departure and step backwards from the aviation screening security system that Congress created in the wake of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in 2001 and the deadly bombing of the Pan Am Flight 103 over Scottland in 1988,” AFGE President Everett Kelley said Tuesday in a written statement.
“Changes of this magnitude should not be made behind closed doors without the input of Congress, the flying public, the local airport authorities, and TSA employees themselves.”
In a statement to the Phoenix, officials with Tampa International Airport said they have opted into the TSA Gold+ program, adding that it “reflects the Airport’s strong commitment to modernization, innovation, and operational resilience in aviation security.”
“The change to privatization not only reduces disruption risks caused by lapses in federal appropriations or government shutdowns but also allows greater flexibility in exploring new screening checkpoint infrastructure and technology to enhance the customer experience,” said Beau Zimmer, the airport’s communications manager.
Project 2025
The AFGE represents 47,000 TSA officers at 400 airports across the country. Their concerns about the Trump administration’s privatization plan arise because such a plan was included in the Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025 document, the conservative policy wish list that surfaced ahead of the 2024 presidential election.
According to the liberal Center for Progressive Reform, the Trump administration had initiated or completed 53% of Project 2025’s domestic administrative policy agenda in the first 12 months following the president’s inauguration in January 2025.
“As part of an effort to shrink federal bureaucracies and bring private-sector know-how to government programs, TSA is ripe for reform,” the document says on page 158. “The US should look to the Canadian and European private models of providing aviation screening manpower to lower TSA costs while maintaining security.”
Project 2025 suggested the TSA could expand the existing Screening Partnership Program to all airports. Currently, 20 U.S. airports are part of that program, including in Sarasota, San Francisco, and Kansas City, according to a May NPR report.
All screening at U.S. airports was conducted by private screeners before the 9/11 attacks. Shortly after the attacks, the U.S. Senate passed the Aviation and Transportation Security Act 100-0 to create the TSA.
The AFGE says the Trump administration’s fiscal 2027 budget proposes to eliminate 8,400 transportation security officer (TSO) positions — roughly 14% of TSA’s screening workforce. About 4,500 of those positions would be replaced by private contractors through a mandatory expansion of the Screening Partnership Program to include all small and non-hub airports. That would expand the SPP from 20 airports to about 220 airports.
At a House Homeland Security Committee hearing held in May, most Democrats said that forced privatization at U.S. airports  would be a mistake that would lead to worse outcomes for both travelers and TSA personnel. Workers at private companies would earn less than most TSA staff, they said, while losing their collective bargaining rights, according to a report from Government Executive.
Right of first refusal 
“The administration’s actions should concern all Americans, and AFGE will continue to speak out against any proposal that threatens our members’ jobs and jeopardizes the safety of the flying public,” Kelley said.
According to officials who have been informed about the plan, TSOs have right of first refusal for jobs with a contractor, and no TSO will lose a job who wants to keep it.
A TSA spokesperson issued this statement to the Phoenix:
“TSA Gold+ presents a new way for TPA to deliver exceptional service to every traveler, while advancing security, efficiency, and the overall airport experience. Throughout this transition, we remain committed to operational stability and supporting our employees.”

title: House eyes passage of bill altering criteria for late-term abortions
authors: Alison Kuznitz | State House News Service
description: The bill would eliminate the existing criteria that allows for abortions to be performed 24 weeks or later into a pregnancy. Instead, leaving it up to the professional judgment of the physician performing the abortion.
text:
HOUSE DEMOCRATS ADVANCED LEGISLATION Tuesday removing restrictions to abortion later in pregnancy, stripping a four-pronged framework that was included in the 2022 shield law that looked to safeguard access to reproductive care.
The one-page bill (H 2370) the House Ways and Means Committee polled out Tuesday morning would eliminate the existing criteria that allows for abortions to be performed 24 weeks or later into a pregnancy. Instead, the bill states that “an abortion may be performed by a physician based upon the professional judgment of the physician.”
The House is slated to vote on the bill during a formal session Wednesday, Speaker Ron Mariano and Rep. Aaron Michlewitz announced.
It cleared the House Ways and Means Committee on a 23-6 vote. Republican Reps. John Marsi, Joseph McKenna, Kelly Pease, Todd Smola, Alyson Sullivan-Almeida, and Steven Xiarhos voted against moving the bill out of committee. Reps. Michael Chaisson and Marcus Vaughn reserved their rights. Reps. Rodney Elliott, Russel Holmes, and Chynah Tyler took no action in the poll. 
“This legislation is about ensuring that in Massachusetts, reproductive health care decisions are made exclusively by the patient and her doctor — unencumbered by a legal framework that, in practice, isn’t always capable of accounting for the complexity and uncertainty inherent to pregnancy-related health care,” Mariano and House Ways and Means Chair Michlewitz said in a statement. “Informed by physicians in Massachusetts with patients who have had to leave the Commonwealth to receive medical care as a result of current law, these reforms will ensure that Massachusetts remains steadfast in our commitment to protecting a woman’s right to choose.”
Under the existing framework, abortions later in pregnancy can only be performed if necessary to preserve the patient’s life, necessary to preserve the patient’s physical or mental health, warranted because of a lethal fetal anomaly or diagnosis, or warranted because of a “grave fetal diagnosis.” The wording of those guardrails were a focal point of conference committee negotiations in 2022, as lawmakers passed the state’s first shield law in response to the Supreme Court overturning Roe v. Wade.
“We look forward to continued conversations with the Membership about this critical issue, and to passing this important legislation tomorrow,” Mariano and Michlewitz said.
The Massachusetts Family Institute said the bill “seeks to remove virtually all remaining protections in Massachusetts for unborn babies and their mothers.” In an email blast, the group said the bill would “eliminate meaningful limitations and accountability for late-term abortions” and “expand abortion access at a stage when unborn children are capable of feeling pain and surviving outside the womb.”
The Senate last month passed a bill aimed at bolstering investments in primary care, boosting access to care and growing the workforce. House leaders have not joined that push and Mariano has given voice to surfacing legislation addressing prescription drug issue. 
Health Care Financing Committee co-chair Rep. John Lawn has said the House is working on reforms for pharmacy benefit managers.

title: Poll finds low public awareness of Colorado’s upcoming 150th anniversary
description: More than two-thirds of Coloradans say they’ve heard “nothing” or “not much” about the Centennial State’s upcoming 150th statehood anniversary, a poll found. Just 6% of respondents said they’ve heard “a lot” about the commemoration, which coincides with the nation’s recent 250th birthday celebration, while the remaining 24% said they’ve heard “some,” the Col[...]
text:
An American flag and a Colorado flag fly at the Colorado Capitol in Denver on June 10, 2025. (Photo by Quentin Young/Colorado Newsline)More than two-thirds of Coloradans say they’ve heard “nothing” or “not much” about the Centennial State’s upcoming 150th statehood anniversary, a poll found.
Just 6% of respondents said they’ve heard “a lot” about the commemoration, which coincides with the nation’s recent 250th birthday celebration, while the remaining 24% said they’ve heard “some,” the Colorado Polling Institute found. Awareness was highest among Coloradans aged 35 to 44, especially parents.
“Schoolchildren may be the ones that are driving some of this awareness and bringing that home to the adults in their lives,” said Lori Weigel of New Bridge Strategies, one of the survey’s pollsters.

With funding from the Rose Community Foundation and the Daniels Fund, the Colorado Polling Institute surveyed 655 respondents from June 26 to July 1 about their views on Colorado’s past, present and future. Despite deep political divisions at the state and national level, nearly two-thirds of voters said they agreed with the statement that “Colorado’s best days are ahead,” and 70% agreed that “As Coloradans, we have more in common than what divides us.”
Click the image to see Newsline’s special reporting project on 150 years of Colorado statehood.
“We had more positive numbers on (those questions) than I was expecting,” Weigel said. “I think a little bit of that might be a glow that we were getting going into July 4th.”
Colorado’s natural beauty, outdoor recreation opportunities and “political and social progressiveness” topped the list of what respondents said was the best thing about Coloradan today. Eighty-four percent said they were proud to be a Coloradan, compared to 75% who said they were proud to be an American.
That gap is driven by the state’s partisan divide, pollsters found. Among self-identified conservative respondents, 97% said they were proud to be an American while just two-thirds were proud to be from Colorado; among liberals, the proportions were almost exactly inverted. Coloradans identifying as socialists were the least likely, at 26%, to say they were proud to be Americans, though 92% of those respondents still said they were proud to be Coloradans.
A 58% majority of voters said Colorado places too little emphasis on civic education, compared to just 5% who said it places too much.
Colorado’s 150th statehood anniversary will be celebrated on Aug. 1 with a flagship celebration beginning at 10 a.m. at the Colorado Capitol, along with events all over the state. A full list of events can be found on the America 250-Colorado 150 website.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Drawn out of congressional district, Cleo Fields will seek old La. Senate seat
description: Fields, 63, would lengthen an already extensive career in politics should he secure his old state Senate seat. He has served three previous stints in the chamber, with the first spanning from 1988-93. Fields was also part of the Senate from 1997-2008 and 2020-25.
text:
U.S. Rep. Cleo Fields announced Tuesday, July 21, 2026, he will seek the Louisiana Senate seat he has held on three previous occasions dating back to 1988. The seat was left vacant by the unexpected death of Sen. Larry Selders earlier this month. (Photo by Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)U.S. Rep. Cleo Fields, D-Baton Rouge, has for weeks indicated he would not run again for Congress after the Louisiana Legislature revised the state’s House districts to favor a Republican candidate. He announced Tuesday he would seek his former seat in the Louisiana Senate, left vacant by the unexpected death of Sen. Larry Selders earlier this month.
In a news release, Fields said he would enter the race to fill the rest of Selders’ term in Senate District 14. He has scheduled a news conference Friday in Baton Rouge to detail his plans.
“I feel my calling to serve the people is better put to use back home than here in D.C., and I intend to answer that,” Fields said.
A special election to fill the remainder of Selders’ term has been called for Dec. 12, with a Jan. 9 runoff if needed. Qualifying for the race takes place Oct. 14-16.
Selders, who died July 7 from a heart condition, succeeded Fields in the state Senate in 2025. Fields left the legislature when he won the 6th Congressional District seat, which the legislature crafted in 2024 to comply with a federal court order requiring a second district that favors a Black candidate among Louisiana’s six U.S. House seats.
A group of white voters challenged how the 6th District’s boundaries were drawn in a case that ultimately went before the U.S. Supreme Court. Gov. Jeff Landry and Attorney General Liz Murrill, who originally defended the 2024 congressional map, sided with the plaintiffs, leading the Supreme Court’s conservative majority to invalidate a foundational premise of the landmark Voting Rights Act in an April decision.
The legislature followed that ruling with a new congressional map, leaving Louisiana with just one majority-Black district, which U.S. Rep. Troy Carter, D-New Orleans, represents. Fields has said previously he would not challenge Carter.
Louisiana’s U.S. House races this year were originally supposed to be part of the state’s party primary elections in May and June, but Landry issued an executive order that moved the contests to the Nov. 3 ballot. Those contests will now be open primaries, with all candidates from every party on the ballot. Runoffs, if needed, will take place Dec. 12
Qualifying for the congressional elections takes place Aug. 5-7.
Fields, 63, would lengthen an already extensive career in politics should he secure his old state Senate seat. He has served three previous stints in the chamber, with the first spanning from 1988-93. Fields was also part of the Senate from 1997-2008 and 2020-25. 
He previously served in Congress from 1993-97 in the 4th District and ran unsuccessfully for governor in 1996, when he advanced to a runoff against eventual winner Mike Foster. 
Fields opted not to run again for Congress when the 4th District was redrawn to favor a white Republican candidate, but he would return to the U.S. Capitol 28 years later.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Hartford residents back police oversight board stuck in union standoff
description: The Civilian Police Review Board investigates misconduct. It's seen its work grind to a halt because it can't get records from the police.
text:
Dozens of community members took to the streets and spoke at a public hearing Monday to call on city leaders to stand behind Hartford’s police oversight board amid an escalating conflict with the police union.
The Civilian Police Review Board, which investigates misconduct and citizen complaints, has seen its work grind to a standstill in numerous cases this year because it can’t obtain necessary records from the police department.
The Hartford Police Union has also challenged powers granted to the CPRB, arguing they conflict with a union contract, and that the panel and its inspector general have overstepped their legal authority to investigate officer conduct.
The deadlock spurred Inspector General Joseph Lopez to seek assistance from members of the City Council, who are weighing changes to a city ordinance that would make clear the CPRB is authorized to issue subpoenas and send cases to binding arbitration.
Residents and local advocacy groups voiced their support for the board Monday during a faith walk organized by the North Hartford Public Safety Coalition in response to a recent spike in gun violence in the area.
Participants included members of the Greater Hartford Interfaith Action Alliance, which advocated to strengthen the CPRB after the murder of George Floyd in 2020.
More than two dozen people also urged council members to support the board during a virtual public hearing that lasted nearly two and a half hours.
Corrie Betts, president of the NAACP Greater Hartford branch, said empowering the board isn’t “anti-police,” but rather supports both officers and the public.
“The strongest institutions are not those that resist independent review,” Betts said. “The strongest institutions are those that welcome transparency because they understand that public trust is earned, not demanded.”
Hartford Police Union President James Rutkauski was the only speaker who offered an opposing view. Rutkauski criticized proposed changes that would grant the inspector general greater independence and a dedicated budget.
Rutkauski directed his remarks at Lopez, contending Lopez drafted the ordinance changes to secure himself a “permanent, untouchable seat of power with an open checkbook,” and asked members of the council to sign off on them without understanding the ramifications.
“We don’t know what he will be spending, and we have no true idea of the financial impact that these ordinance changes could have,” Rutkauski said.
Lopez, a lawyer who previously directed the Complex Litigation Unit in the Office of the Chief Public Defender, responded that he took a pay cut of about $100,000 annually to accept the inspector general position because he believes the work is impactful.
“I’m not here for the salary,” he said. “I’m here to do a good job for the CPRB. They are hardworking individuals, and this is a noble cause.”
Lopez told council members previously that while Hartford has Connecticut’s most robust ordinance establishing its civilian oversight board, the panel hasn’t functioned that way to date.
The board investigates allegations such as excessive use of force in parallel with the Hartford Police Department’s Internal Affairs Division. It renders independent judgments, which it sends to the police chief.
City leaders significantly strengthened the board in 2020, drawing on new state legislation that authorized subpoena power for civilian review boards. They also empowered the CPRB to send cases to arbitration if the chief rejects a charge the board has sustained.
The union has challenged those processes in court and before the State Board of Labor Relations. It also rescinded a previous agreement that permitted the inspector general to attend officer interviews conducted by Internal Affairs.
Changes under consideration by the council would ensure the inspector general has access to evidence, documents and other materials. They would also require the police chief to wait for the CPRB to render findings before issuing a final decision on alleged misconduct, and clarify that arbitration doesn’t conflict with the union’s contract. In cases where the arbitrator sustains a charge, the chief could choose the discipline and would not be bound by mandatory punishments specified under the department’s code of conduct.
Among those who spoke in favor of the proposed changes were a former city councilman and former school board chairperson.
Other supporters included Eric Coleman, a retired superior court judge and former state senator who chaired the legislature’s judiciary committee; and lawyer Sydney T. Schulman, who participated in securing a consent decree for the Hartford Police Department that was in place for five decades before being lifted in 2023.
Community organizer Cherell Banks, a founding member of the North Hartford Public Safety Coalition, said working closely with youth and other residents has shown her that public safety depends on trust. People are more likely to report concerns and cooperate with law enforcement when they believe there is a fair, transparent process for accountability, Banks said.
“This is not about being against the police,” Banks said. “It’s about building a system that supports both residents and officers through fairness, transparency and accountability.”
This story was first published July 21, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Former New Mexico AG says federal prosecutors haven’t honored Epstein investigation agreement
description: Federal prosecutors investigating the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein “to this day” have not upheld an agreement to share New Mexico-related materials with the state’s top law enforcement agency, former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas wrote in a Monday letter to Attorney General Raúl Torrez.
text:
Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas (left) wrote to current AG Raúl Torrez on July 20, 2026, and said federal prosecutors failed to uphold an agreement to share materials related to the late sex-offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Balderas photo by Gino Gutierrez for Source NM/Torrez photo by Danielle Prokop/Source NM)
Federal prosecutors investigating the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein “to this day” have not upheld an agreement to share New Mexico-related materials with the state’s top law enforcement agency, former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas wrote in a Monday letter to Attorney General Raúl Torrez.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Balderas’ letter says that his office was conducting an investigation into Epstein and his Santa Fe County property, Zorro Ranch, in 2019 when they learned of a broader federal investigation into Epstein and his co-conspirator Ghislaine Maxwell.
He wrote that his office and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York subsequently came to an agreement weeks before Epstein’s suicide — Balderas’ investigators would stop interviewing potential witnesses, and the federal prosecutors would refer state-related matters to the New Mexico attorney general’s office at the end of their case.
“The agreement with the SDNY prosecutors was not to simply stop or to stay out of their way. Instead, my administration had a firm agreement with the SDNY that they have not honored to this day,” Balderas wrote to Torrez Monday, adding that partially redacted files released under the federal Epstein Files Transparency Act contain handwritten notes confirming the details of the arrangement. 
Balderas’ letter comes weeks after Torrez accused the federal government of impeding his agency’s investigation into Zorro Ranch. He has contended that the U.S. Department of Justice has delayed the release of relevant records that contain names of witnesses, abuse survivors and co-conspirators that his agency needs if it is to fully investigate and prosecute any criminal matters.
“Former Attorney General Balderas has confirmed something we’ve said all along: New Mexico honored its side of an agreement with the federal government, and the federal government did not honor its own,” Torrez said in a statement Tuesday. “That breach doesn’t weaken our position, it strengthens it. New Mexico is entitled to these records, and we will use every tool available, including litigation, to obtain them.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Wisconsin, coalition of states, win lawsuit against Trump administration cutting federal grants
description: A federal judge ruled late last week that the Trump administration had acted illegally last summer when it cut millions in federal grant money.  U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in the District of Massachusetts ruled on Friday that the White House’s Office of Management and Budget does not have the authority to revoke grants on […]
text:
OMB Director Russ Vought testifies before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Jan. 15, 2025. (Screenshot from committee webcast)A federal judge ruled late last week that the Trump administration had acted illegally last summer when it cut millions in federal grant money. 
U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani in the District of Massachusetts ruled on Friday that the White House’s Office of Management and Budget does not have the authority to revoke grants on a whim. OMB had argued that a line in the federal regulations gave the White House authority to cancel grants to account for shifts in priorities. 
Talwani found that the agency couldn’t cancel grants to achieve priorities that were announced after the grants had been awarded. 
Wisconsin was joined by 22 other states and Washington D.C. in filing a lawsuit against OMB pulling back grant funds. The Wisconsin Department of Justice noted in a press release that the state had lost tens of millions of dollars in federal grant funding meant to help provide Wisconsin-grown food to local food banks, modernize the state’s unemployment system and fund research at UW-Madison. 
“The Trump administration has been recklessly attempting to slash funding that supports important programs,” said Attorney General Josh Kaul. “This decision shuts down an unlawful avenue that the Trump administration was using to try to impose those cuts.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Cyclosporiasis outbreak surpasses 560 cases in North Carolina
description: North Carolina is reporting 561 cases of cyclosporiasis as of July 20, 2026, but the cause of the state’s growing outbreak remains a mystery. Dr. Carl Williams, state public health veterinarian for the N.C. Department of Health and Human Services, told reporters Tuesday that while some states were able to identify lettuce as the source […]
text:
With cases of cyclosporiasis  on the rises, North Carolina health officials recommend people thoroughly wash fresh fruits and vegetables. Cooking your produce can also kill the parasite. (Photo: Getty Images)   North Carolina is reporting 561 cases of cyclosporiasis as of July 20, 2026, but the cause of the state’s growing outbreak remains a mystery.
Dr. Carl Williams, state public health veterinarian for the N.C. Department of Health and Human Services, told reporters Tuesday that while some states were able to identify lettuce as the source for a significant proportion of cases, in North Carolina the outbreak may be caused by several sources.
“Our thought is that it’s likely that there are multiple vehicles for cyclosporiasis. It’s not a single source or a single food product from a single company,” said Williams.
While that can make it difficult to offer advice about what to avoid, Williams says that thoroughly washing fresh produce is a good first step to protecting yourself. Even if the packaging says the produce has been triple washed, that does not guarantee the parasite will be removed entirely.
“[Cyclosporiasis] is shed in feces that could contaminate surface water. In other countries, that surface water may be used for irrigation or it may be used for the application of pesticides,” Williams explained. “That’s how it gets from the human to the surface water onto the surface of the fresh fruit and vegetable. These fresh fruits and vegetables come to the United States, they come to North Carolina, there’s no outward sign of a problem.”
Williams says cases tend to increase in the summer months when more people are enjoying more fresh fruits and vegetables. Cyclosporiasis, like many foodborne illnesses, can be prevented by cooking foods to 165 degrees Fahrenheit.
“If you cook it, you’ll kill it. But most people don’t want to cook their fresh fruits and vegetables,” said Williams.
Cyclosporiasis is one of more than 80 conditions that is reportable to the state by law. Each case is carefully investigated by NCDHHS and local health departments as they work to identify the original supplier or source.
Because most state public health labs cannot do the molecular work needed to trace specific strains of cyclospora, it’s up to the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to establish any genetic linkages between specimens taken in North Carolina and specimens from another state.
Williams says the CDC has been very responsive to NCDHHS, conducting calls twice a week with state health departments as they search for answers.
The microscopic parasite can cause explosive diarrhea and intense stomach cramps that can last for days. That can be especially dangerous for certain segments of the population.
FDA: Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce sample produced a false positive for cyclospora

“Certainly, you want to take extra care if you are immunocompromised or elderly,” Williams told NC Newsline. “Even things that may not be that big of a problem, you can get dehydrated. That alone can create serious problems.”
Sixteen people in North Carolina have been hospitalized because of the parasite.
Some school districts have made the decision not to serve fresh produce until more is known about the source of the outbreak. Durham Public Schools decided to serve frozen or canned vegetables until September.
NCDHHS has been consulting with the NC Department of Public Instruction about the risks cyclosporiasis might pose for schools this fall, but has not issued any formal guidance.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Multi-agency operation yields 14 cocaine arrests, including in South Dakota
description: RAPID CITY — A multi-agency effort to disrupt cocaine trafficking resulted in 14 total arrests of people from Colorado and the South Dakota cities of Pine Ridge, Box Elder and Rapid City, authorities announced Tuesday. Representatives of federal, tribal, state and local agencies gathered in the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Rapid City to speak about […]
text:
Ron Parsons, the U.S. attorney for South Dakota, speaks at a press conference on July 21, 2026, in the Rapid City federal courthouse. Standing behind him are FBI Denver Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski, left, and FBI Minneapolis Special Agent in Charge Christopher Dotson. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)RAPID CITY — A multi-agency effort to disrupt cocaine trafficking resulted in 14 total arrests of people from Colorado and the South Dakota cities of Pine Ridge, Box Elder and Rapid City, authorities announced Tuesday.
Representatives of federal, tribal, state and local agencies gathered in the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Rapid City to speak about the operation.
“Every time I see an amount of drugs seized, the only thing I can think about are the people that were not poisoned by that drug, the families that didn’t suffer because those drugs were taken off the street,” said Ron Parsons, the U.S. attorney for South Dakota.
Federal agencies and tribe partner to clear Pine Ridge Reservation’s ballistics testing backlog

The FBI spearheaded the investigation in coordination with other agencies. The operation seized 5 kilograms of cocaine intended for distribution in South Dakota, authorities said, along with 37 firearms and $61,000. The operation’s first phase happened last month in Colorado, and the latest arrests occurred Tuesday in South Dakota.
Those arrested have all been charged in federal court with conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance, and some face additional charges related to alleged financial crimes and firearms offenses.
The operation was aided by a broader FBI effort known as Operation Steadfast Promise, which launched in April to target violent crime on tribal lands. Some of the people arrested were living on the Pine Ridge Reservation in southwest South Dakota, and the Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety was part of the operation.
Parsons declined to divulge details about the origin of the seized drugs, citing the ongoing investigation, but said illegal drugs in western South Dakota typically come from South America or Mexico via Denver.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Eye-popper traffic stunt intends to draw attention to anti-child sex trafficking effort
description: OMAHA — A convoy of 30 school buses and a semi-truck disrupted traffic flow Tuesday and created a spectacle as it traveled about four miles across southwest Omaha. The highest levels of city government were aware — and in fact were part of the planning that had the parade at one point in the wrong […]
text:
A convoy of more than two dozen school buses, intended as symbols of childhood innocence, traveled about four miles across southwest Omaha to draw attention to child sex trafficking and a stepped up effort to curb the crime. (Photo courtesy of Project Harmony)OMAHA — A convoy of 30 school buses and a semi-truck disrupted traffic flow Tuesday and created a spectacle as it traveled about four miles across southwest Omaha.
The highest levels of city government were aware — and in fact were part of the planning that had the parade at one point in the wrong lane, literally moving against traffic.
The stunt led by nonprofit Project Harmony was designed to highlight a ramped-up effort against child sex trafficking in and around Nebraska’s most populous city. “Omaha Against Traffick” is a new awareness campaign aimed at helping people better identify signs and curb the crime. It is expected to bolster a $12.5 million Project Harmony-led anti-trafficking initiative involving more than 60 organizations.
The initiative, which involves agents of the Omaha Police Department and Douglas County Attorney’s Office, was founded in 2024 after Project Harmony secured buy-in from various groups that serve youth and families. Last year, the effort raised the $12.5 million, mostly from private sources but also government, said Gene Klein, chief executive of Project Harmony.
“We want to make sure the public understands when you say child sex trafficking that we all have a similar definition of what that is and that we would know what to do as a result of seeing someone or suspecting that someone might be sex trafficked,” Klein told the Nebraska Examiner.
Preparing for the convoy that will travel about four miles across Omaha, from Omaha Burke High School to Project Harmony campus in southwest Omaha. (Photo courtesy of Joshua Foo)
Angela Roeber, Project Harmony communications officer, cited results of a community assessment last year. She said the vast majority of respondents reported having heard about the issue, but “knowledge was really low” when it came to deeper questions such as what conditions put kids at greater risk of being trafficked.
She said her team does not want the campaign to be just another headline grabber. Still to come will be billboards, bus wrap ads and continued educational efforts locally and in other markets.
“We want this to be something that lives for quite a few years,” Roeber said. 
Project Harmony has served more than 90,000 youth during the past 30 years. Its campus includes police and federal investigators, Nebraska Health and Human Services Department staff and other professionals who work on child abuse cases.
Supporters drew distance between the Project Harmony initiative and, for example, media announcements that shine attention on potential human trafficking during large events such as the College World Series.
Omaha’s police officials didn’t readily have related data when participating, along with Gov. Jim Pillen, Omaha Mayor John Ewing and top Nebraska law enforcement agents, in a June pre-CWS press conference alerting the public about potential human trafficking during the annual baseball tournament. The department recently provided the information and said Omaha police did not make any human trafficking-related arrests during the most recent CWS or the previous two. 
Police spokesman Lt. Neal Bonacci said the department wants to be proactive. He said officers also are offered additional training to help better recognize signs.
Roeber said the CWS press conference looked more broadly at human trafficking whereas, she said, Project Harmony’s lens is sharply focused on youth.
Omaha police officers prepare to escort 30 school buses down the wrong lanes of traffic on 120th Street. The convoy traveled from Omaha Burke High near 120th Street and West Dodge Road to Project Harmony campus at 120th and Q Streets, marking the launch of a child sex trafficking awareness campaign. (Photo courtesy of Joshua Foo)
Klein defined child trafficking as sexual assault in exchange for something of value such as food, clothes, money or shelter.
He said Project Harmony’s efforts are rooted in a new approach its team took around 2018. He said Omaha police at the time were dealing with a few thousand reports of missing minors, many “running away from something at home or running to something that might not be safe for them.”
At the time, said Klein and Sgt. Brett Schrage of the OPD Missing Persons Unit, common practice had been finding and returning the youths, though the pattern typically continued. They said the Project Harmony team pivoted to focus on that runaway group, recognizing that many engaged in high-risk behaviors that fit the definition of sex trafficking. 
Buoyed by data from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, Roeber said the team came up with criteria that helped better  pinpoint youth most at risk for being trafficked.
Prior to 2018, Klein recalls seeing “zero” child sex trafficking investigations or charges in Omaha. Since the start of 2023, the group said that the Douglas County Attorney’s Office secured 31 convictions associated with sex trafficking. It counted 59 victims of child sex trafficking in the Omaha metro area since then.
Project Harmony said official trafficking numbers likely are undercounted.
Klein said local child trafficking cases don’t resemble TV-style episodes where a youth is abducted and taken overseas. Often they’ve run away from home and are homeless, he said, and are vulnerable to traffickers offering a place to stay and food.
“These are Omaha children that grew up in Omaha,” Klein said. “Their families are pretty fragmented. They don’t have a lot of consistency in their lives.”
 

Take action
To report abuse: 1-800-652-1999, Nebraska child abuse hotline.
For more information: OmahaAgainstTraffick.com.



Tuesday, the convoy traveled from Omaha Burke High School, near 120th Street and West Dodge Road, south to Project Harmony’s campus near 120th and Q Streets. Omaha police stopped east and westbound traffic at Q Street to allow the buses to turn, causing a bit of a traffic buildup.
Vehicles honked. People working on the initiative waved from within the buses. 
“This campaign launch is really to catch people off guard, to spark curiosity and intrigue them enough to learn more and want to be a part of creating a safe community for all of our children,” Roeber said.
The campaign includes partners such as Boys Town, which provides three beds dedicated to high-risk youth who need a safe space to stay, and Creighton University’s Community Connections program, which offers family resources.
Project Harmony said that signs to watch for in children include receiving unusual and extra attention from an adult; isolation from friends because of an adult and adult-youth relationships that reflect dishonesty, dependence and control.
Said Klein:  “In driving against traffic with a convoy of school buses — symbols of childhood innocence — we ask our neighbors to understand that child sex trafficking happens everywhere and to join us in the fight to protect our youth.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont is not in trouble. Vermonters are.
description:
Short-term rentals and wealthy newcomers are pricing out the people who built the state's communities.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont is not in trouble. Vermonters are..
text:
This commentary is by Bob Stannard, a former member of the Vermont House of Representatives who lives in Manchester.
In a recent commentary in VTDigger, the authors advocate that perhaps the only solution to Vermont’s problems is more growth, more development. They point out the obvious: Our population is decreasing, we have fewer kids in school, and we are now suffering from regulations that deter further growth. What they fail to address is the root cause of the problems that they believe growth will solve, but won’t, which is income inequality.
Let’s look at two hypothetical families. One family has lived in Vermont for many generations. They’re still living on the once-thriving family farm, but now, thanks to tax policies and subsidies that favor large agri-corporations, it is no longer viable. They have always worked for themselves and now are doing odd jobs for those who will hire them. In 1950, their farmhouse would have cost $10,000. They lived a very peaceful life, but experienced their share of stress. The weather impacted their crops. Their machinery occasionally broke. There was always something that kept them up at night. Crime was minimal because everyone knew each other in their tight-knit community. As time moved on, this family saw the value of their $10,000 farmhouse increase to $400,000 today, a price still out of reach for most Vermonters.
The other family immigrated to Brooklyn, New York, in 1950. They were able to purchase a brownstone building for the same amount, $10,000. They lived in a nice neighborhood and commuted to Manhattan, where they, their kids and grandkids were able to make a very good living. These folks faced some inconveniences like traffic, potholes and developers tearing down one neighborhood after another to make way for the next big housing project. As neighborhoods changed and crime rose, they experienced one significant benefit: an increase in the value of their real estate. A brownstone in Brooklyn currently sells for between $1 million and $5 million.

READ MORE

In recent years, we’ve witnessed an exodus of people from New York, New Jersey and Connecticut. There are multiple reasons why they may have decided to move. Overcrowding. The hassle of day-to-day city life. High crime rates. Too many homeless people. Polluted air. Perhaps it was the crashing of two planes into the World Trade Center or the pandemic that was the tipping point. Maybe it was just that they could realize a serious windfall if they sold up. 
The Brooklyn family sold their lovely brownstone for $4 million. Add that to their savings from toiling in Manhattan for years, and they could be pretty well set if they could find a reasonably priced house. 
Vermont had a lot to offer these Brooklyn folks. It’s a beautiful state covered in forests rather than asphalt and concrete. People live at a slower pace here, and the best part is that they could buy a really nice house with some land for only $750,000. They couldn’t wait to make the move and a change of lifestyle. 
There are many more people in the aforementioned states than there are in Vermont. The comparison of two families above is skewed. The competition for Vermont land and homes today is fierce. People with money move to New England and are happy to pay exorbitant prices for a place to live or to invest in homes for short-term rentals, adding additional stress to our long-term rental markets. 
Vermont has experienced past immigration. In the 1960s, young kids from down country who wanted a different life flocked to Vermont. It was known as the back-to-the-land movement. They created communes and seriously thought that all they had to do was have a nice garden, a goat or two and smoke some weed, and they could live happily ever after. They did not compete with Vermonters, but instead found ways to assimilate into the community, not try to change it. Some went on to become state senators. Vermonters accepted these kids because they worked hard, got involved with their community and did not price Vermonters out of their homeland. 
That was the Vermont that I once knew. A Vermont of strong communities, highly opinionated locals who were more than willing to share their point of view on just about anything, whether you wanted to hear it or not. It was a state where neighbors helped each other when needed. Oh, sure, there were gates, but they were to keep the cows, sheep and goats from escaping, not to keep people out. The whole point of being a Vermonter is to have a driveway that any friend can drive up for a visit unannounced. 
It’s Vermonters who are in trouble, not Vermont. Vermont will be here just like it always has been, but the people who made Vermont what it was — yeah, they’ll be gone. They’ll be driven out by those of means who can pay high prices and scoff at the cost of living. So build away. Open the floodgates and get going. Time’s a wastin’. 
Move Vermonters outta here and make way for the “New Vermont” — the one that’ll be overdeveloped and undesirable in no time.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont is not in trouble. Vermonters are..

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Workers at CT children psych facility raise concerns about safety, outcomes
description: Union leadership said 66 of the roughly 300 workers at the Solnit South facility are now recovering from injuries.
text:
Employees of the Department of Children and Families gathered in the rain Tuesday to sound the alarm about worker injuries and understaffing at the state’s psychiatric facility for children age 13 to 17. 
SEIU 1199 union leadership said 66 of the roughly 300 workers at the Solnit South facility in Middletown are not currently working while they recover from injuries tied to workers’ compensation claims.
Workers argued many injuries were “preventable” and the result of a lack of resources, funding and appropriate staffing at the facility. 
“Solnit was once recognized as one of the premier public children’s psychiatric programs in the country. It can and must be again,” said Becky Simonsen, vice president of SEIU 1199. “We have the dedicated workforce. We have the clinical expertise. So what’s missing? Investment. Resources.”
Erin Burns, a Solnit South employee, described multiple assaults she experienced there, including one that resulted in a concussion. She said all workers understand there is some risk to working in the facility but added that, “what I cannot accept is preventable danger and harm caused by ineptitude.”
“I believe these assaults were preventable and they were not simply part of doing my job,” she said. “They were the result of chronic understaffing and a lack of leadership.”
A union representative said some workers have been hit in the head with objects or hurt with makeshift weapons, while others got hurt while breaking up fights between patients. Less severe injuries often occur at the facility and don’t rise to the level of workers’ compensation, according to the union.
DCF has struggled to recruit and retain staff across the agency. 
Simonsen said the children at Solnit have serious psychiatric needs and have often survived profound abuse and trauma. In some cases, the kids have been turned away by other providers due to the complex nature of their needs. 
Workers said they do not blame the teenagers, who in some cases have pushed workers to the ground causing concussions, or have used “pieces of the building” as a weapon to cut workers. Rather, employees said they blame DCF and accused the agency of  not adequately staffing the facility and creating an unsafe environment. According to Simonsen, some employees are being asked to work 16 hours every time they show up for an 8-hour shift.
“When there aren’t enough staff, children don’t receive the intensive therapy they need. Group treatment doesn’t happen. Recreation disappears. Other educational and therapeutic programming is reduced,” she said. “Our members who came here to help children heal spend their shifts simply trying to keep everyone safe.” 
Simonsen argued Gov. Ned Lamont has prioritized the state’s fiscal guardrails — budget controls used to govern how spending is appropriated — over the safety of children and the workers who care for them. 
“We are here today to say loud and clear that these children deserve a safety net that meets their needs. Because a safety net is only a safety net if it is there when a child falls,” Simonsen said. 
Simonsen said she has spoken to DCF Commissioner Susan Hamilton and was told that while there is a desire to make improvements, the scope of the issue requires a significant change to the agency’s budget.
Hamilton and Dr. Andrew Agwunobi, who is the CEO and executive vice president for health affairs for UConn Health, affirmed the critical role that Solnit plays in the community in a statement and said that, “our priority is delivering high-quality care for patients while ensuring the safety of staff.”
UConn Health recently took over the facility but Darnell Ford, the children’s services unit supervisor, said that there hasn’t yet been a noticeable change in funding or management — just the facility’s signage. 
Meeting the needs of the children in the facility depends on support from lawmakers “to actually have the true investment that has been awaited for far too long,” Ford said.
In their statement, Agwunobi and Hamilton listed actions that they said reflect the commitment to addressing workforce, safety and operational concerns, including increasing the pace of hiring, contracting security guards for staff safety and formalizing staff to patient ratios.
They also said that they are bringing on a full time independent monitor to evaluate operations and compliance.
Many speakers on Tuesday took time to express their optimism about the facility and services it has the capacity to provide when staffing needs are met. 
“There’s a lot to be preserved about this place. I think it’s built on decades of expertise, experience, resources,” said Dr. Akashdeep Aujla, the principal psychiatrist for Solnit South, but he added that those have been on the decline over the past decade. Many times, Aujla said his patients are ready to discharge but don’t have a place to go because of the decline in public-private partnerships with service providers and the lack of foster homes available.
Two former patients also spoke of the positive experiences they’d had at Solnit, with one saying that activities like photography, swimming and dialectical behavioral therapy  gave her skills that helped in her “healing journey.”
According to the union, activities are sometimes left by the wayside when staffing levels are low. “Because of the short staffing, there’s been reduced programming. Reduced programming and structure creates an environment where more injuries are happening,” said Simonsen.
Employees said the lack of staffing has also made it more difficult for the facility to differentiate between kids who have different needs based on their diagnosis and treatment journey, so they are often “lumped together.”

name: National
title: Citing fraud, feds halt more than $1B in Medicaid money for California, Minnesota
description: The Trump administration announced Tuesday that it is freezing more than $1 billion in Medicaid payments to California and Minnesota in an effort to crack down on fraud. Medicaid is the public health insurance for people with low incomes, including some disabled and elderly people, jointly funded by state and federal dollars. The U.S. Department […]
text:
Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, speaks at the Department of Health and Human Services in Washington, D.C., in December. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced Tuesday that they are freezing more than $1 billion in Medicaid payments to California and Minnesota in an effort to crack down on fraud. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)The Trump administration announced Tuesday that it is freezing more than $1 billion in Medicaid payments to California and Minnesota in an effort to crack down on fraud.
Medicaid is the public health insurance for people with low incomes, including some disabled and elderly people, jointly funded by state and federal dollars.
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services deferred more than $867 million to California and $199 million to Minnesota. The feds say they need more documentation from those states to support some Medicaid claims for services that are at high risk for fraud.
The freeze marks the latest round of withheld payments as the Trump administration continues its crackdown on suspected fraud in publicly-funded social service programs, mostly focusing on Democratic-led states. Earlier this year, the Trump administration launched a fraud task force to look into potential waste or abuse in publicly-funded benefits programs, explicitly naming states such as California, Colorado, Illinois, Maine, Minnesota and New York.
The Trump administration has already deferred Medicaid payments in Minnesota twice this year, totaling nearly $400 million. The deferral process, under which the federal government can withhold funding when questioning claims already billed to Medicaid, had never been used to deny funding for entire service areas until a $243 million deferral in February, the Minnesota Attorney General noted.
A letter delivered Tuesday from CMS to the Minnesota Department of Human Services stated that $195 million of the deferred $199 million comes from specific providers that CMS identified as high-risk for fraud or “aberrant billing practices” based on historical billing and analysis. The money comes from services delivered from January through March and has already been paid. States will have to provide documentation backing up the claims or be forced to reduce future billing to the federal government.
The Trump administration has also threatened to withhold $2 billion in annual Medicaid funding to Minnesota in a separate process. The funding fight in Minnesota centers on 14 Medicaid services deemed high-risk to fraud and are largely designed to give long-term care for elderly and disabled people. But state officials have said that funding freezes could deliver a serious blow to the state’s Medicaid program more generally, which cost $18 billion in 2024 and covers other low-income Minnesotans.
John Connolly, temporary commissioner and state Medicaid director for the Minnesota Department of Human Services, said in a statement that Tuesday’s deferral reflects the federal government’s “unprecedented and punitive ways as part of their war on Medicaid and its recipients.”
“CMS touts their new fraud-detection capabilities, yet has not provided data or explanation on how the deferral amount was calculated or what it was based on. I respectfully ask the federal government to partner with us and share any information about their methods to identify potentially fraudulent providers in Minnesota,” Connolly said.
The federal-state fight over Medicaid funding has affected thousands of Medicaid providers in Minnesota, who were abruptly cut off from funding as the state raced to reach a federal deadline to screen all providers in the “high-risk” services. Providers and their advocates said the process was rushed and left legitimate providers unable to get paid for delivering services to vulnerable Minnesotans.
HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said the Trump administration’s goal is to strengthen the integrity of the Medicaid program and make sure federal funds are spent appropriately.
“States that receive federal Medicaid funding must demonstrate that every dollar meets federal requirements,” Kennedy said in a news release on the deferred funds. “When they cannot, we will not release federal funds until they do.”
California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, called the withheld funds a “recycled political stunt” in a post on X, and said his state was being targeted for political reasons.
Minnesota Democratic Gov. Tim Walz rejected the Trump administration’s framing of the situation in a post on X: “This isn’t about fraud — it’s about cutting your healthcare so that Trump can afford the tax cuts he gave to billionaires.”
CMS said it identified unusually high growth in spending on certain in-home care programs in California, triggering the hold on that state’s funds. It has not provided proof of fraud.
Newsom countered in his X post, arguing that California is saving taxpayer money “by keeping seniors and people with disabilities out of far more expensive nursing homes.”
In Minnesota, a CMS review flagged expenditures that raised “potential eligibility or billing concerns.”
“CMS is done trying to chase down stolen and misused funds after they’ve already left the building,” Dr. Mehmet Oz, CMS administrator, said in a news release, adding that the deferred payments are part of a “proactive new approach to program integrity.”
The pauses in funding don’t affect who is eligible for Medicaid, and they’re not permanent cuts.
Alyssa Chen of the Minnesota Reformer contributed to this story. Stateline reporter Anna Claire Vollers can be reached at avollers@stateline.org.
