name: Nevada Current
title: Clark County, nonprofits launch effort to ease conversion to solar
description: Clark County’s Department of Environment and Sustainability launched a new program to help residents go solar. Through a partnership with nonprofits Switch Together and Solar United Neighbors, residents will be able to compare “no-obligation, competitive pricing on rooftop solar, battery storage, and electric vehicle (EV) charging.”  The partnership emerged[...]
text:
The program is designed to help homeowners and small businesses access discounted rates through group buying to install solar panels. (Photo by Jerod MacDonald-Evoy/Arizona Mirror)Clark County’s Department of Environment and Sustainability launched a new program to help residents go solar. Through a partnership with nonprofits Switch Together and Solar United Neighbors, residents will be able to compare “no-obligation, competitive pricing on rooftop solar, battery storage, and electric vehicle (EV) charging.” 
The partnership emerged from Clark County’s All-In Clark County climate and sustainability initiative, created to address the impacts of climate change in Southern Nevada.  
The program, primarily administered by Switch Together, helps homeowners and small businesses access discounted rates through group buying to install solar panels. 
Nevada has long been among the nation’s leaders in solar power adoption, but  community solar installations declined significantly in the state last year. In Nevada, the Trump administration froze $156 million in grant funding under the Solar for All program which would have financed community solar projects that would benefit low-income households.
Switch Together is an organization that provides homeowners with low-cost solar power. Registration is free, and Switch Together conducts a reverse auction to secure low costs and connect customers with the qualified installer who won the bid. Homeowners will then have over a month to decide whether to accept the offer from the installer and set a date for installation. 
Nevada is the eighth state where a local government is partnering with Switch Together. 
“Switch Together advances the goals of All-In Clark County by helping residents make informed choices and take practical steps toward a more sustainable and resilient Southern Nevada,” Clark County climate and sustainability program manager Robert Burgy said in a press release. 
Nevada Program Director at Solar United Neighbors Julia Hubbard described  the nonprofit’s collaboration with Clark County and Switch Together as an “opportunity for residents to receive an average of a 20% discount, which comes out to be about $6,500.”  
“Any kind of discount on a solar system is going to make things more affordable and really make the difference in terms of someone crunching the numbers to see if this does make sense for their household,” Hubbard said. 
Hubbard also said NV Energy is “targeting solar owners” with its peak demand charge billing method scheduled to take effect January 1. NV Energy has said the new billing procedure is intended to offset what the utility contends is a $50 million annual subsidy paid by full-service customers on behalf of rooftop solar users.
Hubbard noted installation costs have always caused hesitation in residents considering switching to solar. 
“We work in Nevada as well as across the nation to help people go solar, join together, and fight for their energy rights,” Hubbard said. “And really at the heart of that has been consumer protection and education.” 
In addition to the launch of the new program. Solar United Neighbors of Nevada will hold an event at West Las Vegas Library on July 23 to inform residents about solar power, battery storage, and bulk buying. 
“The July 23 event is like a deep dive into the technology and economics of going solar, but it also is going to preview what to expect in the Switch Together program,” Hubbard said. “One thing to know is people can sign up for this program right now, and then get an estimate.” 
Hubbard explained that once met with an estimate, homeowners can choose to move forward with a refundable $150 deposit and meet an installer. After they meet with the installer, residents have over a month to decide whether to sign the contract. Payment plans will also be discussed during the meeting, she said. 
“The idea behind the event is trying to give folks as much information up front as possible so they can make the best decision for their household,” Hubbard said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Mental illness, substance abuse driving New Mexico’s high maternal mortality, new data shows
description: Mental illness, including drug abuse, accounted for nearly 42% of the deaths of 74 mothers between 2018 and 2023, according to new data.
text:
Mental illness, including drug addiction, was the underlying cause of more than 40% of 74 pregnancy-related deaths of New Mexico mothers between 2018 and 2023, according to new data state health department officials presented to state lawmakers on July 20, 2026. (Getty Images)Mental illness, particularly substance abuse, was the biggest contributing factor to 74 pregnancy-related deaths of New Mexico mothers between 2018 and 2023, according to new data presented Monday to a legislative health committee.
New Mexico Department of Health officials presented the most recent figures from the department’s Maternal Mortality Review Committee, a board tasked with investigating all deaths that occur during or within one year of pregnancy and recommending measures to prevent such deaths in the future. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, New Mexico’s maternal mortality rate is well above the national average. Still, the new data shows that New Mexico’s pregnancy-related mortality rate has dropped precipitously since the COVID-19 pandemic.
In 2021, the state’s pregnancy related-mortality rate — was 149.6 per 100,000 live births. By 2023, however, the rate decreased by nearly 84% to just 24.2, according to the new data. 
The rate the New Mexico Mortality Review Committee measures is the number of people who die due to pregnancy complications or from health conditions a pregnancy exacerbated. 
The decline brought levels back to pre-pandemic rates. Nonetheless, the review committee noted that more than 97% of the 74 deaths in that six-year period were “preventable.”
The report identifies mental illness as the biggest factor underlying those deaths, a term that includes includes suicide, substance abuse and post-traumatic stress disorder, among other psychiatric illnesses. 
Mental illness accounted for nearly 42% of the deaths, followed by infections at roughly 16% and heart-related illnesses and hemorrhages or other injuries that each caused approximately 10% of the deaths. 
“Mental health conditions, especially substance use disorders, remain the most significant contributing factor to maternal mortality and the most common underlying cause of death,” NMDOH Chief Medical Officer Miranda Durham told lawmakers.
The review committee also determined that more than three-quarters of the patients who died in that period had no prenatal care or unknown prenatal care, according to the new data. Kevin Peine, executive director at the NMDOH’s Centers for Public Health, noted that the rate of deaths drops sharply even if patients receive prenatal care only in their first trimester. 
“This drives home the point to me that access to prenatal care in the state is critical, and early prenatal care can be a driving factor towards some of those preventions,” he said.
New Mexico Supreme Court tosses challenge to removal policy for drug-exposed newborns

Several Democratic lawmakers on the interim Health and Human Services Committee keyed in on the findings regarding lack of prenatal care and substance abuse to criticize Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham’s 2025 order requiring state officials to take immediate custody of newborns with fetal alcohol syndrome or drug exposure.
Committee Chair Rep. Liz Thomson (D-Albuquerque) said she fears that mothers with drug addictions will opt out of prenatal care to avoid losing custody of their babies. 
“That’s really scary to me, and something I think that we need to keep a close eye on,” she said. 
State Sen. Linda Lopez (D-Albuquerque) also said the report shows the state’s resources would be better placed supporting mothers and babies exposed to drugs, rather than separating them. The report recommended expanding post-birth support, conducting additional screenings and expanding services to high-risk families in the period right before and right after birth.
“Separating a newborn from a new mom is trauma in itself,” Lopez said. “If we’re willing to separate and take away, then what is the state not doing to assist and help these new moms?”
Michael Coleman, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham’s communications director, did not respond to Source NM’s request for comment Monday, though he recently told Source NM that the governor stands behind the directive. 
“The governor believes safety is the top priority — and that means giving parents the space they need to recover, while making sure no baby is left in a home where exposure puts them at risk,” he said.

name: Nevada Current
title: As Jewish Nevadans, Tisha B’Av calls us to remember. Recent events call us to act.
description: Joan Sebastian Guerrero, a 26-year-old father, husband, and delivery driver from Colombia was recently shot and killed by an ICE agent while driving his car in Maine.  A local witness to the murder, Mary Hayes, told The New York Times that she saw a woman and a little girl kneeling beside Guerrero’s bullet-punctured corpse. That […]
text:
People pay respects on Wednesday, July 15, 2026, at a memorial for Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero. The 25-year-old was fatally shot by ICE agents on Monday in Biddeford, Maine. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)Joan Sebastian Guerrero, a 26-year-old father, husband, and delivery driver from Colombia was recently shot and killed by an ICE agent while driving his car in Maine.
 A local witness to the murder, Mary Hayes, told The New York Times that she saw a woman and a little girl kneeling beside Guerrero’s bullet-punctured corpse. That girl was Guerrero’s three-year-old daughter. She was wearing her Bluey pajamas and clutched the handle of a pink backpack on wheels. The girl watched her father’s body get pulled from the car by ICE agents, handcuffed, and dumped on the street. Guerrero’s corpse was left there for five hours.
“I heard agony,” Hayes told the Times. “I heard a howl that came from your soul, that your whole life had just changed and it was never going to be the same.”
We are writing this as Jewish Nevadans who work on migration issues from different perspectives. We are a political philosophy professor and an immigration law professor, respectively. As the sun sets on Wednesday, July 22nd, Jewish communities across the globe will begin to observe Tisha B’Av, the saddest day on the Jewish calendar. On this day, Jews traditionally mourn a long history of injustices experienced by the Jewish people throughout history.
We are writing this piece because Guerrero’s murder reminds us how Tisha B’Av is also a “howl from the soul.” One of us has had the privilege to visit the village where his family came from in Eastern Poland, and from which relatives were taken to be shot in the forest during the Nazi occupation. He is the descendent of those members of his family who were able to migrate before the rise of fascism. Migration is why we survived.
These memories call us to action today. As we mourn the long history of Jewish forced migrations and persecution, we will mourn Guerrero’s death and the countless other migration injustices endured by so many Nevadans and people across the U.S. An attack on the rights, dignity, and the lives of immigrants is an attack on us all.
Tisha B’Av, and Jewish ethics more broadly, compel us to defiantly remember injustice. As philosopher Allison Wolf explains, “Jewish ethics … centers history,” and “a foundational part of Jewish ethics is the obligation to remember … or ‘not to forget’.” Wolf argues that ”living a just life requires remembering tragic histories so they do not repeat themselves—not only against one’s own group but against other communities.”
Tisha B’Av underscores how remembering injustice is, in fact, very hard work. On this day many Jews fast from sundown to sundown. Synagogues will hold special services during which Jews will chant sorrowfully by dim candlelight. In our era of endless doom scrolling, rapid, flashy news cycles, and increasingly limited attention spans, Tisha B’Av encourages us to carve out time and space to actively mourn.
In particular, on Tisha B’Av Jews read passages like this from Lamentations: a text attributed to the prophet Jeremiah, who witnessed corruption and persecution preceding the Babylonian Siege of Jerusalem:
           …we have become orphans, fatherless;
           Our mothers are like widows …
           We are hotly pursued;
           Exhausted, we are given no rest.
These ancient words describe the current situation of many of our neighbors in Las Vegas. Every day in Nevada, around 600 people are forced to go to sleep in ICE detention centers, locked away from their families. Most of them are Latino men. Men are tracked from their homes, arrested on their way to work. Everyday, here and across this country, families must worry whether a father who leaves to earn a living will return. Our neighbors are hotly pursued. There are empty seats at family tables in our community because people have been taken away by the federal government. And that is not the worst case scenario. A child who merely gets in the car with her father now risks seeing him shot by the government. Our neighbors are given no rest.
 We can no longer assume that the government of the United States, our government, will follow the law. A federal judge in Nevada recently stated that in its zeal to arrest and detain, ICE is in “open defiance” of judicial orders and “rebelling against the basic principle underlying our constitutional order.”
When someone has died, it is tradition for Jews to say, “May his memory be a blessing.” Usually this is a reminder to treasure the joy the deceased brought us during their life. But blessings come in many forms. In Biddeford, Maine, Joan Sebastian Guerrero’s neighbors marched in the main street of the town nearly immediately after the government killed him. They howled from their souls. They definitely turned memory into action, and that action is also a blessing. When one of their neighbors howled in agony, they howled back in protest.
This week, we grapple with persecution in our country while remembering the suffering of our ancestors. May their memories be both a blessing, and a call to action for the living. May we all howl for our neighbors. And may all of us, wherever we come from, be allowed to rest.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: More use home colon cancer tests, but skip crucial annual follow-up, Rutgers study says
description: A Rutgers University study found about half of those who use home-based colon cancer tests fail to retest annually, increasing their risk for undiagnosed cancers.
text:
A Rutgers University study found about half of those who use home-based colon cancer tests fail to retest annually, increasing their risk for undiagnosed cancers. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Home tests for colorectal cancer are increasingly popular, but about half of those who use them fail to follow up as recommended with annual rescreenings, according to a new Rutgers University study.
Dr. Ethan Halm, the lead author of the study published in June, examined a decades’ worth of data from nearly 500,000 patients ages 50 to 65 who used a fecal immunochemical test, or FIT test, to screen for colon cancer at home starting in 2010 or 2011.
Halm found 54% of these patients repeated the at-home screenings in future years; 30% did so inconsistently; and 16% failed to perform a second test. All the patients were part of large healthcare systems in California or Texas that offered tests for free, but Halm found that people in a system that proactively mailed home-screening kits to patients who were overdue for retesting were most likely to repeat annual screenings.
“It’s really about making them broadly available,” Halm, a vice chancellor for population health, told the New Jersey Monitor.
Halm’s study also found that patients who repeated home-based tests were more likely to identify early-stage cancers, which are highly treatable, than those who failed to retest. Those who tested less often, or never did, were more likely to find advanced colorectal cancer, which is far more deadly.
Colorectal cancer is among the most common forms of cancer diagnosed and a leading cause of cancer death, especially among men. Nearly 56,000 people die nationwide from colon cancer, including 1,400 in New Jersey, and mortality rates are highest among Black residents.
Colon cancer death rates have declined nationwide and in New Jersey as screening for the disease has increased. By 2024, more than 77% of residents age 50-75 years were testing for colorectal cancer, according to state data.
Home-based FIT tests are the least expensive and easiest option for most patients, Halm said. The study did not include more recent home-based testing options like Cologuard, which cost hundreds of dollars.
The third and most conclusive option is a colonoscopy, an outpatient procedure that involves several days of preparation and anesthesia. The high cost, a limited number of available clinicians, and many patients’ aversion to this test make it a hard sell for doctors, Halm said.
“There are a lot of people who are squeamish about a colonoscopy. The best test is the test that gets done,” he said, noting that insurance covers all options in New Jersey.

title: Almost 5 years after a Utah college student’s suicide, her boyfriend heads to prison
description: After the death of their daughter, Rose and Keith Nguyen urged authorities to take the unusual step of prosecuting her boyfriend.
text:
Rose and Keith Nguyen pose with a portrait of their daughter, Rena Nguyen, at the offices of the Utah State Bar in Salt Lake City on Friday, July 17, 2026. (Annie Knox/Utah News Dispatch)If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988. There is also an online chat at 988lifeline.org.
For more than two years after their 20-year-old daughter Rena died, Rose and Keith Nguyen urged authorities in Utah County to prosecute her boyfriend.


 Domestic violence resources

Help for people in abusive relationships is available in Utah:

Utah Domestic Violence Coalition: A confidential statewide, 24-hour domestic violence hotline can be reached at 1-800-897-LINK (5465)
YWCA Women in Jeopardy program: 801-537-8600
Utah child abuse and neglect hotline: 1-855-323-DCFS (3237)
National Domestic Violence Hotline: 1-800-799-7233



They wanted recognition from the criminal justice system that their daughter took her own life only after Caleb Aidan Rees, knowing she was in crisis, yelled at her as she cried and left a loaded handgun in a room with her, then walked away.
The Nguyens hired attorneys and brought on an expert to help make their case for taking the rare step of holding someone else accountable for a suicide, saying their daughter, a Brigham Young University student from northern California, was a victim of domestic abuse. 
Almost four years later, Rees pleaded guilty to a third-degree felony count of manslaughter in April, along with other drug and weapons charges. And on Friday, in an emotional court hearing, a judge in Provo’s 4th District Court ordered him to serve up to 20 years in prison. 
Rena Nguyen’s parents say they want the outcome to deter others who would do the same to a romantic partner. They also hope other authorities in Utah and beyond will take a fresh look at similar cases already closed without any criminal charges being filed. 
“I believe we must do more than just teach victims to escape abuse,” Keith Nguyen told the judge on Friday. “We must use every tool under the law to deter anyone who even considers harming another person.” 
The Nguyens’ attorney, Richard Lambert, said it’s the first case he knows of in the United States “in which a domestic abuser has driven someone to take their own life, has been held accountable for that action.”
He sees parallels to a case in Scotland where a man is serving eight years in prison after prosecutors argued his wife’s suicide followed physical and emotional abuse in their 18-month marriage. 
In court, prosecutors played part of a phone recording Rena Nguyen had secretly taken in Orem in October 2021 that captured her interactions with Rees in the hours leading up to her death.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Judge Sean Petersen called the recording “nothing short of horrific” on Friday before ordering Rees to four consecutive terms of up to five years in prison. 
“It is not normal or accepted behavior — the repeated threats, demeaning statements, and the ridicule, Mr. Rees, that you heaped upon Rena,” the judge said. He went on to say that “it gives me a lot of pause about your future relationships and the safety of the public.” 
Prosecutors had alleged in charging documents that Rees had known that his girlfriend had held a loaded gun to her head “mere hours before the shooting” and that she’d texted a friend, saying “I can’t keep doing this. I want to live but not like this.”  
When Orem police called to check on her, the charging documents said, Rees told her if the police showed up he’d “spray them” and kill himself, and yelled at her as she sobbed. 
Rose Nguyen told the judge that what happened that night wasn’t a moment of poor judgment but a pattern of cruelty from Rees. Earlier in their relationship, she said, her daughter endured emotional abuse, physical harm, and sexual violence under the threat of a firearm.
But Rees’ attorney Evan Muir rejected that there was a pattern of abuse before that day, saying, “my client never hit her, he didn’t do anything — he never committed a battery upon her.”
Caleb Rees, charged with manslaughter in Rena Nguyen’s death in October 2021, appears during a sentencing in Fourth District Court in Provo on Friday, July 17, 2026. (Pool photo by Francisco Kjolseth/The Salt Lake Tribune)
Addressing the judge, Rees, 31, said he hadn’t wanted her to harm herself that night and said he’s not the same person he was then. 
“The regret, shame, remorse, and loss of that day is something that will never leave my mind,” Rees said. 
The Nguyens detailed her prior calls and interactions with Orem police in a lawsuit they filed against the department — claims that were dismissed after the department argued in court filings that Utah’s governmental immunity law precludes them from culpability.
Rena Nguyen was studying biology at BYU, had graduated at the top of her high school class and wanted to be a radiologist, her mother said Friday at a news conference. 
“That’s not just a loss for the community,” Rose Nguyen said, “but a loss for us and for those that she could help.”
Rose Nguyen concludes her remarks before Judge Sean M. Petersen in the sentencing hearing for Caleb Rees, charged with manslaughter in her daughter Rena Nguyen’s death in October 2021, in Fourth District Court in Provo on Friday, July 17, 2026. (Pool photo by Francisco Kjolseth/The Salt Lake Tribune)

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Neighbors, environmental groups oppose hog confinement planned near scenic Niobrara River
description: Concerns are growing about a 5,000-head hog confinement barn being planned near Valentine, 2.7 miles from the scenic Niobrara River, one of Nebraska’s  top tourist destinations. Critics say the area’s sandy soils and shallow groundwater make it highly susceptible to contamination from hog manure leaching into groundwater or washing into the river, threatenin[...]
text:
Paddlers on Nebraska's Niobrara River. Concerns are growing about a hog operation planned near one of Nebraska's most scenic tourist destinations. (Photo courtesy of Niobrara Council)Concerns are growing about a 5,000-head hog confinement barn being planned near Valentine, 2.7 miles from the scenic Niobrara River, one of Nebraska’s  top tourist destinations.
Critics say the area’s sandy soils and shallow groundwater make it highly susceptible to contamination from hog manure leaching into groundwater or washing into the river, threatening float trips for the 60,000 paddlers who visit the Niobrara each year.
 “We don’t really think it’s going to be possible to build enough safeguards to assure that it will be run safely,” said Sandy Benson, the president of Friends of the Niobrara. “Those Sandhill soils are so different than other parts of the state.”
But the head of the family planning the hog site maintains that complaints are unfounded, and that the design of the facility – capturing manure in a deep pit and piping it to nearby farm fields – will eliminate any issues with odors or leaks.
“It’s all hearsay,” said Tim Marlatt, whose family operation, TK Angus, has raised cattle on the proposed site for 13 years. 
Marlatt said that he is hoping to expand into hog production to keep his family in farming, and to utilize the manure as natural fertilizer on his fields of corn and alfalfa. 
“It’s a way to generate more income with the same acres, and keep more people still in production agriculture,” Marlatt said. 
The planned hog site, southeast of Valentine and adjacent to the Fort Niobrara National Wildlife Refuge, was first proposed 2 ½ years ago. It has stirred controversy since.
But the project now is at its final step of approval – a review by the Nebraska Department of Water, Energy and Environment . That agency has said it intends to approve the project, though is reserving a final decision until reviewing written comments.
Those written comments are due by July 31, and those concerned that a hog confinement operation isn’t safe in the Sandhills are urging others to submit comments. 
“Everybody’s voice matters,” said Sunny Elliott of Valentine, a science teacher who has put up a website, “Protect Cherry County,” about the project. “This is our absolutely last hope.”
As of Monday, five letters have been submitted to the state, all in opposition.
Cherry County is known as “God’s Own Cow Country,” where cowboys on horseback herd cattle to new pastures. Its rolling, grass-covered Sandhills and wet meadows nurture the nation’s largest beef cattle herd, estimated at 165,000 head last year.
But in recent years at least a couple hog sites have begun to be built in the vast county, which – at over 6,000 square miles – is larger than some entire U.S. states, including Connecticut, Delaware and Rhode Island.
The Marlatts’ operation includes three, center-pivot irrigation systems.
Tim Marlatt said that new land is hard to come by, so to increase the profits from their existing property – and to provide a future living for a son and grandchildren – the hog confinement, holding 5,000 hogs weighing 55 pounds or larger, was planned.
He said that because the hog manure will be confined in a pit and then injected into the soil, the chances of odor problems are “slim to none.”
The organic, hog waste, Marlatt maintains, is better for the environment than commercial fertilizer because it will “bind” with the soil, thus retarding any leaching into groundwater.
“We are regulated to apply hog manure. We have zero restrictions on chemical fertilizer,” he said.
But critics of the project question whether there is adequate monitoring of groundwater to detect any leaks and whether steps will be taken to prevent runoff from fields to reach the Niobrara.
In written comments to the Department of Water, Energy and Environment , Casey King said that several nearby homes rely on private wells for their drinking water, and there would be no warning if groundwater became contaminated.
“The proposed confinement is simply too close to existing homes and to the Niobrara River, one of Nebraska’s most valuable natural resources,” King wrote.
The project got an initial OK from the Cherry County Planning Commission but then was rejected by the three-member Cherry County Board.
That generated a lawsuit by the Marlatts and TK Angus.
A year ago, Cherry County District Judge Mark Kozicek overruled the County Board, stating that the county had failed to provide testimony from “one neighboring property owner, user of the river, member of a chamber of commerce or tourist board” about perceived adverse impacts of the hog confinement.
Cherry County was ordered to approve a conditional use permit for TK Angus, and the project proceeded to a final review by the Water, Energy and Environment department .
Tim Marlatt said the family’s hog confinement proposal would not have advanced this far if it wasn’t being built within state environmental standards. Such facilities help the county’s tax base, he added, and keep families on farms.
But critics like Friends of the Niobrara and the Sierra Club disagree, and question if such operations are appropriate in an area of sandy soils that overlie the Ogallala Aquifer. Groundwater is 10 feet or less from the surface, they said.
“The proposed site’s highly permeable soils, shallow groundwater, and direct hydrological connection to the Niobrara River make contamination likely and irreversible,” stated the Friends of the Niobrara in its submission to the Department of Water, Energy and Environment.



Public comment period
Written comments on the project should be sent by July 31 to the Nebraska Department of Water, Energy and Environment, 245 Fallbrook Blvd., Lincoln, NE 68521. 
The application and related materials are available for review at the department’s Lincoln office or by accessing the department’s website, https://dwee.nebraska.gov/, and referring to “public records search” section. The facility ID number is 124885.
Comments should address issues within the department’s authority under the Livestock Waste Management Act.

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA ordered to pay $118M in teacher pension skimming case; state appeals
description: A Washington judge has ordered the state to pay roughly $120 million to thousands of public school teachers for withholding interest on pension contributions they made more than two decades ago. But those more than 26,000 teachers will need to wait for payments, as the state is now appealing the decision. Washington’s Department of Retirement […]
text:
(Photo by HT Ganzo/Getty Images)A Washington judge has ordered the state to pay roughly $120 million to thousands of public school teachers for withholding interest on pension contributions they made more than two decades ago.
But those more than 26,000 teachers will need to wait for payments, as the state is now appealing the decision. Washington’s Department of Retirement Systems concedes it’s liable in some form, but disagrees on the magnitude of the penalty. The agency declined to comment as the litigation remains pending.
The case stretches back to the mid-1990s when most teachers’ transferred their retirement funds to the state’s Teachers Retirement System, or TRS, Plan 3.
For many years, interest didn’t accrue on contributions in the quarter they were deposited. This became clear when the pensions transferred.
“Unbeknownst to anyone, their computer program was only doing the interest based on the ending balance of the last quarter, so you lose out on all of your interest every quarter you made a deposit,” said Alex Strong, attorney for the plaintiffs who has been working on the case for the past 11 years. 
And at the time of the transition, the Department of Retirement Systems did not credit the workers’ interest on their pension contributions for at least a quarter, according to court filings. 
For example, plaintiffs in this case transferred their state-managed retirement accounts from TRS Plan 2 to Plan 3 in 1996, according to court documents. Because they transferred mid-quarter, they had a zero balance in their Plan 2 accounts at the end of that quarter. So the state didn’t credit their accounts for the interest earned that quarter or the one before. 
This interest was supposed to be paid at an annual rate of 5.5%, compounding quarterly. 
The uncredited interest earnings amounted to around $13 million at the time of the transfer. 
But that disputed sum has been earning interest since, as the current and former teachers haven’t had access to the money. Factoring in that compounding interest, Thurston County Superior Court Judge Christine Schaller ruled last month that the state owed the teachers $118 million — an amount that could grow further as the case drags on.
The lawsuit has already been before state and federal appeals courts over various issues several times. In 2018, the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled the state owed teachers the interest “skimmed from their retirement accounts.” 
Given that ruling eight years ago, Strong has been “baffled” the state hasn’t rectified this sooner.
“The teachers are excited to finally get the money that belongs to them, hopefully it happens sooner rather than later,” Strong said. “We’re glad that even after 20 years of litigation that the teachers’ constitutional rights are being vindicated, they’re going to get their property returned to them, and we really do hope that we can finally bring this case to a resolution here.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Over the years, the original $13 million has been withheld and has accrued interest in the state’s commingled trust fund of retirement accounts for many public employees. That money is invested by the Washington State Investment Board and has grown 8.65% per year on average.
The same thing happened to state and local public employees in the Public Employees’ Retirement System plan, but the state long ago settled litigation for some of those workers.
By now, roughly 61% of the teachers covered in the current litigation have retired, Strong said. 
“They really should have been figuring out how to fix the error, rather than hiring outside counsel and spending lots of money to try to keep money that didn’t belong to the Department of Retirement Systems,” he said. “It’s past time for them to return the money that belongs to the teachers and get this case over with.”
A spokesperson for the Department of Retirement Systems noted the ruling, if upheld, wouldn’t affect the health of Washington’s well-funded public retiree pension system.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi Today and Deep South Today launch ‘Black Box,’ a podcast examining opioid settlement spending
description: "Black Box," a new podcast hosted by Mississippi Today Mental Health Reporter Allen Siegler, follows Mississippi's opioid settlement and examines how more than $400 million intended to address addiction, treatment and recovery is being spent.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Mississippi Today and Deep South Today announce the launch of “Black Box,” a new investigative podcast that takes listeners inside one of the most consequential public health and government accountability stories unfolding in Mississippi.
Hosted by Mississippi Today Mental Health Reporter Allen Siegler, “Black Box” follows the money behind Mississippi’s opioid settlement and examines how more than $400 million intended to address addiction, treatment and recovery is being spent across the state. 
The five-part narrative series combines original reporting, on-the-ground storytelling and exclusive interviews with public officials, advocates, families and people directly impacted by the opioid crisis.
The first two episodes launch Tuesday, with the final three episodes launching in coming weeks.
“As states across the country proudly announced using millions of opioid settlement dollars to address addiction, few knew how Mississippi was managing its money,” Siegler said. “This series traces what’s happened since the state received its first settlement check, where the money might go next and what the victims of Mississippi’s opioid epidemic think of these decisions.”
After decades of lawsuits against pharmaceutical companies accused of fueling the opioid epidemic, states began receiving billions of dollars in settlement. Mississippi is expected to receive more than $400 million. The series investigates what happens after the money arrives, examining decisions made by lawmakers, local governments and public agencies tasked with determining how the money is  spent.
Throughout the series, listeners will travel across Mississippi to hear from families affected by addiction, public health experts, recovery advocates and policymakers while exploring questions of transparency, accountability and public trust. Episodes investigate how local governments have spent settlement dollars, whether spending decisions align with public health recommendations and how political decisions may shape the future of addiction treatment and prevention.
“Black Box” is the first major narrative podcast released under the Deep South Today banner, showcasing the organization’s commitment to ambitious, multimedia journalism that serves communities across the South. The project is a collaboration among Mississippi Today, Deep South Today and the award-winning audio production company, Goat Rodeo.
“At Deep South Today, we believe some stories deserve more than a headline,” said Emily Wagster Pettus, Editor in Chief of Mississippi Today. “This investigation combines rigorous accountability reporting with powerful storytelling to help listeners understand not only how public dollars are being spent, but what is at stake for Mississippi communities.”
Mississippi Today has reported extensively on opioid settlement spending since 2023, uncovering how state and local governments have approached one of the largest public health funding opportunities in state history. “Black Box” expands that award-winning reporting into an immersive audio experience designed to bring listeners closer to the people, decisions and consequences behind the story.
Listeners can subscribe on all major podcast platforms.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Uncertain congressional map hangs over Missouri’s crowded 5th District GOP primary
description: The Republican nomination in Missouri’s 5th Congressional District could, in the weeks after the Aug. 4 primary, become a prize not worth having. Six candidates are competing for the nomination in a district Republican lawmakers redrew last year at President Donald Trump’s urging to give their party an advantage over incumbent Democratic U.S. Rep. Emanuel […[...]
text:
The candidates for the Republican nomination in Missouri's 5th Congressional District are, from left, Micah Beebe, Brett Hueffmeier, Taylor Burks, Rick Brattin and Brad Patty (Compiled from submitted and staff photos).The Republican nomination in Missouri’s 5th Congressional District could, in the weeks after the Aug. 4 primary, become a prize not worth having.
Six candidates are competing for the nomination in a district Republican lawmakers redrew last year at President Donald Trump’s urging to give their party an advantage over incumbent Democratic U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.
But Secretary of State Denny Hoskins is expected to decide on primary day whether a referendum petition challenging the map has enough valid signatures. If he certifies it, the courts could be asked to decide whether the new boundaries were ever legally in effect — and which map must be used for the Nov. 3 general election.
Under the new map, the Republican nominee would compete in a 14-county district stretching from Kansas City through rural areas that reliably support the GOP. Under the previous boundaries, the contest would be decided in Kansas City and portions of Jackson and Clay counties, where Cleaver would be overwhelmingly favored to win a 12th term.
Missouri’s congressional districts that will be used Aug. 4 for the primary. The boundaries could shift back to the districts drawn in 2022 if a referendum on the map is placed on the November ballot. The GOP’s goal is to win the 5th District seat currently held by U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, a Kansas City Democrat (Screenshot from Missouri House website).
Since winning election in 2004 with 55% of the vote, Cleaver has fallen short of a majority only twice and not since 2014.
The possibility that the district could change after the primary has not discouraged political spending. Outside groups have poured almost $2.8 million into the contest — more than five times what the six candidates combined have reported raising — but all of it has focused on two candidates: Taylor Burks of Boone County and state Sen. Rick Brattin of Cass County.
The concentration of money has left the other four candidates — Micah Beebe, Brett Hueffmeier, Brad Patty and Berton Knox — trying to convince voters that the primary has not already become a two-person race.
“I went into this race realizing that I was running against some people that had done this before, and that they were probably going to get a lot of endorsements,” Hueffmeier said. 
Brattin is certain the map used on primary day will be the one electing the next 5th District representative in November, arguing that a  referendum on a congressional map violates the federal constitution.
“The sole authority is given only and solely to the legislature and legislature alone,” he said. 
“This isn’t a regular statute on which referendum is applicable, and I’ve said that from the onset.”
Burks said that while a referendum may occur, he expects the courts will keep the districts in place for November.
“Both the attorney general and secretary of state have very clearly said that this is the map that governs this cycle,” Burks said. “What happens with the referendum will be decided by voters. If the secretary of state puts it on the ballot.”
 A two-candidate advertising war

There is little love lost between the two candidates benefiting from — and enduring — million-dollar advertising campaigns.
For Burks, Brattin is defined by his membership in a disruptive faction of Republicans in the Missouri Senate he believes are more interested in garnering headlines than moving the state forward.
“Senator Brattin has a long track record of being a bomb thrower and a disrupter in the state Legislature,” Burks said. “Club for Growth apparently is seeking that and trying to buy this seat for him, which my campaign is going to do everything we can to stop.”
Club for Growth is the funding source behind more than $1.3 million being spent by Win It Back PAC, airing positive ads painting Brattin as “a MAGA Marine” who will fight for Trump’s agenda.
A negative ad funded by Club for Growth accuses Burks of encouraging “woke” activities at Truman State University, where he serves on the Board of Governors. It cites a campus resource center with clothing available to students who are transitioning their gender.
State Sen. Rick Brattin of Harrisonville speaks to reporters in 2024 with Missouri Freedom Caucus members, then-state Sen. Denny Hoskins of Warrensburg, left, and then state-Sen. Bill Eigel (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).
“I obviously have no control over the legal activities of student groups,” Burks said. “And no university funds were used for that, so it didn’t even come before the board. It is a silly, desperate out-of-state attack ad.”
Conservatives for American Excellence, a super PAC backing Burks, has responded with ads attacking Brattin over votes he cast in the Missouri Senate.
One ad says Brattin helped sex offenders get removed from the state registry because he voted for a 2018 bill that changed how long some offenders must remain registered.
The ad also says he voted against child-abuse prevention funding. That claim is based on Brattin joining other members of the Conservative Caucus in opposing an $853 million supplemental spending bill that included about $519,000 for two child-abuse programs.
“Rick Brattin voted to make it possible for sex offenders to be removed from registries. Brattin also voted against funding for child abuse prevention programs,” the ad states. “If Rick Brattin won’t vote to protect our children, then you can’t vote for him.”
Despite the attacks, Brattin believes the race is trending his way.
He has major endorsements, including Gov. Mike Kehoe and Missouri Right to Life, he noted.
“Plus having the track record, the voting record is resonating with people that are tired of people talking the talk and not walking the walk,” Brattin said.
Burks, a commander in the Naval Reserve and chief executive of commercial landscaping company Rost Inc., has financed much of his campaign himself, lending it $900,000 and raising about $250,000 from donors.
Brattin, a two-term state senator who previously held office as a state representative and Cass County auditor, has raised $312,000. 
Hueffmeier, a one-time staff member for U.S. Sens. John Ashcroft and Kit Bond who now works in commercial real estate, loaned his campaign $275,000 and raised about $50,000 more.
Beebe, a commercial real estate investments specialist, raised less than $5,000. 
Patty, a retired Army master sergeant currently pursuing a graduate degree in public administration, raised $7,774 through June 30. He said the loans illustrate the corrupting influence of campaign money because candidates who lend their campaigns heavily may later rely on donors to repay them.
“This job pays $174,000. It’s a two-year term,” Patty said. “So, who’s going to pay the extra money back?”
Patty also said Brattin should be disqualified in the minds of voters because he helped create a district he does not live in and is now seeking to represent.
“So you vote for the map as a state senator, and then you run in it, and you don’t live in the district,” Patty said. “Why wouldn’t you run in your own district? Well, it’s because you lost to Mark Alford, and you know you can’t win.”
 Voters size up the field

At a recent Lincoln Days event in Saline County, five of the six candidates were on hand but the program didn’t give any of them time for a quick stump speech.
That left them quick one-on-one efforts at campaigning. Many Republicans stopped after they shook hands with candidates on their way to the dinner buffet that they need to know more about the candidates before they make a choice.
“Them showing up here in such a small community says a lot, that they want to make change,” said Kaylee Kipping, whose Saline County home is newly in the 5th District. 
She said she’s leaning toward Burks because he’s a “conservative family man.”
Taylor Burks, left, candidate for the Republican nomination in Missouri’s 5th Congressional District, speaks with Jamie Ulbrich on July 2  at the Saline County Republican Lincoln Days dinner in Marshall.(Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).
Wayne Heuman of Saline County said he knows a little bit about the candidates but not enough to decide. He wants a candidate committed to passing the SAVE Act pushed by President Donald Trump to require voters to provide proof of citizenship to register, photo identification to vote and limit mail-in voting. 
“We don’t need illegals coming in and voting and running our country,” Heuman said.
Many did like the idea of gaining another Republican seat in the Missouri delegation.
“It’s a fantastic idea,” said Roger Davenport of Marshall. “It has to reflect the voters of the district, what’s happening across the United States.”
 The issues

There is little daylight among the five candidates interviewed by The Independent on the Republican Party’s core issues. All support Trump’s border policies, oppose abortion and support gun rights.
The differences are largely ones of emphasis, experience and temperament.
Burks’ television ads, for example, focus on China.
He wants to stop China from buying up Missouri farmland, he said. To do so, he says in one broadcast ad, China will have to pry the land “from my cold, dead hands.”
Brattin said his stump speech points out the dangers he sees if Democrats regain control of Congress.
“We now have a party that’s literally electing devout communists, outspoken devout communists. Some of these Democrats are even happy 9/11 occurred, and thought we deserved it,” Brattin said. “They want to see it toppled and think America is disgusting and disgraceful. I think we’ve got to have representation of people who love America, will uphold its values, and combat the crazy left that literally wants to see its destruction.”
Beebe places greater emphasis on federal spending and the national debt.
“I’m not so naive to think that I’m going to show up in Congress and all of a sudden the problems are going to be fixed,” he said.
Hueffmeier said he wants to work on solving rural health care needs. Right now, there are heavy restrictions on doctors owning hospitals. If that were changed, he said, there would be more interest from physicians to serve rural areas.
“It’s just kind of an antiquated law that’s there that really doesn’t need to be there anymore,” he said.
Patty said he wants to cut spending and taxes.
“I am all about reducing taxes and putting money, basically not taking too much money from the people, because it was originally in their hands,” he said.
All five candidates interviewed supported Trump’s decision to use military force against Iran, although Hueffmeier criticized the administration’s preparation and public messaging.
“What the president’s been a little guilty of is that the messaging was not organized, or well organized, in order to do it,” he said.
The U.S.-Israeli relationship helped lead Trump to go to war and the Israeli military actions in Lebanon and Gaza have soured some Americans on the Middle East ally.
None of the candidates said they would reduce or curtail support for Israel. Burks, however, added that the U.S. must be ready to hold Israel accountable for how it uses military aid.
“The United States, as an ally, also has a role to work with Israel and say, ‘hey, what’s what’s proportional, what’s in the best interest of this partnership overall,’” Burks said.
The next Congress will consider what, if anything, should be done to regulate development of artificial intelligence.
For Burks, the area to regulate is online interactions with children and national security. For Brattin, the limits should be to protect humans while allowing full and open development for commercial uses.
Hueffmeier said he learned the need for privacy protection when he returned from China after working as a higher education administrator. His devices were hacked, he said.
AI regulation should protect personal information and privacy, he said.
“We tend to just give up our privacy and our freedoms on an increasing basis without really thinking it through, and just thinking everything is going to be okay but what the public doesn’t understand is that once you do that, you know it’s too late,” Hueffmeier said.
AI development needs data centers, and the candidates are hearing from vocal opponents of data center development. While they sympathize, they questioned whether it is a federal issue.
Congress should not be regulating data center site selection, Brattin said. In his state Senate district, he said, there are communities determined to keep them out and communities that will welcome them.
“Nobody wants a nuclear power plant right in their backyard. They don’t want a coal-fired power plant in a residential community,” Brattin said. “In the same way, they don’t want a big hyperscale data center which looks like a maximum security prison in a residential area. We understand it’s just common sense on all sides, from the developers to the counties and to the state, as to where these things are going to be installed.”
Farmers are reeling from the combined effect of low crop prices, high feed and fertilizer costs and tariffs cutting off markets entirely. The system of farm supports known as the Farm Bill, which also includes authorization of nutrition assistance programs, is three years late for renewal.
Hueffmeier said farm programs should prioritize making farms profitable. The current programs, for farmers who are enrolled, put targets for subsidies at past prices and yields regardless of the profitability of those levels.
More stable support is needed, he said.
“Those are not bad ideas, and those things didn’t really ever cost us an enormous amount out of the federal budget,” Hueffmeier said.
Patty said farmers should face market conditions.
“I personally stand on the principle of having the government being less and less involved,” Patty said.
Brattin said less regulation would ease the burden on farmers.
With little public polling, it is uncertain which candidate has the upper hand as early voting begins Tuesday.
The only thing that would alter the outcome, candidates agreed, is if Trump endorses a candidate.
Hueffmeier, who went to Washington looking for support, said he doesn’t expect the president to make a selection. 
“Here’s what they told me: They said that he will only endorse someone if it’s right at the end, and we know for sure that that person is going to win,” Hueffmeier said. “Otherwise the only time he gets involved is when he’s upset with somebody who’s an incumbent and he wants somebody to run against them.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: In the panic over a talent exodus, Massachusetts is forgetting the underutilized talent it has
description: Most states compete for the workers everyone else wants. Talent activation is a different discipline. It starts not with who might move to the state, but with who is already here.
text:
MASSACHUSETTS IS IN a talent panic. The headlines have been steady for months. 
The Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce reports that 26 percent of young Boston area residents plan to leave the region within the next five years. The Mass Opportunity Alliance, a coalition of the state’s largest business groups, found in a December poll that one in three Massachusetts voters are considering leaving themselves or know someone who is. IRS data show 182,000 net residents left Massachusetts since 2020, with the largest losses among workers aged 26 to 34. Two ballot initiatives backed by some in the business community were slated to ask voters this fall to cut taxes (one was tossed from the ballot on a technicality).  
The conversation about how to respond has narrowed to a single word: affordability. Three-quarters of Massachusetts employers say housing costs are hurting their ability to recruit workers. If people cannot afford to live here, they will not stay. 
The Healey administration is right to lead with affordability. But it is only one part of the story. Massachusetts is so focused on the high-skill talent it stands to lose that it has forgotten the wealth of underutilized talent it already has. 
The young professional in a job that does not use her training. The mid-career worker displaced from one industry who could move to another. The foreign-credentialed immigrant whose qualifications do not transfer. The recent graduate who cannot find a pathway into the sectors she trained for. The resident in a community of color who cannot find her way into the cluster economy growing around her. Connecting them with jobs is not a side initiative or an equity portfolio. It is the most powerful economic competitiveness strategy the state has not yet used. 
In the regions I have worked with, the most consequential talent is almost always the talent that remains untapped. Standard workforce metrics miss most of them. The talent the economy is leaving on the table is invisible to the dashboard. 
Massachusetts has both a talent shortage and an underutilization problem. The state is projected to face a shortfall of roughly 192,000 college-educated workers by 2030, even though nearly half of its adults hold bachelor’s degrees, the highest rate in the country. At the same time, the untapped workforce is everywhere, from underutilized professionals in Greater Boston to mid-skill workers in the state’s 26 Gateway Cities, places like Lawrence, Lowell, Worcester, Fall River, Springfield, Brockton, and New Bedford.  
Many of these residents’ skills and ambitions have yet to be matched to sectors that are hiring nearby. Worcester sits 25 minutes from a biomanufacturing corridor that has been expanding for a decade. Springfield is at the edge of the Pioneer Valley life sciences corridor. Mattapan and Dorchester are a short transit ride from the Longwood Medical Area. The talent is not missing. The infrastructure that could match them with jobs has not been built. 
AI makes that gap even more costly. The jobs most vulnerable to AI are held by precisely the highly educated knowledge class that the Commonwealth has spent the last 40 years attracting. This spring, a Tufts University study identified Massachusetts as the most AI-vulnerable state in the country. At the same time, many mid-skill and frontline jobs are relatively safe, and thousands of them remain unfilled. 
In my work with cities, I have sat in many rooms where business and political leaders strategize about how to attract more biotech PhDs and engineers. The conversation rarely turns to whether a worker living 30 minutes from a biomanufacturing site even knows it has job openings. That asymmetry is no longer survivable. 
Most states compete for the workers everyone else wants. Talent activation is a different discipline. It starts not with who might move to the state, but with who is already here. High-skill talent recruitment runs on incentives and marketing. Talent activation runs on alignment.  
My firm is helping to build an integrated workforce system in Los Angeles that will bring 50,000 residents into the region’s growing economy by 2030, and we are part of a similar effort underway in Austin. The logic is straightforward, even if the work is hard. First, you map the industries that are hiring. Second, you identify the residents who are not connected to them. Then you build a bridge between them. 
Massachusetts has already laid much of the groundwork for such a structure. Since MassReconnect and MassEducate made community college tuition-free, adult enrollment has jumped roughly 40 percent. The governor’s skills-based hiring executive order and the new MassSkills Coalition have brought employers, workforce providers, and labor into the same room. 
Three things remain to be done. First, the state must treat the Gateway Cities and Boston’s immigrant and working-class neighborhoods as the front line of talent activation.  
Every dollar spent on workforce development should move residents into growing sectors. Second, it needs to put the brakes on credential inflation. Bachelor’s degrees are required for more and more jobs that do not need them. Third, workers themselves need a seat at the table. The young workers, apprentices, and mid-career professionals the strategy is meant to serve understand the barriers they face better than the institutions designing around them. Every region I have worked with that closed this gap did it by treating underutilized workers as part of the answer rather than evidence of the problem. 
Massachusetts has built the most enviable knowledge economy in the country. For its next chapter it should ask potential workers in Lawrence, Mattapan, or Chelsea what they could build if the doors were open to them. Then it needs to open the door. 
Steven Pedigo is a co-founder of CivicSol, an economic development and public strategy firm, and a professor of practice at the LBJ School of Public Affairs at the University of Texas at Austin. He joins Northeastern University’s School of Public Policy and Urban Affairs this fall.

name: Maryland Matters
title: As costs balloon, state officials pitch Key Bridge project to key federal lawmakers
description: Maryland officials took two key congressional appropriators on a tour Monday of ongoing work to replace the Francis Scott Key Bridge, as ballooning costs have raised fears that the federal government might not honor its pledge to pay 100% of the project.
text:
From left, Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) Maryland Transportation Authority Chief Engineer Jim Harkness and Gov. Wes Moore (D) tour the Key Bridge site. (Photo courtesy Maryland Governor's Office)Maryland officials took two key congressional appropriators on a tour Monday of ongoing work to replace the Francis Scott Key Bridge, as ballooning costs have raised fears that the federal government might not honor its pledge to pay 100% of the project.
Gov. Wes Moore (D), current and former members of the state’s congressional delegation and state transportation officials took Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) and Rep. Steve Womack (R-Ark.) on a boat tour of the site, where work continues even though the state parted ways this spring with the current contractor over projected costs.
Capito, the chair of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and Womack, the chair of the Transportation, Housing and Urban Development Subcommittee of the House Appropriations Committee, were generally supportive of the project, despite what Capito called “eye-popping” costs on the multibillion-dollar project.
“We have to have a transparent process,” Capito said to reporters after the boat tour. “I want to see why these costs have ballooned and what are the performance measures that are built in … because now, the whole country is paying for this.”
The bridge collapsed into the Patapsco River when it was struck in the early morning hours of March 26, 2024, by a fully loaded container ship leaving the Port of Baltimore, killing six workers who were on the bridge at the time and severing a major East Coast highway route.
In the weeks immediately following the collapse, state officials estimated that replacing the bridge would cost about $1.7 billion. Then-President Joe Biden pledged that the federal government would pay the full cost of replacement, a promise that was made law in late 2024 in legislation passed by Congress.
Since then, however, the state’s official cost estimate has grown to be between $4.3 billion and $5.2 billion — and some unofficial estimates have suggested it might be much higher.
State and federal officials tour the site of the Francis Scott Key Bridge replacement work. (Photo courtesy Maryland Governor’s Office)
The state this spring ended its contract with Kiewit Infrastructure over price disagreements on the job going forward. Kiewit was involved in expedited planning on a replacement bridge, removal of the old bridge structures and placement of piles for a new bridge, and it will continue that work through the end of this year. But state officials are seeking new contractors for subsequent phases of the project.
State officials have blamed a number of pressures for the higher costs, but say the chief culprit are the modern safety measures that were not a part of the original bridge’s 1970s-era design, but have to be built in today to prevent another tragedy like the 2024 collapse from happening.
“If you look at the fact that this next bridge that we’re building, it is going to have additional safety precautions and mechanisms that were not there when  features” that were not there when the bridge was originally built, Moore said Monday.
“It will have to be larger, because it has to accommodate larger ships,” Moore said. “So I know when people say. ‘That’s ambitious, to say you’re going to build a bridge that’s safer and bigger, and build it faster than was done before,’ the answer is, it is ambitious.”
Moore pointed to the work done so far and speed at which crews cleared the shipping channel in and out of the port — in weeks instead of months — and said he is confident the project can still be finished by 2030.
Moore said Capito and Womack have been “with us every step of the way.”
“They were here walking with us after the initial tragedy,” he said. “This is not an introduction to either of these two.”
Both Capito and Womack remained supportive of the project, with Capito noting the 89,000 people who crossed the bridge daily and Womack noting that some of the steel used in the project came from an Arkansas foundry.
“This is not a shirts-and-skins issue. This is not a blue/red issue,” Womack said. “This is a national issue and the sooner we can get this thing built, and they’re track record is pretty good right now, when you consider the speed at which a lot of these things are happening,  this is going to be open in record time and everybody’s going to benefit, particularly the nation.”
Capito said that permitting reform that is working through Congress will be key to dealing with projects like the Key Bridge as the nation continues to grapple with aging infrastructure. For member of Congress it has been a case of “lessons learned” with the bridge, she said.
One of the lessons already learned, Capito said, is “Maybe don’t put an estimate out until you’re really sure what the estimate might be.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: High costs, heavy traffic: New Jersey’s highway system still falls short
authors: Special to the New Jersey Monitor
description: New Jersey residents pay a lot for road maintenance — and we have some of the worst roads in the nation, writes Baruch Feigenbaum.
text:
New Jersey residents pay a lot for road maintenance — and we have some of the worst roads in the nation, writes Baruch Feigenbaum. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)By Baruch Feigenbaum

Anyone who drives the New Jersey Turnpike at rush hour knows the feeling. Traffic slows to a crawl. Brake lights stretch for miles. What should be a short commute becomes an hour of stop-and-go frustration. That’s because New Jersey ranks 50th, dead last in the nation, in urban traffic congestion, a new study of every state’s roads finds. On average, New Jersey drivers waste about 85 hours a year, more than two full workweeks, sitting in gridlock.

These traffic jams come with real economic costs. Time spent stuck in traffic reduces productivity, increases fuel consumption and emissions, and raises shipping costs for businesses and prices for consumers. It also makes daily life harder for commuters just trying to get to work or home to their families, to stores, and to activities. But congestion is only part of the story.
The president, not the governor, is responsible for revived Roxbury ICE jail plan

Reason Foundation’s 29th Annual Highway Report, which grades state highway systems on 13 categories, including bridge safety, traffic fatalities, pavement conditions, and spending efficiency, ranks New Jersey 40th in the nation for overall highway cost-effectiveness and road conditions. That is worse than the state’s 34th overall ranking last year, but a major improvement over New Jersey’s last- and near-last-place finishes in the overall rankings for several years before that.

When you look at nearby states, there are reasons to worry. While New Jersey is 40th out of 50 states, Connecticut has improved its system to the 7th-best road performance and cost-effectiveness in the country. Delaware ranks 32nd, Maryland 34th, and Pennsylvania 36th. New Jersey only manages to beat New York, which ranks a dismal 47th.

For a dense state with one of the nation’s most heavily used transportation networks, New Jersey’s ranking underscores its persistent challenges with congestion, pavement quality, and spending. New Jersey performs reasonably well in some categories, particularly safety. It has the 14th-lowest rural traffic fatality rate and the 16th-best urban traffic fatality rate. It also ranks 17th in rural interstate highway pavement condition, but falls to 42nd out of 50 states in urban interstate highway pavement condition and 41st in urban arterial road pavement condition.

Bridge conditions are closer to the middle of the pack. New Jersey ranks 27th nationally in the percentage of bridges that are structurally deficient, but 44th in capital and bridge disbursements, meaning the state spends far more per road and bridge project than all but a handful of states. That spending should result in better pavement quality and up-to-par bridges.

Unsurprisingly, the other biggest problems for New Jersey’s road system are on the spending side, where taxpayers pay a lot for the 40th-ranked system. New Jersey ranks 42nd in maintenance spending, which includes costs such as repaving roads and repairing potholes.

Spending more is not necessarily a problem if the results are outstanding, but as anyone who has driven on the state’s bumpy roads knows, that isn’t the case.

Politicians and officials will rightly point to the state’s higher cost of living, harsh winters, proximity to New York, and other factors as reasons for higher-than-average spending. But that explanation only goes so far, and the state should continue to reform how projects are prioritized and how transportation dollars are spent.

Improving New Jersey’s highway system does not require reinventing transportation policy. If the state wants to improve quickly, ensuring spending produces smoother pavement on urban roads and fewer structurally deficient bridges would yield significant gains.

In the longer term, reducing traffic congestion has to be near the top of the state’s list. Smart investments in added capacity, better traffic management, and more effective use of technology could move drivers through some of the state’s worst bottlenecks, helping the state’s economic productivity and competitiveness.

New Jersey’s highway system is one of the busiest in the country. Millions of people rely on it every day, and businesses depend on it to move goods across the Northeast. For a state with such a critical transportation network, New Jersey has made some solid gains in recent years, but still has a lot of work to do.
Baruch Feigenbaum is senior managing director of transportation policy at Reason Foundation

name: WyoFile
title: ‘White colonies’ of petri dish bacteria led to data center pollution fine
description:
Cheyenne releases timeline of tests, missteps, retests and rounds of disinfection in data center water pollution case.
The post ‘White colonies’ of petri dish bacteria led to data center pollution fine appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Mysterious, unusual white colonies of bacteria growing in a lab’s petri dish alerted workers at Cheyenne’s water works that something was amiss.
The Jan. 15 discovery kicked off months of investigations, lab tests, disinfections, retests and sampling that led the city to cite operators at the Meta Cheyenne Data Center for “serious noncompliance” with wastewater discharge standards, a $10,000 fine and potentially cleanup costs.
The Cheyenne Board of Public Utilities on Monday released a timeline and list of FAQs related to the Meta citation and fine, plus 612 pages of documents released as a result of records requests.

An artist’s conception of the Meta Cheyenne Data Center as seen on a Meta announcement on Facebook. (Meta)

Meta has appealed the citation and asked for its $10,000 back. It seeks a contested-case hearing and told Cheyenne that Meta should not be on the hook for cleanup costs.
Because of that appeal, utility officials won’t answer any more questions or hold a press conference about the pollution, a utility spokesperson said in a statement.
“The BOPU believes the timeline, FAQ, and accompanying public records provide a thorough account of the events and addresses many of the questions raised by the community,” the statement reads.
Discovery of the bacteria in the wastewater recycling system — not drinking water — and the citation to Meta and its subsidiary have worried some residents upset at the ongoing rezoning of thousands of acres in rural areas for a new industrial use. Cheyenne terminated Meta’s wastewater discharge permit, raising public questions about industry promises, environmental protections and water conservation statewide.
The timeline
The utility’s 13-page timeline recounts how the white colonies of bacteria seen on Jan. 15 first alarmed water workers conducting routine tests on the city’s wastewater treatment system.
It wasn’t until Feb. 12, almost a month later, that the utility sent samples on to the Wyoming Public Health Laboratory. Eleven days later, on Feb. 23, results came back “identifying the white colony bacteria as Cupriavidus gilardii,” an unusual bacterium that’s found in soils and is known to be deadly.
What followed was months of sampling, testing, resampling and retesting, cleansing of water systems and the use of potable water in the reclaimed-water irrigation network.
Four months later, on June 26, the utility issued its first press release about the contamination. The agency explained the timing of its public notice in its FAQs.
“[The board of Public Utilities] determined there was a low risk to public health, which did not justify a public notification that could result in public panic,” the document reads. “As a public agency, BOPU must weigh public safety, impacted area, and level of risk when determining the appropriate nature and extent of public notifications.”
In the course of its hunt for the source of the pollution, utility investigators went quickly to the Meta site. That’s “because they were the newest industrial user discharging to the BOPU wastewater system,” the utility said.
Investigators sampled water from a “predischarge storage tank” at the data center March 18 and it spawned white colony bacteria in a lab petri dish.
Six days later, results came back from Wyoming Public Health Laboratory “indicating that Meta Cheyenne Datacenter CHY1-2 discharge contained Cupriavidus gilardii,” the timeline reads.
“[T]here was a low risk to public health, which did not justify a public notification that could result in public panic.”Cheyenne Board of Public Utilities
Cheyenne, which has limited rights to local water sources, obtains half its water from 115 miles away across the Continental Divide. It reclaims its sewage to irrigate parks and golf courses.
Because of the pollution, Cheyenne disinfected its wastewater recycling system — one pond in the system holds 3 million gallons or about 9 acre-feet of water — by flushing, using chlorine and a solution of sodium hypochlorite. The work was extensive and expensive.
“Based on the significant labor hours and expense required to flush the wastewater collection mains, collect and analyze samples, alteration of operation at the WWTPs, disinfection of the reuse system, utilization of potable water for irrigation in lieu of the contaminated reuse water, and the passthrough of the bacteria to Crow Creek and Dry Creek, BOPU Industrial pretreatment program staff determined that an enforcement action was warranted,” the utility’s timeline states.
Meta calls its Cheyenne center a 715,000-square-foot campus. Most of the space in such complexes is taken up by warehouses of computers that can be used to power artificial intelligence or serve cell phones and computers that need complex software for writing, filming, recording, streaming and number crunching.
The industrial parks are being constructed on thousands of acres that have been used for years as ranch lands, including near Evanston and Wheatland.
Documents indicate that the Cheyenne investigation and citation centered on the filling and flushing of a closed-loop cooling system, a method of cooling computer banks while conserving water.
Meta said it acted as soon as it found out there was a problem. Meta’s construction contractor Fortis “immediately stopped discharging industrial wastewater and began hauling it offsite,” Meta said.
The company began testing through an independent contractor and “found no trace of the substance,” a spokesperson said in a statement.
“Meta is committed to being a good neighbor in Cheyenne,” the statement reads, “including through the protection of local water resources, and will continue encouraging collaboration between Fortis and the board until this situation is resolved.”
