name: WyoFile
title: County’s secret ballot battle lands in court
description:
The Fremont County Library Board remains in limbo as a judge decides whether county commissioners erred by either using a secret ballot or by trying to rectify that action.
The post County’s secret ballot battle lands in court appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
RIVERTON—District Court Judge Jason Conder heard hours of legal arguments in an unusual lawsuit that has placed Fremont County commissioners in the uncommon position of arguing they violated Wyoming’s Public Meetings Act, while the plaintiff insists they followed it.
Conder took three pending motions under advisement at the conclusion of the July 16 hearing, declining to rule from the bench on David Mossburg’s requests for a preliminary injunction and summary judgment or on the county’s motion to dismiss the case.
Instead, Conder repeatedly said the case hinges on what actually occurred during a June 24, 2025, county commissioners meeting and indicated he intends to personally review video and audio recordings of the proceedings before issuing a decision.
“I recognize the strange situation that the individual suing the county commissioners is saying you didn’t break the rules, and the county commissioners are saying, ‘Yes, we did,’” Conder said near the end of the hearing. “It’s understandably awkward.”
The lawsuit stems from the commissioners’ appointment of Mossburg and Karen Wetzel to the Fremont County Library Board on June 24, 2025. Before publicly voting on the appointments, commissioners used anonymous weighted ballots to rank six applicants. The ballots were tabulated during the lunch recess before commissioners reconvened; commissioners then announced the results publicly and unanimously voted to appoint Mossburg and Wetzel.
Secret ballot
After The Ranger questioned whether the anonymous balloting violated the Wyoming Public Meetings Act, commissioners revisited the issue twice that fall. On Oct. 7, they publicly voted to add their names to the previously anonymous ballots and discussed whether anyone wished to change their votes. Two weeks later, on Oct. 21, commissioners held a new public vote that retained Wetzel but replaced Mossburg with Julie Lefevre.
Mossburg served on the library board between the June and October meetings, a fact both parties stipulated during Thursday’s hearing.
Now a Republican candidate for the District 1 Fremont County Commission seat, Mossburg filed suit earlier this year seeking declaratory and injunctive relief. In an email explaining his intent to sue, Mossburg argued that he had been lawfully appointed June 24 and that the October revote unlawfully removed him without any finding of misconduct or neglect, as required for removal of appointed library board members. His complaint also argues that even if the anonymous ballot process was flawed, the commission cured any defect on Oct. 7 by publicly identifying the ballots and affirming the commissioners’ votes.
His motion for a preliminary injunction asks the court to restore him to the library board while the case proceeds, arguing that each day he remains off the board deprives both him and the public of the service of a lawfully appointed board member.
“What directions were commissioners given before they voted?”District Court Judge Jason Conder
Representing Mossburg, attorney Thomas Szott argued Thursday that the central legal question is what constituted the commission’s official governmental action.
“The action,” Szott argued, “is the June public vote.”
According to Szott, the anonymous weighted ballots were merely an informal ranking mechanism used to identify commissioners’ preferences before the legally significant action occurred in open session.
After the ballot results were announced June 24, Vice Chairman Mike Jones moved to appoint Mossburg and Wetzel, Commissioner Clarence Thomas seconded the motion, and commissioners unanimously approved it.
Jones testified that commissioners retained the discretion to reject that motion.
“Absolutely,” Jones said when asked whether commissioners could have voted no.
Szott argued Jones’ testimony demonstrated the public vote was not merely ceremonial.
“The commissioners had the opportunity to change their minds,” he said. “Meaning this is not just a formal rubber stamp of whatever happened in the ballots.”
Heart of the case
Because the official action occurred publicly, Szott argued, there was no Public Meetings Act violation requiring correction. Even if the anonymous ballots were improper, he maintained, they were not themselves governmental action and therefore could not invalidate the subsequent public vote.
Throughout the hearing, however, Conder repeatedly pressed both attorneys on whether that conclusion depended on how commissioners understood the weighted ballots.
“What directions were commissioners given before they voted?” the judge asked. “Doesn’t that matter?”
Conder questioned whether commissioners may have understood the weighted ballot results themselves to determine the appointments, with the later public vote simply formalizing a decision already reached.
Szott acknowledged the importance of the question.
“That’s the heart of the case, for sure,” he replied.
Conder returned repeatedly to that issue, saying he needed to review the June 24 meeting video to determine exactly what commissioners were told before casting their ballots.
The county, represented by attorney Katye Ames, argued that the anonymous weighted ballots effectively decided the appointments before the public vote, rendering the June 24 action void under the Public Meetings Act.
She characterized the subsequent public vote as “a rubber stamp” of decisions already reached privately.
According to Ames, commissioners recognized the legal problem after receiving a September 2025 letter questioning the appointment process.
The remedy
She argued the Oct. 7 meeting, during which commissioners publicly signed the previously anonymous ballots, did not sufficiently cure the defect because it simply reaffirmed the earlier decision.
Instead, she said, the Oct. 21 revote satisfied the Wyoming Supreme Court’s decision in Gronberg v. Teton County Housing Authority, which allows public bodies to cure Public Meetings Act violations through “a new and substantial reconsideration” conducted in compliance with the law.
“The remedy here,” Ames said, “is to then fix it by holding a public meeting and actually taking appropriate action to do what you’re trying to do. That’s exactly what the board did here.”
Conder spent considerable time questioning both attorneys about Gronberg v. Teton County Housing Authority, repeatedly asking what would constitute the “substantial reconsideration” required under that decision.
At one point, he asked Ames what he would actually see on the October recordings, demonstrating meaningful reconsideration rather than another procedural formality. Ames responded that commissioners publicly voted candidate by candidate and ultimately reached a different result, arguing that the different outcome itself suggested genuine reconsideration.
Szott disagreed, arguing that the county was attempting to graft additional requirements onto Gronberg that the supreme court never imposed. He maintained that because commissioners originally reached their decision without extended public deliberation, the law did not require a more elaborate process to cure any defect.
The hearing also focused on Jones’ testimony about the October revote itself. Initially, Jones testified there had been no separate finding declaring the June appointments void. Later, after Conder noted an apparent inconsistency in his testimony, Jones clarified that he believed commissioners effectively accomplished both actions simultaneously.
“I believe we did it in one action, whereas by taking the new vote, we were declaring it void,” Jones testified.
Beyond the legal questions, Conder repeatedly expressed concern about the practical consequences for the library board while the litigation remains unresolved. He noted that whichever side ultimately prevails, the board faces uncertainty over whether actions taken during the disputed appointment period might later need to be revisited.
“The poor library board,” he remarked. “One side is going to think I’m wrong. One side is going to appeal … and the board, the whole darn time, is going to say, ‘Man, we’ve been voting on all these things. We may have to vote again.'”
The hearing also addressed Mossburg’s request for expedited consideration.
Szott argued that allowing the litigation to proceed under a normal timeline could effectively deprive his client of meaningful relief if his would-be-three-year library board term expires before the case is resolved.
Conder acknowledged the concern but cautioned that no immediate ruling should be expected.
“I will work it as fast as I can,” he said, noting the court’s existing calendar and the need to review the meeting recordings before deciding the pending motions. “You’re not going to have an answer this week. You’re not going to have an answer next week.”
Before adjourning, Conder complimented both attorneys on their arguments and reiterated that he would review the record before issuing written decisions on the preliminary injunction, the county’s motion to dismiss and Mossburg’s request for summary judgment.

name: WyoFile
title: One of Wyoming’s million-dollar check writers will be its new congressman
description:
Only self-funded candidates have a shot at succeeding Hageman, who didn’t loan her campaign a dime when she won, writes
columnist Kerry Drake. 
The post One of Wyoming’s million-dollar check writers will be its new congressman appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
I’m getting nostalgic for the type of political campaigning that used to be standard in Wyoming, but is likely gone forever in congressional races.

Opinion

There was a time, not that long ago, when receiving contributions from the most people who actually live in the Equality State was a badge of honor for candidates who wanted to prove they had widespread support. They derided, with some success, opponents who depended on wealthy out-of-state donors.
Widespread support has nothing to do with the 2026 U.S. House race, which attracted 10 Republican candidates. Second-quarter campaign finance reports to the Federal Election Commission show four candidates have each loaned their campaigns more than $1 million to fight for the chance to succeed two-term Rep. Harriet Hageman, who is running for the U.S. Senate.
The House candidates most pundits see as running one-two with less than a month before the Aug. 18 primary are both funded by family wealth. 
Secretary of State Chuck Gray, following the family money recipe for success that helped buy him his current office in 2022, has loaned his current campaign $1.15 million. But that pales compared to the $2 million that Steve Friess has loaned his rookie campaign.
Friess, son of late GOP donor and philanthropist Foster Friess, has only raised $87,000 from individual donors. That’s about $5,000 less than state Senate President Bo Biteman, R-Ranchester, has collected from donors. He has not used any of his own money.
Financial adviser Reid Rasner has loaned his campaign $1.71 million, about 84% of his war chest. Jackson rancher Frank Chapman’s commitment to himself totaled $1.06 million, which accounts for an embarrassing 97% of his campaign funds.
Rasner has spent much of his own money to make fun of Gray, whom he comically calls “China Chuck” for his alleged allegiance to the communist country. If you have a spare million to waste on this pursuit, I guess trolling one of the most obnoxious 2020 presidential election deniers isn’t a bad use of the money. I’d do it.
Rasner’s criticism of Gray would have more meaning, though, if it was coming from a candidate who has a coherent message of his own to convey. Rasner doesn’t.
But the million-dollar-plus loans have undeniably raised the profiles of all four candidates and paid for massive broadcasting campaigns and the ability to overflow mailboxes across the state.
I can’t be the only Wyoming resident who is offended by rich candidates who have such little respect for voters in this state that they callously plan to outright buy the Republican nomination for U.S. House while playing to an audience of one: President Donald Trump.
Every member of this quartet is an unabashed Trump sycophant who would likely stop at nothing to win his endorsement, which is largely seen as game over for the other nine. But what’s in it for the president to get involved in a primary in a state where three of every four voters are Republicans?
Other than another chance to show that he’s the kingmaker who will reward his most loyal servant, not much. But it’s probably enough to make him do it since it’s Wyoming, and Trump famously handpicked Hageman to take out one of his most-hated rivals, former Rep. Liz Cheney.
One of the U.S. House hopefuls who also challenged Cheney was Gray, who Trump notably snubbed. It was enough to drive Gray to drop out of the race in favor of seeking the GOP secretary of state nomination, where he did get Trump’s nod.
Ahead of this primary, he started running campaign ads without even saying what office he wanted. Once Hageman declared her Senate bid, Gray made his move for her House seat.
Gray’s father, Wyoming radio mogul Jan Charles Gray, spent $700,000 on his son’s 2022 race. Wyoming election laws limit how much individuals can donate to statewide campaigns to $2,500. However, there are no limits on direct contributions from immediate family members.
The FEC second-quarter report for Gray’s U.S. House race indicates that his father, who formed the Protecting Wyoming Values PAC in April, has donated $657,000 to the super PAC, which has spent $519,000 on Chuck Gray’s campaign.
Super PACs cannot directly coordinate or donate to political candidates or parties. They can, however, raise and spend unlimited funds to overtly advocate for or against candidates. 
Chapman is the king of super PAC beneficiaries this year, with the Fighting for Wyoming PAC spending $2.42 million to support his candidacy, mostly on TV advertisements. That’s all money from Republican megadonor and hedge fund manager Kenneth Griffin, who has single-handedly helped Chapman make up ground since his late campaign start in March.
So, what candidates have the best chance of gaining Trump’s endorsement? Gray’s commercials typically feature Trump praising the job he’s done, which makes it sound like an official endorsement until you realize that “Good job Chuck” was said at a 2024 Trump rally in Colorado.
The president has previously said positive things about Biteman, whom he encouraged to run for governor. But the candidate Gray is in competition with is Friess, whose father earned the endorsement of Trump in a 2018 GOP gubernatorial primary ultimately won by Mark Gordon. 
Trump is attracted to money, of course, since it can travel back to him, and the Friess family has the most in this race.
How can any hardworking Wyomingite who makes an average wage think they will be best represented by people willing to spend more than a million bucks for the chance at a job that pays $175,000 a year? The winner will also need to keep ponying up every two years to remain a “public servant.”
This is hardly the first time that Wyoming politicians have spent large sums of their personal fortunes to try to win a powerful office. But I can’t think of another time when 85% of the $7.1 million candidates have raised thus far has come from their own wallets.
If voters in the Republican primary aren’t happy with that stark statistic, they should look beyond the four men who have spent the most money. They are basically the same candidate — Richie Riches who will do anything to please the MAGA crowd and have shown 100% loyalty to Trump.
Whoever shows up in the winner’s circle — and it will unfortunately be one of these million-dollar check writers — has helped rewrite the Wyoming federal candidates’ playbook.
It now reads, “If you can’t afford to buy your way into this political poker game, don’t bother. You can’t win.”

title: Trump proposal will turn federal grants into a system of political favors, Democrats warn
text: WASHINGTON — Democrats in Congress are pushing back against a proposed Trump administration rule introduced by the Office of Management and Budget that would substantially change the way federal grants are reviewed and distributed.Over the past few weeks, several groups of lawmakers have written public comment letters to Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought expressing strong opposition to the new draft rule, which would give political appointees the power to decide what institutions receive grant funding, among other revisions. A summary of the rule cites the Biden administration as to why it is needed. “Federal awards were often used during those years to promote a ‘woke’ policy agenda that did not reflect the values of the vast majority of the American public,” it says, pointing to diversity, equity and inclusion, or DEI, policies.Democrats said the proposal exceeds the office’s authority, will make it harder for grant recipients to carry out funding priorities established by Congress and would turn federal grants into a tool for President Donald Trump to “unilaterally advance his partisan agenda and punish political rivals.” The draft rule would allow Trump to “terminate or suspend any grant at any time for any reason and without any notice,” they said.“Ultimately, these changes will make it harder for grant recipients to apply for and manage federal funds – undermining public safety, public health, economic competitiveness, and the government’s ability to address rising costs,” wrote Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York and the entire Senate Democratic Caucus in their July 1 letter to Vought. Maryland Democrats in Congress and members of the Congressional Community Safety Caucus, led by Reps. Summer Lee of Pennsylvania, LaMonica McIver of New Jersey and Gabe Amo of Rhode Island, also wrote letters urging OMB to rescind its proposed new rule. Hundreds of billions in funds affectedThe more than 100-page draft rule, published in collaboration with 41 other federal grant-making agencies on May 29 and titled “Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance,” would change the framework used to evaluate grant applications as well as guidelines for cost sharing.It would potentially affect hundreds of billions of dollars in federal funding at universities, nonprofit organizations and other U.S. institutions, according to SciLine, an independent nonprofit service for journalists and scientists run out of the American Association for the Advancement of Science.Under the proposed rule, federal grants could not be used to “fund, promote, encourage, subsidize, or facilitate” DEI initiatives. Awards would also in many cases have to “demonstrably advance the President’s policy priorities,” and agencies would be allowed to cancel funding that is “not effective at achieving program goals or Federal agency priorities” or “no longer in the Federal Government’s interest.” “The overarching goal of OMB's proposed revisions is to improve transparency, accountability, and oversight for how Federal taxpayer dollars are used in the context of Federal grantmaking,” according to the executive summary of the rule.OMB officials say they could implement the new draft rule as early as Oct. 1. Community violence intervention programs During the public comment period for the draft rule, which ran from May 29 to July 13, congressional Democrats slammed its vague language and the implications it holds for many institutions that rely on federal funds. Maryland’s senators and Democratic representatives in their July 10 letter to Vought denounced the rule for changing a process traditionally based on merit. “The federal grantmaking process includes essential, non-political guardrails that this rule seeks to eviscerate,” they wrote.They also said the proposed rule contains a slew of new undefined standards for grants, including that they must adhere to “gold standard science” and cannot reflect “anti-American values,” that recipients may not be able to understand or comply with. Maryland institutions, often known as hubs for scientific research and innovation, have been hit hard by National Institutes of Health funding cuts and mass federal layoffs since Trump began his second term in 2025. Local governments and schools that receive federal funds have also taken blows, as has the state’s overall economy. In their July 13 letter, members of the Congressional Community Safety Caucus voiced concerns over how the draft rule could specifically affect community violence intervention programs. Community violence intervention programs, local efforts that have been linked to drops in violent crime rates in cities across the country, rely on federal grants for “state and local government investments, hospital partnerships, philanthropy, and research support,” according to the lawmakers’ letter.The new draft rule, they wrote, would jeopardize the operation of these programs by allowing Trump administration officials to “withhold, suspend, or terminate grants, or change terms and conditions mid-implementation, forcing grantees to operate in a tumultuous environment.” The administration has already made cuts to parts of the Office of Justice Programs, further limiting the funds available to community violence intervention programs.Other responses Though opposition to the proposed rule is mainly coming from Democratic lawmakers, some bipartisan criticism regarding the rule’s broad scope and fast timeline exists. Sen. Susan Collins, a Maine Republican, on July 6 asked Vought to extend the proposal’s public comment period at least 90 days and “withdraw portions of the rule that would potentially harm small and rural communities and scientific and biomedical research.”“While I agree these principles should guide the administration and oversight of Federal funds, the rule would impose new, burdensome requirements on award recipients … and conflict with Congress’ control over the federal funding process,” she wrote.  OMB did not respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment on lawmaker pushback to the proposed rule. But Vought took to social media last month to express his view of the opposition. “The freakout by those on the Left subsidized by taxpayer funds over OMB’s update of the regulation governing federal grant making tells you how important it is to keep the bureaucracies from leaking out spending that is woke, wasteful, and contra to the policies of the Trump Administration thru the NGOs,” he wrote.

title: Idaho to receive $3.9 million for AmeriCorps volunteer programs
description: Idaho is set to receive more than $3.9 million in federal funding for AmeriCorps volunteer programs. The move comes just over a year after the program faced abrupt cuts sought by the now-defunct federal Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE.  AmeriCorps is a federal program that funds volunteers for nonprofits and service projects across the […]
text:
Volunteer programs in Idaho are set to receive more than $3.9 million through the federal AmeriCorps program. (Photo courtesy of AmeriCorps)Idaho is set to receive more than $3.9 million in federal funding for AmeriCorps volunteer programs. The move comes just over a year after the program faced abrupt cuts sought by the now-defunct federal Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE. 
AmeriCorps is a federal program that funds volunteers for nonprofits and service projects across the nation. 
Funds announced Monday will go to the Governor’s Commission on Service and Volunteerism, called Serve Idaho, which administers programs in the state. 
More than $2.1 million was awarded as part of a competitive grant process and will go toward expanding programming for Idaho State University and the Student Conservation Association,  according to a press release from the Idaho Department of Labor. 
The state agency also received nearly $1.8 million in formula funding to go toward existing programs at the University of Idaho, Palouse-Clearwater Environmental Institute, Teach for America, and the Central Idaho Mountain Bike Association. 
“We are thrilled that Serve Idaho has received both competitive and formula funding from AmeriCorps to continue advancing national service across our state,” Serve Idaho Program Manager Emily Straubhar said in the press release. “These investments reflect the incredible impact AmeriCorps Volunteers make every day in Idaho communities. We are grateful for AmeriCorps’ continued partnership and look forward to expanding opportunities for service that strengthen communities throughout Idaho.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Federal officials cut Idaho’s AmeriCorps funding last summer, later reinstated the grants 

In April 2025, the federal government abruptly cancelled more than $1 million in grants for Idaho’s AmeriCorps programs, which affected 133 AmeriCorps members across the state, the Idaho Press reported. The move was part of a broader effort by DOGE to terminate federal grants and contracts across a wide spectrum of programs and agencies nationwide. 
Serve Idaho was notified on April 25, 2025, that DOGE terminated $400 million in AmeriCorps grants nationwide, which was just over 41% of the federal agency’s funds for the program. Several Idaho volunteers, who receive a living stipend from the program and educational grants after its successful completion, were terminated from their positions shortly after the notice, the Idaho Press reported. 
The grant cancellations were quickly challenged in court by Democratic state officials from 24 states and Washington, D.C. A judge in June 2025 ordered federal officials to restore funding to the states that sued, which did not include Idaho, the Associated Press reported.  
Idaho’s grant funding was restored in July 2025 when federal authorities decided to reinstate the grants for all states, according to an Idaho Department of Labor spokesperson. 
“The restoration was an executive/ administrative decision and not a new act of Congress,” spokesman Will Hoenike said in an email. “We received funding this year, both competitively and formula-funding, through funds that were appropriated by Congress.”

title: DA declines to prosecute fatal Burger King shooting by Memphis Safe Task Force
description: The Shelby County District Attorney will not pursue charges in the fatal shooting of a man inside a Burger King by a federal agent assigned to the Memphis Safe Task Force, District Attorney Steve Mulroy’s office announced Monday. Darrin Pigram, 41, was killed during his work shift at the restaurant May 13 when Drug Enforcement […]
text:
Shelby County District Attorney Steve Mulroy has declined to prosecute a Drug Enforcement Administration agent's fatal shooting of 41-year-old Darrin Pigram. Pictured: a makeshift memorial outside Burger King, where Pigram was killed by officers serving a warrant as part of the Memphis Safe Task Force. (Photo by Brad Vest for the Tennessee Lookout)The Shelby County District Attorney will not pursue charges in the fatal shooting of a man inside a Burger King by a federal agent assigned to the Memphis Safe Task Force, District Attorney Steve Mulroy’s office announced Monday.
Darrin Pigram, 41, was killed during his work shift at the restaurant May 13 when Drug Enforcement Administration officers entered to serve a warrant.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Pigram’s death was the first of four fatal shootings this year by officers assigned to the Memphis Safe Task Force.  All four deadly encounters were referred to the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, which investigates officer-involved shootings. 
The district attorney concluded “the use of deadly force was legally justified and that the evidence does not support a reasonable likelihood of conviction.” The conclusion was based on a review of evidence, the TBI’s investigation in Pigram’s death and state law governing use of force by law enforcement, a news release from Mulroy’s office on Monday said.
Andre Wharton, a Memphis attorney representing Pigram’s family, said Monday that Pigram’s parents and siblings were “disappointed and befuddled” by the decision. 
Pigram was shot eight times in front of coworkers, Wharton said, citing information shared with the family by the district attorney’s office.
Family demands answers after Memphis Task Force agent kills man at Burger King

Since Pigram’s death, family members have reviewed portions of the restaurant surveillance video in the district attorney’s office. Wharton also reviewed the district attorney’s “declination letter,” describing the office’s decision not to pursue criminal charges.
“The report concludes that deadly force was necessary because Mr. Pigram lifted his shirt, reached for a firearm, and became aggressive,” Wharton said. “The video we viewed does not show those actions. Instead, it shows an encounter that unfolded in seconds, with Mr. Pigram backing away as the agent suddenly rushed toward him before opening fire.”
“We respectfully disagree with the decision not to pursue charges, but today’s report does not end our pursuit of the truth,” he said. “Our focus remains exactly where it has been from the beginning: transparency, accountability, and justice.”
The eight-page declination letter was also released Monday by the Shelby County District Attorney’s office. The letter from District Attorney Steve Mulroy is addressed to the U.S. Marshals Service Director Gadyaces Serralta. The U.S. Marshals Service is the lead agency of the Memphis Safe Task Force, established in September by President Donald Trump to combat crime in Memphis. There are 2,700 personnel currently attached to the task force, according to the Marshals Service.
The letter, which misspells Pigram’s name and cites an incorrect date for his shooting death, describes the sequence of events leading up to and including Pigram’s fatal shooting:
Man fatally shot in second Memphis Safe Task Force use-of-force incident this week

Officers from the Memphis Police Department and Drug Enforcement Administration arrived to serve a warrant on Pigram at his workplace after first attempting to locate him at his home.
The warrant stemmed from a January altercation with neighbors over loud music, according to court records. Pigram allegedly brandished a gun at the neighbors. Court records show Pigram has one previous misdemeanor conviction in Shelby County.
A Memphis police officer first entered the restaurant, then reported back to four DEA agents. All four of the DEA agents then entered the Burger King, according to the letter. None of the DEA agents were wearing body-worn cameras, the letter noted.
Two DEA agents carried rifles in their hands as they entered the restaurant.  Pigram behind the counter. They asked Pigram to step out. Pigram complied, walking to the employee-only door and opening it. According to one of the agents, Pigram then became “visually and verbally aggressive” after learning he was being served an arrest warrant. 
Two agents told investigators that, as they approached an employee door to reach Pigram, he attempted to “push the agents off” and “close the door between himself and the agents.” One agent described a “pulling match” at the door between Pigram and a DEA officer. 
But a footnote in the declination letter notes that “camera footage of the physical activity between Mr. Pigram and (the DEA agent) does not support these claims of aggressive action at the doorway.”
“The video showed that Mr. Pigram walked to the employee-only door, opened it with his left hand, and stood holding the door open,” the footnote said.
The cameras in the restaurant were stationery, capturing Pigram and law enforcement officers as they moved in and out of view. The restaurant cameras did not record audio of the incident, the letter noted.
As one DEA agent stood on the customer side of the front counter with his rifle in his hands, another DEA agent who had been out of view of the restaurant camera “suddenly burst back into view as he surged through the door and appeared to shove Mr. Pigram backward into the front counter area. Mr. Pigram continued to move backward as (the agent) appeared to continue to rush toward Mr. Pigram,” the footnote read.
National Guard troops on patrol in Memphis fatally shoot 20-year-old man,  according to TBI

The report cited three DEA agents reporting Mr. Pigram made statements to the effect of “no” and “shoot me.”
One DEA agent reported that, because Mr. Pigram raised his hands “in fists,” another agent responded by slinging his rifle onto his shoulder “so he could ‘go hands on’ with Mr. Pigram.”
The agent’s action in slinging his rifle onto his shoulder prompted a fellow DEA agent to jump the front counter behind him. “Thereafter, the agents appeared to move forward in tandem,” the letter said. 
The DEA agent who ultimately fired the fatal shots said Pigram began moving his shirt as he approached. The agent said he “saw Mr. Pilgrim’s gun in his waistband and realized Mr.Pigram was reaching for that weapon.” 
The agent fired three shots and then “several more,” he said. He said he feared for his life.
Pigram staggered back and came to rest on the floor under the drive-through window, the letter said.  Other agents said they saw a gun in Mr. Pigram’s waistband. 
“Video confirmed the bulk of the officers’ account, although it did not clearly show the actual shooting itself,” a statement from the district attorney’s office said. The statement noted, based on witnesses, that it was “not unusual for (Pigram) to be armed while working at the Burger King.
Wharton, the Pigram family attorney, noted Monday that Mulroy’s letter contains “factual errors and internal inconsistencies. In several places, its own discussion of the video conflicts with the conclusions it ultimately reaches. Those inconsistencies deserve answers, not silence.”
“The family has never asked for special treatment,” Wharton said. “They have asked only for a complete, transparent, and objective evaluation of what happened on May 13. That request remains unchanged today.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Stitching a life back together: North Carolina’s push to improve reentry services
description: It is hard to imagine finding hope in a steel cargo container. But Shirlye Grandy sees life, fellowship and beauty in the metal box that sits on the Dix Park campus in Raleigh. Grandy served nearly six years in the N.C. Correctional Institution for Women, but now holds the title of public arts project coordinator […]
text:
Two visitors learn about the challenges facing incarcerated women during a visit to the Stitching Stories Reimagined display at Dix Park on July 14, 2026. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)It is hard to imagine finding hope in a steel cargo container. But Shirlye Grandy sees life, fellowship and beauty in the metal box that sits on the Dix Park campus in Raleigh.
Grandy served nearly six years in the N.C. Correctional Institution for Women, but now holds the title of public arts project coordinator for Arise Collective, a Raleigh nonprofit dedicated to helping incarcerated women across the state.
Grandy told members of the N.C. Joint Reentry Council last week that her life was profoundly changed in 2019 when she joined a small group of women at NCCIW crocheting items to be donated and sold. The proceeds were used to help parents on the outside bring children to see those who were incarcerated.
But when COVID-19 hit, everything changed. Prison visits and classes were canceled. There was no outside work. In the minimum custody unit where Grandy and the other women were housed, more than 100 prisoners contracted the virus in one week.
Shirlye Grandy shared her story with the N.C. Joint Reentry Council on July 14, 2026. (Screen grab: North Carolina Department of Adult Correction video)
“But what that did was it brought us together as sisters in incarceration,” Grandy said. “It turned into something much larger. It showed that we are determined, we have life, and we are not giving up.”
The women of H.A.T.S. – that’s Handmade and Totally Special – used each week to crochet. Each colorful section joined together represented a year that a woman served behind bars.
Grandy recalled carefully crocheting six squares to mark her own sentence.
“My friend Faye Brown, who passed away from COVID, had 40,” Grandy told the reentry council.
When the 25-foot-long prison quilt was finished just before Mother’s Day 2021, other incarcerated women were invited to tie ribbons to the squares to recognize the children they left behind and the lives lost by family and friends while they were in prison.
According to research by The Sentencing Project, the U.S. has seen a 525% increase in the number of incarcerated women between 1980 and 2021, roughly twice the rate of increase for men. Eighty percent of incarcerated women are mothers.
Grandy lost her own mother during her incarceration.
Jennifer Jackson, chief executive officer for Arise Collective, says opportunity for the crocheters struck two years later when the Z. Smith Reynolds Foundation and the Mellon Foundation issued a grant proposal to create permanent public art to tell the stories of historically marginalized communities.
“There’s a community of people who have been touched by incarceration across our state that has been hidden,” said Jackson. “We made a pitch that they consider this a community, as we were defining it, as one that fit within their grant guidelines.”
The foundations selected Arise and the Stitching Stories Quilt to be reimagined and transformed for the public.
Four artists — Carlos González García, David Wilson, Eliza Redmann and Owens Daniels — spent the next three years transforming the crocheted quilt into a durable mosaic that captures the lives of the often-forgotten women. On the opposite wall of the shipping container, a mirrored wall portrays the original artists with the phrase, “We are you.”

 







Two visitors learn about the challenges facing incarcerated women during a visit to the Stitching Stories Reimagined display at Dix Park on July 14, 2026. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)









80% of incarcerated women are mothers. Each white ribbons represents a child left behind. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)









Each square represents a year that a woman served behind bars. The red ribbon represents a life lost during COVID. Incarcerated people were infected by COVID at a rate 5 times higher than the national rate. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)









A mirrored wall inside the cargo container portrays the original  artists and the phrase "We are you."  (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)









Two visitors to the art installation read about the women behind the Stitching Stories project. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)









The artwork will be displayed on the Dix Park campus until September when it will move to Wilmington. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)






The work will be displayed on the Dix Park campus until September when it will move to Wilmington.
The project is also an opportunity for the public to learn more about mass incarceration and the challenges that arise after leaving prison.
Each year, more than 18,000 individuals are released from North Carolina state prisons. Without a support network, 49% of those are rearrested within two years.
North Carolina is part of a national initiative to reduce the recidivism rate by 30% by 2030. Its goal is to improve reentry services that help people leaving prison find employment, healthcare and housing. Formerly incarcerated people are up to 10 times more likely to experience homelessness than the general population.
Grandy credits Arise Collective with helping her successfully transition to a better life after her release. This summer, she’s giving tours of the Stitching Stories exhibit.
She told those gathered at the All Faiths Chapel at Dix last week that while she never liked to talk about herself, she was proud of what her quilting sisters had accomplished.
“In a space that could have been the most dangerous and disastrous and dark place, we created light and beauty,” Grandy said.
Later this year, Grandy will complete her master’s program at Duke Divinity School. She said others who have served their time also deserve a second chance.
“None of that would be possible without good transition programs,” Grandy said, ”places where women like me who want to do something different with their life after incarceration have a place to go and grow and learn how to be a person again.”
The artwork will be on display at Dix Park in Raleigh until September. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama birth center licenses still valid despite appellate court ruling, says Montgomery judge
description: A Montgomery County judge ruled Sunday that the state’s birth centers can keep operating despite an appellate court ruling earlier this year that declared them hospitals subject to regulation by the Alabama Department of Public Health. The ruling came after ADPH State Health Officer Dr. Scott Harris sent cease-and-desist letters to the birth centers — […]
text:
A room is seen at the Alabama Birth Center in Huntsville, Alabama on Wednesday, April 15, 2026. A Montgomery County judge on Sunday ruled that the state's birth centers can continue operating despite a higher court's ruling that the centers are hospitals. (Eric Schultz for Alabama Reflector)A Montgomery County judge ruled Sunday that the state’s birth centers can keep operating despite an appellate court ruling earlier this year that declared them hospitals subject to regulation by the Alabama Department of Public Health.
The ruling came after ADPH State Health Officer Dr. Scott Harris sent cease-and-desist letters to the birth centers — which provide an option between home and hospital birth — in June.
ADPH said temporary licenses, granted in 2024 under a 2023 order, were “null and void” and that the birth centers “must ‘cease and desist’ [their] operations as a freestanding birth center until’ they receive a new license based on compliance with the regulations, according to court documents.  
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
But Montgomery Circuit Court Judge Greg Griffin, who granted the temporary licenses in 2024, wrote in his order on Sunday that the law has not changed since those temporary licenses were issued.
“As such, the preliminary injunction assumes that defendant can require birth centers to obtain a ‘hospital’ license to operate but sets limits on the requirements he can impose on birth centers as a condition of receiving such a hospital license, including by preventing the defendant from requiring compliance with the regulations,” he wrote.
Oasis Family Birthing Center in Birmingham and Alabama Birth Center in Huntsville filed the suit against ADPH in 2023, a few months after the agency adopted new regulations requiring centers to be under the oversight of a physician or medical director and to be within 30 minutes of a hospital with OB-GYN services. 
The centers, which provide an in-between option for individuals who do not feel comfortable with a home birth but prefer an out-of-hospital birth, said the regulations would make it difficult or impossible for them to provide services around the state, particularly in rural areas that lack hospitals.  
The Alabama Court of Civil Appeals in January ruled that ADPH can regulate freestanding birthing centers as hospitals under 1949 state law. The lawsuit went back to the circuit court over 12 other complaints after the Alabama Supreme Court declined to take up the main question of the suit, whether or not birth centers are hospitals under state law. 
A message seeking comment from ADPH on Monday was referred to the Alabama Attorney General’s Office. A message seeking comment from Harris’ attorney Ben Albritton was left on Monday. 
Whitney White, an attorney with the ACLU Reproductive Freedom Project representing the clinics, said in a statement Monday that they will continue until access to pregnancy care and birth centers are permanently protected.
“More than two-and-a-half years ago, the court recognized that birth centers provide essential care to their communities, and that preventing them from operating in accordance with national standards while this case is ongoing would cause immeasurable harm to the birth centers and the pregnant Alabamians who need their care,” White said. “Yesterday’s order merely confirms that status quo and that the court’s 2023 preliminary injunction remains in place.”
According to the American Association of Birth Centers, 0.3% of births take place in a birth center in the United States, where midwives and doulas take care of expectant mothers. All patients who give birth in birth centers are healthy and low-risk, while about 85% who give birth in hospitals are considered low-risk.
Alabama has long struggled with high maternal mortality and difficulties in accessing prenatal care. According to state data released in November, the state’s infant mortality rate was 7.1 babies per 1,000 live births in 2024, reflecting the rate of infants who died within their first year of life. That was down from 7.8 deaths per 1,000 births in 2023, according to state data. There were 414 infant deaths in 2024. Of those, 222 of the deaths were white babies and 176 were Black babies, the lowest recorded number for Black infants. 
But infant mortality rates for Black Alabamians remain far higher than those of white Alabamians. The infant mortality rate among white Alabamians was 5.4 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2024. For Black Alabamians, the rate was 11.8 per 1,000. In 2023, the rates were 5.7 and 13.1 deaths per 1,000 births, respectively.

description: Tennessee’s agriculture commissioner used his position to pressure the Tennessee Farm Bureau to cut ties with an agent after a personal dispute, a lawsuit filed in Weakley County alleges.  Bryant Rhodes, a Weakley County insurance agent, filed the lawsuit on July 15 alleging state Agriculture Commissioner Andy Holt, after an altercation at a land auction, […[...]
text:
Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Andy Holt, with hat, is accused in a lawsuit of pressuring the Tennessee Farm Bureau to cut ties with a long term agent. Photo from a Sept. 5, 2025 forum with Republican candidates in a special election for the 7th Congressional District. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee’s agriculture commissioner used his position to pressure the Tennessee Farm Bureau to cut ties with an agent after a personal dispute, a lawsuit filed in Weakley County alleges. 
Bryant Rhodes, a Weakley County insurance agent, filed the lawsuit on July 15 alleging state Agriculture Commissioner Andy Holt, after an altercation at a land auction, pressured the Farm Bureau to cut ties with him.
“Holt, understanding his influence over (the) Farm Bureau as Commissioner of Agriculture… began to use this false story he created to pressure Farm Bureau into terminating Rhodes,” Ross Webster, Rhodes’s lawyer, alleges in the complaint. 
Webster went on to add that as part of the pressure campaign to get Rhodes fired, the Farm Bureau was “already worried about upsetting Holt” because at the time it “would not publicly endorse” U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn for Governor.
The Farm Bureau cut ties with Rhodes shortly after Holt pressured them too, and he has struggled to find work because of the “misinformation campaign.” 
Holt did not respond to the Lookout. 
Tennessee Agriculture Commission Andy Holt. left, and U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, right, at a Blackburn for Governor event. (Photo: Marsh Blackburn Facebook Page, posted on May 30, 2026)
Holt was appointed by Gov. Bill Lee as Agriculture Commissioner in October 2025, after serving as the deputy head at the agency the year before. He replaced retiring commissioner Charlie Hatcher, who is running for the Republican nomination to the 5th Congressional District. 
Prior to that, Holt served a decade in Tennessee’s state House, where he had a reputation for controversy.
He posted a doctored photo in 2019 on social media insulting a former Republican state House candidate’s physical appearance after the candidate criticized an ally of Holt’s, the Jackson Sun previously reported. 
Holt was also accused of dumping more than half a million gallons of hog waste and dead hogs in a creek near his farm and was granted special treatment by state regulators, according to a NewsChannel 5 report in 2015. 
Tennessee’s Little Hatch Act law bans executive office officials from using their “official position, authority, or influence to interfere with an election or nomination for office.”
Holt appeared in a photo with Blackburn at a campaign event earlier this year. 
The Tennessee Farm Bureau has not endorsed any candidate in the race.
The lawsuit alleges that Holt’s push for Rhodes’ firing started after Rhodes publicly called out Holt over his attempt to drive up the price of land Rhodes was looking to purchase in April 2026. Holt then “chased Rhodes and confronted him, calling him childish and overall behaved in an inappropriate and embarrassing manner towards Rhodes.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: A former AIPAC-linked group is now supporting Abdul El-Sayed to elect a doctor to the U.S. Senate
description: 314 Action, a national organization that works to recruit, train and elect scientists, doctors, nurses and healthcare professionals, on Tuesday endorsed the campaign of Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of Detroit. What is surprising about the effort is that 314 Action Fund was once linked to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, and wa[...]
text:
U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks at a rally with U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and U.S. House candidate William Lawrence in Lansing, Mich., on July 19, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)314 Action, a national organization that works to recruit, train and elect scientists, doctors, nurses and healthcare professionals, on Tuesday endorsed the campaign of Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of Detroit.
What is surprising about the effort is that 314 Action Fund was once linked to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, and was one of the groups that AIPAC diverted money to through its super PAC in the 2024 cycle. 
314 Action Fund told Michigan Advance on Monday that it is not affiliated with AIPAC. Given that history, it is notable that the group plans to support El-Sayed and spend on his behalf.
The outside money is sorely needed for El-Sayed as he runs against U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham), whose campaign has seen nearly $50 million in outside spending on her behalf.
314 Action in a news release said that as an epidemiologist and doctor, El-Sayed is one of their Guardians of Public Health, who is answering the call to serve his community. The Guardians of Public Health effort aims to elect 100 new doctors, nurses and healthcare professionals to Congress and down to the local level by 2030. The group has raised and spent more than $25 million on that effort thus far.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“As an epidemiologist and a doctor, Abdul El-Sayed saw firsthand how broken the healthcare system was and how broken policies are making Michiganders sick. He’s already proven he can make change — as a public servant, Abdul secured free glasses for kids, removed lead from Detroit’s elementary schools and spearheaded a program that will cancel up to $700 million in medical debt for 300,000 Michiganders,” Shaughnessy Naughton, president of 314 Action, said in a statement. “As Trump and Republicans gut Medicaid, SNAP, and public health programs, we need new, bold, progressive leaders like Abdul working to create systemic change. He has the vision, grassroots support, and proven experience to win. We’re proud to endorse Abdul for the U.S. Senate and look forward to supporting his campaign.”
El-Sayed praised the organization and thanked them for their support.
“As the only national organization working to elect doctors and scientists, 314 Action understands that electing career politicians isn’t working,” El-Sayed said in a statement. “I never planned on getting into politics, but when I realized that our healthcare system set Americans up to fail, I had to make a change. The reality is that too many working families are facing impossible decisions that are sometimes life or death. Michiganders deserve better. I’m proud to have 314 Action’s support in this fight and I look forward to working with them in Congress.”
In June, Dave Weigel of Semafor wrote a piece detailing what he referred to as the “toxicity” of AIPAC spending in Democratic primaries. The piece noted that 314 Action Fund fell into that “new, messy reality” in 2014, when it received $1 million from the United Democracy PAC, which was labeled as one of AIPAC’s first campaign committees. That effort in 2024 was aimed at helping current U.S. Rep. Maxine Dexter (D-Oregon) get elected. Dexter has since voted against sending military aid to Israel and renounced AIPAC.
314 Action has since moved to distance itself from the controversial American lobby group for Israel.
In a statement to the Advance, 314 Action Executive Director Erik Polyak said that, “for 10 years, 314 Action has focused on one mission: to recruit, train, and elect Democrats with backgrounds in science and medicine.”
“We’re the only national organization doing this work, and we’re proud that we’ve helped elect more than 700 scientists and doctors at every level of government while raising nearly $100 million from over 550,000 supporters,” Polyak said. “We do not screen, evaluate, or prescribe foreign policy positions to our endorsed candidates — that isn’t why we exist and does not determine who we choose to support.”
Polyak also said that 314 Action “has not taken money from AIPAC or any affiliated entity this cycle, and we won’t.”
“From Michigan to Pennsylvania to Maine, we’re watching our opponents weaponize disinformation to smear us in races where we’ve backed strong candidates like Abdul El-Sayed — and we won’t stand idly by and watch that happen.”
Despite its former AIPAC connection, the group said it is now turning to El-Sayed in a bid to propel the first Democratic doctor to the upper chamber of Congress — which hasn’t happened since former U.S. Sen. Ernest Gruening was elected in 1959 to represent Alaska and ended his tenure in 1969. Gruening studied medicine but did not practice.

title: Third round of FEMA funding aids 2025 storm recovery for North Dakota
description: The Federal Emergency Management Agency has approved more than $682,000 to assist North Dakota recover from June 2025 storms, the third round of disaster relief funding this year. The funds awarded, $334,000 to Nodak Electric Cooperative Inc, and  $348,000 to Northern Plains Electric Cooperative, will be used to replace electric poles and power lines damaged[...]
text:
An agricultural outbuilding was damaged near Medina, N.D., during a storm on June 20, 2025. The National Weather Service in Bismarck confirmed a tornado near Medina, with a preliminary rating of EF1. (Photo courtesy of National Weather Service-Bismarck)The Federal Emergency Management Agency has approved more than $682,000 to assist North Dakota recover from June 2025 storms, the third round of disaster relief funding this year.
The funds awarded, $334,000 to Nodak Electric Cooperative Inc, and  $348,000 to Northern Plains Electric Cooperative, will be used to replace electric poles and power lines damaged in the storm, and make other electrical repairs or replacements, according to a FEMA news release on Monday.
In a July 2025 letter sent to President Donald Trump, North Dakota’s federal delegation said the disaster destroyed homes and businesses, but also negatively impacted the state’s rural electric cooperatives. Damage from the June 2025 storms were estimated to have caused $11.7 million in damages.
“While the State of North Dakota put numerous resources and measures in place to protect its residents prior to, during, and after the derecho event, the storm system caused unavoidable damages to infrastructure and property, and tragically took the lives of 4 North Dakotans,” said U.S. Sens. Kevin Cramer, John Hoeven and U.S. Rep. Julie Fedorchak, in a statement.
Governor pledges state support for storm victims while touring eastern North Dakota damage

In June, FEMA also awarded about $822,000 to North Dakota due to the storms last year. More than $422,000 of those funds went to the Minnkota Power Cooperative to restore electrical transmission power systems and about $400,000 to the University of Jamestown to fund repairs to the school sports complex.
The federal agency awarded an additional $650,000 to the state on July 9 in support of community resilience and recovery grants.
The state is also making requests for federal assistance in response to storms in 2026.
Gov. Kelly Armstrong requested Trump declare a presidential major disaster declaration for storms occurring last month, June 7-9, that caused an estimated $4.6 million in damage. The storms damaged parts of Bottineau, Burke, Divide, McLean, Mercer, Oliver and Williams counties. Armstrong declared a state disaster as a result of those storms on June 30.
“Just as communities were starting to clean up from the first round of storms on June 7, another round hit two days later, compounding the damage and complicating response and recovery for our citizens,” Armstrong said in a statement. “We appreciate the administration considering this request to help cover the cost of significant damage to public infrastructure from this one-two punch.”

text:
The August primary election features several hotly contested congressional races and an open governor's seat. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)More than 75,000 Tennessee voters cast their ballots in the first two days of early voting for the August primary election, according to data released by the Tennessee Secretary of State’s office.
That outpaces the same early voting period in the 2022 primary election by nearly 24,000 voters — a 47% increase.
This year’s ballot includes multiple high-profile competitive primaries, including a gubernatorial race with no incumbent and several races for newly redrawn U.S. Congressional districts.
Republicans U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, U.S. Rep. John Rose and state Rep. Monty Fritts are vying for a spot on the November gubernatorial ballot. Democratic primary contenders include Memphis City Council member Jerri Green, Memphian Carnita Atwater, farmer Tim Cyr and Nashville-based steel guitar player Adam Kurtz.
Statewide, voters submitted 48,378 Republican ballots and 24,520 Democratic ballots, according to state data. 

SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE 
The number of Democratic primary ballots eclipsed Republican ballots in four counties, including the state’s two most populous: Shelby County and Davidson County. Both counties have been long-time Democratic strongholds, and 2026 marks the first year that both are gerrymandered into multiple districts in an effort to give Republican candidates the upper hand.
Hardeman and Haywood counties in West Tennessee also saw more Democratic ballots pulled than Republican by a narrower margin.
Tennessee’s 17 urban counties saw primary voter turnout during the first two days of early voting increase 72% from 2022. Rural counties saw a 27% increase.
Notably, Gov. Bill Lee, the incumbent, ran unopposed in the 2022 Republican primary election, which may partly account for lower 2022 voter turnout. On the Democratic primary ballot, Jason Martin narrowly defeated Memphis Councilmember JB Smiley Jr.
But the 2022 primary also debuted a 5th U.S. Congressional district that broke the boundaries of Davidson County. Incumbent Jim Cooper, a Nashville Democrat who represented Nashville for two decades, bowed out of the race. State Sen. Heidi Campbell, a Nashville Democrat, ran unopposed on the Democratic primary ticket, but the Republican ticket was crowded with nine candidates. Maury County Republican Andy Ogles ultimately won the seat.

text:
VTDigger reporters Shaun Robinson and Ethan Weinstein work in the cafeteria at the Statehouse in Montpelier on Friday, January 16, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Dear Reader,
When I accepted the opportunity to become VTDigger’s CEO, I did it because I believe Vermont deserves ambitious, independent journalism.
And I am asking you to help make that possible.
This week, we’re inviting 500 readers to support VTDigger. If you’ve been thinking about making a contribution, please join us today.

Support VTDigger

One of the things I’ve enjoyed most during my first few weeks at VTDigger is meeting readers. Because we live and work in the communities we serve, those conversations happen everywhere from the grocery store to the post office.
Recently, a couple stopped me to say, “We so appreciate all of your work to keep us informed. We don’t know what we’d do without VTDigger.” Another supporter told me they’d lost trust in much of the national media and now rely on VTDigger for accurate, independent reporting about Vermont.
Those conversations stay with me. They remind me that earning and keeping readers’ trust isn’t something we can take for granted. It’s something our newsroom constantly works to earn.
Every day, reporters are asking hard questions, digging into complex issues and helping Vermonters better understand the decisions shaping our communities. That’s the kind of journalism your support makes possible.
And we’re building on that work.
Later this summer, we’ll publish an ambitious reporting collaboration with FRONTLINE examining the lasting impacts of Vermont’s recent flooding. We’re preparing for statewide election coverage that readers will rely on through November. And we’ll continue investing in investigative reporting that helps Vermonters understand not just what happened, but why it matters.
Roughly half a million people rely on VTDigger’s news every month, but only a small percentage financially support this work. Every contribution helps us spend more time reporting, asking questions and holding institutions accountable.
If you believe Vermont deserves that kind of journalism, please make a gift today.

Support Vermont news

Thank you for welcoming me to VTDigger and for being part of the community that powers this newsroom.
Sincerely,

Brendan Kinney

title: Death row inmate seeks replacement of physician in charge of botched execution
description: A death row inmate is asking the Tennessee Supreme Court to replace the physician in charge of a botched execution in May or appoint a special master to consider his claim that a scheduled Aug. 13 execution could be unconstitutional. In a Monday Chancery Court filing, attorneys for inmate Darrell Hines cited the risk of […]
text:
A death row inmate is asking the Tennessee Supreme Court to replace the physician to be use for his August 13 execution by lethal injection. (Photo by Mike Simons/Getty Images)A death row inmate is asking the Tennessee Supreme Court to replace the physician in charge of a botched execution in May or appoint a special master to consider his claim that a scheduled Aug. 13 execution could be unconstitutional.
In a Monday Chancery Court filing, attorneys for inmate Darrell Hines cited the risk of extreme pain and suffering if the state uses the same doctor who was in charge when the state tried and failed to execute Tony Carruthers in May. The move comes after a Davidson County judge required the Department of Correction to reveal whether the same physician will perform Hines’ lethal injection.
Chancellor Russell Perkins granted the request of Hines’ attorneys, compelling the Department of Correction to disclose whether Dr. Mark Fowler will oversee Hines’ execution after they argued that his lack of medical skills contributed to the failed execution of Carruthers and could cause Hines to suffer through a similar botched procedure, according to a release from Hines’ legal team. Carruthers is on death row for a triple murder.
State ordered to state whether it will use doctor involved in failed execution

“It’s unconscionable that TDOC continues to withhold this information,” said Hines’ attorney, Kit Thomas. 
The state has claimed a secrecy law enables it to conceal the physician’s identity and whether it plans to use Fowler, even though it has publicly disclosed his name, according to the release. 
The physician tried for more than an hour to insert backup and central intravenous lines on Carruthers, as required by protocol, before Gov. Bill Lee called off the execution and postponed it for a year. Witnesses called it a bloody “torture.”
Attorneys for Hines, who is convicted of the 1985 rape and murder of motel maid Catherine Jenkins in Kingston Springs, point out that Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol requires the execution physician to be able to insert a central line but that Fowler acknowledged in a court document he had performed the procedure about 12 times in an emergency room but not since 2013 and doesn’t have privileges to conduct one at any hospital.
Lee declined to postpone the Hines execution and two others set for this year even though a group of Republican senators urged him to commission an independent review of the botched execution and correct any problems before the state attempts another one.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Chemours lawsuit settlement: Another round of destructive environmental denialism
description: To say that 21st Century humanity finds itself in a time of dire and unprecedented environmental crisis is an increasingly obvious and undeniable fact. Thanks to climate change, warming and rising oceans, desertification, the poisoning of air, land and water, species extinction, and dozens of other destructive trends, billions of people are confronting life-[...]
text:
An aerial view of the Chemours Fayetteville Works plant in northern Bladen County. For more than 30 years Chemours and its predecessor, DuPont, discharged “forever chemicals” into the Cape Fear River. (Photo: Chemours)To say that 21st Century humanity finds itself in a time of dire and unprecedented environmental crisis is an increasingly obvious and undeniable fact. Thanks to climate change, warming and rising oceans, desertification, the poisoning of air, land and water, species extinction, and dozens of other destructive trends, billions of people are confronting life-altering changes in the world around them that are leading to hardship, the abandonment of long-established ways of life, mass migration and conflict.
Put more simply, we live in a time in which humans are slowly drowning in their own effluent and if we don’t get our act together very soon, the chances that we and our descendants will experience a series of rapidly metastasizing disasters mounts every day.
So, what to do?
Seen from a global perspective, the answers are not that complicated. Humans must bring a rapid end to their opioid-like addiction to fossil fuels, end mass deforestation, develop ways to dramatically curb polluting chemicals, and reduce and manage their solid waste.
Unfortunately, as anyone who’s contemplated cranking down the AC on a steamy, sleepless night can attest, effecting these kinds of fundamental global overhauls in how we live is much easier said than done when it comes to making decisions at the local and individual levels.
And this is especially true when people in positions of leadership pay only lip service to addressing the massive challenges we face or even deny their existence at all.
North Carolinians – particularly those who reside in the state’s southeastern region — are watching this latter scenario play out right now in the way the Trump administration is failing to respond to the problems posed by the chemical pollutant known as GenX and the family of “forever chemicals” to which it belongs known as PFAS.
As award-winning journalist Lisa Sorg has documented over a period of several years for Inside Climate News and NC Newsline, these chemicals – which have been scientifically linked to a host of human health problems – are used to manufacture Teflon coatings, stain-, grease- and water-resistant materials, and other consumer products. They get their “forever” moniker from the fact that, when released into the air or water, they do not break down but instead persist in the environment for hundreds of years.
For decades, a company known as Chemours spewed vast quantities of PFAS into the air and water surrounding its facility in Cumberland County – a fact that has led to what experts say is widespread and dangerous pollution of public water systems and private wells across the surrounding region. A series of lawsuits and regulatory actions designed to make the company clean up its act and compensate the affected people and institutions followed.
Not surprisingly, however, forcing a giant corporation armed with a fleet of lawyers and political connections to admit its errors and the damage those errors have caused – much less pay an adequate sum to rectify them – is always an uphill fight.
This brings us back to the matter of public leadership. As with virtually every other matter of environmental regulation it has touched since January of 2025, the Trump Environmental Protection Agency has sought to downplay the effects of PFAS and other forever chemicals and roll back public safety and health regulations.
And this trend was manifested most recently and destructively in a proposed lawsuit settlement that EPA announced last week.
Under the proposed terms, Chemours would be required to fund a series of water clean-up and pollution mitigation efforts in West Virginia, New Jersey and North Carolina, but as numerous critics have pointed out, none of the thousands of individual plaintiffs in the lawsuit will get their day in court to describe their pain and property loss. What’s more, the ultimate payout toward cleaning up Chemours’ mess will likely amount to a relative pittance.
As North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson rightly observed in a scathing joint statement with Gov. Josh Stein, the proposal gives Chemours vast authority over how funds will be allotted and could end up leading to the expenditure of as little as $2 million per year to address water pollution in North Carolian that’s impacted hundreds of thousands of North Carolinians.
“Our state is ground zero for GenX contamination,” Jackson said, “but this deal does practically nothing to clean up our water. Chemours made this mess, and Chemours should clean it up.”
Stein echoed that assessment, saying, “This deal does nothing meaningful for North Carolinians. This EPA, which has already weakened protections against chemicals like GenX, is now allowing polluters to pick and choose how and where they’ll fix their contamination – leaving North Carolina with no guarantees.”
In short, the proposed settlement – click here to learn more and here to submit a comment – if ratified, stands to become just the latest a long and disastrous series of decisions in which humans have put the toxic combination of corporate greed and head-in-the-sand environmental denialism ahead of the common, near- and long-term good. And as even a casual glance at the world around us makes clear, the window for making these kinds of shortsighted decisions is rapidly closing.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Public Charter School Commission approves new merger policy
description: The Alabama Public Charter School Commission last week approved a new policy that would allow charter schools to merge under one governing board.  APCSC Executive Director Logan Searcy said during the commission’s meeting that the new policy could be used in case of an “enrollment concern.” “Our charter schools and our traditional school systems are […]
text:
A high school classroom in Florida. The Alabama Public Charter School Commission last week approved a new policy that would allow two or more charter schools to merge. (Getty)The Alabama Public Charter School Commission last week approved a new policy that would allow charter schools to merge under one governing board. 
APCSC Executive Director Logan Searcy said during the commission’s meeting that the new policy could be used in case of an “enrollment concern.”
“Our charter schools and our traditional school systems are funded on the number of students we have. So if enrollment declines, then the state funding also declines,” Searcy said in an interview on Friday. “So we don’t want that to be a situation for our charters, so we are just looking toward the future, so that if such a situation were to occur, we would have a mechanism for them to be able to merge, to have an enrollment that would be sustainable financially.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Searcy said lack of awareness of school choice options is why enrollment could be lower with some charter schools, and that the commission is working to increase awareness.
“Enrollment is a matter of awareness of engaging parents, and so we want to have quite a bit of community engagement and parent engagement as well, so that parents know that the charter school is there and can give parents that educational choice, that option, and so I think that we’re working on getting that word out there,” she said.
Under the new policy, two charter schools operating as local education agencies under the same non-profit can also merge to consolidate campuses.
The policy states that merger applications should also be submitted at least 12 months ahead of the proposed effective date to give time for officials to meet Alabama State Department of Education deadlines.
To have a strong application, schools must have a clear, evidence-based reason for wanting to merge; academic results from all participating schools that show why a merger is needed; a detailed budget demonstrating the financial impact of the merger; a detailed implementation plan; clear support from parents, staff and community partners of all schools and must demonstrate the capacity of the remaining governing board that will oversee the schools.
“I think it’s very needed,” Commissioner Charles Knight said during the meeting. “I think that several other schools might take advantage of this,” he said.
Searcy said during the meeting that merger applications would be available for charter schools this summer. 
During the 2026 regular session, the Alabama Legislature passed a constitutional amendment that would allow two or more county boards of education to consolidate into one multi-county board of education. The amendment will appear on a future ballot.

A member asked, “Is that thunder?”
“It’s your tax payers,” someone responded. 
Dozens of residents attended the meeting to protest a contract with Flock Safety, which would cost the city $2.1 million over five years for audio detection, live video cameras, drone services and license plate reader cameras. Not all of the residents could fit into council chambers, so many were upstairs waiting as the meeting lasted from 7:30 p.m. Monday until nearly 4 a.m. Tuesday. 
Two days later, the American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia announced it was filing a lawsuit against the city and Mayor Patrick Farrell, a Republican.
Flock cameras have been around for less than a decade, but have been rapidly expanding. Last October, it was announced that Amazon’s Ring would partner with Flock, trying to spin the partnership as a way for people to help find lost pets. Customers didn’t buy it, and Ring canceled the partnership in February. 
Private businesses are already using them throughout the state. A crowdsourced map by Deflock shows there are about 636 Flock cameras throughout the Mountain State. 
Ever go to Target in Kanawha County? There are three advanced license plate reader cameras in the parking lots at the Trace Fork shopping center in South Charleston. 
After the outcry in Huntington, news outlets all over the state are looking into Flock contracts. Putnam County entered into a contract with Flock in June 2025, and placed eight cameras, which have not been activated yet, according to WOWK. Putnam County Sheriff Bobby Eggleton said the project has been paused.
Obviously people are worried about privacy with these cameras, but as with other types of artificial intelligence, there’s a lot of room for error.
In Minnesota, a man was pulled over by four police cars after his car was flagged by Flock cameras as having stolen plates. It turns out, the license plate number had been entered into the National Crime Information Center database with incomplete numbers, and his plates were not stolen. The driver is a journalist who reviews vehicles, and gave a firsthand account of the experience of being tracked for days. 
In Houston, residents cut down at least six of the Flock cameras. -Here in West Virginia, a man in Morgantown was arrested for allegedly destroying several cameras. 
Some places, like Los Angeles and Macon County, North Carolina, are ending their contracts with Flock Safety over privacy concerns. 
The city of Newport, Kentucky decided that despite the benefits of the surveillance cameras during a pilot program, the police department would not enroll in the permanent program because the public had concerns about privacy, transparency, data retention, oversight and constitutional protections regarding the cameras.
Police misuse of the technology is a big concern, and has already been an issue in other states.
In Atlanta, more than 10 officers have been fired this year for misusing the license plate reader cameras. In South Carolina, two officers were fired, also for alleged misuse.
What does camera misuse mean? So far, it seems to mean police stalking people.
A police sergeant in Texas was accused of using license plate readers to “track and stalk a female officer.” He resigned. 
An officer in Milwaukee looked up his ex’s license plate more than 50 times, and his ex’s former partner more than 100 times. He was sentenced to probation. 
A second officer in Milwaukee was charged with misuse after searching for one license plate 17 times, and admitted to installing a GPS device on that person’s car.
I could go on and on. These reports are all just from this month.
Between the privacy worries and the possibility of police misusing the cameras, the positives aren’t outweighing the negatives.
While Huntington City Council was presented a proposal for the devices about a month ago, a public records request by ACLU-WV Investigative Reporter Kyle Vass found emails between the city’s police department and Flock Safety going back “several months” talking about a “large deployment” of the equipment. Why was a plan being made before council even voted?
Localities in West Virginia need to look into what’s going on in other states with Flock. And if they’re not going to listen to residents’ disapproval, then they at least need to spend more time working on safeguards to make sure the technology won’t be abused.
