name: Connecticut Mirror
title: It’s a bird! It’s a plane! It’s a very expensive collision!
description: After one of CT's most expensive airplane vs. bird strikes, Danbury Municipal Airport’s team is working to ensure it doesn’t happen again.
text:
An occasional look at Connecticut’s remarkable people, places and things

In early July, Danbury Municipal Airport administrator Michael Safranek received a message on his walkie-talkie. It was air traffic control: There were birds congregating on a taxiway. If an airplane hit one, the strike could endanger humans and wildlife alike. Could he shoo them away?
Safranek immediately got into his car and headed for the taxiway. He’s one of just eight workers who serve Danbury Municipal each day. His job means he must ensure that one of Connecticut’s busiest general aviation airports, which he said will accommodate 71,000 flights this year, runs smoothly. Part of that mandate means deterring wildlife — mostly geese, sometimes gulls and occasionally deer, coyotes and other animals — from hanging around.
Airports are not necessarily financially liable for bird strikes as long as they do their due diligence to keep birds off the runway. Safranek feels responsible for ensuring that strikes do not happen under his watch. “It’s on me,” he said. 

Michael Safranek monitors the Danbury Municipal Airport campus for birds.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

A report by the Federal Aviation Administration notes that, between 1990 and 2024, 313,716 wildlife strikes have occurred in the U.S. They’ve killed 82 people, damaged 20,439 aircraft and destroyed 162 of them. In that time frame, they’ve cost Connecticut at least $2.8 million and the U.S. more than $1.2 billion in repairs and delays. 
Safranek has seen, firsthand, the damage wildlife strikes can afflict. On Sept. 7, 2017, Danbury Municipal was the site of Connecticut’s most expensive recorded wildlife strike, according to the FAA’s Wildlife Strikes Database. A Citation 500, a small business jet, was half a mile away from landing when it struck several Canada geese 150 feet in the air. The plane ingested at least one goose into an engine, which immediately shut down. Though the pilot landed safely, the report on the FAA’s database notes that repairs cost the airport $750,000.
The number of wildlife strikes across the country increased by 26% from 2023 through 2025. But in Connecticut, during the same period, the number of strikes decreased by 44% and continues to drop. Safranek believes the state’s airport workers have become more vigilant in taking preventive measures. Almost two years have passed since Danbury Municipal’s most recent wildlife strike, and he wants to maintain that streak.
“It’s a very dangerous, detrimental thing to life and property,” Safranek said. “We better keep up on it.”
Two birds, one propane cannon
On the morning of July 15, Safranek got into an airport police car and began driving around the greenery surrounding the 250-acre airport. Morning patrols have been part of his daily routine since he first began working at the airport in 2005. Most bird strikes in Connecticut happen between 7 a.m. and 10 a.m., which Safranek said coincides with most airports’ busiest times.
Wildlife strikes in Connecticut peaked in 2023 with 138 reported strikes. Safranek attributes at least part of it to increased aircraft activity after the coronavirus pandemic, when more people began traveling again — and, in Danbury Municipal’s case, when private, noncommercial pilots resumed their travels.
Wildlife, especially birds, flock to airports. Big open spaces of grass teeming with insects serve as resting spots and feeding grounds. On rainy days, they bathe in small ponds that form in natural depressions. They do not have to worry about predators, thanks to extensive fencing.
“It’s like being on vacation for them,” Safranek said. 

A map of the Danbury Municipal Airport campus in the air traffic control tower.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Habitat management forms the first line of protection against wildlife strikes. Measures such as removing standing water, putting up deer-proof fencing and mowing grass short make the airport unattractive for different species.
If wildlife choose to stay, harassment is the next move. Some larger airports recruit falcons or border collies to chase birds away, but Danbury Municipal relies on technology. Safranek often fires pyro shells, nonlethal rounds that whistle and crackle in the air loud enough to scare wildlife away. He also uses a propane cannon to emit sonic blasts of up to 120 decibels, mimicking the sound of a gunshot.
During the first half of the year, Safranek and his colleagues focus on disrupting wildlife mating patterns. Birds tend to gather at the airport and start mating in the spring. If the airport team doesn’t drive them away by the summer, birds will give birth to chicks and begin traveling in larger flocks. About 56% of Connecticut’s wildlife strikes occur from July through October, when declining temperatures prompt birds to migrate to warmer places.
“We have a deal with the birds — February, March, April and beginning of May, we push them out using scare tactics, and if they’re here in June and July, we use whatever methods we can,” Safranek said. “We give them free reign for a couple of months, and then it’s time to have them leave.” 
But if wildlife don’t leave and poses an immediate threat to air traffic, Safranek turns to his last resort: depredation. His permit with the FAA allows him to kill any animal except humans and bald eagles, which are federally protected by the Bald and Golden Eagle Act. Safranek estimates that Danbury Municipal uses fewer than three live rounds a year, and most years, that number is zero.
“If there’s geese on the runway and a plane with people on board or landing, it’s a last-minute decision we have to make,” he said. “I don’t like using live rounds if I don’t have to.”

Michael Safranek shoots an air whistler cartridge at the Danbury Municipal Airport.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror


Danbury Municipal Airport administrator Michael Safranek shows a box of air whistler cartridges and the handgun he uses to scare away birds.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror
Michael Safranek demonstrates how to use the airport’s propane cannon, which creates loud bangs to scare away birds.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Eagle eyes
While making his rounds, Safranek spotted a blue heron above the runway. He called the air traffic control tower to get the all-clear before rolling down the window and loading a starter pistol with a nonlethal pyro shell. But when he gauged the distance of the heron from the runway, he put the pistol down.
“He’s far enough away,” Safranek said. “I’m not going to bother him.”
Richard Dolbeer, who is among the world’s foremost experts on wildlife strikes, views such judgment calls as fundamental to the philosophy of wildlife strike prevention. Dolbeer, 80, was one of the creators of the FAA’s wildlife strike database and still consults for the USDA. To him, the question of prevention is not simply “How can we kill as few birds as possible?” but “How can humans and nature coexist?” 
Airport staff have understood the dangers of wildlife strikes for decades, but the issue captured public awareness with the “Miracle on the Hudson” in 2009. A plane leaving New York City’s LaGuardia Airport flew into a flock of Canada geese and immediately lost both engines, forcing the crew to make an emergency landing in the Hudson River. All 155 people on board survived.
After the “Miracle on the Hudson,” Danbury Municipal, which previously hadn’t placed much emphasis on consistent wildlife removal, ramped up its harassment measures. Safranek made sure every airport vehicle had a gun that could shoot sound projectiles and introduced propane cannons, which can be controlled remotely and fired at set intervals.
Michael Safranek monitors security camera footage for the Danbury Municipal Airport and shows a photo of a bird strike that damaged an airplane engine.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror
Danbury Municipal, like other airports across the country, also began documenting wildlife presence more carefully. Each day, Safranek updates a spreadsheet tracking the number of wildlife seen at the airport. And if a plane hits a bird, he must fill out an extensive report for the FAA’s database and photograph “snarge,” or the mangled debris of blood, feathers and flesh. Sometimes, he can’t figure out the species of the crushed bird, so he sends the snarge to the Smithsonian’s Feather Identification Lab for testing.
“Airports in Connecticut have done a good job for a number of years reporting strikes,” Dolbeer said. “For the nation as a whole, we’re seeing greater effort being made in some areas and some airports to report the strikes.”
All airports in Connecticut work closely with the Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection and U.S. Wildlife Service to ensure best practices. Larger commercial airports, such as Bradley International, have hired specialists from the U.S. Department of Agriculture to serve as airport wildlife biologists. And in addition to the several thousand dollars Danbury Municipal budgets each year, the airport has received funding from the FAA to maintain prevention measures, such as a $500,000 grant in 2000 to put up a deer-proof fence.
Dolbeer isn’t sure whether Connecticut’s decreasing wildlife strike numbers represent a long-term trend, noting that strikes in the state have increased slightly over a 10-year period. But he notes that better conservation has led to growing bird populations and growing awareness to more diligent reporting — both of which may contribute to the overall increase in strikes. 
To Dolbeer, the “new frontier” of wildlife strike prevention lies in the aircraft themselves. He hopes to help others devise technology such as bird-detecting radar and ultraviolet landing lights, which he described as similar to flashing lights on a police car. 
“I’m on a mission,” he said. “I have no retirement plans right now.”

Danbury Municipal Airport administrator Michael Safranek poses for a portrait outside of his office on July 15, 2026.  Credit: Julia Levine / CT Mirror

Safranek does not intend to implement any new measures. Strike prevention technology is expensive, and wildlife already seem to have learned to stay clear of aircraft. Half an hour after his morning patrol, a dark blur in the air caught his eye — the heron, returning. 
“If you notice, he stays away from the runway,” Safranek said. “He knows.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Energy policy and reality: How to keep costs down in New Hampshire
description: As the New Hampshire Legislature wrapped up its session this year, Republican representatives and the governor lauded the passage of a bill that is intended to stimulate the development of small modular nuclear reactors and allow our utilities to own them.  Meanwhile some bills that would further enable renewable energy managed to get through, but […]
text:
Along with energy efficiency programs, putting more renewable energy into the grid also helps keep down costs. (Photo by Janelle Stecklein/Oklahoma Voice)As the New Hampshire Legislature wrapped up its session this year, Republican representatives and the governor lauded the passage of a bill that is intended to stimulate the development of small modular nuclear reactors and allow our utilities to own them. 
Meanwhile some bills that would further enable renewable energy managed to get through, but it’s clear that the legislators have a preference for continuing our dependence on fossil fuels and pinning hopes on a nuclear technology that is still in the research and development stage.
Most experts say it will be a decade before the new nuclear plants are ready for commercialization, and even then they will likely be among the most expensive ways to generate electricity.
We have been told for years that electricity rates in New Hampshire are among the most expensive in the country. That’s partly true. We are in the top 10 most expensive along with our neighbors in Massachusetts, Maine, and Connecticut. Getting them down has been a mantra of politicians for decades, but here we are, pretty much in the same place. Interestingly, rates in New Hampshire have increased 15% in the past year while they have declined 3.9% in Massachusetts. Is it coincidence that Massachusetts has the highest adoption of rooftop solar in New England?
So what can we do to bring down rates?
First, it must be said that it’s not the rate that hurts most residential customers, but the total bill they receive every month. Energy efficiency programs are the bedrock of bringing down costs for most homeowners and businesses, and despite some political posturing coming from Washington, D.C., that “energy efficiency is communism” (really, some Republicans actually said that), logic dictates that if you can do a job with less electricity and save money, that’s just common sense.
Putting more renewable energy into the grid also helps keep down costs. Every research report produced in the past year that compares the installation and operation cost of various electrical energy technologies has found that solar and wind are now the lowest cost, pretty much anywhere in the world. Would more robust support for solar bring down our electric bills?
Look at the case of Australia. The country is pioneering the installation of home renewables and battery use, and has become a global leader. Today 1 in 3 homes has solar panels, and in the past year 415,000 homes have had batteries connected. Only China has installed more batteries in the past year.
Industrial scale batteries, solar, and wind have started to bring down the cost of electricity. Recently the Australian energy minister held a press conference to announce that prices for electricity in parts of the country with the most renewable generation would drop by 10%.
There is even a program to provide free electricity days when there will be no charge for electricity, because of the surplus of solar power. The “Solar Sharer Offer” is giving households three hours of free power during the middle of the day,  which is an incentive to run washing machines, dryers, dishwashers, ovens, and heating and air conditioning during hours when there is surplus solar electricity. It is also a good time to charge electric vehicles and home batteries.
Not that many years ago, our politicians used to argue that we should prioritize the power sources that are most cost competitive. They said we shouldn’t “pick winners and losers” with subsidies and incentive programs. Aren’t we doing just that by creating special treatment and massive government subsidies for nuclear power while eliminating those incentives for renewables?
Fortunately, renewables have declined in cost so much that they are now the least cost alternatives, and the market place has taken notice. Too bad so many of our legislators have not been paying attention.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Democratic candidates discuss inclusive politics, bumpy primary campaign
description: Three Democratic candidates for governor told a citizens’ group that communities most affected by state policy decisions should have a greater role in shaping them during a Monday night forum in Madison focused on affordability. The forum was hosted by Kaleidoscope Wisconsin, a coalition of organizations that are “rooted” in marginalized communities in the s[...]
text:
Candidates alongside representatives of Kaleidoscope Wisconsin, a coalition of organizations that are “rooted” in marginalized communities in the state, at the Center for Black Excellence in Madison. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)Three Democratic candidates for governor told a citizens’ group that communities most affected by state policy decisions should have a greater role in shaping them during a Monday night forum in Madison focused on affordability.
The forum was hosted by Kaleidoscope Wisconsin, a coalition of organizations that are “rooted” in marginalized communities in the state, at the Center for Black Excellence in Madison. Angela Russell, founder of the Undercurrent, a consulting and advisory practice for organizations that care about social impact, moderated the event. It took place with just three weeks to go before  the primary election and following a massive shakeup in the race last week, when Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez dropped out because of a financial scandal and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who had previously dropped out, got back into the race with the endorsement of Gov. Tony Evers.
State Rep. Francesca Hong, state Sen. Kelda Roys and former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes participated. Crowley and Joel Brennan, former head of the Department of Administration, did not attend.
Throughout the evening, the candidates stated that Wisconsin’s affordability challenges stem from systemic failures in housing, healthcare, education and taxation, and agreed on the need for more progressive taxation and greater investment in public services.
Roys said she wants to end the state’s private school voucher program, restore collective bargaining rights for public employees and open the state employee health insurance plan to more residents. She criticized state subsidies for data center developers. 
Barnes talked about reforming the manufacturing and agriculture tax credit, expanding BadgerCare through a public option and increasing taxes on wealthy individuals and corporations.
Hong highlighted her plans to tax millionaires and billionaires, expand Medicaid, increase shared revenue for local governments, raise the minimum wage and establish guaranteed paid leave.
While candidates articulated their policy ideas, they also repeatedly turned to a broader question: Who has influence over state government and whose voices are included in decision-making?
Hong said people in local communities know what they need and don’t need to be told what they need. She said politicians should be public servants who ensure people have access to programs, adding that she doesn’t see food, housing, education and healthcare as benefits but instead sees them as rights and “things that are needed in order to build economic security and freedom.”
Hong said an effective governor must listen to communities and that “the people” should be the ones government answers to, rather than “lobbyists” or those with the most access to the governor’s office.
“We need not only a new type of politics, but somebody right now who isn’t answering to industry and who isn’t being pressured by the status quo,” Hong said. 
Barnes said he still sees himself as the community organizer he once was, adding that elected officials need to remain connected to the communities they represent and that it can be easy for politicians to “get into office and lose touch.”
“It’s impossible to lose touch if you’re still going home to the same place every night,” Barnes said, adding that he learned as lieutenant governor how important it was for him to “bring people who are  representative of communities that have been left behind” as well as “people who challenge me” into his circle.
Roys said the solutions to the problem facing Wisconsin are not unknown, but that the “political will” to make change has not been there. She said that Republicans have broken the “positive feedback loop” that should exist between people and lawmakers. She described a cycle in which voters give power to policymakers, who then are expected to deliver results and return to communities to understand what more needs to be done.
“It is up to us to demand change,” Roys said, adding that people should hold her accountable as well.
The candidates were asked what they have learned from each other. 
Hong said she was inspired by remarks Barnes made over the weekend about the dramatic twists and turns in the governor’s race. She recalled a speech he gave in which he commented on Evers’ decision to endorse Crowley, and his reversal of his decision to drop out of the race, saying it showed why “so many people are frustrated and want nothing to do with the Democratic establishment.” Some supporters of Barnes and Hong have complained that Crowley  is being elevated by “establishment” Democrats to stop more progressive Democrats from getting through the primary.
“There’s been a lot of news in the governor’s race,” Hong said. “It’s been a little bit chaotic…I think Mandela gave his strongest remarks at a forum that I’d heard in a while.”
Hong called it “very empowering.”
“He was speaking to a community that I think still feels very much like the elections are just being decided for them,” Hong said. “And to use the time that you’re supposed to talk about yourself, to share remarks with the community… this election belongs to the voters. It should always be about the voters.”
Hong also said she has learned how to explain policy in clearer ways from Roys.
Roys said she has learned how to be more active and authentic on social media from Hong, and agreed with Hong about Barnes’ comments over the weekend, saying he “really distilled out what this is about.”
Barnes, who noted that the candidates have known each other for a long time, said Hong has brought “newness” to the forefront.
“If you want to build a real democracy, it is about not just working with the basic folks that you’ve known forever, of course, that’s the foundation of the work, but we’re in the business of addition,” Barnes said. “For so long, people hadn’t wanted to be a part of our politics… Over the last week, the people are fired up. People are ready for change, and I think it would be unwise for some people to seek to dismiss that.”
Barnes said he appreciated that Roys has sharp “elbows” and is willing to be critical and fight, including with members of her own party. He noted the primary has been very long, but said that it is good for democracy.
“These long primaries suck,” Barnes said, but he added, “it is good for people to be able to push each other, to challenge each other, to be able to generate ideas from one another, to have a moment to see what works, what doesn’t work, and ultimately to give people a choice. The more that choice is taken away the more we do to undo all the good work that has happened.”
All three Democratic candidates, along with Brennan and Crowley, are competing for a spot on the November ballot to take on U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, the presumptive Republican nominee. In-person absentee voting starts on July 28. The primary is Aug. 11.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Pushing judicial amendment, Kansas GOP officials cite anonymous website tied to high-profile lawyer
description: William Allen White changed his mind very publicly. Once an ardent anti-populist — the equivalent of a conservative today — he eventually embraced the progressive cause — more or less a modern political liberal. What White didn’t do was obscure his identity or opinions. He proudly credited himself as editor and publisher of The Emporia […]
text:
This statue of "Justice" sits in the lobby of the Kansas Judicial Center in Topeka. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)William Allen White changed his mind very publicly. Once an ardent anti-populist — the equivalent of a conservative today — he eventually embraced the progressive cause — more or less a modern political liberal.
What White didn’t do was obscure his identity or opinions. He proudly credited himself as editor and publisher of The Emporia Gazette. His name was emblazoned on dozens of books and on the Gazette masthead besides.
That’s why I find it peculiar to find White misquoted by an anonymous website that long surfaced as the first result of Google searches about the Kansas judicial selection amendment. The “Kansas Information Network” includes no names or email addresses. It offers scant content beyond a lengthy page about potentially voting for state Supreme Court justices.
According to the Secretary of State’s Office, the group behind that website was incorporated in 2025 by Josh Ney, a high-profile lawyer who has represented Republican lawmakers and spoken publicly in support of the amendment. He also incorporated the similarly named “Kansas Information Network Action,” which promoted the other group’s website via Google.
You might know Ney as the “N” of KN Law Group. The “K” was once Ryan Kriegshauser, recently appointed by President Donald Trump as the U.S. attorney for Kansas. Ney served as the state’s securities commissioner under Gov. Sam Brownback and has made his presence felt during the Statehouse session.
All Kansans have the right to speak out on issues of public importance. That’s a good thing.
But with the amendment vote set for Aug. 4 and fundamental rights for Kansans at stake, the anonymity and curious approach of the website leave a sour taste. Republican officials have taken the bait, with Rep. Adam Smith, R-Weskan, citing it as authoritative on Facebook. His post was then reshared by the Cowley County Republican Party.
Ney has been a outspoken advocate of changing the Kansas Supreme Court selection process, as he told the Rotary Club of Wichita on Monday.
“For the for the past 17 years, I’ve been asked to testify at various times as we’ve debated this, whether it’s nominating commission reform, federal model for the court of appeals and ultimately transparency issues with the current system,” he said.
The website doesn’t mention Ney’s role as incorporator, or his continued advocacy. It doesn’t say who created the content or paid for the associated advertising.
 
The Kansas Supreme Court, whose future membership rests on an amendment vote next month, meets at Topeka’s Kansas Judicial Center. (Photo by Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)
What’s in a name?
Let’s sort through this all piece by piece. The title caught my eye first.
“Kansas Information Network” contains three nouns, all of which also appear in the name of an actual state agency: the “Information Network of Kansas.” That group aims “to enable digital access to Kansas state and local government information and services for public use and benefit.”
Kansas Public Radio once hosted its own “Kansas Information Network,” although the project appears not to have published any stories since late 2017.
Neither the state agency nor the public radio project have any connection to the new, amendment-focused, website. Nevertheless, the bland, utilitarian design of its website conveys bored authority. Kansans learning about the amendment debate might confuse the new site for a long-running, authoritative resource.
But there’s more
On its “About” page, the website includes the following misquotation from William Alan White: “The facts are fairly and honestly presented; truth will take care of itself.”
The source of this quote is a memoir by legendary journalist George Seldes titled “Witness to a Century: Encounters with the Noted, the Notorious, and the Three SOBs.” In it, he quotes the Emporia newspaperman as saying: ‘That’s it, that is our formula: ‘The facts fairly and honestly presented; truth will take care of itself.”
You’ll notice that the Kansas Information Network adds an “are” to the quote, presumably for ease of reading. That still makes the quote incorrect. You can also read White’s words each and every day in the Kansas Reflector’s email newsletter. We use the correct version as our motto.
Let’s place quibbles about verbiage aside. The citation of a legendary Kansas journalist and political progressive lends implicit assurances of the website’s handedness. White’s name looms even larger given the surrounding pages’ anonymity.
Perhaps most humorously, the Kansas Information Network includes a page of “Helpful Resources.” It includes the names, numbers and websites of Kansas public officials — with the notable exception of judicial selection amendment supporter and state Attorney General Kris Kobach. Finally, it includes a link the KTWU public TV show “Sunflower Journeys.”
That struck a nerve with me because the producer and host of the show for 27 seasons, Dave Kendall, has written columns for Kansas Reflector. Kendall no longer works for KTWU or the program, but he was surprised and amused to see it mentioned in such a context.
“To me personally, it’s just another laugher and SMH (shaking my head) moment,” he wrote me via email. That being said, he wrote later, “it would be unfortunate for those who see SJ on this list as some sort of stamp of approval.”
I reached out to Ney multiple times for comment on the site and his connection to it. I emailed twice, sent a text message, and left a voicemail.  He didn’t respond.
 
Attorney Josh Ney has been a prominent supporter of changing the selection process for Kansas Supreme Court justices. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)
Advocacy for change 
Ney’s connections with both organizations has been previously reported.
The Sunflower State Journal’s Brad Cooper wrote about Kansas Information Network Action — and its $264,000 ad buy backing the amendment — on June 15. He noted that Ney had incorporated it.
Former state Rep. Jason Probst, D-Hutchinson, wrote about the website and Ney on a Substack blog entry titled “When Truth isn’t good enough to win…” from July 12. Want to know how the Kansas Information Network misleads? Read this piece. Probst details how a supposedly unbiased information source can manipulate voters.
Ney himself spoke out about the amendment in an interview with KAKE-TV posted June 22 He added his name to an open letter released July 14 from Kansas attorneys supporting the measure. The day before, he commented for a piece by my pal Joel Mathis in the Kansas Leadership Center’s Journal. 
He submitted testimony in favor when the amendment was being debated in 2025. All the way back in 2009, he wrote an article titled “Does the Kansas Supreme Court Selection Process Violate the One Person, One Vote Doctrine?” published in the Washburn Law Review.
Most recently, he spoke at the Wichita Rotary event. Over the course of an hour, he offered about as good of a case for changing the Kansas Supreme Court nomination process as I’ve heard.
“In Kansas and in any constitutional republic, do we need an exception to democracy?” he asked the audience. “I think the burden of proof ultimately needs to be on the person who is asking the people to cede their inherent authority to someone else. Another way of asking that is: Are Kansans in 2026 capable of picking their own government?”
With all of this being said, I don’t know why the Kansas Information Network needed to be anonymous.
I might not agree with Ney’s conclusions, but that’s the way our nation’s marketplace of ideas works. His experience with the Kansas legal system makes him a more persuasive messenger than a random website. Nothing prevents the Kansas Information Network from trumpeting Ney’s experience or reprinting that law review piece.
As a longtime tiller in the fields of professional opinion, I don’t understand how someone both wants to passionately express their opinions on one hand and help incorporate a secretive group supporting such opinions on the other.
Perhaps amendment advocates prefer obfuscation.
The misleading rhetoric around the vote suggests as much. Why come out of the shadows when you can instead rely on the goodwill generated by Kansas icons such as William Allen White and durable programs such as “Sunflower Journeys”?
Political operatives can list good reasons to vote for the amendment and good reasons to vote against it. But Kansans should show consistency and moral clarity in identifying themselves in making their cases to the public. It might also help if they refrain from telling total fibs about what passage would mean.
As Ney ended his speech to the Rotary on Monday afternoon, he recommended the audience check Ballotpedia’s summary of the amendment as a worthwhile, unbiased source. For some reason, he didn’t mention the Kansas Information Network.
Clay Wirestone is Kansas Reflector opinion editor. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: ICE is asking to be sued. Milwaukee is just the city to oblige.
description: Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made its position clear. The agency refuses to require its agents to follow Milwaukee’s law banning masks. Since it is unable to come to this common sense conclusion itself, the remedy is for Milwaukee City Attorney Evan Goyke to sue. This is how we keep secret police at bay. […]
text:
Religious leaders in Milwaukee protest ICE arrests in the city (Photo courtesy Michael Pointer Mace) Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made its position clear. The agency refuses to require its agents to follow Milwaukee’s law banning masks. Since it is unable to come to this common sense conclusion itself, the remedy is for Milwaukee City Attorney Evan Goyke to sue. This is how we keep secret police at bay.
Goyke has taken the first step. In a July 17 letter to the U.S. Department of Justice, he defends the ICE out MKE ordinance, stating that masked law enforcement “increases the risk of dangerous interactions with the public, undermines accountability and police community relations, and stokes confusions, fear, and intimidation.”
Milwaukee prohibits ICE agents from wearing masks. The Department of Homeland Security staunchly refuses to follow this sensible rule despite a Milwaukee Police Department standard operating procedure that models this basement level of transparency. We need to know what ICE is doing. We need to know who you are. We need to see your faces.
DHS claims that it won’t follow Milwaukee’s ordinance because of the Supremacy Clause. Their claim asserts that municipalities cannot create rules that prevent employees from performing federal duties and, in most cases, the Supremacy Clause makes sense.
We wouldn’t want a city ordinance to keep the U.S. Census Bureau from collecting population data. We wouldn’t want municipalities to prevent the National Weather Service from studying tornados. At the same time, identifiable and transparent federal law enforcement is not at odds with the rule of law. 
Clarity and accountability is at the heart of our Fifth Amendment’s promise of due process. The Supremacy Clause does not supersede our Constitution’s protections. The clause itself is a component of our Constitution (Article VI, Clause 2) and no article or clause may violate the Bill of Rights. 
The Mask-Free MKE ordinance took time to create. Over and over again, our church members returned to the Common Council’s galley seats as the rule was amended, re-written and reviewed by our city attorney, Evan Goyke. Goyke’s job is to make sure that the proposed ordinance is constitutional and enforceable. Goyke’s verdict is that the people of Milwaukee can prohibit masked law enforcement.
Consider the current situation of Giovanni Sosa, a 20-year old with no criminal record. Gio came to the United States when he was 4 years old. Recently, he was snatched by masked ICE agents, leaving his wife Litzy without her husband and his 2 year old daughter without her father.
Gio has worked construction jobs since he was 14 and has never run afoul of law enforcement. Last week, while heading to the barber, his car was surrounded and blocked. His window was smashed and he was handcuffed and dragged to  detention. As he was shoved into a government car, Gio had the presence of mind to yell out his mother’s phone number. Had he not done so, he simply would not have returned home from the errands he was running. Who took him? Where was he? Was his detention legal? Was the use of force necessary?
Our Constitution protects us from having to ask these questions. The Fifth Amendment states that “no person” shall be deprived of life or liberty without protections against arbitrary government actions. Surely, masks cross this line.
DHS claims that it must allow its employees to wear masks for their safety. Lauren Bis, a DHS spokesperson, states, “Sanctuary politicians attempting to ban our federal law enforcement from wearing masks is … a flagrant attempt to endanger our officers.” 
The Trump administration’s immigration enforcers fear that without masks, their employees’ actions would instigate such a strong public outcry that they would be forced to hold officers accountable. They don’t want the public to identify officers responsible for using excessive force. How can DHS officials be opposed to basic transparency before the public it serves?
This is where City Attorney Evan Goyke can help. DHS has convinced itself that the Supremacy Clause supersedes the Constitution. Its insistence that secrecy and obfuscation is a means to serve the people is a slippery rationalization that leads to a secret police force. City Attorney Goyke should sue ICE and require the agency to comply with the law. It is for the good of the residents of Milwaukee, for ICE’s own agents, for MPD officers and for our democratic heritage. This moment of trial will turn our commitment to defend our rights into steel. Our’s is a nation without a secret police. Masks cross a line. At this pivotal hour, Milwaukee must lead.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Tax change would spur Ohio development — and help low-income families most, new study says
description: Taxing buildings less and land more in Ohio would encourage development such as more housing, and most of the benefits would flow to people who need them most, like renters in low-income neighborhoods.  That’s the conclusion of a study of Cincinnati that was made public last week. The study by the University of Notre Dame’s […]
text:
Vacant buildings in Columbus. Proponents of a land-value tax say it would create incentives for owners to develop such properties. (Photo by Marty Schladen, Ohio Capital Journal.)Taxing buildings less and land more in Ohio would encourage development such as more housing, and most of the benefits would flow to people who need them most, like renters in low-income neighborhoods. 
That’s the conclusion of a study of Cincinnati that was made public last week.
The study by the University of Notre Dame’s Student Policy Network in conjunction with the Center for Land Economics used data from the Hamilton County Auditor’s office to simulate the effects of a specific kind of “land-value tax.” 
It would tax land at four times the rate of the buildings and other improvements on it. Currently, valuations of land and improvements are added together and taxed.
The goal of a land-value tax is to create a financial incentive to develop unused or underused land in otherwise developed neighborhoods. The tax mix would be different, but it would provide the city with the same revenue it’s getting currently.
Most Ohio economists appear to think it’s a good idea.
Ohio state Sen. Louis Blessing III, R-Colerain Township, is proposing a constitutional amendment that would allow Ohio communities to opt into a version of a land-value tax.
The researchers found that Cincinnati has more than $1.87 billion in vacant or underdeveloped land, and they found some striking incongruities.
For example, a low-income apartment building in the hip Over the Rhine neighborhood is taxed at 22 times the rate of the parking lot next door.
“When we went parcel by parcel through Cincinnati’s assessor data, the pattern was impossible to miss,” Curtis Brashaw, co-leader of the student team, said in a written statement accompanying the report. “A downtown lot worth millions can pay less tax per square foot than the apartment building next to it.”
The principle behind a land-value tax is straightforward. Taxing land at a greater rate than improvements makes development more financially attractive. And particularly in urban areas, that discourages a gap-toothed landscape in which prime land is underused. 
“When a property owner chooses to improve their land, whether by constructing a new apartment building or renovating a deteriorating structure, the tax bill rises as a direct result,” the report said. “In this way, the tax code treats investment as a liability rather than an asset, discouraging development. Over time, this creates a financial disincentive for development that contributes directly to vacant lots, surface parking, and urban blight. We tax the wrong thing.”
Changing the tax mix would create winners and losers.
Under the student group’s simulation, median taxes on vacant land would increase 126%. And median retail and commercial property taxes would increase 39% — largely because land with that zoning and in those locations is valuable.
On the other side of the coin, homeowners and apartment dwellers would benefit. The median single-family home would see a 10% drop in property taxes, while taxes on multi-family units would decrease more than 16%.
The study also found that the biggest benefits flow to those who need them most.
“The burden shifts progressively,” it said. “The lowest-income neighborhoods see median cuts near 17% and middle-income neighborhoods 10% to 11%, while only the highest-income quintile sees a median increase of about 11%.”
In places where a land-value tax has been implemented, there’s some evidence that it helped the overall economy. For example, Allentown, Pa., implemented such a scheme in 1996. 
Tax cuts flowed to nearly 75% of properties and building permits increased by 32%, the Strong Towns Archive quoted former U.S. Sen. Pat Toomey, R-Pa., as saying. The Notre Dame students’ report said that new development in Allentown far outstripped that in nearby communities such as Bethlehem. 
Blessing, the Ohio state senator promoting a land-value tax option, said the new report helps prove his case that it’s a smart idea.
“This is exactly the kind of evidence Ohioans deserve as we look for real answers on property taxes,” the report quoted Blessing as saying. “This amendment doesn’t impose anything on anyone. It simply gives communities the option to stop penalizing the families and businesses who improve their property. This report shows Cincinnati what that choice could look like, and I believe Ohio’s voters should be the ones to make it.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio approved $1 million in emergency funds to help 16 children from Vinton County
description: The Ohio Controlling Board approved $1 million in emergency funds to help the 16 children from Vinton County who were recently found by law enforcement authorities in terrible conditions.  The children range in age from 18 months to 18 years and were allegedly found in a roughly 12-foot by 12-foot room inside a Hamden house […]
text:
The Ohio Statehouse. (Photo by Megan Henry, Ohio Capital Journal). The Ohio Controlling Board approved $1 million in emergency funds to help the 16 children from Vinton County who were recently found by law enforcement authorities in terrible conditions. 
The children range in age from 18 months to 18 years and were allegedly found in a roughly 12-foot by 12-foot room inside a Hamden house when law enforcement conducted a search warrant for a parallel investigation on June 30. 
The $1 million is going into a special fund that is being set up for Vinton County for the 16 children, said Joel Potts, the chief government and external affairs officer at the Ohio Department of Children and Youth. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“These resources are specifically for this emergent need,” he said during Monday’s Controlling Board meeting. 
“We know that many of them will be needing therapeutic foster care for quite some time to come. That is $150 a day to $250 a day on average per child. So those costs alone would bankrupt the county when you see them doubling the number of cases.” 
Potts said he has never seen anything like this before in his 40 year career. 
“A child off the radar is terrible enough,” he said. 
“Sixteen kids in one family in one household to be off the radar is something that I’ve just not seen.” 
Livestock was kept in better conditions than the children, Vinton County Sheriff Ryan Cain said during a press conference earlier this month. 
“Extremely high presence, I’m sure, of bacterial and human feces,” he said. “It was just a disgusting scene.” 
Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson said it’s something we’re not used to seeing in America. 
“It really looked third-world,” he said. “I think if they would have waited another 24 hours, there was a very high probability that we’d be dealing with a death or multiple deaths of these children.” 
The children were not enrolled in school, authorities said, adding that some of the children can’t speak and that the 18-year-old can’t spell their name. 
“It was terrible,” Wilson said. “They really looked almost like feral animals … so when we’re talking reading and writing and education, we’re talking a whole ‘nother level of expectations here.”
Vinton County’s location in rural Southeast Ohio.
Ohio state Sen. Kyle Koehler, R-Springfield, asked if $1 million is enough money to help the 16 children. 
“What happens when the youngest of the children are in their teens and things start coming forth that we didn’t expect?” 
Potts stressed the $1 million is for the children’s immediate needs.  
“Over the next several months we are going to have a much better sense of what these particular children are dealing with, and what their long-term needs are going to be,” he said. 
Ongoing costs will be necessary, Potts said. 
“This is unprecedented,” he said. “We’ve seen a county agency literally double the number of kids in temporary custody overnight.”
Vinton County is Ohio’s least populated county with about 12,600 people.
All of the children are currently in foster care and the hope is the children will get adopted, Potts said. 
“As horrendous as these types of cases are, it does give us that opportunity to ask those hard questions, and it’s time for us to ask those hard questions,” he said. 
“You can’t look at something like this and not think that we need to do more.”
During the state budget process last year, Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine originally proposed an additional $83 million to Ohio counties for child protective services, but lawmakers did not fully fund the request in the last year’s budget, said Ohio state Rep. Bride Rose Sweeney, D-Westlake.
“I do know that this was a very large discussion in our state budget that we heard from county officials across the state about the dire needs of protective services and not having enough money,” Sweeney said.  
Ohio state Sen. George Lang, R-Butler County, said he spent his early years in foster care. 
“I do believe this is one of those rare exceptions where we need to err on the side of helping rather than err on the side of fiscal prudence,” he said. 
Ohio state Rep. Mark Johnson, R-Chillicothe, was in Hamden over the weekend and saw the house is on a dead-end road with only one other house at the end of the road. 
“No neighbor, the hardware store guy, the fire department had never visibly seen a child here,” he said. “It’s rather bizarre, to say the least.”
Making sure the children are taken care of is the top priority, Wilson said. 
“We’ve got to ensure the kids are safe,” he said. “We’ve got to make sure they’re placed in good, solid therapeutic placements. And we have to hold accountable the people who are looking to do this to their own family.”
Gary Siders Sr., 73, Catherine Siders, 67, Gary Siders Jr., 36, and Elizabeth Siders, 33, are each facing 16 counts of felony endangering children in Vinton County Common Pleas Court. They have all pleaded not guilty.
A Vinton County judge signed a gag order on July 14 after Gary Siders Jr.’s attorney filed a motion for the order.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio doesn’t need to scrap managed care. It needs to sharpen it.
description: In committee rooms at the Statehouse, Ohio lawmakers have been debating a measure that would upend the state’s Medicaid managed care system altogether. Ohio Senate Bill 386 and its House companion, the bipartisan Medicaid Savings Act, would move Ohio away from the managed care system that currently serves roughly three million Medicaid enrollees and toward [[...]
text:
The Ohio Statehouse. (Photo by Jake Zuckerman, Ohio Capital Journal.)In committee rooms at the Statehouse, Ohio lawmakers have been debating a measure that would upend the state’s Medicaid managed care system altogether. 
Ohio Senate Bill 386 and its House companion, the bipartisan Medicaid Savings Act, would move Ohio away from the managed care system that currently serves roughly three million Medicaid enrollees and toward an administrative services model, similar to one Connecticut adopted years ago. 
The sponsors argue it could save the state hundreds of millions of dollars a year by cutting out what they call the “middleman.” 
They’re not wrong that Ohio’s managed care program has room for improvement and there may well be room for direct state/provider partnerships, but scrapping it altogether, in this particular moment, would be a mistake. 
This debate isn’t happening in a vacuum. It’s happening just as Ohio finalized a new two-year state budget ahead of the July 1 constitutional deadline, and just as federal Medicaid cuts signed into law last year begin working their way through state budgets, with Ohio expected to lose tens of billions of dollars in federal Medicaid funding over the next decade and hundreds of thousands of Ohioans expected to lose coverage.
At its core, managed care works like a fixed payment plan for a state’s health care spending. 
Instead of absorbing the seasonal swings and unpredictable spikes of a fee-for-service system, Ohio pays managed care plans a set amount per member, per month, and the plans largely absorb the risk of what happens after that. 
In a time when the state’s fiscal footing feels shakier than usual, that kind of predictability isn’t a nice-to-have. It’s a hedge against the very volatility Ohio is trying to manage.
And even more importantly, Ohio’s managed care contracts create real incentives to measurably improve the population’s health while decreasing costly inefficient care — a real boon to the people covered by Medicaid and to Ohio’s taxpayers. 
Ohio requires its Medicaid health plans to share financial rewards with providers that deliver high quality care while lowering costs, and health plans tout specific innovative provider partnerships as selling points when bidding on state contracts.  
Those commitments should be treated as exactly that — commitments, not marketing copy.

Ensuring that plans follow through on the value-based partnerships and other population health solutions in their winning bids isn’t a nice-to-have; it’s central to whether managed care delivers on its promise.
When done right, managed care is one of the few tools Ohio has that actually aligns incentives, improves outcomes, and creates budget stability for the people who need it most.
The transparency critique is fair — but there is a fix
One of the strongest arguments for the Medicaid Savings Act is that the state has too little visibility into how managed care dollars are actually spent. 
That’s a legitimate frustration, and I saw it firsthand when managed care plans’ pharmacy benefit managers failed to serve the public interest and hid highly questionable business practices behind “proprietary” labels. 
But Ohio’s General Assembly and the Department of Medicaid have spent the last seven years building tools to fix exactly that problem, including ensuring state legislature’s access to plan-level eligibility, billing, and spending data. 
ODM also holds the health plans accountable to the highly detailed terms of their contracts and the promises they made when bidding to secure the work. 
Better transparency is achievable through better oversight. It doesn’t require walking away from a model that, when done right, does something a Connecticut-style administrative services organization wouldn’t: put plans’ own money on the line for outcomes.
What Ohio would actually lose
Ohio’s Next Generation Medicaid and MyCare managed care programs tie substantial financial incentives to outcomes: increasing preventive screenings that save lives, delivering blood pressure and diabetes management that help people feel better while lowering costs, and providing care coordination for people with serious mental illness and complex chronic conditions.
Ohio’s MyCare program, for example, fully integrates Medicare and Medicaid benefit access and financing for dually eligible members, closing a gap where a bifurcated system creates fragmentation across Medicare and Medicaid and removing incentives to shift costs between programs rather than actually reduce them. 
MyCare’s coordination greatly improves member experience and streamlines access to needed care while reducing administrative burden for the state, for members, and for the care teams advocating on their behalf. 
As federal rules tighten Medicaid eligibility and coverage, that kind of integration becomes more valuable, not less.
In Connecticut, while the administrative costs have been reduced relative to managed care, the state is still facing high costs with individuals using home and community-based services — a similar population to the Ohioans served through MyCare. 
Ohio has already addressed this gap with this mature integrated program to serve these exact members — why cut off our nose to spite our face? 
Reform the model. Don’t demolish it.
None of this means the status quo is good enough. 
Legitimate questions remain about whether managed care plans are saving money on the right things and the state should keep pushing for more transparency and for plans to create more downside risk among the value-based providers, so everyone in the chain has real skin in the game. 
With over half of the state’s budget dedicated to Medicaid, member advocates and policy experts alike should continually push for systems that deliver better results at a lower cost, and alternative delivery systems, including the ASO model, may emerge as a viable solution for certain populations in certain circumstances. 
But lawmakers should be honest that the Medicaid Savings Act is a big bet — one being made at the exact moment Ohio can least afford budget uncertainty. 
Before trading a system built around aligned incentives and shared risk for one built around administrative efficiency alone, the state should make sure it isn’t solving a transparency problem by giving up the very structure that gets results for the Ohioans who need them most.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT’s pre-K endowment diverts pension dollars
description: The state’s new early childhood education fund could add $900 million in pension costs while still falling short of funding universal pre-K.
text:
Connecticut’s Early Childhood Education Endowment (ECEE) was created to further the state’s efforts to subsidize early childhood education. The goal is commendable. Childcare is expensive, and surely many families in Connecticut could benefit from additional support. 
But the financing structure of this endowment is troubling. It redirects surplus dollars that would otherwise have gone toward paying down Connecticut’s severely underfunded public pension systems, setting up the state for future problems.
Connecticut already funds early childhood education through its operating budget. The state approved $418 million for fiscal year 2026 and $443 million for fiscal year 2027, separate from the endowment. These funds are part of the regular budget process, where spending is debated, appropriated, and subject to the state’s fiscal guardrails.
The endowment is different. Starting in fiscal year 2026, it is set to receive any unappropriated General Fund surpluses once the Budget Reserve Fund is at its statutory cap. Before the endowment was created, those surpluses would have continued to support additional contributions to pay the state’s massive pension system debt that is owed to public workers.
Connecticut’s State Employees Retirement System and State Teachers’ Retirement System have a combined unfunded liability of $31.5 billion. These are not optional obligations. These are pension benefits already earned by public employees that are legally binding claims on future state revenues.
Unfunded pension obligations are among the state’s most expensive fiscal risks. When pension funding falls short, the state forgoes investment earnings that would have accrued on contributed assets, increasing long-term costs and shifting a larger burden to future taxpayers. For decades, Connecticut did exactly that, using funding practices that lowered near-term budget pressure while pushing debts and costs into the future.
The fiscal guardrails adopted in 2017 were designed to change this trajectory. By directing volatile revenues and year-end budget surpluses toward unfunded pension liabilities, Connecticut began to reverse decades of pension underfunding. These additional contributions improved both systems’ funded status and contributed to multiple credit rating upgrades. In the last few years, budget surpluses accounted for about 30% of total additional pension contributions.
But Connecticut is not out of the woods. Even after recent progress, the state government remains the most indebted in the nation on a per-capita basis, according to Reason Foundation. It carries about $24,000 in long-term debt per resident, more than four times the national average for state governments. A state carrying this much debt cannot treat surpluses as discretionary windfalls.
A new paper by Reason Foundation and Yankee Institute finds that the forgone pension contributions redirected to the endowment increase inflation-adjusted pension costs by roughly $300 million to $900 million relative to the pre-endowment trajectory.
Furthermore, according to the paper, the endowment is unlikely to generate spending at the scale implied by current policy goals anytime soon. Even under favorable assumptions, in 20 years, the spending enabled by the endowment would still not be enough to cover Connecticut’s current pre-K spending. According to our modeling, in the best-case scenario, the endowment’s annual inflation-adjusted spending capacity reaches only about $240 million by 2035 and $369 million by 2045—still less than the $418 million appropriated for 2026. 
That creates a second risk. Not only did the establishment of the endowment delay the payment of public pension debt, but it also created a political expectation. Many families may now expect free or heavily subsidized childcare. If the endowment cannot fund that promise, future lawmakers may face pressure to increase contributions or redirect additional surplus dollars away from pensions.
A third risk is the budgetary precedent it sets. This expansion of early childcare funding was done outside the traditional budget process. Connecticut’s fiscal guardrails set the pace for state government spending growth. This endowment circumvents that, moving spending growth outside the ordinary appropriations process. If this model is replicated for other priorities, the spending cap could be weakened, if not practically nullified.
Connecticut’s fiscal guardrails exist for a reason. Built through hard-won political consensus, they helped rebuild reserves, improve pension funding, and restore fiscal credibility after years of turmoil. 
Early childhood education may be a worthy priority, but this endowment poses many risks. It slows the pace of pension debt reduction, creates expectations the state may not be able to meet, and sets a precedent for shifting future spending priorities outside the fiscal discipline that helped stabilize Connecticut in the first place.
Mariana Trujillo is managing director of government finance at Reason Foundation. She is the lead author of the study “The Impact of the Early Childhood Education Endowment on Connecticut’s Pension Funding and Fiscal Health,” published by Yankee Institute in collaboration with Reason Foundation.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: State land ownership doesn’t equal stewardship
description: Connecticut keeps treating preservation and public access as competing values. They aren't.
text:
Sing it with me:   Let’s go fly a kite.   Louder now!   Up to the highest height! 
 That’s the kind of image public land can conjure at its best – a joy for anyone who shows up, regardless of what they earn or where they live. Connecticut has the land for all of this. What it lacks is the will to build it. 
 Instead, the state has developed a habit of acquiring remarkable properties, congratulating itself for saving them from development, and letting them decay into passive parkland – or into nothing at all. Hammonasset Beach, with its campground, nature center, and two miles of beach, generates more revenue for Connecticut’s state park system than any other park in the state. The state just doesn’t act on what it knows. 
Consider Sunrise Resort in East Haddam, a beloved campground nestled in the “Catskills of Connecticut,” where families swam in the Salmon River and the pool for generations. Purchased by the state in 2009, it sat vacant for years. The riverside cabins were eventually demolished. Just 1.4 miles away, a private operator opened 45 tiny cabins in December 2021 – no river frontage, no restaurant, just cabins and a dog park. Marriott bought that company in 2024. The state had the better property. It tore it down instead. It was the right land to protect. What followed was an abdication.
Or consider Seaside Sanatorium in Waterford. The famed Gilded Age architect Cass Gilbert designed the Tudor Revival complex as the country’s first heliotropic hospital for children with tuberculosis (treatment through sunlight and sea air). Listed on the National Register of Historic Places since 1996, it continues to sit abandoned after closing nearly 30 years ago. Less than ten years ago, the Department of Energy & Environmental Protection’s own master plan for Seaside endorsed a destination park – commissioning a feasibility study that concluded a roughly 100-room lodge with a restaurant and spa would attract developers, then issuing a formal Request for Proposals calling Seaside “an attractive” candidate for a hotel. 
In 2023, the state reversed course and announced it would demolish the historic buildings for passive parkland instead. A lawsuit sought to block it – and while it has since been settled, the buildings still stand (for now). DEEP wrote the playbook for a successful Seaside Park. They just declined to follow it.
The state frames this as a choice between buildings and open space. It isn’t. Seaside’s buildings already occupy their footprint. Demolishing them doesn’t add a single acre, but it destroys the reason to visit – reviewer after reviewer cites the buildings, not the shoreline, as Seaside’s draw. 
At Medfield State Hospital in Massachusetts, a similarly left-for-dead complex, the historic campus is being reimagined rather than razed, with Bellforge Arts Center animating the grounds with concerts, festivals, community events, and trails. A hotel at Seaside with a ground-floor restaurant and public shoreline and grounds access, or an arts venue anchored in those Tudor Revival halls, would do the same. 
Connecticut keeps treating preservation and public access as competing values. They aren’t. Other states are building the infrastructure Connecticut already has – Alabama just broke ground on a new lodge at Cheaha State Park. Connecticut has Cass Gilbert buildings sitting on Long Island Sound. The state just lacks the vision to use them.
Enter Hartford’s Batterson Park – and a rare chance to get this right. It just reopened after a $10 million largely state-funded renovation, and is operated by Riverfront Recapture under a public-private partnership with DEEP. It has trails, picnic areas, a splash pad, and kayak launches. 
What it doesn’t have is swimming, which is still prohibited due to water quality issues from I-84 runoff that a 2024 state study says could be addressed with long-term stormwater remediation. Meanwhile, 86 acres adjacent to the park, deeded by the City of Hartford to its pension fund in 2017 in lieu of a $5 million cash contribution it couldn’t afford, remain in limbo – a proposed truck stop sale fell through, but the land’s future is unresolved. 
Should the city look to sell, the state should be first in line, because protecting that land is what makes the long-term vision possible. DEEP’s own master plan for Seaside identified swimming as an undersupplied amenity statewide. Protect the land, fix the water, and build the activated public space that Sunrise and Seaside never became. Batterson could be the crown jewel Ritter described – a place where residents can get in the water on a hot summer day. The state just has to decide to finish what it started.
Passive parkland is fine, when it’s the deliberate answer. But it is not the solution to every parcel of open space within our borders. Not everyone wants to go for a stroll. Not every day is right for flying a kite. Some days, you need to get in the water – and not every family has a private pool or a shoreline community. Public swimming is not a luxury. It is exactly the kind of thing the state exists to provide. 
Connecticut has the land. The gesture of protection, however, cannot become a substitute for the harder work of stewardship.
Leah Beckett is a Hartford resident and planner at IMEG, the founder of Herd Supply Co., and co-owner of Beckett Farms.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT ratepayers pay the price when utility bullying goes unchecked
description: Since engaging in a well-funded bullying campaign to run the lead regulator at the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority out of town, Connecticut’s monopoly utility corporations are now on the prowl for more of our hard-earned money to pad their record high profits. If we let these out-of-control bullying tactics continue, we will all pay the […]
text:
Since engaging in a well-funded bullying campaign to run the lead regulator at the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority out of town, Connecticut’s monopoly utility corporations are now on the prowl for more of our hard-earned money to pad their record high profits. 

Tom Swan, executive director of CCAG

If we let these out-of-control bullying tactics continue, we will all pay the price. We need reforms now to ensure that service delivery and value for Connecticut residents is at the center of decision making, not undue influence by these corporations.
The bullying was in full view last year when Eversource and Avangrid successfully forced out PURA Chair Marissa Gillett with arguably the most aggressive smear campaign undertaken by corporations in Connecticut history. These monopoly utility companies did not respond well as Gillett implemented policies to protect utility customers and closely scrutinized their rate hike and bill increase proposals.
Since they ran out Gillett, Eversource and Avangrid have already reaped the benefits. In March, PURA caved to Eversource in a gas rate case. PURA also modified its draft decision giving Yankee Gas an additional $4 million and eliminating penalties that had been imposed on the utility for management and compliance issues. Also in March, PURA reconsidered a United Illuminating case, increasing the utility’s profits by $2 million, and fully erased the penalty for the company’s repeated failures to remediate contamination at English Station in New Haven.
The utilities flexed their influence in another rate case. WFSB recently reported another draft decision moved significantly in favor of Avangrid and against ratepayers following multiple communications between an executive at Avangrid and a PURA commissioner, now retired. The final decision on the PURA docket cost ratepayers millions of dollars more than the initial draft decision. 
It would be illegal for their discussion to have included the pending docket. This reporting has been met with shocking silence by other policy makers in Connecticut. At a minimum there should be an investigation into this matter and the case should be reopened to be considered by the new PURA commissioners, especially since the only other commissioner that voted to overturn the draft was a lobbyist for Avangrid just before being appointed.
The utilities are also challenging laws aimed at providing relief for ratepayers. In 2025, Connecticut enacted a law that requires them to participate in the ISO New England regional transmission system, thereby cancelling a “bonus” incentive payment for voluntary participation. This would save ratepayers $4.5 million a year.  Yet, the utilities have continued to collect these incentive payments from ratepayers.  
Gov. Ned Lamont, the Consumer Counsel Claire Coleman, PURA and Attorney General Tong have called on FERC to end the utilities charging ratepayers for these fees. After these officials petitioned FERC, the utilities filed a lawsuit challenging the law they have been ignoring.
In March, Eversource backed out of three solar contracts selected by the state to provide clean and renewable electricity. The refusal to execute these contracts denies Connecticut ratepayers access to lower cost solar power, and is a thumb in the nose of the state.
In the latest rate case before PURA, Eversource is requesting a double digit rate increase that will result in rates rising by over a half a billion dollars. To make matters worse they have called for more than 300,000 documents to be withheld from public disclosure. Ratepayers cannot afford, nor should we allow, rate cases to be secreted away from the public, and decided under undue influence, bullying and threat of reprisal.
What can be done? There are several proposals on the table from key decision makers. These include:

Regular review of monopoly status. This would mandate a process for utilities to reapply to maintain their monopoly status every 15 years. It would allow municipalities to choose another entity to deliver electricity.


Granting the Consumer Counsel subpoena power. This will give this consumer advocate a powerful tool to ensure they have all the information they need to represent ratepayers before PURA..

In addition, we propose several important concrete next steps:

PURA’s website is outdated and falls far short of the level of accessibility and transparency the public deserves. It should be redesigned to be intuitive, searchable, and genuinely consumer-friendly.


All communications between PURA and regulated companies, including their representatives and lobbyists, should be publicly disclosed in a timely manner. The public should not have to file public records requests or navigate unnecessary barriers to understand how regulatory decisions are being made.


End the revolving door. Ratepayers have not been well served by the cozy relationship between the utilities and government. We need legislation that will forbid legislators and executive branch staff from going to work for the utilities and PURA. 

Without action, the utilities will continue to bully their way to great profits that Connecticut cannot afford. These simple and common sense reforms will help restore trust in the process and save ratepayers significant money.
Tom Swan is the Executive Director of the Connecticut Citizen Action Group.
