name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: ‘Thoroughly disappointed,’ Wyoming Game and Fish urges reversal of Grand Targhee expansion approval
description: Wyoming wildlife managers were blunt in their objection to a Caribou-Targhee National Forest draft decision that lets a ski area expand its boundaries into vital habitat for Teton Range bighorn sheep. The decision left Wyoming Game and Fish Director Angi Bruce “thoroughly disappointed,” she wrote in a July 13 comment letter about Grand Targhee Resort’s appro[...]
text:
Skiers stop to take in the view of Teton Canyon from the slopes at Grand Targhee Resort on Dec. 31, 2017, near Alta. (Photo courtesy of Ryan Dorgan via WyoFile)Wyoming wildlife managers were blunt in their objection to a Caribou-Targhee National Forest draft decision that lets a ski area expand its boundaries into vital habitat for Teton Range bighorn sheep.

The decision left Wyoming Game and Fish Director Angi Bruce “thoroughly disappointed,” she wrote in a July 13 comment letter about Grand Targhee Resort’s approved expansion. The state agency’s memo suggested a single solution.
“The only effective remedy to the Department’s Objection Points is to avoid [ski area] expansion and the subsequent development into South Bowl,” Bruce wrote.
South Bowl is one of the two expansion areas that Grand Targhee Resort has been working to get approved for nearly six years. The plans were unpopular from the beginning, in part because of known incursions into the talus slopes used by the Teton’s bighorn sheep, which are part of a small and disease-free core native herd in Wyoming.
 Two proposed Grand Targhee expansions would add nearly 700 acres 

The U.S. Forest Service approved new developments and expansion of Grand Targhee’s boundaries in late May. The OK’d changes to the 57-year-old ski area include a host of new lifts, runs, an on-slope restaurant and mountaintop guest building and are intended to make Targhee more competitive as a destination resort. The two tentatively approved expansions would stretch Grand Targhee’s permit area by 694 acres, a 28% addition to its existing 2,517-acre footprint.
Bighorn sheep regularly move along the path in purple on their way to a natural Teton Canyon mineral lick, marked with a star. This view of Grand Targhee Resort’s proposed expansion, which has since been shrunk, is from the Table Mountain trail. (Image courtesy of the Wyoming Game and Fish Department)
Caribou-Targhee Supervisor Kim Pierson reduced the proposed expansions in response to bighorn sheep-related and other environmental concerns, such as the loss of federally “threatened” whitebark pine: the Mono Trees area was reduced 24% to 459 acres. And the South Bowl area was trimmed 12% to 235 acres “to reduce the likelihood of human and bighorn sheep interactions,” Pierson wrote in the draft decision.
In that document, Caribou-Targhee officials disclosed potential bighorn sheep population declines as a result of the ski area’s expansion.
“Loss of habitat within and in the vicinity of the project area, particularly in South Bowl and in Teton Canyon, which is likely accessed through South Bowl, has the potential to harm viability of the Teton Range Herd,” the draft decision stated.
 Objections to the resort’s expansion voiced by county and wildlife officials

Wyoming wildlife officials were unsatisfied with that outcome.
The agency’s wildlife biologist for the Jackson Region, Aly Courtemanch, studied the impacts of backcountry skiing on Teton sheep for her University of Wyoming master’s degree research, concluding that out-of-bounds skiing in the Tetons is directly displacing bighorn sheep.
Game and Fish’s objection letter stated that “minimization measures” and the removal of 31 acres of the South Bowl expansion “do not meaningfully mitigate impacts to bighorn sheep.”
A forthcoming review process could make the Targhee expansion more favorable to Bruce and her Wyoming Game and Fish colleagues.
“There’s an opportunity for the final record decision to be different than the draft, if substantial issues are shown,” Caribou-Targhee spokesman Jared Fisher told WyoFile. “Maybe something was missed in the analysis.”
It’s the forest’s job to address those potential deficiencies, he said.
Game and Fish argued in its objection that the tentatively approved Grand Targhee plans “not only run counter to Wyoming state law but also the shared agreements between the State of Wyoming and the Forest Service regarding management of bighorn sheep and their habitats.”

Wildlife managers argued the draft decision violated the Caribou-Targhee National Forest Plan and Forest Service policy for sensitive species. Game and Fish officials also objected to the forest’s exclusion of technical data they provided.
Wes Livingston, a wildlife capture expert, places a collar on a bighorn sheep in the Tetons as part of a research project monitoring the herd’s health. (Photo by Mark Gocke/Wyoming Game and Fish Department)
Caribou-Targhee’s draft decision was met by over 1,200 comments. Some of those bits of public input won’t have any real impact, because the submitting parties lacked standing or provided remarks that lacked substance, Fisher said.
But substantive remarks from other objectors could sway the final outcome. Objecting parties include both Teton Counties, which border each other opposite the Idaho-Wyoming state line, according to the Jackson Hole News&Guide.
There are also numerous comments from wildlife-focused advocacy groups that objected to the high-profile Teton bighorn sheep herd’s expected habitat loss.
“Of all the negative impacts a Grand Targhee expansion would cause for wildlife, the harm to bighorn sheep habitat is the most acutely concerning,” Wyoming Outdoor Council Wildlife Program Manager Meghan Riley wrote in a comment letter. “The Targhee Bighorn Sheep Herd exists as a small, isolated population confined to high elevations in the Teton Range where they remain year round.”
During surveillance flights, Wyoming biologists last tallied only about 80 animals in the herd, though DNA analyses of scat samples suggest some animals were missed and the population is somewhat larger.
The Greater Yellowstone Coalition, Idaho Conservation League and The Wilderness Society also objected to an expansion, arguing the boundary change “unnecessarily impacts” Teton bighorns.
“The only way to truly protect the Teton bighorn herd would be to remove the South Bowl expansion from the decision,” the groups wrote.
If that’s not possible, they suggested mitigation measures: Restricting summer operations, not allowing backcountry gates in the area and identifying suitable replacement habitat for displaced sheep.
A collaborative objection letter from the Wyoming Wild Sheep Foundation, Wildlife Wildlife Federation, Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership and Wild Sheep Foundation also details misgivings “specifically and exclusively” about the Targhee expansion’s potential harms to Teton Range bighorns. The herd is “one of the most ecologically irreplaceable wildlife populations in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem,” the groups wrote.
“The expansion of Grand Targhee Resort into South Bowl is irreversible in any meaningful management timeframe,” the groups wrote. “The loss of the Teton Range bighorn sheep herd, or its reduction to a remnant population requiring augmentation, is permanent.”
Grand Targhee owner Geordie Gillett did not respond to WyoFile’s request for comment.

title: Former state Sen. John Polk dies at 77
description: Senate Accountability, Efficiency, Transparency Committee Chairman John Polk, R-Hattiesburg, glances up at a completed committee report that he is proof reading in the Supreme Court Chamber at the Capitol in Jackson, Miss., Monday, March 29, 2021. (AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis)
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Businessman and former state Sen. John Polk of Hattiesburg died, Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann said in a social media post on Monday. Polk was 77.
“The Senate and I have lost a close friend, confidant, and outstanding person in former Senator John Polk of Hattiesburg,” Hosemann wrote. “We will always remember him for his unwavering dedication to Mississippi, his strong convictions, and his willingness to say what needed to be said even when it was difficult.”
During a special session last week, Sen. Josh Harkins had announced to his colleagues that Polk had entered hospice care for his illness, and Harkins praised Polk’s service, saying “he’s carried himself with dignity … and was a genuinely kind man.”
Public Safety Commissioner Sean Tindell, a former senator who served with Polk, said: “John Polk was a distinguished businessman, statesman, devoted family man, and man of God. He will be deeply missed, but I take comfort in knowing he is at peace.”
Polk, a Republican served as District 44 senator for Lamar County from 2012 to early 2026. The Legislature redrew the district in 2025, a move Polk had said played into his decision to not seek reelection.
“Serving district 44 as your Senator has been the honor of my life,” Polk said, announcing his decision to his constituents last year. “I know there were times I didn’t vote the way you individually wished I had, but I always had the people of the district and state’s best interest when I voted.”
Polk was a veteran of the Mississippi National Guard and served as an executive at his family’s business, Polk Meat Products, and was a longtime business and community leader in the Pine Belt area and big supporter of his alma mater, the University of Southern Mississippi.  
Arrangements were pending as of Monday.

title: Judge’s ruling in Shekarchi’s bid to quash ethics probe expected in one week
description: WARWICK — The fate of the state Ethics Commission’s investigation into whether former House Speaker K. Joseph Shekarchi can join the Rhode Island Supreme Court will be determined within a week, a Kent County Superior Court judge said Monday. Judge Richard Licht heard arguments in Shekarchi’s lawsuit seeking to halt the Ethics Commission’s investigation into[...]
text:
Former House Speaker K. Joseph Shekarchi leaves a Kent County Superior Court courtroom following a nearly two-hour hearing on his lawsuit seeking to halt a state ethics investigation into his Rhode Island Supreme Court application on July 20, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)WARWICK — The fate of the state Ethics Commission’s investigation into whether former House Speaker K. Joseph Shekarchi can join the Rhode Island Supreme Court will be determined within a week, a Kent County Superior Court judge said Monday.
Judge Richard Licht heard arguments in Shekarchi’s lawsuit seeking to halt the Ethics Commission’s investigation into whether his bid for a seat on the state’s highest court violates Rhode Island’s “revolving door” law, which restricts lawmakers from accepting certain state positions.
Licht, who sought and received an Ethics Commission advisory opinion before joining the Superior Court in 2014, said he plans to issue his decision no later than the end of day Monday, July 27 — the day before the state’s Judicial Nominating Commission is set to interview Shekarchi and four other finalists seeking to fill the vacancy created by the March retirement of Justice Maureen McKenna Goldberg.
“They have a right to know at least what this court thinks, whatever that may be,” Licht said. 
Shekarchi, a Warwick Democrat, stepped down as House speaker on May 7, three days after applying to the bench. That same day, Roger Williams University School of Law Professor Michael Yelnosky filed his complaint arguing that the leap from one branch of government directly to another would violate the revolving door rule written into state law in 1992.
The law prohibits sitting legislators from seeking or accepting employment with any state government agency for at least one year after leaving elected office. But it exempts lawmakers who seek or accept election to a constitutional office.
The commission voted to authorize a full investigation June 2, concluding that the complaint states facts that, if true, are sufficient to constitute an ethics code violation. After the Ethics Commission twice refused to end its investigation, Shekarchi’s attorney Thomas M. Dickinson filed a Superior Court lawsuit seeking to halt the probe and have a judge declare that Shekarchi did not violate the state ethics code.
Shekarchi has repeatedly insisted his application is eligible under the law. Jason Gramitt, the Ethics Commission’s executive director and chief prosecutor, argues the exemption does not apply to appointed positions such as the Supreme Court.
“They are not positions that are elected by the general electorate,” Gramitt told Licht.
Superior Court Judge Richard Licht questions Rhode Island Ethics Commission Executive Director Jason Gramitt during a hearing in Warwick on July 20, 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)
Dickinson again made the case the Supreme Court is indeed a constitutional office exempt from revolving door rule. He also pointed out that the General Assembly didn’t take any action to modify the law after then-Sen. Erin Lynch Prata was appointed to the high court in 2020.
“You can infer legislative assent from silence in certain circumstances,” he said.
Licht too questioned the inaction taken by the commission.
“There could have been another vote for another advisory opinion, or to amend the initial one,” he said. “Nothing happened.”
Gramitt responded that the Lynch Prata case was different from Shekarchi’s since she sought an initial advisory opinion from the Ethics Commission. The commission did not issue a formal opinion, so the case did not create precedent.
“To say that one case of non-prosecution means that the door is wide open for everyone else after that, that’s not how the law works,” he said.
As Licht weighs his decision, he’s already predicted the outcome: “It’s probably going to the Supreme Court.”
“Fifty percent will like it, fifty percent won’t, whatever I decide,” he said. “That’s the job and I don’t mind.”

title: Much of Arkansas under extreme heat warnings; cooling centers opening across state
description: Some Arkansans may be in need of community cooling centers this week as the heat index is forecast to eclipse 100 degrees across large swaths of the state.  Parts of eastern, central and western Arkansas are under extreme heat warnings until Tuesday evening, while the rest of the state is under a heat advisory. The […]
text:
A graphic illustrating the heat advisories and warnings in Arkansas on July 20, 2026. (Graphic Courtesy of the National Weather Service North Little Rock office)Some Arkansans may be in need of community cooling centers this week as the heat index is forecast to eclipse 100 degrees across large swaths of the state. 
Parts of eastern, central and western Arkansas are under extreme heat warnings until Tuesday evening, while the rest of the state is under a heat advisory. The National Weather Service’s office in North Little Rock has warned that overnight temperatures may not dip below 80 degrees in many places.
“Simply put, this leads to oppressive conditions as overnight lows will offer little to no relief from the intense, daytime heat,” the office wrote in a Sunday post on X.
As temperatures have spiked this summer, public cooling centers have opened in several cities, including West Memphis, Pine Bluff, Little Rock, Russellville and North Little Rock. North Little Rock’s and Russellville’s cooling stations are their city-owned community centers, which are operating under their normal business hours.
“Our community centers are open to residents who need respite from the heat during the summer months,” Little Rock spokesperson Aaron Sadler said.
Northwest Arkansas residents can find relief at 7hills Homeless Center’s Day Center or the Salvation Army of Northwest Arkansas. The city of Fayetteville provides funding to these organizations to open cooling centers when temperatures reach an actual or “feels-like” temperature of 100 degrees or more.
Tuesday will be hotter than Monday, according to the National Weather Service. A Wednesday cold front will lower temperatures, but the heat index is expected to rise back into the 100s again over the weekend in Little Rock. 
Little Rock is experiencing an average of seven more days of extreme heat each year compared to 1970 according to Climate Central, a policy-neutral nonprofit that researches climate change and analyzes local climate data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). The organization defines an extreme heat day as one where the temperature rose above 85.7 degrees, which is different from the criteria the weather service uses for issuing extreme heat warnings. 
When the heat index gets above 91 degrees, precautions such as going inside and increasing fluid intake should be taken to avoid issues like heat exhaustion and heat stroke, according to the Mayo Clinic.
More information about cooling centers is available by contacting your local city or county officials.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Judge questions Jackson officials about Lake Hico data center discussion
description: Lake Hico and adjacent cooling ponds are being drained by Entergy because the Brown power plant that used the water is being closed.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
U.S. District Court Judge Henry Wingate, who’s overseeing the federal Jackson water lawsuit, wanted answers Monday about reported discussions of a potential data center on a historically significant property in the city.
WLBT reported Friday on emails exchanged between Jackson Mayor John Horhn and a local tech nonprofit that detail the benefits a hyperscale data center at Lake Hico would bring, including up to $15 billion in private investment and up to $20 million a year in revenue for the city.
Wingate said he called a status conference to ensure any discussions of a data center in Jackson consider impacts on the city’s rehabilitating water and sewer systems.
Horhn, though, appearing as a witness Monday, said such questions were “very, very premature.” The mayor explained that a developer who recently leased the Lake Hico property, which is 16th Section land owned by Jackson Public Schools, is taking the next three years to explore what to do with the land. The options being considered include residential and industrial uses, Horhn said. 
Just three days before the WLBT report, the Jackson City Council voted to pass Mississippi’s first moratorium on new data centers, which is set to start in August and last for six months.
Given the large amount of tax revenue the industry could bring, Horhn said it “would be foolish” for the city to not at least consider bringing in a data center. But he also emphasized that the city, during the moratorium, is developing new rules to account for the public’s concerns around noise, water footprint and energy consumption.
Horhn added he’s sensitive to the significance of Lake Hico and understands why residents would be concerned over the property’s future. Decades ago, the area served as a recreation hub for the city until integration saw white communities abandon the lake for the Ross Barnett Reservoir, the mayor recalled. More recently, Entergy used the property as a cooling pond for one of its power plants. In 2020, the company announced it was draining the lake because JPS wanted to pursue other development. 
Jackson City Attorney Drew Martin said the city would consult with JXN Water — the third-party manager of the local water and sewer systems — on the new regulations it plans to enact for data centers. Martin, echoing Horhn, also reiterated to Wingate that the city has received no proposal or application to build a data center at Lake Hico.

name: Source New Mexico
title: PNM, private equity firm extend merger deadline to mid-2027 after regulators deem stock sale illegal
description: The parent company of New Mexico’s largest electricity provider and the private equity firm looking to acquire it are extending the deadline for their pending merger to mid-2027.
text:
Officials with PNM’s parent company and Blackstone Infrastructure announced they’re extending the deadline for their proposed merger to mid-2027, after the New Mexico Public Regulation found a $400 million stock sale violated state law. (Photo by Danielle Prokop for Source NM)The parent company of New Mexico’s largest electricity provider and the private equity firm looking to acquire it are extending the deadline for their pending merger to mid-2027.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The announcement came weeks after state regulators found that TXNM Energy Inc., which owns PNM, and private equity firm Blackstone Infrastructure violated state law by conducting a $400 million stock sale in 2025 without first gaining approval from the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission. After the commission’s decision on the stock sale earlier this month, neither PNM nor Blackstone officials would say if they intended to continue pursuing the merger.
However, in a joint announcement Friday, officials for TXNM and Blackstone said they extended the deadline for the acquisition to May 31, 2027.
“We remain committed to our proposed partnership with Blackstone Infrastructure because it is critical to TXNM Energy’s long-term ability to provide clean, affordable and reliable power to the customers we serve,” TXNM Energy President and CEO Don Tarry said in a statement. “We appreciate the NMPRC’s careful review of this case and look forward to further demonstrating why this partnership will strengthen the grid, support long-term investment and deliver meaningful benefits for customers and communities across New Mexico and Texas.”
Officials with PNM and Blackstone had long said the deal adhered to state law and contended the pending $11.5 billion merger, first announced in 2025, presented an efficient way to quickly infuse much-needed cash into the state’s aging electric grid.
TXNM has taken out a $400 million loan to undo the 2025 stock sale, according to the joint announcement. The PRC also imposed $300,000 in penalties against the companies in its early July decision.
“Blackstone Infrastructure’s extension of our merger agreement is a sign of our commitment to continue to work collaboratively with stakeholders as we demonstrate the significant benefits of the proposed merger,” Sean Klimczak, global head of Blackstone Infrastructure, said in a statement.

title: Iowa farmer sees culture shift toward water conservation
description: MADRID – Nick Helland and his father have embraced a slew of conservation practices – bioreactors, saturated buffers, cover crops and a nutrient reducing wetland — on their farm in the Greater Des Moines Watershed.  Helland said he feels there has been a “shift in the culture” among farmers from judging one another on how […]
text:
Nick Helland explains how a nutrient reducing wetland on his property took about six acres out of crop production and filters nutrients from about 170 acres. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) MADRID – Nick Helland and his father have embraced a slew of conservation practices – bioreactors, saturated buffers, cover crops and a nutrient reducing wetland — on their farm in the Greater Des Moines Watershed. 
Helland said he feels there has been a “shift in the culture” among farmers from judging one another on how black they could till their soil, to now, how frequently they till and how much cover they leave on the fields. 
“It’s really starting to shift the culture, demonstrate to some of our neighbors and peers that hey, this can be done,” Helland said. 
Gov. Kim Reynolds and Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig toured the Helland farm Monday to demonstrate the conservation tools and incentives they boosted with the implementation of the “farm-to-faucet” act. 
The water quality program, passed as an amendment to the annual budget for the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship and Iowa Department of Natural Resources, represented a $319 million investment into conservation practices, water quality monitoring and water system infrastructure upgrades over a 12-year period. 
The allocation included an estimated $52 million, over the 12-year period, to expand cover crop incentives, a streamside buffer program, wetland implementation and grazing systems in the 22-county Greater Des Moines Watershed. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Helland, a seventh-generation farmer, said his family has been implementing conservation practices, like no-till farming, since the mid-1990s. 
Nick Helland, left, shows Gov. Kim Reynolds a nutrient reducing wetland nestled between corn and soybean fields on his property near Madrid on July 20, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
He said the farm has planted cover crops since cost-share programs first launched in the early 2010s, but he said with the expanded cost-share this year, and several other conservation programs, he plans to put cover on all of his cropland, as opposed to the 20% to 30% he typically seeded with cover crops. 
“I think it’s taken us years to kind of figure out how to build these pieces and how to build the house correctly, but we’ve laid the right foundation, and pieces are coming together,” Helland said. 
As part of the Farm to Faucet program, IDALS expanded cover crop incentives so that farmers in the Greater Des Moines Watershed can now receive $25 an acre on up to 500 acres – an increase from a previous cap of 160 acres. IDALS also expanded a streamside buffer pilot project to pay farmers in the 22-county region for implementing either harvested or non-harvested streamside buffers, another conservation method present at the Helland farm. 


Popular conservation strategies 
Bioreactor: An excavated pit connected to a tile line and filled with wood chips that filter the water from the tile. The water is denitrified by bacteria as it passes through the wood chips. It can reduce 24% to 43% of nitrogen. 
Saturated buffer: A strip with vegetation that helps to filter and absorb nutrients from the water out of a tile line. Practice can reduce 45%-50% of nitrogen.
Cover crops: A crop planted in between cash crops to keep roots in the soil that help lock in nutrients and soil in a field. Practice can reduce 25%-30% of nitrogen and 29% of phosphorus.
Wetlands: Strategically located to collect water from tile lines and runoff from a field, wetlands can filter nutrients from the water before it runs into a waterway. Practice can reduce up to 52% of nitrogen. 
Buffers and wetlands also create additional wildlife habitat. Information and figures from IDALS and the Iowa Nutrient Reduction Strategy non-point source assessment. 


Naig, speaking in front of Helland’s woodchip bioreactor constructed along the Big Creek, said the farm to faucet program is about “investing more into things that are working,” like the strategies on the Helland farm. 
“Clean water is nonnegotiable,” Naig said. “ … We really are here today to talk about that farm-to-faucet approach – so to get a chance to hear the ag side of the story, what’s happening on this farm, but know that this farm is not the only farm where these things are happening.” 
Figures from IDALS show 147 water quality wetlands have been implemented in the state, along with 484 saturated buffers or bioreactors, more than 220,000 acres of streamside buffers and nearly 4 million acres planted with cover crops. All of these practices help to trap nutrients, namely phosphorus and nitrogen, that would otherwise flow off of fields, through tile lines and into waterways. 
Reynolds said the Helland farm showcases the partnerships and “everything that our farmers are doing to protect our natural resources and water quality.” She said farmers and the state need to “be flexible” to adjust programs based on what is working to improve soil health and water quality. 
“Do more of what works — it’s that simple,” Reynolds said.
Helland and Naig said sharing farmer-to-farmer knowledge and working with a conservation professional are important in helping a producer find the right conservation approach.
A recent report showed Iowa lost 17% of the county-level USDA staff that work with farmers to find and apply for conservation funding, loans or other programs. Naig said it’s important these offices are staffed, but also that the state is “efficient” in delivering programs. 
While some water quality advocates have argued conservation practices should be obligatory, rather than just incentivized for farmers, Helland said he feels a mandate would lead farmers to implement practices that don’t work for their farm. 
“If you’re using incentives and you’re starting to kind of help the farmers change the culture and everything, you’re going to be more apt to get the right tool onto that right acre,” Helland said.
Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig, second from right, stands along the top of a dam supporting a nutrient reducing wetland at Helland Farms July 20, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
At the faucet 
The Farm to Faucet legislation also allocated a one-time, $25 million investment to Central Iowa Water Works to expand its infrastructure and increase nitrate removal capacities over the next three years. 
Naig and Reynolds, along with Iowa Department of Natural Resources Director Kayla Lyon, visited the water treatment facility in Grimes that is planning an expansion of its reverse osmosis treatment capabilities. 
Central Iowa Water Works, which serves more than 600,000 customers in the Des Moines region, has twice issued a lawn watering ban due to high concentrations of nitrate in the Des Moines and Raccoon rivers, which serve as source water for some of the water treatment systems in the area. 
Naig said the farm to faucet program aims to “prevent pollutants from ever getting into our streams” with the implementation of conservation work in the watershed and to ensure there is an “appropriate amount of treatment infrastructure” downstream.  
“Because that’s how you actually can deliver clean, safe drinking water to Iowans,” Naig said.
Tami Madsen, CEO of Central Iowa Water Works, said the investments upstream are an “essential part of Iowa’s water story.” 
“While advanced treatment technology is essential, treatment plants are not expected to solve every water quality challenge alone,” Madsen said. “… The future of Iowa’s water will be built through partnerships like the ones represented here today: farmers, landowners, conservation organizations, utilities, water treatment professionals, researchers, local governments, and state leaders working together for that common goal.”

title: Wife of former Michigan House speaker sentenced for embezzling from campaign fund he controlled
description: Stephanie Chatfield, the wife of former Michigan House Speaker Lee Chatfield, was sentenced Monday after pleading guilty last month to embezzling from the Peninsula Fund, a nonprofit campaign fund controlled by Lee and his associates, Robert and Anné Minard. Stephanie Chatfield was initially charged in April 2024 with one count each of embezzlement from a […[...]
text:
Former Michigan House Speaker Lee Chatfield (right) and his wife Stephanie Chatfield (left) leave court after their preliminary exam as the couple face multiple charges related to embezzlement on Feb. 28, 2025 | (By Anna Liz Nichols/Michigan Advance) Stephanie Chatfield, the wife of former Michigan House Speaker Lee Chatfield, was sentenced Monday after pleading guilty last month to embezzling from the Peninsula Fund, a nonprofit campaign fund controlled by Lee and his associates, Robert and Anné Minard.
Stephanie Chatfield was initially charged in April 2024 with one count each of embezzlement from a nonprofit organization and conspiracy to commit embezzlement from a nonprofit organization. She and Lee Chatfield were set to go to trial later this year, but in June Stephanie Chatfield agreed to a plea agreement that saw the state drop two of the felony charges, one for embezzlement and another for conspiracy to commit embezzlement.
Instead, she agreed to plead guilty to embezzling from a political nonprofit organization, which remains a felony that carries prison time and a fine of between $200 and $1,000.
On Monday, Ingham County Circuit Court Judge Morgan Cole sentenced Chatfield to six months of probation and 25 hours of community service. She must also pay a $2,000 fine.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Anyone who is granted access to non-profits and their funds must obey the law,” Attorney General Dana Nessel said in a statement. “Proximity to influence does not grant immunity from accountability, and no one can use their nexus to power to unlawfully enrich themselves. Mrs. Chatfield was a willing participant on the Peninsula Fund gravy train, enjoying a lifestyle funded by money meant to support public welfare. My office remains committed to pursuing and prosecuting those who treat these types of accounts as personal piggy banks.”
Lee Chatfield has pleaded not guilty to the charges filed in 2024. The attorney general’s office declined to comment on whether he was also pursuing a plea agreement.
Nessel’s office alleged that the couple funneled money from their political nonprofit accounts to fund a lavish lifestyle. They were both set to stand trial in September for embezzlement and other charges related to their activities, but Stephanie Chatifield’s guilty plea eliminated the need for her trial.
Chatfield aides sentenced to probation after pleading guilty to felony charges

The Department of Attorney General’s case against the Chatfields asserted that, beginning in 2021, the couple allegedly used nonprofit money to reimburse themselves for purchases at luxury retailers including Coach and for expenses at attractions such as Universal Studios. Prosecutors also alleged Lee Chatfield spent lavishly at strip clubs and partied with associates and his brothers.
An investigation into Chatfield began after his former sister-in-law reported to Lansing police an allegation that he had sexually assaulted her for years, starting when she was 14 or 15 years old. 
Michigan State Police looked into the allegations and found evidence of potential financial improprieties – an investigation that was later taken over by Nessel. However, she said her office did not find sufficient evidence to pursue charges for criminal sexual conduct.
The Minards recently pleaded guilty to lesser charges and agreed to testify against the Chatfields. The Minards were initially charged with conducting a criminal enterprise for their role in allegedly misappropriating funds from three nonprofit organizations and two political action committees tied to Lee Chatfield.

title: State Police recruitment opens for next training academy class
description: The Rhode Island State Police is expected to graduate 17 new troopers in August. Applications to join the Class of 2027 are now open.
text:
Rhode Island State Police Training Academy recruits march during the 2025 Newport St. Patrick's Day Parade. (Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current) 

Learn more
Interested applicants to the Rhode Island State Police can speak with troopers from a variety of different specialty units and learn more about a career during the following events:
Open Houses
Saturday, Aug. 15, 10 a.m. – 2 p.m.
Saturday, Sept. 19, 10 a.m. – 2 p.m.
Rhode Island State Police Headquarters, 311 Danielson Pike, North Scituate, R.I.

Women troopers are available to talk about their experience with the Rhode Island State Police.
Tuesday, Sept. 8, 6-7 p.m.
Walter Stone Conference Room
Rhode Island State Police Headquarters, 311 Danielson Pike, North Scituate, R.I.
 
Additional information about the selection process is available at www.risp.ri.gov/academy
To apply, visit: www.PoliceApp.com/RISP.
Applications must be properly completed and received no later than Sept. 30.


Seventeen new Rhode Island state troopers are expected to graduate 17 from the State Police training academy in August — up from 16 last year. Class sizes are still down from the 29 troopers who graduated in 2024.
Now recruitment is happening for the Class of 2027, with a new academy set to start in March, marking the fifth consecutive year of training classes. Classes were previously held in 2019 and 2022.
Trainees admitted to the academy undergo 22 weeks of training at the State Police Training Academy in Foster and are only allowed off the campus on weekends. Recruits must complete a law enforcement educational curriculum, as well as physical and skills training, according to the State Police website.
The deadline to apply is Sept. 30. Before applicants can begin training at the academy in March, they must undergo a physical assessment, written examination, oral interview, background check and psychological testing.
Applicants must also be U.S. citizens between 18 and 35 years old, hold a high school diploma or equivalency, meet vision requirements, have a driver’s license and have not been convicted of a felony.
Since a $5.6 million project started in 2018 to upgrade the academy, the state’s budgets have earmarked an increasing flow of funds for the academy. The budget allocated the Department of Public Safety $535,000 for “training academy upgrades” in fiscal year 2021 and $750,000 in 2022. That jumped to around $1.4 million in fiscal years 2023 and 2024, and almost $1.6 million in 2025 and 2026.
Upgrades included providing new air conditioning and heating systems and new firearms simulators and safety renovations, according to a 2022 report from the Senate Fiscal Office.
In his budget recommendation for fiscal year 2027, Gov. Dan McKee requested more than $1.6 million to fund operations and pay personnel for another year of training. But the fiscal 2027 budget McKee signed in June included $650,000 for academy upgrades.
Increased funding and wider recruitment campaigns haven’t increased academy applications in recent years. In 2024, 456 people applied to join the academy, according to an Access to Public Records Act request from Rhode Island Current that year. That marked a 27% decrease from the 629 applications in 2023.
Data on the number of applicants in the 2025 admissions cycle was not immediately available.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Wu, feds unveil plan to tackle sea level rise in Boston
description: The draft plan is set to act as a roadmap for how New England’s largest city can navigate the more than four feet of sea level rise the Army Corps projects will hit Boston by 2090.
text:
IF BOSTON IS going to avert the most catastrophic impacts of projected sea level rise this century, it needs to get building. 
A new landmark draft plan set to be released this week from the US Army Corps of Engineers in partnership with the city recommends 20 specific projects to shore up the most flood-prone parts of Boston. 
Some 20,000 buildings and 40 percent of the city — more than a quarter-million residents — at risk of flooding are depending on it. 
“Today marks a major milestone in Boston’s fight to protect our city from climate change,” Mayor Michelle Wu said at a press conference along the waterfront in the North End. “This study … will give us the clearest picture we’ve ever had of how rising seas and stronger storms threaten our neighborhoods, and importantly, the report also will lay out a plan for Boston to become the greener, healthier, more resilient city our residents deserve.” 
The draft plan is set to act as a roadmap for how New England’s largest city, one-sixth of which is built on filled tidelands, can navigate the more than four feet of sea level rise the Army Corps projects will hit Boston by 2090 as the world continues to warm. It’s also a glimmer of cooperation between the federal government under President Trump and a deep-blue city in a state with a Democratic trifecta in what has otherwise seen a souring relationship. 
If all goes to script and the draft plan for Boston — which has an estimated price tag of $10 billion — is finalized in roughly its current form, in the years and decades ahead, new floodwalls up to nine feet high could dot the edges of the harbor in Charlestown, the North End, and South Boston. Levees could be built at Pattens Cove, Tenean Beach, and Pope John Paul II Park in Dorchester. And floodgates could go up right outside Logan Airport in East Boston.
There’s a key sweetener, too: Boston can pass up to 65 percent of the tab on to the federal government for the construction of the infrastructure that the Army Corps recommends to protect the city from flooding. 
Delivering the final study to Congress in two years from now — which will mark a six-year process that kicked off in 2022 — is just the first step. Federal lawmakers will need to appropriate money to fund the suite of flood control projects every two years, requiring Boston to continue to make the case and compete with other cities for funding. 
The plan comes as Massachusetts is hitting a critical crossroads with respect to the adverse economic consequences of flooding around the state, from rising insurance costs to lost property value for homeowners and businesses. That’s now prompting state officials to consider more sweeping and potentially contentious reforms, including a voluntary buyout program now under discussion and efforts to require property owners to disclose their flood risk and prior flooding history.   
“I always like to bring the perspective that we are protecting people,” Gabriela Coletta Zapata, a city councilor who represents East Boston, Charlestown, and parts of the downtown waterfront, said at Monday’s press conference. “These are folks. These are lives. This is decades of memories of folks living in one place that are at risk. And this investment in climate resilience is more about just seawalls and infrastructure. It’s about protecting them.” 
Areas along the Boston waterfront are vulnerable to more severe flooding in the decades to come. (Jordan Wolman/CommonWealth Beacon)
The Army Corps estimates that the cost of closing Boston’s floodways through these 20 projects located along 16 miles of the city’s 47-mile coastline is $10 billion for the baseline infrastructure alone — which doesn’t include upgrades city officials said they would want in order to improve public access to Boston Harbor and integrate the infrastructure into parks and public spaces on the water. 
On a statewide basis, a study released last year from Gov. Maura Healey’s administration found that between $90 billion and $130 billion will be needed in resilience investments through 2050. 
The cost of inaction, though, is far greater. Boston could otherwise experience $54 billion in losses by the end of the century, if nothing is done, according to the draft plan. Key regional assets like Logan Airport, hospitals, I-93, I-90, and rail stations remain highly vulnerable. Neighborhoods more than a mile from the ocean could experience severe flooding in the next 25 years.  
And the prospect of significant buy-in from the federal government further helps take the financial sting out of the billions of dollars necessary to close Boston’s most vulnerable points where water can spill onto land and snake its way through streets. 
Yet even if Congress appropriates the full 65 percent of the funding needed for the projects, how Boston pays for the rest under constrained state and local budgets is an open question. 
Boston’s Green Ribbon Commission has embarked on finding some of the answers, hiring a consultant team last month to develop a coastal resilience financial blueprint that will identify financing options from public and private sources to support the 35 percent the federal government won’t cover. Brian Swett, Boston’s climate chief, stressed to reporters last week that Boston taxpayers alone wouldn’t need to shoulder the burden — the private sector, the state, and the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority would all be expected to chip in, too.  
The Army Corps will be accepting public comment on the draft report through September 18 once it is released in full on Friday. But there are already early signs that some stakeholders will want changes. 
Conservation Law Foundation said in a statement Monday that it wants to see an approach that better reflects “years of community planning” and prioritizes nature-based solutions, like salt marsh restorations and open spaces. 
Top city officials don’t necessarily disagree: Wu said that Boston has stepped up its efforts around permeable pavements and improving tree canopy, while Swett pointed to a “living” seawall that’s attracted new species and led the Boston Harbor to become a fishing hotspot.  
Long before the new draft plan from the Army Corps, Boston has been working to improve its resilience in the face of rising seas and more extreme weather events. Fourteen of the 24 severe storms in Boston that triggered disaster declarations since 1991 have caused major flooding. 
The city has touted a slew of projects along the waterfront either in the works or completed over the past decade designed to mitigate flood risk.  
But with Boston mostly dodging the worst of the devastating consequences of some of the biggest storms in recent years, the scope of what needs to be done to insulate the city’s residents and economy from rising seas is much broader than what’s been accomplished to date — and in need of more financial muscle. 
Hurricane Sandy, which battered the Northeast in 2012 with historic flooding and led to at least 43 deaths in the New York area, is what underscores the urgency of the moment for Swett.  
“In Boston, we missed a massive cataclysmic flooding event not by 500 miles, but by five hours,” he said. “If that same storm, that same trajectory, had hit at our high tide, we would have had the worst flooding in Boston. That was that ‘A-ha’ moment.”

name: VTDigger
title: After penalty kicks in Seattle, Vermont Green FC women end first season as runners-up
description:
“Burlington and Vermont in general are a real current — and I think future — cultural powerhouse for women's soccer,” said the club’s co-founder.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  After penalty kicks in Seattle, Vermont Green FC women end first season as runners-up.
text:
The Vermont Green FC women’s team competed in the USL W championship on July 18, 2026, in Seattle. Photo courtesy Kevin Ng/Vermont Green FC

Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
When Waterbury-born Louisa Thomsen equalized for Vermont Green FC in the United Soccer League women’s national championship Saturday, pandemonium ensued. 
The substitutes’ bench erupted, dashing to embrace the Vermonter as the clock wound down in normal time. Fans who made the trip to Salmon Bay FC’s home stadium in Seattle added to the noise. And back in Vermont, a capacity crowd at Zero Gravity brewery — among many other watch parties — waved their flags with renewed hope.
“It’s one of those, like, storybook things,” club co-founder Patrick Infurna said of the homegrown midfielder Monday. “It had to be her.”
“It was pretty awesome,” Thomsen reflected in an interview.
In the end, though, the women in green fell just short of a national title. Despite holding Salmon Bay to a draw in open play, the Vermont team lost 5-4 in a penalty shootout, marking the team’s first ever defeat.
“It’s never a fun way to lose a match,” said head coach Abby Carchio. But despite all that, and the subsequent cancellation of her entire team’s return flights due to weather, she said her defining emotion Monday was gratitude at the end of the team’s inaugural season.
After topping the Northeast Division of the USL W, a 96-team nationwide women’s summer league largely featuring collegiate players, the Green mounted a deep run into the playoffs. After the team defeated Pennsylvania-based Eagle FC to win the league’s Eastern Conference at the first time of asking, a win against North Carolina’s Asheville City SC in front of a sold-out crowd in Burlington propelled Carchio’s squad to the national final. 
Support from the club’s owners and supporters, as well as her team’s growth in both togetherness and tactical execution, powered the extraordinary first season, Carchio said.
“The player group has been incredibly special,” she said of the newly assembled squad.
For Thomsen, playing in this league for a Vermont-based club in front of family and friends realized an improbable dream. 
“It’s never been something that I thought was even an option,” she said.
The 21-year-old plays for Bucknell University in Pennsylvania during the academic year. Having spent years seeking out the highest available level of soccer in Vermont, Thomsen said, the news that Vermont Green FC was preparing to launch a women’s team was exciting in itself. And after making the roster this summer, she worked her way off the bench to start in many of the squad’s most important games.
Beyond technical development, the exposure Vermont Green offers can help young players access other playing opportunities, or even land a professional contract, Thomsen said. 
“You never know who’s watching,” she said of the playoff games her club played this summer.
But more immediately, she’s excited for Vermont Green’s continued growth in coming years. Recruitment will only strengthen with time, she said, and the club’s management is already “top tier.”
“There’s a national championship in the future, 100%,” Thomsen said. 
Infurna agrees. The stories and excitement generated by this early success can only help the club’s momentum going forward.
“Burlington and Vermont in general are a real current — and I think future — cultural powerhouse for women’s soccer,” he said. 
He commended the players, coaching staff and fans alike for their dedication to the club’s project this season. Virtue Field’s bleachers, which hold 2,500, sold out for nearly every home women’s game this season as a distinct fan culture formed around the women’s team, according to Infurna.
“We didn’t fail by not winning the final,” he said. “We are so proud.”
The Vermont Green men’s team, still boasting an undefeated record of its own this season, will face Asheville City in Laredo, Texas on Friday for the Eastern Conference championship in the United Soccer League’s second men’s tier.

title: Federal government approves condensed timeline for overseas ballots in SC primary
description: COLUMBIA — South Carolina can go ahead with a condensed timeline to get ballots to overseas voters for the upcoming special U.S. Senate primary, the federal Department of Justice said. An agreement the agencies signed Monday resolves a conflict between state and federal law over the election’s timing. Under South Carolina law, the special primary […]
text:
The federal Department of Justice agreed not to sue South Carolina over a law setting special primary elections before the federally required deadline for overseas voters on Monday, July 20, 2026. (File/Photo by Seanna Adcox/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — South Carolina can go ahead with a condensed timeline to get ballots to overseas voters for the upcoming special U.S. Senate primary, the federal Department of Justice said.
An agreement the agencies signed Monday resolves a conflict between state and federal law over the election’s timing.
Under South Carolina law, the special primary to elect a GOP nominee to replace Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died unexpectedly July 11 after winning the June primary, must take place Aug. 11.
But that didn’t leave enough time to fulfill a federal requirement that overseas voters, including members of the military, have 45 days to request and send in a ballot, either physically or online.
The federal agency, which is responsible for enforcing election laws, agreed not to sue the state for failing to allow the 45-day window.
By Friday, election officials must reach out to everyone who requested a mailed Republican ballot for the June 9 statewide primary election or June 23 runoff to ask if they’d like to participate again.
Anyone who voted in the Democratic primary can’t vote for the Republican nominee, the Election Commission has decided.
Officials will have until Aug. 1 to send out requested ballots, according to the agreement.
The state and federal agencies agreed the deadlines “will provide sufficient time” for overseas voters to receive and fill out their ballots.
Ballots must be sent back by 7 p.m. Aug. 11, which is election day. If a runoff is necessary, votes for that must be cast by 7 p.m. Aug. 25.
All but 48 of the 1,051 overseas voters participating in the June primary did so online, the elections agency said previously.
Voters will likely have a crowded slate of candidates to choose from in South Carolina’s first open U.S. Senate race in 22 years. Filing officially opens Tuesday, but five candidates had announced by Monday they intended to run.
Early voting begins Aug. 5.

title: US Education Department veterans blast Trump plan to transfer programs
text:
WASHINGTON — Former U.S. Department of Education officials in Republican and Democratic administrations sounded the alarm Monday over the agency’s efforts to outsource its special education programs and civil rights enforcement to other agencies. U.S. Democratic Sen. Patty Murray of Washington state convened the former officials, along with advocates and educators, at a virtual press conference to blast those sweeping moves, which are part of a broader effort by President Donald Trump’s administration to dismantle the 46-year-old Education Department. Murray rebuked the transfers as “outrageous” and “completely unacceptable,” noting that while she is fighting “tooth and nail” against any effort to dismantle the agency, she is “especially concerned about what this could mean for all students, especially students with disabilities.” The agency in June said the Department of Health and Human Services will administer programs under Education’s Office of Special Education and Rehabilitative Services, or OSERS, while civil rights enforcement under its Office for Civil Rights will be transferred to the Department of Justice. The Education Department had announced 10 earlier interagency agreements, or IAAs, with HHS, Labor, Interior, State and Treasury, which transfer several of Education’s responsibilities to those agencies.The department has said it “will continue to perform all statutorily required duties and responsibilities” involving special education programs and civil rights enforcement.

 






U.S. Sen. Patty Murray, a Washington Democrat. (Photo by Kayla Bartkowski/Getty Images)

OSERS is responsible for administering the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, or IDEA, which guarantees a free public education for students with disabilities. The umbrella unit OSERS includes the Office of the Assistant Secretary, Office of Special Education Programs and the Rehabilitation Services Administration. The civil rights office is tasked with investigating complaints from students and families. 'Learners, not patients'Katy Neas, CEO of The Arc of the United States, an advocacy group for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities, said that the transfers “would split apart the offices responsible for making disability rights real in schools, leaving families chasing answers across the federal government instead of getting accountability from one education agency.” Neas was the deputy assistant secretary and acting assistant secretary at OSERS during the Biden administration. “The stakes have never been higher,” she said. “If we allow the Department of Education to be dismantled, we not only undo decades of progress, we also risk abandoning the promise that every child deserves a chance to try and to succeed.” Catherine Lhamon, executive director of the Edley Center on Law and Democracy at the University of California, Berkeley, School of Law said the “new interagency agreement between the Department of Education and the Department of Justice is what someone would create if the person were designing a system to fail.” Lhamon served as assistant secretary for civil rights during the Obama and Biden administrations. “The principal harm of this new agreement is that it guarantees lengthier continued silence from the federal government on the classic kinds of discrimination cases families experience,” Lhamon said. Examples include restraining or secluding students, she said.It raises “the core question (of) whether students with disabilities have the free appropriate public education to which the law entitles them,” Lhamon added.Stephanie Smith Lee, co-director of policy and advocacy at National Down Syndrome Congress, pointed out that “IDEA is an education and civil rights law, not a healthcare program.” “Students with disabilities are learners, not patients,” added Lee, who served as director of the Office of Special Education Programs under the George W. Bush administration. “Moving special education and vocational rehabilitation to the Department of Health and Human Services would separate them from the rest of federal education policy and weaken the expertise and coordinated oversight that students, families and states depend on,” she said. Savannah Newhouse, a spokesperson for the Education Department, dismissed the criticism, saying in a statement to States Newsroom that Murray and the former officials were part of a failing status quo. “As Senator Murray is well aware, the Department of Education’s interagency partnerships do not alter the Trump Administration's dedication to students with disabilities and federal civil rights laws,” she wrote. “These agreements simply ensure that well-positioned agencies can support the workload, pool their expertise, and ultimately strengthen protections for students.” US House bills ‘dead’ in Senate  Meanwhile, earlier in July the House Committee on Education and Workforce advanced a package of 10 bills permanently transferring several of Education’s functions to other departments and largely reflecting many of the earlier IAAs. Notably, that package does not include any efforts to transfer Education’s responsibilities regarding special education programs and civil rights enforcement to other agencies. “As long as this former preschool teacher is a United States senator, every one of those bills is dead on arrival,” Murray said.

title: Canadian hockey sticks, wine and cement subject to new Trump tariffs
text: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump ordered 50% tariffs on several Canadian products Monday in response to what his administration describes as retaliatory restrictions on imports of American goods, including alcohol, dairy and automotives.Trump’s three separate proclamations to impose steep tariffs on items like hockey sticks, wine and cement, came just days after he threatened to slap more tariffs on Canada as smoke from raging wildfires in Ontario blanketed much of the northeastern U.S. through the weekend. But a senior administration official denied the new tariffs were in response to the smoke.“These are not the so-called wildfire tariffs. The president has asked for options on that, and options are being shared with him. These tariffs are in response to discriminatory treatment by Canada against U.S. products,” the senior administration official said on a call with reporters Monday afternoon.The tariffs will go into effect Aug. 19.Trump appeared alongside Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney Sunday at the FIFA World Cup trophy ceremony in East Rutherford, New Jersey, but the two leaders did not discuss White House plans for the new tariffs, according to the senior administration official.Trump triggered the new tariffs under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, a Depression-era provision that authorizes the president to impose duties up to 50% of a product’s value in response to discrimination against U.S. commerce. The provision has been long forgotten since the 1940s and has never been enforced, experts say. “To our knowledge, Section 338 has not been used for this purpose before,” the senior administration official told reporters. “It’s been on the books for a long time. In our view, the terms are clear: It gives the president this authority in situations where a country discriminates against the United States relative to the treatment given (to) a third country.”Trump’s unprecedented sweeping tariffs on global goods, including from Canada, imposed in April 2025 under the 1977 International Economic Emergency Powers Act, or IEEPA, were found illegal and overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court in February.The administration was ordered by the U.S. Court of International Trade to refund roughly $166 billion in duties paid by importers under the IEEPA tariffs.Since the Supreme Court’s major blow to Trump’s trade agenda, the White House has sought other routes to impose tariffs. Almost immediately after the court’s decision, Trump announced a temporary base 10% tariff on all imports under section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974. Those tariffs are now being litigated in trade court.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: State declares its seven-year takeover of Providence Public Schools a success. What the metrics say.
description: By some metrics, things are looking up for the Providence Public School District (PPSD). Students are coming to class more often. Their standardized test scores are rising. And more of them are graduating high school. These are a few of the accomplishments the Rhode Island Department of Education (RIDE) highlights in a 62-page report released […]
text:
Mount Pleasant High School in Providence is seen under construction on Friday, July 17, 2026. The $110 million project is set for completion next summer. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)By some metrics, things are looking up for the Providence Public School District (PPSD). Students are coming to class more often. Their standardized test scores are rising. And more of them are graduating high school. 
These are a few of the accomplishments the Rhode Island Department of Education (RIDE) highlights in a 62-page report released Friday — an epilogue to the agency’s intervention in the capital city’s public schools, which went under state control in 2019. 
“The measurable progress made under the state intervention is undeniable,” Education Commissioner Angélica Infante-Green wrote in the introduction to the report. “PPSD has not only stabilized, but it is moving forward with real momentum.”
On the other end of the takeover’s nearly seven-year timeline is a different report: A 93-page dossier prepared by a team of Johns Hopkins University researchers who documented a school system plagued by systemic issues — problems severe enough that the report garnered national attention when released. 
Infante-Green writes in the introduction to her agency’s new report that its Johns Hopkins predecessor was a “heartbreaking” and “devastating” document, one that showcased “deteriorating buildings, inconsistent curriculum, ineffective central-office practices, and systemic inequities that created barriers to the academic success for the district’s historically underserved students.”
Some of the most tangible transformation in Providence has been made on that first bullet point: Six new or renovated schools opened during the intervention, compared to only one built in the 15 years prior to the takeover. According to the RIDE report, there are 14 additional school construction or renovation projects still underway or planned. Seven projects are slated for completion in the next two years, while the remainder have no projected completion date yet. 
Overall, across all 20 projects finished and unfinished, the state’s contributions to capital improvement in the district could reach nearly $984.6 million — an investment buoyed by $665 million in school construction bonds approved by the city’s voters between 2020 and 2024.
A less flashy but still important quality-of-life improvement made during the takeover: A drinking fountain in all 37 of the district’s schools. The “bubblers,” RIDE’s report notes invoking a Rhode Island colloquialism, supply clean and filtered water for all schools, addressing the numerous reports of brown and often lead-contaminated water that poured from school taps back in 2019, per the Johns Hopkins report. 
What the metrics say
Buildings improved during the takeover, but what was happening inside? RIDE’s new self-assessment gives a less concrete answer as to how much academics have improved since 2019. 
Students’ math proficiency rose from 11.9% in 2019 to 16.4% in 2025. English language arts proficiency inched up, from 17.2% to 17.7%. Both numbers translate to more than four out of five Providence students remaining below grade-level expectations.
A four-year graduation rate of 79% in 2024, however, was the highest in district history, the report noted. The statewide rate that year was 84.1%.
Chronic absenteeism, which peaked at 57.1% during the 2021-22 school year, in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic, fell to 29.3% in 2024-25.
Pre-K capacity also increased during the takeover, from 352 available seats in 2019 to 940 in the 2025-2026 school year. Dual-language enrollment also grew, expanding into high schools and rising from 1,065 to 1,968 seats across grade levels in the district. 
In a Monday email, Providence School Board President Ty’Relle Stephens said the report “did a strong job highlighting many of the accomplishments achieved during the state intervention,” including “historic investment” in facilities and expanded career and technical education (CTE) and dual language programs and offerings. 
“These are meaningful accomplishments that represent real progress for Providence students and families, and that progress deserves to be recognized,” Stephens wrote. 
Still, the academic data was not entirely celebratory for Stephens, who noted that most Providence students currently fail to meet grade-level expectations. Third-grade English Language Arts proficiency “remains below where it was when the takeover began,” he said.
Stephens also pointed out a somewhat deceptive statistic: 14.3% of the city’s high school juniors met or exceeded expectations on the SAT math exam last year. But that rate fell to 3.8% when excluding scores from Classical High School, which has consistently placed first statewide in national ranking lists.
An easel pad is filled with Providence high schoolers’ thoughts on their public schools at an OurSchools community event on Dec. 10, 2024. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
‘Organizational paralysis’
RIDE’s report is also intended to serve as a blueprint for Providence leaders to build upon now that the district is back under local control.
Some of the sharper instructions from RIDE come near the end of the report, on page 51, which outlines “Roles and Responsibilities” upon the district’s return to local control, which formally resumed July 1. 
The 2019 Johns Hopkins report “called out overlapping spheres of authority among the mayor, superintendent, school board and union,” RIDE recaps in its new report, adding that this helped inflict an “organizational paralysis” on the district. 
“It is critical that PPSD doesn’t return to a state of competing authority and organizational paralysis,” the RIDE report reads, and references a declaratory order issued on June 30, the final day of state control.
The order bars Providence from reclaiming unspent money for its general fund, and it also specifies that only the superintendent — not the School Board — has the authority to appoint administrators in the district. 
The order derived in part from a proposal from Stephens earlier in the year that would have eliminated a labor and employment counsel role at PPSD, and redirected those funds to two staff positions, a director and coordinator, who would report to the School Board. 
The order did not give a final legal interpretation of Stephens’ proposal, citing “the absence of a more complete evidentiary record,” but added that “would appear to usurp the Superintendent’s express statutory powers.”
​​The recommendations in RIDE’s new report cites the declaratory order in its outline of shared authority going forward, but “it is important to be clear that they are recommendations,” Stephens wrote. 
“They are advisory and do not, on their own, carry the force of law,” the school board president added. “Nevertheless, the Board has taken them seriously. We developed a public transition dashboard and have already addressed, or begun addressing, many of them.”
To sustain the district’s successes, RIDE’s report states the city must commit long-term funding — something that remained a big question for state officials when determining whether to relinquish control back to local officials.
Then-Providence-Mayor Jorge Elorza and the City Council engaged the state in a court battle in 2021 over the city’s alleged underfunding of its schools, which ultimately led to the state securing a $15 million settlement in 2024.
“One area I would have welcomed more guidance on is the academic path forward,” Stephens noted, adding that “clear recommendations around accelerating student achievement and closing persistent opportunity and achievement gaps would be valuable” to both the school board and the district. 
Wrote Stephens: “[I]n the end, our success will not be measured simply by who governs Providence Public Schools, but by something far more important: whether our children are learning, whether they are thriving, and whether every student, in every neighborhood, has a genuine opportunity to reach their fullest potential.”

text:
A border patrol agent with what appears to be an extra magazine strapped to his chest stands with other federal agents near the scene of 26th Street West and Nicollet Avenue, where federal agents shot and killed a 37-year-old man Saturday, Jan. 24, 2026, the third shooting in as many weeks. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)A Trump-appointed federal judge on Monday tossed out a Department of Justice lawsuit that aimed to invalidate state and local “sanctuary” policies, which limit information-sharing and cooperation between local law enforcement agencies and immigration enforcement.
The lawsuit, filed in September, was one of at least 27 such cases filed against more than 20 cities, counties and states during the first year of President Donald Trump’s second term. It preceded Operation Metro Surge, during which thousands of immigration agents arrested thousands of immigrants; shot three people, killing two; and sparked major protests. 
Leaders at the Department of Homeland Security repeatedly pointed to state and local governments’ refusal to assist in immigration enforcement as a reason for not ending the operation sooner.
In its complaint, the DOJ challenged several state and local policies: a Minnesota law preventing the state Department of Driver and Vehicle Services from sharing data with immigration agencies; Minneapolis and St. Paul policies barring local police from enforcing immigration laws; an attorney general’s legal advisory prohibiting Minnesota law enforcement agencies from holding someone based on a request from federal immigration authorities if the person would otherwise be released from custody; and a Hennepin County policy modeled on that attorney general’s advisory. 
Eric C. Tostrud, chief judge for the District of Minnesota, dismissed all of the claims. He primarily cited the Tenth Amendment’s anticommandeering doctrine, which prohibits the federal government from forcing state and local authorities to carry out tasks — such as immigration enforcement — which are the sole responsibility of the federal government.

name: VTDigger
title: Why do animal rights groups hate Vermont?
description:
Animal rights groups, not hunters and anglers, are driving the divide over Vermont wildlife policy.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Why do animal rights groups hate Vermont?.
text:
Dear Editor,
Recent letters and commentaries in VTDigger show disdain and contempt for hunters, trappers and anglers, as well as the Vermont Fish and Wildlife Department. They use what I believe is innuendo and misinformation to make a case that the department doesn’t serve their wishes and that those of us who hunt, fish and trap are responsible for the divisions in our communities. 
In a survey conducted by Responsive Management for the Vermont Fish and Wildlife Department in 2015, only 3% of Vermonters were dissatisfied with the department. Eleven years ago, there was little division among Vermonters over how the department conducted its mission to manage and regulate fish and wildlife. A more recent study, in 2022, shows dissatisfaction ticking up to just 5%. 
Despite claims by animal rights groups, most Vermonters are happy with the department. So why suggest otherwise?
These animal rights groups are backed by members with lots of time to lobby our legislators and oodles of dollars. They harass the department and write letters attacking Vermont values. They cite one-off situations and repeat them as if they represent all of us who participate in the activities regulated by the department.  
Hunters, trappers and anglers, as a group, do not condone the willful mistreatment of their prey.  We do not condone breaking the fish and wildlife laws set by the department. I have yet to hear these animal rights groups condemn the lawbreakers in their group. 
Animal rights groups are activists, not conservationists. It seems to me they care more about their agenda than wildlife, and it shows up in how they criticize the department for focusing on population-based models rather than individual animals.

READ MORE

What have they done to protect the environment? What funds and time have they dedicated to conservation? All we hear from them is opinion and derision directed at their fellow community members who fish, hunt and trap. 
Vermont sportsmen and women work to protect wildlife habitat, to promote responsible sportsmanship and to be good citizens.   
Jerry D’Amico  
Roxbury, Vt.
