name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Army vet running for U.S. Senate slams ‘rigged system,’ ‘political insiders’
description: TOPEKA — A U.S. Army veteran and outspoken critic of Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall has focused his campaign for the U.S. Senate by approaching issues from a veteran’s perspective as he competes with 10 other Democratic candidates in the Aug. 4 primary. Noah Taylor said he is running a campaign grounded in grassroots […]
text:
Noah Taylor, Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, appears on the Kansas Reflector podcast on July 17, 2026. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A U.S. Army veteran and outspoken critic of Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall has focused his campaign for the U.S. Senate by approaching issues from a veteran’s perspective as he competes with 10 other Democratic candidates in the Aug. 4 primary.
Noah Taylor said he is running a campaign grounded in grassroots support, and he pledged to take no corporate PAC money. In social media videos and ads, Taylor has taken swings at “big corporations and the Epstein class,”  a “rigged system” and “political insiders” as he speaks on the war in Iran, high gas prices and floundering rural health systems.
Taylor said on the Kansas Reflector podcast he decided to run for public office because he “was tired of having people at the federal level that don’t understand our lives, our values and our experiences.”


“I’ve traveled all across this state multiple times, and what I’ve come to realize is people aren’t looking for someone to come riding in on a white horse and save the day,” he said. “We’ve been sold that lie time and time again. They’re looking for someone to stand up, stand tall and fight like hell with them, and that’s what I bring to the table.”
Taylor has signed onto “Unrig Washington,” a 2026 midterm agenda from End Citizens United, the liberal PAC focused on changing campaign finance policies. The agenda has gained broad support from Democrats across the country. It requires its candidates to publicly support banning congressional stock trading, refuse corporate PAC money and root out dark money.
He said his campaign isn’t accepting corporate PAC money or special interest dollars.
“We’ve focused on grassroots organizing and building that campaign with individual contributions because we want power to belong to the people,” Taylor said.
A super PAC, the 1861 Initiative, with an address in Wichita has spent almost $1 million on Taylor’s campaign, paying for digital and TV advertising, paid search results and text message outreach, according to federal election filings. The Civil War began in 1861.
Helena Buchmann, a senior adviser to Taylor’s campaign, said in response to a question from Kansas Reflector about how the super PAC’s spending aligns with Taylor’s pledge against corporate PAC support: “Noah is running to end corruption and get money out of politics. That’s why he’s the only candidate in this race that End Citizens United — the premier organization leading the fight against corporate money in politics — put on their ‘Unrig Washington’ candidate list.”
Taylor grew up in El Dorado, the son of a pipe fitter and a nurse and the product of public schools. After one year of community college, he entered the military, where he fought with the U.S. Army in Afghanistan. He spent more than three years as an infantryman and around three more years as a counterintelligence analyst. He now lives in Kechi outside of Wichita with his wife and two kids, working for a small business operator.
In social media posts, Taylor frequently weighs in on foreign policy. He has condemned Marshall’s inaction on stricter sanctions for Russia, critiqued military spending and faulted the Trump administration for its justifications for the war in Iran.
“If we’re going to be sending American lives, we’ve got to be fighting something that’s worth fighting for,” he said on the Kansas Reflector podcast.
If elected to the U.S. Senate, Taylor said, he wants to improve fellow veterans’ transition from the military into civilian life.
“Right now, we kind of just kick them to the curb and say thank you,” he said, “and it’s such a tough transition.”
He said aid for service members leaving the military means ensuring they know about benefits available to them, or encouraging a “buddy system” like he had in the Army, through which newly discharged service members can access a community and assistance with the basics of life.
Taylor supports legalizing recreational and medicinal marijuana, partially because he has seen it benefit veterans dealing with the lasting effects of their military careers, he said. He also said he supports abortion access, preserving voting rights and eradicating President Donald Trump’s tariffs.
He said he opposes defunding public education, the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement approach and the constitutional amendment on Kansans’ primary ballots that asks if voters want to shift the way Kansas Supreme Court justices are selected to a popular vote.
His military background translates into many of his campaign talking points, as he underscores a need to fight.
“Fifty years from now, our grandkids are going to ask us what we did in this moment, and the only acceptable answer is fight with every fiber of our being for not only our future but for our Constitution,” he said.
He said he wants to fight for affordable healthcare and housing. If progress is made, he said, it won’t be “because it was handed to us.”
“We had to fight for it,” he said, “and that’s uncomfortable to talk about, but we’ve got to fight.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Civil rights groups ask to intervene in lawsuit over majority-Black DeSoto County  judicial subdistrict
description: An attendee holds a  sign at a rally for voting rights at the Jackson Convention Center, Wednesday, May 20, 2026, in Jackson.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Civil rights groups on Monday announced a move to intervene in a federal lawsuit filed by a former Republican gubernatorial candidate and others from DeSoto County aiming to dismantle a majority-Black judicial subdistrict..
The American Civil Liberties Union, ACLU of Mississippi, Legal Defense Fund and NAACP moved to intervene on behalf of the DeSoto County NAACP and the Delta Sigma Theta Sorority Inc. in Foster v. Mississippi, the groups announced in a Monday news release. A federal judge is set to hear arguments Wednesday on whether to block the DeSoto County map from going into effect.
The lawsuit was filed on July 2 in the U.S. Northern District of Mississippi by several DeSoto County residents, including former Republican gubernatorial candidate and current county Supervisor Robert Foster. It was filed against the three-member state Board of Election Commissioners, which is comprised of Gov. Tate Reeves, Secretary of State Michael Watson and Attorney General Lynn Fitch, all of whom are Republicans.
The plaintiffs argue the Legislature’s creation of majority-Black subdistricts for the state judiciary violates the Voting Rights Act. The lawsuit came after the U.S. Supreme Court’s May Louisiana v. Callais decision rolled back protections for minority voters during redistricting.
Before that ruling and the new legal landscape it delivered, legislative leaders in 2025 redrew court districts. They changed the districts to account for population shifts and caseload data, but they also allowed for majority-Black subdistricts in certain areas to give Black voters a chance to elect candidates of their choice. A subdistrict is used for a judge to be elected from a smaller area in the main district, but the judge can still hear cases from anywhere in the district.
The Legislature’s actions were “racially motivated and mathematically problematic,” the plaintiffs argue. 
In response, the civil rights groups maintain that the plaintiffs are distorting the scope of the Supreme Court’s ruling in Louisiana v. Callais. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the use of race to draw Black-majority districts remains constitutional when required by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, the civil rights attorneys said. 
In DeSoto County, home to the growing Memphis suburbs of north Mississippi, Black people make up about 36% of the population. DeSoto County also has the highest rate of growth in its Black population in Mississippi.
Since almost all judgeships in DeSoto County are elected countywide, Black voters effectively have no opportunity to elect their preferred candidates and would be shut out from representation on the circuit and chancery courts, the attorneys argue. 
“Black voters in DeSoto County make up over one-third of the County’s population,” said Joshua Tom, legal director at the ACLU of Mississippi. “We are seeking to ensure all voters have the ability to elect candidates of their choice in DeSoto County.” 
The DeSoto County lawsuit is now before U.S. District Judge Sharion Aycock for consideration, the same judge who previously ruled that Mississippi’s state Supreme Court districts violate the federal Voting Rights Act because they don’t give Black voters a chance to elect a candidate of their choice.
The U.S. Court of Appeals overturned Aycock’s initial ruling in light of the U.S. Supreme Court’s April Louisiana v. Callais decision. Aycock is now evaluating how that case should proceed.
The DeSoto County plaintiffs asked Aycock to block the DeSoto County map from going into effect. Aycock would likely have to rule quickly because judicial elections will take place in November.
Mississippi Today reporter Taylor Vance contributed to this report

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska’s largest county reports sudden jump in cyclospora infections
description: OMAHA — A “rapid increase” in infections of the parasite cyclospora among residents of Nebraska’s most populous county prompted the Douglas County Health Department to issue an alert Monday. Douglas County officials said 12 out of 27 confirmed cases were reported in the past four days, prompting a public health investigation. The county said it is […]
text:
Nebraska's Douglas County Health Department on Monday notes a sudden rise in cyclospora infections among county residents. On July 17, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it has linked an outbreak of cyclosporiasis in five states to shredded iceberg lettuce from Taco Bell restaurants. (Photo courtesy Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)OMAHA — A “rapid increase” in infections of the parasite cyclospora among residents of Nebraska’s most populous county prompted the Douglas County Health Department to issue an alert Monday.
Douglas County officials said 12 out of 27 confirmed cases were reported in the past four days, prompting a public health investigation.
The county said it is working with the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services, federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and U.S. Food and Drug Administration to determine if the county cases are related to the ongoing multistate cyclospora outbreak.
Douglas County epidemiologists identified eating at Taco Bell as the most common exposure among people interviewed to date, with nearly two-thirds of that group reported eating at Taco Bell during the two weeks before becoming ill.  The county said it has shared the findings with state and federal partners as it continues to determine whether local cases are associated with the ongoing multistate outbreak.
Federal officials are investigating a multistate outbreak of the infection linked to shredded iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell locations in five states: Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan Ohio and West Virginia.
A spokesman for the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services said Monday that since May, Nebraska has identified 91 cases of cyclosporiasis, the illness caused by the parasite. Jeff Powell said that DHHS is working with federal and local public health partners to determine if any local cases share exposures linking cases together. At this time, he said, there have been no confirmed local cases related to the national outbreak.
The news release from the Douglas County Health Department did not specify any particular store or site of reported infections, and a spokesman for the department said the investigation is ongoing to help determine a local source.
“Cyclospora is not uncommon during the summer months; however, the number of cases reported over the past several days is higher than we would typically expect in such a short period of time,” said Dr. Justin Frederick, deputy health director and chief of epidemiology and preparedness for Douglas County. 
Cyclospora is a microscopic parasite that causes an intestinal illness known as cyclosporiasis. People typically become ill about a week after consuming contaminated food or water. The illness does not spread from one person to another. Common symptoms include frequent watery diarrhea, loss of appetite and weight loss, stomach cramps and bloating, nausea, fatigue and low-grade fever.
Cyclospora can cause illness that lingers for weeks if left untreated, said Dr. Lindsay Huse, county health director. She said anyone experiencing prolonged diarrhea should contact their healthcare provider, as she said that early diagnosis and treatment can help reduce complications. Infection can be effectively treated with prescription antibiotics, the county said.
According to the CDC, Taylor Farms started a recall of all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico, including those sold at retail stores and restaurants. 
The FDA said Monday that a false positive of cyclospora announced over the weekend from a sample of Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce does not change the basis for the agency’s ongoing investigation. 
People with questions can contact Douglas County Health Department at 402-444-7471.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Lawmakers consider how to prevent Legionnaires’ Disease in Pennsylvania
description: Legionella, the bacteria behind Legionnaires' Disease, has been found in cooling tanks, hot tubs, water faucets and dental offices.
text:
Legionella, the bacteria behind Legionnaires' Disease, has been found in cooling tanks, hot tubs, water faucets and dental offices. (Photo by Sarah Ladd/Kentucky Lantern)Fifty years after a devastating Pennsylvania outbreak that gave Legionnaires’ Disease its name, state legislators met on Monday less than a mile from the Philadelphia site where it happened to discuss the practicality of minimum standards that could prevent future cases. 
Legionnaires’ Disease, caused by the Legionella bacteria, got its name following a 1976 outbreak at an American Legion convention in Philadelphia that killed 29 people. Most people exposed to Legionella don’t get sick and most reported instances are sporadic, not widespread. 
It doesn’t typically spread from person-to-person, but rather through aerosolized droplets of unclean water — complicating efforts to minimize it because the bacteria can grow anywhere from the water source to the final faucet, including pipes or cooling tanks. 
Bill McQuade, an engineer and former president of the American Society of Heating, Refrigeration, and Air Conditioning Engineers, pushes for greater effort to reduce cases of Legionnaires’ Disease on July 20, 2026. (Screenshot from livestream)
“Pennsylvania has a unique place in the history of this disease. It should also have a leadership role in preventing it,” said Bill McQuade, an engineer and former president of the American Society of Heating, Refrigeration, and Air Conditioning Engineers. 
McQuade, who also is on the board of the Alliance to Prevent Legionnaires’ Disease, and others support House Bill 2085, by Rep. Ismail Smith-Wade-El (D-Lancaster). It would impose new minimum standards on public water systems and certain building owners, similar to a recent law in New Jersey. 
Smith-Wade-El pointed to previous outbreaks at the Lancaster County Prison and an ongoing outbreak in New York City, noting that people in institutional settings are at risk for the disease. 
“I want us to get to a version of the bill that prioritizes protecting vulnerable people, regardless of where they are,” he said. “If we don’t know what specific … approaches work to protect people in their homes, I want us to figure it out.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
But utility providers warned of the extra cost imposed by such regulations, adding that those expenses could be passed to consumers. Several also emphasized that they alone couldn’t be held responsible for preventing Legionnaires, since many cases are linked to individual properties. 
“As drafted, (it) assigns responsibility to public water systems for building-level risks that they cannot control, and may divert resources away from the systems and facilities where prevention must occur,” said Charlotte Katzenmoyer, the CEO of Harrisburg-based Capital Region Water.
Smith-Wade-El said in committee he intended to work with stakeholders, including those who testified, to “get this right.”
 More on Legionnaires’ Disease

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that one in every 10 people who get sick from Legionnaires’ Disease die from complications, but noted that maintaining healthy water standards is key to preventing the disease’s spread. 
The serious form of pneumonia can be treated with antibiotics, usually developing within two weeks of exposure. Symptoms include cough, fever, headaches, muscle aches and shortness of breath. Some people also report confusion, nausea and diarrhea. 
Legionnaires cases peaked in 2018, briefly fell and then rebounded close to record levels last year. It is most prevalent in the northeast, with New York City and West Virginia reporting the highest number of cases. 
Kristina Zwolenik, a waterborne epidemiology research associate with the state Department of Health, spoke about the growing number of Legionella cases identified in Pennsylvania before a committee on July 20, 2026. (Screenshot from livestream)
According to Kristina Zwolenik, a waterborne epidemiology research associate with the state Department of Health, Pennsylvania recorded 1,231 confirmed or probable Legionella infections between 2021 and 2023, with an average annual infection rate double the national average. 
Initial state reports identified as many as 450 cases in 2025, higher than previous years. 
“In the majority of the outbreaks that we have successfully identified the source of the exposure, the root cause has been poor maintenance inside the building itself,” said Zwolenik. “We routinely trace cases back to poor, irregular or non-existent maintenance of hot tubs, ice machines and cooling towers as well as building renovations that leave water stagnant in unused spaces.”
But Zwolenik reported that the burden of the legislative proposal on her department “would exceed our current capacity,” adding that the agency would need to increase staffing.
With so many variables and unknowns, experts shared that it can also be difficult to narrow in on one specific regulation that might reduce Legionella cases. It’s unknown why the Mid-Atlantic, for example, reports the highest prevalence of cases.
But the threat is increasing as water-based heat waves, which are periods of abnormally high water temperatures, increase in intensity and frequency due to climate change.
Researchers like Charles N. Haas, an environmental engineering professor at Drexel University in Philadelphia, emphasized the “shared responsibility” for prevention efforts, noting that water utility oversight ends at an individual’s property line. 
Charles N. Haas, an environmental engineering professor at Drexel University in Philadelphia, speaks about ways to mitigate Legionella at a legislative hearing on July 20, 2026. (Screenshot from livestream)
Between property pipes, water heaters, air conditioning units, showers and more, Haas said, “there’s a lot of potential for the water to sit warm (and) stagnant,” conditions that allow Legionella to multiply. Other cases are linked to dental offices, HVAC systems, decorative fountains or even misting systems, but upstream actions from water utilities can potentially dislodge old biofilm growths, risking exposure.
“Under a shared responsibility model, both parties need to get their acts together,” continued Haas. “I think what the bill gets right is the requirement for high-risk facilities to have a water management plan. That’s where the science says the fight belongs.”
The slim odds of contracting Legionnaires’ Disease can make it more difficult to investigate, since most people don’t get sick. Those most at risk include current or former smokers, people with certain health conditions and anyone over the age of 50.
 Preventative action

Haas and others panned an additional proposal that would increase the statewide minimum level of chlorine, which is used as a disinfectant against Legionella — with Katzenmoyer calling it “especially concerning.”
“Disinfection requires careful technical judgment to balance microbial control, water age, corrosion control, taste and odor, infrastructure conditions and compliance with disinfection limits,” said Katzenmoyer. “These decisions belong to the scientific and regulatory process, not in statute.” 
Charlotte Katzenmoyer, the CEO of Harrisburg-based Capital Region Water, shares concerns about proposed regulations on July 20, 2026. (Screenshot from livestream)
Increased chlorine levels could create byproducts, which comes with its own regulations, or increase the long-term risk of cancer for water consumers, she continued. 
Not all of Katzenmoyer’s colleagues agreed. Bill Murray, the executive director of the Reading Area Water Authority, called the Smith-Wade-El’s bill “thoughtful and necessary,” but called for refining its language to provide “clear accountability.” 
“Make no mistake, Legionnaires’ disease is the enemy of every one of us … it exploits vulnerabilities where they exist and, when it does, families suffer,” continued Murray. 
Murray noted local limits when it came to oversight of building projects, adding that a developer could decide to use a reservoir over local water sources to save money, though it comes with additional risks. 
Steve Chintaman, the vice president of government affairs with the Pennsylvania Apartment Association, similarly spoke about the need for amendments that, “would improve the legislation by ensuring compliance requirements are practical, risk-based and appropriately allocate responsibility among all parties involved.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We encourage consideration of implementation approaches that achieve the bill’s objectives while recognizing the operational realities facing housing providers,” said Chintaman. 
Lower-risk shared housing communities, such as student housing, could be caught up in regulations, Chintaman added, pushing for “tailored” compliance requirements based on risk, not on building type or size. 
The development of water management programs, requirements for sampling and monitoring and coordinating inspections would also add to the expenses of apartments and property management companies — and would be particularly onerous for affordable housing developments, Chintaman continued. 
But McQuade, the engineer, pushed for comprehensive legislation, rather than policies that “focused too narrowly on a few pieces of equipment.”
“Any water-using system or equipment in a building that can create spray, mist, bubbles, droplets or aerosols need to be identified, evaluated and managed,” said McQuade. “At the same time, the building is only one part of a larger water pathway. Legionella risk must be managed from the source through public water systems, home plumbings and finally to the fixtures and equipment where people can be exposed.” 
He added that the proposed legislation “moves Pennsylvania in the right direction” by requiring shared responsibility, with utilities, building owners and public health agencies playing a role. 
“If implemented well, this legislation can create a culture of prevention, fewer illnesses, fewer emergency responses and better coordination among utilities, building owners and public health officials,” McQuade continued. 
Lawmakers didn’t vote on Monday, and it’s unclear what the next steps for House Bill 2085 might be. Though committees are meeting, the full chambers of the House and Senate aren’t set to convene until September.

title: Forest fire realities: The more carbon we release, the more likely we’ll have catastrophic burns
description: As smoke from wildfires in Canada billowed across the central and eastern parts of the United States, President Donald Trump once again demonstrated his utter ignorance of wildfires. Detroit remained the most polluted city in the world, according to tracker IQAir. Other major cities like Washington, D.C., and Chicago were equally polluted. Trump declared: “W[...]
text:
Smoky haze from wildfires in Canada diminishes the visibility of the Empire State Building on June 7, 2023 in New York City. New York topped the list of most polluted major cities in the world on Tuesday night, as smoke from the fires continues to blanket the East Coast. (Photo by David Dee Delgado | Getty Images)As smoke from wildfires in Canada billowed across the central and eastern parts of the United States, President Donald Trump once again demonstrated his utter ignorance of wildfires.
Detroit remained the most polluted city in the world, according to tracker IQAir. Other major cities like Washington, D.C., and Chicago were equally polluted.
Trump declared: “We are holding Canada responsible for the fact that they are not properly maintaining their Forests, and Brush therein, and the United States is being unnecessarily invaded by filthy, polluted, and unhealthy air, the quality of which is dangerous, and totally unacceptable!”
Trump suggested that he will increase tariffs on Canada to pay for the “willful negligence” ensuring even more animosity towards the U.S. from our best neighbors and allies. Will Trump increase tariffs this winter if a “polar express” sweeps out of the Arctic and across the U.S. driving up heating costs? I am surprised he hasn’t immediately shipped more rakes to Canada so they can clean up their forests and make them tidy.
All cynical comments aside, Trump’s response demonstrates how clearly he fails to understand the relationship between fossil fuel burning, warming climate and wildfires. He has repeatedly declared that climate warming is a “hoax.”
Worse for the planet, his energy policies that promote fossil fuels are willfully increasing climate warming.
The first problem with Trump’s irrational response is his failure to understand the scope of the wildfire issue. Canada’s boreal forest encompasses 1.3 billion acres. That’s almost the size of the lower 48 states combined (1.9 billion). Thus far wildfires have burnt 7 million acres of Canada. Across most of this vast area there are no roads, not even much forestry. It is impossible to have any substantial impact on wildfires burning across such a huge area.
Climate and weather is the controlling variable, not fuels.
Second, wildfires are a natural part of the boreal forest. These forests do burn on occasion when conditions are “ripe.” And those conditions include drought, high temperatures, low humidity and wind. All those conditions exist across much of Canada today.
Third, though high severity burns release carbon into the atmosphere, which is one factor driving climate warming, much of the carbon in burnt forests remains locked up in snags, roots and charcoal.
By contrast, logging and wood products production which Trump is proposing should be increased both in Canada as well as here in the United States releases a far higher percentage of the carbon locked in forests. For instance, in Oregon the Wood Products Industry releases more carbon than all the transportation sections in the state.
Plus, there are substantial economic and ecological costs associated with logging that are often ignored.
However, the other major problem with Trump’s cognitive dissidence are his energy policies. Trump has basically unleashed massive new inputs of carbon from burning fossil fuels.
He has attacked energy efficiency requirements of the transportation sector. He has canceled wind energy and solar projects. He has supported elimination of tax incentives to support electric automobile conversion, solar energy on homes, energy conservation measures in building construction and other renewable energy policies.
According to a report by the Bluegreen Alliance 223 clean manufacturing, energy, and industrial projects across the country—representing at least $82.8 billion in capital investment—have been canceled or stalled.
Trump is even paying $2. 3 billion of taxpayer dollars to cancel wind farm projects.
Worse for American consumers, his unnecessary war in Iran has driven up energy costs for all Americans. While he gloats that America is the largest producer of crude oil, implying this will result in lower gas and energy costs, it ignores the basic economic reality that the global market sets oil and gas prices. Energy producers in the United States may produce a lot of oil and gas, but they sell it at the global price. And that price has risen due to the uncertainty about oil supplies resulting from the Iranian War.
There is evidence from over millions of years that adding carbon to the atmosphere, whether from natural sources or human emissions, can increase wildfires. If we continue to release carbon into the atmosphere, we can anticipate more large wildfires and smoke into the future.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: 2 SC congressmen launch bids for US Senate, as Darline Graham says ‘I’m in’
description: U.S. Rep. Russell Fry's announcement brought on criticism for running a simultaneous reelection bid in the House.
text:
U.S. Reps. Ralph Norman, left, and Russell Fry, right, both announced they would run for Senate following Sen. Lindsey Graham's death. (LEFT: Photo by Mark Susko/Special to the SC Daily Gazette, RIGHT: Photo courtesy of Rep. Russell Fry's office)COLUMBIA — U.S. Sen. Darline Graham confirmed Monday she will seek election to the U.S. Senate. Her opponents in the race to replace her late brother on November’s ballot will include two Republican congressmen, who launched bids ahead of candidate filing.
“I’m in,” Graham told Fox News for a segment airing Monday night.

Darline Graham Nordone, center, accepted the appointment by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster, right, at the Statehouse Monday, July 13, 2026, to serve out the remainder of the term of her late brother, U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)

She was sworn in last week to fulfill the remainder of Lindsey Graham’s fourth term, which ends in January. She told host Sean Hannity she decided to seek the next six-year term after much prayer and discussion with her family.
“It is a tremendous amount of pressure,” she said about President Donald Trump’s “ask” that she jump in.
“I know I’m a hard worker,” Graham said in a portion of Hannity’s interview released Monday afternoon. “I learned that from Lindsey.”
Graham, 62, who lives in Lexington, has led the state Commission for the Blind since 2019 but has never run for office: “Will it be difficult? Yes, absolutely,” she said about a campaign.
“I feel like I can do it,” she added, noting her three decades in state government. “I feel an inner peace about it.”
The televised interview comes after U.S. Reps. Ralph Norman and Russell Fry launched their own campaigns for the Republican Party’s nomination in the Aug. 11 special election. Graham’s sudden death July 11 from a ruptured aorta created South Carolina’s first open race for U.S. Senate in 22 years.
Filing opens at noon Tuesday and closes July 28. Early voting begins Aug. 5. A primary runoff, if needed, will be Aug. 25.
The winner will face Democrat Annie Andrews in November. People who voted in last month’s Democratic primary, which put the Lowcountry pediatrician on the ballot, can’t participate in next month’s contests. Voters can help decide the new GOP nominee if they voted in the June Republican contests, which Graham easily won, or didn’t vote in either party’s primary.
Both Norman and Fry touted their support of Trump in their campaign announcements, but neither enters the race with the president’s backing. Instead, Trump gave his “Complete and Total Endorsement” to Darline Graham on Friday.
President Trump encourages Sen. Darline Graham to seek full, 6-year term

“RUN, DARLINE, RUN!” his social media post concluded.
She released a letter Saturday thanking South Carolinians without specifying her decision. The Fox News interview cleared that up.
Ralph Norman
Norman’s bid, launched Saturday, comes after an unsuccessful run for governor. He placed third in last month’s GOP gubernatorial primary. His tenure representing the 5th District ends in January.
The 73-year-old has a reputation as a fiscal hawk, with seats on the House budget, financial services and rules committees. He’s also a member of the ultra-conservative U.S. House Freedom Caucus and helped launch a South Carolina chapter of the group, which has spent the past several years warring with the House majority GOP caucus.
Norman entered politics after growing his father’s construction business into one of the state’s most successful commercial real estate firms. A former state House representative, the Rock Hill Republican was first elected to Congress in a 2017 special election to represent the district that spans 10 counties from Spartanburg southeast to Sumter.
Norman touted his ultra-conservative record in a news release, adding that he would push for the Senate to pass a bill adding ID requirements for voters, which the House has already advanced. Sen. Lindsey Graham co-sponsored the Senate version.
“South Carolina has always been a rock-solid conservative stronghold, and at this critical moment we MUST SEND A PROVEN AMERICA FIRST FIGHTER to the U.S. Senate to help President Trump,” Norman said in the news release.
Norman was never expected to get Trump’s endorsement for Senate. An ally to Gov. Nikki Haley while in the state House, Norman backed her over Trump in the 2024 GOP presidential primary, and Haley endorsed his gubernatorial bid.
Russell Fry
But there was wide speculation that Fry would again get Trump’s endorsement. The president’s surprise pick of Darline Graham didn’t stop his campaign launch.
Fry, an attorney who lives in Murrells Inlet, announced his run for the Senate seat Monday morning.
“South Carolinians need a conservative fighter in the U.S. Senate who actually delivers results,” Fry said in a news release. “There’s too much at stake to take a chance, so I’m answering the call.”
A former state representative, Fry first won the 7th Congressional District seat in 2022. He had Trump’s endorsement in ousting 10-year incumbent Rep. Tom Rice, who voted to impeach the president after the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol.
In his campaign announcement Monday, the 41-year-old focused on the rising prices of gas and groceries. He aligned himself with Graham, saying they both came from humble beginnings — Graham from his parents’ bar in Central and Fry from parents living paycheck to paycheck in Surfside Beach.
“There is no other way to put it: Lindsey Graham was one of a kind,” Fry said. “There is no replacing him. But I believe the best way to honor his legacy is to fight alongside the President just as steadfastly as he did.”
It’s official: SC Republicans already on the ballot can run for Senate too

Questions over timing
Fry is not withdrawing his bid for reelection to the House, spokesman Luke Byars said, meaning Fry could be on the ballot twice in November.
After receiving the question multiple times, the State Election Commission confirmed last week that candidates can run for more than one seat simultaneously.
If Fry were to win both seats in November, he would have to choose one. That would trigger another special election, potentially leaving the seat vacant for the opening months of 2027.
The exact timing would depend on when Fry resigned his House seat. State law requires special elections take place 20 weeks after a seat becomes empty, though the U.S. Constitution gives governors authority to declare a U.S. House vacancy and order a special election.
The last time a resignation created a vacancy in the U.S. House was 2017, when 5th District Rep. Mick Mulvaney resigned to join the first Trump administration. Gov. Henry McMaster’s Feb. 16 order followed the timeline in state law, and Norman won the special election four months later.
Norman criticized his primary opponent for seeking a job that could leave House Republicans temporarily without a vote.
“This would leave his constituents unrepresented, jeopardize President Trump’s agenda, and put the House at risk of being led by a Speaker Hakeem Jeffries,” Norman said in a social media post. “We can’t let that happen!!”
U.S. Rep. Nancy Mace, who also lost her bid for governor last month, echoed Norman’s concern that a dwindling number of Republican representatives could allow Democrats to elect Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaker.
“If you’re running for two offices at once, you’ve already told us who you are,” Mace, whose term representing the 1st District ends in January, said in a social media post. “That’s not about politics anymore — that’s about power.”
Mace announced Monday that she is not running for Senate.
John Vincent of Myrtle Beach, a Democrat challenging Fry for the 7th Congressional District, said Fry’s run for Senate made his reelection campaign seem like a fallback option in case of a loss.
“The families of the Pee Dee and the Grand Strand deserve a congressman who actually wants this job, not one holding onto it as a consolation prize,” Vincent said in a news release.
Fry had no primary challengers last month.
Other candidates
Also publicly announcing a bid are Mark Lynch, an appliance center owner who challenged Graham during the June primary, and Duke Buckner, who has previously run against U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn.
Lynch said he planned to “finish the fight.” He received far more votes than any of the other five Republicans challenging Graham in June, though Lynch was still 28 percentage points behind Graham, who won with nearly 57% of ballots cast.
“I’m committed to finish what God has called us to since February of 2025,” Lynch wrote in a social media post.
Buckner is also coming off unsuccessful congressional campaigns. Although he didn’t run for office this year, he has twice challenged Clyburn, the state’s longest-serving representative, in the heavily Democratic 6th District.
Buckner, a Walterboro attorney, made the decision to run for Senate, which he announced over the weekend, “after much prayer,” he said in a social media post.
The list could get much longer before filing ends at noon July 28.

title: Louisiana gets SNAP waiver from Tropical Storm Arthur for hot meals
description: Louisiana residents who receive federal food assistance will be able to use their benefits to purchase hot meals or prepared foods as the state recovers from Tropical Storm Arthur, state officials announced Monday.  The Louisiana Department of Health has received a temporary waiver from the U.S. Department of Agriculture to allow expanded use of Supplemental[...]
text:
A Louisiana Purchase EBT food stamp SNAP card. (Photo by Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)
Louisiana residents who receive federal food assistance will be able to use their benefits to purchase hot meals or prepared foods as the state recovers from Tropical Storm Arthur, state officials announced Monday. 
The Louisiana Department of Health has received a temporary waiver from the U.S. Department of Agriculture to allow expanded use of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program through Aug. 13. Participants can purchase eligible hot and prepared foods at authorized Louisiana SNAP retailers, though not at restaurants.
The waiver is effective immediately and applies to SNAP recipients statewide. It does not provide any additional funding. 
President Donald Trump issued a disaster declaration July 2 to make federal assistance available to residents and businesses in certain parishes after Tropical Storm Arthur produced heavy rainfall and spawned tornadoes in Louisiana on June 17. 
“After a major weather event like Tropical Storm Arthur, even simple tasks like preparing a meal can become difficult,” Health Secretary Bruce Greenstein said in a news release. “We’re grateful to the USDA for approving this temporary waiver, which gives SNAP recipients greater flexibility to purchase hot, prepared foods as communities recover. We’ll continue working with our federal partners to ensure Louisianans have access to the resources they need throughout the recovery process.”
The SNAP waiver comes as the state braces for a second storm in the Gulf of Mexico. 
As of noon Monday, a tropical depression 110 miles south of the Florida Panhandle was moving  northwest at 3 mph with sustained winds of 35 mph. The system is forecast to strengthen into Tropical Storm Bertha as soon as Monday evening before turning west. 
The National Hurricane Center expects Bertha to make landfall in southeastern Louisiana around 7 p.m. Wednesday.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: PODCAST: In New Haven, a push to identify unmarked graves
description: WSHU talks to CT Mirror's John Moritz about efforts to identify the people buried at a cemetery that has headstones marked only with numbers.
text:
Hundreds of headstones in a New Haven cemetery are marked only with numbers. Some community members are working to change that.
WSHU’s Ebong Udoma spoke with CT Mirror’s John Moritz to discuss his article, “The story behind rows of unmarked stones at New Haven cemetery,” as part of the collaborative podcast Long Story Short. Read John’s story here.
WSHU: Hi John, this is a fascinating story, but it’s not your beat. So how did you come across it?
JM: So I came across this story because I was living in New Haven, and some people from the city and local community who I’ve been following had been posting some blogs that this woman Sherill Baldwin had been writing on her website, where she’d been detailing the lives and the history of some of the people that she’d been discovering who were buried at Blake Street Cemetery, which is an old pauper cemetery, a place where the city buried poor and indigent people between 1884 and 1931. And I was really interested, and so I contacted Sherill to learn more about her work.
WSHU: And you got to visit with her a couple of times at the cemetery. Tell us a little bit about this. Describe the cemetery to us first.
JM: So, for people who may be more familiar with Westville Cemetery in New Haven, it’s a fairly large cemetery off Whaley Avenue. There’s also a connecting cemetery owned by the Congregation Mishkan Israel. So it’s a it’s a big piece of property. There’s actually several cemeteries located on the property. But around the back on a side street called Blake Street, there’s a small hill, and on that hill are about 2,200 gravestones, and they’re small, you know, little, you know, bland stones that are just, for the most part, inscribed with numbers, because the people who were buried there didn’t even have their names etched onto the stones. The city kept records of who was buried there, but only inscribed the stones with the numbers that corresponded with a name that was on a piece of paper.
WSHU: So let’s start with Sherill. Who is she, and give us a little bit of her background.
JM: So Sherill is an amateur genealogist from the city of New Haven. She told me she’s been interested in genealogy her whole life, from when she grew up on Cape Cod, she would, you know, research old family family plots and cemeteries around there. She later went out and she got a research certificate from Boston University. But for her, genealogy has always been kind of a side project. It’s not her, you know, full time career. And what she told me was that during the pandemic, during the lockdown, she was unable to make it back home to Massachusetts to continue some of the research on her own family. So she started exploring cemeteries, old cemeteries around New Haven where she lives, and that’s how she came upon Blake Street.
WSHU: Now you tell us the story of one of the gravestones, Anna Horan. Could you just tell us about her story and how Sherill was able to get the family to know what had happened to their ancestors?
JM: Yeah. So this is one of the stories that really got me interested in Sherill’s work. Anna Horan was a child of Irish immigrants who was born, I believe, in the 1880s in New Haven, and she lived a fairly rough life. Her father died in her infancy, and her mother died just before she was married, I believe, in her early 20s, and she was married to a man named Thomas Horan, who came from New York City. And by all accounts, you know the family never had much money, but settled in New Haven, had a child. At one point, Thomas left the family in such circumstances that it actually made the local newspapers that reported him as a cruel husband for leaving his family, taking all the furniture and essentially leaving them out in the streets. Based on the records Sherill was able to find, at some point the couple got back together, had a few more children. He left again. Anna Horan ended up in the Springside Almshouse, which was the place for poor people who essentially couldn’t afford to care for themselves back in the day, and her children were sent to the orphanage.
WSHU: And something else that’s really fascinating is that the oldest person buried there was actually one of the last people sold on the New Haven Green as a slave.
JM: Yes, so you’re referring to the story of Lois Tritton. She was buried in the cemetery in 1894, and she died at the age of 95. So that made her the oldest person buried at Blake Street. And it was interesting. I spoke to another woman named Jill Snyder, who’s been researching a lot of the history of Lois Triton and her mother Lucy. Who, as you mentioned, were the last slaves who were sold at auction on the New Haven Green in 1825. It wasn’t until 1848 that Connecticut formally abolished the practice of slavery. And at the time, you know, what Snyder has found is there seems to be some discrepancy in the record of whether they were actually freed upon sale. They were sold to a man who claimed to be an abolitionist, but based on some of Snyder’s research and some newspaper articles at the time, it appears that Lois Tritton actually had to work off as an indentured servant the debts that were incurred to purchase her freedom. But she was actually a notable figure later in life in New Haven, there were several newspaper articles, not only in the city of New Haven but around the country, that were written about this woman who, you know, in 1895 was kind of a historical curiosity. But when she died, her family didn’t have enough money to pay for a private funeral, so she ended up at Blake Street, and recently, Trinity Church on the Green and St. Luke’s actually banded together and were able to purchase a new headstone for her and her family to honor their legacy.
WSHU: And St. Luke’s Episcopal is one of the oldest Black churches in New Haven. This is really great stuff. Thank you so much, John, for doing this.
JM: Well, I have to give a shout out to the work of local historians such as Sherill and Jill, who have been really uncovering some of the stories of you know the people, the everyday people who built up the city of New Haven.
WSHU: Well, thank you so much, John.
JM: Thank you for having me.

title: What’s that smell? Tracking hydrocarbons in Yellowstone National Park
description: More than just thermal water discharges from Yellowstone’s hydrothermal system—there are gasses like water, carbon dioxide, and hydrogen sulfide, minerals that precipitate from thermal waters as they cool (sinter, travertine, sulfur, orpiment, and many more), and, in some rare places, hydrocarbons. In other words, oil. The excerpt from geoscientists Eugene A[...]
text:
Calcite Springs thermal area in Yellowstone National Park. Calcite Springs is the white altered ground. Dark deposits (not apparent in this photo) are sometimes discharged from fumaroles and are made of either oxidized sulfur or hydrocarbons. (USGS photo by Mike Poland, May 15, 2022.)

        “The deep narrow canyon, with the rushing green river at its bottom and the sheer towering cliffs on its further side, forms an unusual setting for this little group of springs….all the springs and visible steam vents are confined to the lower parts of the area. Especially along the lower third of the slope, sulphur lining cracks and vents may be seen in many places. Breaking into fumaroles with the pick, one finds well-crystallized masses of it, mixed with bitumen of tarry appearance and odor. On the bench above the river’s edge, sinuous trails, resembling the marks of burrowing moles, follow the lines of cracks where the same products have been deposited. No evidence regarding the origin of this tarry substance in the fumaroles is at hand. A unique occurrence in Yellowstone Park, it seems to be best explained as a distillate from organic matter buried in sediments.” – Allan and Day (1935) describing Calcite Spring hydrothermal deposits 
More than just thermal water discharges from Yellowstone’s hydrothermal system—there are gasses like water, carbon dioxide, and hydrogen sulfide, minerals that precipitate from thermal waters as they cool (sinter, travertine, sulfur, orpiment, and many more), and, in some rare places, hydrocarbons.
In other words, oil.
The excerpt from geoscientists Eugene Allan and Arthur Day above describes Calcite Springs in the northeastern part of Yellowstone National Park, where these scientists found sulfur and bituminous hydrocarbons in the deposits around the spring.
But where did this material come from and why is it only rarely observed in Yellowstone thermal waters?
Hydrocarbons are chains of carbon and hydrogen atoms bonded to one another. They form the building blocks of petroleum, natural gas, oil, and coal, and they occur naturally from the thermal maturation of buried organic matter. Hydrocarbon seeps are common in the deep seafloor where the material is consumed by specialized organisms for energy (methanogenesis).
Hydrocarbon seeps occur on land as well—a famous example is the La Brea tar pits in Los Angeles. In that location, oil discharged at the surface created asphaltic tar pits that trapped many plants and animals (including mammoths!) that scientists now study as an important fossil record of that time. Terrestrial seeps, including Calcite Springs and the La Brea tar pits, are typically found where faults or fractures form a pathway for hydrocarbons to ascend from a subsurface reservoir to the surface. Hydrocarbon seeps can occur anywhere organic-bearing geologic units are buried.
The thermal maturation of buried organic matter into hydrocarbons depends on temperature and proceeds through three stages — diagenesis, catagenesis and metagenesis. Diagenesis is the first and lowest-temperature and pressure stage. As sediments with organic material are shallowly buried they are compacted, water in the pore spaces between particles is expelled, and microbial action decomposes organic matter into methane and other hydrocarbons. At this stage, organic-rich sediments (usually from large land plants) can form peat or lignite.
With continued burial of the sediments to greater depths, the pressure and temperature will increase. In a basin without volcanic activity to add extra heat, catagenesis will be achieved once the sediments are buried in several kilometers of overburden sediment and they reach temperatures of 50 to 150°C (122 to 302°F). This is the stage at which liquid petroleum, methane, and various types of coal can form. Hydrocarbons formed during catagenesis are the materials that power most of the energy needs of humans.
The last stage, metagenesis, occurs where sediments are buried so deeply that the temperature and pressures climb high enough that hydrocarbons are “cooked off”, leaving only methane and carbon residue or high-grade coal called anthracite (the most energy-dense coal possible, and one that burns with little smoke or soot). With even higher pressures and temperatures, hydrocarbons are transformed into graphite.
Just east of Yellowstone National Park is the Bighorn Basin, where there are many productive oil and gas wells. These hydrocarbons are thought to be sourced from Permian (the geologic period 299 to 252 million years ago) marine shales and other units. Permian organic-bearing marine shales likely exist in the subsurface underneath northeastern Yellowstone National Park as well and may be a source of the hydrocarbons that discharge at Calcite Springs. There are probably also some additions of hydrocarbons from buried Eocene (the geological epoch 56 to 33 million years ago) lake sediments to the hydrocarbons discharging at Calcite Springs.
You may wonder if there are hydrocarbon seeps in other hydrothermal areas around Yellowstone National Park. Although some recent studies have found trace amounts of hydrocarbons in Yellowstone Lake, Lower Geyser Basin, and Norris Geyser Basin, there are no known surface discharges of oil like at Calcite Springs. This makes sense, as other hydrothermal areas within the Park are located within the caldera, where an active magmatic system is sustained, the heat flux is elevated, and volcanic activity has taken place for roughly the last 2.1 million years. All this heat and magmatism would likely have pushed any buried organic material in the subsurface into the third stage of hydrocarbon maturation, metagenesis, where it is transformed into graphite or was broken down into carbon dioxide and methane that then discharged at the surface as volcanic degassing.
The carbon cycle in action!
Yellowstone Caldera Chronicles is a weekly column written by scientists and collaborators of the Yellowstone Volcano Observatory. This week’s contribution is from Phillip Kondracki, graduate student, and Lauren Harrison, assistant professor, in the Department of Geosciences at Colorado State University.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: ‘Iowa is acting different’: Political expert discusses Democrats’ chances in Iowa
description: Political expert Charlie Cook, the founder of the nonpartisan Cook Political Report, said Monday he thinks Democratic State Auditor Rob Sand will win Iowa’s gubernatorial election, but the U.S. Senate race between State Rep. Josh Turek and U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson may not be as competitive as Democrats might think. Cook said Iowa is no […]
text:
Charlie Cook, founder of Cook Political Report, spoke about the 2024 election season at Drake University in Des Moines Nov. 29, 2023. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Political expert Charlie Cook, the founder of the nonpartisan Cook Political Report, said Monday he thinks Democratic State Auditor Rob Sand will win Iowa’s gubernatorial election, but the U.S. Senate race between State Rep. Josh Turek and U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson may not be as competitive as Democrats might think.
Cook said Iowa is no longer considered a “swing” state and “hasn’t been for a long time,” adding that he does not believe Iowa’s open U.S. Senate seat will flip due to hyperpolarization in modern politics.
“I’m a bit more skeptical in federal races because to me, if a Republican is disaffected this year, they’re a heck of a lot more likely to not show up or to skip over various offices on the ballot than they are to vote for a Democrat,” Cook said. “We’ll have to wait and see whether the Iowa Senate flips, but I’d give it probably a 1 in 4 chance.”
The Cook Political Report changed its rating of Iowa’s U.S. Senate race from “likely Republican” to “leans Republican” on June 3. Polls released in early July showed a tight race, with Turek leading a FOX News poll released July 2 by 4 percentage points and Hinson leading a July 1 New York Times/Siena poll by 2 points.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Cook participated Monday in a Zoom call with the Iowa Writers’ Collaborative where he discussed the national political landscape, saying the party of the president typically sees lower turnout during midterm elections.
“What typically happens is that people that either belong to, or lean towards a president’s party, sometimes they’re a little complacent,” Cook said. “Sometimes they’re a little disappointed. Sometimes they’re deeply disillusioned. Rarely are they fired up, energized, and so they just simply don’t turn out in midterm elections nearly the way they do in presidential years.”
Cook said Iowa is behaving “differently” in the 2026 election cycle compared to other states, opening the door for the governor’s seat and a couple of U.S. House races to flip to Democrats. Cook did not cite specific Iowa congressional districts he believes will flip.
“The governor’s race, I think it probably will flip,” Cook said. “There’s some House races that may skip over a little bit, but we’re not seeing as much of that in other states as we are in Iowa, and we’ll have to wait and see whether the Iowa Senate (seat) flips.”
Cook highlighted the importance of independent voters, a small number of people who often sway elections.
Cook said “ticket splitting,” voting for candidates in both parties, is rare nowadays, and independents will vote for one specific party “90 to 95% of the time.”
“Really, only 10% of all registered voters are really independents that vote,” Cook said. “They tend to be fickle. They tend to get buyer’s remorse. They tend to turn against a president on a moment’s notice, and stay that way, so they disproportionately break for the opposition party these days.”
Cook cited that Trump’s average disapproval rating hovers around 50%, while his approval across multiple polls sits at approximately 39 to 40%. Based on those numbers, Cook said he believes Republicans will lose seats in Congress.
Cook added that the party that controls the presidency has lost House and Senate seats in all but two midterm elections since World War II.
“Any polling data you look at, the energy level difference between Democrats and Republicans is huge this year, with Democrats hyper-motivated and Republicans not so much, and independents breaking very solidly against the president and Republicans as well,” Cook said. “This midterm seems to be shaping up exactly like the historic norm.”
Ranked-choice voting
Cook also discussed his displeasure with the current voting system in the U.S., citing Maine and Alaska as two states that have successfully implemented ranked-choice voting. Ranked-choice voting is an alternative voting system where if a candidate receives at least 50% of first-place votes, they win the election. If no candidate receives a majority, a series of instant run-off elections are held until a candidate receives 50%.
The purpose of ranked-choice voting is to fight against the United States’ two-party system by encouraging more third-party candidates, with the hope that Republicans and Democrats would look to appeal to a broader coalition.
“I think ranked choice is a good thing,” Cook said. “I think primaries where independents are allowed to vote in either party’s primary, I think that’s pretty healthy. Our system was designed by the founders, and it worked really well for 200 years, and for the last 50, it has not.”

title: Alabama Attorney General’s Office defends effort to execute Jeffrey Lee by lethal injection
description: The Alabama Attorney General’s Office urged a federal court Friday to allow it to pursue the execution of a death row inmate by lethal injection after it was barred from using nitrogen gas. In a filing with U.S. District Judge Emily Marks,  attorneys argued that Jeffrey Lee, sentenced to death for the 1998 murders of […]
text:
An oxygen mask. Alabama attaches a similar-looking mask to a condemned inmate when conducting executions using nitrogen gas. The Alabama Attorney General's Office argued in a filing on Friday that the state could execute Jeffrey Lee, 49, by lethal injection after federal courts stopped the state from using nitrogen gas. (Getty Images)The Alabama Attorney General’s Office urged a federal court Friday to allow it to pursue the execution of a death row inmate by lethal injection after it was barred from using nitrogen gas.
In a filing with U.S. District Judge Emily Marks,  attorneys argued that Jeffrey Lee, sentenced to death for the 1998 murders of two people during a pawn shop robbery, can be executed by lethal injection after the federal courts ruled that executing Lee by nitrogen gas would constitute cruel and unusual punishment.
“Lee elected nitrogen hypoxia in 2018, waited seven years, and then challenged the very method he elected,” attorneys for the state wrote. “He won, so the state predictably moved to execute him by lethal injection instead. Now, contradicting himself a second time, Lee says his election still binds the state, which must ‘devise a new and unspecified means of carrying out’ his execution by hypoxia.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Attorneys representing Lee on July 7 filed a motion to expand Marks’ injunction against nitrogen gas executions, arguing that an agreement in 2018 to dismiss Lee’s earlier lawsuit against the state’s lethal injection protocol prevented the state from using that method to put him to death. Lee has proposed being executed by firing squad, a form of capital punishment not currently authorized in the state.
In the motion, Lee’s attorneys said Alabama is bound by the terms of the 2018 agreement. Attorneys for the state wrote on Friday that Lee never raised the issue of executing him by lethal injection.
“On his own telling, the motion raises a wholly ‘new controversy,’” the state’s motion said. “But a new controversy requires either amending the complaint, which Lee disclaims, or a new lawsuit.”
The AG’s Office also said the federal district court’s injunction only extends to the nitrogen gas execution method and not to the other methods currently available in Alabama, including lethal injection, which uses three drugs including midazolam, a sedative.
“The court correctly declined to limit ADOC’s methods of execution to those Lee provided,” the AG’s Office said in its motion. “There was nothing before the Court to suggest that ADOC’s midazolam protocol (the Glossip protocol) is unconstitutional—or, for that matter, that its electrocution protocol is unconstitutional.”
Marks had not ruled on the motion as of early Monday afternoon. The deadline for Lee’s attorneys to file the reply is Wednesday.

text:
Utah Gov. Spencer Cox speaks during a news conference announcing a fireworks ban on June 25, 2026. (Alixel Cabrera/Utah News Dispatch)Ahead of the Pioneer Day holiday this week, Utah lifted its default personal fireworks ban and returned the authority over restrictions to cities, Utah Gov. Spencer Cox announced Monday. However, some caveats will remain, and the state forester will still be allowed to place restrictions in areas facing wildfire risk.
The existing firework restriction maps that municipalities have drawn for their boundaries will prevail from this week on. However, areas of the state that still have a substantial wildfire risk “may work with the state forester to request additional restrictions beyond their existing authority,” Cox’s office said in a news release.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We were hopeful conditions would improve enough to safely return more decisions to our local communities, and in many parts of Utah, that’s exactly what’s happened,” Cox said in a statement. 
“Recent storms have brought meaningful relief to many areas of the state. At the same time, other communities remain at serious risk,” the governor said. “This approach recognizes that wildfire conditions now vary across Utah while ensuring we still have the tools to protect lives and property where the danger remains highest.”
Utah Gov. Cox orders July 4 fireworks ban amid devastating wildfires

The update comes after the governor ordered a default ban ahead of the Fourth of July holiday through a state of emergency declaration amid one of the most wildfire-prone seasons the state has ever seen. The order enabled the governor to suspend a portion of statute to allow the state forester to ban fireworks throughout the whole state.
That was an action that was criticized by some lawmakers, including West Valley City Republican Rep. Matt MacPherson, a professional firework display operator and owner of a firework manufacturer, who said the governor didn’t have the authority to make such a decision.
MacPherson told Utah News Dispatch in a text message in late June that he’s not against firework restrictions, but he believed “the governor did it in the worst way possible and most likely to face legal challenges.” 
But wildfire season isn’t over, Cox said, urging Utahns to use good judgement.
“If you live in an area that remains dry or windy, consider skipping fireworks altogether or attending a community fireworks show instead,” he said. “Our firefighters have carried an incredible burden this summer, and every preventable fire matters.”
Utahns are encouraged to never use fireworks in restricted areas or near dry vegetation, and to immediately report any wildfire by calling 911.
Fireworks are still banned on all federal, state and unincorporated lands, the Utah Department of Public Safety said. Those who start wildfires through illegal or negligent use of fireworks may be subject to civil and criminal penalties.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Gov. Sherrill signs bill restricting landlords’ use of rent-setting software
description: The new law aims to curb landlords’ use of rent-setting practices that critics say amount to unlawful collusion.
text:
Gov. Mikie Sherrill on Thursday called landlords’ use of rent-setting software “collusion by algorithm.” (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed legislation Monday restricting landlords’ use of algorithmic software to set rents, a move state officials say is part of a push to rein in housing costs.
The new law bars landlords from using software to analyze competitor’ pricing and vacancy data to set rent levels, a practice opponents argue has let landlords who would otherwise compete against each other effectively coordinate rent increases.
The law also prohibits landlords from sharing sensitive pricing data that feeds these algorithms, and bans price-fixing agreements between landlords.
Sherrill said New Jersey’s rent prices have gotten “out of control.”
“The problem is that these tools put competing landlords on the same team against renters,” Sherrill said before signing the bill in Newark. “Landlords can use these algorithms to coordinate prices, move in lockstep, and push rent higher and higher. It’s collusion by algorithm, and it’s illegal, and it stacks the deck against renters.”
The law, which passed the Legislature on June 30, will go into effect in July 2027. Some municipalities, like Hoboken and Jersey City, already have laws in place to bar landlords from using these programs to set rental prices.
Sherrill, a Democrat who took office in January, said the bill won’t “single-handedly fix our housing crisis” but made a claim that it will stop some of the “relentless price hikes” that are aggravating the housing market.
The new law comes about one year after the state Attorney General’s Office filed a lawsuit against RealPage, a software company that landlords have used to set rent prices, and nearly a dozen of the state’s largest landlords, arguing that they used the software to inflate rents in violation of antitrust and consumer protection laws.
A spokesman for RealPage did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the new law. The lawsuit against the company is ongoing.
Ana Maria Hill, the state director for 32BJ SEIU, the largest union of property service workers in the nation, said many of the union’s members struggle to keep up with rent increases and live close to where they work.
“The housing crisis wasn’t created by algorithms, but algorithms are contributing to it,” she said. “Today, we are saying no to them.”
Sherrill brushed off any concerns that the law could face legal battles, saying it was worded narrowly to avoid unintended consequences for real estate agents and other businesses not engaging in coordinated pricing. She said state officials learned “from some of the court cases in other states so that we could make this more resilient.”
“I think we’ve crafted this incredibly carefully to both fit within the legal system, as well as protect renters from collusion and wrongdoing,” she said.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Tucked in the state budget, a win for pharmacies looking for PBM regulation
description: “It’s a very good thing for probably several dozen pharmacies throughout the state,” said Rob Frankil, executive director of the Philadelphia Association of Retail Druggists.
text:
In light of ongoing provider shortages, some pharmacists are taking on additional duties to close the gap. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Pennsylvania’s most recent state budget includes a number of policy provisions agreed to by negotiating lawmakers.
One is aimed at helping pharmacies that say they have been arbitrarily prevented by a pharmacy benefit manager from accepting certain Medicaid plans.
The new provision will require pharmacy benefit managers, or PBMs, to allow pharmacies that they previously ended contracts with to reapply to their networks after 12 months, assuming they’re in good standing with state and federal laws.
While the measure does not address many of the issues pharmacists have raised about PBMs, including low reimbursement rates for medications they dispense, it does address an issue facing a handful of struggling Pennsylvania pharmacies.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“It’s a very good thing for probably several dozen pharmacies throughout the state who are having network problems with PBMs that don’t allow them to be in the MCO network,” said Rob Frankil, executive director of the Philadelphia Association of Retail Druggists.
Pharmacy benefit managers, or PBMs, are middlemen in the pharmaceutical supply chain. They’re hired by insurance companies to handle the prescription drug sides of their healthcare plans. 
In that role, PBMs reimburse pharmacies when patients pick up drugs that are covered by their insurance. If a pharmacy wants to accept a patient’s insurance, they have to sign a contract with the PBM that represents them, agree to the reimbursement rates they set, and follow any other rules they outline.
Pharmacists have long blamed PBMs for declining revenues and rising drug costs. The three largest PBMs — CVS Caremark, Express Scripts and Optum — are part of massive healthcare conglomerates and collectively process about 80% of all prescription drug claims in the United States. 
That means pharmacists must maintain good standing with them if they want to accept large numbers of their patients’ insurance plans.
But a number of pharmacists have warned that PBMs can be capricious with their contracts, kicking pharmacies out of their networks for reasons that can appear arbitrary.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A spokesperson for the Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, a trade group that represents the largest PBMs, declined to comment for this story.
For the last several years, attempts to regulate PBMs have brought Democrats and Republicans together. 
Since 2020, more than 1,000 pharmacies have closed across the state. Pharmacists and the trade groups that represent them have been pushing the legislature to pass legislation reining in PBMs.
The provision in the budget was championed by Republican Sen. Dave Langerholc (R-Clearfield) and Democratic Rep. Frank Burns (D-Cambria).

name: Mississippi Today
title: Hinds sheriff misses judge’s deadline to provide jail death records
description: A Hinds County Sheriff's Office van passes by the entrance to the Hinds County Detention Facility in Raymond, Miss., Monday, Aug. 1, 2022. On Friday, July 29, 2022, U.S. District Judge Carlton Reeves, placed the center into receivership after citing "severely deficient" conditions at the facility.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
The Hinds County Sheriff’s Office withheld jail death records from a legal advocacy organization for nearly a year. Then a local judge ordered the sheriff to turn the records over by July 9. But nearly two weeks later, the Southern Poverty Law Center is still waiting. 
The missed deadline is the latest instance of the county and the sheriff failing to produce jail death records, which the SPLC has been seeking since last summer to learn more about the number of people who’ve died in recent years at the Hinds County Detention Center in Raymond.
“We’re just scratching our heads about why we don’t have the records,” said Andrea Alajbegovic, a senior staff attorney at the SPLC. “It’s a little confounding at this point.”
The dispute over the records comes after 18-year-old Mielun Butler was stomped to death in the Raymond center earlier this month, two days after he was arrested and charged with a shooting death at a south Jackson apartment complex.  
The sheriff’s office’s failure to respond to the SPLC’s lawsuit – much less produce the records – has alarmed at least one local attorney who specializes in Mississippi’s government transparency laws. 
The county’s failure to respond to the SPLC’s records request is egregious, said Leonard Van Slyke, a retired attorney who practiced media law in Mississippi for decades. He said the chancery judge could hold the county in contempt of court, levy fines or even order jail time. 
Van Slyke added that in his experience, it’s common for public officials to claim records are exempt or find other ways to evade a public records request. 
“But to totally ignore a request is very unusual,” he said.
The SPLC first requested the documents in May 2025. Though the Mississippi Public Records Act gives government entities seven business days to respond to public records requests, the sheriff’s office did not acknowledge the SPLC’s inquiry until January.
In March, the SPLC filed a lawsuit in Hinds County Chancery Court over the sheriff’s failure to produce the records. After the sheriff and a county attorney did not respond to the lawsuit, Judge J. DeWayne Thomas ordered the county to turn over the jail death records. 
Hinds County Sheriff Tyree Jones listens to opinions on possible crime deterrents during a Violent Crime Prevention Summit held at the Two Mississippi Museums, Thursday, Jan. 5, 2023, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
When Mississippi Today first contacted Hinds County Sheriff Tyree Jones in March about the lawsuit, he said he was not aware. The SPLC did not issue a summons to the sheriff and instead served an officer manager, according to the court docket. In a Friday text message to Mississippi Today, Jones wrote he didn’t know the county had missed the deadline, adding “that’s a legal matter and the county attorneys would have to address that.” 
Tony Gaylor, the Hinds County attorney, said the county has been inundated with public records requests, but he said he didn’t know how long the backlog is. He said the county would respond to the court’s order. 
“That particular request is not something that’s being hid in any way, shape or form,” he said. 
Gaylor also speculated the SPLC did not submit its records request through the county’s online portal until a Mississippi Today reporter informed him the organization had filed the request through that system. 
Gaylor then said the SPLC should seek the records from the federal receiver who took over daily operations of the jail in October. 
John Hall, a private attorney for the sheriff’s office, did not respond to an email and a call from Mississippi Today. 
In mid-December, an attorney for the SPLC who knew Hall emailed him in an effort to obtain the records. According to exhibits attached to the SPLC’s complaint, Hall spoke to the SPLC on Jan. 7 and sent an email acknowledging the organization’s records request on Jan. 8, writing, “We’re on it.” 
But the SPLC did not get the records or any further communication from the county, the emails show. The organization then sought the information from the Mississippi Department of Public Safety in early March but did not obtain the records. 
Two days after SPLC filed the lawsuit in March, DPS provided jail death records. The SPLC subsequently removed the state agency from the suit. 
Under a federal law, DPS is responsible for reporting the number of in-custody deaths in Mississippi to the U.S. Department of Justice. But the state agency gets its numbers from the sheriff, Alajbegovic said, necessitating the need for cross-checking. 
“The full picture of people who have died in the facility seems to be extremely opaque,” she said. 
Butler’s killing occurred the same day Thomas granted the SPLC default judgment. 
A video of the attack circulated on Facebook, drawing renewed attention to the violent conditions at the jail. The Hinds County Detention Center has been subject to a federal consent decree since 2016. 
Butler’s mother, Janice Bradley, joined prominent Jackson attorney Dennis Sweet III at a press conference last week to announce that she had filed a wrongful death claim against the sheriff’s office. 
Sweet pledged to use the potential lawsuit to force the county to be more transparent. 
“We’re going to get at it,” he said. “We will do depositions. We’ll get it all.”
