name: Kansas Reflector
title: What to know about the excommunicated Catholic sect known as SSPX and its ties to Kansas
description: One of the most sweeping excommunications in worldwide Catholic history is concentrated in the small, northeast Kansas town of St. Marys, where the ultra traditionalist sect Society of St. Pius X has built a huge church and taken over local politics.  In early July, the Vatican declared that priests, deacons, bishops, and lay people who […]
text:
A Virgin Mary statue stands positioned at the top of the Immaculata in St. Marys. The rogue sect that built it, the Society of St. Pius X, has been excommunicated.  
(Photo by Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)One of the most sweeping excommunications in worldwide Catholic history is concentrated in the small, northeast Kansas town of St. Marys, where the ultra traditionalist sect Society of St. Pius X has built a huge church and taken over local politics. 
In early July, the Vatican declared that priests, deacons, bishops, and lay people who formally adhere to the teachings of the Society of St. Pius X, or SSPX, are excommunicated. 
SSPX has been at odds with the Vatican for decades, after it was founded in opposition to the Catholic Church’s move toward modernization. 
Their 66,400-square-foot church, the Immaculata, costs $42 million. It seats 1,500 people and hosts a traditional Latin Mass where priests face away from the congregation and women wear head coverings. 
The Kansas Bureau of Investigation said in 2023 it had been looking into accusations of child sexual abuse in SSPX and four Catholic dioceses for four years. The SSPX investigations have since been turned over to Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach’s office, according to a spokesperson for KBI. At least one of those cases is “still under review,” a spokeswoman for Kobach’s office said, but declined to give a timeline for potential charges. 
Kansas Reflector’s attempts to reach SSPX leaders for comment were unsuccessful. 
Here’s what to know about SSPX, the excommunications, and what it means in Kansas. 
SSPX in St. Marys 
SSPX formed in the 1970s as a backlash to a gathering of Ca
The main street in St. Marys has restaurants and plenty of shopping options for religious literature and modest dresses. (Photo by Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)
tholic leadership known as Vatican II. This gathering resulted in the Vatican allowing Catholic churches to host Mass in local languages instead of Latin, and began a
more tolerant approach to other religions. 
SSPX settled into St. Marys in 1978, where they started St. Mary’s Academy and College. 
Outside of Mass, women are encouraged to dress modestly and have large families. At the SSPX-run schools, students are separated by gender and discouraged from dating. 
Members of SSPX have taken over elected positions. The SSPX-dominated city commission forced the local library to ban youth books that mention LGBTQ+ people from the local library. They shut down the community golf course and swimming pool, in part due to the lack of modest clothing at the sites. 
Catholics are steadily leaving the church. They’re leaving in large part due to the Catholic Church’s teachings — especially on social and political issues — and scandals involving religious leaders.  
While most other rural communities in Kansas have shrunk, St. Marys has seen a population jump of 50% to 2,800 since 1980, which the church and others attribute to SSPX. 
“Traditional Catholicism is growing,” said Laura Garrison, who moved to St. Marys 10 years ago. “Many Catholics feel like they have been robbed of the rich and beautiful history of our faith since Vatican II.”
The late Pope Francis, who died last year, was widely considered a progressive pope. The current pope, Pope Leo XIV, is seen as more of a centrist. 
“There is a clear animus, toward tradition, coming out of Rome,” Garrison said. 
The excommunication
The official reason for the excommunications was SSPX consecrating new bishops without the pope’s approval. 
A sign in the center of St. Marys advertises the location of the Immaculata, a towering structure just a few streets away. (Photo by Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)
Before the excommunication, SSPX had two aging bishops and announced their plans to consecrate new ones. The Vatican warned that officials involved in the consecrations would be excommunicated if they did. 
Leo pleaded with the group not to move forward, but they did anyway on July 1 at an SSPX seminary in Écône, Switzerland. Each of the four new bishops — including SSPX Bishop Michael Goldade, who grew up in St. Marys — and the two who performed the ceremony were automatically excommunicated. 
A day later, on July 2, the Vatican released a decree officially stating all SSPX priests, deacons, and all lay Catholics who “formally adhere” to SSPX are excommunicated, too. 
There’s a difference between someone who may “formally adhere” and someone who attends SSPX Mass, though Kansas City Archbishop Shawn McKnight wrote that participation is sinful. Experts in canon law have said that an excommunication of a lay person would only happen if they reject the authority of the pope. 
In an open letter, the superior general of the society, Rev. Davide Pagliarani, said the church will remain faithful to the Catholic Church. 
This wasn’t the first time SSPX members were excommunicated. 
In 1988, SSPX founder Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre consecrated four bishops without the pope’s approval. In response, Pope John Paul II excommunicated Lefebvre and other officials involved. In 2009, Pope Benedict XVI lifted the excommunications in an attempt at reconciliation — but full communion was never restored. 
Two of the bishops that were excommunicated in 1988 — then lifted in 2009 — were excommunicated again this month. 
The Vatican left the door open for reconciliation, stating the church would “welcome with sincere affection and deep concern all those who wish to return to full communion.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: While Landry and New Orleans fight over pride, Louisiana’s children pay for It
description: “Used to be, the saying was, ‘Where goes New Orleans, where goes the state,'” Gov. Jeff Landry told reporters this month. “That has changed.”  If New Orleans’ standing has fallen, it fell on his watch. A governor dismissing his own state’s largest city is not a burn. It is a confession. And the audience is […]
text:
Gov. Jeff Landry speaks to reporters during a news conference at the State Capitol on Feb. 25, 2026. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)“Used to be, the saying was, ‘Where goes New Orleans, where goes the state,'” Gov. Jeff Landry told reporters this month. “That has changed.” 
If New Orleans’ standing has fallen, it fell on his watch. A governor dismissing his own state’s largest city is not a burn. It is a confession.
And the audience is bigger than he thinks. Not just the state. Not just the country. The world is watching Louisiana right now — watching a sitting attorney general indicted on 16 felony counts in a fight over who controls a New Orleans courthouse. 
Watching a governor veto $36 million in New Orleans projects — early learning centers, housing, a healthcare hub — and call it discipline.
Shakespeare opened “King Lear” with a ruler who carved up his own kingdom to feed his ego, demanded performances of loyalty and banished Cordelia, his daughter who refused to flatter him. The realm collapsed while he collected compliments. 
“Nothing will come of nothing,” Lear warned. 
Nothing is precisely what this feud produces for the people of Louisiana.
This state has been calling New Orleans a distraction since before the Civil War, through fights over bonds, tourism and recovery money ever since. The rivalry is the oldest blues song ever written in Louisiana. Landry is simply its newest performer. 
New Orleans is not an island. It is not extracted from Louisiana. Every blow aimed at it lands on all of us. Because here is the truth: Louisiana is hurting. Rural parishes, urban parishes, suburban parishes  — there is not one parish doing better than the other. All of us are on the same floor.
The state’s own legislative auditor found the child welfare system short at least 129 caseworkers, with frontline caseloads climbing from 9.3 cases a month to nearly 16 — well past the auditor’s standard of 10. 
The state’s own agency reports roughly 4,600 children in foster care, children now represented in a class-action lawsuit describing a system its own former leadership called a “death spiral.” 
These are not New Orleans numbers. These are Louisiana numbers.
Keep looking. Louisiana has the worst maternal mortality rate in America — 41.9 deaths per 100,000 births. The state’s own health department says 93% of those deaths were preventable. 
Nearly a third of our parishes are maternity care deserts, and the strongest predictor is population density, not race. That crisis lives in Cajun country and the Delta as surely as it lives in any city. 
Louisiana ranks dead last — 50th of 50 — in women’s and children’s health. Meanwhile, the state proposed cutting $125 million from K-12 education while growing the corrections budget 9%. Lawmakers left a teacher pay cut in place while raising pay for prison guards 
And after repealing Raise the Age, nearly 70% of the 17-year-olds arrested as adults in the state’s three largest parishes were charged with nonviolent offenses. 
This is what a kingdom looks like when the king is distracted by his own performance.
Every hour spent on this feud is an hour pulled away from that ledger. Conflict is not free. It drains the very resources — time, attention, political will — that a hurting state cannot spare, and it pushes us further from every goal we claim to hold. 
Criminologists call the result strain and structural violence. Psychologists call it adverse childhood experiences. A foster child sleeping in a state office calls it Tuesday.
Before we write this off as just another petty rivalry, we must ask: while we are busy looking at the courthouse fight in New Orleans, what policies are quietly slipping through the backdoor in Baton Rouge? Who truly benefits when the public is too distracted to notice a state in decline?
Let’s be real: New Orleans’s economic weight is a real conversation. Ports, tourism, culture — that is not nothing. But it cannot be the only conversation this government is capable of having. A state that can find the energy to fight over a city’s bond authority can find the energy to fund a caseworker.
Louisiana does not have the luxury of a government distracted by its own reflection. The world is watching what we do next. More importantly, sp are our children. Not just Black children. Not just white children. All of our children — in every parish, of every color, in the country and the city alike. 
They did not choose this feud. They are simply paying for it, in caseloads and care deserts and courtrooms. Nothing will come of nothing. Our children deserve something.
The governor says Louisiana will now determine the fate of New Orleans, and not the other way around. Look at where Louisiana is going — 49th in child well-being, 50th in health, last in mothers surviving childbirth. 
The saying needs updating — and not the way the governor thinks: Where go Louisiana’s children, there goes Louisiana.

name: Nevada Current
title: Judge hits the brakes on land sale near polluted Anaconda site
description: A federal court temporarily blocked the sale of more than 2,000 acres of public land in and around a polluted former copper mine to a multi-national petroleum company on Thursday while a lawsuit against the sale is decided in court.  In April, the Bureau of Land Management approved the direct sale of 2,062 acres of […]
text:
An old sediment pond at the Anaconda Mine in Nevada, prior to being relined in 2012. (Environmental Protection Agency photo) A federal court temporarily blocked the sale of more than 2,000 acres of public land in and around a polluted former copper mine to a multi-national petroleum company on Thursday while a lawsuit against the sale is decided in court. 
In April, the Bureau of Land Management approved the direct sale of 2,062 acres of public land near the Anaconda Copper Mine site in Lyon County — and the underlying mineral rights — to the Atlantic Richfield Company (ARC). 
Several environmental groups — the Great Basin Resource Watch, Prayer Horse Inc., and Taboosi Dikudu NO’Obatu Numma Cooperative — responded by suing the federal government to prevent the sale, which was slated to go through after July 27, 2026.
On Thursday, U.S. District Judge Miranda Du ruled the lawsuit raised serious questions about whether the sale complied with federal land disposal requirements and if BLM failed to take a “hard look” at the impact of future mining on the site before approving the sale of public land to a private company. 
The federal judge agreed the sale of the site before a final decision is made on the overall sale would cause “irreparable harm and that the requested relief serves the public interest” by cutting off access to public land. 
ARC purchased and operated the Anaconda Copper Mine in the late 1970s before it eventually sold to Arimetco, which abandoned the heavily polluted site after filing for bankruptcy. ARC remains responsible for the contaminated sites’ clean-up along with the BLM, the state of Nevada, and the Environmental Protection Agency.
Federal land managers have argued the land sale would benefit the public because it would facilitate a more effective and timely clean-up of the contaminated former copper mine, which is set to be completed in 2030.
However, during a hearing last week attorneys representing BLM noted the sale would not make clean-up efforts faster, while attorneys for ARC said the sale would largely benefit the company by easing administrative burdens created by having “another cook in the kitchen” due to BLM oversight. 
The court determined the federal government officials “have not provided a satisfactory explanation” for their decision to sell the land or how “BLM’s ownership has or will hinder the clean-up,” thus potentially violating provisions of the Federal Land Policy Management Act of 1976.
BLM and ARC did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the blocked sale. 
In her decision, Du noted even if clean-up efforts were measurably slower under BLM oversight than private oversight “public ownership has been the status quo for decades, which cuts against any argument that it would now cause irreparable harm.”
The court also determined the federal government potentially violated the National Environmental Policy Act by failing to take a “hard look” at the impact of future mining on the site before the sale when evidence exists that the sale will likely result in future mining operations.
Lion Copper and Gold Corp and its wholly owned Singatse Peak Services (SPS) have developed plans to mine the Anaconda site, according to an economic assessment prepared by AGP Mining Consultants for the company.  
“Upon acquisition, ARC will convey title to all minerals to SPS and the parties will execute a Surface Use Agreement allowing SPS the right to explore and mine the property,” the report says.
Singatse Peak Services filed a motion to join the case on Thursday after the court blocked the sale while the overall case against the sale makes its way through court. 
John Hadder, the executive director of the Great Basin Resource Watch, said SPS’s intervention suggests a mining interest, which he said was further supported by the company’s water right’s applications and historical exploration reports.
“It really does also point to the fact that this mining company is interested,” Hadder said. “It’s reasonably foreseeable that re-mining on the site will occur.”
“Our view is the real reason for the land sale is to facilitate plans to re-mine the site with no environmental impact statement. That’s  what we think is going on,” Hadder said. 
Johanna Emm, the executive director of Taboosi Dikudu NO’Obatu Numma Cooperative, said he was “glad that the court understood that ARC/BLM did not provide evidence of how the land sale would make the Anaconda mine clean-up better.”
Joshua Dini, the executive director of Prayer Horse Inc., said blocking the sale would prevent “any further contamination.”
“I appreciate the court’s finding in preserving my ability to stay connected to my homelands,” said Dini, who is a member of Walker River Paiute Tribe.
For decades, toxins from the Anaconda Copper Mine have seeped into the nearby land, polluting the groundwater and forcing the responsible parties – BP America and Atlantic Richfield Company — to take responsibility for the clean up, including providing bottled water for the Yerington Paiute Tribe’s reservation about 2 miles north of the abandoned Anaconda Copper Mine.
In 2002, the Nevada Division of Environmental Protection, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, and BLM agreed to coordinate oversight of the site’s clean-up. In 2005, BLM closed about two-thirds of the Anaconda Copper Mine site to the public due to environmental hazards. 
In 2018, the Environmental Protection Agency and the state of Nevada agreed to keep the site off the federal Superfund National Priorities List in favor of allowing the state to oversee the remaining cleanup by Atlantic Richfield Company. However, the site is still managed under Superfund guidelines.

name: Nevada Current
title: CD2 fundraising reports suggest momentum may be on Democrats’ side
description: No Democrat has ever won Nevada’s second congressional district, and the nation’s most prominent House rating groups assume the seat will be safely Republican again this year. But in a sign the district might be more competitive this year,  Nevada CD2 Democratic candidate Teresa Benitez-Thompson and Republican candidate David Flippo raised roughly the same a[...]
text:
In Nevada's traditionally safe Republican House district, Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson raised slighly more than Republican David Flippo in the second quarter. (Campaign photos) No Democrat has ever won Nevada’s second congressional district, and the nation’s most prominent House rating groups assume the seat will be safely Republican again this year.
But in a sign the district might be more competitive this year,  Nevada CD2 Democratic candidate Teresa Benitez-Thompson and Republican candidate David Flippo raised roughly the same amount in the weeks immediately before and after their competitive primaries, according to federal campaign finance reports filed last week.
Benitez-Thompson, a former Nevada State Assembly member, reported receiving $154,000 between March 31 and June 30, the period covered by the most recent reports due July 15. Flippo reported raising $153,000 during that time period.
Flippo also loaned his campaign an additional $350,000 during that period. That’s on top of $1.28 million in previous loans. Benitez-Thompson loaned her campaign $20,000 shortly after entering the race in February but has not loaned herself anything since.
Even factoring Flippo’s self funding, Benitez-Thompson reported ending June with more cash on hand — $140,000 — after campaign spending. Flippo reported having $118,000 on hand.
Those reported amounts don’t include third-party spending in support or opposition of the candidates. Three PACs — American Honor, Turning Point, and Freedom Caucus — supported Flippo through the competitive Republican primary against former Nevada State Sen. James Settelmeyer. A fourth PAC, Conservatives for American Excellence, backed Settelmeyer by running attack ads against Flippo.
U.S. Rep. Mark Amodei, the sole Republican in Nevada’s congressional delegation, announced in early February he would not be running for reelection, sparking a competitive scramble from both parties. Settelmeyer emerged as the establishment choice and had the backing of Amodei and Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. Flippo, who had been running against U.S. Rep. Steven Horsford in Nevada’s 4th Congressional District, swapped to CD2 after Amodei’s exit and received the backing of President Donald Trump and the MAGA crowd.
On the Democratic side, Benitez-Thompson entered the race, defeating Gregg Kidd, who’d previously ran for CD2 as an independent candidate, and nine other candidates.
In a statement provided by her campaign last week, Benitez-Thompson said she is encouraged by the grassroots support she has received.
“I am well on my way to having sufficient resources to compete on the airwaves,” she said, adding that “Las Vegan David Flippo will never have the community connection to compete with me on the ground.”
Benitez-Thompson’s campaign has also highlighted that only six of Flippo’s donors during the most recent reporting period live in CD2. Notably, one of those donors was Robert Beadles, the right-wing political activist known for touting conspiracy theories and hiring a private investigator to GPS track Reno Mayor Reno Mayor Hillary Schieve.
When asked for comment, Flippo’s campaign pointed to total receipt amounts, which includes the self loans, and ignored the spending amounts. Through that lens, Flippo has outraised Benitez-Thompson 2 to 1.
“No prediction market gives her more than a 28% chance of winning,” added Rory McShane in the emailed statement. “The Flippo campaign will have plenty of resources to expose Mrs. Benitez-Thompson for the radical socialist she is.”
Other House races
In Nevada’s 1st, 3rd and 4th Congressional Districts, Democratic U.S. Reps. Dina Titus, Susie Lee, and Steven Horsford maintain healthy fundraising leads over their Republican challengers.
Lee reported raising $508,000 in the weeks immediately before and after the June primary and having $3.69 million on hand. Her Trump-endorsed challenger, video game composer Marty O’Donnell, reported raising $381,000 during that time period and having $2.38 million on hand at the end of June. That amount is buoyed by an earlier $3 million loan to himself.
Horsford reported having $1.5 million on hand going into the third quarter, compared to rancher Cody Whipple’s $285,000. Horsford also outfundraised Whipple 3 to 1 during the most recent reporting period.
Finally, Titus continues to have a significant monetary advantage over her Republican challenger, Nevada State Sen. Carrie Buck. Titus reported having $1.3 million on hand compared to Buck’s $626,000.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Bear sightings are increasing in CT. Here’s what you need to know.
description: The Department of Energy and Environmental Protection has received reports of more than 7,300 bear sightings so far in 2026.
text:
Connecticut officials estimate the state’s black bear population at between 1,000 and 1,200. And they often come face-to-face with the state’s human population. The Department of Energy and Environmental Protection has received reports of more than 7,300 bear sightings so far in 2026. 
That’s comparable to bear sightings last year, when state environmental officials received more than 12,000 reports, according to its “State of the Bears” report. West Hartford had the most sightings in 2025 with 1,098. Glastonbury had the most notable increase in sightings, jumping to 248 in 2025 when in previous years sightings were considered “rare.” 
The report also noted an increase in bears entering homes, a trend the agency found “concerning.”
As bear encounters become more common in Connecticut, here’s what you should know.
Have there always been bears in Connecticut?
Bears were native to Connecticut, but habitat loss from colonization drove them to densely forested parts of western Massachusetts. 
Jason Hawley, wildlife biologist with the DEEP, said bears were historically hunted for food and fur. They were also commonly killed out of fear, Hawley said.
“They were intentionally extricated just because they were viewed as competitors for whatever animals the Europeans were raising,” Hawley said. 
By the mid-1800s, Connecticut’s bear population had almost dwindled entirely. Then, about 100 years later,  bears and habitats around the Connecticut River Valley were given protected status, which allowed them to expand their wandering range in the state once again.
Why have bear sightings increased over the last few years? 
An increase in bear sightings and encounters doesn’t necessarily correlate with an increase in the bear population. Sightings occur more frequently as human populations move into areas with more wildlife. 
“[In] towns where bears have sort of recently expanded their range, where bears are more of a novelty, people aren’t used to seeing them,” Hawley said. “It’s more about the number of people that live in that town that then report it.” 
Most bear sightings and human interactions happen in the summer months as bears come out of hibernation and move around more. During this time of year, females who are nursing cubs travel in search of extra calories and males travel in search of mates for breeding season. 
How can residents prevent bear encounters?
Bears can become habituated in days, meaning they get used to people or an area quickly. If they are intentionally fed or know where to find food, they’ll come back. 
Residents should clean and store outside grills when they’re not in use, keep pet food and compost inside, secure trashcans and remove birdfeeders entirely. Lock cars and house doors and close windows and garages. For people who raise chickens, goats or bees, Hawley recommends installing electric fencing. 
“Their sense of smell is incredible, so they know that food is associated with a human in some way,” Hawley said. “They’ll start seeking out human houses, businesses and restaurants where there’s dumpsters.” 
Black bears rarely get aggressive with humans, but they can become more dangerous when they’re habituated. 
If you encounter a bear outside, Hawleys recommends making noise by yelling or blowing an air horn so it creates a negative experience around humans. 
“Make yourself look big. It’s about letting them know that you’re there,” he said. “We don’t want the bear to be comfortable in your yard.”
Is it legal to hunt bears in Connecticut?
Yes and no. 
DEEP launched the Agricultural Bear Damage Permit Program in 2024, which allows farmers to file permits for lethal bear removal to address damage to crops, livestock or apiaries when non-lethal options fail. Since 2025, DEEP has allowed permit applicants to kill 15 bears. 
This spring, state lawmakers tried to expand farmer bear hunting permits, but the bills failed. Connecticut and Rhode Island are the only two states in the Northeast that don’t allow recreational bear hunting.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ e-bike law requiring registration, insurance now in effect
description: New rules for e-bike riders went into effect Sunday. They require registration and in some cases insurance.
text:
New rules for e-bike riders went into effect Sunday. They require registration and in some cases insurance. (Photo by Spencer Platt/Getty Images)New Jersey’s overhauled e-bike rules are now in effect, meaning thousands of riders across the state must be licensed, registered, and in some cases insured for the first time.
Under a law signed by then-Gov. Phil Murphy before he left office in January, e-bikes fall into two groups: low-speed electric or pedal-assist bikes that top out at 20 miles per hour, and faster, throttle-powered bikes that can reach up to 28 miles per hour.
The lower-speed bikes must now be registered with the state Motor Vehicle Commission. Riders of the higher-speed bikes must register them and obtain liability insurance to ride them.
Riders of both types must be at least 15 years old, hold a valid driver’s license or a special e-bike license issued by the Motor Vehicle Commission, and wear a helmet regardless of age. Riders can face fines of up to $50 per violation.
As of July 15, the commission had issued more than 4,100 e-bike registrations and 250 e-bike permits, said agency spokesman William Connolly.
“MVC is working hard to service as many riders as quickly and efficiently as possible,” Connolly said.
Out-of-staters who bring their e-bikes across state lines will have to register their bikes in New Jersey and get licenses if they don’t have a regular driver’s license.
The push for tighter regulations followed a string of fatal e-bike crashes around the state. Murphy’s office cited “numerous dangerous crashes” when he signed the bill, while bill sponsor state Senate President Nick Scutari (D-Union) has argued that e-bikes have gotten faster and more powerful and that younger, inexperienced riders are using them.
Nationally, e-bike injuries rose by 293% from 2019 to 2022, according to Columbia University researchers.
Bike advocates opposed the new law, saying it adds unneeded barriers for cyclists.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Why Sen. Evan Vickers, of southern Utah, wants to be the state’s next Senate president
description: Senate President Stuart Adams’ unexpected primary loss sent shockwaves through the Legislature, leaving a leadership void that Senate Republicans will decide how to fill — but not until a closed-door caucus election after the November general election.  Even though those leadership elections are roughly five months away, one longtime senator is already makin[...]
text:
Senate Majority Leader Evan Vickers, R-Cedar City, is pictured on the first day of the legislative session at the Capitol in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Jan. 16, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Senate President Stuart Adams’ unexpected primary loss sent shockwaves through the Legislature, leaving a leadership void that Senate Republicans will decide how to fill — but not until a closed-door caucus election after the November general election. 
Even though those leadership elections are roughly five months away, one longtime senator is already making it known he’ll be vying to take Adams’ place: Sen. Evan Vickers, R-Cedar City, who served as Adam’s second, as majority leader, for years before he lost that position to Sen. Kirk Cullimore, R-Sandy, in 2025. 
So far, both Vickers and Cullimore are considered likely contenders for the Senate presidency. However, Cullimore, through a Senate spokesperson, declined to comment for this story. 
Stuart Adams is out: Utah Senate president concedes to Republican challenger

In an interview with Utah News Dispatch last week, Vickers pointed to his 18 years in the Legislature (four in the House and 14 in the Senate), as well as six years he spent as Senate majority leader before he lost the position to Cullimore. 
“It was a close race,” he said. “You know, I have to admit, anytime you lose it’s a little painful and it’s taken me a while to get here, but I really do think that that was one of the best things that happened to me because I was able to sit back and kind of observe the caucus, the Senate in general and the Legislature and see what was working and what wasn’t.” 
He said if he’s elected Senate president, he’d work to “get the public’s trust back.” 
“It seems like we’ve lost that recently,” he said, adding that on some issues “the public has not been on our side” and that the Legislature has “never done a very good job of telling our story.” 
From efforts to change an anti-gerrymandering initiative known as Proposition 4, to a controversial anti-collective bargaining bill for public unions that lawmakers repealed amid outcry, to bills expanding the Utah Supreme Court and giving the Senate and governor a say over who the high court’s next chief justice, Vickers said all those moves came with good policy arguments, “but the public didn’t understand that.” 
Unpacking Utah’s primary upsets: The race that’s sending ‘shockwaves’ through the Legislature

“So I would like to do a better job (with the public), if we can, as we push forward,” Vickers said, whether that includes preparing for the Olympics in 2034, making sure public and higher education budgets are sound, and increasing resources for water infrastructure and transportation. 
“Those are things that are going to take some effort and a lot of work within the Legislature,” he said. “But also, we need to do a really good job of helping the public understand what we’re doing and why we’re doing it.” 
Vickers, from Cedar City in Southern Utah, also said senators who represent more rural areas off the Wasatch Front are hungry for more representation in Senate Republican leadership. 
“So we were looking at ways that we might be able to leverage some opportunity to have more say,” he said. 
After Adams lost his primary, that “changed the dynamics,” Vickers said, and he started making some phone calls and asking his fellow senators if they’d support his run. 
“It certainly appears feasible. It doesn’t mean I’m going to win, but it certainly appears feasible,” he said. 
Adams, Vickers said, has been an “amazing leader” who has “done some really wonderful things, and a lot of things that a lot of people will never even know what he’s done because they were behind the scenes … but he’s made the state a better place.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
But Vickers said he would differ from Adams in style, which he described as “a bit more controlling.” 
“President Adams is very, very effective. His style — it really works for him, and he’s done well with it — is he is a little bit more controlling, I think, and he wants to be more engaged in a lot of the individual discussions,” Vickers said. “I’m a little different. I would like to have more people engaged in the process.” 
Vickers pointed to Adams’ predecessor, former Senate President Wayne Niederhauser, as being a good delegator — and that’s what he said he would focus on rather than having “my finger on every pulse.” 
Vickers also said he would continue making sure Senate Democrats are able to voice their opinions, and he said he would likely continue holding daily media availabilities during the session. 
He also said he would only hold the position for up to four years, until his current term ends. 
“Whether I end up being the Senate president or just being a senator in the body, I hope I can continue to build on what I’ve learned from (Adams) and others,” he said. “Yeah, I would like to see a few modest changes in how we function as a Senate and a Legislature, but on the same token I really want the Senate and the Legislature to continue doing really good policy for the state.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: Audit paints troubling picture of WA’s overcrowded youth prison system
description: Nearly half of front-line staff at Washington’s overcrowded juvenile detention facilities leave within a year. Many report feeling unsafe, unprepared and unsupported.  That’s according to a sobering, if not shocking, audit of the state’s youth prison system that has faced years of issues stemming from trying to fit too many young people into facilities not [[...]
text:
A sign and fence at the Green Hill School for juvenile offenders, in Chehalis, Washington. (Photo by Jake Goldstein-Street/Washington State Standard)Nearly half of front-line staff at Washington’s overcrowded juvenile detention facilities leave within a year. Many report feeling unsafe, unprepared and unsupported. 
That’s according to a sobering, if not shocking, audit of the state’s youth prison system that has faced years of issues stemming from trying to fit too many young people into facilities not set up to hold them all safely. 
This capacity strain led to a quadrupling of fights, assaults and contraband incidents at the state’s Green Hill School in Chehalis between 2022 and 2024, according to the report from the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Committee. Training from the state Department of Children, Youth and Families, which runs the detention center, doesn’t prepare staff to handle these situations.
“Without enough experienced staff, facilities struggle to maintain order, build trust with residents, and effectively deliver rehabilitative programs,” the report says.
The audit also found disparate treatment of confined youth of color and invalid assessments that don’t properly predict risk of recidivism and eligibility for release into the community for each incarcerated young person.
State juvenile rehabilitation officials argued progress has been made since much of the work on the audit, released this month, was done in 2024 and 2025.  
“Their points about the lack of safety for staff and for young people when there is overcrowding, we completely agree, and we’ve been shouting from the rooftops about that,” Tana Senn, secretary of the Department of Children, Youth and Families, told lawmakers last week.  
She said her agency will need increased funding from them to address overcrowding and other issues.
Green Hill School, with a safe operating capacity of 180, held 196 people at the end of June, according to state officials. The facility’s population, which holds boys and men ages 17 to 25, had long sat well above 200. At one point in 2024, overcrowding reached such a high level that the agency transferred dozens of young men from Green Hill to an adult prison run by the state Department of Corrections, a move that drew wide backlash and lawsuits.
A change in state law to allow youth convicted of crimes to be kept in juvenile detention, instead of adult prison, until they turn 25 is one reason for the ballooning population in recent years. State forecasts show a potential for continued overcrowding in the coming years.
(Graphic courtesy of the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Committee)
And more and more of the young people incarcerated at Green Hill face longer sentences for violent crimes like murder, sex offenses and robbery, meaning fewer beds open up.
A state appellate court last year ruled the overcrowding at Green Hill violated state law, as young people held there reported having to remain in their cells for hours and urinate in bottles amid staffing shortages that also resulted in diminished programming.
Despite the cascading concerns, the Legislature hasn’t passed substantial policy changes to help address them in recent years. 
Last year, the state did open Harbor Heights, a new, smaller facility on the campus of an adult prison as a release valve for crowding at Green Hill. 
And lawmakers did approve some money to design a new juvenile rehabilitation facility that could serve fewer than 50 people. This comes as national trends have pointed to smaller facilities being more conducive to rehabilitation. A top option to accomplish this in Washington has been renovating the shuttered Mission Creek Corrections Center in Mason County. A new detention center could mean closing Harbor Heights.
Legislators have also tasked the Department of Children, Youth and Families with planning for another facility east of the Cascades.
This year’s budget also included state funding for over a dozen more staffers at Green Hill to address concerns.
Both Echo Glen Children’s Center in Snoqualmie, which houses girls and women ages 11 to 25 and boys from 11 to 17, and Harbor Heights were below capacity at the end of last month.
The audit
The Joint Legislative Audit and Review Committee found a direct link between increasing population at Green Hill and safety issues. 
Every 10 new people held there would result in five to six more assaults or fights and six drug and alcohol incidents. Echo Glen saw more mild upticks with crowding.
Green Hill is also where staff turnover has been most extreme. Employees reported as a result of understaffing they suffered burnout and felt undervalued. Uncompetitive salaries for some positions and limited promotion opportunities added to their frustration, according to the report. In spite of complaints, Washington’s juvenile detention vacancy rates are still below other states.
The agency has taken steps to improve retention, including increasing pay and adjusting shift schedules to reduce burnout, according to the audit. Turnover could make it harder to develop relationships with incarcerated youth. Young people who reported they trusted staff were much more likely to say they felt safe than others.
Turnover at the top is a problem, too. Juvenile rehabilitation has had multiple leaders since 2020, including an assistant secretary who alleged she was fired in an act of whistleblower retaliation. Green Hill has had three leaders since 2020. Echo Glen has had nine. The first superintendent at Harbor Heights has already been replaced, as well. 
Beginning this year, new juvenile detention staffers have to attend a six-week training, the audit says. Previously, the training was five weeks or less, which staff reported didn’t properly prepare them for the job. They said trainers didn’t have front-line experience, didn’t accurately depict what these facilities are like and left them uncertain how to handle safety concerns like assaults. Agency procedures also lacked clear instruction in how to intervene in these situations.
This lack of clarity opens the door for significant staff discretion, creating potential for disparate treatment for young people of color, who are disproportionately confined in juvenile detention. At Green Hill, the audit found Native American, Black, Hispanic and multiracial residents are more likely to be confined to their rooms than their white counterparts.
(Graphic courtesy of the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Committee)
The new training is “evolving based off of staff feedback and the emerging research about what needs to be trained to in these settings,” Jennifer Redman, the state’s assistant secretary of juvenile rehabilitation, told an oversight board last week.
Refresher training for existing employees has also been lacking, but the state says it is working to improve that.
Meanwhile, a survey of 268 young people held in state custody late last year found 63% felt safe, but fewer than half thought their peers felt safe. 
The audit also concluded that the Department of Children, Youth and Families’ assessments of its incarcerated youth are poor. These assessments help determine a young person’s security level in detention, whether they can transfer to a less secure setting, like a community facility, and their likelihood of recidivism. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
But they can both understate and overstate a young person’s risk, allowing them to be eligible for a less restrictive placement when they shouldn’t be, according to the report. They also incorrectly identify their suitability to share a cell in detention.
“It sounds like we’re really not at DCYF following best practices,” said Sen. Keith Goehner, R-Dryden.
The state report found issues in programming offered at the detention centers. Programs include drug and mental health treatment, education as well as life skills and vocational training. But Green Hill and Echo Glen both have waitlists for drug treatment, and young women at Echo Glen don’t have access to higher education opportunities like men at Green Hill. And instead of matching young people to programs based on their needs, they’re more often just matched with what’s available.
A lack of data and oversight also hampers the state’s ability to track the efficacy of these programs, according to the audit.
Senn acknowledged her agency’s juvenile detention is “definitely not perfect.”
“We have improvements to make, and we’re looking forward to improving our practice,” she said.
Recommendations
The report includes advice for the Department of Children, Youth and Families as well as the Legislature to improve juvenile detention.
For lawmakers, auditors suggest funding additional capacity through smaller, community-based facilities, and look at when the department can transfer young people to adult prisons and when they are eligible for community facilities.
As for the state agency, the report suggests doing more to improve staff training and retention. Officials should develop clearer procedures for responding to assaults and riots, and use valid assessments to better predict risks. 
The department should also ensure its programs align with the needs of its detainees, given the population is getting older and has more acute needs. And these programs should be tailored to each young person’s individual needs. 
“The problems identified in this review do not exist in isolation,” the audit says. “Addressing any one of these challenges without attention to the others would likely be insufficient.”
Auditors want the department to report back by summer 2027 on its progress on their recommendations.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Whites-Koditschek joins as fellow with Deep South Today Investigative Reporting Center
description: Sarah Whites-Koditschek is joining Mississippi Today and the Deep South Today Investigative Reporting Center as part of The New York Times Local Investigations Fellowship.
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
Sarah Whites-Koditschek is joining Mississippi Today and the Deep South Today Investigative Reporting Center as part of The New York Times Local Investigations Fellowship.
Sarah Whites-Koditschek
Whites-Koditschek begins her work Monday in Mississippi Today’s newsroom in Jackson. She is part of the six-person fellowship class that The New York Times announced June 22.
The fellowship program, led by Dean Baquet, a former executive editor of The New York Times, gives journalists the opportunity to produce signature investigative work focused on the state or region they’re reporting from. Their reporting will be published by The Times and made available free for co-publication by local newsrooms.
“This is the program’s fourth fellowship class, and we’re thrilled to work with them on producing important accountability reporting from their communities,” Baquet said. “Their work will add to the fellowship’s strong roster of investigative journalism from regions across the country, and we’re excited to help foster this next generation of investigative reporters.” 
The fellows are based in Illinois, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas.
Whites-Koditschek is a former investigative reporter for AL.com in Birmingham, Alabama. She has won national awards from the Society for Professional Journalists and the Public Media Journalists Association as well as a Regional Edward R. Murrow award. She previously worked in public radio as a reporter and producer at WHYY in Philadelphia and KUAR in Little Rock. She is a graduate of the Columbia School of Journalism’s Stabile Center for Investigative Journalism, and she completed a fellowship in investigative reporting at Wisconsin Public Radio and the Wisconsin Center for Investigative Journalism.
 “Sarah digs into important issues, even when facing bureaucratic obstacles,” said Mississippi Today Editor in Chief Emily Wagster Pettus. “She is an outstanding addition to an already strong investigative team, and we look forward to the work she will do in Mississippi.”
Whites-Koditschek joins Bobbi-Jeanne Misick, Mukta Joshi and Rosemary Westwood as local investigations fellows of the Deep South Today Investigative Reporting Center created in collaboration with The New York Times. Joshi is reporting for Mississippi Today, while Misick and Westwood are reporting for Verite News in New Orleans.
Investigative reporting that was produced through the fellowship has received national recognition. A yearslong examination of abuses by sheriffs departments in Mississippi was a finalist for the 2024 Pulitzer Prize for Local Reporting the Goldsmith Prize for Investigative Reporting in 2024 and 2026. The team was also awarded the Peter F. Collier Award for Ethics in Journalism, the First Amendment Coalition’s Free Speech and Government Award and the Investigative Reporters and Editors Tom Renner Medal for Outstanding Crime Reporting.
The Times will continue collaborating with Big Local News, a data-sharing journalism program based at Stanford University. Big Local News will be working again with the fellows on obtaining and analyzing data for their projects and providing ongoing training on investigative data techniques.
Applications for the 2027-28 group of fellows opened July 1. Journalists interested in a fellowship based in Mississippi or Louisiana can visit this application form year round.

name: VTDigger
title: In Vermont’s Democratic primary for lieutenant governor, leading candidates’ past work takes center stage
description:
Molly Gray, who held the job from 2021-2023, says she’d be ready to hit the ground running. Ryan McLaren thinks otherwise: “We can do better than politicians from the past.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  In Vermont’s Democratic primary for lieutenant governor, leading candidates’ past work takes center stage.
text:
Molly Gray, left, and Ryan McLaren, democratic candidates for lt. governor, participating in a housing forum in South Burlington on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Photos by Glenn Russell
The two leading Democratic candidates for Vermont’s second-highest office don’t disagree much over policy. But they say there are key differences in the experience they’d bring to the job — and one of them disputes who should get credit for some past successes.
Molly Gray, who’s from Newbury and now lives in Burlington, was the first to announce a bid for lieutenant governor this year. Gray held the office once before, from 2021 to 2023, and in that time ran unsuccessfully for an open seat in the U.S. House.
Also seeking the job is Ryan McLaren of Essex Junction. The highest public office he’s held is a school board seat, but he’s making the case that his most recent job as a top aide for U.S. Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., shows he has the know-how to make an impact on a statewide level.
For Gray, the pitch to be lieutenant governor is in some ways straightforward. She’s done the job before. But that hasn’t stopped McLaren from describing himself as better qualified, sometimes in brash terms.
“Having a title is very different than getting shit done,” he said in an interview. “And I get shit done.”
A third candidate is also in the race: Esther Charlestin, who lives in South Burlington. Charlestin is a consultant and was the Democratic Party’s nominee for governor against Republican Gov. Phil Scott in 2024. Scott won that election handily.
The primary for lieutenant governor has drawn in a substantial amount of money so far this year, with Gray and McLaren both having raised more than $275,000 each, according to the latest reports filed with the Vermont Secretary of State’s Office. Charlestin has raised about $35,000, giving Gray and McLaren a clear advantage with just weeks until voters head to the polls on Tuesday, Aug. 11. 
At the same time, Charlestin pointed to a late June poll from the University of New Hampshire which ranked her as likely primary voters’ second choice, with 11% support. Gray polled highest 39% and McLaren was third with 7% support. 
Another 42% of likely voters surveyed were undecided, Charlestin noted — and she thinks her consulting experience “facilitating hard conversations” in schools and nonprofit organizations will sway those people that she’s the best fit to oversee policy debates, too.
‘Hit the ground running’
The lieutenant governor job involves few day-to-day responsibilities beyond presiding over the state Senate — though officeholders use the post to advocate for their favored legislation and call attention to issues of statewide import.
Several senators will be new to the chamber starting next year, Gray noted in an interview, and the body will also have a new president pro tempore in the wake of the retirement of Sen. Phil Baruth, D/P-Chittenden Central. It makes sense then, she said, to have a parliamentarian who is already familiar with the rules.
“I’m prepared to hit the ground running. I know how to do the constitutional aspects of the job — and do them really well,” Gray said.
Before serving as lieutenant governor, Gray worked as an assistant Vermont Attorney General and clerked for a federal judge. In the years before that, she worked abroad on humanitarian missions for the International Committee of the Red Cross and after college was a scheduler for Welch’s office, when Welch was in the U.S. House.
McLaren has also worked for Welch, though for far longer and most recently as one of his principal aides. He left the senator’s office to run for lieutenant governor. Earlier, McLaren worked in constituent services for former Democratic Gov. Peter Shumlin and was a field organizer for the state chapter of the Democratic Party.
Mollly Gray, democratic candidate for lt. governor, speaks during a housing forum in South Burlington on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell
On the campaign trail, McLaren has been vocal about having a disability. A skiing accident in 2017 at Mad River Glen left him with little to no function below the knees and limited function between his waist and knees. His condition has improved since then, he has said, though he continues to use a wheelchair to get around.
He said he hopes that serving in a top office with a visible disability would be important for others who are disabled, too, “because there’s not a lot of us in public life as examples of what’s possible.”
Charlestin describes herself as a daughter of immigrant parents who raised her in the U.S. after traveling to the country from Haiti. That gives her “a deep understanding” of the challenges facing immigrant communities in Vermont that have only grown more pronounced since her last bid for office in 2024, she has said.
“I plan on bringing all of that knowledge that I’ve built on since my last run — to bring that to work as lieutenant governor,” she said in an interview.
In addition to her consulting business, Charlestin chairs the Vermont Commission on Women, which is a state panel that advocates for gender equity. She previously worked as dean of climate and culture at Middlebury Union Middle School, though resigned after experiencing racism on the job. She’s also served on the Middlebury Selectboard.
Federal focus
After leaving the lieutenant governor post, Gray became a mother — making “crystal clear” the high costs of raising children that are burdening Vermont families, she said — and served as the first executive director of the Vermont Afghan Alliance, a Burlington-based nonprofit that supports Afghan refugees who are resettling in Vermont. 
By working with the Afghan community, Gray said she knows how to stand up for people in the state against harmful policy changes by the Trump administration.The Afghan Alliance was one of the organizations that pushed to restart access to federal food benefits last year for certain visa holders after Vermont curtailed access to those benefits in line with the state’s interpretation of a federal policy change. The organization’s other work includes translation assistance, driving lessons geared toward women who were banned from driving in Afghanistan and legal aid. 
Her leadership of the organization distinguishes her from the other candidates in the primary, she said. 
“They haven’t seen — in the way that I have — the deep cruelty and inhumanity of this administration up close,” Gray said. “I believe I have the experience to help us stand strong against the Trump administration. To hold the line.” 
Some of Gray’s accomplishments at the Afghan Alliance have been questioned by McLaren, both in recent candidate forums and in an interview.
McLaren commends the organization’s driving program, but has said it only exists in the form it does because of a 2013 Vermont law that allows non-U.S. citizens to obtain state driver’s licenses. After the law was passed, according to McLaren, he played a key part in rolling out its provisions as the top advisor to the head of the state Department of Motor Vehicles.
Molly Gray, democratic candidate for lt. governor, speaks during a housing forum in South Burlington on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell
Credit for the Afghan Alliance’s driving program is due just as much to him as to Gray, he said.
“The fact that those 60 Afghan women could get driver’s licenses is because I was the No. 2 at the DMV,” McLaren said in a candidate forum in Montpelier earlier this year, referring to a number of drivers Gray referenced earlier in the discussion.
Gray pushed back against McLaren’s characterization in an interview, saying that, “Vermonters deserve a lieutenant governor who cares more about getting results and lifting people up than taking credit.” She added, “I welcome the work of anyone who wants to support our new neighbors and start their lives here.”
McLaren has continued to make the case he’s the one with the strongest track record of results from the decade he worked in Welch’s office. He’s argued he has made a more direct impact on federal policy than Gray because he worked closely with a member of Congress. 
The difference between himself and the other candidates is “receipts,” he said, pointing to “a laundry list” of federally-funded projects he worked on for Welch’s office over the past decade. 
From the most recent round of congressionally directed spending, also known as earmarks, McLaren’s campaign highlighted a $5.2 million award to help build 21 affordable apartments in Middlebury, $1 million to expand childcare slots in Craftsbury and just shy of $1 million for the University of Vermont to bolster staffing of a program that provides healthcare services to farmworkers, among others.
“Everywhere I go, there’s a project I got to work on that made an impact,” he said. 
A launching pad?
All three candidates said in interviews that the lieutenant governor’s job has historically been “underutilized,” though offered varying explanations for how they’d use it differently if elected this fall. 
McLaren said he wants to use the job similarly to the role of “public advocate” that exists in New York City and other governments around the country. In New York, the office provides oversight of city agencies and investigates citizens’ complaints. He said he also wants to use the office to call out ethical violations by members of the Legislature, should they commit them. 
The lieutenant governor’s post “is not some great launching pad for political ambition. It hasn’t proven to be in recent history,” he said, noting the exception of Gov. Scott, who went from No. 2 to governor in 2016. 
“Everyone else in this race has run for some other office, lost, and has fallen backward into running for lieutenant governor in 2026,” he continued, referring to Gray’s bid for Congress and Charlestin’s bid for governor. “I just think we can do better than politicians from the past.”
Charlestin said she would model the approach that the lieutenant governor of Illinois, Juliana Stratton, took in recent years to address the disparity in maternal mortality rates facing Black women in that state. Stratton convened a group of Black women birth workers for a forum that later informed a state budget proposal — something Charlestin said she wants to do with issues that are prevalent in Vermont, such as a lack of access to affordable housing.
Esther Charlestin, democratic candidate for lt. governor, speaks during a housing forum in South Burlington on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell
Gray described a somewhat less adversarial approach than McLaren, saying she would be eager to “give both the Legislature and other statewide electeds support and cover” if they are at odds with federal policy changes or steps taken by Scott. 
She pointed to how Lt. Gov. John Rodgers, who’s a Republican, has been closely aligned with Scott since taking office in 2024. Scott endorsed Rodgers’ reelection campaign earlier this week. 
Gray said she is not interested in running for governor or for Congress again, as she did in 2022.
She pointed as an example of her political priorities to solving the rural-urban divide that defined debates this year over Vermont’s land use laws, making a case that she is well positioned to navigate that dynamic because she was born in a small town.
“When I think about access to healthcare in a rural community, or what it would mean to have a school close or what are the needs of rural communities in building housing, I get that,” Gray said. “I’ve lived it.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: PAC attack mailers bring backlash in GOP primary race for Missouri’s 28th state Senate District
description: Sam Alexander paints a grim picture of Missouri’s 28th Senate District.  Alexander, an emergency room physician and farmer running for state Senate, said he lays awake at night thinking of the hospitals in financial straits, young people leaving their small towns behind for more work opportunities and senior citizens living month-to-month. “We’re America. We[...]
text:
The 28th state Senate District Republican primary candidates are, from left, state Rep. Brad Pollitt, Dr. Sam Alexander and Chuck Lentz. (Submitted photos)Sam Alexander paints a grim picture of Missouri’s 28th Senate District. 
Alexander, an emergency room physician and farmer running for state Senate, said he lays awake at night thinking of the hospitals in financial straits, young people leaving their small towns behind for more work opportunities and senior citizens living month-to-month.
“We’re America. We can do a lot better than we’re doing here in this district,” Alexander said. “… We’re dying out here. We really are.”
Alexander’s chief primary competitor, state Rep. Brad Pollitt of Sedalia, chuckled at the assertion that the district has one foot in the grave.
Pollitt, a cattle farmer and former educator, said during his eight years in the Missouri House representing Pettis County, he’s brought more than $150 million back to constituents, including to State Fair Community College, the Boys and Girls Club, Bothwell Hospital and a couple of major road projects.
“We’ve got a budget shortfall, so a lot of these projects aren’t gonna happen here in the future,” he said. “But I was proud that none of my budget asks were withheld or vetoed. How many representatives can say that?”
But while Alexander sees Pollitt as part of a political system that has failed the district, a political action committee backing Pollitt is asking voters to view Alexander as an irresponsible scofflaw who shouldn’t be elected to office. The negative tone of those direct mail messages from the Rocker P Brand PAC have created a rift with some of his backers who don’t want to be associated with the message.
Pollitt and Alexander are joined by Chuck Lentz, a professor and administrator, who said he was in-part motivated to join the race after hearing from his college students who were feeling defeated over how unattainable homeownership was and how costly starting a family can be.
“We have real poverty in these counties,” Lentz said. “And people don’t address rural poverty, and what’s happening to our rural communities, and our small families.”
 The 28th District encompasses nine counties in southwest Missouri and includes the cities of Sedalia, Bolivar and Clinton. Incumbent state Sen. Sandy Crawford must leave office due to term limits. The winner of the primary race will face Democrat Mike McCaffree, a real estate agent from Nevada. 
Second-quarter campaign finance reports show Pollitt had raised $372,656 and had nearly $172,000 cash on hand at the end of June. A political action committee working on Pollitt’s behalf, Rocker P Brand PAC, has raised $272,447 since the start of 2025 and had $240,241 on hand at the end of the quarter.
Alexander has raised $249,791, including a $120,000 personal loan to the campaign, with about $170,000 cash on hand. 
Lentz, raised $13,757 by July.
As of Thursday, Pollitt had placed about $42,000 in ad buys across three TV stations.
 Amendment 5 

The median household income of the 28th District is $55,156, and about 17% of the district’s 188,345 constituents live below the poverty line, according to data from the US Census Bureau. 
“The 28th District is just filled with really good people who just want the government to provide the bare essentials and let them live their lives,” Pollitt said. “They want God in their lives, they want family, and they want life protected. They want their gun rights protected. It’s a huge agricultural Senate district. There’s a lot of cattle in the 28th District.”
Alexander and Pollitt have many of the same priorities on paper: they support gun rights and anti-abortion laws. 
Their views diverge slightly on education and taxation. 
Pollitt said many people are voicing concerns around Amendment 5, which would eliminate the state income tax if approved by a simple majority of Missouri voters in August. He said he can see both arguments for and against the amendment, but won’t share how he plans to vote.
Pollitt voted for the Amendment 5 legislation each time it was before the House on a roll call.
“I think it would be disingenuous if I tell them how to vote. I think they need to look at their own situation. I do believe that the statistics say that states without income taxes, that their economies are stronger than Missouri’s, and their population is growing,” he said. “Their concerns that they’ve said back to me is, ‘we don’t know what you all will tax, and it’s kind of hard for us to say yes when we’re not sure.’”
Alexander said while the state needs to find a way to bring in more industry and people, he wouldn’t have approved of the plan as it stands. He said he would have advocated for a slow roll-out, perhaps by cutting income tax by half a percent at a time to give lawmakers longer to figure out how to adjust the budget accordingly.
“I don’t think it’s right to change one tax for another tax without knowing what that tax is gonna be, and how it’s gonna work,” he said. It may have a bad effect on folks who are lower income or elderly and on a fixed income, he said. 
Chuck Lentz, picured with his wife and three children, is self-funding his grassroots campaign for Missouri’s 28th District Senate seat (provided photo).
Lentz said he’s the only candidate to oppose both Amendment 5 and Amendment 4, which would raise the threshold for passing constitutional amendments proposed by citizen-led initiative campaigns from a simple majority of all votes in the state to a majority in every congressional district.
On principle, Lentz said he’s a no “because it takes some of that power out of people’s hands,” adding that he’s also wary because congressional district boundaries can change.
He’s also firmly against Amendment 5.
“There is real poverty that people are ignoring in rural America and rural Missouri specifically,” Lentz said. “But these are people who don’t want a bunch of handouts, they just want to be able to live … they don’t want everything taxed. Does that make sense?”
 Education issues

Arguments over school choice remain a point of contention in many of this year’s primary races.
Pollitt, who previously worked as superintendent for the Sedalia school district, sponsored a bill several years in a row seeking to allow some Missouri students to enroll in neighboring school districts. 
“Should your home address be the main determination in what public school district your children attend? I don’t believe it should,” he told a House committee last year. “Should the child and family be at the center of the educational focus? I believe it should.”
The bill has gained considerable momentum, but it has never passed. 
State Rep. Brad Pollitt, a Republican from Sedalia, speaks on cuts to child care funding during the House’s budget debate March 26, 2026. (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
Alexander painted himself as “a rare breed of Republican” because he disagrees with school choice. However, Republicans remain split on the issue.
“We can do better than what we’ve been doing for our schools and stuff,” Alexander said. “I’m for improving the grades, for sure, but I’m also for backing these small rural schools that are struggling. A lot of these programs that a lot of the Republicans are pushing, that are being harmful to a lot of these little schools that are doing a good job.”
Lentz, said “school choice” laws could lead to school closures in rural towns, which he fears would decimate small communities.
“We have school choice right now, 100%,” he said. “ Anybody can choose in Missouri to go where they want. But I’m not asking other people to pay for it. That’s the difference.”
 Anti-establisment vs experience

Alexander has run for public office before, previously losing campaigns for Congress and for a state representative seat. This time, he’s launched a substantial campaign, leaning on messaging that he’s everyday folk up against the establishment. 
It’s a campaign message not uncommon in Missouri Republican races.
Alexander, who is also a pilot, preacher and handyman, waxes poetic about a return to his vision of the American Dream: where people know how to work with their hands, and neighbors stop by to help one another out. 
“My entire life I’ve been preparing for this job,” he said, brushing off any criticism at his lack of legislative experience.  

Alexander paints himself as a man of the people, and portrays Pollitt’s support from PACs as an entanglement. He said there should be limits on PAC spending, which he said mutes “the common folks’” voices.
One example, he said, is a campaign attack ad sent to homes in the district by Rocker P Brand PAC. It reads, “guilty,” across Alexander’s face, claiming that he failed to appear in court on trespassing charges. 
Under Missouri campaign finance law, candidates can solicit donations for the PAC but cannot direct how it uses the funds or the message it conveys.
Pollitt asked political friends in Sedalia to set the PAC up in 2022 and prior to the launch of his state Senate campaign, it had raised modest sums. One person who agreed to help in 2022 was Megan Page, who became vide president because Pollitt was a friend and they had worked together on different community boards. In January 2025, Gov. Mike Kehoe appointed her the Pettis County Clerk.
Page said she’s not been involved in the PAC since her appointment as clerk. The day she learned of mailers being sent out funded by the PAC, she called the treasurer and asked to have her name stricken from the PAC records.
Filings with the Missouri Ethics Commission show paperwork to remove Page and PAC President Kim Lyne was filed on July 8.
“Really it boils down to, I do not want to be involved in something politically that I have no control over what they say, when they say it or how they say it,” she told The Independent. “So I needed to step away because it was getting negative and I didn’t want anything to do with that. I didn’t want to be associated with it.”
Page said a consulting company recently took over the PAC. Reports from the Missouri Ethics Commission show the PAC recently paid more than $36,000 for mailers to Catamaran Consulting, a company based out of Los Angeles that was also hired in 2024 as part of an effort in Iowa to fund a Republican candidate to oppose Trump.
Candidates are not responsible for the messages from PACs. But Pollitt is mired in the community outrage that’s followed.
“Pettis County is very different from other counties in Missouri,” Page said of the public outcry. “Historically Pettis County does not do well with smear campaigns and negative campaigns, especially when you’re talking about local people.”
Pollitt said he, like many candidates, created a PAC and then turned it over to others, as is the law.
“PACs can do whatever they want,” he said. “I have no control over them … Once the PAC is taken over, then the candidate no longer has any authority or any contact or any say so about what goes on.”
Pollitt said he’d hoped for a campaign based on issues, and he still hopes it ends that way.
“I said from the beginning, I hoped it would be a positive campaign,” Pollitt said. “And, you know, apparently it hasn’t turned out that way.”
As for the trespassing mailer, Alexander said the charge stemmed from an incident three decades ago in Benton County in which his bird dog ran onto someone’s property while he was quail hunting.
The landowner threatened to shoot his dog, Alexander said, so he crossed  the property line to retrieve the animal. He rebuts any accusation that he failed to appear in court, instead taking the opportunity to decry the “swamp” in Jefferson City funded by political action committees.
Another mailer was sent out over the weekend compared Alexander to Anthony Fauci, attacking his role on the Webster County COVID-19 task force during the pandemic.
“There’s a lot of money that’s flowed into that campaign for Brad, and there’s state senators that are giving money out of their PAC money, and that’s, again, part of the problem with Jeff City,” Alexander said. “There’s too much money floating around that buys votes and stuff.”
All of Pollitt’s largest donations came from political action committees, with more than 30 PACs writing checks for the maximum contribution of $2,4000 to his campaign. They include farming, utility, healthcare, realtors, cannabis, sports betting and conservative committees. 
Candidate committees for state office are limited in the amount of money they can accept from any one donor. PACs can accept donations in any amount.
Pollitt pushed back on any criticism of his funding sources, saying that the variety of PAC support shows he can work well negotiating at many different tables. His endorsement list includes the Missouri Farm Bureau, Missouri Fraternal Order of Police, Campaign Life, Americans for Prosperity, the Missouri Chamber of Commerce and the Missouri State Teachers Association. 
Missouri House speaker faces conservative challenge in key state Senate primary

His connections and experience benefit the district, Pollitt said.
“I’m the only candidate that’s been in the arena,” he said. “I don’t think the Senate is a place where you should send people to learn how to legislate. I think you learn that in the House.”
Fewer of Alexander’s donations come from PACs, but his highest donors include Scope PAC (a physician-led committee), MO Osteopathic PAC and MO State Orthopedic Association. Many of his highest individual donations are from surgeons and physicians. 
His endorsements include Missouri Right to Life, Pettis County First, Cedar County Sheriff James McCrary and the Cedar County Commissioners. 
Lentz leans into his own humble beginnings: he grew up for a time in public housing and he’s raised a family on a school teacher’s salary.
“Why am I the best candidate? Because I’ve lived that way,” he said. “I’m the candidate with the right principles. It’s not because I’m the smartest person, and I’m committed to representation, not ruling over people.”
 Data centers and Medicaid cuts

Pollitt was among 16 state representatives who signed a letter last month asking Gov. Mike Kehoe to call a special session on data centers. 
Pollitt said in a May television appearance that one of his biggest disappointments of the session was an inability to move a solar panel bill that would’ve put parameters on solar fields in rural Missouri.
In July he told The Independent that finding a needle to thread when it comes to property rights and solar panel fields and data centers is still one of his top priorities.
Lentz said AI datacenters must not be allowed to buy farmland without a detailed study of the costs to the state. 
“Calling it ‘the right to sell your property to whoever you want’ is the velvet glove,” Lentz said on social media. “The iron fist beneath it is giving corporations and special interests a clear path to buy up the Ozarks one property at a time.”
Alexander, who opposes data centers, is perhaps most concerned about likely cuts to Medicaid funding coming down from the federal government. 
“We’re gonna see some really, really tough times,” said Alexander, who previously served on the Missouri Oversight Committee for Medicaid, “unless we are wise and look ahead and make sure that we do the right things now to address the problems before they become bigger and bigger and bigger.”
